- Header-only C++03/C++11 codebases that want a drop-in std::sort replacement without adding a build/link dependency
- Large arrays (1000+ elements) where branch-misprediction overhead in a naive quicksort partition loop matters
- Need a guaranteed O(n log n) worst case (heapsort fallback) without giving up quicksort's average-case speed

**Skip it when:**
- Need a stable sort (equal elements keep relative order) — no stable variant is provided, unlike std::stable_sort
- Comparator itself is expensive (e.g. calls into an interpreted-language callback) — issue #20 shows pdqsort can invoke the comparator more often than glibc qsort/introsort, making it slower than std::sort or qsort when comparison cost dominates
- Data shaped like a 'pipe organ' (ascending then descending) sorted against libstdc++ std::stable_sort — the verified README chart shows pdqsort ~2.3x slower there, and roughly tied on 'push front'
- Need MSVC 64-bit builds warning-clean — open issue #22 (int64->int conversion warnings) is unresolved
- Need std::execution parallel policies or a maintained upstream — no commits since 2021-03-14 and issue #16 (C++17 parallel execution) is still open

**Integration:** header-only · none (standard library only: <algorithm>, <cstddef>, <functional>, <utility>, <iterator>, plus <cstdint>/<type_traits> under C++11) · C++03 compiles (branch-based path only); C++11+ enables automatic branchless dispatch and move semantics · any (portable C++, no SIMD/architecture-specific intrinsics); MSVC 64-bit builds emit C4244 int64->int conversion warnings (open issue #22)

**Vs siblings:** Prefer pdqsort over Highway (vqsort) when you can't require AVX2/AVX3 hardware or want to avoid a SIMD library dependency, and over ska_sort when your keys aren't specifically skewed/geometric-distributed integers. vergesort is the closest comparison (same libstdc++ pattern-detection premise, also unstable-vs-stable tradeoffs), but pdqsort additionally documents a branchless partitioning fast path for arithmetic types with default comparators.

**Gotchas:**
- Branchless auto-dispatch only triggers for arithmetic value types compared with std::less/std::greater under C++11; custom structs or comparators always take the slower branch-based path unless you call pdqsort_branchless explicitly
- Can make more comparator calls than a plain qsort/introsort in some cases (issue #20), so it loses to std::sort/qsort when the comparator itself is costly, even though it does fewer swaps
- Switches to std::make_heap/std::sort_heap after O(log n) highly unbalanced partitions, so pathological inputs degrade to heapsort speed, not quicksort speed
- Comparator ordering requirements (strict weak ordering vs. total order) are not documented in the README (issue #28, open question, unanswered as of last commit)

**Status:** Abandoned: no commits since 2021-03-14, the same day an integer-overflow fix (issue #13) landed; a later MSVC-warning issue (#22, 2022) and a C++17 parallel-execution request (#16, 2024) remain open and unaddressed. zlib-licensed and a single ~350-line header, so it's cheap to vendor and patch yourself if needed.

[repo](https://github.com/orlp/pdqsort) · [benchmark](https://github.com/orlp/pdqsort)

#### string-search-and-hashing

##### HighwayHash  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

SIMD-based keyed hash function; ~5x faster than SipHash at 1 KiB while keeping DoS-resistant strong-hash security claims.

**Beats:** SipHash — On a single idle core of an Intel Xeon E5-2690 v3 (2.6 GHz) compiled with a patched GCC 4.9, the README's own benchmark table shows HighwayHashAVX2 at 0.24 cycles/byte for 1024-byte inputs vs SipHash's 1.26 cycles/byte (~5.25x) and 0.95 vs 1.93 cycles/byte at 64 bytes (~2x), consistent with the linked arXiv paper's stated 5.2-5.3x speedup at 1 KiB.

**How:** Mixes input using SIMD 32x32->64-bit multiplies and permutes over a 1024-bit internal state held in AVX2/SSE4.1/VSX/NEON registers, with specialized handling of partial vectors for small inputs. The AVX2 build reaches 0.24 cycles/byte at 1024 bytes vs SipHash's 1.26, more than twice as fast as the repo's own SipTreeHash variant. A runtime dispatcher (instruction_sets.h) selects AVX2, SSE4.1, VSX, NEON, or a portable fallback at first use so one binary can exploit the widest available SIMD without recompiling.

**Use it when:**
- Hash-flooding-resistant hashing where a strong keyed hash faster than SipHash is needed, especially for inputs >=64 bytes where the AVX2 speedup is largest
- x86-64 targets with AVX2 or SSE4.1, or POWER (VSX) / ARM/AArch64 (NEON) where the corresponding source file is included
- Applications that persist hashes long-term: output format is declared frozen forever, so stored hashes never break on upgrade
- Need 128- or 256-bit digests (checksums/integrity) from a single pass, not just a 64-bit hash
- Willing to vendor an archived Apache-2.0 source drop and pin a validated compiler rather than depend on a maintained package

**Skip it when:**
- Need a literal std::hash / std::unordered_map drop-in swap — HighwayHash needs explicit key management and its own state object, not a hasher functor substitution
- Target platform has none of AVX2/SSE4.1/VSX/NEON: falls back to a portable path the README says runs at ~10% of AVX2 throughput
- Building with a modern stock compiler without validating output first: open issue #94 (filed 2020, still open) reports a Portable-target hash mismatch on GCC 10.2, and the archived repo will never fix it
- Need the 'cryptographically strong' framing to hold at typical hash-table bin counts — the repo's own issue #28 is an unresolved dispute over that security claim
- Need active maintenance or security patching — GitHub shows the repository archived (read-only) and the hash output is explicitly frozen, so no further algorithmic or compiler-compat fixes will land

**Integration:** source-drop / static lib (Makefile and CMakeLists.txt build lib/libhighwayhash.a; CMake's BUILD_SHARED_LIBS option can produce a shared lib instead) · none beyond the C++ standard library; pthread is linked for the optional ThreadPool/profiling utilities, not required for hashing itself · C++11 (Makefile and CMakeLists.txt both pass -std=c++11); CMake >= 3.18 for the CMake build path; GCC/Clang new enough for AVX2/SSE4.1/NEON intrinsics as needed per target · x86-64 (AVX2 or SSE4.1), ARM/AArch64 (NEON), POWER (VSX), plus a portable C++ fallback for any other architecture

**Vs siblings:** Pick HighwayHash over komihash/MUM-hash/t1ha/rapidhash when the requirement is specifically SipHash's DoS-resistant strong-hash security framing plus multi-width (64/128/256-bit) SIMD output beating SipHash, not just the fastest possible non-cryptographic hashmap key hash; those sibling hashes target xxHash/CityHash/wyhash-class baselines for general-purpose hashing and are actively maintained, unlike this archived, output-frozen project.

**Gotchas:**
- Output is declared 'frozen forever' in the README: no future release will ever change existing hash values, but also none will ever improve speed or security further
- Intrinsics-using headers must be compiled into separate per-target translation units with matching flags (README 'Dispatch' section); mixing this up risks an ODR violation and crashes
- AVX2 carries a ~56K-cycle warmup penalty on Haswell-era CPUs per the README, so the authors recommend against AVX2 for infrequent/sporadic hashing in an otherwise non-AVX2 application
- Repository is GitHub-archived (read-only); open issue #94 (GCC 10.2 Portable-target hash mismatch, filed 2020) has no fix and, given the archival, never will

**Status:** Abandoned: the GitHub repo is archived (read-only), last commit 2024-04-18, and the hash output is explicitly declared frozen forever; it is Apache-2.0 licensed and small enough to vendor as a source drop, but pin and test the exact compiler version given the open, unresolved GCC 10.2 output-mismatch report (issue #94).

[repo](https://github.com/google/highwayhash) · [benchmark](https://github.com/google/highwayhash/blob/master/README.md)

##### komihash  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only, non-cryptographic 64-bit hash beating wyhash and xxHash on short keys (0-31 bytes) via full 128-bit multiply accumulation.

**Beats:** xxHash (XXH3_64 / XXH64) and wyhash_final4 — Author-run README benchmark across 10 compiler/CPU/OS combinations (GCC 11.5, Clang 18/19, ICC 19, clang-cl 18, Apple Clang 15 on Ryzen 3700X/9950X, Xeon E-2386G, Core i7-7700K, Apple M1) shows komihash 5.34 averaging 7.2 cycles/hash (0-15 bytes) and 8.6 cycles/hash (8-28 bytes) versus wyhash_final4 13.5/18.0, XXH3_64 14.2/21.8, and XXH64 10.2/15.0 — roughly 1.9-2.5x fewer cycles on short keys. On 256,000-byte bulk buffers komihash (19.3-42.7 GB/s) loses to XXH3_64 (28.0-68.4 GB/s) on all 10 platforms and to wyhash_final4 on 8 of 10.

**How:** Unlike wyhash/CircleHash/lehmer64-style hashes, komihash keeps the full 128-bit result of each internal multiplication instead of folding it back into one 64-bit state word, so consecutive internal states stay distinguishable rather than losing entropy. It parses the input message without overlapping reads, which the author argues avoids the seed-value flaws overlap-based parsers can hit, while keeping branch count low on the 0-15/8-28 byte fast paths. It's scalar C99 (no SIMD requirement), so short-key speed comes from a tight instruction sequence rather than vector width.

**Use it when:**
- Hash table/map/Bloom-filter keying where short keys (0-31 bytes) dominate and you want lower cycles/hash than wyhash_final4 or XXH3_64 without requiring AVX2/SIMD
- Need identical hash values on both big- and little-endian platforms (e.g. hashes stored/compared across architectures)
- Hashing values whose total length isn't known upfront, or hashing many independent fixed-size fields incrementally (discrete-incremental API)
- Want a single dependency-free header (MIT) that's trivial to vendor into a C or C++ codebase
- Portable/scalar targets (no SIMD available) where a branch-light, non-vectorized hash is required

**Skip it when:**
- Bulk/large-buffer hashing (files, big blobs): on the README's own 256,000-byte test komihash (19.3-42.7 GB/s) loses to XXH3_64 (28.0-68.4 GB/s) on all 10 tested platforms and to wyhash_final4 on 8 of 10
- Adversarial or untrusted input where seeded collision-resistance matters: issue #23 (opened 2026-09-18, open as of this review) demonstrates a fixed 64-byte message pair that collides for ~91% of uniformly-random hidden 64-bit seeds, which weakens the README's 'seed it and hash-flooding risk is minimized' guidance
- Need a std::hash<T> drop-in for unordered_map/unordered_set without writing a wrapper — komihash exposes plain C functions, not a functor
- 32-bit target platforms, where the README states throughput is 'considerably lower' than 64-bit (no number given)
- Need cryptographic collision resistance — explicitly a non-cryptographic hash

**Integration:** header-only · none (standard C headers only: stdint.h, string.h) · ISO C99 (C++98 supported via a stdint.h fallback path; full auto C++ compatibility, with extra branch optimizations under C++11+) · x86, x86-64 (Intel/AMD), AArch64 (Apple Silicon); tested on Windows 10/11, AlmaLinux 9.6, macOS 26.4; scalar code, no SIMD required; 32-bit builds work but are notably slower per README

**Vs siblings:** Pick komihash over t1ha/CityHash/MUM-VMUM when you want the widest reproducible compiler/CPU benchmark matrix (10 combos) for short-key throughput and don't need SIMD. Pick rapidhash or another sibling instead if the open seed-dependent collision report (issue #23) is disqualifying for your threat model, or if bulk-buffer throughput matters more than short-key speed.

**Gotchas:**
- Open issue #23 (filed 2026-09-18, unresolved as of this review): a fixed 64-byte message pair collides under komihash for ~91% of uniformly-random hidden seeds, reproduced independently by the reporter against the released 5.34 header — a real gap in the 'seed it for collision-attack resistance' advice
- Default seed is 0 (no randomization) unless the caller passes one; self-seeding is required for any hash-flooding resistance, and per the issue above that resistance is weaker than the README implies
- No identity/passthrough hashing: README explicitly recommends using raw key values directly for fixed-size keys rather than hashing them, since komihash adds overhead a no-op wouldn't have
- Big-endian systems pay a ~20% bulk-throughput penalty from byte-swapping, which can be disabled via a macro but then breaks cross-platform hash-value portability

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-08-04, MIT-licensed, 286 stars) and trivial to vendor as one header, but an unresolved collision report (issue #23, opened 2026-09-18, six days before this review) is a live caveat for any security-relevant use.

[repo](https://github.com/avaneev/komihash) · [benchmark](https://github.com/avaneev/komihash/blob/master/README.md)

##### MUM/VMUM hash  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C multiply-mix hash family (MUM/VMUM) rivaling xxHash3, beating CityHash and SipHash24 on most key sizes.

**Beats:** xxHash3, Google CityHash (City64), Bob Jenkins SpookyHash, SipHash24, MetroHash, t1ha2 — widely-used non-cryptographic hash functions used in place of std::hash for hash-table keys — Hashing 1,280M keys (3-1024 bytes) plus 10,000x16MB bulk keys, GCC -O3 (-flto added only for the competing hash functions, not MUM/VMUM), pinned single-core runs, minimum of 3 repeats kept: VMUM-V2's geomean relative throughput (1.00 baseline) is xxHash3 0.79, CityHash 0.38, SipHash24 0.21 on Apple M4 (GCC 14.2.1), and xxHash3 0.93, CityHash 0.48 on IBM Power10 (GCC 11.5.0) -- i.e. VMUM-V2 is ~1.3x faster than xxHash3 and ~2.6x faster than CityHash on M4, and roughly on par with xxHash3 on Power10.

**How:** MUM (Multiply and Mix) randomizes each 64-bit chunk with a 64x64->128-bit multiply, mixes the high/low halves with addition, and XORs into a running state, using a table of pre-generated random factors; the main loop is written to be unrolled by the compiler for out-of-order scheduling, with no per-byte branching. VMUM extends this with target vector instructions (AVX2 32x32->64 multiplies on x86-64, NEON on aarch64, Altivec on ppc64) processing multiple lanes per step, and runs two unrolled loops in parallel to keep OOO execution units busy; targets without vector support fall back to scalar emulation.

**Use it when:**
- Very short keys (3-16 bytes) where MUM/VMUM's fast startup wins on every benchmarked machine (ratio ~1.00 vs xxHash3's 0.7-0.95)
- Long keys (512-1024 bytes) and 16MB bulk hashing on AVX2 (x86-64) or NEON (aarch64) hardware, where VMUM-V2 is ~1.1-1.9x faster than xxHash3
- Apple M4 / aarch64 targets specifically, where VMUM-V2 beats xxHash3 by ~1.3x geomean and CityHash/SipHash24 by 2.6x/4.8x
- Hash-table implementations that want a header-only C hash with no crypto/library dependency and are willing to hand-write the call sites
- Cases wanting the collision-attack-resistant fixed hash by default (Nov 2025 fix), with the ability to opt back into the faster pre-fix variant via VMUM_V1/MUM_V3 macros for controlled environments

**Skip it when:**
- Mid-size keys, roughly 32-128 bytes (16 bytes on Power10): xxHash3 is faster there, e.g. 128 bytes is 1.98x faster on AMD, 1.81x on M4, 2.03x on Power10
- Targets without AVX2/NEON/Altivec and without a compiler 128-bit-integer extension: VMUM drops to scalar emulation and MUM needs GCC/Clang-style __int128 to hit its documented numbers
- Projects that require a real drop-in for std::hash/xxHash's call signature without touching call sites -- MUM/VMUM's API shape is different
- Teams uncomfortable with no LICENSE file at repo root (MIT is only asserted in per-file header comments; GitHub's own license detector shows none)
- Cross-platform byte-identical hashes across BE/LE or 32/64-bit targets, unless [V]MUM_TARGET_INDEPENDENT_HASH is explicitly defined (with a performance cost on BE/no-int128 targets)

**Integration:** header-only (single file: mum.h or vmum.h) · none beyond the C standard library (stddef.h, stdlib.h, string.h, limits.h, stdint.h) · C99; GCC or Clang recommended to get the 128-bit-integer multiply path (checked via __GNUC__); MSVC compiles via typedef shims but takes the non-__int128 fallback path · x86-64 (AVX2 needed for VMUM's full speed, e.g. -mavx2), aarch64 (NEON), ppc64 (Altivec); scalar emulation on any other target

**Vs siblings:** Pick VMUM over rapidhash, t1ha, or CityHash when hashing very short keys (<=16 bytes) or long/bulk keys on AVX2 or NEON hardware, where it edges out xxHash3 and clearly beats CityHash/SipHash24/t1ha2. Prefer xxHash3, rapidhash, or komihash instead for the common 32-128 byte range, where VMUM-V2 loses to xxHash3 by up to ~2x.

**Gotchas:**
- The pre-Nov-2025 VMUM/MUM-V3 variants have a collision-attack weakness (issue #18: an adversary can zero one operand of _vmum to force identical hashes); the fix is now default and costs ~10% throughput, old fast variants are opt-in via VMUM_V1/MUM_V3 macros
- No LICENSE file at repo root; MIT terms live only in the header comment of each source file (mum.h, vmum.h, mum512.h, mum-prng.h)
- Hash values are not target-independent by default (differ across BE/LE and 32/64-bit, and with/without int128 support) unless [V]MUM_TARGET_INDEPENDENT_HASH is defined
- VMUM needs an explicit compile flag (e.g. -mavx2 on x86-64, -mcpu=native/NEON on aarch64) to use its vector code path; without it, it silently falls back to slower scalar emulation

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-06-02, with a collision-attack fix shipped Nov 2025); MIT-licensed via per-file source headers (no repo-root LICENSE file) and small enough as single headers to vendor directly.

[repo](https://github.com/vnmakarov/mum-hash) · [benchmark](https://github.com/vnmakarov/mum-hash#vmum-and-mum-benchmarking-vs-other-famous-hash-functions)

##### sse4-strstr (SIMD-friendly algorithms for substring searching)  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

SIMD substring-search kernels (SSE2-AVX512, NEON) from a blog article; beats glibc strstr by ~1.3-1.8x on x86.

**Beats:** std::strstr / libc strstr (same problem as std::string::find and the default std::search) — On an Intel Skylake i7-6700 with GCC 5.4.1 (-O3 -mavx2), the repo's own speedup_avx2 benchmark scanning data/i386.txt for data/words shows glibc std::strstr at 0.662s vs the "AVX2 (generic)" kernel at 0.364s across three runs with identical checksums (~1.82x faster); "SSE2 (generic)" is 0.489s (~1.35x faster). std::string::find is not measured on this run -- the harness skips it on GCC/x86.

**How:** SWAR and SIMD kernels (SSE2, SSE4.1 MPSADBW, SSE4.2 PCMPESTRM, AVX2, AVX512F/BW, NEON) scan 16-64 bytes per iteration instead of glibc strstr's byte-at-a-time loop. The fastest "generic" kernel behind the cited 1.82x number (avx2_strstr_v2 -> avx2_strstr_anysize) broadcasts the needle's first and last byte across a 32-byte AVX2 vector, compares both in one pass to get a lane mask of candidate offsets, then verifies each candidate with a short memcmp -- a vectorized two-byte filter (0x80.pl's "SIMD-friendly Karp-Rabin" scheme), not a per-byte scan. Needles of length 2-12 get separate template-specialized SSE4.1/AVX2 kernels tuned per exact length.

**Use it when:**
- Exact single fixed-needle search over large in-memory byte buffers (logs, text corpora) on x86-64 with SSE4.1/AVX2/AVX512, or ARMv7/AArch64 with NEON, where the scan itself is the bottleneck
- You want reference/teaching code for SIMD substring-search techniques (the vectorized Karp-Rabin-style first/last-byte filter) rather than a dependency
- You can vendor a handful of individual .cpp/.h files into your own build instead of linking a packaged library
- Needle length and target ISA are known ahead of time so you can pick/compile the matching kernel (SSE4, AVX2, AVX512BW, NEON) for your CPU
- You're willing to own and patch the code yourself going forward -- no upstream maintenance since Jan 2022

**Skip it when:**
- You need a drop-in for std::string::find/strstr with wide-char support, custom predicates, or a std::string_view-friendly API -- none of that exists here
- You need multi-needle or streaming search; only a single fixed needle against a fully-buffered haystack is implemented (open issue #18 asks for multithreading, #19 for combining with Raita's algorithm -- both unaddressed)
- You need a maintained, packaged dependency: no releases, no build-system package config, last commit 2022-01-04, and confirmed bugs (#11, #16) are unfixed
- Needle length 1 passed directly to the low-level avx2_strstr_anysize kernel (bypassing the dispatcher) hits a confirmed bug: k-2 underflows (issue #11)
- On current hardware/libc the maintainer himself says (issue #12, 2020) "AVX2 won't help much" over a decent modern strstr -- re-benchmark on your own CPU/libc before adopting

**Integration:** source-drop · none (uses <immintrin.h>/<arm_neon.h> intrinsics and the C++11 standard library only) · C++11; GCC or Clang with the matching ISA flag per kernel (-msse4.2, -mavx2, -mavx512bw, -mfpu=neon) · x86-64 (SSE2 baseline; SSE4.1/4.2, AVX2, AVX512F/AVX512BW variants gated by build flags), ARMv7 (NEON) and ARMv8/AArch64

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over StringZilla or Boost.Algorithm's Boyer-Moore/Boyer-Moore-Horspool searchers only when you specifically want the raw, ISA-specific kernel source to vendor one function with zero dependencies (no Boost, no StringZilla) or to study the 0x80.pl vectorized Karp-Rabin technique; both siblings are actively packaged and maintained, and StringZilla in particular reports larger, more current speedups over std::string::find.

**Gotchas:**
- Raw per-length kernels (e.g. avx2_strstr_anysize, sse4_strstr_anysize) assert needle_size > 4 or > 0 depending on variant; only the top-level dispatchers (avx2_strstr, avx2_strstr_v2, sse4_strstr_anysize's callers) special-case short needles (0-4 bytes) via strchr/strstr/memcmp -- calling a raw kernel directly with a short needle is unsafe (issue #11, confirmed bug for k=1)
- The vectorized loops load fixed 16/32-byte windows (_mm256_loadu_si256 at s+i and s+i+k-1) per iteration, which can read past the logical end of the haystack near its tail; the README/code does not document a guaranteed-safe overread margin, so vendoring into a tightly-sized buffer needs care
- Open, unanswered GitHub issue (#16) questions whether the `next1` vector in avx2_strstr_eq (the 2-byte-needle path) is read before being fully initialized
- The repo's own speedup.cpp deliberately skips std::string::find on GCC/x86 builds ("proven to be utterly slow, don't waste our time"), so its own benchmark has no std::string::find numbers to compare against on x86

**Status:** Abandoned: last commit 2022-01-04, not archived, two confirmed/unanswered bugs (#11, #16) unaddressed; BSD-2-Clause and small enough to vendor a single kernel file, but the maintainer himself notes (2020) that on modern CPUs/libc the AVX2 advantage over strstr is small.

[repo](https://github.com/WojciechMula/sse4-strstr) · [benchmark](https://github.com/WojciechMula/sse4-strstr/blob/master/results/skylake-i7-6700-gcc5.4.1-avx2.txt)

##### t1ha (Fast Positive Hash)  `C`  `Zlib`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Portable C hash family (t1ha0/1/2) beating xxHash/Murmur on bulk throughput; modest edge on tiny keys.

**Beats:** xxHash32 (also xxHash64 and the Murmur2/Murmur3 family) in SMHasher speed tests — On SMHasher speed tests run in 2016 (GCC 5.4.0, -march=native -O3 -fPIC, Intel Core i7-6700K), t1ha_aes averaged 33.03 cycles/hash and t1ha 35.55 vs xxHash32's 43.72 over 1-31 byte keys (~1.2-1.3x fewer cycles), while on a 262144-byte bulk block t1ha_aes reached 34,636 MiB/s and t1ha 12,229 MiB/s vs xxHash32's 5,514 MiB/s (~6.3x/~2.2x) and xxHash64's 11,123 MiB/s (~3.1x/~1.1x). The verification pass found the source record had mislabeled those bulk MiB/s figures as the 'small keys' result; the real small-key edge over xxHash32 is only ~1.2-1.3x.

**How:** The t1ha0_ia32aes_* variants use AES-NI instructions for hardware-accelerated mixing (this is the 't1ha_aes' benchmark line); each AES-NI variant is compiled with its own flags (-maes plus -mavx/-mavx2 per meson.build) and t1ha0 picks among them, plus 32-bit and big-endian fallbacks, at runtime via T1HA0_RUNTIME_SELECT (optionally using GNU ELF indirect functions to cut call overhead). The core mixing uses a NH/UMAC-style multiply-add construction that the README's FAQ says was deliberately fixed to avoid the 'blinding multiplication' entropy-loss flaw it attributes to plain NH-family designs (and, per the README, to wyhash).

**Use it when:**
- Bulk hashing of large buffers (KB+: checksums, content fingerprinting, dedup) on x86_64 with AES-NI, where the 2016 SMHasher bulk numbers show t1ha_aes far ahead of xxHash32/64
- Need a single API that gives both a 64-bit and a 128-bit digest via the same streaming context (t1ha2_init/update/final)
- Already a portable C (not C++) codebase, or need a C-callable hash with existing Rust/Erlang/Go/Kotlin bindings (linked from the README)
- Willing to vendor a small, frozen, Zlib-licensed source drop (3 .c files) since no upstream fixes are coming
- Mixed/heterogeneous CPU fleet where t1ha0's automatic best-available-implementation dispatch is worth its small indirection cost

**Skip it when:**
- Tiny keys (a few bytes to ~31 bytes) on a modern CPU: the maintainer's own later self-check (i7-4600U, GCC 9.3, in the README) shows t1ha2_atonce at 17.25 cycles/hash already behind xxhash32 (16.55), xxh3_64 (15.1) and wyhash_v7 (14.1) -- the 2016 small-key win over xxHash32 was only ~1.2-1.3x and has since been erased by newer hashes
- Cryptographic or adversarial-input use: the header explicitly states 't1ha' is 'Not suitable for cryptography'; no hash-flood resistance is claimed
- Need active upstream maintenance: GitHub deleted the author's account in 2022 and this repo is a restored read-only mirror; the true origin moved to GitFlic, whose current activity is unverified (a GitFlic fetch timed out during verification)
- Need std::hash-style implicit drop-in: t1ha is an explicit C function call with a seed argument, not something ADL or template specialization picks up automatically
- About to reach for t1ha0_32le/32be or t1ha0_ia32aes without checking the table: the author flags several dispatch targets ('alien' 32-bit/big-endian variants) as niche, and picking the wrong one can be slower than a portable hash

**Integration:** source-drop (3 .c files from /src, or link as a static/shared lib via the provided Makefile/meson.build/vcxproj) · none (pure C, standard headers only: stdint.h, stddef.h, limits.h) · C99 (meson.build passes -std=c99); README recommends GNU C 5.5+, Clang 5.0+, or MSVC 2017 15.6+ for proper performance, older GNU C / VS2013+ also supported · any CPU with native 64-bit arithmetic (portable fallback); accelerated paths for x86/x86_64 (AES-NI, AVX/AVX2) and Elbrus/e2k; separate 32-bit little/big-endian and 64-bit big-endian variants exist but are marked non-primary

**Vs siblings:** Pick t1ha over MUM/VMUM, rapidhash, komihash, or CityHash when you specifically want the AES-NI bulk-throughput path on x86, a plain-C (not C++) implementation with existing Rust/Go/Erlang/Kotlin ports, or a Zlib license; the MUM/VMUM sibling entry directly reports beating t1ha2, and rapidhash/komihash report better small-key numbers than xxHash on modern CPUs, so for tiny-key or newest-hardware workloads check those siblings first.

**Gotchas:**
- t1ha0's chosen implementation depends on the host CPU's detected features, so its output is not guaranteed reproducible across machines; the README says t1ha0 results should only be used at runtime, never persisted or sent over a network -- use t1ha1/t1ha2 for stable, portable results
- t1ha2_atonce's 64-bit result and t1ha2_atonce128's 128-bit result are unrelated values (the 64-bit hash is not a truncation of the 128-bit one), per the header comment
- t1ha1 is documented to fail the strict avalanche criterion in some cases (per the README, discovered via Reini Urban's SMHasher fork); it is kept for compatibility but t1ha2 is the recommended, higher-quality successor
- The AES-NI variants need per-file compiler flags (-maes plus -mavx/-mavx2), not just runtime CPU detection -- building them without the matching flags for your toolchain silently loses the AES-NI path

**Status:** GitHub lists this repo as abandoned/archived, but per its own README that's because GitHub deleted the author's account in 2022 and this is a restored read-only mirror -- the stated true origin moved to GitFlic, whose activity level is unverified. Zlib-licensed and small (3 .c files), so it is cheap to vendor and self-maintain regardless.

[repo](https://github.com/erthink/t1ha) · [benchmark](https://github.com/erthink/t1ha/blob/master/README.md)

##### rapidhash  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Header-only, wyhash-derived 64-bit hash beating xxh3 on latency and throughput on most CPUs; ties or loses on AMD Ryzen.

**Beats:** xxh3 (xxHash3) — not literally std::hash, but the widely-used fast non-cryptographic hash function developers use in place of std::hash — README benchmarks (bench/ harness adapted from xxHash's benchHash, compiler/flags unstated) show rapidhash beating xxh3 on average per-hash latency for 4/8/16-byte keys on Apple M1 Pro, M3 Pro, ARM Neoverse V2, and AMD Turin (roughly tied on Ryzen 9700X), and beating xxh3 on peak throughput hashing 16KB-2MB files on M1 Pro, M3 Pro, M3 Ultra, M4, and Neoverse V2 (xxh3 wins on Ryzen 9700X, 78 vs 68 GB/s). Independently, rurban/smhasher's default-build results table (AMD Ryzen 5 3350G) also shows rapidhash ahead of xxh3 on both bulk throughput and small-key cycles/hash, without stating compiler flags.

**How:** The core is a wyhash-style multiply-mix: a 64x64->128-bit multiply (rapid_mum) folded with XOR (rapid_mix), deliberately avoiding AES-NI/CLMUL or other vectorized instructions so the same code path runs on x86-64 and aarch64. Clang 18+ compiles rapidhash to roughly 185 instructions on both architectures (rapidhashMicro ~140, rapidhashNano under 100, both stack-free). An optional RAPIDHASH_UNROLLED macro trades code size for large-input throughput; RAPIDHASH_PROTECTED trades speed for extra entropy protection against the multiply's zero-collapse cases.

**Use it when:**
- General-purpose in-memory hash-table/hash-map keys needing a fast, SMHasher-passing 64-bit hash as an xxh3 or wyhash replacement.
- Mixed key-size workloads (roughly 4 bytes to 2MB) on x86-64 or aarch64 where one algorithm should cover both tiny keys and large buffers.
- Latency-sensitive small-key hashing (4/8/16 bytes) on Apple Silicon, ARM Neoverse V2, or AMD Turin, where README numbers show rapidhash ~5-9% faster than xxh3.
- Code-size-constrained embedded/mobile targets hashing keys up to ~48 bytes: use rapidhashNano (<100 instructions, no stack usage).
- Cache-miss-sensitive HPC/server code hashing keys up to ~512 bytes: use rapidhashMicro (~140 instructions, no stack usage).

**Skip it when:**
- Streaming/incremental hashing where input length isn't known upfront and can't be buffered whole: no streaming API ships despite the README's 'Streamable' framing (maintainer confirms in issue #39 that the C/C++ side has no streaming implementation and the hash targets short, whole-buffer runs).
- Adversarial or untrusted-input contexts needing DoS resistance: with the default secret, same-length inputs above 16 bytes admit a documented collision construction (issue #25); mitigate by generating a per-process secret with the bundled secret.h.
- Any context requiring cryptographic hashing or collision resistance guarantees: explicitly non-cryptographic.
- Need for a 128-bit or 32-bit hash output: not offered (open issues #26 and #46, no stated plans).
- Peak throughput on AMD Zen5 desktop parts (Ryzen 9700X): xxh3 leads there in the README's own table (78 vs 68 GB/s).

**Integration:** header-only · none (stdint.h, string.h; intrin.h + _umul128 intrinsic on MSVC) · C99 or C++11; constexpr evaluation additionally needs C++14. README claims support for GCC, Clang, Intel icx, and MSVC; the ~185-instruction codegen figure is specifically for Clang 18+. · x86-64 and aarch64 are the tested/optimized targets (no AVX/AES-NI/CLMUL required); the header compiles generically elsewhere via its endianness macros, consistent with the README's 'platform-independent' claim, but only x86-64/aarch64 numbers are published.

**Vs siblings:** Pick rapidhash over komihash or MUM/VMUM when you want the specific hash already vendored into Chromium, Node.js, Folly's F14, Fuchsia, Ninja, JuliaLang, and Zig, plus size-tuned Micro/Nano builds for cache- or code-size-constrained targets. Pick HighwayHash instead if AVX2-level throughput matters more than portability, since HighwayHash depends on vector instructions rapidhash deliberately avoids; pick t1ha or CityHash if a longer independent track record matters more than the newest peak-speed numbers.

**Gotchas:**
- README markets the family as 'Streamable,' but no streaming API exists for C/C++ (open issue #39) — it's designed for short, whole-buffer runs, not incremental hashing.
- Default secret permits a documented collision construction for same-length inputs over 16 bytes (issue #25); use secret.h to generate a custom secret for any adversarial-input exposure.
- rapidhash, rapidhashMicro, and rapidhashNano only produce matching output below 80 and 48 bytes respectively — swapping variants for larger keys silently changes hash values.
- An older header-only revision could produce 'multiple definition of rapid_secret' linker errors across translation units (issue #6, fixed via a static/const macro); the vendored old_version/rapidhashV1.h may not carry that fix.

**Status:** Actively maintained single header (last commit 2026-08-19, V3 released 2025), MIT-licensed and trivial to vendor; open issues (no 128-bit or 32-bit output, no streaming API) mark real feature gaps rather than signs of abandonment.

[repo](https://github.com/Nicoshev/rapidhash) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Nicoshev/rapidhash#outstanding-performance)

### storage-and-data

#### caches

##### go-sieve  `Go`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `active`  `Tier A`

Fixed-capacity generic Go SIEVE cache whose mutex-free Get path out-scales hashicorp/golang-lru LRU/ARC under concurrent reads.

**Beats:** hashicorp/golang-lru (LRU and ARC) — The author ran these on an Apple M4 (10 cores, 4P+6E) with go1.26.3 darwin/arm64 at GOMAXPROCS=10, from a pre-v0.6.5 working tree, and nobody has reproduced them independently. Warm-cache parallel Gets replayed from 18 MSR Cambridge and Meta storage traces took 2.24-12.20 ns/op versus 105.7-384.9 ns/op for hashicorp/golang-lru v2.0.7 LRU/ARC (13-55x faster than the better of the two). Cold mixed replay (Probe vs Get+Add) was 2.0-6.1x faster, and the synthetic 8192-entry uniform-int Get_Parallel was 5.76 vs 144.2 ns/op. All of these are aggregate throughput (wall time divided by b.N across goroutines), not per-call latency.

**Known shortcoming:** The 13-55x is vs golang-lru under contention (at 10 cores 7.53 vs 182.1 ns); on hit ratio ARC is best on 11 of 18 traces.

**Known shortcoming:** Misses, Add, Delete and eviction all take one global mutex, so the author's Mixed_Parallel time worsens with cores (33 to 92 ns/op from 1 to 10 cores) and Delete loses to LRU (81 vs 69.5 ns). 'Lock-free Get' is really a per-slot spinlock; under Zipf 1.5 hot-key skew the lead is ~6%; the eviction scan is unbounded under adversarial reads. Hit ratio trails ARC (best on 11 of 18 traces).

**Known shortcoming:** The zero key is reserved and unchecked (spurious zero-value hit); ProbeFunc is not singleflight; full capacity is preallocated; no TTL/callback/Peek/Resize. Pre-1.0 (v0.6.6), 41 stars, no CI; the latest tag needs Go 1.27.1; benchmarks are author-run on an M4 only from a dirty v0.6.4 tree.

**How:** SIEVE only sets a visited bit on a hit, so reads never reorder a list and never take the global mutex. `Get` does one load from a concurrent puzpuzpuz/xsync map (key to int32 slot index), then one atomic OR on a per-slot uint64 that packs a bit-63 spinlock with the visited counter, then an atomic AND to unlock. Nodes live in a pre-allocated array linked by int32 indices, with a bump allocator and freelist, so steady state makes no per-entry heap allocations and, for scalar K/V, gives the GC no pointers to trace. Misses (insert), eviction (the SIEVE 'hand' walks the FIFO clearing visited bits until it finds an unvisited node) and Delete all go through one global sync.Mutex.

**Use it when:**
- Read-dominated in-process caches hit by many goroutines at once, where golang-lru's single mutex is the bottleneck. The author's examples are HTTP response, DNS resolver and authz decision caches. The gap grows with cores: Get_Parallel is 14.9 vs 31.4 ns/op (LRU) at GOMAXPROCS=1 and 7.5 vs 182.1 at 10.
- Warm caches with high hit rates. The big win is on the hit path (13-55x on trace-replayed parallel Gets); on cold mixed read/write replay it drops to 2-6x.
- Large entry counts with scalar or fixed-size keys and values (ints, [16]byte, small structs), where GC scan cost matters. At 1M entries the heap is 78.4 MB vs 112.4 MB for LRU, and the GC-impact benchmark is 4.37 vs 9.46 ms/iter.
- Get-or-insert code paths. Probe/ProbeFunc do check-then-insert in one TOCTOU-safe call and return the evicted entry synchronously, so the caller can clean it up without channels or callbacks.
- Teams that want a small BSD-2 library with one dependency (the core is sieve.go + slotstate.go) that they can read or vendor, rather than a full caching framework.

**Skip it when:**
- Write-, miss- or delete-heavy workloads. Every insert of a new key, every eviction and every Delete takes one global mutex. In the Mixed_Parallel sweep (60% Get/30% Add/10% Delete), SIEVE's own aggregate time gets worse as cores are added, from 33.3 ns/op at 1 core to 92.3 at 10 (LRU goes to 222.8). Delete_Parallel is slower than LRU (81.2 vs 69.5 ns/op).
- When hit ratio matters more than CPU. With the cache at 10% of unique keys, ARC had the lowest miss ratio on 11 of 18 traces and LRU on 5 (all Meta storage traces). SIEVE k=1 beat LRU on only 10 of 18 traces and was never best in its row.
- Very hot-key read skew. Readers spin on the same slot word: at Zipf s=1.50 the lead over LRU shrinks to about 6% (94.2 vs 100.4 ns/op), and at s=1.01 SIEVE's own ns/op rises from 8.2 at 2 cores to 26.6 at 10.
- When you need TTL/expiry, cost- or weight-based capacity, eviction callbacks, Resize, statistics, or loading/refresh. None of these exist, and capacity is a fixed entry count. New() also allocates the full node array, 8 bytes of slot state per entry and a presized map up front, even if the cache never fills.
- Risk-averse production use. It is pre-1.0 (v0.6.6) with 41 stars and one known importer on pkg.go.dev. The repo has no CI workflow directory, and the API has changed between 0.x releases (v0.5.0 replaced the eviction channel with synchronous return values).

**Integration:** module · github.com/puzpuzpuz/xsync/v4 (v4.5.0 at v0.6.6). The benchmarks are a separate bench/ module that also pulls in hashicorp/golang-lru v2.0.7 and opencoff/go-mmap. · go.mod on main/v0.6.6 declares go 1.27.1, the current Go release (v0.6.4-v0.6.5 declare go 1.26.3, and v0.6.3 declares go 1.26.1). All() needs Go 1.23+ iterators. · Pure Go plus one go:linkname to runtime.procyield, so any Go target in principle. It was benchmarked only on Apple M4 darwin/arm64; x86-64 performance is not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Against otter (the other catalogued golang-lru beater, with adaptive W-TinyLFU, TTL, loading, refresh and stats), pick go-sieve when you only need a fixed-count, read-heavy cache and want a tiny single-dependency codebase with zero steady-state allocations; pick otter when hit ratio or expiry matters. Against golang-fifo (also SIEVE in Go, with TTL and a reader-lock hit path per its README, backed only by a README table), go-sieve has the mutex-free hit path and stronger reproducible evidence: raw results are committed and there is a trace-replay harness.

**Gotchas:**
- The zero value of K is reserved ("" for strings, 0 for ints, the zero struct) and is not checked. Freed slots have their key zeroed, so a Get racing with the eviction of a zero key can return a spurious hit with a zero value. Offset or wrap such keys.
- The README calls Get 'lock-free', but it takes a per-slot test-and-set spinlock that backs off with runtime.procyield (via go:linkname) and then Gosched. Every attempt sets the visited bit, even a failed one or one on a stale index, so an unrelated entry can get an undeserved mark. The source comment also says the eviction scan is not strictly bounded under adversarial read load, and that scan runs while holding the global mutex.
- ProbeFunc is not singleflight: concurrent misses on the same key can each run the constructor. Only one value is stored, and the other callers get it back flagged as CacheHit.
- Purge does not zero old key/value slots, so the objects they point to stay reachable until the slots are reused. String and pointer K/V still leave GC-traced pointers in the node array; the GC savings are mainly for scalar types.

**Status:** Actively maintained by a single author (v0.6.6, last commit 2026-09-08), BSD-2-Clause, and small enough to vendor, but still pre-1.0 with API changes between 0.x releases and the latest tag requiring Go 1.27.1.

[repo](https://github.com/opencoff/go-sieve) · [benchmark](https://github.com/opencoff/go-sieve/blob/main/bench-results.md)

##### AdaptSize  `C`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Size-aware probabilistic admission for Varnish's memory cache; raises CDN object hit ratio 47-91% over stock LRU Varnish.

**Beats:** LRU (via unmodified Varnish Cache, a concurrent-LRU CDN memory cache with no admission control) — The NSDI'17 paper replays two private Akamai edge traces (Hong Kong and US, about 440-450M requests each) on a university testbed: FUJITSU CX250, dual Xeon E5-2670, 32 GiB RAM, RHEL 6.5, gcc 4.4.7 with unstated flags. With a 1.2 GiB hot object cache, AdaptSize-patched Varnish raised object hit ratio by 47% (HK) and 91% (US) over stock Varnish 4.1.2 (LRU, admits everything) and by 30-48% over offline-tuned Nginx 1.9.12. Hit-ratio variability fell 1.9x (HK) and 3.8x (US), and throughput stayed equal (17.5 Gb/s peak on hits; misses within the 95% CI). The README's separate example (OHR 0.42 to 0.66, variability 23% to 5%) does not appear in the paper.

**Known shortcoming:** The search record's figures (0.66 vs 0.42 hit ratio, CoV 5%/23%) are not in the paper and were replaced with its numbers (object hit ratio +47-91% vs Varnish, +30-48% vs Nginx, same throughput) (verifier downgrade).

**Known shortcoming:** The win is hit ratio (+47-91% vs stock Varnish at 1.2 GiB); throughput is only equal. The tuner at HEAD does not compile (fprint typo with -Werror, issue #6 open since 2019); the cache-size argument is documented in GB but multiplied by 2^20 and rejects values <=1 or >1000, so the paper's 1.2 GiB cannot be entered without editing code.

**Known shortcoming:** The tuner keys objects by atol(URL), so it only works with numeric-ID replay URLs; admission uses integer division, so the enforced policy is a step function rather than the modelled curve; responses without Content-Length are always admitted; drand48 is not thread-safe. Varnish 4.1.2 only, self-described proof of concept, abandoned since 2018; maintained ports exist in libCacheSim and webcachesim.

**How:** The gain is in hit ratio, not CPU speed. Turning away large, rarely requested objects stops one big object from evicting thousands of small ones. To tune c, AdaptSize models each object as its own Markov chain over LRU positions, all linked by a single shared 'pushdown' rate (a mean-field / characteristic-time approximation). That turns the object hit ratio (OHR) into a closed-form function of c. Every ∆ requests (about 250K in the paper; in the code the interval grows with cache size), the tuner evaluates this curve using a Padé approximant for the exponential and a 20-step fixed-point solve, scans integer values of log2(c), then refines the best one with a golden-section search. This avoids the local optima that trap hill climbing with shadow caches. Statistics come from a read-only scan of Varnish's shared-memory log, so the request path only gains one random draw and one exp() call.

**Use it when:**
- Research or reproduction work on size-aware admission in a Varnish 4.1-based memory cache, driven by trace replay such as the author's webtracereplay tool.
- A memory cache in front of a disk tier or origin where object sizes span many orders of magnitude (bytes to GBs, e.g. mixed web, video chunks and downloads), so large objects keep flushing out small ones. The paper's case is a 1.2 GiB hot object cache.
- The cache is small relative to the working set. The paper's gains are largest near 1.2 GiB and fall to 13-14% over Varnish at 32 GiB (they hold when cache size and traffic grow together).
- The traffic mix shifts during the day (e.g. web in the morning, web plus video in the evening), so any single size threshold is wrong part of the time and hill-climbing tuners get stuck.
- You want a documented model for size-aware admission to port into your own cache. The Padé-approximated OHR(c) model and golden-section search fit in a few hundred lines of C.

**Skip it when:**
- Production deployments. The README calls it a proof of concept that is not ready for production, the last commit was January 2018, it only targets Varnish 4.1.2 (released March 2016), and one of its Varnish patches comments out an internal VSL assertion as a 'pseudo bug fix'.
- Your goal is throughput or latency on hits. Throughput matches stock Varnish (both peak at 17.5 Gb/s on hits) and never exceeds it. The paper's latency gains come from more hits and lighter disk-tier load, not from a faster request path.
- You optimize byte hit ratio or origin/WAN bytes rather than object hit ratio. The paper shows no change in the disk tier's byte hit ratio, and the disks transfer about 30% more bytes, although disk utilization drops about 20%.
- Object sizes fall in a narrow range. The admission curve only tells objects apart by size, so there is little to gain. This is inferred from the paper's motivation, not measured.
- You use anything other than Varnish (Nginx, Memcached, Redis, CacheLib): there is no integration. One user who replicated it on their own datasets (issue #3) first saw it below LRU, S4LRU and LFU-DA; that was settled privately by email and the cause is not documented.

**Integration:** source-drop (three patches to the Varnish 4.1.2 source + a Varnish VMOD built with autotools + a separate tuner daemon) · Varnish 4.1.2 source tree, patched and rebuilt from scratch (the tuner links Varnish's vut/libvarnish objects and libvarnishapi); autotools, libtool, pkg-config; libm, librt, pthread; varnishadm at runtime · C99/gnu99 with GCC. The tuner Makefile uses -std=gnu99 -O2 -Wall -Werror. The paper used gcc 4.4.7. · Linux. It was tested on x86-64 RHEL 6.5 with kernel 2.6.32. Other platforms are not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick AdaptSize when the problem is admission of wildly varying object sizes in front of a Varnish-style LRU memory cache. Cacheus, LHD, S3-FIFO and SIEVE change eviction instead, and LRB is a simulator-based learned policy. To try the idea without Varnish 4.1.2, libCacheSim (home of the GL-Cache, S3-FIFO and SIEVE entries) and the author's webcachesim both ship C++ AdaptSize implementations (an admission module in libCacheSim, an AdaptSizeCache policy in webcachesim).

**Gotchas:**
- The tuner at HEAD does not compile. adaptsize.c calls fprint (a typo for fprintf) with a '%l' format under -Werror. Issue #6 has been open since 2019, with more reports in 2021. Fix the typo before building.
- Cache-size units disagree. The README and usage text say the cachesize argument is in GB, but the code multiplies it by 1024*1024 (MiB) and rejects values <=1 or >1000. As written, the paper's 1.2 GiB cache cannot be entered correctly without editing the code.
- The tuner identifies objects by atol() of the request URL; the header says 'ASSUMPTION: request URLs already hashed to UInt!'. Real URL paths all parse to 0 and are told apart only by size, so it only works with numeric-ID URLs like those from trace replay. Its statistics-tree comparator (cmp_key) still subtracts longs into an int, the same overflow that PR #5 fixed only in the shadow-cache comparator.
- The VMOD computes exp(-r / opt_threshold) with integer operands (long / unsigned). The enforced admission probability is therefore the step function exp(-floor(size/c)), not the smooth e^(-size/c) that the tuner's model assumes. Responses without a numeric Content-Length (e.g. chunked) are always admitted.

**Status:** Abandoned since January 2018, with a build break open since 2019. The top level is BSD-2-Clause and the VMOD directory carries an Unlicense file. The code is small enough to read in an afternoon but is a self-described proof of concept tied to Varnish 4.1.2, so for new evaluations the C++ ports in libCacheSim or webcachesim are the practical route.

[repo](https://github.com/dasebe/AdaptSize) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/nsdi17/nsdi17-berger.pdf)

##### CacheLib  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Meta's in-process C++ caching engine with an optional SSD tier; the authors report up to 60% more throughput than Memcached.

**Beats:** Memcached — In the authors' OSDI 2020 paper, CacheBench drove CacheLib and an in-process, minimally modified Memcached 1.6.6. Both used LRU eviction and 32 threads, with a 100M-object working set and caches of 8-144 GB. CacheLib served up to 60% more requests per second at similar hit ratios; Figure 12's throughput axis spans 0-2 M ops/s. The run used the 60 s promotion delay, and the paper gives no CPU, compiler or build flags; no independent reproduction was found.

**Known shortcoming:** The 'up to 60% more req/s than Memcached 1.6.6' ran Memcached in-process via CacheBench for 60 s; no CPU/compiler given.

**Known shortcoming:** A library only (no server, no Memcached protocol), so not a drop-in. Heavy build: getdeps pulls folly, fbthrift, fizz and wangle; C++20 and libnuma required; CI Ubuntu only; the unstable folly API means upgrading the whole stack in lockstep. The only evidence is the authors' own paper with no third-party reproduction.

**Known shortcoming:** The hash table is untuned by default; warm restart needs a clean shutDown() and is lost on any format-version bump; flash-tier handles can block. A user reported get throughput dropping from 22.2M to 12.7M ops/s between versions (#257), closed without public explanation. The S3-FIFO and SIEVE papers report beating CacheLib's own LRU.

**How:** The paper credits most of the gain over Memcached to lower lock contention. Each slab class keeps its own LRU, protected by a folly::DistributedMutex. Its lock_combine() does flat combining: the thread holding the lock runs the critical sections that waiting threads have queued. A promotion delay (lruRefreshTime, 60 s by default) moves a hot item to the LRU head at most once per window. An optional tryLockUpdate setting skips the promotion when the lock is busy. The DRAM index is a chained hash table with compressed pointers and lock striping (locksPower). Memory comes from a custom slab allocator with 4 MB slabs and size classes set per workload, and each item carries about 32 B of intrusive metadata (hash-chain hook, LRU hooks, refcount, timestamps).

**Use it when:**
- A many-threaded C++ service (Rust bindings also exist) that needs a large in-process look-aside cache, tens to hundreds of GB, with many cores reading the same hot keys. This is where a Memcached-style global LRU lock becomes the bottleneck. The 60% gain was measured at 32 threads.
- Working sets bigger than DRAM, where an SSD is cheaper capacity. Navy stores objects under 2 KB in a set-associative Small Object Cache and larger objects in a region-based Large Object Cache. Flash admission is probabilistic to limit write wear.
- Services that deploy often and cannot afford a cold cache. Warm restart keeps the DRAM cache in POSIX shared memory across process restarts on the same host.
- Multi-tenant caches that need per-workload memory isolation (pools), automatic slab rebalancing and OOM-aware memory release, rather than one global LRU.
- Evaluating cache hardware or eviction policies against production-like or trace-driven workloads. The CacheBench tool ships in the repo.

**Skip it when:**
- You want a networked, protocol-compatible replacement for Memcached or Redis. CacheLib has no server, protocol, sharding or replication.
- You are not on Linux, or you want a light build. getdeps.py builds folly, fbthrift, fizz, wangle, boost and more. The build needs C++20 and libnuma, CI runs only on Ubuntu, and a vcpkg port is Linux-only. folly has no stable API, so the whole stack has to be upgraded at matching versions.
- Your values are pointer-rich or not memcpy-safe, or your code base is C. The core allocator stores flat bytes, and the paper says ad-serving teams (nested data) and RocksDB (C-style code versus RAII handles) could not adopt it. The newer ObjectCache only partly addresses this.
- The cache is small or single-threaded. Pools, allocation classes, hash-table sizing and the rebalancer are overkill there, and there is about 32 B of overhead per item plus the bucket array (256 MB for up to 32M items at the recommended bucketsPower 26).
- Your bottleneck is how well the eviction policy scales. The S3-FIFO and SIEVE sibling entries report prototypes that beat CacheLib's own optimized LRU, S3-FIFO by more than 6x at 16 threads.

**Integration:** shared lib (CMake, built through getdeps.py; installs libcachelib_allocator.so etc. plus headers; templates instantiated per eviction trait) · folly, fbthrift, fizz, wangle, fmt, glog, gflags, boost, googletest, zlib, zstd, libnuma, sparse-map, xxHash, magic_enum; liburing optional · C++20 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20); GCC 10+ or Clang 10+; CMake 3.14+; Python 3.6+ for getdeps.py · Linux only in practice. CI runs Ubuntu on x86-64, and the docs list Ubuntu 18.04-22.04, CentOS 8 and Debian 10/11. macOS and Windows are not supported, and aarch64 is not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick CacheLib over Pelikan/Segcache, Dragonfly or Pogocache when the cache lives inside your own C++ service and you need an SSD tier, warm restarts or per-tenant pools. Those siblings are ready-to-run network servers, and Segcache, MemC3 and MICA report much larger multiples over Memcached (close to 8x, almost 3x) for DRAM-only small-object serving. Look at S3-FIFO or SIEVE, or CacheLib's own 2Q/TinyLFU traits, when scaling the eviction policy matters more than features.

**Gotchas:**
- The default hash-table settings are deliberately unoptimized. Call setAccessConfig(expectedItems) or set bucketsPower to about 2x the item count, or find() and insert slow down. This is the FAQ's first answer to 'why is my cache so slow'.
- Warm restart only works if you drain accesses and call shutDown() before the allocator is destroyed. Otherwise the shared-memory segments are deleted. Any RAM or NVM format-version bump drops the cache on upgrade (kCachelibVersion is now 19, but CHANGELOG.md stops at V17).
- With the SSD tier on, find() can return a not-ready handle that blocks when you touch it (use toSemiFuture() to avoid blocking). findToWrite() is always synchronous and invalidates the flash copy. allocate() returns a null handle instead of throwing when it finds no evictable item, for example when items are pinned by outstanding handles.
- Performance depends on configuration and version. The paper notes that dropping the promotion delay from 60 s to 10 s raised the hit ratio but lowered throughput. One user measured 22.2M to 12.7M gets/s between a Dec-2022 commit and v2023.08.21.00 on a 48-thread CacheBench config (issue #257, closed without a public explanation). ThreadSanitizer reports false races because DistributedMutex is not TSAN-annotated (issue #148).

**Status:** Actively maintained by Meta, with weekly vYYYY.MM.DD tags (latest v2026.09.21.00, last commit 2026-09-26) and Apache-2.0 licensing. Using it in practice means building with Meta's getdeps toolchain and upgrading in lockstep with folly/fbthrift, not vendoring a few files.

[repo](https://github.com/facebook/CacheLib) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi20-berg.pdf)

##### Garnet  `C#`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Multi-threaded Redis-protocol (RESP) cache-store in C# from Microsoft Research; up to ~100x Valkey/Redis throughput on many-core servers.

**Beats:** Redis — In the authors' own PVLDB 2026 paper, run on Azure F72s_v2 VMs (72 vCPUs, 144 GB, Ubuntu 24.04, accelerated TCP; CPU model and .NET version not stated), Garnet's GET throughput at 128 client sessions was 108x Valkey 8.1, which stood in for Redis. A memtier run (1:9 SET:GET, 256M 8-byte keys, 6400 clients) showed at least 20x the throughput and 3x lower P99 than standalone Valkey; checkpointing 256M keys took 1.06 s against 273.1 s, and migrating all slots between two nodes was 94x faster. Most figures come from Garnet's own Resp.bench tool, and none of the sources read here show an independent reproduction.

**Known shortcoming:** Evidence is the authors' own paper (all Microsoft Research): Redis mostly not run (Valkey 8.1 stands in), most figures from Garnet's own Resp.bench, website numbers with --no-obj --no-pubsub and batches up to 4096; no independent reproduction. Best-latency numbers use an eRPC/DPDK kernel-bypass prototype not in the OSS release. Not a full drop-in: ~100 commands unsupported (Streams, FCALL/FUNCTION, CLIENT TRACKING, SORT, WAIT), no modules, MSET not atomic, passive cluster without failover. Open disk-tier bugs: cross-db corruption with multi-db + storage tier (#2152), crash on ZADD over an expired record read from disk (#2163). Eviction is log order, not LRU; storage tier off by default (overflow dropped); AOF acks before commit unless --aof-commit-wait. C#/.NET, not C++.

**How:** Sessions are shared-nothing and the store is shared-everything. Each connection's packet is TLS-decrypted, parsed and executed on the .NET socket I/O completion thread (SocketAsyncEventArgs), with no hand-off to per-core shard workers, so every core can serve every key and a pipelined batch runs without thread switches. Storage is Tsavorite, from the FASTER lineage: a latch-free hash index of 64-byte cache-line buckets (7 tagged entries plus an overflow/lock word) over a 'hybrid log' of records. Records in the mutable in-memory region are updated in place, new records are linked with CAS, and epoch protection (epoch-protected state machines) handles index resize, page flush/eviction, checkpoints and slot migration without blocking. The parser matches whole RESP headers for hot commands (GET, SET, DEL, INCR...) with Vector128 SIMD compares and falls back to a CRC32-hashed command table. Checkpoints use CPR-style version shifts instead of fork() and write with io_uring.

**Use it when:**
- Tens to hundreds of concurrent client connections doing small GET/SET, ideally pipelined or batched, on a many-core box where single-threaded Redis/Valkey saturates one core (the paper measures 108x Valkey GET throughput at 128 sessions on a 72-vCPU VM).
- Datasets larger than RAM that still need a RESP interface: --storage-tier keeps hot records in memory and spills older log pages to SSD or Azure storage.
- Frequent snapshots or warm restarts where Redis fork-based SAVE doubles memory or stalls: the paper checkpoints 256M keys in 1.06 s against Valkey's 273.1 s.
- .NET teams that want to embed the cache in-process (Microsoft.Garnet NuGet) or write atomic server-side logic as C# stored procedures instead of Lua.
- Sharded clusters that rebalance often: slot migration is server-to-server and measured 94x faster than Valkey's client-driven migration (paper).

**Skip it when:**
- Apps that use Redis Streams (every X* command is unsupported), Redis Functions (FCALL/FUNCTION), client-side caching (CLIENT TRACKING), SORT, WAIT/WAITAOF, CLIENT PAUSE or loadable Redis modules.
- Cluster deployments that expect built-in failover: cluster mode is passive, with no leader election, so you must run your own control plane (for example a Kubernetes operator) to detect failures and promote replicas.
- Tiered storage combined with multiple logical databases (SELECT n): open bug #2152 (Sept 2026) says all databases share one log file, so a read on db 0 can return db 1's value. Open #2163 is an IndexOutOfRangeException on ZADD over an expired record read back from disk. The disk-tier paths are less mature than the in-memory path.
- Teams that rely on exact Redis semantics or eviction policies: MSET is not atomic, eviction follows log order (FIFO for read-only records unless --copy-reads-to-tail) rather than Redis maxmemory-policy choices, and with the storage tier on, reads may run out of order relative to earlier writes in the same pipeline.
- Environments that cannot run or tune a managed runtime: Garnet needs the .NET 8/10 runtime with server GC, and large indexes and logs live on the pinned managed heap by default (the native allocator is opt-in and then needs GC hard-limit tuning).

**Integration:** standalone server (dotnet run, the garnet-server dotnet tool, or the repo's Dockerfiles) or a NuGet library (Microsoft.Garnet) hosted in your own .NET process · .NET runtime 8 or 10; NuGet packages including CommandLineParser, Microsoft.Extensions.Logging, Azure.Storage.Blobs, Azure.Identity, Microsoft.IdentityModel/System.IdentityModel.Tokens.Jwt, KeraLua (Lua scripting) and diskann-garnet (vector sets) · .NET 10 SDK to build (global.json pins 10.0.400, roll-forward to latest major); assemblies target net8.0 and net10.0; C# latest with unsafe code · Linux and Windows are both documented as first-class; the paper also lists x64/ARM and macOS. Dockerfiles exist for Alpine, Ubuntu, Azure Linux, chiseled and Nano Server. The io_uring checkpoint path and huge-page hints are Linux-only.

**Vs siblings:** Pick Garnet over KeyDB when you want many-core throughput, larger-than-memory tiering or fast checkpoints. In the Garnet paper, KeyDB (a multi-threaded network layer over a lock-guarded store) scored 0.6x Valkey throughput and took 481.7 s to checkpoint, against Garnet's 108x and 1.06 s. KeyDB's own headline is a TLS-specific 7x over Redis. Pelikan/Segcache is a memcached-protocol TTL cache and Caffeine is an in-process JVM cache, so Garnet is the one to pick when you need Redis data types, persistence and clustering over the network.

**Gotchas:**
- Memory is set with two knobs: the hash index (-i, rule of thumb 16 bytes per expected key; it never shrinks, and auto-grow only runs if --index-resize-freq is set) and the log (-m). The storage tier is off by default, so records pushed out of memory are simply dropped.
- Durability defaults are weak: with AOF on, writes are acknowledged before the log commits unless --aof-commit-wait is set. Checkpoint and AOF formats are compatible only from 2.1.0 onward within 2.x, and an older binary cannot read a newer checkpoint.
- Published headline numbers ran Garnet with --no-obj --no-pubsub (the object store disabled) and large batches of up to 4096 requests (website Resp.bench setup). The paper switched from memtier to its own Resp.bench because memtier became client-bound, so re-measure at your own batch size and command mix.
- The lowest-latency results in the paper (4-5x lower P99 PING) use an eRPC/DPDK kernel-bypass path that the paper calls a prototype, not part of open-source Garnet.

**Status:** Very active: v2.1.8 shipped 2026-09-16 with commits landing daily. MIT-licensed, about 12k stars, used widely inside Microsoft and offered as the managed Azure Cosmos DB Garnet Cache. Usable today via the dotnet tool, Docker or NuGet, but the storage-tier and multi-database paths still have open correctness bugs.

[repo](https://github.com/microsoft/garnet) · [benchmark](https://badrish.net/papers/garnet-vldb2026.pdf)

##### GL-Cache  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Learned eviction (XGBoost over write-time object groups): higher hit ratio than LRU, slower than LRU, 228x faster than LRB.

**Beats:** LRU — The FAST'23 paper replays 118 production traces (103 CloudPhysics and 14 MSR block-I/O traces, plus 1 Wikimedia CDN trace) in a closed loop. In the libCacheSim micro-implementation (CloudLab m510, Xeon D-1548; compiler and flags not stated), GL-Cache raises hit ratio well above LRU's single-digit gain over FIFO but runs slower than LRU, and its throughput wins (228x/586x over LRB, 64% over the fastest other learned cache) are against learned caches, not LRU. In the Segcache-based Rust prototype (CloudLab c6420, Xeon Gold 6142, one CloudPhysics trace, release profile opt-level 3 with LTO), it gets up to 40% higher hit ratio than the best baseline, at throughput similar to Cachelib's throughput-optimized LRU and to Segcache.

**Known shortcoming:** The 64% throughput gain is over the fastest other learned cache (vs LRB it is 228x); against LRU it wins hit ratio only and is slower on throughput; not better than Belady. Split hardware across two testbeds; the paper artifact repo (Thesys-lab/fast23-GLCache) has no licence (verifier downgrade).

**Known shortcoming:** Beats LRU on hit ratio only; throughput is below LRU (0.3-0.8x FIFO; Wikimedia 2.5-4.2 vs FIFO 7.6-9.7 MQPS). Speed wins are only against other learned caches (228x/586x vs LRB). The libCacheSim module is a metadata-only simulation policy, opt-in (-DENABLE_GLCACHE=ON, needs XGBoost), never built in CI, no locks.

**Known shortcoming:** Training runs synchronously inside get() (10-50 ms) and inference inside evict; behaves as plain FIFO until the first model (needs one day of trace timestamps). Defaults differ from the paper's configurations; README says retrain every 2 days, code every 1; 6 features vs the paper's 7. Artifact license is muddled (none detected, README says Apache-2.0, micro-impl/LICENSE is GPL-3.0); the libCacheSim copy was relicensed Apache-2.0 on 2026-09-13. Bad parameters exit(1); range checks are asserts.

**How:** It uses group-level learning. Objects are grouped by write time into fixed-size segments, laid out like a log as in Segcache. A gradient-boosted tree model (XGBoost, regression with squared-error loss, retrained from scratch once a day) predicts each group's utility, defined as the sum over its objects of 1/(time to next access x size), from 6-7 cheap group features: age, mean object size, hits, active objects, and the request rate, miss ratio and write rate when the group was created. One inference ranks all groups and is reused until a fraction F_eviction (2-10%) of them has been evicted. Each eviction merges the lowest-utility group with its N_merge-1 neighbours in write time and keeps only the best objects, scored by 1/(size x age). Per-object metadata is about 5 bytes (a 4-byte last-access time plus under 1 byte of amortized group features), against 16 for LRU's list pointers and 189-192 for LRB. A hit only updates the access time, plus the utility for groups sampled for training.

**Use it when:**
- Simulating or evaluating eviction policies on block-I/O or CDN traces in libCacheSim, where hit ratio matters more than CPU per request (in the paper, LRU and Cacheus gained only single-digit % over FIFO on the median trace; GL-Cache gained much more)
- You want a learned eviction policy but cannot afford LRB: GL-Cache-E is 228x faster than LRB on average at the small cache size, GL-Cache-T 586x, with a 7% higher mean hit ratio
- Segment or log-structured caches (Segcache-style) where evicting whole segments is natural: on one CloudPhysics trace the prototype raised hit ratio by 60% over plain Segcache at 8 GB
- Variable-size objects and workloads whose mix of recency, frequency and size changes with cache size (the model re-weights features per trace and per cache size)
- Traces with real timestamps covering several days, since training uses wall-clock intervals (first model after one day of trace time, then daily retraining)

**Skip it when:**
- If you need more requests per second than LRU gives: in the micro-implementation LRU runs close to FIFO, while GL-Cache runs at 0.3-0.8x FIFO (paper Table 1), and GL-Cache-E reaches only 2.55-4.20 MQPS against FIFO's 7.62-9.68 on the Wikimedia trace
- Short traces or ones without meaningful timestamps: until the first model is trained (one day of trace time) it evicts segments in plain FIFO order
- As a production in-process cache: the libCacheSim module is a metadata-only simulator policy with no locking and no value storage, and the Rust prototype is a research benchmark frozen since May 2023
- Builds that cannot take on an XGBoost dependency or an opt-in build flag: GLCache compiles only with -DENABLE_GLCACHE=ON, CI never builds or tests it, and XGBoost installs have broken on macOS (issue #180)
- Latency-sensitive paths: libCacheSim calls train() synchronously inside get() (10-50 ms per training in the paper) and runs inference inside eviction (0.4-3 ms), and each group eviction removes hundreds to thousands of objects at once

**Integration:** shared lib (the glcache C module inside libCacheSim, built only with -DENABLE_GLCACHE=ON; BUILD_SHARED_LIBS defaults to ON) · XGBoost C API (find_package(xgboost) REQUIRED when enabled), glib, zstd, tcmalloc (per README), CMake; the Rust prototype uses a fork of rust-xgboost (1a1a11a/rust-xgboost) and forks of Twitter's rustcommon · CMake 3.12+ with a C compiler (C standard not stated; C++17 set for libCacheSim's C++ parts); prototype: Rust 2021 edition · Linux and macOS (libCacheSim CI builds both, but without GLCache; PR #280 in July 2025 fixed compiling GL-Cache on macOS)

**Vs siblings:** Pick GL-Cache over LRB when you want learned eviction without LRB's per-object cost: it is 228-586x faster with a similar or higher hit ratio. Pick it over LHD or Cacheus when hit ratio on diverse block traces matters: up to 37.8% above LHD, and 60% higher on the median MSR trace at the small cache size. Pick S3-FIFO or SIEVE (same repo) instead when you need throughput and multi-threaded scaling beyond LRU and no ML dependency.

**Gotchas:**
- libCacheSim's defaults (segment-size=100, n-merge=2, rank-intvl=0.02, retrain-intvl=86400) match neither paper configuration (GL-Cache-E: 60 objects/2/0.02; GL-Cache-T: 200/5/0.1). Set parameters explicitly to reproduce the paper.
- The code has drifted from the paper: the GLCache README says it retrains every two days but the code default is one day, and libCacheSim uses 6 features, dropping write rate as redundant, where the paper lists 7. It runs 20 boosting rounds; the Rust prototype runs 8.
- Bad parameters: an unknown key makes the parser call exit(1), and the range checks are assert() calls, which disappear in NDEBUG builds.
- The artifact's license is unclear: GitHub detects no license for Thesys-lab/fast23-GLCache, its README says Apache-2.0, and micro-implementation/LICENSE is GPL-3.0. Use the libCacheSim copy, which is Apache-2.0 (relicensed in PR #324 on 2026-09-13).

**Status:** libCacheSim is actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-26, Apache-2.0, 347 stars), and the GLCache sources were last touched 2026-09-13. The module is still opt-in, untested in CI and simulator-only, and the paper's Thesys-lab artifact has been frozen since 2023-05-12.

[repo](https://github.com/1a1a11a/libCacheSim) · [benchmark](https://junchengyang.com/publication/fast23-glcache.pdf)

##### Hyperbolic Caching  `C`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Research Redis 3.0 fork plus simulator whose cost-aware 'hits over time-in-cache' eviction beats Redis's sampled LRU on miss rate.

**Beats:** Redis — Setup: a rack of Intel Xeon E5620 2.40 GHz Ubuntu 14.04 servers, PostgreSQL 9.3 backends, no compiler or flags given. Django-Wiki replaying a 600k Wikipedia trace against a 1 GB cache: HC Redis reached 23.7 vs 21.1 req/s (+12.3%, miss rate 0.637 vs 0.681). A NodeJS look-aside app (5M requests, 10 runs): +3.2% to +13.5% (e.g. Dynamic Intro, 5k objects: 11.3 vs 10.0 kreq/s, miss rate 0.27 vs 0.33). The baseline is 'default' Redis sampled LRU; the runner scripts start it from a 'redis-default' build of the same fork, not stock Redis and not Redis 4.0+ LFU.

**Known shortcoming:** This repo is the Python simulator and runners; the Redis C patch lives in kantai/redis-hyperbolic-caching. Last commit 2017-07.

**Known shortcoming:** A 2015 fork of Redis 3.0.3; both repos archived; not production. The priority clock is a 24-bit lookup count that wraps every ~16.8M lookups. Policy is fixed at compile time and still named allkeys-lru; costs need nonstandard SET CX/CC or SETCOST commands.

**Known shortcoming:** Plain HC loses to LRU on an expire-once trace (0.60 vs 0.55 miss rate); HC-Expire exists only in the simulator. Noisy per-item cost gives HC-Cost +0% on Django-Wiki. Baseline is likely the same fork's default build, not stock Redis or Redis 4.0+ LFU; no compiler/flags. Shipped configs use 32 samples (paper says 64); size-aware mode computes object size per sampled key.

**How:** Hyperbolic caching (Blankstein, Sen, Freedman, USENIX ATC'17) gives each item the priority n_i / t_i: hits since insertion divided by time since insertion. The priority is computed lazily, only for keys that Redis's existing random-sampling eviction pool draws, so no ordering structure is kept even though priorities decay at per-item rates. Extensions multiply by the per-item cost (HC-Cost), use a per-class exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) of cost (HC-Class, weight 0.2 in code), divide by byte size (HC-Size), and seed a new item's count from the last evicted priority (beta = 0.1). The throughput gain comes from fewer backend (PostgreSQL) fetches, not faster cache operations.

**Use it when:**
- Look-aside web caches where miss cost varies a lot by item and the app can measure it. In the paper's NodeJS lookup-vs-join app, HC-Cost reached 9.4 kreq/s vs 5.0 for plain HC, despite a 57% higher miss rate.
- Backends whose cost shifts for a whole group of keys, e.g. one overloaded replica. HC-Class updates a class's EWMA cost and reprioritizes all its cached items at once.
- Zipf-like, frequency-driven key-value workloads sized for roughly 70-90% hit rates, where Redis's LRU approximation leaves misses behind. NodeJS tests gained 3.2-13.5% throughput.
- Caches with very uneven object sizes (the HC-Size mode). In simulation on Memcachier app traces it 'drastically outperforms LRU'.
- Trying out a new eviction priority function offline. The Python simulator replays Zipf, ARC/SPC, Wikipedia and Memcachier workloads against many policies.

**Skip it when:**
- Any production Redis deployment. This is an archived fork of Redis 3.0.3 (2015) with none of the later Redis releases, fixes or policies. Redis 4.0+ ships its own allkeys-lfu with counter decay.
- Items read about once before they expire, as in the MSN Decision Service trace. Plain HC missed 0.60 vs 0.55 for LRU. The expiration-aware HC-Expire exists only in the simulator; the Redis patch has no TTL term.
- Noisy per-item costs. On Django-Wiki, HC-Cost gave +0.0% throughput vs +12.3% for plain HC, because render times varied (570 ms mean, 180 ms deviation on one page).
- Cost-free traces where ARC or LFU are options. In simulation HC trailed ARC on the P1-P4 traces and LFU on Viral Search.
- Memory-tight caches. The code adds a uint32 cost to every redisObject, plus a double hit counter in hyperbolic builds; the paper cites two doubles per item.

**Integration:** source-drop — a patched Redis 3.0.3 server tree (branch cost-cache) built with make.sh; there is no library. The simulator is plain Python scripts. · Redis 3.0's bundled deps (hiredis, linenoise, Lua) plus libstdc++ (a C++ std::set wrapper is compiled and linked). The benchmarks also need PyPy/NumPy, NodeJS 4.x and PostgreSQL 9.3. · C99 (-std=c99 -pedantic) plus a C++ compiler; the patch adds -Werror. No compiler version is documented (the paper's servers ran Ubuntu 14.04). · Linux (evaluated on Intel Xeon E5620); other platforms not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over LHD, SIEVE or LRB when misses differ in backend cost and you want the app to tell a Redis-protocol cache that cost, per item or per class; those policies are cost-oblivious miss-rate optimizers. Garnet, Dragonfly, KeyDB and Pogocache make the server itself faster, while this only changes which keys get evicted. It helps only when backend misses, not cache CPU, limit throughput, and in practice you would port the roughly 380-line priority function rather than run this fork.

**Gotchas:**
- REDIS_LRU_CLOCK_LOGICAL is hard-wired to 1. 'Time' is the count of key lookups, kept in a 24-bit field that wraps every ~16.8M lookups, after which the age of long-resident keys aliases. The same clock applies to the make.sh 'default' build.
- The policy is chosen by make.sh flags (hyper | size-aware | classes). CONFIG still reports allkeys-lru; only `INFO`'s priority_func line shows the real policy. volatile-ttl and random policies are unchanged.
- Costs are uint32 integers; the Django backend sends int(100*seconds). In class builds, CX without CC is rejected, and class ids must be 1-31.
- Eviction internals change: the pool shrinks from 16 to 4 entries and the shipped confs use maxmemory-samples 32 (the paper says it samples 64). Size-aware builds call rdbSavedObjectLen (rdbSaveObject with a NULL target) on every sampled key, which can be costly for large values.

**Status:** Both repos are archived. The simulator was last committed 2017-07-14 and the Redis 3.0.3 fork 2017-05-18. The simulator is MIT; the Redis changes are MIT per their README, while GitHub tags the Redis repo BSD-3-Clause. Treat it as reference code to port into a modern Redis eviction path, not as a deployable server.

[repo](https://github.com/kantai/hyperbolic-caching) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/atc17/atc17-blankstein.pdf)

##### LHD (Least Hit Density) / RankCache  `C++`  `MIT (verbatim MIT text, Copyright 2017-2018 Carnegie Mellon University, plus a non-binding request to cite the LHD paper; GitHub reports NOASSERTION)`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Trace-driven simulator for LHD, a size-aware eviction policy needing ~8x less cache than LRU for equal hit rate.

**Beats:** LRU — There are two separate results. First, an idealized simulation on a weeklong Memcachier trace and MSR block traces (512M requests after a 128M warm-up): on average LHD+ needed 8x less space than LRU to match hit rate, and 2.4x/2.5x/2.9x less than GDSF/Hyperbolic/AdaptSize. Second, RankCache, a modified memcached v1.4.33 that is not in this repo, was run on one server with the network bypassed, same-size objects and a synthetic Zipfian trace: at 16 threads it gave 8x (abstract) or 16x (intro) the throughput of list-based LRU, and 2x CLOCK at a 90% hit ratio. The paper gives no CPU, compiler or flags for these runs.

**Known shortcoming:** The repo is a single-threaded simulator only; RankCache (the memcached 1.4.33 fork behind the 8x/16x throughput claim) was never released, so the throughput claim cannot be reproduced.
