Throughput runs used synthetic Zipf, same-size objects and bypassed the network; no CPU/compiler/flags; abstract says 8x vs LRU, intro says 16x.

**Known shortcoming:** Fixed 2^20-access reconfiguration gives 4% vs 49.7% hit rate on the LIRS loop trace (issue #1, unanswered). example.cfg keys appClasses/ewmaDecay/accsPerInterval are never read (constexpr); trace paths hard-coded. Linux x86-64 only, -Werror, needs libconfig++, ~61 MB fixed tables, no TTL. Baselines weak (no ARC/TinyLFU/segmented LRU); libCacheSim vendors this code and is the easier way to run it.

**How:** Hit density = hit probability / (object size x expected time in cache). It is estimated from online histograms of hit ages and eviction ages. There is one histogram per class, 16 last-hit-age classes x 16 app-id classes. The histograms are EWMA-decayed and turned into a rank table indexed by coarsened age, in one linear pass every 2^20 accesses. To evict, it samples ASSOCIATIVITY random objects plus the last 8 low-ranked admissions and evicts the lowest, so there is no global ordered list and eviction cost is constant. ASSOCIATIVITY is 32 in lhd.hpp; example.cfg and RankCache use 64. The throughput gain belongs to RankCache: because eviction is by sampling, a hit only writes a per-object timestamp. Evictions use memcached's version-check optimistic concurrency instead of the serialized list operations of LRU or the serialized evictions of CLOCK, and a compact separate tag array makes 64 samples cost about 4 cache misses.

**Use it when:**
- Deciding whether a size-aware policy would beat LRU on your own key-value traces, where object sizes vary from a few bytes to ~1 MB (the Memcachier trace had a 100 B median), before building anything.
- Building your own sampled-eviction cache (Redis-style random sampling) and wanting a reference implementation of a principled ranking function to port; the core is about the first 200 lines of lhd.cpp.
- Workloads that mix scans with Zipf-like reuse, or that show LRU performance cliffs: the paper shows LHD avoiding the cliffs that LRU, GDSF and Hyperbolic hit on MSR src1_0 at 96 MB and proj_2 at 128 MB.
- Memory-bound cache tiers where hits per GB matter more than CPU per request: averaged across cache sizes, LHD+ had 45% fewer misses than LRU and 23-27% fewer than AdaptSize, GDSF and Hyperbolic.
- Multi-tenant caches where each request carries an app or tenant id, since LHD+ also classifies objects by app id (hashed into 16 classes).

**Skip it when:**
- You need a working cache or a faster memcached now: this is a single-threaded simulator. The RankCache server behind the 8x/16x throughput numbers (built on memcached v1.4.33) is not published here.
- Short traces or loop/scan-heavy traces. In open issue #1, Caffeine's author reports that the fixed 2^20-access reconfiguration interval gave 4% hit rate on a LIRS loop trace at cache size 512. Reconfiguring every 1,024 accesses raised that to 49.7%, but runtime rose from 2 s to 26 s. On his unit-size ARC and LIRS traces, LHD never had the best hit rate and was about on par with ARC at higher runtime cost.
- Anything that needs TTL/expiry, deletes or concurrent access: the simulator has none of them. libCacheSim's port of this code aborts on short TTL configurations ('LHD does not support expiration').
- Tight metadata budgets: the simulator allocates about 61 MB of fixed tables before any object is cached (256 classes x 20,000 ages x 3 float arrays), plus a 56-byte Tag struct (by field layout) and a std::unordered_map entry per object. RankCache reports 6.4 MB of rank tables plus 12.6 MB of counters per thread.
- You need comparisons against strong modern baselines. The paper compares against list-based LRU, GDSF, Hyperbolic, AdaptSize and CLOCK, not ARC or TinyLFU. An HN commenter noted it also misses memcached's modified-2Q LRU, which was the default from 1.5.0.

**Integration:** source-drop · libconfig++ (linked with -lconfig++ and used for config parsing); otherwise the STL only. lhd.cpp depends on the simulator's own cache::Cache and parser::Request types. · C++14 (the Makefile runs g++ -std=c++14 -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -funroll-loops -mcmodel=medium -Wall -Werror). Supported compiler versions are not documented. · Linux x86-64 as shipped: parser.hpp uses stat64 and ioctl, and the Makefile hard-codes -march=native and -mcmodel=medium. Other platforms are not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick LHD only as a research reference, to test hit-density eviction on your own traces or to port its ranking into your own sampled cache. For something deployable, use Pelikan/Segcache (memcached replacement, about 8x Memcached's throughput at 24 threads) or Caffeine (JVM); for a simple, scalable replacement for LRU, use SIEVE. libCacheSim (the SIEVE entry) already includes this LHD code behind its common C API next to many other policies, and is the easier way to run it.

**Gotchas:**
- example.cfg sets repl.appClasses, ageCoarseningErrorTolerance, accsPerInterval and ewmaDecay, but the code never reads them. The real values are constexpr constants in lhd.hpp (16, 0.01, 2^20, 0.9). Only repl.type, cache.assoc, cache.admissionSamples, cache.capacity (in MB) and the trace.* keys are read.
- Trace paths are hard-coded in cache.cpp (/n/memcachier/snia/msr/<file>.trace and others), so running your own trace means editing cache.cpp or matching one of the binary header formats in parser.hpp. The full-format reader loops back to the start of the file at EOF, objects over 1 MB are trimmed, and 74 B of memcached overhead is added to every object size.
- rank() samples only 8 candidates until 50 reconfigurations (about 52M accesses) have passed, and explorer objects are admitted only during that window. The code comment calls this a warm-up hack that 'doesn't belong in a real system'. Age coarsening is re-tuned only at reconfigurations 5 and 25.
- reconfigure() prints stats to stdout every 2^20 accesses, errors are handled with assert(), and std::hash<candidate_t> hashes only the object id and ignores appId.

**Status:** Abandoned: one 'Initial LHD release' commit on 2018-07-23 and one open 2019 issue with no reply. It is MIT-licensed (with a request to cite the paper) and about 40 KB of source, so easy to vendor, but it is simulation code, not a cache library.

[repo](https://github.com/CMU-CORGI/LHD) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/nsdi18/nsdi18-beckmann.pdf)

##### LRB (Learning Relaxed Belady) / webcachesim2  `C++`  `BSD-2-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

ML (LightGBM) CDN cache-eviction policy approximating relaxed Belady; cuts simulated WAN traffic 4-25% vs Bloom-filter LRU.

**Beats:** LRU — In the authors' webcachesim2 simulations of six production CDN traces (Wikipedia plus five from two anonymous CDNs, 64 GB-4 TB caches, metadata subtracted from cache size), LRB cut WAN traffic 4-25% vs B-LRU (LRU with Bloom-filter admission), by over 13% on average. The 44% average and 43% p95 bandwidth cuts come from the ATS 8.0.3 prototype with a 1 TB NVMe cache on three GCP n1-standard-64 VMs, compared with unmodified ATS, which the paper says approximates FIFO rather than LRU; throughput was tied (11.72 vs 11.66 Gbps), peak CPU rose from 9% to 16%, and the CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** The 44%/43% WAN-bandwidth gains are against Apache Traffic Server's FIFO-like cache, not LRU; against LRU-family policies the gain is 4-25% in simulation. Fork of dasebe/webcachesim; last commit 2023-01 (verifier downgrade).

**Known shortcoming:** The win is miss ratio (WAN bytes), not CPU: the 44% cut is vs ATS (about FIFO); vs the LRU family it is 4-25% in simulation. GL-Cache (FAST'23) measured LRB at 0.01-0.07 MQPS vs FIFO's 7.6-9.7 on a Wikimedia trace (about 775x slower than LRU, ~200 us per eviction) with the smallest hit gain across 118 traces.

**Known shortcoming:** Metadata is 25-214 B per object; memory_window must be tuned per trace and cache size; the uint32 request clock wraps after 4.29B requests. Heavy dependencies (LightGBM, MongoDB drivers, Boost, libprocps), Ubuntu 18 only, uses VLAs, globals shared across LRBCache instances. Abandoned since 2023-01; libCacheSim has a maintained port (-DENABLE_LRB=ON).

**How:** It does not make eviction cheaper in CPU terms; it lowers the miss ratio, and that cuts WAN bandwidth. The relaxed-Belady idea: instead of finding the object requested farthest in the future (Belady's MIN), evict any object whose next request falls beyond a 'Belady boundary'. So LRB samples 64 cached objects at random and predicts log(time-to-next-request) for each with a LightGBM gradient-boosted-tree regressor (32 iterations, 32 leaves, L2 loss), then evicts the one predicted farthest. Features are 32 inter-request deltas, 10 exponentially decayed counters, object size and optional categorical fields. Labels come from sampled objects inside a sliding memory window, and the model retrains every 128K labeled samples.

**Use it when:**
- Large flash CDN or object caches (the paper evaluates 64 GB to 4 TB, with mean object sizes of 33-644 KB) where WAN egress or byte miss ratio costs more than CPU. The prototype's peak CPU rose from 9% to 16%.
- Workloads where the best heuristic changes from trace to trace. In the paper, LRU4 wins on Wikipedia but is among the worst elsewhere, and TinyLFU and LFUDA each win only on some traces. LRB had the lowest byte miss ratio in all 33 trace/size combinations.
- Moderate eviction rates. Each eviction runs a LightGBM batch prediction: the paper puts it at 30 us for 64 candidates, and GL-Cache measured about 200 us per eviction on one core, which caps it near 5,000 evictions/s.
- Research: comparing a new eviction policy against LRB and around 20 baselines (B-LRU, LFUDA, S4LRU, LeCaR, LHD, AdaptSize, Belady) in the paper's own simulator, on the released 14-day Wikipedia trace (2.8B requests).
- You can spare a validation prefix of the trace (the paper uses the first 20%) plus a MongoDB-backed parallel search to tune memory_window for each cache size.

**Skip it when:**
- DRAM or key-value caches with high request rates. On the Wikimedia trace, GL-Cache (FAST'23) measured LRB at 0.01-0.07 MQPS against 7.6-9.7 MQPS for FIFO, and reported a 775x slowdown vs LRU.
- Small objects or tight metadata budgets. Per-object metadata grows with request history, from 25 B for single-request objects up to 214 B (paper Table 3), against 16 B of pointers for LRU. It stayed under 3% of cache size only because CDN objects are large.
- Block-I/O-style workloads. Across 118 traces, GL-Cache found LRB gave the smallest hit-ratio gain over FIFO among LRB, LHD and GL-Cache-E, and GL-Cache improved on LRB's hit ratio by 7% on average, up to 87%.
- When you need a library replacement for an LRU container. There are no values and no get/put API, the dependency stack is heavy (LightGBM, Boost, mongo-c/cxx drivers, libbf, libprocps), and the install targets Ubuntu 18.04.
- When you need a maintained dependency. The last commit was 2023-01-20, known simulator bugs are still open (#12 S4LRU size accounting, #25 LHD oversized request), and the latest issue (#29, March 2024) has no reply.

**Integration:** shared lib · LightGBM, sparsepp, libbf, mongo-c-driver and mongo-cxx-driver (all pinned as sunnyszy fork submodules), fast-cpp-csv-parser, Boost and libprocps. OpenJDK 8 is needed only for the Adaptive-TinyLFU baseline. Memory-window tuning also needs pywebcachesim (Python), GNU parallel and MongoDB. · C++17 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17) and CMake 3.2.2+. Documented only on Ubuntu 18 and the ubuntu:18.04 Docker image; the GCC version is not documented. LRBCache::rank() uses variable-length stack arrays, a GCC/Clang extension that is not standard C++. · Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 18.04 per INSTALL.md and the Dockerfile; it links libprocps). Other OSes and architectures are not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick LRB over LHD, SIEVE or W-TinyLFU only for large flash CDN caches, where the bytes it saves on the WAN outweigh roughly 100x lower eviction throughput and up to about 200 B of metadata per object. GL-Cache measured TinyLFU and LHD far faster than LRB, and those simple policies suit DRAM caches better. To simulate LRB alongside those policies, libCacheSim (the SIEVE entry) ships a maintained LRB port (-DENABLE_LRB=ON) that is easier to build than this repo.

**Gotchas:**
- memory_window matters a lot and has to be tuned for each trace and cache size. The code default is 67,108,864; the README's Wikipedia values run from 58.7M at 64 GB to 671M at 1 TB. Tuning on the full trace (LRB-OPT) gained another 1-4%.
- Logical time is a uint32 request counter (`uint32_t current_seq = -1`) and metadata positions are 31-bit bitfields, so traces longer than about 4.29B requests wrap. The paper's largest trace is 2.8B requests.
- It evicts plain LRU until the first model is trained (128K labeled samples) and whenever the LRU tail is older than memory_window. LightGBM inference defaults to 4 threads per prediction; a code comment says 1 thread is 2-3x slower.
- The default objective is byte miss ratio; object miss ratio needs --objective=object_miss_ratio. The trace sanity check aborts if a key's size changes (issue #15). The paper subtracts metadata from cache size, which the simulator exposes as the is_metadata_in_cache_size flag.

**Status:** Abandoned BSD-2-Clause research code (last default-branch commit 2023-01-20). It works as a simulator through the sunnyszy/webcachesim Docker image, but embedding it means carrying LightGBM and the MongoDB drivers; libCacheSim's actively maintained port is the easier way to use it.

[repo](https://github.com/sunnyszy/lrb) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi20-paper-song.pdf)

##### MemC3  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

NSDI'13 research fork of Memcached 1.4.13: optimistic cuckoo hashing plus CLOCK eviction; ~3x read-heavy throughput, incomplete protocol.

**Beats:** memcached — The server was a 2x6-core Xeon L5640 with 1GB of item memory. 50 client machines on 10GbE replayed a pre-generated YCSB Zipf trace (95% GET / 5% SET) using 100-key libmemcached multi-gets. MemC3 peaked at 4.4 MOPS vs 1.5 MOPS for stock Memcached 1.4.13, almost 3x. Local microbenchmarks showed cuckoo+CLOCK holding ~40% more 16B/32B items than chaining+LRU and ~5M lookups/s per thread. The server compiler and flags are not stated. The baseline predates Memcached 1.4.15 (Sept 2012), which already reworked read scalability, and Memcached's maintainer argues the stock-Memcached number may have been handicapped by benchmark setup.

**Known shortcoming:** The 3x is 4.4 vs 1.5 MOPS against stock Memcached 1.4.13 (2013); abandoned since 2014-06.

**Known shortcoming:** Can return wrong or corrupt data: refcounts were removed and GET sends zero-copy from slab memory (the Memcached maintainer's 2020 review includes a repro script); delete leaks memory; CAS/incr/decr/add/replace are stubbed and slab rebalancing removed. The SET path takes no lock (item_lock is a no-op for cuckoo) although the paper assumes a single writer.

**Known shortcoming:** Fixed-size index (default ~1.25 GiB), no resize, assert(false) when full. Linux x86 only, workers pinned to core 6+i, GCC 10+ link failure without -fcommon. The Memcached 1.4.13 baseline predates the 1.4.15 read-scaling work; libcuckoo is the maintained successor.

**How:** The index uses optimistic concurrent cuckoo hashing, a form of partial-key cuckoo hashing: each key has two 4-slot buckets, the alternate bucket is b XOR hash(tag) so moving an entry never requires reading its key, and lookups compare 1-byte tags before following a pointer (about 2 cacheline reads per lookup). Readers take no locks; they read one of 8192 striped version counters before and after scanning the buckets and retry if it changed. A writer first finds the whole cuckoo path and then moves keys backward along it, so no key is ever missing from the table mid-insert. CLOCK only sets a recency bit on a hit instead of relinking an LRU list, which removes the LRU mutex, the two LRU pointers and the 2-byte refcount from each item; integer-cast key comparison and optional 2MB hugepages add smaller gains.

**Use it when:**
- Studying or re-implementing a read-mostly (90%+ GET), many-threaded cache index: it is a compact working reference for optimistic cuckoo hashing and CLOCK wired into a real memcached-shaped server.
- Reproducing the NSDI'13 numbers or using MemC3 as a historical baseline in a paper. The repo ships the YCSB trace settings, a trace generator and a libmemcached multi-get bench client.
- Controlled experiments with tiny, fixed-size objects (the paper used 16B keys and 32B values), where per-item header overhead dominates and roughly 40% more items per GB of item memory is the point.
- Pure GET/SET traffic on Linux x86-64 hardware with more than 6 cores, when you don't need delete, CAS, incr/decr or add/replace semantics.

**Skip it when:**
- Any production cache. Memcached's maintainer showed (2020 review, with a repro script) that MemC3 can return wrong or corrupt data. Refcounts were removed, yet GET responses are still sent zero-copy from slab memory, so a concurrent overwrite can change a value while it is being sent.
- Workloads that need delete, CAS/gets, incr/decr, add/replace/append/prepend or slab rebalancing. These are stubbed, broken (the review reports that delete leaks the item's memory) or removed outright.
- Write-heavy or miss-heavy caches, because inserts and evictions are single-writer. The paper's own 1GB cache with ~15% misses peaks at 6 MOPS at about 6 threads and falls off after that. With 10% inserts the hash table peaks at 20 MOPS at 10 threads.
- Caches that are small relative to the working set. Table 3 shows LRU beating CLOCK on miss ratio at 256MB and below (e.g. 64MB: cuckoo+LRU 35.87% vs cuckoo+CLOCK 36.46%).
- Growing datasets, or non-Linux / non-x86 / little-core hosts. The cuckoo index never resizes, worker threads are hard-pinned to CPU cores 6+i, x86 intrinsic headers are included, and key comparison assumes little-endian.

**Integration:** source-drop — an autotools build of a standalone server binary (memc3), not a library. The cuckoo table (assoc_cuckoo.c) is tied to memcached's item and slab code. · libevent for the server. The bench tools also need libmemcached, YCSB (to pre-generate traces), and OpenSSL/zlib for the trace generator. · C99 (AC_PROG_CC_C99) with GCC __sync builtins and autoconf/automake. Under GCC, configure adds -Wall -Werror -pedantic, and GCC 10+ needs -fcommon because memcached.h defines globals without extern. The last known-good compiler is not documented. · Linux x86-64 in practice: the code includes xmmintrin.h/immintrin.h, uses pthread_attr_setaffinity_np/sched_getcpu, pins worker i to core 6+i, and has a little-endian-only integer key compare. Hugepage support is Linux-only (SHM_HUGETLB).

**Vs siblings:** Pick MemC3 only to study or reproduce the optimistic-cuckoo-plus-CLOCK design inside a memcached-shaped server. For a running cache, Pelikan/Segcache (maintained, about 8x Memcached at 24 threads per NSDI'21) or current Memcached is the safer choice, and MICA (same efficient/ GitHub org) goes much further on tiny items (65.6-76.9 Mops) with a different design. If you only want the concurrent cuckoo table, the README points to its maintained successor, libcuckoo.

**Gotchas:**
- The index is allocated at full size at startup. The default hashpower of 25 means 2^25 packed 40-byte buckets (~1.25 GiB), whatever -m is set to. There is no expansion: when a 500-displacement cuckoo search fails, assoc2_insert prints 'hash table is full ... need to increase hashpower' and do_item_link_nolock hits assert(false). Size the table up front with -o hashpower=N.
- The lookup's version check covers only the index read. GET builds iovecs that point into slab memory, and the refcounts are commented out. The memcached.org repro shows a 200KB value turning from '1's into '2's partway through a large multiget.
- Configuration is compile-time #defines in memc3_config.h: cuckoo vs chaining, CLOCK vs LRU, lock mode, hugepages. The shipped config leaves hugepages off, although the paper's full-system run used MemC3 'with all optimizations enabled'.
- It may not start or build as-is. Creating worker thread i fails on hosts without a core 6+i (the memcached.org reviewers had to comment out the affinity line). Globals such as keyver_array and hashpower are defined in a header, which breaks linking under GCC 10's default -fno-common.

**Status:** Abandoned: the last commit was 2014-06-28, it sits on a 2012 Memcached base, and an issue from 2021 is still unanswered. It is BSD-3-Clause and readable as a reference but unsafe to deploy, and its authors point to libcuckoo as the maintained re-engineering of its hash table.

[repo](https://github.com/efficient/memc3) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/nsdi13/nsdi13-final197.pdf)

##### MICA  `C`  `Apache-2.0 (license text embedded in README; no separate LICENSE file in the repo)`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Research in-memory key-value cache/store over DPDK UDP; 65-77 Mops on tiny items per 16-core server, far above Memcached.

**Beats:** memcached — NSDI'14 Fig. 10 tested a dual 8-core Xeon E5-2680 server with eight 10GbE ports, running DPDK 1.4.1 with 16 EREW partitions, 8B/8B items and no client batching. MICA's cache mode served 75.5-76.9 Mops on uniform keys and 65.6-70.5 Mops on Zipf-0.99. Memcached rev 87e2f36, ported to MICA's DPDK stack and at its best with 2 cores, reached 0.7-1.3 Mops, and the next-best system, Masstree, reached 16.5 Mops. The paper does not give the compiler version; the repo's flags are -O9 -msse4.2 -march=corei7. MICA was network-bound (54.9-66.4 Gbps used), so the gap narrows for 16B/64B and 128B/1024B items (8.6-14.6 Mops on the large set). The latency comparison (MICA at 24-52 us) was against stock Memcached on the kernel network stack.

**Known shortcoming:** Baseline is Memcached, which peaks at 2 cores in the paper's setup; 16 partitions, and Memcached's latency is flat, so the 'more stable latency' claim does not hold.

**Known shortcoming:** Not a memcached drop-in: its own UDP protocol with client-computed key hashes, no TCP, no client library beyond benchmarks. Needs an Intel ixgbe NIC with Flow Director, a DPDK 1.5-era build and hugepages at /mnt/huge; will not build on current DPDK without porting.

**Known shortcoming:** Lossy cache mode: a full bucket evicts its oldest entry; a too-small GET buffer truncates the value but still returns success; TTL is stored but never enforced. A plain cmake build keeps asserts and aborts on GETs of values >1500 B, while NDEBUG turns assert(false) error paths into no-ops. Log pool rounds up to a power of two; 'typedef int bool' breaks C++. Abandoned (master 2014); the successor mica2 is idle since 2017.

**How:** It partitions data by keyhash in EREW mode, so each core owns its partitions outright with no locks or cache-line sharing. Clients help the NIC route requests: the Intel Flow Director perfect-match filter sends each packet to the owning core's RX queue based on its UDP port, over DPDK with burst I/O (up to 32 packets) and zero-copy replies built inside the request buffer. In cache mode, items live in a per-partition circular log on hugepages (FIFO, or approximate LRU by re-appending, with no garbage collection). That log is indexed by a lossy set-associative hash index: 15 tag+offset slots per 128-byte bucket, where a collision evicts the oldest entry instead of being resolved, and 48-bit offsets let dangling pointers be detected cheaply. Multi-stage software prefetching overlaps the packet, bucket and log-entry cache misses across a burst, and store mode swaps in segregated fits plus bulk chaining (spare buckets sized at 10% of the main buckets).

**Use it when:**
- You control both clients and servers and can give a cache tier dedicated Intel 10GbE (ixgbe, Flow Director) NICs and hugepages for kernel bypass.
- Many tiny or small items (8-64 B values, keys of 255 B or less) under write-heavy or Zipf-skewed traffic where lock-based stores stop scaling. The paper shows MICA holding 65.6-76.9 Mops, losing at most 14% to skew.
- Cache semantics are acceptable: silent eviction on a full hash bucket or on log wrap-around is fine for your data.
- You need high throughput with a single round trip per request: the paper measured 24-52 us average end-to-end latency while serving tens of Mops.
- You want a compact reference implementation (about 12K lines of C) of EREW partitioning, client-steered NIC request direction, and a circular log with a lossy set-associative index.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a memcached drop-in. It has no memcached text or binary protocol, no TCP, and no client library beyond the benchmark clients, so applications must adopt its UDP format and handle loss and retries themselves.
- You need values larger than one packet, multi-get, CAS, range queries, persistence or replication. The paper lists durability and multi-packet items as non-goals.
- Cloud VMs, non-Intel NICs or current DPDK. The build links only DPDK's ixgbe PMD and relies on Flow Director and a 2014-era DPDK make-based setup (>= 1.5.0). gen_confs.py hard-codes the paper's testbed (8 server ports, a 16-core server, 12-core clients, 10.0.0.x addresses).
- Anything that needs upstream support. master was frozen on 2014-03-03, the isca2015 branch on 2016-01-18, no issue or PR has ever been filed, and Apache-2.0 appears only as README text with no LICENSE file.
- Store mode where writes must never fail for lack of space. Spare buckets are fixed at 10% of the main buckets, and once they run out a SET is rejected with an out-of-space error.

**Integration:** source-drop · Intel DPDK >= 1.5.0 (paper used 1.4.1; rte_eal, rte_mempool, rte_ring, rte_mbuf, ethdev, ixgbe PMD), libcrypto, librt, libm, pthread, hugetlbfs mounted at /mnt/huge, cmake >= 2.6, Python 2.7 and bash 4 for config generation · GNU C with gcc >= 4.6.0 and cmake >= 2.6; repo builds with -O9 -msse4.2 -march=corei7 · x86-64 Linux >= 3.2 only (SSE4.2, Nehalem or newer); peak results need a dual-socket NUMA server with Intel 10GbE ixgbe NICs that support Flow Director, plus 2 MiB hugepages

**Vs siblings:** Choose MICA over MemC3 (same CMU group, memcached-compatible) or Pelikan/Segcache (a production memcached replacement) only when you own the NIC, the client library and the hardware, and peak tiny-item ops per server is the goal. For anything that has to work with standard clients or on commodity cloud hosts, Pelikan, Dragonfly or Pogocache are the practical choices.

**Gotchas:**
- Build mode matters. configure_all.sh sets NDEBUG=yes, but a plain `cmake ..` leaves asserts on, and the debug path in mehcached_get deliberately asserts on any value longer than 1500 bytes. With NDEBUG=yes, error paths written as `assert(false)` (such as hugepage allocation failure during table or pool init) print a message and keep going instead of aborting.
- Cache mode is lossy by design. A SET into a full 15-slot bucket evicts that bucket's oldest entry even when the log has free space. A GET with a too-small output buffer returns success with a silently truncated value (partial-value handling is marked TODO).
- expire_time is stored and echoed back to clients but never enforced by the server (netbench_server.c: 'TODO: use expire_time'), so clients must check staleness themselves.
- Log pool sizes are rounded up to the next power of two (and a 2 MiB multiple), so memory use can nearly double. Init also shells out to `rm /mnt/huge/mehcached_shm_*`. basic_types.h does `typedef int bool`, which breaks when included from C++ or alongside stdbool.h.

**Status:** Abandoned: master was last committed 2014-03-03 and the isca2015 branch 2016-01-18, no issues or PRs have ever been filed, and Apache-2.0 is stated only in the README. It is a copyable C reference to learn from rather than a deployable service, and its C++ successor efficient/mica2 (DPDK 16.11, g++ >= 5.3) has also been idle since 2017.

[repo](https://github.com/efficient/mica) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/nsdi14/nsdi14-paper-lim.pdf)

##### Pelikan / Segcache  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Rust cache-server framework whose pelikan-segcache speaks memcached's text protocol over Segcache, a TTL-segmented store with 5-byte-per-item metadata.

**Beats:** Memcached — The NSDI'21 paper replayed Twitter production traces against the storage layer only (no networking) on dual Xeon Gold 6230R hosts. The multi-thread test used trace c, with 7% writes. In it, the legacy C Segcache (twitter/pelikan, archived at thesys-lab/segcache) reached over 70 MQPS at 24 threads. Memcached 1.6.6 levelled off at 9 MQPS after 8 threads. On one thread, Segcache was up to 40% faster than Memcached. Compiler and flags are not stated. None of these numbers were measured on the current Rust code, which keeps the segment design and 5-byte metadata but not the per-thread write segments. The Rust engine's only published scaling data (i5-13500H E-cores, rustc 1.97.1, engine only) shows reads scaling 8.19x on 8 cores while writes do not scale.

**Known shortcoming:** Paper numbers (70 vs 9 MQPS at 24 threads) come from the legacy C Segcache; no Rust Pelikan vs Memcached benchmark exists. The Rust engine dropped the paper's per-thread write segments (one shared tail per TTL bucket), so writes run 0.82x on 8 cores while reads are 8.19x (cache-rs journal, #85 open). Multi-worker shared engine only since 2026-08 (segcache 0.4.0-0.4.2 yanked; 7 engine bugs found in rollout; false NotFound on cas, #101). add/replace not atomic across workers (32.7% double-win at 8 workers); data port text protocol only. The README's ADQ p999 claim measured C pelikan_twemcache (slab), not Segcache; cache-rs docs still say single-threaded.

**Known shortcoming:** The NSDI'21 paper's C artifact is github.com/Thesys-lab/Segcache (folded into this entry).

**How:** Segcache appends items to fixed-size segments (1 MiB by default). Each segment holds only items with similar TTLs, grouped into 1024 TTL buckets. Per-item metadata is therefore a 5-byte header plus an 8-byte hash slot, instead of Memcached's roughly 56 bytes of pointers, LRU links and timestamps. A whole expired segment is freed in one step. Eviction uses merge-based eviction, which scans a run of segments and copies only frequently used items (1-byte approximate frequency counter) into a new segment; S3-FIFO and simpler policies are optional. The Rust engine uses a lock-free 2-choice hash table of 64-byte buckets with SIMD tag scans (AVX2/NEON), and since segcache 0.4 (August 2026) N worker threads share one engine through `Arc` with no storage thread in between.

**Use it when:**
- Memcached-style look-aside caches with many small objects (tens to a few hundred bytes), where per-item metadata is a large share of DRAM.
- Workloads where items carry TTLs and expired data should leave memory quickly (the paper's Twitter traces used TTLs from 2 minutes to 30 days).
- Read-heavy traffic: the current engine's reads scale almost linearly (8.19x on 8 cores for uniform gets in the maintainers' own harness).
- Teams that want to build a custom cache server in Rust from reusable protocol, storage and runtime crates, or embed the `segcache` crate directly.

**Skip it when:**
- Write-heavy traffic, or traffic that overwrites the same keys often, on many cores. The maintainers measured writes to one shared engine at 0.82x of single-thread throughput on 8 cores: every writer in one TTL bucket reserves space at one shared tail segment (cache-rs issue #85, open). The 2021 Segcache blog already lists a very high overwrite rate as a weak spot.
- Large objects, or data with no TTLs: the Segcache authors say these see limited benefit from the design.
- When you are counting on the paper's multi-core numbers. The paper's C engine gave each thread its own active write segments; the Rust engine does not do this yet, and nobody has published a Rust Pelikan versus Memcached throughput result.
- Code that uses `add` as a distributed lock or needs atomic add/replace: with more than one worker, two concurrent `add`s on one key can both return STORED (32.7% of hot-key races at 8 workers, in the maintainers' own test).
- Risk-averse production use, or clients that need the memcached meta or binary protocol, `touch`/`gat`, or stats on the data port. The concurrent engine is about a month old. Its rollout found seven engine bugs (lost increments, a deadlock, resurrected deletes, false misses), and some correctness issues are still open (for example cache-rs #101, a false NotFound on cas). The server wires only the text protocol: get, set, add, replace, append, prepend, cas, incr, decr, delete, flush_all, version and quit.

**Integration:** server binary built from a Cargo workspace (the Pelikan crates are not on crates.io); storage engine is the `segcache` crate (crates.io 0.4.x) · segcache 0.4.3 and keyvalue (pelikan-io/cache-rs), mio, rustls with AWS-LC (needs a C toolchain and cmake), metriken, clocksource, serde/toml · Rust stable, edition 2021; no MSRV declared; CI uses dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable; cmake and a C compiler for AWS-LC · CI builds on ubuntu-latest and macos-latest; SIMD tag scan on x86-64 (AVX2) and aarch64 (NEON) with a scalar fallback; Windows not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick this over Garnet or KeyDB when you run a Memcached-protocol cache of many small TTL'd objects and memory per item costs more than the Redis data-structure features those two provide. Caffeine is an in-process JVM library rather than a network server, so it fits a different case.

**Gotchas:**
- Rust Pelikan runs no periodic expiry. Expired items become invisible on access, and their memory comes back only under write pressure, so a lightly loaded server shows expired segments as used memory.
- The hash table has a fixed size (`hash_power`, default 16 in code, 22 in the sample config) with no overflow chains. Set it too low and you lose capacity with no warning (issue #29 asks for a log message). Segment ids are 18 bits, and segments over 8 MiB used to alias item locations silently in release builds (cache-rs #79, closed 2026-08-20).
- The engine metrics evict_time, expire_time and clear_time used a 1-second clock and reported 0 or exactly 1 s (cache-rs #75, fixed upstream). Check which segcache version you run before trusting them.
- Some cited evidence does not match the code. The README's p999 < 5 ms at 1M QPS result (the Intel ADQ post, 2020) was measured on the C pelikan_twemcache slab server, not on Segcache or Rust. The segcache crate's docs/segcache.md still describes a single-threaded `&mut self` engine, although the 0.4 API takes `&self`.

**Status:** Active (commits in September 2026, Apache-2.0) and buildable with stable Rust, but multi-worker storage only landed in August 2026 on a young concurrent engine, and the peer-reviewed numbers belong to the unmaintained C code.

[repo](https://github.com/pelikan-io/pelikan) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi21/presentation/yang-juncheng)

##### quick-cache  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Sharded concurrent Rust cache with S3-FIFO/CLOCK-Pro-style eviction; beats Mutex-guarded LRU mainly on hit ratio and thread scaling.

**Beats:** LRU+Mutex (hashlink crate LruCache + std::sync::Mutex) — The author ran mokabench (the Moka project's ARC-trace replay harness; both caches used an xxh3 hasher) on x64 Linux with an i9-12900H; rustc version and flags are not stated. On the ARC S3 trace at 100k capacity, QuickCache hit 12.84% in 2.196 s with one client, vs 2.33% in 2.422 s for hashlink LruCache behind a Mutex: about 1.1x faster and 5.5x the hit ratio. Across all traces the hit-ratio gain was 1.2-5.5x (equal at SPC1 30M), but LRU+Mutex was only ever run with one client and was faster in 3 of 9 configurations. Also, the README says LRU+Mutex used std::sync::Mutex, but mokabench's hashlink driver actually uses parking_lot::Mutex.

**Known shortcoming:** Single-client wall time is only ~1.1x (2.196 vs 2.422 s), not ~3x, and LRU+Mutex is faster in 3 configurations; the real wins are hit ratio and concurrency. Evidence is mokabench, a small suite (10 stars).

**Known shortcoming:** The win is mostly hit ratio (1.2-5.5x); the LRU+Mutex baseline was never run multi-client and actually used parking_lot::Mutex (not std as the README says); author-run with rustc/flags unstated. Per-shard capacity (default 4x cores) rejects heavy items and evicts early (#26/#55/#65); tables never shrink (#99); no TTL. Pre-1.0 (0.7.0 broke the Lifecycle API), MSRV 1.85, ~47 unsafe sites despite the 'trivially verifiable' claim (Miri/fuzz/shuttle in CI).

**How:** The eviction policy is a modified CLOCK-Pro that the crate docs call very similar to S3-FIFO. Resident entries live in hot and cold FIFO rings (the hot target defaults to 97% of weight) and carry a small reference counter capped at 2 (the source notes CLOCK-Pro uses 1 and S3-FIFO 3). A ghost ring holds hashes of recently evicted keys (sized at 50% of estimated items by default), and a key that returns while still in it is readmitted straight to hot. This scan resistance is where the hit-ratio gains over LRU come from. A hit only does a relaxed atomic increment of that counter under a shard read lock, and skips it when the counter is already saturated, so reads never need exclusive access or list relinking the way LRU does. The sync cache is split into power-of-two shards (default 4x detected cores). Each shard is a hashbrown HashTable of indices into a linked slab, behind a parking_lot RwLock. Per-entry overhead is 21 bytes, and the cache does not allocate once the table stops growing.

**Use it when:**
- Rust services where many threads share one cache on a hot path: in the README's mokabench runs on the ARC S3 trace at 100k capacity, QuickCache took 2.196 s with 1 client, 1.279 s with 3 and 0.798 s with 6.
- Traces with scans or one-hit wonders (storage block traces, buffer caches) where LRU hit ratio collapses: on ARC S3 at 100k entries QuickCache hit 12.8% vs 2.3% for LRU+Mutex, and on DS1 at 1M entries 14.9% vs 3.1%.
- Caches sized in bytes rather than item count, using a `Weighter` such as value length. Zero-weight items are kept apart from eviction and never evicted.
- Loaders that must compute each missing value only once (thundering-herd protection), sync or async, via `get_or_insert_with` / `get_or_insert_async` / `get_value_or_guard_async`.
- When you want a small dependency tree and no background threads. The README contrasts it with Moka, which has more features.

**Skip it when:**
- You need TTL/TTI expiry or time-based invalidation: the README says these are partially or not implemented and points to Moka. Eviction listeners exist only as a `Lifecycle::on_evict` hook that you write yourself.
- You need strict LRU order or a guarantee that a just-replaced item stays resident: the maintainer confirms replaced entries can still be evicted (issue #50), and `insert` vs guarded insert could pick different victims before fix #95 (issue #93).
- Tiny caches, or item weights that vary widely on high-core machines: capacity is divided per shard, so an item heavier than one shard's hot budget (about 97% of capacity/shards) is rejected outright, and a shard can evict while other shards still have room (issues #26, #55, #65).
- Single-threaded speed is the goal: single-client LRU+Mutex finished faster in 3 of the 9 README configurations (S3 800k: 2.613 vs 3.207 s; DS1 1M: 8.901 vs 9.883 s; SPC1 2M: 10.768 vs 14.611 s).
- Processes that must hand memory back after shrinking: evicting or draining drops the items but does not shrink the internal tables (issue #99), and the documented footprint (K+V+21)*(len*1.5).next_power_of_two() includes ghost slots.

**Integration:** crate · equivalent 1.0 and hashbrown 0.17 always. Default features add foldhash 0.2 (default hasher) and parking_lot 0.12. Optional: crossbeam-utils 0.8 (`sharded-lock`) and shuttle 0.8 (testing only). · Rust 1.85 for 0.7.0 (rust-version in Cargo.toml, checked by cargo-msrv in CI). 0.6.x declared 1.71 but in practice needed 1.80 until fix #121 (issue #118). · Any Rust std target with no architecture-specific code. CI builds and tests on Linux, macOS and Windows. wasm32 is not documented; an older version failed on wasm32-unknown-unknown through ahash/getrandom (issue #32).

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when you are in Rust and want an in-process S3-FIFO-style cache library. The closest siblings are Caffeine (JVM, W-TinyLFU with expiry and listeners) and otter or golang-fifo (Go); the S3-FIFO and SIEVE entries are libCacheSim research prototypes, not embeddable Rust crates.

**Gotchas:**
- The shard count defaults to 4x detected cores, so `capacity()` is rounded and can differ between machines. Keep `estimated_items_capacity` within about 1-2 orders of magnitude of reality, or set `shards()` explicitly (the maintainer suggests 0 estimated items in tests to force 1 shard).
- `Weighter::weight` must be cheap and stable: changing a resident item's weight is documented as undefined behavior (except inside `before_evict`), and so is overflowing the weight sum in release builds.
- `Lifecycle` hooks such as `on_evict` and `is_pinned` run inside the eviction path under the shard write lock, so keep them tiny (the eviction-listener example sends to a channel). 0.7.0 broke the Lifecycle API: `RequestState` must now implement Default and is passed by &mut.
- The README says it uses 'only trivially verifiable' unsafe, but the source has about 47 unsafe sites (unreachable_unchecked, unchecked slab access, raw pointers in the placeholder waiters). CI runs Miri, cargo-fuzz and shuttle. Recent fixes include a JoinFuture race (#104), a leak when a guard was dropped without inserting (#120) and weight_capacity=1 storing nothing (#106).

**Status:** Actively maintained: v0.7.0 shipped 2026-06-27, it is MIT-licensed, and crates.io shows about 27.2M downloads and 115 reverse dependencies. It is still pre-1.0, and minor releases have broken the API (0.7.0 Lifecycle reshape).

[repo](https://github.com/arthurprs/quick-cache) · [benchmark](https://github.com/arthurprs/quick-cache#benchmarks)

##### RAMCloud  `C++`  `ISC`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Distributed, durable in-DRAM key-value store with kernel-bypass RPC; beats Redis 2.6 on read-heavy YCSB, not on writes.

**Beats:** Redis — FAST '14 Figure 12 measured aggregate YCSB throughput from 24 client nodes against 12 storage nodes: 1 KB objects, triple replication, on an 80-node cluster (Xeon X3470, ConnectX-2 InfiniBand, Linux 2.6.32). The baselines were Redis 2.6.14 (AOF with 1 s fsync, asynchronous replicas) and HyperDex 1.0rc4, both over kernel sockets. RAMCloud beat Redis on the read-heavy workloads B, C and D, and its Verbs transport more than doubled read throughput versus its own kernel-socket runs, but it lost or tied on the write-heavy workloads A and F. Results are given only as bars, no compiler or flags are stated, and the caption gives both 100M and 10M for the key count (the TOCS rerun says 10M operations on 10M keys).

**Known shortcoming:** The wiki names memcached only in prose; the measurable evidence is the FAST'14 YCSB comparison vs Redis 2.6.14 (Fig. 12), where RAMCloud wins read-heavy B/C/D but trails or ties write-heavy A/F. Needs low-latency NICs for its headline latency; abandoned; GitHub shows no license although the code is ISC.

**Known shortcoming:** On write-heavy YCSB A/F kernel sockets lose to Redis and Verbs only ties at 75% memory (25% slower on A at 90%). Over kernel TCP the latency edge mostly disappears (+50-100 us per TOCS); needs InfiniBand/kernel bypass and a full cluster (coordinator, ZooKeeper/LogCabin, backups). No scans, eviction/TTL or Redis protocol.

**Known shortcoming:** Support ended 2019-10-07; built for g++ 4.9-5.4 and breaks on newer distros (RAM-553); Python bindings are Python 2 only. The default build is debug (no -O3); idle servers burn a core polling; durability assumes backups flush buffers after a power-fail warning.

**How:** The main latency technique is kernel bypass plus polling. InfRcTransport drives Mellanox NICs from user space through InfiniBand Verbs reliably-connected queue pairs, and both clients and servers busy-poll instead of taking interrupts or waking threads (the TOCS paper puts a condition-variable wakeup at about 2 us). On each server, one dispatch thread polls the NIC and hands each RPC to a worker thread. Objects live in log-structured memory: 8 MB segments built from 64 KB seglets, indexed by a hash table with cache-line buckets and one pointer per object. Two-level cleaning (in-memory segment compaction plus an LFS-style cost-benefit combined cleaner) runs in parallel threads, which keeps memory use at 80-90%. A write is acknowledged once it reaches the backups' in-memory buffers, and the backups write whole 8 MB segments sequentially later.

**Use it when:**
- Online requests that make long chains of dependent small reads (graph walks, multi-step lookups), where the TOCS paper's 4.7 us median read of a 100 B object over InfiniBand changes what is feasible
- Small objects (about 100 B to 1 KB; it is tuned for a few hundred bytes or less) that must be durable and strongly consistent on write, replacing a memcached-plus-database cache-aside setup and its invalidation logic
- Datacenters with InfiniBand (Mellanox ConnectX-2/3) or other kernel-bypass NICs and a spare core per server for polling
- Datasets larger than one machine's DRAM that can be sharded into tables across many servers; batched multiRead reached about 6M objects/s from a single server in TOCS
- Research or teaching on log-structured memory, fast crash recovery or microsecond RPC, where the code and papers are the reference implementation

**Skip it when:**
- Write-heavy workloads: on FAST '14 YCSB A and F, RAMCloud over kernel sockets trailed Redis, and with Verbs it only matched Redis at 75% memory use and was 25% slower on workload A at 90%
- Commodity Ethernet with kernel TCP only: TOCS says the advantage 'drops significantly' on 1 Gb/s kernel TCP, and TcpTransport adds about 50-100 us over InfRcTransport
- Caching use cases that need eviction or TTLs, range scans, or Redis data types: RAMCloud is a durable store with no eviction and no scans (YCSB E was omitted for this reason)
- Anything that needs vendor support or a modern toolchain: support ended 2019-10-07, the wiki links a known build break on newer Ubuntu and OpenSuse (RAM-553), the Python bindings are Python 2 only, and there is no georeplication
- Small or single-box deployments: it needs a coordinator, ZooKeeper or LogCabin, and storage servers with backup devices of about 2 x DRAM x replication factor, and it was only ever tested on an 80-node cluster

**Integration:** shared lib (libramcloud client library plus separate coordinator and storage-server daemons, built from source with GNU make) · Boost (program_options, filesystem, system), Google protobuf, pcrecpp, OpenSSL (libssl/libcrypto), ZooKeeper C client (on by default; LogCabin is an optional submodule), gtest submodule; optional libibverbs (auto-detected), DPDK, SolarFlare OpenOnload. At runtime it also needs a ZooKeeper or LogCabin cluster. · C++11 (GNUmakefile defaults to -std=c++11); the wiki lists GNU g++ 4.9.x, and the last CI config used g++ 5.4 on Ubuntu 16.04. Newer compilers are not documented. · Linux only; x86-64 with SSE4.2 (the build defaults to -msse4.2 -march=native). Best on Mellanox InfiniBand with Verbs; DPDK, UDP and kernel TCP transports also exist.

**Vs siblings:** Garnet, Dragonfly and KeyDB are catalogued as Redis replacements and measured on ordinary server hardware, and MICA, MemC3 and Pelikan are single-node caches with eviction. Pick RAMCloud only when you need writes synchronously replicated before they are acknowledged, data sharded across many nodes' DRAM with 1-2 s crash recovery, and an InfiniBand or kernel-bypass fabric to realise the latency.

**Gotchas:**
- The default build is a debug/test build (DEBUG=yes: -DTESTING=1, -fno-builtin, no -O3), and the wiki warns this 'slows the system down considerably'. Build with DEBUG=no before measuring anything.
- A coordinator started without -x (external storage) loses all cluster data if it crashes. The backup -f target is treated as a raw block device and overwritten, and undersized backup space (below about 2 x DRAM x replication factor) can eventually stop writes from being served.
- Write durability assumes backups can flush their DRAM buffers after a power failure is detected (or that NVDIMMs are fitted); without that, a datacenter power loss can drop writes that were already acknowledged.
- Servers busy-poll and use a full core even when idle. TOCS reports 30-100 us tail spikes (about 1 in 1,000 reads and 1 in 100 writes) when Linux deschedules the server threads, and the single dispatch thread caps small-read throughput at about 950K reads/s per server.

**Status:** Abandoned: the repo is marked 'No Longer Maintained', the wiki says support ended 2019-10-07 and the last commit was 2019-10-16. It is ISC-licensed but is about 100K lines of C++11 with Boost, protobuf and ZooKeeper dependencies, so it is a system to operate rather than something to vendor, and the last CI-tested toolchain is g++ 5.4 on Ubuntu 16.04.

[repo](https://github.com/PlatformLab/RAMCloud) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/fast14/fast14-paper_rumble.pdf)

##### RobinHood (tail-latency-aware cache repartitioning)  `Go`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Research controller that resizes per-backend memcached partitions by request-blocking count, cutting request P99 versus one shared cache.

**Beats:** OneRFpolicy: a single shared off-the-shelf memcached cache per application server, matching Microsoft OneRF's production configuration. Also compared: TAO++ (static per-backend allocation) and emulated LAMA++, Cliffhanger++ and FAIR++. — On a 50-VM Azure D16 v3 testbed (2.4 GHz E5-2673v3, 16 app servers with 32 GB local memcached, 34 backend servers across 20 services, ~200k queries/s replaying Microsoft OneRF statistics with injected backend load spikes), RobinHood broke a 150 ms P99 request SLO under 0.3% of the time versus 30% for the next best policy, OneRFpolicy (one shared memcached cache per app server). The result is SLO attainment, not a speed ratio, and no compiler matters (Go + Python, versions not given); in other runs it was under 1.5% vs 38% (LAMA++) for fast load ramps and 5% vs 24% (TAO++) for random multi-backend spikes.

**Known shortcoming:** The metric is SLO attainment (99.7% vs 70% of requests within the P99 target), not speed; the 'next best' is a single shared memcached cache (OneRF), not static partitioning. Go research prototype.

**Known shortcoming:** Research testbed, not drop-in; the author says it is not production-ready. controller.py's algorithm named 'robinhood' is not the paper's (the paper's RBC is crit_path_window, P98.5-P99.5); the example config uses crit_path at a 1 s interval, not 5 s. The paper's 20-backend configs and traces, simulator and baseline labels are unpublished (issues #2-#4, no reply).

**Known shortcoming:** Dead stack: Python 2, a pymemcache fork 316 commits behind, golang 1.8/1.9 images, GOPATH. Costs: hit P99 +13-28% on resized partitions; miss latency on cache-rich backends up to 2.55x; 5 s windows miss sub-5 s spikes.

**How:** Every window (5 s in the paper) it 'taxes' 1% of every partition and hands the pooled space out in proportion to each backend's request blocking count (RBC): how often that backend produced the slowest query among requests whose latency lies between P98.5 and P99.5. A backend whose allocated space exceeds its used space by more than 30% has its RBC ignored, so space is not wasted on backends that already have high hit ratios. Since request P99 is almost entirely made of cache misses on whichever backend is overloaded at the moment, shifting cache from cache-rich to cache-poor backends lowers the miss load where it hurts. No cache operation gets faster; P99 hit latency actually rose 13-28% on the partitions being resized.

**Use it when:**
- Application-layer caches in front of many heterogeneous backends (databases, recommenders, KV stores) where each user request fans out into dozens of queries and you have a request-level P99 SLO.
- Backend latency spikes caused by other tenants' load, not correlated with your own query rate, so hit-ratio-maximizing or static per-backend allocations do not react to them.
- OneRF-style layouts where each app server queries only its local cache, and the cache can be resized online per partition (memcached with `cache_memlimit` and slab reassignment, or a cache you control).
- You already log each request's latency and which backend's query was slowest, so computing the RBC is nearly free (paper: under 8 KB/s of stats per app server at 1000 requests/s).
- As a reference design for tail-latency-driven cache allocation: the paper reports the best clairvoyant static split needs 73% more cache to give every backend its peak RobinHood allocation.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a faster cache server or a better eviction policy. RobinHood only changes partition sizes; per-op throughput is memcached's, and hit P99 goes up 13-28% on partitions being resized.
- Single-backend or low-fan-out workloads (nothing to rebalance), or backends that share one underlying storage bottleneck, which the paper says breaks its assumption of independent query latencies.
- Production use as-is. The author says it is not production-ready and not running in production. The controller is Python 2, and the Dockerfiles use golang:1.8/1.9 with the removed go-wrapper script, the deprecated base/archlinux image and GOPATH builds with no go.mod.
- Latency spikes shorter than a few seconds. Reallocation runs in 5 s windows, and moving 1% of a 32 GB cache (up to 327 1 MB pages) can take up to 5 s because of memcached lock contention.
- When cache-rich backends cannot absorb extra misses: RobinHood raised query latency on the least-queried backend by up to 2.55x and by up to 61% on the top 5 backends.

**Integration:** source-drop · memcached (needs the cache_memlimit and slabs reassign commands; version not pinned, installed from Arch packages); Python 2 with a fork of pymemcache (bsb20/pymemcache: 1 commit adding slabs/cache_memlimit calls, 316 behind upstream) and requests; Go with bradfitz/gomemcache and go-sql-driver/mysql; MySQL and Docker Swarm plus a container registry for the full testbed · Python 2 (controller); Go 1.8/1.9 GOPATH-era builds (golang:1.8/1.9 images); authors used Docker 18.03 on Ubuntu 17.10 · Linux x86-64 in Docker Swarm (repo ships linux_amd64 prebuilt Go archives and a 9.6 MB appserver binary); other platforms not documented

**Vs siblings:** S3-FIFO, SIEVE, LHD, AdaptSize and Hyperbolic Caching improve one cache's eviction or admission, and Pelikan/Segcache, Garnet and Dragonfly are faster cache servers. RobinHood leaves the cache alone and decides how much memory each backend's partition gets so that request P99 drops across a fan-out. Pick its approach when the tail comes from whichever backend is overloaded right now, not from cache speed or overall hit ratio; it can run on top of any resizable cache, including one of those.

**Gotchas:**
- The algorithm named "robinhood" in controller.py is a simple latency-sort heuristic (even split, double share to the highest-P99 backend), not the paper's algorithm. The RBC-proportional policies are the crit_path* variants: crit_path_window uses the paper's P98.5-P99.5 window, but the shipped example config selects crit_path (P99-P100) with a 1 s interval instead of 5 s.
- Only a 2-backend example config and a small trace are published. The 20-backend configs and traces behind the paper are not (issue #4, unanswered), the simulator was never released (issue #3), and the Cliffhgr++/FAIR++/LAMA++ baselines are not labelled in the repo (issue #2, unanswered).
- The controller disables memcached slab automove and shrinks partitions by randomly reassigning slab pages. memcached does not free pages immediately (multi-MB memory bursts, paper Sec. 5.6), and shrinking blocks some concurrent cache operations.
- Each partition keeps a 30 MB floor and moves in 1 MB steps. The stats server keeps a fixed 10M-entry ring of queries plus requests (the paper says the last 1M requests) and copies and sorts all of it every 3 s.

**Status:** Abandoned research testbed (last commit 2019-07-08, 53 commits, three open issues with no author reply), BSD-3-Clause; the core idea sits in ~600 lines of Python 2 that are easier to port than to run, because the full testbed needs Docker Swarm, a registry and dozens of VMs.

[repo](https://github.com/dasebe/robinhoodcache) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi18-berger.pdf)

##### S3-FIFO  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

SOSP'23 three-FIFO-queue eviction policy: lower miss ratios than LRU, and over 6x CacheLib LRU's throughput at 16 threads.

**Beats:** LRU (Meta CacheLib's optimized LRU; also CacheLib's optimized 2Q and TinyLFU, plus Segcache) — Throughput was measured with the authors' S3-FIFO container in a 2023 CacheLib fork (linked lists for S and M, hash table for the ghost). It replayed a synthetic Zipf(1.0) trace of 100·n million requests over n million 4 KB objects in a closed loop, filling misses from pre-generated values. On CloudLab c6420 nodes (two 16-core Xeon Gold 6142 at 2.6 GHz per CloudLab's docs; turbo off, threads pinned, memory bound to one NUMA node) it exceeded 6x the throughput of CacheLib's optimized LRU at 16 threads, at LRU miss ratios of both 0.02 and 0.21. The build was RelWithDebInfo; the compiler is not named. Miss ratios come from libCacheSim simulation over 6594 traces, ignoring object size, against the lab's own reimplementations of the baselines (for example, W-TinyLFU without a doorkeeper or hill climbing). There S3-FIFO had the best mean on 10 of 14 datasets at a cache of 10% of the footprint and on 7 of 14 at 0.1%.

**Known shortcoming:** The >6x throughput over CacheLib's optimized LRU at 16 threads comes from a synthetic Zipf 1.0 run only (not the CDN/Twitter/Meta traces); CloudLab c6420 with the CPU unnamed; benchmark code is Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23 (RelWithDebInfo). The paper evaluates 6594 traces from 14 datasets (the record's '1559' was wrong).

**Known shortcoming:** Algorithm only: the libCacheSim code is a simulator that stores no values, and the CacheLib prototype is a fork stale since 2023-12 that was never upstreamed. The paper's 6x prototype differs from the paper's algorithm (5% small queue, one access bit, ghost sized to half the object count). libCacheSim's 's3fifo' changed in 2024-10; the paper's numbers correspond to 's3fifov0'.

**Known shortcoming:** Loses on loop/block traces (DS1, S3), where the author concedes W-TinyLFU is better. Otter's lock-free S3-FIFO design lost to BP-Wrapper caches and Otter v2 dropped S3-FIFO; the s3fifo.com adoption list is stale. libCacheSim never caches objects >=10% of the cache; worst-case eviction is O(n).

**How:** The algorithm rests on 'quick demotion'. Across 6594 production traces, a median 72% of objects in a window holding 10% of the trace's objects are one-hit wonders, so new objects go into a small FIFO S that takes 10% of the space. When an object reaches the tail of S, it moves to the main FIFO M if it was hit (threshold 2 in libCacheSim); otherwise it is evicted and its id goes into a ghost FIFO G, and a later miss that finds the id in G inserts straight into M. M works like CLOCK/FIFO-reinsertion with a 2-bit counter capped at 3. A cache hit only increments that counter atomically, so it moves no list node and takes no lock, whereas LRU promotion serializes on a lock. Insertion and eviction are queue-tail operations that can be done lock-free. The CacheLib prototype uses atomic doubly-linked lists and an atomic FIFO hash table for the ghost, which the paper says can hold 4-byte fingerprints.

**Use it when:**
- Web, key-value and CDN object caches with skewed (Zipf-like) popularity and many one-hit wonders. At a cache size of 10% of the footprint, the paper finds S3-FIFO best by mean miss ratio on 10 of 14 datasets, and the author says it suits web workloads best.
- Read-heavy, many-core in-memory caches where LRU's promote-on-hit lock is the bottleneck. A hit writes only a 2-bit counter, and the CacheLib prototype beat CacheLib's optimized LRU by more than 6x at 16 threads.
- Flash caches that need an admission filter: keep S and the ghost in DRAM and write only objects hit twice to a FIFO flash tier. On the Wikimedia and Tencent Photo CDN traces this gave both fewer flash writes and a lower miss ratio than probabilistic admission or Flashield, even with DRAM at 0.1% of the cache size.
- Replacing LRU in a slab-based cache when you want one static knob. Per the paper, miss ratios change little for most traces with S anywhere from 5% to 20% of the cache.
- Evaluating candidate policies on your own traces first: libCacheSim runs s3fifo next to about 30 other policies (LRU, ARC, LIRS, W-TinyLFU, SIEVE...) in one command.

**Skip it when:**
- Database, search, analytics or old block workloads with loops or large scans. On the ARC DS1 and S3 traces, the author concedes that W-TinyLFU beats S3-FIFO. The Otter maintainer measured a 'quite serious' loss on DS1, and Caffeine's author calls its results across broader workloads 'great, good, bad, awful'.
- Workloads where most objects are requested exactly twice, with the second request arriving after the object has left S. The paper names this as its adversarial pattern: the second request becomes a miss, which matters most for small caches (thousands of objects).
- When you need a ready library from the authors. libCacheSim's version is simulation-only (ids and sizes, no values, glib dependency), and the CacheLib prototype is a research fork last pushed in December 2023. Upstream facebook/CacheLib ships no S3-FIFO container.
- When multi-core speed is the main goal of a general-purpose library. Otter's author found that the paper's lock-free-queue design lost to BP-Wrapper caches (Ristretto, Theine) and rewrote Otter around BP-Wrapper. Otter v2.0.0 (June 2025) then replaced S3-FIFO with adaptive W-TinyLFU, and Caffeine's author reports close to 1B reads/s at 16 threads with a W-TinyLFU design.
- Variable-size objects without slab classes: the paper's evaluation ignored object size. A ring-buffer implementation also wastes space under delete-heavy workloads, because deleted slots are not reused until eviction (paper, Sec. 4.2).

**Integration:** source-drop (an algorithm; the reference C module is compiled into libCacheSim's CMake library and cachesim binary, and the CacheLib prototype is a templated MM container header inside a CacheLib fork) · libCacheSim: glib-2.0, argp, Threads, zstd (on by default for compressed traces), optional tcmalloc. CacheLib prototype: CacheLib's full stack, including folly (MPMCQueue, DistributedMutex). · libCacheSim: CMake 3.12+, a C compiler plus C++17 for its C++ parts, Ninja recommended, Release build by default. CacheLib prototype: CacheLib's contrib/build.sh toolchain, built RelWithDebInfo with Ninja; compiler not stated. · libCacheSim CI runs on ubuntu-latest and macos-latest (clang); Windows not documented. The algorithm itself is portable C. The prototype's build.sh uses apt, so Debian/Ubuntu.

**Vs siblings:** Pick S3-FIFO over SIEVE (same repo, one queue) when the workload has scans or block-style access: its small queue plus ghost gives scan resistance, which the S3-FIFO paper says SIEVE lacks. Pick it over Caffeine or the W-TinyLFU C++ port when building a web/CDN/KV cache that needs lock-free hits and a single static knob, but keep adaptive W-TinyLFU for mixed database and analytics workloads, where S3-FIFO loses on loop-heavy traces such as DS1.

**Gotchas:**
- Two versions exist. libCacheSim's 's3fifo' changed in October 2024 to insert new objects into M once S fills, before the first eviction. The SOSP'23 numbers come from the original, now 's3fifov0' (S3FIFOv0.c), so use that name to reproduce the paper.
- Implementations differ from the paper. Algorithm 1 uses a 10% S, a 2-bit counter, promotion when freq > 1, and a ghost as large as M. libCacheSim sizes the ghost in bytes (0.9x cache size). The CacheLib prototype behind the 6x number uses a 5% S (pRatio_ = 0.05) and a single accessed bit, and sizes the ghost to half the object count at first eviction. Otter traced its hit-ratio jumps to ghost sizing.
- libCacheSim will not cache an object whose size is at least the small queue's size (10% of cache bytes): insert returns NULL and can_insert returns false. Tiny caches or very large objects silently get no caching.
- Evicting from M reinserts every tail object with a nonzero counter until it finds one at zero, so an eviction can walk a long run of recently hit objects (worst case O(n); counters capped at 3). Otter v1 advertised an O(1) worst case as a change from the paper's O(n).

**Status:** libCacheSim is actively maintained (Apache-2.0, 347 stars, pushed 2026-09-26), but it is a simulator, so production use means porting the roughly 500-line policy or adopting a third-party implementation such as quick_cache or TinyUFO. The CacheLib prototype fork has not been updated since December 2023 and never reached upstream, and s3fifo.com's adoption list still names Otter, which dropped S3-FIFO in v2.

[repo](https://github.com/1a1a11a/libCacheSim) · [benchmark](https://junchengyang.com/publication/sosp23-s3fifo.pdf)

##### SIEVE  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Parameter-free FIFO-plus-moving-hand eviction policy that beats LRU on miss ratio and multi-thread throughput for web caches.

**Beats:** LRU — Throughput: a CacheLib-based C++ prototype (Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23) ran on a CloudLab c6420 (dual Xeon Gold 6142 @ 2.6 GHz, 384 GB DDR4, turbo off, threads pinned to one NUMA node; compiler and flags not stated). It replayed Meta and Twitter KV traces with a cache of 4 GB × threads (miss ratios 7% and 2%), and SIEVE beat CacheLib's optimized LRU by 16% (TwoQ by 17%) at 1 thread and more than 2x at 16 threads on the Meta trace. Miss ratio was measured separately in the libCacheSim simulator over 1559 traces: a mean 21% lower than FIFO on CDN1 at the large cache size, and up to 63.2% (mean 1.5%) lower than ARC.

**Known shortcoming:** The '>2x LRU throughput at 16 threads' compares with an unoptimized LRU (optimized CacheLib LRU scales 6x to 16 threads); SIEVE's >2x holds only on the Meta trace (125% per the paper) and it is 16% faster at 1 thread. Its miss-ratio edge over ARC (1.5% mean) is smaller than ARC's over LRU. Throughput came from a CacheLib prototype (Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23), not libCacheSim; no compiler/flags (verifier downgrade).

**Known shortcoming:** libCacheSim is a simulator only (stores no values). SIEVE is not scan-resistant (paper section 7) and on block/page workloads is sometimes worse than LRU. At tiny caches (0.1%) TwoQ/LHD win; LRB wins byte miss ratio at 1-2% cache; bigger miss spike than LRU/ARC on popularity shift.

**Known shortcoming:** The CacheLib prototype is a research fork, stale since 2023-12, with abort()/printf paths; the head-insert race is fixed only in AtomicDList, SieveList still inserts lock-free; not in upstream CacheLib. Compiler/flags unstated; the >2x at 16 threads is on the Meta trace only. Third-party ports vary (the kassane C++ port copies a shared_ptr on every get, sets the global pmr default resource and has no lock).

**How:** A hit only sets the object's visited bit. Nothing moves in the queue, so the hit path takes no list lock. In the CacheLib prototype a hit is a flag write, inserts use a CAS on the list head, and only eviction and removal take a folly::DistributedMutex. On a miss the hand walks from the tail toward the head, clearing visited bits and evicting the first unvisited object; objects that survive keep their position instead of being reinserted at the head as in CLOCK/FIFO-Reinsertion. The paper calls the result 'lazy promotion' plus 'quick demotion': new objects sit between the head and the hand and get examined soon after insertion, so one-hit wonders leave quickly, and in the simulator SIEVE ran up to 40% fewer instructions per request than LRU.

**Use it when:**
- Object, CDN or key-value caches with skewed (Zipf/power-law) popularity and few scans. This is the paper's domain: 1559 traces from Twitter, Meta, Wikimedia, Tencent and two CDNs, where SIEVE had the lowest miss ratio of 10 algorithms on more than 45% of traces.
- Swapping out a doubly-linked-list LRU in an in-process cache when you want no tuning parameters and a change of about 20 lines (12-21 lines in the paper's four library ports).
- Multi-threaded caches where LRU's move-to-head on every hit causes lock contention. The CacheLib prototype was 16% faster than CacheLib's optimized LRU at 1 thread and more than 2x faster at 16 threads on the Meta KV trace.
- Mid-to-large caches, around 10% of the trace footprint, where the gains are largest: a mean 21% lower miss ratio than FIFO on the CDN1 dataset, against 15% for CLOCK.
- As a building block that replaces the LRU queue inside ARC, TwoQ or LeCaR. ARC-SIEVE cut ARC's miss ratio by a mean of 3.7% (up to 62.5%) over the 1559 traces.

**Skip it when:**
- Block, page or file caches with scans or loops, such as database buffer pools or backup reads. The paper's §7 says SIEVE is not scan-resistant (it has no ghost queue) and sometimes has a higher miss ratio than LRU on block workloads. A co-author wrote on HN that when the hand sits near the head it evicts new objects in an MRU-like way and 'may not be robust'.
- Very small caches (0.1% of footprint): TwoQ and LHD sometimes beat it because new objects are evicted before they can show popularity. On two Wiki CDN traces, LRB beat it on byte miss ratio at 1-2% cache sizes.
- Workloads whose popular set changes abruptly. When the paper switched between two Zipf workloads, SIEVE had a larger transient miss-ratio spike than LRU or ARC because the hand has to travel back to the tail before old objects can go.
- When you need a ready-made C/C++ cache library. libCacheSim is a simulator, the CacheLib prototype is a research fork last pushed in December 2023, and SIEVE is not in upstream facebook/CacheLib (its tree has no MMSieve).
- Ring-buffer or log-structured stores. SIEVE evicts from the middle of the queue, so it needs a linked list (17 B of per-object metadata in the paper's Table 3), and a co-author called circular-buffer or log-structured implementations 'not trivial'.

**Integration:** source-drop (the algorithm). In the catalogued repo, Sieve.c is one policy inside libCacheSim, a CMake/Ninja-built C library and cachesim binary, and it holds no values. The CacheLib prototype is a full CacheLib fork. Third-party ports include kassane/sieve-cache-cpp (header-only, C++17, MIT). · The algorithm has none. libCacheSim needs glib-2.0 and zstd (zstd trace support is on by default); tcmalloc is optional. The CacheLib prototype needs CacheLib's full dependency set (folly, etc.), installed through contrib/build.sh. · libCacheSim: CMake 3.12+ with CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17 for its C++ parts; the minimum C standard and compiler versions are not documented. CacheLib prototype: CacheLib's 2023 build script, tested on CentOS 8, Ubuntu 18.04 and Debian 10. kassane/sieve-cache-cpp: C++17 (uses std::pmr). · The algorithm runs anywhere. libCacheSim documents installation on Ubuntu and macOS; the Node binding ships a prebuilt binary for Linux x64 only; Windows is not documented. The throughput results were measured on x86-64 (Xeon Gold 6142).

**Vs siblings:** Pick SIEVE over LHD or W-TinyLFU/Caffeine when you are patching an existing C/C++ linked-list LRU for web or KV traffic and want a parameter-free change of about 20 lines with a lock-free hit path. LHD has tuning parameters and far more code (192/81/64 lines for hit/evict/insert against SIEVE's 4/9/3) but wins at very small caches. Caffeine is a complete concurrent JVM library, and W-TinyLFU is the safer choice when scans or an unknown workload mix are likely.

**Gotchas:**
- Because eviction happens in the middle of the queue, deleting an object the hand points at must move the hand to its neighbour (libCacheSim's Sieve_remove_obj sets hand = prev). Ports that skip this leave a dangling hand. Eviction is also worst-case O(N) when most objects have their visited bit set.
- The CacheLib prototype is research-grade code. SieveList::getEvictionCandidate printf's and abort()s after more than two full sweeps, and unlink() calls try_lock() then abort() as its lock-held check. A null-tail race between lock-free linkAtHead and unlink was reported and fixed only in the sibling AtomicDList (PR #1, Dec 2023); SieveList still inserts at the head lock-free.
- Third-party ports vary in quality. kassane/sieve-cache-cpp's get() allocates and returns a shared_ptr copy of the value on every hit, its constructor calls std::pmr::set_default_resource (a process-wide side effect), and it has no mutex.
- Most of the headline miss-ratio results ignore object size (the paper assumes slab-style caches). Byte miss ratio is shown only for the CDN traces, and the paper's mean ARC-over-LRU reduction appears as both 6.7% and 6.3%.

**Status:** libCacheSim is actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-26, Apache-2.0, 347 stars), but Sieve.c has had only cosmetic edits since January 2024, and the CacheLib throughput prototype (Apache-2.0, 11 stars) has not been pushed since 2023-12-13. The algorithm is small enough to copy into your own cache, which is how the listed adopters (TiDB, Ceph, DragonFly, PostgREST, DNSCrypt-proxy, Immudb and others) use it.

[repo](https://github.com/1a1a11a/libCacheSim) · [benchmark](https://junchengyang.com/publication/nsdi24-SIEVE.pdf)

#### columnar-analytics

##### ALP (Adaptive Lossless Floating-Point Compression)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Reference C++ primitives for ALP, a lossless double/float column encoding that decodes 17-66x faster than Zstd, Gorilla, Chimp and Patas.

**Beats:** Zstd, Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128, Patas (existing lightweight and general-purpose floating-point compressors) — In the authors' SIGMOD 2024 micro-benchmark (Ice Lake Xeon 8375C on AWS i4i.4xlarge, clang -O3, one L1-resident 1,024-value vector timed 300K times, Zstd level 3 given about 1 MB), ALP averaged 0.487 values/cycle compressing and 2.609 decompressing: 8-251x faster compression and 7-66x faster decompression than Zstd (0.035/0.101), Gorilla (0.052/0.047), Chimp (0.042/0.039), Patas (0.060/0.157) and PDE (0.002/0.387), at 21.7 bits/value against Zstd's 20.6 (ratios computed from a size formula, not written bytes). Inside DuckDB 0.10 the gain shrank to 2-4x faster decompression than Patas, and a query over ALP data (0.020 s) was still slower than over uncompressed data (0.012 s).

**Known shortcoming:** Zstd compresses slightly better (20.6 vs 21.7 bits/value); the 14x/26x vs Zstd and 55x decode vs Gorilla are from Table 5 on a Xeon 8375C; clang-only build.

**Known shortcoming:** Primitives only: no byte-level API, stream format, spec or releases (compressor.hpp was deleted in 2024-09). The library ships only the scalar kernels; the SIMD kernels live in publication/ and fail to link from the library. CMake is Clang-only, needs clang-tidy on Linux and exports -march=native/-mavx512dq publicly, so binaries are not portable.

**Known shortcoming:** Loses on POI lat/lon (ALP_rd) and many-repeat columns (NYC/29 40.4 vs 20.5 bits/value). In DuckDB 0.10 it was only 2-4x faster than Patas and an ALP query took 0.020 s vs 0.012 s uncompressed. Zen 4 VPCOMPRESSPD slowdown open (#45); an encoder race was fixed only in 2025-10; an unchecked int64 cast is UB (as in duckdb#24634).

**How:** Most real-world doubles began as decimals. ALP multiplies each value by 10^e and 10^-f and rounds with the branch-free magic-number add/subtract trick (2^52+2^51 for double). It keeps the integer only if decoding reproduces the exact bits; values that fail are stored as exceptions and patched in afterwards. The int64s are frame-of-reference bit-packed in FastLanes' interleaved layout and decoded by a generated, branch-free, auto-vectorized kernel per bit width that fuses unpacking with the multiply (a median 40% gain from fusing in the paper). A two-level sample keeps the (e,f) search off the hot path: 8 vectors × 32 values per 102,400-value row group shortlist at most 5 pairs, and each vector tries only those, stopping after two worse ones; non-decimal data switches to ALP_rd, which dictionary-encodes the top 1-16 bits of each value into at most 8 entries and bit-packs the rest.

**Use it when:**
- You are building a columnar format, database or time-series store and need a float codec whose unit is one 1,024-value vector, so scans can skip or decode single vectors. Zstd, by contrast, must decompress a whole block. The paper's example is 32 vectors of 8 KB inside a 256 KB block.
- Doubles that originate as fixed- or low-precision decimals, such as prices, sensor readings, temperatures and stock ticks. Examples: City-Temp takes 10.7 bits/value against 16.2 for Zstd and 59.7 for Gorilla. Averaged over the 13 time-series datasets, ALP takes 16.4 bits/value against 17.2 for Zstd.
- Scan- or aggregate-heavy analytics where decode CPU dominates. In the authors' Tectorwise run on City-Temp (Ice Lake), single-threaded SCAN over ALP ran at 1.337 tuples/cycle against 0.565 uncompressed and 0.044 for Zstd, and SUM at 0.233 against 0.197 uncompressed.
- Replacing Gorilla, Chimp, Chimp128 or Patas in an existing lightweight float slot. ALP beat Chimp128 and PDE on compression ratio on 27 of 30 datasets and is faster in both directions. DuckDB made exactly this swap in v0.10.
- Mixed hardware fleets: the decoder is plain C++ that auto-vectorizes. The paper measured it on Ice Lake (AVX-512), Zen3 (AVX2), Apple M1 and Graviton2/3 (NEON), and Ice Lake was fastest.

**Skip it when:**
- You want a compress(buf)/decompress(buf) library like zstd. There is no container or stream format, no bitstream specification (issue #32, left to contributors), and no tags or releases (issue #43). Use FastLanes, or an engine that already ships ALP: DuckDB picks it automatically for FLOAT/DOUBLE at checkpoint since 0.10, and ClickHouse has it as a beta codec behind enable_alp_codec since 26.9.
- High-precision 'real' doubles with no decimal structure, such as radians, simulation output or ML values. POI-lat and POI-lon fall back to ALP_rd at 55.5 and 56.4 bits/value (about 1.15x), worse than Zstd's 48.1 and 53.1. ALP_rd is also about 3x slower to compress and 4x slower to decompress than regular ALP.
- Columns full of exact repeats. On CMS/1, Medicare/1 and NYC/29 ALP needs 35.7, 39.4 and 40.4 bits/value, against 24.5, 28.7 and 20.5 for Zstd and 28.2, 32.3 and 28.7 for Chimp128. You need your own dictionary or RLE stage in front; the paper's cascade reaches 33.1, 35.7 and 24.7.
- Cold storage where ratio beats speed. Across all 30 datasets Zstd level 3 averages 20.6 bits/value against 21.7 for ALP alone. ALP only wins (18.8) when cascaded with dictionary or RLE, which this repo does not provide.
- float16, bfloat16 or fp8 data, or GPU decoding. Reduced-precision types are unsupported (issue #38), and the GPU kernel PR #23 has been open and WIP since October 2024.
