**Known shortcoming:** Unimplemented pandas methods fall back by squashing the whole frame to one chunk on one worker (OOM at TB scale). Not a Dask drop-in (no dd.*, .compute(), map_partitions), though ~96.7% pandas-compatible. Stale: last release 0.8.2 (2024-12), last main commit 2025-04, 84 open issues including correctness bugs (#691 reset_index, #671 head), no Python 3.13 wheels. First-party paper with no CPU model, compared only with pandas-API frameworks (never DuckDB/Polars), and TPC-H ratios skip queries where baselines failed.

**How:** Data is split into chunks that plain pandas/NumPy runs in separate worker processes, so there is no GIL, and intermediate results go to a shared-memory storage service (disk, mmap or Vineyard backends are optional). The core idea is dynamic (iterative) tiling: Xorbits executes the first chunks, collects their real shapes, sizes and dtypes, and only then tiles the rest of the graph. That lets it choose tree-reduce or shuffle-reduce for groupby.agg, merge small chunks up to chunk_store_limit (512 MB by default), and handle skewed joins that Dask and Modin partition blindly. It adds coloring-based graph-level fusion of the chunk graph into subtasks, operator fusion through NumExpr/JAX/CuPy, column pruning, and breadth-first plus locality-aware scheduling onto NUMA-node or GPU 'bands'. The paper's ablation credits dynamic tiling with 7.08x (TPC-H Q2, SF1000) and 10.59x (Q7, SF100), and graph fusion with 3.80x (Q7) and 2.04x (Q8).

**Use it when:**
- Existing pandas code on 100 GB-1 TB Parquet/CSV that no longer fits one node, when you want to keep the pandas API rather than rewrite into Spark SQL or Dask idioms.
- Merges between a huge fact table and a tiny dimension table (skewed keys). There Dask and Modin stall on one core; the paper measured 29x and 37x on TPCx-AI UC10 (34 GB joined to 3.2 MB).
- Single-node multi-core speedup on 20 GB-class CSV feature-engineering pipelines. The paper reports 2.65x over Modin on census and 3.86x over PySpark on plasticc, with single-threaded pandas slowest.
- Mixed dataframe and distributed-array work (QR, linear regression) where you would otherwise pair Dask DataFrame with Dask Array. The paper reports 5.88x and 1.74x average throughput over Dask Array.
- Teams already running Kubernetes, SLURM or a plain supervisor/worker cluster (the xorbits-supervisor and xorbits-worker CLIs) that want a pandas-shaped front end.

**Skip it when:**
- Data that fits comfortably in one machine's RAM when raw speed is the goal. The paper compares only against pandas-API frameworks, never DuckDB, Polars or SQL engines, and it calls pandas-API TPC-H 'fundamentally unfair' against SQL systems.
- Small or interactive workloads. Startup is slow (the docs say to call xorbits.init() before timing), and too many chunks make the supervisor spend its time scheduling.
- Anything that needs an actively maintained dependency. The last release was 0.8.2 (2024-12-26) and the last main commit 2025-04-21. There are 84 open issues, including open correctness bugs (#691 reset_index on unexecuted groupby output, #671 head(100) wrong on TPC-H Q18 output).
- Python 3.13+: PyPI has wheels only for CPython 3.9-3.12.
- GPU (cuDF/CuPy) production use. Many GPU-labelled bugs are still open, such as nunique failing on GPU (#344), cuDF NA deserialization errors (#406) and CUDA memory not being released on shutdown (#377).

**Integration:** module · xoscar (actor runtime), numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, pyarrow, fsspec, cloudpickle, pyyaml, psutil, tornado, sqlalchemy, defusedxml, tqdm, uvloop (non-Windows). Optional: ray, kubernetes, vineyard, jax, numexpr/lz4, s3fs, adlfs, datasets. · Python >=3.9. PyPI 0.8.2 wheels cover CPython 3.9-3.12, and building from source needs Cython >=0.29.33. setup.cfg declares pandas >=1.0, but CI carries a TODO that pandas 2.2.3 does not work well with numpy 2.2 / pyarrow 19. · Wheels for Linux x86-64/aarch64 (manylinux2014), macOS x86-64/arm64 and Windows amd64. Cluster deployment is via CLI, Kubernetes (including EKS) or SLURM. Optional NVIDIA GPU through cuDF/CuPy (gpu=True on loaders).

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Modin when data exceeds one node or merges are skewed: in the paper Modin on Ray OOMed on SF1000 and was 37x slower on skewed UC10, even though both reach 96.7% pandas-API coverage. FireDucks and cuDF (cudf.pandas) are single-machine pandas accelerators with much larger speedups over pandas, so Xorbits is only the right choice when you need multi-node scale-out behind the pandas API.

**Gotchas:**
- Silent-scale fallback: any pandas method Xorbits has not implemented is emitted as a RuntimeWarning '<Type>.<method> will fallback to Pandas'. It then runs after rechunking the whole object into one chunk (core/adapter.py), so a single worker must hold the full frame. On 1 TB data that means OOM.
- Deferred execution plus iterative tiling means a statement can trigger partial execution mid-plan whenever metadata such as a post-filter shape is unknown. Errors and cost appear later than they would in pandas. Call xorbits.run() to force evaluation, and warm up with xorbits.init() before benchmarking.
- Performance depends on chunk_store_limit (512 MB by default). The docs say raising it helps little on CPU but should be raised on GPU. chunk_size= on constructors is meant for debugging.
- Open operational bugs include 'Too many open files' (#769, #731), gzip read_csv using only one core (#738), and read_parquet memory-allocation errors (#729).

**Status:** Stale: last release 0.8.2 in December 2024, last main commit April 2025 (cuDF 25.2 compat), later pushes are dependabot branches only. It is Apache-2.0 and pip-installable with prebuilt wheels, but the large Mars-derived codebase is not something you can realistically vendor or maintain yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/xorbitsai/xorbits) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.00865)

#### embedded-kv

##### PsiTri (arbtrie)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

C++20 embedded transactional KV store (radix trie, node-level COW) with a RocksDB-API shim; 1.6-3x RocksDB on bank transfers.

**Beats:** RocksDB — The project's own TPC-B-style bank benchmark counts 5 KV ops per atomic transfer, uses triangular skew and runs with sync=none. At batch=1 on an 8-core AMD EPYC-Turin Vultr VM (Clang 20, -O3 -flto -march=native), the RocksDB-API shim PsiTriRocks wrote 2.3x as many transfers/s as RocksDB (369K vs 158K), and its concurrent reader did 4.9x as many reads/s (1.42M vs 290K). At batch=100, native PsiTri was about 2.98x RocksDB 9.9.3 on an Apple M5 Max (Clang 17, -O3 -flto=thin) but only about 1.57x on the EPYC VM, where MDBX (239K) and TidesDB (167K) beat it (164K).

**Known shortcoming:** Workload is TPC-B (not TATP); the 2.3x/4.9x come from a separate batch=1 run and the 4.9x is reader throughput under a concurrent writer, with sync=none. TidesDB and MDBX beat it on EPYC.

**Known shortcoming:** All benchmarks run with sync=none, and the RocksDB shim ignores WriteOptions::sync and use_fsync, so unflushed WAL is lost on crash. The shim's WriteBatch drops the column family (writes go to the default root), OpenForReadOnly opens read-write, Merge is treated as Put, and Bloom/compression/stats options are ignored; source-compatible only, cannot open RocksDB data.

**Known shortcoming:** Files are 2-4x live data (1,088 vs 320 MB); loses bulk load to RocksDB; MDBX beats it on EPYC and on scans. CMake says clang only (README says GCC 12+), -march=native by default, no Windows, CI Ubuntu only. Pre-1.0, 4 stars, no independent replication; snapshots shrink fan-out; recovery time grows with DB size.

**How:** The index is an adaptive radix trie crossed with a B-tree. Inner nodes route on 1-byte dividers found with a SIMD lower_bound (NEON, SSE2/SSSE3 or AVX-512, chosen at compile time), and leaves are sorted ~2 KB nodes with hash-accelerated lookup. Copy-on-write happens per node in 64-byte multiples instead of 4 KB pages. Every object is reached through a 32-bit ID in a control-block table, so the segment allocator (SAL) can move an object with a memcpy plus one CAS, while writers bump-allocate in private 32 MB segments. The DWAL write path puts commits into a writer-private in-memory ART buffer plus a buffered WAL append with no fsync. Two background merge threads then drain 100K-entry batches into the COW trie, so there is no LSM compaction and readers get lock-free MVCC snapshots.

**Use it when:**
- Small read-modify-write transactions (ledger or balance updates, blockchain or game state) that touch a few keys atomically, where durability via a periodic flush is acceptable instead of an fsync per commit.
- One writer plus concurrent point readers that need consistent snapshots. In the bank runs, native PsiTri's write throughput did not drop with a reader attached (+1.5% on M5 Max, +10.7% on EPYC).
- A RocksDB app that only uses Put/Get/Delete/WriteBatch/iterators/snapshots on the default column family and wants to try another engine by relinking.
- Workloads that count or delete key ranges often, or that store hierarchical data (nested subtrees, O(1) snapshot of a subtree).
- Linux or macOS on x86-64 or ARM64 with a dataset up to about 2x RAM. The scale benchmark held >300K inserts/s and >11M reads/s (12 threads) up to that point.

**Skip it when:**
- You need durability on every commit. All published benchmarks use sync=none, and unflushed DWAL WAL entries are lost on crash. PsiTriRocks ignores WriteOptions::sync and Options::use_fsync; only Flush() syncs the WAL.
- Disk space is tight. Data is never compressed, and files run 2-4x the live data under sustained writes: 1,088 MB for PsiTri vs 320 MB for RocksDB in the M5 bank run, and 76.7 GB vs 51.5 GB at 200M random upserts.
- Your code depends on RocksDB merge operators, bloom filters, block cache, compression, statistics or compaction tuning. PsiTriRocks accepts these silently and ignores them, and Merge behaves as Put.
- Scan-heavy or bulk-load-heavy work. MDBX scanned 2-4x faster in the bank runs, and RocksDB bulk-loaded faster than PsiTriRocks on both machines (1.96M vs 1.80M and 1.16M vs 0.96M ops/s).
- You need a proven production engine. It is pre-1.0 (the authors say the API may change and it is not battle-tested), has 4 stars and no independent replication, and native PsiTri lost to MDBX on the x86 VM (164K vs 239K transfers/s). Writes to the same root are serialized by a mutex.

**Integration:** static lib · Threads plus in-repo libraries (sal, ucc, art, hash, bundled xxhash). A standalone build also requires Boost.program_options, Catch2 3 (tests are on by default) and fetches abseil via CMake FetchContent; PsiTriRocks links absl::btree privately. The SQLite and DuckDB layers are optional. · C++20 and CMake 3.16+. The README says Clang 15+ or GCC 12+, but the top-level CMakeLists states that LLVM clang is required and GCC is not supported, and on macOS it hard-codes Homebrew LLVM's clang++. The benchmarks used Clang 17 and Clang 20. · Linux and macOS (POSIX mmap/mlock; no Windows code path found). Runs on x86-64 (SSE2/SSSE3/AVX-512 paths) and ARM64 (NEON), with scalar fallbacks. -march=native is on by default, so binaries are not portable unless you turn it off. CI runs on Ubuntu only.

**Vs siblings:** Pick PsiTri over SplinterDB, KVell or F2 when the workload is small multi-key atomic transactions with concurrent readers that need snapshots. Those siblings' catalogued wins measure raw insert or lookup throughput, while PsiTri's evidence is on transactions. If you rely on merge operators, compression or bloom filters, or need to reopen existing RocksDB data, prefer an engine that keeps RocksDB's feature set and format, because PsiTriRocks drops them.

**Gotchas:**
- In PsiTriRocks, WriteBatch drops the column-family argument (Put(cf, k, v) forwards to Put(k, v)), and DB::Write always writes to root 0, so column-family writes made through a batch land in the default column family.
- OpenForReadOnly just calls Open, which opens the database read-write. Flush() and CompactRange() are accepted but only sync the WAL or do nothing; to reclaim disk space you must call compact_and_truncate (the psitri.compact_and_truncate property through the shim).
- Long-lived snapshots compete with live nodes for cacheline slots, and inner-node fan-out can drop from 256 to as low as 16 until they are released. Recovery after a crash scans the whole database, which the docs estimate at minutes for a 100 GB database.
- Write sessions are heavy (32 MB buffer each, backed by thread_local storage). Do not create them per request or pass them between threads. DWAL merges also stall: in the 200M-key random-upsert run the minimum round throughput was 24,791 ops/s, vs 85,161 for RocksDB.

**Status:** The project is actively developed but pre-1.0: the last main commit (2026-04-28) was one of a burst of MVCC and recovery fixes, the repo has 4 stars and is still named arbtrie, and it is MIT-licensed and installable as a CMake static library, though the authors warn the API may change and it has no production track record.

[repo](https://github.com/gofractally/arbtrie) · [benchmark](https://gofractally.github.io/arbtrie/benchmarks/bank/)

##### TurboKV  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Async (Tokio) Rust LSM key-value store whose unsynced-WAL mode acknowledges single-caller writes 2-4x faster than fjall 2.11.

**Beats:** fjall (the page's like-for-like peer); redb shown only as architectural context — The author's harness pits TurboKV 0.6.0 durable (unsynced mmap WAL) against fjall 2.11.2 PersistMode::Buffer. Setup: one caller, 200,000 x 20-byte keys / 400-byte values (84 MB), compression and block cache off, rustc 1.88.0 at opt-level 3 with thin LTO, Apple M4 / macOS 15.3.2 / APFS, 3 repetitions. The README table shows median write-acknowledgement throughput of 3.7x (sequential fill), 2.0x (random fill), 2.1x (overwrite), 4.5x (100-key batches) and 4.2x (1,000-key batches) over fjall. But the TurboKV column comes from a later separate run: within the single shared run the ratios are 1.8-4.4x, and counting forced flush and compaction ('settled' throughput) they shrink to about 1.1-1.6x.

**Known shortcoming:** The ~27x headline compares TurboKV's Fast mode with redb and is not like-for-like; against fjall at matched durability the gain is ~2-4.5x, and Paranoid mode loses to redb at 1/100 keys.

**Known shortcoming:** The default durable() mode does not fsync per write (recent acknowledged writes can be lost on power loss); paranoid() manages ~210 ops/s for a single caller, below redb Eventual (1,397). README fjall ratios mix two runs (same run 1.8-4.4x; ~1.1-1.6x counting flush and compaction); tested only against fjall 2.11.2 with 84 MB of data on a 32 GiB box (no RocksDB/LMDB/sled, nothing larger than RAM). redb is faster on reads (246k vs 183k); reopen ~1 s vs ~0.1 s; disk amplification 2.14x vs fjall 1.43x. Build fails without AES RUSTFLAGS (gxhash); needs Tokio; pre-1.0, one maintainer, agent-driven PRs.

**How:** In durable mode, each record goes into a WAL segment that is physically preallocated (fallocate on Linux, F_PREALLOCATE on macOS) and shared-memory-mapped, with a record CRC and a commit tag written last. So an acknowledgement is a memcpy into the page cache, not a write(2) or fsync. Encoding uses a thread-local buffer, and a coarse cached clock stamps WAL records; the changelog measures that clock at 599,648 vs 541,401 ops/s for sequential writes. The memtable is a lock-free crossbeam skip list guarded by 65,536 striped per-key mutexes, and fast mode stages inserts in 64-entry per-thread buffers. Reads use mmap'd SSTables, a sharded LRU block cache and exact-key Bloom filters hashed with gxhash (AES-NI/NEON). Flush and leveled compaction are deferred to background tasks, so the headline acknowledgement rate does not include that work.

**Use it when:**
- A Rust service already on Tokio that needs a local ordered byte-key store and whose bottleneck is write ingest from one or a few callers.
- You can accept losing recent acknowledged writes on power loss or a kernel crash, but not on a process crash. That is the durable() contract, the same class as fjall's PersistMode::Buffer.
- Bulk loads or grouped writes: atomic batches of 100-1,000 keys reached about 2.3M keys/s in durable mode and about 0.16M keys/s in paranoid mode (1,000/batch) on an Apple M4.
- Rebuildable caches or scratch data, where fast() (no WAL) acknowledged 1.2-3.9M keys/s for 400-byte values.
- Prefix- or range-scan access patterns over small-to-mid values (the tests used 20-byte keys and 400-byte values).

**Skip it when:**
- You need every acknowledged single write to survive power loss from one caller: paranoid() managed about 210-226 ops/s on the M4 (sync-latency bound), below redb Eventual's 1,397-1,549.
- Read-heavy or restart-sensitive workloads. In the older 0.5.0 full matrix, redb beat TurboKV on random point reads (246,119 vs 183,154 ops/s, with fjall at 184,160 tied), and TurboKV reopened about 1 time/s (~0.97 s per reopen) vs about 10/s for fjall and 12/s for redb. 0.6.0 has no published read or recovery numbers.
- Space-constrained or larger-than-RAM datasets. Disk amplification at the measurement boundary was 2.14x (3.22x for overwrites) vs fjall's 1.43x. Only an 84 MB dataset on a 32 GiB machine was tested, and mmap reads beyond RAM are unmeasured.
- Non-Tokio or no_std environments, multi-process or replicated access, or CPUs/targets without AES+SSE2 or AES+NEON. gxhash has no software fallback, so the crate does not build there.
- You need a mature engine: it is pre-1.0 with about 540 total crates.io downloads and one maintainer. 0.6.0 removed many public APIs, and its v5 WAL cannot be opened by older TurboKV versions.

**Integration:** crate · tokio (rt-multi-thread, fs, sync, time), crossbeam-skiplist, parking_lot, memmap2, lz4_flex, snap, zstd (builds the zstd C library via zstd-sys), gxhash 3, crc32fast, lru, bytes, byteorder, serde/serde_bytes, thiserror, tracing, libc, num_cpus; windows-sys on Windows · Rust 1.85 (MSRV, gated in CI; edition 2021), plus RUSTFLAGS -C target-feature=+aes,+sse2 (x86) or +aes,+neon (ARM), or -C target-cpu=native · Linux, macOS and Windows are built and tested in CI. Needs x86/x86-64 with AES-NI+SSE2 or ARM/AArch64 with AES+NEON. The preallocated mapped-WAL fast path is used where native reservation exists; other filesystems fall back to ordered file writes.

**Vs siblings:** Pick TurboKV over SurrealKV or Badger when you want a Rust/Tokio store and single-caller write acknowledgement under process-crash durability is the metric that matters. Prefer SurrealKV (Rust) or Badger (Go) when you need published point-read and update numbers against RocksDB, which TurboKV does not have; its only current cross-engine data is write ingest against fjall 2.11.

**Gotchas:**
- The default preset, durable(), does not fsync each write. The WAL is synced only on memtable flush (checked every 60 s, rotation near 64 MiB), on 1 GiB segment rotation and on clean close, and the README says there is no exact loss bound. Use paranoid() if every acknowledgement must reach stable storage.
- A plain `cargo build` fails unless RUSTFLAGS enables AES (gxhash). The persisted Bloom-filter bits depend on gxhash 3's hash, so the on-disk format is tied to that hash.
- Dropping a Db is not a clean shutdown; call close() or close_with_status(). A failed or cancelled mutation may already be in the WAL, so check state before retrying a non-idempotent write. A paranoid group-commit error poisons the handle until reopen.
- Streaming iterators advance synchronously inside async code, doing mmap reads, checksums and decompression, and they pin snapshot readers. Creating a scan can freeze the active memtable, so frequent small scans add flush work. Media or mapping faults on the mmap'd WAL can terminate the process instead of returning an error.

**Status:** Actively developed (0.6.0 released 2026-08-28, last commit 2026-08-29) under Apache-2.0 and installable with `cargo add turbokv`. It is a young, pre-1.0, single-maintainer crate that needs AES RUSTFLAGS and Tokio, and was developed largely through agent-driven PRs (codex/* branches, 'ready-for-agent' issues).

[repo](https://github.com/kingroryg/turbokv) · [benchmark](https://github.com/kingroryg/turbokv#benchmarks)

##### ZoneTree  `C#`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Pure-C# LSM-tree ordered key-value engine for .NET; beats RocksDB (via RocksDbSharp) and SQLite on its own indexed profile-store benchmark.

**Beats:** RocksDB, SQLite — On the project's own 2M-profile run (one worker, .NET 10.0.9 Release with Server GC, AMD EPYC 4345P 8C/16T, 60.4 GB, Ubuntu 24.04), ZoneTree finished the full live insert/read/index-scan/query/update workload in 181,390 ms. RocksDB 6.2.2 via RocksDbSharp took 429,036 ms and SQLite 3.50.3 took 1,062,037 ms, all with identical checksums. Id reads ran 3.6x faster than RocksDB and email lookups 2.8x faster; raw inserts tied, and RocksDB led on insert-plus-stabilize readiness (154,360/s vs 141,281/s). At 100M profiles the read lead shrinks to about 1.9x and updates tie, and at 20M and 50M RocksDB wins the raw insert and update phases.

**Known shortcoming:** The 'raw insert 154,360/s' is insert plus stabilize; raw inserts tie RocksDB (182,070 vs 181,662/s). Baseline is RocksDB 6.2.2 via RocksDbSharp; the repo moved to ZoneTree/ZoneTree.

**Known shortcoming:** Memory-heavy: peak 3.3 GB vs RocksDB 1.1 GB at 2M keys, 33 vs 3.6 GB at 20M, 56.3 vs 11.1 GB at 100M (on-disk data only 7.4 GB). Writes lose at scale (RocksDB wins raw insert+update at 20M/50M; a user in #108 saw batched RocksDB inserts 4.5 s vs ZoneTree 7.8 s). Weak baseline: RocksDB 6.2.2 via RocksDbSharp P/Invoke, 5 instances, no Bloom/block-cache options.

**Known shortcoming:** Mutable reference values stay in memory, so mutating after Upsert changes data without the WAL and rollback will not undo it (#120). The default async WAL can lose writes on crash; Sync WAL is only an OS-kernel flush. A custom comparer needs a matching hasher (else Bloom false misses); package renamed Tenray.ZoneTree to ZoneTree at v1.8.7.

**How:** It is a classic LSM tree. Writes land in an in-memory B+Tree mutable segment (128-entry nodes, node-level monitor locks by default) that sits behind a concurrent Bloom filter and a background async Zstd-compressed WAL. A background maintainer then freezes these segments and merges them into sorted, compressed disk segments. Disk segments are 'multipart': each logical segment is a set of immutable key-range parts, so a merge rewrites only the parts whose range changed and carries clean parts forward, which bounds write amplification. Reads go through a sparse index (step 16 in the benchmark, 1,024 by default), a cache of decompressed 4 MB blocks, 16-entry materialized key/value chunks, per-segment circular key/value caches and prefetch hints for sequential lookups; the project attributes its higher peak memory to the decompressed-block caching.

**Use it when:**
- .NET services that need an embedded, ordered, persistent key-value store with seek/range scans and reverse iteration, and want only managed dependencies (K4os LZ4 and ZstdSharp ports, no native RocksDB binaries). It supports NativeAOT on net7.0 and later.
- Read-heavy point lookups and ordered index scans with a working set that fits in RAM with room to spare. At 2M profiles it did 970,010 id reads/s vs RocksDB's 272,133/s and 388,867 email lookups/s vs 138,471/s.
- Live, unbatched single-record writes where SQLite autocommit becomes the bottleneck. At 2M profiles it inserted 182,070 rows/s vs SQLite's 6,231/s (WAL journal, synchronous=NORMAL).
- Building your own index, queue, event-store, TTL or full-text layer on an ordered keyspace. There is an official ZoneTree.FullTextSearch package, plus operation indexes for async replication and live backup of non-transactional trees.
- Cache, temporary or rebuildable data. The NoWAL mode removes WAL cost entirely.

**Skip it when:**
- Memory-constrained hosts. Peak process memory vs RocksDB was 3.3 GB vs 1.1 GB at 2M profiles, 33.0 GB vs 3.6 GB at 20M, and 56.3 GB vs 11.1 GB at 100M on a 60.4 GB machine, where ZoneTree's on-disk data was only 7.4 GB.
- Write-dominated workloads at tens of millions of rows. On the project's own 20M and 50M runs, RocksDB's raw insert and update phases were faster (20M: 173,190 vs 156,633 inserts/s and 44,044 vs 39,440 updates/s). At 100M, updates were a tie. In issue #108 a user loading 10M string-to-byte[] records measured 7.8 s for ZoneTree vs 4.5 s for RocksDB with batched writes. Without batching, ZoneTree was about 4x faster, and random lookups were about even.
- You need SQL, native secondary indexes, joins or cross-language access. ZoneTree is a .NET-only key-value engine, and the benchmark maintains every secondary index in application code as a separate tree.
- Strict per-write power-loss durability. The default AsyncCompressed WAL can lose recent writes on a crash. Even Sync WAL only flushes to the OS kernel (maintainer, issue #116), and SyncCompressed writes its tail every 500 ms.
- If you are comparing against a tuned modern RocksDB, the published numbers do not tell you the answer. The harness uses RocksDB 6.2.2 through the RocksDbSharp P/Invoke wrapper as five separate instances and sets no block-based-table options (no Bloom filter, no enlarged block cache). Meanwhile ZoneTree runs with a dense sparse index and a block cache bounded by lifetime, not size.

**Integration:** shared lib (NuGet package `ZoneTree`, managed assembly) · K4os.Compression.LZ4 1.3.8, ZstdSharp.Port 0.8.8 (both managed NuGet packages) · .NET 6 (multi-targets net6.0 through net10.0; library built with C# 14 / LangVersion 14.0) · any .NET 6-10 runtime (managed code with unsafe blocks). Published benchmark runs are Linux x64 and Windows 11 x64.

**Vs siblings:** Pick ZoneTree when your code is .NET and you want an ordered, embedded, managed-only store with range scans. Most siblings here (Badger, Pogreb, SurrealKV, Speedb, ToplingDB, SplinterDB, NuDB) are Go, Rust or C/C++ engines and would need a native binding such as the RocksDbSharp wrapper this benchmark used. F2/FASTER is the other .NET-relevant sibling; the ZoneTree repo ships a ZoneTree-vs-FASTER harness for Int64 point inserts and lookups but publishes no results from it, so that head-to-head is unmeasured.

**Gotchas:**
- Values in in-memory segments are held by reference. Mutating an object after Upsert, or one returned by TryGet or ReadCommittedTryGet, silently changes what readers see: no WAL record, and a transaction rollback does not undo it (issue #120). Use immutable records or structs, or clone before upserting.
- The comparer, serializers and value types are part of the database identity and cannot change behavior on an existing store. A custom comparer also needs an IKeyHasher that agrees with its equality (for example, a case-insensitive string comparer needs a case-insensitive hasher), or the mutable-segment Bloom filter can wrongly report misses.
- Memory limits are record counts, not bytes: MutableSegmentMaxItemCount defaults to 1,000,000, which is far too much for large string or document values. You also need a maintainer (CreateMaintainer) or your own maintenance loop, or read-only segments pile up. .NET keeps freed memory, so process RSS stays high after merges.
- In v1.8.7 the package and namespace were renamed from Tenray.ZoneTree to ZoneTree, and in v1.9.0 the repo moved from koculu/ZoneTree to the ZoneTree org. TotalRecordCount counts physical versions, not live keys (use Count()). Built-in live backup does not cover transactional trees.

**Status:** Actively maintained: v1.9.8 released 2026-09-15, 99 NuGet versions, zero open issues, authored by Ahmed Yasin Koculu under the ZoneTree GitHub org. MIT-licensed and installed from NuGet with no native binaries.

[repo](https://github.com/koculu/ZoneTree) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ZoneTree/ZoneTree/blob/main/docs/benchmark/reference/2m/2m.md)

##### DobLIX  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause (RocksDB 5.x-era 'BSD License For rocksdb software' LICENSE text; GitHub reports NOASSERTION) plus Facebook PATENTS file (Additional Grant of Patent Rights Version 2)`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Research RocksDB fork replacing the SST index with a block-aware learned string index; paper: 2.21x read-only throughput vs RocksDB.

**Beats:** RocksDB — The PVLDB 2025 paper ran RocksDB 8.1.1 built with GCC 9.4.0 (C++17, flags not stated) and 4 background threads on a 64-core Threadripper Pro 5995WX with 256GB RAM and a Samsung 980 Pro NVMe, using SOSD datasets (64M 8-byte keys, 64-byte values) and 10M-operation Zipfian workloads; against RocksDB's default index it averaged 2.21x throughput on RO, 1.22x RH, 1.31x BA, 1.04x WH, 2.02x on YCSB B/C/D and +42.8% on YCSB-E. These numbers come from the unreleased paper build with the tuner and RocksDB 8.1.1, not the public repo.

**Known shortcoming:** The repo is a RocksDB 5.1.2 tree while the paper says 8.1.1, and it has no DobLIX benchmark harness. The listed 2.67x is TridentKV tail latency; against RocksDB it is 2.21x read-only and 1.04-1.31x on mixed workloads. BSD-3 plus Facebook's PATENTS file.

**Known shortcoming:** The public repo is not the paper's build: the authors say (issue #2) the tuner and PRA were withheld for confidentiality. It is a RocksDB 5.1.2 fork with a changed SST footer and Get() always going through the learned index, so it is no drop-in for modern RocksDB. Error bound 128 and 4 KB blocks are hard-coded; the paper's last-mile/prefix optimisations are computed but unused.

**Known shortcoming:** The builder copies the whole SST into RAM before Finish; srand() reseeds the global RNG; mismatched delete[] in the reader; the README build is reported broken (issue #1, no reply). Gains: 2.21x read-only but 1.04x write-heavy and only +42.8% on YCSB-E (scans use the normal index).

**How:** The index is a Radix String Spline: a trie of RadixSpline models, each built with Neumann and Michel's GreedySplineCorridor PLA over 8-byte big-endian key chunks, with common prefixes stripped at each node. The 'dual objective' is that a spline segment is also cut when its bytes would exceed a max block size. Each spline segment then becomes its own data block, so the model predicts the block directly and a Get reads one small block instead of searching an index block and then a possibly large data block. The paper also adds a Q-learning agent that picks PLA or piecewise regression (PRA), the error bound and the max block size, plus model-guided last-mile search inside the block, but none of these three are in the public code.

**Use it when:**
- Studying or prototyping learned indexes inside an LSM SST. learned_index/ is a compact header-only RadixSpline and Radix String Spline already wired into RocksDB's table builder and reader.
- Read-only or read-mostly point-lookup workloads on small fixed-size keys where index lookup plus block load dominate Get latency. The paper reports 2.21x average RO throughput and 2.02x on YCSB B/C/D vs RocksDB's default index.
- Read workloads with a larger block cache. The paper measured +81% over RocksDB at 512MB cache (RO, Zipfian, AMZN), where index cost is a larger share of each lookup.
- Long string keys with shared prefixes. Prefix stripping per trie node gave a 25.9% smaller index at 64-byte keys and 1.32x-1.62x throughput on variable-size KV mixes modeled on UDB, ZippyDB and UP2X.
- Only as a starting point you will port to a current RocksDB and complete yourself (the PRA model and RL tuner are missing).

**Skip it when:**
- Production use. The base is RocksDB 5.1.2, years behind current releases in fixes and features. The authors state in issue #2 that the public code is not the version used in the paper.
- Write-heavy workloads. The paper's own WH gain over RocksDB is only 1.04x, and the builder buffers each whole SST in RAM before writing it (see gotchas).
- Range-scan-heavy workloads. Iterators still use the regular binary-search index block. The paper's YCSB-E gain is 42.8%, and it notes all systems perform alike during the scan phase.
- Existing RocksDB databases. The SST footer gains a third block handle and Get() always goes through the learned index. Reading SSTs written by stock RocksDB, and migrating them, is not documented.
- Expecting workload-adaptive tuning. The RL tuner and PRA model are withheld, and the public builder hardcodes error bound 128 and a 4KB max block.

**Integration:** static lib (the whole RocksDB 5.1.2 fork, built with CMake or Make; not a plugin or separable patch) · RocksDB 5.1.2 build deps per README: gflags, snappy, zlib, bzip2, lz4, zstd. No ML/RL libraries, since the tuner is not included. · CMakeLists sets -std=c++11. The paper used C++17 with GCC 9.4.0. Issue #1 reports the README build failing and was closed without a reply. · Paper tested Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu 20.04). learned_index/ uses GCC/Clang builtins (__builtin_clz/__builtin_clzl), so MSVC is not supported as written. Other platforms are not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick DobLIX over write-focused siblings (PebblesDB, MatrixKV, Titan) only when the bottleneck is point-lookup index and block reads in a read-mostly RocksDB workload and you want to study learned SST indexes. For anything deployable, Titan is a maintained RocksDB plugin, and SplinterDB claims 2-2.6x faster point queries plus 6-10x faster inserts in a maintained codebase.

**Gotchas:**
- BlockBasedTableBuilder::Add copies every key and value of the output SST into a std::vector<pair<string,string>>, plus another copy of each user key for training. Data blocks are only written in Finish(), so flush/compaction memory grows with SST size.
- Data-block boundaries come from spline segments via a hardcoded FinalizeRSSModel(128, 4*1024), not from BlockBasedTableOptions::block_size. The only tuning is editing and recompiling.
- The paper's last-mile optimizations are inactive in the public reader. GetKeyFromBlock computes a model search bound and prefix length, then ignores both and calls the standard BlockIter::Seek. The table-open loop that fills per-block key counts also never increments block_num, so those counts are wrong; this is harmless today only because nothing uses them.
- Every RadixStringSplineNode constructor calls srand(time(NULL)), which reseeds the process-global C RNG on each SST build. The table reader also frees a new char[] buffer through std::unique_ptr<char>, a mismatched delete.

**Status:** Stale research code drop (one code commit in Feb 2025, README edits to Sep 2025) whose Huawei authors say the tuner and PRA are withheld for confidentiality; it is BSD-3 with Facebook's old PATENTS grant, so read or copy learned_index/ but do not deploy it.

[repo](https://github.com/ah89/DobLIX) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05369 (PVLDB 18(11): 3965-3978, 2025, DOI 10.14778/3749646.3749667))

##### F2 (FASTER v2)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

Microsoft's two-tier hash-and-log KV store for skewed, larger-than-memory point workloads; its paper reports ~11.8x RocksDB throughput at 10% memory.

**Beats:** RocksDB — Setup, from the PVLDB 18(12) 2025 paper: CloudLab node with a 16-core Xeon Silver 4314 and 4 PM9A3 NVMe drives in RAID-0, 250M 8 B-key/100 B-value YCSB records (A/B/C/D/F/W) plus MixGraph, 16 threads, memory capped at 10% of the data. Every system ran with Direct I/O and no WAL, compression or checksums, and RocksDB v8.11.4 was tuned with 10-bit Bloom filters and the data-block hash index. F2 averaged 11.8x RocksDB's throughput, and single-thread latency was 1.4x lower on reads and 3.5x lower on writes. The compiler is not stated and the RocksDB harness is not published.

**Known shortcoming:** Venue is PVLDB 18(12) 2025 (not VLDB 2023). The 11.8x is an average over YCSB and MixGraph; latency gains are 1.4x read and 3.5x write. The RocksDB harness and compiler are not published.

**Known shortcoming:** No longer actively maintained: since 2026-08 the README points to Garnet/Tsavorite (C#); the only C++ change since the F2 merge (2025-02) is overflow hardening. Open bug #944 (F2 compaction hang, failing RMW test) has only an unmerged draft fix (#947, since 2025-09); the paper admits no production-workload testing.

**Known shortcoming:** The public benchmark_f2.cc differs from the paper (8 B values vs 100 B, read cache off, 4+12 GiB in-memory split, workloads A/B/C/RMW only), so the paper's numbers are not reproducible from the repo. Point operations only (no scan/iterator/transactions/compression); durability is manual Checkpoint with no WAL; the context+callback+session API is not a drop-in for RocksDB. Linux (libaio) and Windows x64 only, max 96 threads. Gains shrink at low skew and FASTER ties F2 at >=20% memory.

**How:** Write-hot records stay in a FASTER HybridLog, which is updated in place in its in-memory mutable region, flushed append-only to disk and indexed by a latch-free in-memory hash table. Background hot-cold compaction moves write-cold records to a separate cold log. That log uses a two-level hash index: an in-memory table points to 256 B 'hash chunks' kept on disk, costing under 1 byte of RAM per cold key versus FASTER's 8 bytes. Compaction is multi-threaded and lookup-based, built on a Conditional-Insert primitive that copies a record only if no newer version of its key has been appended; the paper measures it 5.2x faster than FASTER's scan-based compaction while using 25x less memory. A second-chance FIFO read cache, chained into the hot index, serves read-hot records that live on disk, so a hot key needs no I/O and a cold key needs about two (index chunk plus record) instead of an LSM level probe.

**Use it when:**
- Point-only traffic (get/put/delete/RMW) with Zipfian-like skew on a dataset roughly 5-40x larger than the RAM you can give it. The paper used 250M keys (~30 GiB) under a 3 GiB cap.
- Update- or RMW-heavy state such as counters, per-entity or per-function state, or streaming join synopses, where RocksDB's compaction write amplification hurts. Paper: 3.3-3.9 us single-thread write latency vs RocksDB's 6.7-17.3 us, and write amplification of 1.2-2.4 vs 2.5-5.8.
- Workloads where the read-hot and write-hot key sets differ; the read cache keeps disk-resident read-hot records in memory without pulling them back into the write log.
- Billions of keys where index RAM is the constraint: the cold-log index is tunable to under 1 B per key.
- A Linux x86-64 NVMe server running a custom C++ service (up to 96 threads) where you control the per-thread loop (sessions, Refresh, CompletePending).

**Skip it when:**
- You need range scans, prefix seeks, ordered iteration, snapshots, transactions, column families or compression. F2Kv exposes point operations only; the paper even dropped MixGraph's 3% seeks.
- Low-skew or uniform read-heavy access. Every cold-log read costs about two extra I/Os, the paper shows YCSB-B throughput falling as skew drops (alpha <= 50), and once memory reaches 20% or more of the dataset, the original FASTER matches F2.
- Production use that needs a maintained engine. Since Aug 2026 the README says the repo is no longer actively maintained and points to Garnet/Tsavorite (C#). The F2 infinite-compaction/RMW-test-failure issue #944 is still open, its fix #947 has been an unmerged draft since Sep 2025, and the paper says F2 has not been tested on production workloads.
- macOS or other non-Linux/non-Windows targets. The POSIX I/O backend requires Linux libaio (or liburing), and Windows CI runs only the in-memory tests, not the F2 tests.
- You want a drop-in RocksDB swap. The callback/context API, compile-time key/value types and manual checkpointing make a port a rewrite.

**Integration:** static lib · Linux: libaio, libuuid, Intel TBB, stdc++fs, pthread (optional liburing via USE_URING). Windows: rpcrt4. CMake FetchContent downloads toml11 v4.3.0 and googletest v1.14.0 at configure time. The optional Azure blob device also needs cpprestsdk and azure-storage-cpp. · CMake 3.14+. On Linux, GCC in -std=c++17 mode (the headers also use designated initializers, which GCC accepts as an extension). On Windows, Visual Studio 2022 with /std:c++20. CI uses Ubuntu 22.04 g++ and windows-2022. · Linux x86-64 (libaio or io_uring) and Windows x64. No macOS I/O backend. ARM is not documented, and the io_uring spinlock uses the x86-only __builtin_ia32_pause.

**Vs siblings:** Pick F2 over KVell and SplinterDB for pure point/RMW traffic with heavy skew and RAM around 10% of the data: in the same paper it averaged 11.9x KVell's and 4.6x SplinterDB's throughput, though SplinterDB had slightly lower single-thread YCSB-B read latency (42.1 vs 45.3 us). Pick SplinterDB, whose entry reports it matching RocksDB on small range queries, or another LSM sibling when you need ordered scans.

**Gotchas:**
- Reads of disk-resident keys return Status::Pending, and the callback fires only when that same thread calls CompletePending(). The bundled benchmark calls Refresh() every 64 ops and CompletePending() every 1,600.
- Auto-compaction is on by default, with disk budgets of only 1 GiB (hot) and 8 GiB (cold). The paper set them to 125% of dataset size (5 GiB / 35 GiB for 30 GiB of data), and budgets under 64 MiB throw. The read cache is off by default (DEFAULT_READ_CACHE_CONFIG.enabled = false) and has to be enabled and sized explicitly.
- The hot index table_size must be a power of two and at most INT32_MAX or the constructor throws std::invalid_argument. The paper advises sizing both indexes to the expected unique-key counts to avoid extra I/Os per lookup. Misuse is reported through C++ exceptions.
- The F2 configuration samples on the docs page do not compile as written (for example the typos hlog_copaction_config and hot-config). Start from cc/benchmark-dir/benchmark_f2.cc instead. That harness also differs from the paper's setup: 8-byte values, read cache disabled, 4 GiB hot + 12 GiB cold in-memory logs (its comment says 6/10 GiB), and only workloads A, B, C and 100% RMW.

**Status:** MIT-licensed and public, but the README has said since Aug 2026 that the repo is no longer actively maintained (successor: Garnet/Tsavorite, in C#), not 'active' as recorded. The only C++ source change since F2 merged in Feb 2025 is an integer-overflow hardening patch, and the F2 compaction-hang fix (#947) is still an unmerged draft.

[repo](https://github.com/microsoft/FASTER) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01516)

##### HyperLevelDB  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

HyperDex's LevelDB 1.17 fork with parallel writers and cheaper compaction; about 3.4x faster bulk writes than LevelDB, but slower reads.

**Beats:** LevelDB — InfluxData, which is independent of HyperLevelDB, ran a 2014 test on a 2-core, 4 GB DigitalOcean SSD droplet with default, untuned settings; compiler, flags and engine versions are not stated. It wrote 100M 24-byte keys with small protobuf values in 1,000-item batches. HyperLevelDB wrote them in 10m45s vs 36m08s for LevelDB (~3.4x) and 21m19s for RocksDB, but range-queried them ~4.7x slower than LevelDB (13m49s vs 2m55s) and lost on delete and compaction. In the same gist, the 3M-point SSD run had HyperLevelDB writing slower than LevelDB (21.0s vs 18.0s), and only the magnetic-disk 3M run showed a write win (30.4s vs 46.1s).

**Known shortcoming:** The win is writes (~3.36x load); queries are ~4.7x slower than LevelDB and deletes/compaction are slower too.

**Known shortcoming:** Reads lose badly (100M range query 13m49s vs LevelDB 2m55s) and the write win is inconsistent (a 3M SSD run took 21.0 s vs LevelDB 18.0 s; DB 206 MB vs 78 MB after load). x86-only inline-asm atomics (maintainer declined std::atomic/arm64, #19/#21); no Windows (#18).

**Known shortcoming:** Abandoned since 2016, frozen at LevelDB 1.17, pre-C++11 (tr1). Background threads are never joined, so each open/close leaks ~24 MB of virtual memory (#4); only a soft L0 throttle; shares LevelDB's namespace and C symbols, so both cannot be linked into one binary. PebblesDB (built on it, active 2024) is usually the better choice.

**How:** Writes: in LevelDB, the writer at the head of a FIFO does all the work behind one mutex. Here each writer reserves a sequence-number range with an atomic fetch-add, appends to an mmap-backed log that hands out non-overlapping regions, and inserts into a concurrent skip list that traverses without the lock and only validates under it. Only visibility (last sequence) and ordering are serialized. Compaction: the picker chooses the contiguous run of level-N files with the highest bytes(N)/bytes(N+1 overlap) ratio, capped at 16x the level's file size, so each compaction rewrites as few bytes as possible; it does trivial moves first. Memtable flush and level compaction run on two separate background threads, using per-level locks. Level sizes are hard-coded larger than LevelDB's: L0 64 MB, L1 128 MB, L2 512 MB, then 8x per level, with SSTs of up to 64 MB.

**Use it when:**
- An existing LevelDB C++ codebase on x86-64 Linux where ingest throughput is the bottleneck and a move to RocksDB is not on the table.
- Write-once, read-later bulk loads such as time-series or event logs written in batches. In InfluxData's 2014 test, 100M small points loaded in 10m45s vs 36m08s for LevelDB.
- Many application threads writing at once. The authors' own 4-thread, 128-byte-value test showed 2-4x the throughput of LevelDB, RocksDB and Basho's fork (first-party graphs only).
- You need a cheap live backup (hard links) or a change feed (ReplayIterator from a timestamp) on a LevelDB-style store, as HyperDex did.
- As a research or reference baseline: PebblesDB is built by modifying HyperLevelDB and stays API-compatible with it.

**Skip it when:**
- Read- or scan-heavy workloads. In the same InfluxData run, range-querying 100M values took 13m49s vs 2m55s for LevelDB (~4.7x slower), and delete and compaction were also slower (6m00s vs 3m48s, 6m33s vs 4m00s).
- Non-x86 hardware or Windows. util/atomic.h is hand-written x86 inline assembly (mfence, lock cmpxchg, MMX for 32-bit). The maintainer declined std::atomic and arm64 ports (issues #19, #21), and Windows support was never planned (#18).
- Anything that needs a maintained engine. The last commit (2016-02-16) fixed a memory leak. In 2018 the maintainer declined to tag a release because he could not vouch for its quality (#22). The code is frozen at LevelDB 1.17.
- Processes that open and close the DB often. Background threads start at Open and are never joined, so each open/close cycle leaks thread stacks. In #4 that was about 24 MB of virtual memory per cycle, and the fix was 'keep it open'.
- Small or single-threaded workloads and tight disk budgets. In the gist's 3M-point SSD run, writes were slower than LevelDB's (21.0s vs 18.0s), and the DB was 206 MB vs 78 MB after the load.

**Integration:** shared lib (autotools/libtool build of libhyperleveldb; a static archive is also produced) · pthread; Snappy is optional and auto-detected by configure. Building from git needs autoconf 2.62+ and libtool 2.2+. The optional 'benchmark' tool also needs libe, popt and ygor. · Pre-C++11 code: it uses std::tr1::shared_ptr unless built against libc++, plus GCC __sync builtins and GCC-style inline asm, and configure sets no -std flag. Last fixed for GCC/Clang in 2014 (OS X Mavericks, FreeBSD commits). Whether it builds on current compilers is not documented. · x86-64 (and 32-bit x86) on Linux. There are 2014 build fixes for FreeBSD and OS X, but the maintainer said in 2016 he had not tested macOS. No Windows, ARM/aarch64 or PowerPC support.

**Vs siblings:** PebblesDB is HyperLevelDB plus FLSM guards, with the same API, reports higher write throughput, and was updated as recently as 2024, so it is usually the better pick in this lineage. Choose HyperLevelDB only when you want the smallest, simplest step from LevelDB (no guard layer), or to match an existing HyperDex deployment. For a new project, a RocksDB-based sibling (Speedb, Titan, ToplingDB) avoids being stuck on a 2014 LevelDB codebase.

**Gotchas:**
- L0 is only soft-throttled: a writer sleeps one microsecond per L0 file above 8, and db_impl.cc never uses kL0_StopWritesTrigger. A long ingest can therefore pile up overlapping L0 files that later reads must check, which fits the slow queries seen right after the bulk load.
- Seek-triggered compaction only kicks in after more than 10 consecutive reads with no write in between (kStraightReads), so mixed read/write workloads rarely get read-driven cleanup.
- With manual_garbage_collection=true, compaction keeps deleted and overwritten data until the application calls AllowGarbageCollectBeforeTimestamp. Forgetting that call makes disk usage grow without bound.
- Known build snags: linking against Ubuntu's Snappy fails with 'DSO missing from command line' until -lsnappy is added to LIBS (#15/#16). Level sizes, file sizes and triggers are compile-time constants in version_set.cc/dbformat.h, not Options.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2016 and never re-released (the maintainer declined in 2018). It is BSD-3-Clause and small enough to vendor, but it is x86-only, frozen at LevelDB 1.17, and has no known-good modern compiler documented.

[repo](https://github.com/rescrv/HyperLevelDB) · [benchmark](https://www.influxdata.com/blog/2014/06/20/leveldb_vs_rocksdb_vs_hyperleveldb_vs_lmdb_performance.html)

##### KVell  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier B`

SOSP'19 research key-value store for NVMe/Optane SSDs that has no LSM compaction; 2-8x RocksDB throughput on YCSB point workloads.

**Beats:** RocksDB — In the SOSP'19 paper, on a 4-core 4.2 GHz i7 with an Optane 905P (memory capped by cgroups to 1/3 of a 100 GB, 100M x 1 KB dataset), KVell sustained about 420K req/s on YCSB A. That is 8x RocksDB 6.2 and 5.8x PebblesDB, with 2.2-2.7x on YCSB B/C, about 4x on Nutanix production traces, rough parity on uniform YCSB E, and 3.9 ms max latency versus RocksDB's 9.6 s. RocksDB was run through a modified db_bench (SILK fork; the author's issue-tracker command uses --sync=0 and no compression). The paper names no compiler; the repo builds with clang -O2 and TCMalloc, and only the KVell side of the harness is published.

**Known shortcoming:** Research prototype (author: don't use in production), dormant since 2020, source drop that builds a bench binary, async callback C API, no RocksDB drop-in. Index and worker routing use only the first 8 key bytes (keys sharing that prefix abort; scans are uint64 order, not lexicographic). Items over 4 KB abort and growing past a slab class asserts; the paper's multi-block/migration never shipped. Bug on master: ADD_OR_UPDATE falls through into DELETE (benchmarks don't call it). No fsync, checksums, transactions or snapshot scans; slabs never shrink; needs 4 KB power-atomic SSDs; Linux AIO + x86 rdtsc only; compile-time config, 30 GB page cache reserved at start, pinned busy-spinning workers. Weak on small-item and SATA scans (3K vs RocksDB 15K) and when the index exceeds RAM (15M to 109K lookups/s). RocksDB baseline via the SILK db_bench fork with --sync=0 and no compression.

**How:** It is shared-nothing: keys are split across worker threads by their first 8 bytes, and each worker owns its own in-memory B-tree index (Google cpp-btree, about 19 B per key), its own LRU page cache and free lists, and slab files on a single disk. Items are not sorted on disk. They sit in size-class slab files (100 B to 4 KB) and are updated in place, so there is no compaction, no commit log and no write amplification beyond the 4 KB page. Each worker batches up to 64 requests per Linux AIO io_submit/io_getevents call with O_DIRECT, which amortizes syscall cost and keeps the device queue deep without overfilling it. The bet is that random I/O on modern NVMe is as cheap as sequential I/O, so CPU cycles spent keeping data sorted are wasted.

**Use it when:**
- Point-read and update-heavy workloads (YCSB A/B/C/F style) on NVMe or Optane drives where RocksDB is CPU-bound on compaction and cannot saturate the device.
- Items of roughly 100 B to 4 KB where you need bounded worst-case latency: the paper reports 3.9 ms max versus 9.6 s for RocksDB, because nothing runs in the background.
- Write-heavy mixes with medium values, such as the Nutanix 57:41:2 write:read:scan workloads (250 B-1 KB items), where KVell was about 4x RocksDB.
- Machines with several NVMe drives and many cores. Each worker is tied to one disk, and the design scaled to 8 drives and 5 B keys on i3.metal.
- As a design reference or starting point for your own NVMe store (for example, porting it to io_uring or SPDK) when your keys are naturally unique 8-byte integers.

**Skip it when:**
- Keys whose first 8 bytes are not unique (for example, string keys with a common prefix like 'user0000'). The index and worker routing use only an 8-byte prefix, and the code dies on 'Adding item that is already in the database' or on key mismatch during updates.
- Values above about 4 KB including the 24-byte header (it dies with 'Item is too big'), or values that grow past their slab class on update (assert). The paper describes multi-block items and slab migration, but the released code does not implement them.
- Scan-heavy workloads with small items, or older SATA SSDs. Each scanned item costs one random 4 KB read, so RocksDB wins with 64 B items, uniform YCSB E is only about even (13.9K vs 14.4K scans/s), and on a SATA S3500 KVell managed 3K scans/s against RocksDB's 15K.
- Datasets whose index does not fit in RAM. Index lookups fall from 15M/s to 109K/s when the index is 5x RAM. The page cache is also reserved up front from a compile-time size (30 GB by default).
- Anything production-grade. The author says 'don't use it in production'. There are no transactions (those are in the KVell+ osdi branch), no snapshot-consistent scans, no checksums, no fsync, slab files never shrink, and it relies on the drive writing 4 KB pages atomically on power failure.

**Integration:** source-drop · libc, pthreads, libm, libstdc++ (the Google cpp-btree is vendored). Linux AIO is called through raw syscalls, so libaio is not needed. gperftools TCMalloc is optional but recommended (the run script LD_PRELOADs it). · Makefile defaults to clang/clang++ with -std=c++11 for the B-tree index code. GCC needs -fno-strict-aliasing (per a Makefile comment). README targets Ubuntu 18.04. No minimum compiler version is documented. · Linux only (linux/aio_abi.h, io_setup/io_submit syscalls, O_DIRECT, fallocate, pthread_setaffinity_np). In practice x86-64 only, because the timing code uses rdtsc inline asm. It assumes SSDs whose 4 KB writes are atomic on power failure.

**Vs siblings:** Pick KVell over the LSM siblings (PebblesDB, MatrixKV, TerarkDB, Titan) when you run a point-operation-heavy workload on fast NVMe and care most about worst-case latency. It has no compaction, and its paper measured PebblesDB directly on YCSB A (KVell 5.8x faster). Pick SplinterDB, an LSM sibling or NuDB instead when you need a real embeddable library, arbitrary keys, values above 4 KB or small-item range scans. KVell is a prototype you would have to finish yourself.

**Gotchas:**
- On master, kv_add_or_update_async is broken: the ADD_OR_UPDATE case in slabworker.c has no 'break' and falls through into DELETE, so an existing key is updated and then deleted. The bundled benchmarks never call it (they use add, update and read), so the paper numbers are unaffected.
- All configuration is compile-time #defines in options.h: the data path pattern /scratch%lu/kvell/..., PAGE_CACHE_SIZE, queue depth and PINNING. With PINNING=1, workers are pinned to cores 0..W-1 and busy-spin even when idle. You need a core for every worker and injector, or you must turn pinning off.
- Data is split statically by key prefix modulo the worker count. Changing the number of disks or workers means deleting the database, and every start rebuilds all indexes by scanning every slab (the paper measured 6.6 s for 100 GB on 8 NVMe drives).
- Scans are not snapshots: they return each key's latest value. Keys are ordered by their first 8 bytes read as a native uint64, which on little-endian x86 is not lexicographic byte order. The caller's thread does the merge across workers, so the scan benchmark uses 12 injector threads instead of 4.

**Status:** The repo is effectively dormant: master has only an initial 2019 commit, a 2020 README update and a December 2025 fix to a workload random-number generator, and the 8 open issues are mostly user questions the author answered in 2020. It is an MIT-licensed C prototype, with a core engine of about 1.8K lines, that is easy to vendor and study, but you would own every fix (including the ADD_OR_UPDATE fall-through), and the author explicitly says not to use it in production.

[repo](https://github.com/BLepers/KVell) · [benchmark](https://github.com/BLepers/KVell/blob/master/sosp19-final40.pdf)

##### MatrixKV  `C++`  `GPL-2.0 OR Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

RocksDB 5.18 fork that moves L0 into Optane persistent memory with fine-grained column compaction; 3.6x NVM-assisted RocksDB random-write throughput.

**Beats:** RocksDB — In the USENIX ATC'20 paper's db_bench test (80 GB of 16 B-key / 4 KB-value inserts in uniform random order, RocksDB defaults, 8 GB of NVM per store), MatrixKV reached 3.6x the random-write throughput of RocksDB with an 8 GB L0 placed in Optane (1.86-3.61x across 64 B-64 KB values) and 2.6x NoveLSM, and 3.29x on YCSB load. YCSB-A p99 at about 20K req/s was 405 us, against 786 us for RocksDB-L0-NVM, 2,080 us for NoveLSM and 11,055 us for stock RocksDB on SSD, and SSD write amplification was 3.43x versus 8.78x for stock RocksDB. Hardware: two unnamed 24-core 2.2 GHz Intel CPUs, 32 GB DRAM, an Intel SSDSC2BB800G7 SSD and Optane DC PMM on Fedora 27 / Linux 4.13.9; compiler, flags and client thread count are not stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Needs Optane-class persistent memory, which Intel wound down in 2022; frozen at RocksDB 5.18.3, not a plugin. Uses ~18.6 GB of NVM, not 8 GB (master preallocates 2x slots; issue #2 reports ~20 GB plus a crash when freed L0 space isn't reclaimed, unanswered); the paper's 4 KB paging exists only on an unmerged branch with 256 KB pages. Speedup is write-only: reads roughly equal RocksDB, sequential writes lose to stock RocksDB on SSD, full gain needs an 8 GB L1. Fragile recovery (a missing pmem pool only prints and continues). Debug logging always on in the working directory; the shipped script puts the WAL on SSD (paper: NVM) and uses threads=1; the paper gives no compiler, flags, CPU model or thread count (#4).

**How:** Flushed MemTables are written to NVM as sorted 'RowTables' in a matrix container. When the receiver half fills up it becomes the compactor, and its data is merged into L1 by column compaction: one small key range at a time, taken across all RowTables and matched with the overlapping L1 SSTables, rather than all of L0 against all of L1. In the paper this meant 467 compactions of about 0.33 GB each, versus RocksDB's 52 compactions averaging 3.1 GB. Because a column's cost does not grow with level width, L1 is widened to 8 GB, which flattens the tree from 5 levels to 3 and lowers write amplification. Cross-row hint search stores a forward pointer from each key into the previous RowTable, in the style of fractional cascading, so point lookups in the large unsorted L0 need no Bloom filters.

**Use it when:**
- Sustained random-insert or update-heavy workloads (bulk load, YCSB load/A/F-like) where RocksDB's L0-L1 compaction stalls cause throughput troughs and p99/p99.9 spikes.
- You already have Optane DC PMM (or equivalent byte-addressable persistent memory mounted for PMDK), several GB of it free, and a comparatively slow SSD for the lower levels (the paper's SSD managed 68 MB/s for 4 KB random writes).
- Any value size from 64 B to 64 KB, since the paper's random-write gain over RocksDB with L0 on NVM was 1.86-3.61x across that whole range (3.6x at 4 KB).
- Research or prototyping: reproducing the ATC'20 results, or as a reference design for column compaction and cross-row L0 search when adding a persistent-memory tier to an LSM engine.

**Skip it when:**
- Machines without persistent memory. Intel wound down Optane in July 2022, so new deployments need other hardware, and pmem_map_file's msync fallback on an ordinary file is not the configuration that was measured.
- Read- or scan-dominated workloads. In the paper, random and sequential reads roughly matched RocksDB and YCSB B-E were only 'adequate'. An open issue (#3) reports high read latency under YCSB-C++.
- Sequential-insert workloads. In the paper, stock RocksDB on SSD beat every NVM variant, MatrixKV included, on sequential writes.
- Production systems. The code is frozen at RocksDB 5.18.3 with none of RocksDB's later fixes. Issues about NVM overuse and a crash when freed L0 space was not reclaimed (#2) have had no answer since 2021, and debug logging is compiled in.
- Many column families on a small NVM device, because each named column family maps its own pool file sized from the L0 stop threshold.

**Integration:** static lib (the whole RocksDB v5.18.3 tree plus utilities/nvm_mod, built with the Makefile; the README says CMake is not supported) · PMDK libpmem (Makefile links -lpmem), pthread; RocksDB's usual optional compression libraries (snappy, lz4, zstd) if present · C++11 (build_detect_platform and the Makefile force -std=c++11); the paper used Fedora 27 / Linux 4.13.9; the compiler version is not documented · Linux with PMDK and a DAX-mounted persistent-memory path (tested on x86-64 with Optane DC PMM); other platforms not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick MatrixKV only when you have Optane-class persistent memory and the problem is RocksDB write stalls and tail latency under random inserts. It is the only sibling built for a DRAM/NVM/SSD hierarchy, and in the paper's all-NVM comparison it led while PebblesDB gained little over RocksDB. On plain SSDs, SplinterDB, KVell or PebblesDB are the write-throughput alternatives, and Titan is the maintained plug-in choice if your problem is large values.

**Gotchas:**
- NVM footprint is much larger than the 8 GB L0 budget. Master pre-allocates (L0_stop_size / write_buffer_size + 1) * 2 slots of write_buffer_size + 8 MB each, about 18.6 GB with the defaults (8 GB stop, 64 MB memtables), which fits issue #2's report of nearly 20 GB. The page-granular space management described in the paper exists only on the unmerged MatrixKV-Pager branch, which uses 256 KB pages rather than 4 KB.
- The paper's full speedup depends on also flattening the tree. The shipped script sets max_bytes_for_level_base to 8 GB; with RocksDB's default 256 MB L1 you get only the write-stall reduction, and the paper reports 25% more throughput with the 8 GB L1. L0 thresholds are byte sizes (7 GB trigger, 7.5 GB slowdown, 8 GB stop by default) instead of RocksDB's file counts.
- Recovery is fragile. If the pmem pool file is missing while the manifest still lists L0 files, RecoverFromStorageInfo prints 'can't recover' and carries on. It also copies each L0 table's key metadata into a stack variable-length array, which could overflow the thread stack for small-value tables. A RowTable flush returns IOError if its data plus about 52 bytes of metadata per key (with 16 B keys) exceeds its fixed slot.
- Debug logging is hard-wired: my_log.h defines LZW_DEBUG and LZW_INFO, so the library appends to NVM_LOG in the working directory, opening and closing the file for every line, on each L0 table add or delete and each column-compaction pick. The paper says the WAL lives on NVM, but the shipped script puts --wal_dir on the SSD, and utilities/nvm_mod contains no WAL code.

**Status:** Abandoned since August 2020 (3 open issues with no maintainer replies) and tied to discontinued Optane hardware. The code inherits RocksDB's GPLv2 / Apache-2.0 dual license and is best treated as a vendorable research reference for its column-compaction and L0-search design, not as a production engine.

[repo](https://github.com/PDS-Lab/MatrixKV) · [benchmark](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/atc20-yao.pdf)

##### Nova-LSM  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

LevelDB-based LSM KV server split into RDMA-linked compute and storage parts; beats LevelDB/RocksDB under skewed access.

**Beats:** RocksDB — With YCSB 1 KB records on CloudLab c6220 nodes (2x Xeon E5-2650v2, 64 GB, one 1 TB HDD, 56 Gbps InfiniBand), logging off for all systems and compiler and RocksDB version unstated, Nova-LSM beat LevelDB/RocksDB by 2.3x to 18x under Zipfian access on a 2 TB, 10-node database, and on one node reached 105x over a single LevelDB instance on SW50 Zipfian but only about 1.4x over 64-instance RocksDB*. Under Uniform access throughput was roughly equal or lower, and the RocksDB/LevelDB wrapper binaries (rocksdb_main, leveldb_main) are not in the repo, whose checked-in RocksDB script sets block_cache_mb=0.

**Known shortcoming:** The 105x outlier is one server with 10 GB under a skewed Zipfian workload against a single LevelDB instance; in the same cell it is ~1.4x vs the tuned RocksDB* and ~17.5x vs RocksDB (derived, Fig. 18a). The 2.3-18x headline is 2 TB across 10 nodes with RDMA. Repo builds with -g and no optimization level; stale since 2021.

**Known shortcoming:** Not embeddable: an RDMA server exposing only GET/PUT/SCAN over a socket with a Java YCSB client. Keys must be decimal integers (the lookup index is a dense array sized upper_key-lower_key). Delete writes an empty value (no tombstone); no write batches. Logging is off by default, the paper's index/Drange flags default to false, and the build uses -g without -O.

**Known shortcoming:** On uniform/CPU-bound workloads it is equal or 10-30% slower; RocksDB* beats it on SW50 on tmpfs; the 105x vs one LevelDB is about 1.4x vs RocksDB*. Abandoned 2021 with unanswered issues (ConnectX-5 segfault, local run); the RocksDB harness is not in the repo and ran with block_cache_mb=0.

**How:** It builds dynamic ranges (Dranges) inside each range, each with its own active memtables; writes are load-balanced across them, and Level0 SSTables from different Dranges do not overlap, so Level0-to-Level1 compaction runs in parallel and write stalls shrink. Hot keys stay in memory because memtables with fewer than 100 unique keys are merged rather than flushed, giving 65% less data written under skew. A lookup index sends each get to the single memtable or L0 SSTable that holds the latest version, and a range index lets scans skip stale versions of hot keys. SSTable blocks are scattered across rho StoCs, picked by power-of-d on disk-queue length, and compaction can be offloaded to StoCs.

**Use it when:**
- You have a multi-node RDMA/InfiniBand cluster and want to reproduce or extend the SIGMOD 2021 disaggregated-LSM results. The repo ships CloudLab profiles, configs and experiment scripts.
- Range-partitioned data with heavily skewed (Zipfian 0.99) access, where in a shared-nothing setup the node holding the hot range saturates its own disk. Pooling StoCs gave 9x or more over shared-nothing on a 1 TB, 10-node setup.
- Write-heavy ingest with large memtable memory that stalls on Level0 compaction. With 10 StoCs, raising LTC memtable memory from 32 MB to 2 GB took W100 Uniform from 8.9K to 246K ops/s.
- Scan-plus-write workloads on skewed keys (SW50 Zipfian), where LevelDB/RocksDB iterate every version of a hot key and Nova's range index skips them.
- As a design reference for ideas you want to port into your own LSM engine: Dranges/Tranges, the memtable lookup index, power-of-d SSTable placement.

**Skip it when:**
- As an embedded RocksDB/LevelDB replacement inside an application process. It is a server with a static partition config, integer-only keys, and no atomic write batches (listed as future work in the paper).
- Uniform-access, CPU-bound workloads. The paper reports a 15% range-index overhead on single-node SW50 Uniform and 20-30% lower throughput on CPU-intensive uniform workloads. On tmpfs it is 10-30% slower under Uniform, and RocksDB* (64 instances) beats it on SW50.
- Clusters without RDMA, or with newer NICs. The setup scripts target mlx4 (ConnectX-3) packages. Open issue #3 reports an IBV_WC_RETRY_EXC_ERR segfault on ConnectX-5 CloudLab nodes, and open issue #2 asks how to run it on one local machine. Neither has an answer.
- Anything that needs durability, deletes or ongoing support. Log replication is off by default (--log_record_mode=none), Delete does not write a tombstone, and the project has no releases or tags and no activity since 2021.

**Integration:** static lib + server binary (CMake builds libleveldb plus nova_server_main); used in practice as a standalone server · libibverbs (RDMA verbs; linked unconditionally), libevent, gflags (static .a required), fmt (script installs 6.1.2 from source), pthreads; optional crc32c and snappy. Clients use the separate Java NovaLSM-YCSB-Client binding. · C++11 (-std=c++11), CMake 3.9+; compiler hard-coded to /usr/bin/g++, version not documented · Linux only (tested on CloudLab R320 and c6220 x86-64 nodes); multi-node mode needs an RDMA NIC (scripts load mlx4/ConnectX-3 drivers)

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only when the bottleneck is one node's disk under skewed, range-partitioned load and you have an RDMA cluster to pool disks across nodes. Otherwise KVell, SplinterDB, PebblesDB, MatrixKV and Titan are far easier single-node engines to adopt (Titan loads as a RocksDB plugin; MatrixKV attacks the same write-stall problem with an NVM tier instead of Dranges).

**Gotchas:**
- Keys must be decimal-integer strings. The comparator (YCSBKeyComparator) and the Drange code parse keys with str_to_int. The server routes keys by numeric range from a static config file and asserts the key is within it. The lookup index is a dense array with one 4-byte slot for every integer in [lower_key, upper_key), allocated when the DB opens.
- Delete is not a real delete. DB::Delete calls WriteMemTablePool(key, Slice()), and every write path adds kTypeValue, so a deleted key reads back as an empty value rather than NotFound. The socket protocol has no DELETE at all.
- The paper's features are off by default. --enable_lookup_index, --enable_range_index and --enable_subrange all default to false, and logging defaults to none. The paper's comparison ran with logging disabled for every system. A failed Put hits NOVA_ASSERT and aborts the server.
- The default build is unoptimized: CMakeLists sets -g with no -O level and no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, and also builds -pg profiling binaries. nova_server_main multiplies --max_stoc_file_size_mb by 1024 only once; open issue #3 asks whether that is a bug, with no answer.

**Status:** Abandoned research prototype (last master commit 2021-06-20, a contributed db_bench branch merged 2021-12-15, no releases, two open issues unanswered) under BSD-3-Clause, so it can legally be copied, but it is tied to CloudLab/mlx4 scripts and is not realistically usable as a dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/HaoyuHuang/NovaLSM) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01305)

##### PebblesDB  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

LevelDB-API embedded KV store on a Fragmented LSM tree; several times RocksDB's random-write throughput with less write IO.

**Beats:** RocksDB — In the SOSP'17 paper's db_bench runs (Dell Precision 7810 with an unnamed Xeon 2.8 GHz, 16 GB RAM, Linux 4.4, ext4 on RAID0 of two Intel 750 SSDs, compression off, datasets 3x RAM; RocksDB version, compiler and flags not stated), single-threaded random inserts of 50M pairs (16 B keys, 1 KB values) reached 6.7x RocksDB's throughput with 2.4-3x less write IO, and the paper's insert table shows 56.18 vs 14.12 KOps/s (about 4x). Those runs used HyperLevelDB's default parameters (4 MB memtable) unless noted; with RocksDB's own defaults and 4 threads the lead shrinks to 3.3x, and on YCSB loads to 1.5-2x.

**Known shortcoming:** The 6.7x headline ran RocksDB on HyperLevelDB defaults (4 MB memtable); with RocksDB defaults and 4 threads it is 3.3x, and YCSB load 1.5-2x; RocksDB version unstated. Sequential inserts 3x slower; short seeks after compaction 30-47% slower. Open unfixed bugs: bloom-map thread race crashes (#19), torn-write power-loss corruption (#28), crashes on values over tens of KB (#29), small-KV memory leak (#24). Bloom filters are memory-only and rebuilt at open (~1.2 s/GB), and off unless filter_policy is set. Tuning is compile-time only; POSIX only; g++ 4.7-5 era. Abandoned since 2019; LevelDB API, only a partial RocksDB drop-in.

**How:** It uses a Fragmented Log-Structured Merge tree (FLSM): each level is split into skip-list-style 'guards', chosen by hashing each inserted key with MurmurHash3 and checking for runs of trailing set bits, with more guards at deeper levels and overlapping sstables allowed inside a guard. Compacting a guard merge-sorts its sstables and appends the resulting fragments to the child guards in the next level without rewriting sstables already there, so most data is written once per level (the last two levels are the exception). Less write IO means compaction finishes faster and foreground writes stall less. Reads get back to LSM speed through per-sstable bloom filters (about one sstable read per level), seek-triggered forced compaction, optional parallel seeks within a guard, and larger sstables that miss the table cache less often.

**Use it when:**
- Write-heavy ingest of random (hashed or UUID-like) keys into an on-SSD store much larger than RAM, where compaction write IO or SSD wear is the bottleneck. The paper measured 2.4-3x less write IO than RocksDB and 2.5x lower write amplification at 500M keys.
- Update-heavy workloads: in the paper, PebblesDB kept 75% of its initial insert throughput across two full update rounds, while the other stores fell to about 50%. Its update throughput was 2.15x HyperLevelDB's.
- Existing LevelDB or HyperLevelDB code that needs more random-write throughput with no API changes. Point-read throughput stayed equal or slightly higher in the paper's runs.
- Mixed YCSB-like workloads whose range scans do many next() calls after each seek, or that interleave writes. The paper measured only 6% overhead on YCSB workload E.
- Research or reproduction of FLSM ideas: the repo ships db_bench and YCSB bindings, and there are companion JNI and MongoDB (mongo-pebbles) layers.

**Skip it when:**
- Sequential or append-ordered key inserts: 3x lower throughput than HyperLevelDB, because guards force sstables to be split and rewritten where LSM stores just move files. The paper itself recommends RocksDB for this case.
- Short seek-heavy range queries on a fully compacted store: 30% slower than HyperLevelDB, 40% on an aged file system or with scarce RAM, and 47% on seeks for fully cached small datasets.
- Large values or tiny KV pairs: only 1 KB values were tested. Open issue #29 reports crashes with values over a few tens of KB, and issue #24 documents a memory leak with many small key-value pairs.
- Durability-critical deployments: open issue #28 shows torn log writes after a simulated power failure leaving partially persisted values after RepairDB. LevelDB fixed the same bug in 1.23.
- When you need RocksDB features or a maintained engine: there are no column families, transactions or compression other than Snappy. Median CPU was 171% vs 98-110% for the others, memory was about 300 MB above HyperLevelDB at 100M keys, and the code has been untouched since 2019.

**Integration:** shared lib (autotools/libtool builds libpebblesdb shared and static; a CMake target is also provided) · Snappy (optional, auto-detected) and pthreads; autotools with libtool, or CMake 3.9+, to build · C++11 (-std=c++11). The README says it was tested with g++-4.7, 4.9 and 5 and 'may not work' with other compilers. A 2019 commit fixed a g++-7 build error, and PR #18 for a g++-6 test build error was never merged. · POSIX only (LEVELDB_PLATFORM_POSIX). The old Travis CI built on Linux and macOS. atomic_pointer.h has x86, ARM-Linux and PPC paths and falls back to <atomic> elsewhere. No Windows port.

**Vs siblings:** Pick PebblesDB only if you already code against the LevelDB/HyperLevelDB API and want a no-code-change boost in random-write throughput with less write IO. For new designs that start from RocksDB, SplinterDB (maintained, 6-10x RocksDB inserts while matching it on small range queries) or Titan (a RocksDB plugin for large values) are safer, and KVell reports beating PebblesDB itself on both read- and write-dominated workloads.

**Gotchas:**
- Almost all tuning happens at compile time, not through Options. kMaxFilesPerGuardSentinel (default 2) is in db/dbformat.h, and the FILE_LEVEL_FILTER, SEEK_PARALLEL and DISABLE_SEEK_BASED_COMPACTION macros are in db/version_set.h. The guard-density constants top_level_bits=27 and bit_decrement=2 are hard-coded in db/write_batch.cc, and the paper says to raise top_level_bits above about 100M keys or guards become skewed.
- The per-sstable bloom filters live only in memory (a std::map). DB::Open rebuilds them by scanning every sstable: the paper measured about 1.2 s per GB, or 62 s for 52 GB. They are built only if Options.filter_policy is set, and it defaults to NULL, so without NewBloomFilterPolicy the main read optimization is off.
- Guard deletion is not implemented, so deleted key ranges leave empty guards behind. The paper saw no read slowdown with 9,000 empty guards, but they are never reclaimed.
- Everything is declared in namespace leveldb with LevelDB's class names, so linking it into one binary with LevelDB would likely clash (not documented). It is also unrelated to CockroachDB's Go 'Pebble' despite the similar name.

**Status:** Abandoned since the last commit on 2019-08-03, with 13 issues and PRs open (including crash-consistency and thread-safety bugs) and a CockroachDB Pebble author calling it 'a research project and ... dead' on HN in 2020; it is BSD-3-Clause and about 9.1k changed lines on top of HyperLevelDB, so it can be vendored, but you own the fixes.

[repo](https://github.com/utsaslab/pebblesdb) · [benchmark](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~vijay/papers/sosp17-pebblesdb.pdf)

##### SplinterDB  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Embedded C key-value store for NVMe SSDs; paper reports 6-10x RocksDB insert throughput and 2-2.6x point-query throughput.

**Beats:** RocksDB — The USENIX ATC'20 paper replayed YCSB-derived traces (load and A-F, 24B keys, 100B and 1KiB values) against an unnamed version of RocksDB (and PebblesDB) on a Dell R720 with a 32-core 2.0 GHz Xeon and an Optane 905p SSD, memory capped at 4GiB by a cgroup: SplinterDB was 6-10x faster on inserts, 2-2.6x on point queries, roughly equal on short scans, with half the write amplification. Compiler and flags were not reported; the repo's tests/functional/ycsb_test.c is a SplinterDB trace replayer, but the traces and the RocksDB side of the harness are not in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** No crash recovery: log replay is 'not wired yet' in src/core.c, an uncleanly closed DB refuses to mount, WAL off by default, no fsync API. ~15% slower than RocksDB on YCSB E short scans; the paper names no RocksDB version, CPU model, compiler or flags; traces and the RocksDB harness are not public. Linux-only (libaio), x86-64 CI only, Release uses -march=native -ffast-math. Open critical assert on small-pair inserts (#560) and segfault on YCSB-C (#585) since 2023. No releases; 'not for production before 1.0'.
