The default hasher is gxhash (AES-NI/NEON) instead of the upstream's SipHash-1-3.

**Use it when:**
- A Rust service needs a 'definitely absent' pre-check with deletions for a key set that grows without a known final size, for example in front of an index or WAL write path, as the README's example shows.
- String or byte-slice keys (the bench used random 8-128 byte keys) on hardware with AES instructions, where hashing dominates the cost of a lookup.
- Lookups that are mostly for keys that are present. The deferred second hash pays off most there, because most positive lookups hit the first bucket.
- You already use sile's scalable_cuckoo_filter and want the same layout and memory footprint (both 353 KB in the bench) with faster operations, and you can rename a few calls.
- Servers or Apple Silicon builds where you control RUSTFLAGS (e.g. -C target-cpu=native).

**Skip it when:**
- Portable x86-64 binaries built without extra RUSTFLAGS. The default gxhash feature does not compile there, and turning it off falls back to std's SipHash, which voids the published numbers.
- Static or rarely changing sets. In the bench it used about 29 bits per key (353 KB for 100k keys at 0.17% measured FPP, because bucket counts round up to a power of two and the filter was 38% full), and immutable xor/binary-fuse filters are far smaller.
- Workloads dominated by keys that are absent. These were never benchmarked; every miss hashes twice and probes both buckets in every layer, so the cost grows with the number of growth layers.
- Concurrent writers. There is no concurrent API: mutation takes &mut self, so you need an external lock or sharding.
- Projects that are strict about maturity or licensing: 3 stars, about 1.1k downloads, MulanPSL-2.0 declared only in Cargo.toml and the README with no LICENSE file, and the upstream's MIT notice is not reproduced.

**Integration:** crate · fastrand, bitcode (derive); gxhash by default (optional); museair optional · Rust 2024 edition (rustc 1.85+); no rust-version declared; benchmarked on rustc 1.98.0 · Default gxhash feature: x86/x86-64 with aes+sse2 or ARM with aes+neon enabled at compile time; a stock x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu build fails. Built out of the box on Apple M2 Max (the author's bench machine). With default-features = false or museair it should build anywhere Rust std does (not tested).

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over xorf (static xor/binary fuse, smaller and faster but immutable) or fastbloom (no deletion) when a Rust set must take inserts and deletes and grow without a known size. The C++ efficient/cuckoofilter reference and CGCL's Dynamic Cuckoo Filter cover the same ground outside Rust, and no head-to-head numbers against them exist.

**Gotchas:**
- `cargo add autoscale_cuckoo_filter` does not build on default x86-64 targets. gxhash 3.5 raises compile_error! unless aes+sse2 are enabled, and docs.rs builds of 0.5.26 and 0.5.27 failed for this reason, so recent versions have no hosted docs. Set RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" (or +aes,+sse2) or use default-features = false.
- The README is wrong about the hasher and serialization. It says the default hasher is RapidHash and advertises optional serde, but the code uses gxhash::GxHasher (std SipHash with no hash feature) and supports bitcode only. The hasher field is skipped when encoding, so a filter built with a custom or seeded hasher decodes with H::default() and returns wrong answers. The gxhash docs also say hashes may change across its major versions and warn that the unseeded default hasher is open to DoS.
- The branchless one-load bucket path only applies while fingerprint bits x entries <= 64 (16-bit fingerprints at 4 entries). Each growth layer adds one fingerprint bit, so an FPP below about 2.4e-4, or a fourth layer at the default 0.001, falls back to a per-entry loop.
- The usual cuckoo deletion hazards apply, and the README documents them at length. `add` stores duplicates. Removing a key that was never inserted can delete a colliding fingerprint and cause a false negative. `len()` is approximate.

**Status:** Actively released (19 crates.io versions from 2025-12-29 to 0.5.27 on 2026-09-06), but it is a 3-star monorepo crate whose per-crate CI file sits in a subdirectory that GitHub Actions does not run. It is about 2,000 lines of Rust including tests, so it is easy to vendor under MulanPSL-2.0 once the gxhash build flags are handled.

[repo](https://github.com/js0-site/rust/tree/main/autoscale_cuckoo_filter) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/js0-site/rust/main/autoscale_cuckoo_filter/README.md)

##### BuRR (Ribbon Filter)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Static bumped-ribbon retrieval/filter library: 0.06-1.4% space overhead against Xor's 23% and Bloom's 44%+, with slower sequential queries.

**Beats:** Bloom filter, xor filter — Table 2 of arXiv 2109.01892 (lorenzhs/fastfilter_cpp harness, clang++ 11 -O3 -march=native, 64-core AMD EPYC 7702) shows BuRR 2-bit w=64 at 0.25% space overhead at about 1% FPR, against 23% for Xor, 14.4% for Xor+, 40-46% for Cuckoo12 and 45-52% for blocked Bloom. At 10^8 keys, run sequentially, it built faster than Xor (115 vs 159 ns/key) but queried about 2x slower (82/74 vs 41/41 ns); only in the 64-thread, 1280-filter run did it also beat Xor on queries (215 vs 386-392 ns). Plain Bloom is not in the table: the claim that BuRR Pareto-dominates it comes from the paper's parallel-workload summary (Figure 1).

**Known shortcoming:** Static only (bulk build, no insert/delete). Sequential queries ~2x slower than Xor at 1e8 keys and ~4x at 1e6; only the 64-thread run beats Xor. Linux/glibc with GCC/Clang only (bits/stdint-uintn.h, __uint128_t); needs system libxxhash plus submodules; CI builds but runs no tests. Duplicate keys are checked only by assert (with NDEBUG the base layer likely retries forever, from code reading). uint32 index caps one structure at ~4.29B slots; retrieval values over 16 bits need a new instantiation; a non-inline operator<< in a header likely causes duplicate-symbol link errors; weak serialization; ~17 B/key peak build memory. A GCC 15 -O3 miscompile was fixed on main only on 2026-09-13 (the parallel branch lacks it).

**How:** Ribbon ('Rapid Incremental Boolean Banding ON the fly') gives each key a w-bit (32/64/128) random coefficient window at a hashed start slot. On-the-fly GF(2) Gaussian elimination keeps a banded row-echelon system using word-wide XORs, and back-substitution then produces the solution. Bumping keeps this compact. Start positions are grouped into buckets of about w^2/log w and radix-sorted by bucket (ips2ra). When a bucket hits a linear dependency, the keys below a threshold are rolled back and pushed to a smaller recursive layer, and only 1-2 bits of threshold metadata are kept per bucket. That lets the table be overloaded (fewer slots than keys), so almost no slots stay empty. A query hashes once (a 64-bit master hash code, remixed per layer) and checks the bucket threshold. Each result bit is then the parity of the coefficients ANDed with an interleaved, column-major solution block, touching at most two adjacent blocks, and filter queries stop at the first mismatching bit.

**Use it when:**
- Immutable key sets built in one bulk pass (read-only indexes, per-file filters, shipped lookup tables) where bits per key matter most. At about 1% FPR, BuRR 2-bit w=64 measured 0.25% over the n*r-bit lower bound, against Xor's 23% and blocked Bloom's 45-52%.
- Retrieval / static-function use: storing 1-16 bits per key without the keys, for example as a building block for perfect hashing or compact key-to-small-value maps where non-member queries do not need to be detected.
- Many sharded filters queried from all cores, where memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. In the paper's 64-thread run over 1280 filters of 10^7 keys, BuRR 2-bit w=64 answered queries in 215 ns (Xor r=8: 386/392 ns) and built at 190 ns/key (Xor: 586).
- Large inputs (around 10^8 keys) where build time matters: BuRR 2-bit w=64 constructed at 115 ns/key, against Xor's 159 ns/key, sequentially.
- Linux builds with GCC or Clang, where you can vendor templated headers, git submodules and a system libxxhash.

**Skip it when:**
- Any need for inserts, deletes or counting after construction. The whole key set must be present at build time; blocked Bloom, cuckoo or Prefix Filter handle incremental inserts.
- Single-threaded, latency-critical lookups, especially on cache-resident filters. At n=10^6, positive/negative queries took 19/24 ns, against Xor's 5/5 and blocked Bloom's 3/3. At n=10^8 they took 82/74 ns, against Xor's 41/41 and blocked Bloom's 24/24.
- Large r (very low false-positive rates). Query and build time grow with the number of result bits, and the paper's heatmap hands the large-r region to Xor and cuckoo filters.
- Memory-tight builds. Construction holds an 8-byte hash per key plus a CoeffRow and a ResultRow per slot (about 17 bytes/key for w=64, r=8) before BackSubst compacts to roughly r bits/key, on top of your own input array.
- Windows/MSVC, macOS, or teams wanting a hardened library: headers include glibc's <bits/stdint-uintn.h>, configuration is compile-time and, in a maintainer's words, 'a bit of a mess' (issue #3), and the project is small research code (52 stars, 4 issues).

**Integration:** source-drop (templated headers plus sorter.cpp compiled to sorter.o with explicit ips2ra instantiations, linked with a CMake-built libtlx.a; the third-party SimpleRibbon repo wraps a few configs as a CMake static library) · system libxxhash >= 0.8.0 (XXH3); git submodules tlx (built and linked), ips2ra (radix sort), DySECT (cuckoo table for 1+-bit thresholds), pcg-cpp; vendored RocksDB headers; pthread; gtest for tests. CI also installs libtbb-dev. · C++17 (Makefile -std=c++17 -Werror). CI builds (build only, no tests) with GCC 10-14 and Clang 16-18 on Ubuntu 24.04, and the paper used clang++ 11. GCC 15 -O3 miscompiled until the 2026-09-13 fix (issue #4). · Linux/glibc with GCC or Clang: the code uses <bits/stdint-uintn.h>, __uint128_t, ssize_t and GCC builtins. x86-64 is the only tested target (the paper used AMD EPYC, and the Makefile sets -march=native). BuRR's own code has no ISA-specific intrinsics, but aarch64, macOS and MSVC are not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick BuRR over Xor/binary fuse (xor_singleheader) when space dominates: 0.1-0.5% overhead against about 23% for xor and 7.5-12.5% for binary fuse. Also pick it when you need retrieval of small values, or when many shards are queried under heavy parallel load. Prefer xor_singleheader for the fastest single-threaded queries from one dependency-free header, and Prefix Filter when keys arrive incrementally on AVX-512 hardware.

**Gotchas:**
- Deduplicate input. Unique master hash codes are only checked with assert(), so -DNDEBUG builds skip the check. By our reading of the code, a duplicate row is always linearly dependent, so the non-bumping base layer keeps retrying with 0.05 more slots per item and never succeeds. Distinct keys whose 64-bit XXH3 hashes collide behave the same way.
- Size limits are compile-time. RConfig fixes Index to uint32_t, so one structure is capped at about 4.29 billion slots unless you write a custom config (issue #3). Retrieval presets link only against sorter.cpp's explicit Sorter instantiations for 8- and 16-bit values, so wider values need an added instantiation.
- Serialization is 'not meant as a robust storage and transfer format' (binary_format.txt): there are no corruption checks and the hash function is not recorded. Deserializing with a different compile-time config throws config_error, and endianness conversion is untested.
- Header hygiene: config.hpp defines a non-inline operator<< for __uint128_t inside namespace std, so including ribbon.hpp from two translation units should give duplicate-symbol link errors. The default configs also print construction timings (DefaultConfig::log = true). The GCC 15 miscompile workaround (XXH_FORCE_MEMORY_ACCESS=0) is on main only; the 'parallel' branch is 3 commits behind main.

**Status:** Active but low-traffic research code: a few maintenance commits a year, the latest (2026-09-13) fixing a GCC 15 -O3 miscompile; all 4 issues are closed. It is Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor, but you must wire up submodules, a system libxxhash and compile-time configs yourself, or use the SimpleRibbon CMake wrapper.

[repo](https://github.com/lorenzhs/BuRR) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.01892)

##### Cascaded Learned Bloom Filter (CLBF)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Learned Bloom filter: pruned boosted-tree cascade plus Bloom filters; less memory than Bloom/PLBF, faster rejects than PLBF.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — arXiv 2502.03696 v2 setup: Intel i9-11900H, GCC 11.4.0 -O3, single-threaded; 100-round depth-4 XGBoost; 10,000 held-out non-keys. At the same FPR, CLBF used up to 17% less total memory (model plus filters) than the best PLBF configuration (Ember, F=0.005). Its mean reject time was up to 14.6x lower than PLBF's at about 9,250 kB on Higgs, and 65x in an appendix shallow-NN variant. Against the classical fastfilter_cpp Bloom filter it is mostly just plotted; the one quoted number is Kitsune [SSDP] at F=0.01, 3.3 kB vs 1,684 kB, an easy dataset. Reject time includes inference but is measured in a batch over pre-extracted feature vectors, so feature extraction is not counted.

**Known shortcoming:** Code (Apache-2.0, C++) was found by the verifier at github.com/atsukisato/CascadedLBF; the paper reports GCC 11.4 -O3 on an i9-11900H.

**Known shortcoming:** Research code, not a library: 6 commits, 0 stars, no CI/tests; single add()/contains() throw 'Not implemented' (batch only, static set). The BloomFilter destructor is commented out (never freed; copies share bit arrays); non-inline headers; fixed /tmp scratch files clobber concurrent builds. Needs a trained XGBoost model and per-query feature vectors; changed features cause false negatives.

**Known shortcoming:** The only quoted Bloom comparison is an appendix result on an easy dataset (Kitsune SSDP 3.3 kB vs 1,684 kB); the 17%/14.6x/65x figures are all vs PLBF, and reject time excludes feature extraction.

**How:** The query runs through a cascade of up to D boosted weak learners. Before each tree, a 'trunk' Bloom filter rejects non-keys without running inference. After each tree, a query whose running score exceeds a threshold exits early to a 'branch' Bloom filter. Queries that survive reach a PLBF-style final stage with K=8 score-partitioned Bloom filters. A dynamic program over discretized FPRs (powers of 0.5, 20 levels) chooses how many trees to keep, which prunes an over-sized ensemble, and sets each filter's FPR. It minimizes lambda*memory/M_BF + (1-lambda)*reject_time/R_BF at target FPR F. Thresholds come from quantile candidates, with optional Optuna refinement. The memory saving comes from right-sizing model versus filters; the reject-time saving comes from early rejection, whereas PLBF runs the whole ensemble on every query.

**Use it when:**
- Static blocklist-style sets whose members are predictable from features: malicious URLs or files, intrusion-traffic signatures (the paper's URL, Ember and Kitsune data). Memory must be scarce and rebuilds rare.
- You would otherwise use a PLBF or Sandwiched LBF with boosted trees and don't want to hand-tune the tree count. CLBF prunes a 100-tree XGBoost model to the depth D that minimizes total memory.
- The filter is a pre-filter in front of an expensive exact lookup and non-key reject latency matters. Lower lambda below 1 to trade memory for faster rejects (lambda=0 falls back to a plain Bloom filter).
- Reproducing or benchmarking learned Bloom filters: Docker scripts rebuild CLBF and C++ baselines (Bloom, PLBF, Sandwiched LBF, G-PLBF, ELBF, PHBF, HABF) on 14 datasets.

**Skip it when:**
- Keys carry no predictive features (random IDs, hashes). No classifier can separate them, and the optimizer's best case is a plain Bloom filter; use a xor, ribbon or blocked Bloom filter instead.
- The key set changes often. Single-key add() and contains() throw 'Not implemented', and the paper says updates shift the distribution and need a rebuild. Construction includes model training and calibration: even Sandwiched LBF builds 180x-1,100,000x slower than a Bloom filter, and CLBF is 1.003x-1.23x on top of that.
- The query distribution can drift from the calibration non-keys, or is adversarial. The FPR target is met only in expectation on calibration data.
- You need a production library. It is research code with 6 commits and 0 stars, no tests or CI of its own, filter memory that is never freed, hard-coded /tmp scratch files, and headers that link from only one translation unit.
- You need the smallest possible filters: every internal filter is a classical Bloom filter (about 1.44x the information-theoretic bound). The paper says any AMQ could be used, but the code hard-wires Bloom.

**Integration:** source-drop · XGBoost C API (libxgboost, dmlc/xgboost git submodule), nlohmann/json, and the vendored fastfilter_cpp Bloom filter (modified for runtime bits-per-key). The experiments additionally need Eigen3 (PHBF baseline) and Python (preprocessing, Optuna variant). · C++17, CMake 3.12+ for the example; paper and Docker image use GCC 11.4.0 on Ubuntu 22.04; fast range reduction uses __uint128_t (GCC/Clang), with a modulo fallback otherwise · Tested on Linux x86-64 (Docker Ubuntu 22.04; experiments build with -march=native). The example CMake also links libxgboost.dylib on macOS. Hard-coded /tmp paths assume POSIX.

**Vs siblings:** Over PLBF (kapilvaidya24/PLBF), pick CLBF when your model is a boosted ensemble: at matched memory it rejects up to 14.6x faster and needs up to 17% less memory, with no hand-picked tree count. The paper skipped Ada-BF because PLBF dominates it. Pick non-learned siblings (Xor/xor_singleheader, BuRR, Prefix Filter, ChainedFilter) when keys lack predictive features, the set changes, or you need a maintained library.

**Gotchas:**
- Every query must pass the exact feature vector used when the key was inserted. The path through the cascade depends on the running score, so changed features can produce a false negative. Keys are uint64; the experiments hash strings with djb2 first.
- The vendored BloomFilter holds a raw new[] array and its destructor is commented out. Filters are never freed, and copying a CLBF (the example does clbf = calibration_manager.configure_lbf_assembly(...)) gives shallow copies that share bit arrays.
- Headers define non-inline functions and a global variable (warn_too_many_false_positives). Include them from exactly one .cpp file, or linking fails with duplicate symbols.
- The custom tree evaluator ignores XGBoost's default_left, so NaN features always go right and scores can differ from XGBoost's own output. Configuration also times a plain Bloom filter (n keys, 1M queries) at build time, so with lambda < 1 the chosen layout depends on the machine.

**Status:** Active research code: 6 commits from January to August 2026, 0 stars, no issues, Apache-2.0. You can copy src/ plus the vendored Bloom header and link libxgboost, but it is not a packaged library. The arXiv v2 abstract links this repo.

[repo](https://github.com/atsukisato/CascadedLBF) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03696)

##### Cuckoo-GPU  `C++`  `BSL-1.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only CUDA cuckoo filter with lock-free batched insert/query/delete; outpaces multi-threaded CPU cuckoo filters and GPU TCF/GQF.

**Beats:** cuckoo filter — On an NVIDIA GH200 (H100, 96 GB HBM3, CUDA 13.0; Meson -O3, C++20; host compiler unstated) at 95% load with 16-bit fingerprints and uniform random 64-bit keys already in device memory, Cuckoo-GPU inserted 175x faster and answered positive queries 351x faster than the 120-thread Partitioned Cuckoo Filter on a Xeon W9-3595X at 4M items (L2-resident), and 69x and 143x faster at 268M items (DRAM-resident); the CPU side times a bulk construct(), GPU timings exclude host-to-device transfer, and negative queries run at roughly half the positive-query rate in the DRAM case. Against GPU filters on the same GH200 it was 2.1-378x faster than TCF and GQF but slower than the append-only Blocked Bloom filter on inserts.

**Known shortcoming:** The ~350x is mostly the GPU-vs-CPU hardware jump (GH200 / RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell vs a partitioned cuckoo filter on a 120-thread Xeon W9-3595X); against the GPU Bloom filter GBBF in DRAM it is 0.7x on inserts and 0.9x on queries. Host compiler version unstated.

**Known shortcoming:** Kernels receive the host-side filter object pointer, so they likely need HMM/ATS unified memory and fault elsewhere (inferred from code, undocumented). A failed insert (>500 evictions) drops a carried fingerprint of an older key, causing false negatives (no stash); errors call exit(); every call synchronizes the stream; concurrent query with insert/delete gives torn reads.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarks time keys already on the device (no transfers) and bulk-construct the CPU baseline. Slower than cuCollections' blocked Bloom filter on inserts (0.35x/0.7x); FPR 0.045% vs 0.011% for the CPU partitioned cuckoo filter; the XOR placement policy forces power-of-two sizing. CUDA/Linux only, v0.1 with no tags.

**How:** Each key gets one thread that does partial-key cuckoo hashing with xxHash64: the upper 32 bits give the fingerprint and the lower 32 bits give the primary bucket; buckets hold 16 slots packed into 64-bit words, so SWAR bit tricks find empty or matching slots and each insert or delete is a single-word atomic compare-and-swap, with no locks. Unlike GQF and TCF, which organise memory for cache locality, it accepts random access and relies on HBM/GDDR bandwidth. Queries use non-atomic 128-bit vector loads (256-bit ld.global.nc on compute capability 10.0+), so a positive hit often needs one memory transaction. At high load a breadth-first eviction heuristic first checks up to bucketSize/2 candidates for a free alternate slot before extending a chain, which the paper says cut tail eviction lengths and gave up to 25% higher insert throughput than greedy DFS on GH200.

**Use it when:**
- Your keys are fixed-size integers (for example 64-bit IDs or 2-bit-packed 31-mers), they are already in GPU memory, and you need approximate membership with deletions in batches of millions of keys or more.
- You now use a dynamic GPU filter such as GQF or TCF. On the same GH200 the README reports 2.1-4x faster inserts and 9.9-35x faster queries than TCF, and 2.6-378x faster operations than GQF, at 16-bit fingerprints and 95% load.
- The filter ranges from a few MiB (L2-resident) up to tens of GiB on a high-bandwidth GPU (H100/GH200 HBM3, RTX PRO 6000 GDDR7), or is spread over several GPUs with FilterMultiGPU.
- The pipeline is throughput-oriented, such as k-mer indexing, GPU join/semi-join prefiltering or deduplication, and one kernel launch plus a stream sync per batch is acceptable.
- You run near capacity (about 95% load) and still want steady insert throughput. The BFS eviction policy is designed for this case.

**Skip it when:**
- You have no NVIDIA GPU. The library is CUDA-only, and most of the quoted 69-351x gain over the CPU filter comes from the GH200 vs Xeon hardware jump.
- Your workload only inserts and queries. The append-only cuCollections Blocked Bloom filter inserts faster (Cuckoo-GPU runs at 0.35x of its speed L2-resident and 0.7x DRAM-resident) and roughly matches on DRAM-resident queries, though its FPR is much higher (2.5-6% vs about 0.045%).
- Keys start on the host or arrive in small batches. The benchmarks keep keys in device memory, excluding transfer time, and every API call ends in cudaStreamSynchronize, so small batches pay launch and sync overhead.
- You need a very low or finely tuned FPR per bit. The default 16-bit tags in 16-slot buckets give about 0.045% FPR vs about 0.005-0.011% for the CPU partitioned cuckoo filter with 4-slot buckets, and tags can only be 8/16/32 bits with power-of-two bucket sizes.
- You need queries to run at the same time as inserts or deletes (the paper warns of torn reads), variable-length or string keys, Windows support, or a versioned stable release. The Meson project version is 0.1 and there are no tags.

**Integration:** header-only · The single-GPU filter needs only the CUDA Toolkit (Thrust, CUB, libcu++). FilterMultiGPU needs gossip (Funatiq/gossip), and the top-level meson.build always pulls it in. The experimental IPC server uses POSIX shared memory, semaphores and cudaIpcMemHandle. Tests and benchmarks also pull cuCollections, BGHT, saltsystemslab gpu-filters (TCF/GQF), tum-db partitioned-filters, Google Benchmark, GoogleTest, CLI11 and KMC as Meson wraps. · The README requires CUDA Toolkit 12.9+, a C++20 compiler and Meson 1.3+ if you use its build. The dev shell moved to CUDA 13.2 in June 2026, and the paper used CUDA 12.9 and 13.0. The project compiles with -std=c++20 --expt-relaxed-constexpr --expt-extended-lambda, so mirror those flags. The host compiler version is not documented. · NVIDIA GPUs only. The build targets sm_80, sm_90 and sm_120 plus compute_75 PTX, and 256-bit loads are used only on compute capability 10.0+. Evaluated on Linux x86-64 (EPYC 7713P + RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell) and aarch64 (GH200). Windows is not documented, and the IPC path is POSIX-only. Single-GPU kernels appear to need HMM or ATS (see gotchas).

**Vs siblings:** Every catalogued sibling (Prefix Filter, Xor/xor_singleheader, BuRR, Morton, Vacuum, Windowed Cuckoo, Ada-BF, SuRF, ChainedFilter) runs on the CPU. Pick Cuckoo-GPU when both the keys and the code that consumes the filter are already on an NVIDIA GPU and you need deletes at billions of operations per second. If keys live on the host, a CPU cuckoo variant such as Morton or Vacuum avoids the transfer and the GPU dependency, and Xor/BuRR/Prefix target lower space or faster builds.

**Gotchas:**
- Kernels receive `this`, the host-side Filter object (the README and tests create it on the stack), and read numBuckets and d_buckets through that pointer. This only works if the GPU can read pageable host memory: ATS on Grace Hopper, or HMM (per NVIDIA: Linux with the open r535+ driver, CUDA 12.2+, kernel 6.1.24+, x86-64). Elsewhere you should expect illegal-address faults. FilterMultiGPU avoids the problem by placing each Filter in cudaMallocManaged memory. This is inferred from the code and not documented.
- A failed insert (after maxEvictions, default 500) is not rolled back. The new fingerprint has already been swapped in, and the one being carried, which belongs to a previously stored key, is dropped, so a reported failure can cause a false negative for a different key. There is no victim stash. The repo's own NearCapacityInsertion test only requires 99% of inserted keys to be found, and the paper lists insertion failures at extreme load as a limitation that needs a fallback.
- Every CUDA error inside the library, including a failed cudaMalloc in the constructor, goes through CUCKOO_CUDA_CALL, which prints and calls exit(). There are no exceptions or error codes to handle.
- The default XorAltBucketPolicy rounds the bucket count up to a power of two, so memory can almost double just past a 2^n boundary. OffsetAltBucketPolicy avoids this at the cost of one fingerprint bit; it has about 34% slower positive queries when L2-resident and equal speed when DRAM-resident. Keys are hashed as raw bytes (xxHash64 over sizeof(T)), so use trivially copyable key types without padding. Thread indices are 32-bit, so keep each batch under 2^32 keys.

**Status:** Actively maintained research companion code for an ACM-published paper: last commit 2026-09-13, 40 stars, one merged PR, no open issues, no tagged releases. It is BSL-1.0 and header-only, so vendoring include/cuckoogpu/ is easy, but expect research-grade APIs that call exit() on errors.

[repo](https://github.com/tdortman/Cuckoo-GPU) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tdortman/Cuckoo-GPU#performance)

##### cuSBF (GPU Minimizer-Aware Super Bloom Filter)  `CUDA/C++ (header-only)`  `BSL-1.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only CUDA Super Bloom filter for DNA k-mers; 7.6-9.1x faster than cuCollections' GPU blocked Bloom on RTX PRO 6000.

**Beats:** Bloom filter (NVIDIA cuCollections GPU Blocked Bloom Filter, GBBF) — On an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (96 GB GDDR7, AMD EPYC 7713P host, CUDA 13.2, -O3), Google Benchmark runs of Config<31,28,16,4> at 16 bits per k-mer (256 MiB filter for C. elegans, 8 GiB for CHM13), with device-resident input and transfers untimed, showed cuSBF inserting 9.1x/8.2x and querying 7.7x/7.6x faster than cuco::bloom_filter<uint64_t> on its default policy, which was fed pre-packed 64-bit k-mers. The same unreviewed, first-party preprint reports only 1.37-2.36x on GH200.

**Known shortcoming:** GPU-only (CUDA 13.2); the headline ranges are vs other GPU filters (Cuckoo-GPU 7.8-3427x, GQF 11-69x) and vary widely by workload.

**Known shortcoming:** The 9.1x lead holds only with input already on the GPU; with host input over PCIe 87-94% of throughput is lost (paper). On GH200 (HBM3) the lead over cuCollections is only 1.37-2.36x. Worse FPR than Cuckoo-GPU (~24x) and the CPU Super Bloom (~30x) at 2^31 bits; size rounds up to power-of-two shards (5 GiB becomes 8 GiB).

**Known shortcoming:** Sequence-only API (k-mers of DNA sequences, no arbitrary keys), forward strand only (no canonical/reverse complement), any non-ACGT byte drops spanning k-mers; no delete/merge/save. Immature: v0.4.0, no tags, 7 stars; Linux, sm_80+, CUDA 13.1+ only.

**How:** It implements the Super Bloom filter: a minimizer hash picks one 256-bit shard per k-mer, so a super-k-mer (about 8.5 consecutive k-mers at k=31, m=16) hits the same shard, and the Findere scheme sets H bits for each of the k-s+1 overlapping s-mers. Each thread block loads a coalesced shared-memory tile of T+k-1 symbols; inserts OR together the masks of adjacent same-shard lanes with CUB HeadSegmentedReduce so only the run head issues four 64-bit atomicOr calls, and queries use __match_any_sync so one lane loads the shard (256-bit ld.global.nc on Blackwell) and shuffles it to its peers. Shards are split into four 64-bit sectors (hash i sets a bit in word i mod 4) using bit-slices of one 64-bit hash, with compile-time-unrolled loops. The paper's speed-of-light profile shows cuSBF compute-bound at about 85% SM throughput on insert, while cuco's blocked Bloom drops below 10% SM throughput once the filter outgrows L2.

**Use it when:**
- GPU-resident genomic pipelines that need k-mer presence tests over whole reads or genomes (contamination or host-read screening, read-classification pre-filters) with the sequence bytes already in device memory
- DNA with k <= 32, ideally the paper's Pareto point k=31, s=28, m=16, H=4, and filters from hundreds of MiB to several GiB (benchmarked at 256 MiB and 8 GiB, 16 bits per inserted k-mer)
- Append-only workloads that bulk-insert and then bulk-query, where throughput matters more than single-key latency
- Discrete Ampere-or-newer NVIDIA GPUs with many SMs (the largest lead was on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell), or cache-coherent CPU-GPU systems such as GH200 when the input starts in host memory
- When you want a lower false-positive rate than cuco's blocked Bloom at the same memory: README shows 0.848% vs 3.069% at 21.4 bits per k-mer

**Skip it when:**
- General keys (integers, strings, URLs): the API only indexes k-mers cut from sequences, with no per-key insert or contains
- You need deletions, counting, merging two filters, or saving and loading a filter: none exist (the only reset is clear())
- Host-resident input on a PCIe GPU: the paper measured an 87-94% throughput loss on the RTX PRO 6000 (6.3/7.1 GKmer/s host input vs 48.5/112 GKmer/s device-resident). On GH200 (HBM3), the lead over cuco shrinks to 1.37-2.36x, and cuSBF itself ran slower there than on the RTX PRO 6000
- Tight false-positive budgets: at 2^31 bits Cuckoo-GPU has about 24x fewer false positives and the CPU Super Bloom about 30x fewer. A k-mer one base away from an indexed k-mer falls back to the single-s-mer false-positive rate
- Non-Linux hosts, pre-Ampere GPUs, CUDA older than 13.1, or projects that need a mature dependency: v0.4.0, no git tags or releases, one main author, 7 stars

**Integration:** header-only · CUDA Toolkit 13.1+ (Thrust, CUB, libcu++ cuda::std::expected) and zlib (for gzip FASTX input; pulled in as a Meson subproject). Benchmarks and tests also pull cuCollections, Google Benchmark, GoogleTest, CLI11, saltsystemslab gpu-filters, Cuckoo-GPU and a vendored Rust CPU Super Bloom. · CUDA 13.1+ nvcc (-std=c++20 --expt-extended-lambda --expt-relaxed-constexpr); GCC or Clang host compiler with C++20 including std::format, which the headers call; Meson >= 1.3 plus Ninja for the bundled build · Linux x86-64 or aarch64 with an NVIDIA GPU of compute capability 8.0+ (Ampere, Ada, Hopper, Blackwell; default gencode sm_80/sm_90/sm_120). WSL2 is described as a reasonable dev setup. Native Windows and macOS are not supported.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Cuckoo-GPU (same author) for insert-heavy, duplicate-heavy genomic k-mer streams where deletions don't matter (80x to 3427x faster inserts, about 8x faster queries on the RTX PRO 6000), and pick Cuckoo-GPU for deletions, arbitrary 64-bit keys, or lower FPR at mid-size budgets. The CPU filters (CQF, Xor, BuRR, Prefix) are the better fit unless you are on an NVIDIA GPU with sequence data.

**Gotchas:**
- Capacity is rounded up to a power-of-two number of 256-bit shards, so a 5 GiB request allocates 8 GiB. You size the filter in bits yourself (the paper used 16 bits per inserted k-mer); there is no sizing helper based on item count or target FPR.
- The headers have no canonical or reverse-complement k-mer handling, so the filter is strand-specific. Canonicalize yourself or insert both strands. Any non-ACGT byte (N, IUPAC codes) invalidates every k-mer spanning it, and those windows query as 0. A/C/G/T are case-insensitive.
- Config limits: HashCount must be 4, 8, 12 or 16; k times bits-per-symbol must be <= 64 (k <= 32 for DNA, 12 for 5-bit protein); s and m must be <= k. Each Config is a separate type and kernel instantiation. The paper notes that larger alphabets force short minimizers and raise the FPR.
- The constructor throws std::runtime_error through CUSBF_UNWRAP(clear()) if clear() fails, and the thrust allocation can throw; other calls return Result. The CUSBF_TRY/CUSBF_UNWRAP macros use GNU statement expressions. Per-k-mer queries produce one output byte per k-mer, about 3 GB of device memory for a 3.1B k-mer genome.

**Status:** Active single-author research code (last commit 2026-09-26; versions 0.2.0 to 0.4.0 bumped in meson.build during Aug 2026 but never tagged), with 7 stars and no issues or PRs; BSL-1.0 and header-only, so it is easy to vendor at a pinned commit.

[repo](https://github.com/tdortman/cuSBF) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tdortman/cuSBF#performance)

##### fastfilter (hexops)  `Zig`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Zig binary fuse and xor filters; binary fuse builds 1.7-3.8x faster than xor, with smaller filters and equal lookups.

**Beats:** xor filter — The README's own harness (src/benchmark.zig, Zig 0.12.0-dev.706, -O ReleaseFast) builds over consecutive keys 0..N-1 and probes random, nearly all-miss u64s. On a 2019 MacBook Pro (2.3 GHz 8-core Core i9), BinaryFuse8 populates 1M/100M keys in 37.5 ms/7.4 s vs 103.4 ms/28.0 s for Xor8 (~2.8x/~3.8x); on a Ryzen 9 3900X the gaps are ~1.7x/~2.8x, and lookups tie. Both sides are this library's own Zig code, with nothing measured against the C reference, Bloom or cuckoo filters, and the tables predate the current benchmark.zig, which drops the fuse rows and parses only --num-trials.

**Known shortcoming:** The real ratio is ~3.8x (28.0 vs 7.4), not ~19x, and both sides are its own Zig code; the published tables were made with Zig 0.12-dev and the bench code has since been ported; the GitHub repo is archived (moved to Forgejo).

**Known shortcoming:** No comparison against the C reference, Bloom or cuckoo filters; the win is build speed and memory (22 vs 52 MiB at 1M keys) while lookups tie. Bench keys are sequential 0..N-1 with probes that are nearly all misses; the current benchmark.zig drops fuse rows and ignores --xor/--num-keys. The README install URL points to a GitHub mirror that now holds only a 'Moved' README (empty package); needs Mach Zig 2026.4.10 (0.16-dev) while CI pins 0.14 with no runs. Immutable, no C ABI, arity 3 only, u32 slot math caps ~3.8B keys, fixed seed; contain() on an empty filter reads uninitialized memory.

**How:** Binary fuse filters (Graf & Lemire, arXiv 2201.01174) map each key to 3 slots in three consecutive power-of-two segments, a spatially coupled 'fuse' layout after Dietzfelbinger & Walzer. That lets the array hold about 1.125n slots instead of the xor filter's 1.23n (9.0 vs 9.84 bits/key at 8-bit fingerprints). Construction groups hashes by segment (high hash bits), peels the 3-hypergraph with a queue of cells hit by a single key and assigns fingerprints in reverse. Its per-slot scratch is a 1-byte count, an 8-byte xor-of-hashes and a 4-byte queue entry, vs xor's 16-byte sets plus 16-byte queue and stack entries, hence 22 vs 52 MiB peak at 1M keys. A query is one murmur64 mix, a 64x64->128 multiply-high and 3 XORed loads, the same work as an xor filter, so lookups tie.

**Use it when:**
- A Zig codebase that needs a read-only membership pre-check (a skip-the-disk or skip-the-network test) over a key set that is rebuilt in batches rather than updated.
- Build time and build memory matter: BinaryFuse8 populated 1M keys in 37.5 ms vs 103.4 ms for Xor8 and 100M in 7.4 s vs 28.0 s (2019 MacBook Pro), using roughly 23 vs 55 bytes/key of scratch.
- You want about 0.39% false positives at about 9.0 bits/key (BinaryFuse8). BinaryFuse(u16) gives about 0.0015% at 18 bits/key, and BinaryFuse(u32) gives effectively zero at 36 bits/key.
- The key set is too large to keep as a contiguous array: populateIter streams keys from any iterator. You can also give the filter storage and the build scratch separate std.mem.Allocator instances, for example an mmap-backed one for scratch.

**Skip it when:**
- You need inserts, deletes or incremental growth: the filters are immutable, so use a cuckoo or quotient filter instead.
- You expect faster lookups than an xor filter: contains() measured 24.0 vs 25.0 ns at 1M keys and 145 vs 153 ns at 100M. At 10M+ keys with 16/32-bit fingerprints, lookups cost 100-175 ns, dominated by 3 random memory loads.
- You are not writing Zig: the library exports no C ABI. Use FastFilter/xor_singleheader for C/C++, xorf for Rust or FastFilter/xorfilter for Go. For 100M+ key xor builds, the README itself points to the C library's xor8_buffered_populate, which is not implemented here.
- Memory-tight or huge builds: peak build scratch for BinaryFuse8 is about 2 GiB at 100M keys, on top of the finished filter (and the keys, unless you stream them). init() computes the slot count as a u32, so a single filter tops out at about 3.8 billion keys.
- You need minimum space or a stable toolchain. Arity is hard-coded to 3, so the 4-wise variant that the paper puts within 8% of the lower bound is not available, and ribbon filters such as BuRR get closer. The code also tracks Mach-nominated Zig nightlies, currently 0.16.0-dev.

**Integration:** module · none (Zig std only) · Zig 2026.4.10-mach (identical to 0.16.0-dev.3142+5ccfeb926), per build.zig.zon's mach_zig_version and meant to be installed via anyzig. benchmark.zig uses std.Io and std.process.Init, so older Zig will not build the whole package. The last tag, v0.11.0, targets Zig 0.12.0-dev.706. · Any Zig target: pure scalar Zig with no SIMD or intrinsics (it uses a u128 multiply-high). The CI config targets Linux x86-64 only, and the README benchmarks ran on macOS and Windows x86-64.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when your code is Zig and you want iterator-based population with separate filter and scratch allocators. Otherwise use a sibling: FastFilter/xor_singleheader (the C reference it ports, which also has buffered xor construction) for C/C++, xorf for Rust, FastFilter/xorfilter for Go, and BuRR or a ribbon filter when bits/key matters more than build speed.

**Gotchas:**
- The README install snippet uses github.com/hexops/fastfilter/archive/$LATEST_COMMIT.tar.gz, but the archived GitHub repo's HEAD now contains only a README saying 'Moved to https://code.hexops.com/hexops/fastfilter' (which 301s to code.hexops.org). Point build.zig.zon at the Forgejo repo instead. The README's exe.addModule build snippet also predates the current build API.
- Xor(T) requires unique keys and returns error.KeysLikelyNotUnique after 100 seeds otherwise; run AutoUnique first. BinaryFuse(T) deduplicates automatically.
- Custom populateIter iterators must return null at the end and then restart from the first key, because construction rescans on every seed retry. This is enforced only in Debug builds (a panic); ReleaseFast does not check it.
- Seeds come from a fixed SplitMix64 starting constant, so builds are deterministic and the caller cannot supply a seed. Calling populate() with zero keys returns before the seed or fingerprints are set, so contain() on an empty BinaryFuse reads uninitialized allocator memory. The tests pass only because page_allocator returns zeroed pages.

**Status:** Maintained only through Zig-version bumps: the last algorithm fix was v0.10.2, the changelog stops at v0.11.0, and the last commit (April 2026) moved to Zig 2026.4.10-mach. It lives on a self-hosted Forgejo with no issues, PRs or CI runs, next to an archived GitHub mirror with issues disabled. It is dual MIT/Apache-2.0 and about 70 KB of dependency-free Zig, so vendoring src/ is easy.

[repo](https://code.hexops.org/hexops/fastfilter) · [benchmark](https://code.hexops.org/hexops/fastfilter/raw/branch/main/README.md)

##### Morton Filter  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

AMD Research's compressed, cache-line-blocked cuckoo filter with batched APIs; beats Fan et al.'s cuckoo filter on large, DRAM-resident filters.

**Beats:** cuckoo filter — In the VLDB'18 paper, on an AMD Threadripper 1950X fixed at 3.4 GHz (g++ 5.4.0, -Ofast -march=native, single-threaded, 128M-slot filters, average of 5 trials), Morton3_8 at 11.71 bits/item was 1.3x to 2.5x faster than Fan et al.'s 12-bit reference cuckoo filter on negative lookups, 1.6x to 2.4x on positive lookups, 0.9x to 15.5x on inserts and 1.3x to 1.6x on deletes, measured over load factors 0.05 to 0.95. The same paper's Skylake-X run shows smaller gains (lookups 1x to 1.8x, deletes about 1.2x, inserts about 0.67x to 3x), and a later deletion correctness fix cut peak Morton delete throughput from about 38 to about 28 MOPS, so current code may not reach the paper's delete numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** Batch API needs key counts that are multiples of 128 (else reads past the input) and insert_many always returns true. No stash/victim cache: after 300 kicks a dropped fingerprint (possibly an earlier key's) causes false negatives. Non-inline functions in headers cause duplicate-symbol link errors; no copy constructor (copies double-free); exit(1) on errors; Morton1_8 doesn't compile (#4). Abandoned since 2020-12, g++/x86 only.

**Independent measurement:** Independent: the Xor filter paper (i7-6700) measured single-query Morton at 47/65 ns vs cuckoo CF12 31/38 ns; the Prefix filter paper (Ice Lake) found it strictly worse than VQF; an own Skylake-X run had inserts ~0.67x cuckoo at low load.

**How:** Each 512-bit (cache-line) block holds a compressed Fingerprint Storage Array (46 x 8-bit slots in Morton3_8), a Fullness Counter Array (64 x 2-bit counters for 64 logical 3-slot buckets) and a 16-bit Overflow Tracking Array. Buckets are logically underloaded but empty slots are not stored ('decoupled logical sparsity'), and a bucket's offset is found by a branchless popcount-based prefix sum over the counters. Insertions are heavily biased to the primary hash H1, and the OTA records overflows, so most lookups, positive or negative, touch one cache line (about 1.05 to 1.11 lines per query at 0.95 load in the paper). The alternate bucket is chosen with a bounded odd offset rather than Fan et al.'s XOR, which keeps both candidates on the same page (fewer TLB misses) and drops the power-of-two table size requirement; keys are processed in batches of 128 (the paper's Fig. 14 credits batching with about 2x and the popcount reduction with another 2x to 3x).

**Use it when:**
- Filters of hundreds of MB (the paper uses 128M slots, about 187 MB) that live in DRAM, where memory bandwidth rather than hashing limits throughput.
- Workloads that can issue operations in batches of 128 uint64 keys, such as bulk loading or batched probes in a join or LSM lookup path.
- Dynamic sets that need deletions and are filled to high load (0.75 to 0.95), where the paper measured inserts about 3x to 15x faster than a stock cuckoo filter.
- Sets whose size you cannot predict and cannot rebuild from source keys: in-place 2x/4x/8x growth works without a backing store, at the cost of roughly one fingerprint bit of false-positive accuracy per doubling.
- About 0.3% false-positive rate at about 11.7 bits/item (Morton3_8), or about 10 bits/item with Morton7_8, on AMD Zen-class CPUs where the paper's tuning was done.

**Skip it when:**
- One-at-a-time queries. The README discourages them, and the Xor filter paper (i7-6700, GCC 8.1) measured Morton single queries at 47 and 65 ns/key (10M and 100M keys) against 31 and 38 ns for a 12-bit cuckoo filter and 23 and 32 ns for Xor8.
- Intel servers without retuning. The paper's own Skylake-X run shows lookups only on par to 1.8x faster and inserts at about 2/3 of the cuckoo filter's speed below 0.5 load; the Vacuum Filter paper (Xeon E5-2687W) measured Morton at about 6x Bloom-filter throughput vs about 10x for cuckoo; the Prefix Filter paper (Ice Lake) dropped Morton as strictly worse than the vector quotient filter.
- Static sets built once: xor, binary fuse or ribbon filters use less space (Xor8 about 9.8 bits/key at a similar FPR) and query faster.
- Production code that must be robust. The author calls it an academic prototype; errors, including allocation failure, call exit(1); the repo has no unit tests; nothing has been committed since December 2020.
- MSVC or non-x86 builds: the code depends on __uint128_t and GCC vector extensions, the README says only g++ is supported (Clang fixes came in late 2020), and only x86-64 has been tested.

**Integration:** header-only · none for the filter itself; the benchmark harness clones Fan et al.'s cuckoofilter at a pinned commit and links -lcrypto · C++11 (Makefile uses -std=c++11), GCC with GNU extensions; the README recommends g++ 5.4 and reports a GCC 8.x slowdown; Clang fixes (the issue #2 128-bit-shift UB and a non-constexpr log2) landed only in the final Dec 2020 commit · x86-64 is the only tested target (benchmarks built with -march=native -mpopcnt; BMI2 is used if present); no MSVC (__uint128_t, GCC vector extensions); other architectures not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Xor/Binary Fuse and BuRR when the set changes after construction (they are static), and over Prefix Filter when you need deletions (Prefix Filter is insert-only by design). Otherwise its only distinctive feature is in-place growth without the source keys: on Intel, the Vacuum Filter paper (Xeon E5-2687W) puts Morton at about 6x Bloom-filter throughput against about 10x for cuckoo and 11x for Vacuum, with Vacuum also supporting deletions and resizing, and the Prefix Filter authors found Morton strictly worse than the vector quotient filter.

**Gotchas:**
- The batch loops always process full 128-key chunks and read keys[i..i+127]. If num_keys is not a multiple of 128 they read past the end of the input (a README known issue). insert_many always returns true, so check the status vector, which must be pre-sized.
- There is no stash or victim cache. After 300 cuckoo kicks the insert returns false with the fingerprint it was carrying dropped, and that fingerprint can belong to an earlier key, which can cause a false negative. Deleting a key that was never inserted can also delete another key's fingerprint.
- util.h and test_util.h define non-inline functions (operator<< for __uint128_t, Test::pass) in headers, so including the library from more than one .cc file gives duplicate-symbol link errors unless you patch them to inline.
- The class owns raw aligned_alloc buffers and has a destructor but no copy constructor or assignment operator, so copying a filter double-frees. Resizing is compiled off in every preset (resizing_enabled = false), so double_capacity() calls exit(1) unless you flip it. Issue #4 (open since 2021): Morton1_8 fails to compile because of an over-broad static_assert.

**Status:** Abandoned: the last commit is a December 2020 bug-fix merge (the author no longer has write access) and one issue remains open; the code is an MIT-licensed academic prototype that is small enough to vendor but needs local patches (the multiple-of-128 batch limit, inline fixes for the header ODR problem, and copy safety) before production use.

[repo](https://github.com/AMDComputeLibraries/morton_filter) · [benchmark](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol11/p1041-breslow.pdf)

##### Prefix Filter  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Insert-only AVX-512 filter with a fixed ~0.37% false-positive rate; builds over 3.2x faster than cuckoo filters in similar space.

**Beats:** Bloom filter, cuckoo filter — The paper's authors measured single-threaded runs on one Xeon Gold 6336Y (Ice Lake) core, built with GCC 10.3 using -Ofast -march=native, inserting 0.94*2^28 (about 252M) random 64-bit keys. The prefix filter built more than 3.2x faster than every cuckoo filter setup (Fan et al.'s own code and a flexible variant) and 1.39-1.46x faster than the authors' vector quotient filter, using 11.55-12.13 bits/key at a 0.37-0.39% false-positive rate. It won on negative queries against CF-12 at every load up to 95% (+55% at 50% load, +2.8% at 90%), but lost 46-60% to CF-12 on positive queries at full load. There is no C++ standard library baseline for this kind of structure.

**Known shortcoming:** Needs AVX-512 including VBMI, x86 Linux only, no fallback (build failure #1 open since 2024). No delete (Remove throws), fixed ~0.37% FPR, no serialization, per-instance /dev/urandom hash seed. Hard capacity: a full spare throws logic_error; allocation failure calls exit(-3). No copy/move constructors but frees a raw buffer in the destructor, so copying double-frees; no duplicate-key check. Not packaged as a library (class lives in Tests/wrappers.hpp with bundled Bloom/cuckoo headers; README clone URL 404s). Positive queries at full load 46-60% slower than CF-12; blocked Bloom is 2x faster at 3-6x the FPR. Last commit 2022-09; a copy also lives in FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp.

**How:** It has two levels, following the Bercea-Even (BE) filter. The first level is a table of 32-byte pocket dictionaries (Elias-Fano/quotienting encoding: Q=25 lists, 8-bit remainders, 25 slots per bin), which holds about 94% of the fingerprints. A small second-level 'spare' filter holds the rest; by default the spare is TwoChoicer, the authors' own vector quotient filter. When a bin is full, an insert evicts the largest fingerprint among the bin and the new key to the spare. This keeps the 'Prefix Invariant': each bin holds the smallest fingerprints mapped to it, so a query can tell from the bin alone whether it needs the spare. As a result, about 92% of negative queries touch one cache line; cuckoo filters and vector quotient filters touch two. Inside a bin, a query broadcasts the 8-bit remainder and runs one AVX-512 byte compare over the body. That answers most negatives without a Select (PDEP/TZCNT) on the 50-bit header.

**Use it when:**
- Filters built once for immutable data, such as per-run filters in an LSM tree, where build time matters and about 12 bits/key at about 0.4% false positives is acceptable.
- Keys arrive one at a time and the filter fills to 90-95% of capacity. In the paper's tests, cuckoo filter inserts slow down more than 27x at high load, while prefix filter inserts decline only 1.9-2.8x from their plateau.
- Mostly-negative lookups in front of a slow store, on filters larger than the last-level cache. Negative queries were 55% and 40% faster than CF-12 at 50% and 70% load.
- Keys cannot all be gathered before building, which rules out static xor, binary fuse and ribbon filters.
- Single-threaded use on Linux, on an Intel server CPU with full AVX-512 including VBMI (the paper used Ice Lake).

**Skip it when:**
- You need deletions or counting. The Prefix Invariant makes deletion impossible (paper Sec. 4.1), and Remove throws.
- No AVX-512: AVX2-only x86, ARM or Apple Silicon. There is no scalar fallback, and the build fails with 'target specific option mismatch' on _mm256_permutexvar_epi8 (issue #1, open since 2024-01 with no fix).
- Mostly-positive lookups on a full filter. At 100% load, positive queries are 28-40% slower than CF-12-Flex and 46-60% slower than CF-12. If raw speed matters more than space, the blocked Bloom filter is about 2x faster on every operation, at a 3-6x higher false-positive rate in the paper's configuration.
- You need a tunable false-positive rate, or you don't know the key count. The 8-bit remainder fixes the rate near 0.37-0.39%. The spare is sized for the declared capacity, so going past it makes the spare insert fail and throw std::logic_error.
- Concurrent writers. The code has no synchronization. The paper (Sec. 4.4) sketches per-bin locking but did not implement it.

**Integration:** source-drop · No external libraries. Tests/wrappers.hpp, which holds the Prefix_Filter class, also #includes the bundled Bloom, blocked Bloom and cuckoo filter headers. Python (matplotlib, pandas, brokenaxes) is needed only to plot results. · C++17 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17) and CMake 3.10+. The paper used GCC 10.3; the README says GCC 9.3 works, recommends newer releases, and names Clang as an option. CMake sets -march=native for everything. · x86-64 Linux only. It needs AVX-512F/BW/VL plus VBMI (512-bit ops in the TwoChoicer spare, the 256-bit byte permute in the pocket dictionary) and BMI2 (PDEP/TZCNT/BZHI). The README says 'Intel. Support of AVX512 is a must.' Hash seeds are read from /dev/urandom.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over xor/binary fuse (xor_singleheader) or BuRR only when keys must be inserted one at a time. Those two are static and need the whole key set before building. When the key set is known up front, they are smaller: Xor8 is 9.8 bits/key and BuRR is under 1.5% over the optimum, while the prefix filter is 11.55-12.13 bits/key, about 3.6 bits over the optimum. They also run without AVX-512.

**Gotchas:**
- Prefix_Filter and TC_shortcut own a raw posix_memalign buffer, free it in the destructor, and define no copy or move constructors. Copying one, for example by pushing it into a std::vector that reallocates, double-frees. Construct it in place or hold it through a pointer.
- Capacity is a hard limit. The spare holds 1.08 x 5.86% / 0.935 of max_items. Once it is full, Add prints to stdout and throws std::logic_error. If allocation fails, Prefix_Filter calls exit(-3). TC_shortcut instead returns with an uninitialized buffer (its assert is compiled out under -DNDEBUG).
- Add does not deduplicate: the paper assumes distinct keys, and inserting the same key twice uses two slots. Each instance seeds its Dietzfelbinger multiply-shift hash from /dev/urandom, so two filters over the same keys differ, and there is no way to persist or reload a filter.
- The README's build steps clone TheHolyJoker/Prefix-Filter with -b master. That repo returns 404; the real source is TomerEven/Prefix-Filter, and its only branch is main.

**Status:** This is an abandoned research artifact: the last commit was 2022-09-12, and the one open issue (an AVX-512 build failure) has had no fix since 2024. It is Apache-2.0 per LICENSE.md (GitHub reports NOASSERTION) and about 4k lines, so it can be vendored. FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp carries a copy in its benchmark harness (added 2022-07-11), compiled only when AVX512BW/VL/CD/DQ are enabled.

[repo](https://github.com/TomerEven/Prefix-Filter) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.17139)

##### RocksDB Ribbon Filter  `C++`  `Apache-2.0 OR GPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

RocksDB's built-in Ribbon SST filter: same FP rate as its Bloom filter in about 30% less memory, at 3-4x CPU.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — arXiv:2103.02515 Table 2 used a 2021 copy of RocksDB's ribbon code in the fastfilter_cpp fork (Xeon D-2191 Skylake DE, GCC 8.4.1 -O3 -march=skylake-avx512, FP rate about 1%). Standard Ribbon w=128 had 6-8% space overhead vs 49.8% for RocksDB's FastLocalBloom, but cost 166 vs 21 ns/key to build and 58 vs 10 ns/key to query at n=10^6, and 235 vs 72 and 140 vs 36 ns/key at n=10^8. The RocksDB blog's filter_bench figures (no hardware stated) are 7 vs 10 bits/key, 140 vs 32 ns/key to construct and 600 vs 500 ns/key to query; no std:: baseline applies.

**Known shortcoming:** Ribbon trades speed for space: 6-8% space overhead vs 49.8% for RocksDB's FastLocalBloom, but build costs 166 vs 21 ns/key and queries 58 vs 10 ns/key (arXiv:2103.02515 Table 2). The blog's 4.4x/20% ratios are derived; the record's 'ESA 2021' venue could not be confirmed.

**Known shortcoming:** Ribbon costs CPU: builds are 3-8x Bloom's and queries 58 vs 10 ns/key at 1e6 keys (140 vs 36 at 1e8); the wiki warns it can slow peak writes. Build temp memory is ~230 vs ~75 bits/key (3 GB vs 1 GB at 100M keys), untracked unless cache charging is on. With the default bloom_before_level=0 flushes stay Bloom, and it silently falls back to Bloom above 950M keys, for tiny filters, after 256 reseeds or at the cache limit.

**Known shortcoming:** Static filters only (the memtable filter stays Bloom); no RocksJava Ribbon class; RocksDB <6.15 reads Ribbon filters as no filter; open MSVC C4723 issue (#14065). The paper's numbers come from a 2021 fastfilter_cpp copy, not the in-database path, and the blog's filter_bench gives no hardware.

**How:** The win is space, not speed. Ribbon (Rapid Incremental Boolean Banding ON-the-fly) is a perfect-hash static function over GF(2). Each key hashes to a start column and a 128-bit coefficient row, which approximates a band matrix (Dietzfelbinger-Walzer). The system is solved by on-the-fly Gaussian elimination that behaves like linear-probing hash insertion, followed by back-substitution. A query computes the parity of an r-bit window in an 'interleaved' column-major solution that spans 1-3 adjacent cache lines. The XOR construction avoids Bloom's roughly 1.44-1.5x space factor. Splitting between b-1 and b solution columns gives fractional bits/key.

**Use it when:**
- RocksDB databases where SST filters stay resident in RAM for a long time (defaults, or cache_index_and_filter_blocks with optimize_filters_for_hits) and filter blocks take a large share of block cache; the blog's example LOG shows 14% of a 9 GB cache.
- Leveled or universal LSMs with long-lived lower levels. Use the hybrid (bloom_before_level=N) so flushes and L0 get Bloom and deeper levels get Ribbon. The blog's cost model puts the break-even at about 1 hour of filter lifetime.
- FP rates around 1-10%. Standard Ribbon w=128 is 6-8% over the information-theoretic minimum there, against about 50% for blocked Bloom.
- Roughly 10K-10M keys per filter, the range r=128 is tuned for. The blog says even 100M keys in one filter save 27% vs Bloom.
- Outside RocksDB: a static key set known up front, when you want portable C++ with fractional bits/key and are willing to vendor util/ribbon_*.h the way pdillinger/fastfilter_cpp did.

**Skip it when:**
- Short-lived filters (flush/L0 output, data living under about an hour) or write-bound workloads. Construction costs 3-8x Bloom CPU, and the wiki warns it 'could slow peak write rates in some cases.'
- CPU-bound point lookups on memory-resident data. Paper Table 2 has queries at 58 vs 10 ns/key (n=10^6) and 140 vs 36 ns/key (n=10^8) against RocksDB's FastLocalBloom, and Ribbon queries get relatively costlier at low FP rates.
- Sets that grow after build. Ribbon is static, and RocksDB's memtable filter stays Bloom.
- Compaction hosts that are tight on memory and build huge unpartitioned filters. Construction needs about 230 bits/key of temporary memory vs about 75 for Bloom: 3 GB vs 1 GB for 100M keys in one filter, untracked unless cache charging is enabled.
- Partitioned filters over cold data without optimize_filters_for_hits, where only some filters are resident; the blog says the benefit is 'not as clear' there.

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (built into RocksDB); standalone use is a source-drop of the templated util/ribbon_alg.h + ribbon_impl.h headers · Inside RocksDB: RocksDB itself (compression libs and gflags optional). Standalone: a handful of RocksDB support headers (math128.h, fastrange.h, port.h, etc.; the fastfilter_cpp fork ships coding_lean.h, fastrange.h, lang.h, math.h, math128.h, port.h) · Current RocksDB: C++20, GCC >= 11 or Clang >= 10 (INSTALL.md; CMake defaults to C++20). The Ribbon headers themselves say they are written for C++11, and the 2021 paper copy built with GCC 8.4.1. · Any platform RocksDB supports (Linux, macOS, Windows VS2017+, AIX, BSDs per INSTALL.md). The Ribbon code uses no processor intrinsics, only compiler built-ins for prefetch, clz/ctz and parity, with native 128-bit ints when available and a fallback otherwise. Open issue #14065: an upcoming MSVC flags a potential divide-by-zero (C4723) in ribbon_impl.h, which fails warnings-as-errors builds.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over BuRR, which gets below 1% overhead with bumped Ribbon but is research code, and over xor/binary fuse (xor_singleheader: faster queries, about 13-23% overhead, single header), when you already run RocksDB or want a production-hardened C++ Ribbon with Bloom-like fractional bits/key. Choose BuRR for minimum space and xor/binary fuse for the fastest static-filter queries; ribbonGo is the Go option.

**Gotchas:**
- Default bloom_before_level=0 still writes Bloom filters for memtable flushes under leveled and universal compaction, so savings only appear as compaction rewrites files. Use -1 for all-Ribbon. Since 8.7 the option can be changed at runtime through SetOptions.
- It silently falls back to Bloom, with only an info-log warning, when a filter has more than 950M keys, when a small filter (<1024 slots) would be smaller as Bloom, after 256 failed re-seeds, or when cache charging for the banding memory hits the limit.
- Temporary construction memory is untracked by default. Enable block-cache charging for filter construction (reserve_table_builder_memory in 6.27, now cache_usage_options / CacheEntryRole::kFilterConstruction), or use partitioned filters or smaller SSTs.
- Downgrading to RocksDB < 6.15 reads Ribbon filters as 'no filter' until compaction rebuilds them. RocksJava has only a BloomFilter class and no dedicated Ribbon class.

**Status:** RocksDB is actively maintained (last push 2026-09-25). The Ribbon code itself is stable: the headers have only had reformat/modernize commits since 2024 and filter_policy.cc last changed in Nov 2025. It has been production-ready since 6.22, its SST schema has been long-term supported since 6.20, and it is dual GPLv2/Apache-2.0, so the headers can be vendored.

[repo](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.02515)

##### Xor Filter (xor_singleheader)  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C99 xor and binary fuse filters: static membership filters with fewer bits/key and faster lookups than Bloom/cuckoo.

**Beats:** Bloom filter, cuckoo filter — The xor paper's Table 3 benchmarks the C++ fastfilter_cpp release 1.0 code (GCC 8.1 -O3 -march=native, i7-6700 Skylake, single thread, non-inlined queries, 25% of queried keys present). At 10M keys, Xor8 took 23 ns/query at 9.8 bits/key, against 40 ns for Bloom12 (12 bits/key) and 31 ns for Cuckoo12 (12.8 bits/key); at 100M keys the figures were 32, 58 and 38 ns. The binary fuse paper (GCC 10 -O3, same i7-6700 plus an EPYC 7262) shows, in plots only, that 3-wise fuse reaches about 9 bits/key with xor-level query speed and builds more than 2x faster than xor. Neither paper benchmarked this C header; its own query benchmark prints no Bloom or cuckoo comparison, and the README sample output looks like placeholder numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** Paper numbers are for the C++ fastfilter_cpp code, not this header (the papers say so); the repo's own query bench has no Bloom/cuckoo comparison. The header has only 3-wise binary fuse (4-wise, 8.6 bits/key, is C++-only, #69) and no 32-bit fingerprints (#8, #75). fuse16 populate failed on 20-40% of key sets near 11.5k keys until v2.2.0 (2026-09-21, #77), so older vendored copies are affected. The dedup fallback compares u64 keys with an (int)(a-b) qsort comparator and mutates the caller's keys in place; fuse populate needs the exact allocated size; deserialize() has no length check; serialization format changed in v2.0.0 and is native-endian only; ~24 B/key temporary build memory, single-threaded; below ~20k keys xor may be smaller than fuse.

**Known shortcoming:** Packaging note: oschonrock/binfuse wraps this header's binary fuse filters in a C++ library with persistence; its own benchmark reports absolute numbers only.

**How:** Each key maps to three array slots, and construction stores fingerprints so that the XOR of those three slots equals the key's fingerprint. A query is one hash, three independent memory loads and a compare, with the same cost for hits and misses; a Bloom filter needs up to k probes and slows down when most queried keys are present. Construction is hypergraph peeling: slots touched by exactly one key are removed repeatedly, then assigned in reverse order, retrying with a new seed if peeling stalls. Binary fuse filters (spatially coupled, after Dietzfelbinger and Walzer) keep the three slots in consecutive small segments and pre-bucket hashes by segment, which improves cache locality and shrinks the array from about 1.23n to 1.125n slots. Index reduction uses multiply-shift instead of modulo.

**Use it when:**
- The key set is known up front and read-only: SSTable or segment filters in an LSM/columnar store, leaked-password lists, precomputed deny-lists shipped to clients.
- Memory per key matters: binary_fuse8 is about 9 bits/key at 0.39% FPP for sets of 1M keys or more, against 12 bits/key for a Bloom filter at a similar (0.31%) FPP.
- Most queried keys are present: xor and fuse lookups always do exactly three loads, while standard Bloom filters get slower on hits (xor paper Fig. 4).
- You want a dependency-free file to vendor into C or C++ (nDPI and InfiniFlow Infinity embed binaryfusefilter.h), with serialization and mmap-friendly loading.
- You need a very low FPP without a big filter: binary_fuse16 gives about 0.0015% at roughly 18 bits/key.

**Skip it when:**
- You need inserts, deletes or filter unions: there is no add/remove, and filters built on partitions cannot be OR-ed together the way Bloom filters can (issue #35). Rebuilding needs the full key set.
- Lowest query latency matters more than memory: the blocked Bloom filter was faster in both papers (16 ns vs Xor8's 23 ns at 10M keys) at 10.7 bits/key and about 0.94% FPP.
- Construction memory or time is tight: binary fuse needs about 24 bytes/key of temporary memory (2.4 GB for 100M keys), construction is single-threaded, and at 10M keys xor construction took 110-120 ns/key, against 10 ns for blocked Bloom and 40-90 ns for standard Bloom (xor paper, Table 2). Binary fuse builds more than 2x faster than xor.
- You need the smallest possible filter: this header ships only 3-wise fuse (about 12.5% over the lower bound). The 4-wise variant (7.5%) exists only in C++ fastfilter_cpp (issue #69), and BuRR/ribbon filters go below 1%. For sets under about 20,000 keys, the paper says xor may even beat binary fuse on size.
- You need an FPP below 1/65536 or cross-endian files: there are no 32-bit fingerprints (issues #8 and #75 are open), and serialization is native byte order only.

**Integration:** header-only · C standard library plus libm (binaryfusefilter.h calls log, floor and round; the CMake INTERFACE target links m) · C99 (CMake c_std_99, Makefile -std=c99). CI uses GCC 13 and Clang 18 on Ubuntu 24.04 and MinGW-w64 GCC on Windows. It uses __uint128_t where available, __umulh on MSVC x64/ARM64, and a portable fallback otherwise. · Any platform with a C99 compiler. CI covers only Linux x86-64 and Windows MinGW 32/64-bit; macOS, ARM and MSVC are not in CI. No SIMD required.

**Vs siblings:** Choose this over BuRR when you want a single dependency-free C99 file and faster lookups: the binary fuse paper measured ribbon queries slower than 3-wise binary fuse. BuRR still wins clearly on space, with overhead under 1% against about 12.5%. Choose it over Prefix Filter when the set is static and you cannot require Intel AVX-512 and C++17, which the Prefix-Filter README mandates; Prefix Filter supports incremental inserts and this library does not.

**Gotchas:**
- populate() can return false, so always check it. The source comment calls failure rarer than a cosmic ray, but issue #77 showed binary_fuse16_populate failing on 20-40% of distinct key sets at about 11,480-11,521 keys. That was fixed only in v2.2.0 (2026-09-21), so update any vendored copy made before then.
- Deduplicate keys yourself. When populate() sees duplicates, it sorts and deduplicates your array in place. xor8/xor16 first waste 10 failed seeds before trying that. The qsort comparator returns (int)(a - b) on uint64 keys, which is not a consistent ordering, so this fallback cannot be relied on.
- binary_fuse*_populate() returns false unless the key count equals the size passed to allocate(); despite the 'up to size' comment, that size must be exact. Sizes are uint32_t, so one filter holds under about 4 billion keys.
- Serialization changed format in v2.0.0 (a Size field was added). deserialize() takes no buffer length and trusts ArrayLength from the buffer, so never feed it untrusted bytes. The README's 16-bit example also names binary_fuse8_contain/free where it means the fuse16 functions.

**Status:** Actively maintained: v2.2.0 shipped 2026-09-21 with a construction-failure fix. It is Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor, as nDPI and InfiniFlow Infinity do; Pebble and Databend, named in the README, use the Go and Rust ports rather than this header.

[repo](https://github.com/FastFilter/xor_singleheader) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.08258)

##### Better Choice Cuckoo Filter (BCF)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Research patch to efficient/cuckoofilter: inserts go to the less-loaded bucket, claiming 35% fewer relocations, 25% lower insert latency.

**Beats:** Cuckoo filter — The only published numbers are in the abstract of the paywalled ICDCS 2019 paper: 35% fewer average relocations and 25% lower average insertion latency than the standard cuckoo filter on large real-world data sets. The README repeats them and names an Intel Xeon E5-2670 @ 2.60GHz on RHEL 6.2, but gives no compiler, flags, absolute timings or baseline configuration. The repo has no BCF-vs-CF harness. example/test.cc only times windows of about 100 BCF inserts at each ~1% load step of a 2^20-slot, 12-bit table. It uses gettimeofday, calls Contain() before every Add, sleeps 1 s between windows, and is built at -g by default.

**Known shortcoming:** A modified copy of efficient/cuckoofilter; the Makefile's default is a debug build; gains are fewer relocations/lower insert latency vs the standard cuckoo filter.

**Known shortcoming:** A copy of early-2017 efficient/cuckoofilter whose only change is that Add() picks the less-loaded bucket. False-negative bug: after 1000 kicks InsertFail drops an evicted fingerprint and the victim cache is unreachable. Misses upstream's padding fix (PR #27), so a 64-bit read overruns the last bucket; no num_buckets>=1 guard. Six extern global counters break linking (benchmarks/ will not link) and are not thread-safe even across instances; PackedTable is broken.

**Known shortcoming:** No BCF-vs-CF harness in the repo and the paper is paywalled (abstract only); the Makefile defaults to -g; the README's data path differs from test.cc. The checkout includes ~690 MB of .vscode/ipch junk; abandoned since 2019.

**How:** Upstream puts the fingerprint in the first candidate bucket i1 and only moves to i2, then to random-walk eviction, when i1 is full. BCF's Add() first counts the occupied slots in both candidate buckets and inserts into the emptier one, with ties going to i1. This is the 'power of two choices' (balanced allocation) principle. Bucket occupancy stays more even, so at high load fewer inserts find both buckets full, which means fewer cuckoo kick-out chains and lower insert latency. Lookups and deletes are unchanged upstream code: two bucket probes with SWAR tag matching (the haszero/hasvalue12 bit tricks) on 64-bit loads.

**Use it when:**
- You already vendor efficient/cuckoofilter with SingleTable and want a roughly 10-line change to Add() that cuts relocations when tables run near full. The repo's own test fills a 2^20-slot table until inserts fail.
- Insert latency at high load factor is the pain point, and the lookup path and memory layout must stay exactly the same as upstream's (same 12-bit, 4-way bucket format and the same two-probe Contain).
- Filters are sized with little or no headroom. BCF removed upstream's rule that doubles the bucket count, so the table has about as many slots as the requested capacity, and that is the regime where fewer relocations matter.
- Research or teaching: reproducing the ICDCS 2019 power-of-two-choices result. An IPv4 trace (input/ip_final.txt, addresses as decimal integers) and the relocation-logging example are included.

**Skip it when:**
- Any use that must never give a false negative. After 1,000 kicks, AddImpl returns InsertFail even though it has already evicted a stored fingerprint. The victim-cache code upstream uses to keep that fingerprint is now unreachable, so an item inserted earlier can silently disappear.
- Production or memory-safety-sensitive code. SingleTable predates upstream's November 2017 padding fix (efficient/cuckoofilter PR #27, 'avoid buffer overrun'), so the unaligned 64-bit bucket reads run past the end of the allocation at the last bucket. The constructor also lacks upstream's num_buckets >= 1 guard.
- Concurrent inserts, even into separate filter objects. Every successful Add writes process-wide globals (NumberOfBuckets_0..4 and NumberOfRelocations), and there is no locking.
- Semi-sorted filters (PackedTable). BCF's Add() calls NumTagsInBucket, which is commented out in packedtable.h, so CuckooFilter<..., PackedTable> no longer compiles once Add is used.
- Low-load or read-heavy filters. Every insert now scans both buckets (8 tag reads) and recounts the destination bucket for statistics, even when the first bucket has room. The claimed gain comes only from avoiding relocations at high load.

**Integration:** source-drop · OpenSSL (hashutil.cc wraps EVP MD5/SHA1, and the Makefile links -lssl -lcrypto). The Makefile also passes -lpthread. · C++11 (Makefile --std=c++11, CMake CXX_STANDARD 11). Needs GCC or Clang on a 64-bit target, because the default hash uses unsigned __int128 and the buckets use __attribute__((packed)). · x86-64 little-endian as written. singletable.h includes <xmmintrin.h>, and the tag code relies on unaligned little-endian 64-bit loads ('only works for little-endian' comments). Developed on RHEL 6.2 with a Xeon E5-2670.

**Vs siblings:** Pick BCF only when you are patching an existing efficient/cuckoofilter deployment (the Cuckoo Filter sibling) and need its exact layout and query path with fewer relocations near full load. Better port the balanced-choice rule than vendor this snapshot. For new code, Morton Filter (1.3-2.5x faster lookups than the reference cuckoo filter), Vacuum Filter (about 25% less space at similar throughput) or Prefix Filter (more than 3.2x faster builds than any cuckoo configuration) are better evidenced.

**Gotchas:**
- It does not link out of the box. cuckoofilter.h declares extern NumberOfBuckets_0..4 and NumberOfRelocations, and only example/test.cc defines them. The unchanged upstream benchmarks/ files (bulk-insert-and-query, conext-*) call Add() without defining them.
- The README says the example reads ./input/ip_final.txt, but example/test.cc opens ./ip_final.txt, so ./test run from the repo root prints 'Error opening file'. The Makefile also defaults to OPT = -g -ggdb with -O3 -DNDEBUG commented out, so turn on optimization before timing anything.
- The README lists NumTagsInBucket() as a filter operation, but it is a method of the private table_ and CuckooFilter does not expose it. The worst-case kick chain before failure is twice upstream's (1000 vs 500).
- A checkout brings seventeen 40 MB .vscode/ipch IntelliSense caches (about 690 MB), a CLion cmake-build-debug directory and prebuilt benchmark .exe files. Copy src/ rather than adding the repo as a submodule.

**Status:** Abandoned: three commits in May-June 2019, no issues or PRs ever, 12 stars. Apache-2.0 via upstream's CMU/Intel LICENSE (GitHub shows NOASSERTION). The idea is about 10 lines in Add(), so porting it onto current efficient/cuckoofilter is safer than vendoring this pre-2017-fix snapshot.

[repo](https://github.com/CGCL-codes/BCF) · [benchmark](https://github.com/CGCL-codes/BCF#overview)

##### Counting Quotient Filter (CQF)  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

C counting quotient filter: approximate membership plus per-item counts, faster and smaller than counting Bloom filters.

**Beats:** counting Bloom filter (and Bloom filter generally) — The SIGMOD 2017 paper by the CQF's authors (as quoted on the morning paper) reports in-memory inserts and queries up to an order of magnitude faster than the original quotient filter, several times faster than a Bloom filter, and similar to a cuckoo filter. It also reports at least 2x over every other structure it tested (Bloom, QF, cuckoo, counting Bloom) on SSD, on uniform-random and Zipfian inputs. The figures are qualitative: the paper PDF returned 403, so compiler and hardware are unknown, and the repo's bm.c benchmarks only the CQF (built with gcc -Ofast -msse4.2).

**Known shortcoming:** The repo's bm.c has no Bloom baseline, so the 'order of magnitude faster than Bloom' comes only from the SIGMOD 2017 paper.

**Known shortcoming:** Linux x86-64 only (x86 asm even with NH=1; partitioned_counter.c uses sched_getcpu). Open segfault on resize/merge since 2019 (#9); qf_malloc does not zero memory (call qf_reset); qf_use/qf_usefile leave num_locks at 0 so lock flags overrun the lock array (from source reading); queries take no locks. Full at 95%; the library calls exit() and prints to stdout.

**How:** It is a rank-and-select quotient filter (RSQF). Each hash is split into a quotient, which picks a home slot, and a remainder. Remainders sit in sorted runs placed by linear probing. Each block of 64 slots stores occupieds and runends bitvectors plus one 8-bit offset (2.125 metadata bits per slot), so finding a run costs one POPCNT rank and one PDEP+TZCNT select within a block or two, instead of k random probes as in a Bloom filter.
