That locality also explains the SSD result, and it lets the filter run up to 95% full, compared with about 75% for the original quotient filter. Counts are stored inside the remainder slots with a variable-length encoding, so an item with no duplicates costs nothing extra, and skewed counts grow roughly logarithmically.

**Use it when:**
- Approximate counting over large multisets such as k-mer counting in genomics. splatlab's own Squeakr and Mantis vendor this code under include/gqf.
- Skewed or Zipfian streams, where a counting Bloom filter wastes fixed-width counters. Here 1 to 3 copies use 1 to 3 slots, and larger counts use about 2 + log(C)/r slots (maintainer, issue #4).
- Filters larger than RAM: qf_initfile/qf_usefile mmap the filter from a file, and the paper reports at least 2x over every other structure it tested on SSD.
- When you need deletes, resize (manual or auto-doubling), a linear-scan merge of several filters, or iteration. QF_HASH_INVERTIBLE gives exact answers when keys fit in key_bits.
- Insert-heavy multi-threaded workloads on Linux x86-64 using QF_WAIT_FOR_LOCK or QF_TRY_ONCE_LOCK, which use region spinlocks instead of a global lock.

**Skip it when:**
- Any target other than Linux x86-64. popcnt, bsr and rdtsc are unconditional x86 inline asm, and even the NH=1 build only removes PDEP/TZCNT. partitioned_counter.c includes <sys/sysinfo.h> and <linux/unistd.h> and calls sched_getcpu, so macOS, aarch64 and MSVC need porting.
- Static sets built once: xor or ribbon filters are smaller. For pure membership at loose false-positive rates, a Bloom filter can also be smaller; the paper says the RSQF only beats Bloom on space below about a 1/64 false-positive rate (as quoted in an HN comment).
- Reads that must be consistent with concurrent writes: qf_query and qf_count_key_value ignore the lock flags and read without locking.
- Production code that cannot absorb maintenance risk. Last commit was 2022-09-22, and issue #9 (segfaults during auto-resize and merge, open since 2019) is unresolved. The library calls exit() on allocation failure and writes resize messages to stdout and stderr.
- Keys wider than 64 bits or string keys used directly: the API takes a uint64_t key, and the maintainers said in 2024 (issue #17) that 128-bit support is not on the roadmap.

**Integration:** source-drop · The core (gqf.c, gqf_file.c, hashutil.c, partitioned_counter.c) needs only libc, libm and pthreads. libssl/libcrypto are used only by the bundled test programs (RAND_bytes), but the Makefile links them into every target. There is no library or install target. · GCC or Clang with GNU extensions (-std=gnu11, __uint128_t, GNU inline asm). The Makefile uses gcc -std=gnu11 -Ofast -msse4.2. No minimum version is documented. · Linux x86-64. The fast select path needs BMI2 PDEP plus TZCNT (Haswell or newer); build with NH=1 for a broadword select fallback on older x86 CPUs.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over the Cuckoo Filter (efficient/cuckoofilter), Vacuum Filter or Xor/BuRR filters when you need true multiset counts, deletes, resize or merge, or an SSD-resident filter; the paper puts its in-memory speed close to the cuckoo filter. Prefer Xor/BuRR for static sets where space is what matters, and the cuckoo filter for portable pure-membership C++ with no counting.

**Gotchas:**
- qf_malloc uses malloc, and qf_init's memset of the buffer is commented out, so a new filter can start with garbage metadata. Open issue #9 (segfaults in shift_remainders/run_end during resize and merge) went away for one user after switching to calloc. Call qf_reset after qf_malloc; resize still goes through qf_malloc internally.
- qf_use and qf_usefile allocate the lock array while num_locks is still 0, and never set it afterwards (only qf_deserialize does). Locking flags on a reopened or mmapped filter can therefore index past that array, so use QF_NO_LOCK there. This comes from reading the source and is not documented.
- The filter counts as full at 95% of nslots, or when an insert lands more than 1000 slots from its home slot. Occupancy and element counters are batched per CPU with a threshold of 100, so qf_get_* values lag until qf_sync_counters is called.
- In QF_HASH_NONE mode, keys must already be reduced modulo the filter's range; the issue #3 segfault came from skipping this. The header also warns of very bad performance on skewed inputs in this mode. QF_HASH_INVERTIBLE only gives exact answers for keys that fit in key_bits.

**Status:** Abandoned: last commit 2022-09-22 (a merge of README build-instruction fixes), with an unresolved 2019 segfault issue. It is BSD-3-Clause and only about four C files, so vendoring it, as splatlab's Squeakr and Mantis do, is the realistic way to use it on Linux x86-64.

[repo](https://github.com/splatlab/cqf) · [benchmark](https://blog.acolyer.org/2017/08/08/a-general-purpose-counting-filter-making-every-bit-count/)

##### Cuckoo Filter (efficient/cuckoofilter)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Reference C++ cuckoo filter from the CoNEXT'14 authors: a Bloom-filter replacement that supports deletes and does faster positive lookups.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — In the CoNEXT'14 paper (2x Xeon L5640, compiler and flags not stated, random 64-bit keys hashed with CityHash, 192MB filters), the cuckoo filter at 12.60 bits/item builds at 5.00M keys/s vs 3.91M for a standard Bloom filter at 13.00 bits/item and the same 0.19% FPR. Plot-read lookup throughput is about 1.45x-2.4x the standard Bloom filter's, and the gap grows with the share of positive queries. The Bloom baseline code is not in the repo. An independent run in the Xor Filters paper (i7-6700, GCC 8.1.0 -O3 -march=native, 10M keys, 25% found) measured a size-flexible Cuckoo 12 at 31 ns vs Bloom 12 at 40 ns, and the original power-of-two version at 30 ns but 20.1 bits/key.

**Known shortcoming:** Figure 5 is overstated in the original record: cuckoo ~12/~10.5 MOPS vs Bloom ~8.3 falling to ~4.9, so at most about 2.4x (not 2.75x). The Bloom baseline code is not in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Table size rounds up to a power of two (up to ~2x memory; the repo's own bench wastes 46-138%; the Xor paper measures 20.1 bits/key). Only fingerprint widths 2/4/8/12/16/32 work; others compile but give false negatives (#6, #34). Cannot resize: after 500 kicks a victim stash is used and then Add fails permanently, sometimes below advertised capacity (#9).

**Known shortcoming:** The same repo's SIMD blocked Bloom filter has ~2x faster lookups; semi-sorted mode is ~2.5x slower than the plain filter. Default hash takes uint64 keys only; no serialization, no locking, and no copy constructor (a copy double-frees). Needs OpenSSL headers; little-endian, GCC/Clang only; abandoned.

**How:** The filter is a cuckoo hash table of 4-slot buckets holding short fingerprints, filled with partial-key cuckoo hashing: an item's alternate bucket is its current bucket XOR a hash of its fingerprint, so entries can be moved without the original key. Every lookup reads exactly two buckets, which the paper counts as at most two cache misses. Both 64-bit loads are issued before comparing, and SWAR has-value bit tricks check all four fingerprints of a bucket in one word, so lookup cost stays flat as the share of positive queries grows, whereas a Bloom filter must probe all k bits for each hit. The optional PackedTable ('semi-sorting') sorts each bucket's low 4-bit nibbles and permutation-encodes them, saving 1 bit per fingerprint at a large speed cost.

**Use it when:**
- You need deletions (a counting-Bloom replacement) over 64-bit integer or pre-hashed keys, and you can guarantee that you only delete keys that were actually inserted.
- Lookup-heavy workloads where many queries hit present keys: in the paper's 192MB test, CF stays at about 10.5-12 MOPS while a standard Bloom filter falls to about 4.9 MOPS at 100% positive queries.
- Target FPRs of roughly 0.01-3%, served by 12- or 16-bit fingerprints. Below 3% FPR the semi-sorted variant needs fewer bits per item than a space-optimized Bloom filter (paper Fig. 4, 7.2-bit crossover).
- Capacity known up front and close to 4 x 2^k keys (at most ~0.96 of that), so the power-of-two table is not half empty.
- You want the canonical implementation to reproduce the CoNEXT'14 numbers or to serve as a baseline in your own filter benchmarks.

**Skip it when:**
- Arbitrary or memory-tight capacities. The bucket count rounds up to a power of two, so memory can reach ~2x the ideal. The repo's own bulk-insert-and-query output shows 46-138% wasted space, and the Xor Filters paper measured the original Cuckoo 12 at 20.1 bits/key vs 12.8 for a size-flexible rewrite at 10M keys.
- Growing or unbounded sets. The filter cannot resize: after 500 relocations the next Add fails for good. Issue #9 reports failures before the capacity the constructor promises, and the Xor paper lowered max load from 0.96 to 0.94 to stop construction failures.
- Raw lookup speed with no deletes. The repo's own AVX2 SIMD blocked Bloom filter runs ~2x faster than Cuckoo12 in bulk-insert-and-query (about 74 vs 37 M finds/s in the file's sample output). The paper's blocked Bloom filter ties CF at 0% positive queries and builds faster (7.64 vs 5.00 M keys/s), though at 2x the FPR of a standard Bloom filter.
- Semi-sorted mode where speed matters. In the repo's figure-5 benchmark, ss-CF lookups run at 9.4-10 MOPS vs 24.8 for plain CF on an i7-4790. At 10M keys the Xor paper measured Cuckoo semiSort 13 at 57 ns vs Bloom 12 at 40 ns.
- Concurrent writers, std::string keys, persistence, big-endian targets or MSVC. None is supported: there is no locking, the default hash accepts only uint64 (issue #39), serialization is missing (issue #28 still open), the bit tricks assume little-endian, and the code uses unsigned __int128.

**Integration:** source-drop (src/*.h plus src/hashutil.cc; `make install` also builds a static libcuckoofilter.a) · OpenSSL headers: hashutil.h includes <openssl/evp.h>, so even including cuckoofilter.h needs them. Link with -lssl -lcrypto if you compile hashutil.cc. Nothing else. · C++11 (both Makefiles use -std=c++11). GCC or Clang, because the code relies on unsigned __int128 and __attribute__((packed)). No MSVC support is documented. · Little-endian 64-bit only: code comments say the bucket reads work only on little-endian, and they use unaligned 64-bit loads. The benchmarks target x86-64 (-march=core-avx2), and simd-block.h needs AVX2, but the cuckoo filter itself uses no intrinsics. Other architectures are not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Xor Filter (immutable, per its paper) or the same repo's SIMD blocked Bloom filter when you need deletes, or a lower FPR per bit than a blocked Bloom filter. Among dynamic cuckoo-style siblings, Morton Filter (1.3-2.5x faster lookups than this reference in its paper) and Vacuum Filter (about 25% less space at similar throughput) are catalogued improvements. This one wins mainly as the simple, widely cited reference.

**Gotchas:**
- Only some fingerprint widths work, and nothing checks at compile time. SingleTable reads tags only for 2, 4, 8, 12, 16 and 32 bits; other widths compile but give false negatives (issue #6; the static_assert PR #35 was never merged). PackedTable at 5, 7 and 9 bits also fails (issue #34), and the Xor Filters authors could get only the 13-bit semi-sorted variant to work correctly.
- When an insert fails after 500 relocations, Add() still returns Ok and parks the displaced fingerprint in a one-entry victim stash. From then on every Add() returns NotEnoughSpace until a Delete frees a slot.
- Deleting a key that was never inserted can remove another key's matching fingerprint, which creates a false negative. Inserting the same key 2b+1 = 9 times fails.
- The class owns a raw table pointer but defines no copy constructor or copy assignment, so copying a CuckooFilter double-frees. The root Makefile also defaults to -g -ggdb, not the -O3 -DNDEBUG used by the benchmarks.

**Status:** Abandoned: the last commit (2021-11-12) only removed an include flag, the last real fixes landed in 2017, and 22 issues and PRs remain open. The Apache-2.0 src/ is about 2k lines and easy to vendor, but expect to patch sizing, width checks and serialization yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/efficient/cuckoofilter) · [benchmark](http://www.cs.cmu.edu/~binfan/papers/conext14_cuckoofilter.pdf)

##### SIMD Blocked Bloom Filter (src/simd-block.h, Impala-derived)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

AVX2 split-block Bloom filter: one 32-byte block per key, about 2-3x faster queries than a standard Bloom filter.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — The Xor Filters paper (Graf & Lemire, ACM JEA 2020) benchmarked a modified copy of this kernel (fastfilter_cpp's SimdBlockFilterFixed: non-power-of-2 sizing, 10.7 bits/key, Murmur-finalizer hash) single-threaded with GCC 8.1.0 -O3 -march=native on an Intel i7-6700 Skylake at 3.4 GHz. With 25% of queries present it took 16 ns per query vs 31 ns (Bloom, 8 bits/key) and 40 ns (Bloom, 12 bits/key) at 10M keys, 20 ns vs 53/58 ns at 100M keys, and 10-20 vs 40-90 ns/key to build, at 0.94% FPP vs 2.2% (Bloom 8) and 0.31% (Bloom 12).

**Known shortcoming:** The paper's blocked Bloom filter is not simd-block.h (added 2016-12); independent numbers come from the Xor filter paper (arXiv 1912.08258): 16 ns vs 31/40 ns at 10M keys, measured with fastfilter_cpp.

**Known shortcoming:** From code reading (not run): the move constructor never nulls the source pointer, so a move double-frees; Add is not thread-safe. Power-of-two sizing (its own bench: 8.95-15.79 bits/key, 0.14-2.07% FPR); FPR below 0.4% is costly (0.1% needs 16.9 bits/key per the Parquet SBBF spec). AVX2 + POSIX + GCC/Clang only; needs OpenSSL headers; per-instance random seed prevents merge/serialize.

**Known shortcoming:** Abandoned; a +15% PR (#32) is unmerged. Maintained successor: jbapple/libfilter.

**How:** It is a split block Bloom filter, combining Putze et al.'s cache-blocked Bloom filter with Broder-Mitzenmacher split filters. One hash picks a 256-bit block, and one AVX2 multiply (_mm256_mullo_epi32 by eight odd constants, shift right 27) turns the rest into eight 5-bit indices that set one bit in each 32-bit lane. Insert is a single OR-store and lookup a single _mm256_testc_si256, so each operation touches one 32-byte-aligned block with a fixed, branch-free instruction count. A standard Bloom filter does k scattered memory probes instead, which is why the gap grows from about 2x at 10M keys to about 2.7-2.9x at 100M keys.

**Use it when:**
- Read-heavy membership pre-checks (join or semi-join filters, skipping disk or LSM or Parquet-style reads) where a false-positive rate of roughly 0.4-19% is acceptable, the range its author gives. fastfilter_cpp's tuning notes put its lowest space overhead near 1-1.4% FPP.
- Large filters that spill out of cache (10M-100M+ keys), where the single-block access pays off most: 20 ns vs 53-58 ns per query at 100M keys in the Xor Filters paper.
- Insert-heavy or streaming construction: 10-20 ns/key vs 40-90 ns/key for standard Bloom. Unlike a cuckoo filter, Add never fails.
- x86-64 servers with AVX2 (Haswell or later) whose keys are already 64-bit integers or 64-bit hashes.
- As a ~140-line reference kernel to vendor. The same block scheme (identical salt constants) is standardized as Parquet's split block Bloom filter and is used in Impala, Kudu, Arrow and StarRocks.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a false-positive rate below about 0.4%. With a fixed 8 bits set per key, space grows fast: Parquet's SBBF table needs 16.9 bits/key for 0.1% and 26.4 for 0.01%, while an optimal standard Bloom filter needs 1.44*log2(1/eps), about 14.4 bits/key for 0.1%.
- Memory is the binding constraint. In the paper it used 10.7 bits/key at 0.94% FPP, while Xor8 used 9.8 bits/key at 0.39%. The author's note says a standard Bloom filter reaches 0.63% in the space this filter needs for 1.0%.
- You need deletes, counting, serialization, or OR-merging of filters. The hash seed is random per instance, so two filters built separately cannot be unioned.
- Non-AVX2 x86, ARM, MSVC or Windows. The code uses AVX2 intrinsics, posix_memalign, unsigned __int128 and GCC builtins, and the constructor throws std::runtime_error on CPUs without AVX2.
- You want maintained code. simd-block.h has not changed since Dec 2016 or the repo since Nov 2021, and PR #32 (a hashing change the author reports as 15% faster) was never merged.

**Integration:** header-only · OpenSSL headers, pulled in transitively by hashutil.h (#include <openssl/evp.h>) even though the filter does not use them. The repo Makefiles also link -lssl -lcrypto. The filter needs nothing else. · C++11 (the repo builds with --std=c++11). Needs GCC or Clang extensions (__builtin_cpu_supports, [[gnu::always_inline]], unsigned __int128); MSVC support is not documented. · x86-64 with AVX2 only (the benchmarks compile with -march=core-avx2), on POSIX systems (posix_memalign). fastfilter_cpp's derived SimdBlockFilterFixed adds aarch64 NEON and SSE4.1 variants.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over the Cuckoo Filter in the same repo when you never delete and can live with about 1% FPR: the repo's own benchmark shows 55-74M adds/sec vs 23-35M for Cuckoo8, and inserts cannot fail. Pick it over the Xor Filter or BuRR/Ribbon when keys arrive incrementally or build and query speed beat space (10 vs 110 ns/key build, 16 vs 23 ns query at 10M keys vs Xor8); pick those when bits/key matter.

**Gotchas:**
- The move constructor copies directory_ without nulling the source's pointer, so both destructors free the same buffer if a move actually runs. Returning the filter by value, as the repo's benchmark does, only works because of copy elision.
- Size is always 2^log_heap_space bytes, so bits/key and FPR jump with n. The repo's own benchmark, using the same sizing rule, shows 8.95-15.79 bits/item and 0.14%-2.07% FPR across runs. Overfilling degrades FPR silently rather than failing; Parquet's spec cites about 18% at 5 bits/key.
- The default TwoIndependentMultiplyShift hash is seeded from std::random_device in every constructor, so filters are not reproducible across runs or processes and cannot be merged. It is only 2-independent, and the repo's random.h warns that multiply-shift behaves non-randomly on some structured inputs. The paper's benchmark used a Murmur finalizer instead.
- Build flags: it needs -mavx2 (or -march) and, per its own comment, -fno-strict-aliasing, because of the __m256i reinterpret_casts. It also relies on transitive includes for memset and std::runtime_error, since there is no <cstring> or <stdexcept>.

**Status:** Abandoned (simd-block.h untouched since Dec 2016, repo since Nov 2021) but Apache-2.0 and about 140 lines, so easy to vendor; for maintained code, use the author's jbapple/libfilter (C/C++/Java/Go, last push Aug 2023, with an NDV/FPP sizing API) or fastfilter_cpp's non-power-of-2 variant.

[repo](https://github.com/efficient/cuckoofilter) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1912.08258)

##### SuRF (Succinct Range Filter)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Static trie-based range filter (SIGMOD'18); beats Bloom filters on range seeks in RocksDB, loses on point lookups.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — The SIGMOD'18 paper replaced RocksDB's Bloom filters with SuRF at equal memory (14 bits/key; SuRF with a 4-bit suffix; public efficient/rocksdb fork on RocksDB 5.8) on a synthetic 100 GB time-series (2K sensors, 128-bit keys, 1 KB values, Snappy) running on an Intel i7-6770HQ with 32 GB RAM, an Intel 540s SSD and a 1 GB block cache; compiler not stated. Open-Seek throughput went from 1.97 to 3.10 Kops/s (about 1.5x) and Closed-Seek was up to 5x faster with 99% empty ranges, but all-miss point queries fell from 32.9 to 19.8 (SuRF-Hash) or 16.4 (SuRF-Real) Kops/s; the paper measured throughput and I/Os per operation, not latency.

**Known shortcoming:** Wins only on range queries (open seek ~1.5x, closed seek up to 5x at 99% empty); on all-miss point queries Bloom is faster (32.9 vs 19.8/16.4 Kops/s). Static: keys must be pre-sorted, unchecked under NDEBUG, giving false negatives (#6); no insert/delete. x86-only (SSE2 + POPCNT hard-coded). Non-inline functions in headers cause link errors across translation units. lookupRange/approxCount share a member iterator, so not thread-safe (#5). Manual memory: empty destructor, partial destroy(), shallow copies double-free (#11 open); a false-negative bug was fixed only in 2022-03. Code defaults differ from the paper (ratio 16 vs 64); the RocksDB fork is frozen on 5.8 since 2018.

**How:** It is built on the Fast Succinct Trie (FST), a hybrid LOUDS-DS encoding: the few hot upper levels use LOUDS-Dense (256-bit label and child bitmaps per node, so a child lookup is one array access plus a rank), and the large lower levels use LOUDS-Sparse at about 10 bits per node. Rank is a single-level lookup table over 512-bit blocks plus POPCNT, select uses a table sampled every 64 set bits, sparse-node label search compares 16 labels at a time with SSE2, and lookups prefetch across the parallel bit sequences. The filter keeps only the shortest unique prefix of each key, plus optional hashed suffix bits (fewer point-query false positives) or real key-suffix bits (these also help range queries). The RocksDB gain is avoided I/O: moveToKeyGreaterThan gives each SSTable's smallest candidate key >= the low bound without reading a data block.

**Use it when:**
- LSM-tree or sorted-run storage (SSTables, immutable segments), where the filter is built once per file from already-sorted keys and you want to skip files on Seek. The paper measured Open-Seek at 1.5x and Closed-Seek at up to 5x over Bloom filters in RocksDB.
- Time-series or event stores that often ask 'did anything happen in [t1, t2]?' and where most short ranges come back empty. The 5x gain was measured with 99% of ranges empty.
- You need an approximate count of keys in a range. The code comment says it can undercount by at most 2 at the boundaries.
- Static key sets of variable-length byte strings, or integers encoded big-endian with the bundled uint64ToString helper so byte order matches numeric order. Budget about 10 bits/key (random 64-bit ints) to 14 bits/key (emails) before suffix bits.
- Many threads doing point lookups or iterator seeks on one shared, read-only filter. The paper's Appendix C shows point-query throughput scaling across 10 cores and 20 hyper-threads.

**Skip it when:**
- Point-lookup-only workloads. The paper says 'the Bloom filter is usually a better choice than SuRF'. In the RocksDB all-miss test at 14 bits/key, throughput was 32.9 Kops/s for Bloom, 19.8 for SuRF-Hash and 16.4 for SuRF-Real, because I/Os per operation were 0.022 vs 0.047 and 0.056.
- Dynamic sets. The filter is static and needs a full rebuild to add keys; there is no delete. Appendix A only sketches how updates could be added.
- Long keys with long shared prefixes, such as emails or URLs. The paper shows SuRF slower than Bloom on email keys and with higher false-positive rates, and SuRF-Base size has no theoretical upper bound because it depends on the key distribution.
- Adversarial or key-correlated range queries, or anywhere you need a guaranteed range false-positive rate. SuRF's rate depends on the stored and queried key distributions. Later work such as Grafite (arXiv 2311.15380) targets bounded, distribution-independent range false-positive rates.
- Production use without your own hardening. This is research code: x86-only (SSE2 and POPCNT hard-coded), no releases, and correctness bugs fixed as late as March 2022 (issue #13: false negatives from uninitialized label-vector tail bytes). Issue #11, a double free when destroying a deserialized SuRF, is still open. It also gives no benefit for long scans, because the paper saw no speedup on Next.

**Integration:** header-only · none for the filter itself (C++ standard library and SSE2 intrinsics); GoogleTest for the unit tests; YCSB, Python and the ARF git submodule for the benchmarks; the RocksDB integration lives in the separate efficient/rocksdb fork · C++11 with GCC/Clang builtins (__builtin_popcountll, __builtin_bswap64, __builtin_ctz, __builtin_prefetch) and -mpopcnt; CMake 2.6+ for the tests and benchmarks; CI config used GCC on Ubuntu 16.04 (xenial); no MSVC support documented · x86-64 only as written (unconditional <emmintrin.h> SSE2 label search, -mpopcnt required); no aarch64 or other fallback

**Vs siblings:** Every sibling here (Prefix, Xor/Binary Fuse, BuRR/Ribbon, Morton, Vacuum) is a point-membership filter; SuRF is the only one that answers range emptiness, seek-to-next-key and approximate counts, so pick it only when range queries matter. For point-only filtering a sibling will be smaller and faster, since SuRF's own paper concedes point queries to Bloom.

**Gotchas:**
- Input must be sorted in byte order, and release builds set -DNDEBUG, so nothing checks this. Issue #6 built from std::to_string(0..9999), which is not in lexicographic order, and got 9 false negatives out of 10,000. Duplicates are skipped. An empty key list or an empty-string key is only guarded by assert.
- The header defines functions that are not inline (config.hpp align/uint64ToString, SuRF::create, LabelVector::search, ...). Including surf.hpp from more than one .cpp gives duplicate-symbol link errors, so wrap it in a single translation unit, as the RocksDB fork does in util/surf.cc.
- Memory is managed by hand. ~SuRF() is empty, so you must call destroy() and then delete. destroy() frees the arrays but not the inner LoudsDense/LoudsSparse/bitvector objects. Copying a SuRF copies raw pointers, which leads to a double free. serialize() returns a new[] buffer the caller owns, in a raw native-endian format with no version or checksum.
- The shipped defaults differ from the paper: kSparseDenseRatio is 16 (the paper says R=64, and the 64 line is commented out) and the LOUDS-Dense rank block is 512 bits, not the paper's 64. Re-tune before comparing against the published numbers.

**Status:** Abandoned (last commit 2022-03-11, no releases or tags, 4 open issues, RocksDB fork frozen since 2018-12) but Apache-2.0 (the GitHub API says NOASSERTION; LICENSE is the plain Apache text) and only about 3.5k lines across 12 headers, so it can be vendored if you accept x86-only and hand-managed memory.

[repo](https://github.com/efficient/SuRF) · [benchmark](http://www.cs.cmu.edu/~huanche1/publications/surf_paper.pdf)

##### Vacuum Filter  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier B`

Deletable cuckoo-filter variant allowing any table size; ~25% less space than cuckoo on average, smaller than Bloom below 3% FPR.

**Beats:** Bloom filter, cuckoo filter — The PVLDB 2020 paper ran on an Intel Xeon E5-2687W (3.0 GHz, 30 MB L3) with the compiler and flags not stated, using 0.95x2^27 random 64-bit keys in 192 MB filters with 12-bit fingerprints (13-bit semi-sorted), against Fan et al.'s CF code, the authors' own Bloom/BBF/DIBF and the published MF/CQF code. VF-ss did positive lookups 1.1-1.8x faster than CF-ss and tied on deletes, and VF had the highest lookup throughput below 90% occupancy and the highest insert throughput below 65%. The ~25%-less-space-than-CF result comes mainly from CF's power-of-two table rounding. The '>10x vs Bloom' headline uses the authors' own Bloom implementation, which an xor-filter co-author on HN called un-optimized (other papers show about 2x for CF over Bloom). No std:: container is compared.

**Known shortcoming:** Correctness: a failed insert evicts an older fingerprint (vacuum.h insert, Add_many/evict), causing false negatives. *_many batch calls overrun unless arrays are padded to 128. Headers aren't ODR-safe (non-inline functions, global max, macros, using namespace std); the fast constructor prints to cout and calls srand(1); the fast version needs OpenSSL headers and __int128 (GCC/Clang only). The paper's resize and duplicate-insert variants (IUPR/DVF) aren't in the repo; no serialization or thread safety; fixed unseeded hashes. The '>10x vs Bloom' used an unoptimized Bloom (per an xor-filter co-author), and the space win mostly comes from cuckoo's power-of-2 rounding; cuckoo ties or wins above 90% occupancy. Code frozen since 2019-10 (only a 2024 LICENSE commit).

**How:** The table is split into power-of-two chunks, and the alternate bucket is B1 XOR (H(f) mod L), so both candidate buckets sit in the same chunk. The table then only needs to be a multiple of L, not a power of two. A multi-range alternate function uses the fingerprint's low 2 bits to pick one of 4 range sizes, each sized with a balls-into-bins bound for 95% load. Most keys get small ranges and so better cache/TLB locality: the paper's Table 2 reports 75% of bucket pairs in the same 4 KB page, versus 0.83% with a single range. Insertion looks one step ahead, checking the alternates of all 8 fingerprints in the two full buckets before a random-walk kick; bucket indexes use the multiply-shift (x*m)>>32 range reduction; lookups use the CF's SWAR bit-trick tag compare; and optional semi-sorting saves 1 bit per item.

**Use it when:**
- Dynamic sets of 64-bit integer (or pre-hashed) keys that need deletes, where the item count is known up front and is not near 3.8x2^k: there a cuckoo filter must round up to a power-of-two table (the paper's 274,926-cert set: VF-ss 12.9 vs CF-ss 21.0 bits/item at 0.1% FPR, similar lookup speed).
- Target false-positive rates below about 3% (e.g. 0.1%-0.01%), where VF-ss needs about 2.07 + 1.05*log2(1/eps) bits/item and beats Bloom on space.
- Filters much larger than the last-level cache, or on SSD/mmap, where two-bucket locality matters (the paper measured 1.86-2.13x faster lookups than CF on SSD with a 100 MB memory limit).
- Bulk loads and probes that can use the 128-key batch APIs with padded arrays.
- Research or prototyping where you will vendor and patch the headers yourself.

**Skip it when:**
- Static or build-once sets: xor/binary fuse or ribbon filters are smaller and faster to query.
- Filters run near full (>90% occupancy for lookups, >65% for inserts): the paper shows cuckoo filters tie or win there.
- You need resizing, duplicate-insert tolerance, serialization or concurrent access: the paper's IUPR/dynamic-VF framework is not in the repo, there is no save/load API, and there is no locking. Inserting the same key 9 times overflows its 8 candidate slots.
- Tiny filters, or FPR above 3%: the fast version rounds the table up to a multiple of at least 1,024 buckets (wasteful below about 4k keys), and above 3% FPR Bloom is smaller.
- Space is not tight and raw lookup speed is the goal: TUM's 2021 partitioned-filters study found that non-power-of-two addressing mostly slows cuckoo/Morton filters and recommends power-of-two tables in that case.

**Integration:** source-drop (header-only templates: vacuum.h + hashutil.h, or ModifiedCuckooFilter/src/*.h; no CMake/package, only demo makefiles) · vacuum.h: standard library only. Fast version: ModifiedCuckooFilter/src/hashutil.h includes <openssl/evp.h>, so it needs OpenSSL headers to compile (it links -lssl -lcrypto only if hashutil.cc is used). · C++14 per the top-level makefile (C++11 in the CF subdirectory). GCC/Clang only: needs unsigned __int128, __attribute__((packed)), and <bits/stdc++.h> in the demo. No tested compiler versions are documented. · 64-bit little-endian. The paper tested x86-64 (Xeon E5-2687W) and the makefile uses -march=native -mpopcnt. No SIMD intrinsics are needed, but the code does unaligned 64-bit loads.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Xor/Binary Fuse and BuRR when the set changes and you need deletions, since those are build-once. Pick it over Prefix Filter when you need deletes: Prefix Filter's README calls it an incremental (insert-only) filter. Against Morton Filter, the other deletable cuckoo variant, the VF paper reports lower memory in all its tested cases and support for arbitrary fingerprint lengths; SuRF solves range queries, a different problem.

**Gotchas:**
- A failed insert silently drops an older key. When vacuum.h insert() or the batch Add_many()/evict() runs out of kicks, it returns false after placing the new fingerprint and discards the last evicted one, so a previously inserted key can start returning false negatives. Rebuild on any failure.
- The batch APIs assume key and result arrays padded to a multiple of 128. Contain_many always processes full 128-key batches, and all *_many calls memcpy 128 results, so unpadded arrays are read and written out of bounds. Contain_many also ignores the victim slot.
- The headers are not ODR-safe. Non-inline free functions (upperpower2, solve_equation, proper_alt_range, a global max(int,int)) break linking if included in 2+ translation units. They also define global macros (MIN, MAX, ROUNDUP, debug), and hashutil.h does a global 'using namespace std'. vacuum.h uses assert/log without including <cassert>/<cmath>, and its include guard is named CUCKOO_H.
- Side effects and fixed hashing: the fast constructor prints alt ranges to std::cout and reseeds rand(). Each vacuum.h object embeds 512 KiB of encode/decode tables (the demo puts one on the stack). Hash seeds are fixed (mt19937(1), constant MurmurHash64), so adversarial keys can force insert failures. Deleting a key that was never inserted can remove another key's fingerprint.

**Status:** Research code frozen since October 2019: the only later commit (2024-11-23) added the MIT LICENSE, and a 2021 license question is still open with no reply. It is MIT, with an Apache-2.0 subdirectory derived from CMU/Intel's cuckoofilter, and small enough to vendor, but expect to patch the ODR, batch-overrun and stdout issues before production use. A Java port exists in Alibaba's mpc4j, and TUM's partitioned-filters repo vendors the code.

[repo](https://github.com/wuwuz/Vacuum-Filter) · [benchmark](http://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol13/p197-wang.pdf)

##### Vector Quotient Filter (VQF)  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier B`

SIMD two-choice quotient-style filter with deletes; about 2x faster inserts than the Morton filter and steady throughput to 90% load.

**Beats:** Morton filter — The authors' raw data in the repo (scripts/Performance.gnumeric: 2^28 slots, 8-bit tags, CPU and compiler not recorded, pre-2024 hashing code) backs the paper's claims: 40.1 ns vs 80.1 ns per insert against the Morton filter (2.0x), and 3.4x insert scaling from 1 to 4 threads; it also shows lookups at 34.3 ns vs 25-31 ns for the cuckoo filter, so VQF is slower on lookups rather than at parity. An independent run of the current code (Schmitz et al. 2025, AMD Ryzen 9 9950X, 2^30 slots) measured 22.1 M inserts/s and 25.4 M lookups/s, behind the Prefix filter (33.2 / 39.1) on both; the paper PDF itself returned 403, so its setup is unverified.

**Known shortcoming:** The full SIGMOD paper is paywalled (ACM 403), so CPU/compiler are unseen; last commit 2024-05.

**Known shortcoming:** The authors' own raw sheet shows inserts 2x Morton (40 vs 80 ns) but lookups slower than cuckoo (34 vs 25-31 ns); an independent 2025 run (Ryzen 9950X) puts it behind the Prefix filter on both and behind every cuckoo variant on lookups. In thread mode only insert is locked (query/remove unlocked). The 8-bit AVX-512 path uses vpermb (VBMI) behind an avx512bw check; GCC + Linux + x86 BMI2 only; a 2024 hashing rewrite was never re-benchmarked; no destroy/resize/serialize.

**How:** Each 64-byte block holds 48 8-bit fingerprints plus a 128-bit metadata bitvector that unary-encodes run boundaries for 80 buckets. That is quotient-filter/Robin Hood layout confined to one block (the paper's 'mini-filter'). A lookup broadcasts the fingerprint, compares it against the whole block in one AVX-512 compare (two AVX2 compares on the fallback path), and masks the hits to the bucket's run using BMI2 pdep/tzcnt rank-select on the metadata; power-of-two-choices hashing means it checks two blocks. An insert picks the less-loaded of the two blocks, looking at the alternate only once the primary is about 75% full, then shifts tags with one vpermb permute from precomputed shuffle tables and updates the metadata with pdep. There are no cuckoo kick-out chains, so insert cost stays nearly flat as the filter fills.

**Use it when:**
- Dynamic filters (inserts plus deletes) filled to high load: in the authors' 2^28-slot data, VQF inserts run at about 22 Mops up to 60% load and about 17 Mops at 90%, while the cuckoo filter falls from 33 Mops to about 2 Mops.
- Insert-heavy ingest on x86-64 servers with AVX-512 (the 8-bit fast path needs VBMI) and hardware-speed BMI2 (Intel Haswell or later, AMD Zen 3 or later), where a roughly 0.44% false-positive rate (8-bit tags) or roughly 0.002% (16-bit tags) is acceptable.
- Multi-threaded, insert-only build phases: the THREAD=1 build uses per-block spinlocks, and the authors' TXN data shows 62.3 ns/insert on 1 thread vs 18.4 ns on 4 threads.
- Keys you can already reduce to a well-mixed 64-bit hash, such as k-mers or IDs, with sizes from about 2^21 to 2^30 slots (the range the authors and later papers benchmarked).
- A reference or baseline implementation when evaluating quotient- or pocket-dictionary-style filters.

**Skip it when:**
- Lookup-dominated workloads: in the authors' own data the cuckoo filter answers lookups faster (25-31 ns vs 34 ns at 2^28). Schmitz et al. 2025 measured 25.4 M lookups/s for VQF vs 32-44 M/s for their cuckoo variants and 39 M/s for the Prefix filter.
- Insert-only or static sets: the Prefix filter builds 1.39-1.46x faster at similar space, and xor or binary fuse filters are smaller and faster for static sets.
- Non-x86 targets (ARM, Apple Silicon), MSVC or clang-only toolchains, and AMD Zen 1/Zen 2, where PDEP/PEXT are microcoded at about 18-cycle latency.
- You need a tunable FPR, counting, resizing, merging, serialization or enumeration. Only 8- or 16-bit tags exist, fixed at compile time; the CQF covers the rest.
- Production use needing maturity: no tests, releases or library target, and the May 2024 commit rewrote bucket and alternate-bucket hashing after the paper's measurements, with no published re-benchmark from the authors.

**Integration:** source-drop · vqf_filter.c needs only libc and x86 intrinsics headers. libssl/libcrypto (RAND_bytes), pthread and libitm are linked by the Makefile for the bundled benchmark drivers. · GCC/g++ with -std=c++11: vqf_filter.c is C++ despite its .c extension (reinterpret_cast, references, <algorithm>). The Makefile hard-codes gcc/g++ with -fgnu-tm and -march=native. · x86-64 only; BMI2 (pdep/pext/tzcnt) and at least AVX2 are required. The fast 8-bit path needs AVX-512 VBMI. The Makefile detects AVX-512 with Linux lscpu.

**Vs siblings:** Pick VQF over the cuckoo filter (efficient/cuckoofilter) or the Morton filter when you need deletes and insert throughput that holds at 80-90% load, and over the Prefix Filter when you need deletions or an AVX2 fallback (the Prefix Filter is insert-only and needs AVX-512). Choose the CQF instead for counting, resizing or merging, the cuckoo filter for lookup-bound workloads, and xor/binary fuse filters for static sets.

**Gotchas:**
- The caller supplies the hash. Bucket = hash % range and tag = bits 32-39 (tag 0 is remapped to 1), so a poorly mixed 64-bit hash raises the FPR. Duplicate inserts consume extra slots, and removing a key that was never inserted can delete another key's fingerprint.
- The AVX-512 path is guarded by __AVX512BW__, and the Makefile checks for avx512bw. The default 8-bit code, however, calls _mm512_permutexvar_epi8, which GCC places under avx512vbmi, so -march=native builds on BW-only CPUs (Skylake-SP, Cascade Lake) will likely fail to compile (inferred from the code, not tested). TAG_BITS is a hard #define in vqf_filter.h, so switching to 16-bit tags means editing the header.
- Library hygiene: vqf_init prints 'Size: N' to stdout and checks malloc only with assert. There is no destroy function (call free()). A failed insert prints 'vqf filter is full.' to stderr and returns false. The 64-byte blocks start 48 bytes after the malloc'd header, so whether each block fits in one cache line depends on the allocator.
- The full-block check in vqf_insert runs only inside the branch taken when the alternate bucket is in a different block. If both candidate buckets map to the same full block, the insert proceeds without a capacity check and can overwrite the last stored tag. This comes from code reading and was not tested.

**Status:** Stale: the last commit (2024-05-19) rewrote the hashing, and the repo has 0 open issues and 13 stars. It is BSD-3-Clause and small (vqf_filter.c is about 630 lines), so it is easy to vendor, but it ships no library target, tests or releases.

[repo](https://github.com/splatlab/vqf) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/swkim101/cspapers.org/main/index2/2021/sigmod/Vector%20Quotient%20Filters%3A%20Overcoming%20the%20Time%20Space%20Trade-Off%20in%20Filter%20Design)

##### xorfilter (Go binary fuse / xor filter reference implementation)  `Go`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Pure-Go binary fuse and xor filters: static membership filters at ~9 bits/key (0.39% FPR) vs ~11.5 for Bloom.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — The storage overheads over the information-theoretic minimum (13% binary fuse, 23% xor, 44% Bloom) and the 'more than twice as fast' build vs xor filters come from the authors' C++ fastfilter_cpp runs in JEA 2022 (GCC 10 -O3 -march=native, single-threaded, Intel i7-6700 Skylake, 100M random 64-bit keys), not from this Go code; the paper only says the Go port was checked qualitatively. The Go repo itself has only a README bits-per-key chart and construction benchmarks in PR threads (about 36 M keys/s at 1M keys on an Apple M1), with no head-to-head against a Go Bloom filter.

**Known shortcoming:** The 13/23/44% space overheads are from the paper; the JEA 2022 paper says the Go port was checked but reports no Go timings.

**Known shortcoming:** No Go-vs-Bloom benchmark in the repo; Go numbers exist only in PRs (~36M keys/s build on M1), where a blocked Bloom filter builds ~130M keys/s (~3.6x faster). Build needs ~24 B/key scratch. Static only (no add/delete); FPR fixed at 2^-8/16/32 (tunable-rate issue #19 open since 2020); 3-wise only.

**Known shortcoming:** Gotchas: the keys slice is sorted/deduplicated in place; a builder-built filter aliases builder memory; Load does no validation (can panic or over-allocate); construction can fail with 'too many iterations' (boundary-size retries fixed 2026-01). Below ~10k keys the space advantage over Bloom mostly disappears.

**How:** Each key maps to three slots in three consecutive segments of a fingerprint array of about 1.125n entries (the binary fuse layout the paper builds from Dietzfelbinger and Walzer's work). Construction 'peels' the resulting 3-hypergraph by repeatedly removing slots that hold a single key, then assigns fingerprints in reverse order so that fp(x) = H[h0] xor H[h1] xor H[h2]. A query is one murmur-style mix, three loads and two xors, with no loop over k hash functions as in a Bloom filter. The Go build buckets keys by segment for cache locality, derives peeling indexes with branchless bit tricks and can reuse scratch buffers (Jan 2026 releases); only the 3-wise variant is implemented (arity is hard-coded to 3), not the paper's denser 4-wise variant (~8.6 bits/key).

**Use it when:**
- Static key sets, or sets rebuilt per batch, in Go: per-SSTable filters in an LSM store (Pebble uses it for sstable table filters), per-segment or per-partition indexes, shipped allow/deny lists.
- Memory-bound deployments of roughly 100k+ keys, where the README's ~9 bits/key (8-bit) and ~18 bits/key (16-bit) figures hold and ~20% less space than a Bloom filter at the same FPR matters.
- Read-heavy concurrent lookups: the built filter is immutable, so many goroutines can call Contains without locks.
- Filters stored on disk or sent over the network: Save/LoadBinaryFuse use a portable little-endian format, and the README says the fingerprint arrays compress with gzip or zstd.
- Services that build many filters: BinaryFuseBuilder reuses scratch slices to cut GC churn. Single-threaded build speed is roughly 28-57 M keys/s depending on CPU and set size (PR #54 benchmarks on M1, AMD Turin, Intel Emerald Rapids and Axion).

**Skip it when:**
- Sets that grow incrementally or need deletes: there is no Add or Remove, so any change means a full rebuild. A Bloom, cuckoo or quotient filter fits better.
- Paths sensitive to build time or build memory. Building 1M keys allocated about 25 MB for a ~1.1 MB result (PR #48), and Pebble's wrapper budgets ~24 bytes per hash. On the same M1, a cache-line-blocked Bloom built at ~130 M keys/s vs ~36 M keys/s here (PR #48 note).
- Small sets (a few thousand keys or fewer). The code's size factor rises to 1.25n at 10k keys and 1.375n at 1k keys, plus segment rounding, so most of the space edge over Bloom disappears. The paper notes xor filters can be smaller below ~20k keys.
- FP rates other than 2^-8, 2^-16 or 2^-32: the width is fixed by the fingerprint type, and issue #19 (tunable rate) has been open since 2020. Ribbon filters are configurable.
- Lowest possible query latency: in the paper's C++ runs, an AVX2 blocked Bloom filter queried faster than 3-wise binary fuse (one cache line vs three scattered loads).

**Integration:** module · none at runtime (stdlib only; cespare/xxhash and testify are test-only) · Go 1.22 (go.mod); CI runs Go 1.22.x, plus 1.24.x for the big-endian job · any Go target. CI covers linux, macOS and windows (amd64), linux/386, and ppc64 big-endian under QEMU; Drone builds arm and arm64. The package imports unsafe on every target.

**Vs siblings:** In Go, pick this for a static key set when you want the production-tested option (Pebble, Oracle Coherence Go client, MatrixOne) at fixed 8- or 16-bit FP rates. Pick go-qfext if you need inserts after the build, ribbonGo if you need arbitrary FP rates or lower space overhead (its README claims ~4.7% over the minimum at r=7, vs ~12.5% here), and xorf or xor_singleheader for the same algorithm in Rust or C.

**Gotchas:**
- NewBinaryFuse, PopulateBinaryFuse8 and Populate may sort and deduplicate your keys slice in place. Pass a copy if you need the original.
- With BuildBinaryFuse, the returned filter's Fingerprints slice belongs to the builder and is overwritten by the next build. Copy it, or use one builder per live filter; Pebble guards its builders with sync.Pool and a mutex.
- LoadBinaryFuse has no integrity check (per the README) and trusts the stored length and segment fields. Corrupted or untrusted input can trigger a huge allocation or an index-out-of-range panic in Contains, so add your own checksum.
- Construction is randomized and returns 'too many iterations' after MaxIterations (1024, a mutable package-level var). Before the Jan 2026 fix (PR #50), some sizes near segment-length boundaries averaged ~110 retries; a 2023 false-negative bug on duplicate-heavy input (issue #35) is fixed. Use v0.5.1 or later. Xor8 has no Save/Load.

**Status:** Actively maintained: v0.5.1 was tagged 2026-01-26 after a Dec 2025-Jan 2026 run of build-speed and buffer-reuse PRs, one issue is open, and it is Apache-2.0 with under 1,000 lines of stdlib-only Go, easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/FastFilter/xorfilter) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.01174)

### toolchain-and-build

#### build-systems

##### Mill  `Scala`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

JVM build tool for Java/Scala/Kotlin; 4-44x faster clean/incremental compiles than Maven, 3.6-10.2x than Gradle.

**Beats:** Apache Maven and Gradle — Mill's own docs page (mill-build.org/mill/comparisons/performance.html) benchmarked Mill 0.12.9-native (Java 17) against each project's default Maven/Gradle version on a 2021 M1 MacBook Pro (10 CPU, 32GB RAM), median wall time of 3 runs after warmup. Netty (~500k LOC, 47 modules) vs Maven: 4.0x-44.0x across sequential/parallel/single-module clean, incremental, and no-op compile. Mockito (~100k LOC, 22 modules) vs Gradle: 3.6x-10.2x for the same five scenarios.

**How:** Mill runs a persistent JVM background daemon, avoiding per-invocation JVM startup and classloading. It memoizes every build step as a fine-grained Task in a dependency graph, so unchanged tasks are skipped entirely (no-op compiles finish in ~0.1s). For Java/Scala incremental compiles it uses the Zinc incremental compiler to recompile only files whose changes affect downstream code. Unlike Maven, it works directly with classfiles on disk rather than round-tripping through .m2 jar packing/unpacking, and it parallelizes independent tasks by default.

**Use it when:**
- Multi-module Java/Scala/Kotlin monorepos where edit-compile-test iteration speed matters
- CI pipelines bottlenecked by Maven/Gradle daemon startup or full-module recompilation on every run
- Teams that want built-in selective test execution, test parallelism, and Chrome-trace build profiling without extra plugins
- New JVM projects willing to adopt a non-XML/non-Groovy build DSL from the start
- Want a self-contained native (Graal) launcher with fast CLI startup and no local JDK requirement

**Skip it when:**
- Large existing Maven/Gradle codebase with heavy reliance on the Maven Central/Gradle Plugin Portal plugin ecosystem, which Mill's is much smaller than
- Non-JVM projects (C++/CMake/Cargo, etc.) - not applicable at all
- Windows-ARM machines: Mill has no native executable there (upstream GraalVM limitation) and falls back to the slower JVM launcher, which also needs a system JDK 17+
- Teams running very high task parallelism on newer Mill versions: an open issue (#7381, 1.2.0-RC1) reports up to ~20x slowdown and thread-pool blowup at large --jobs values
- Projects needing mature BSP/IDE tooling parity - several Metals/BSP integration bugs have been filed (mostly closed, but recent)

**Integration:** source-drop (CLI tool + build.mill config file per project, not a library) · none for the default launcher (self-contained Graal native binary, downloads its own JVM for module builds); the '-jvm' launcher variant requires a system JDK 17+ · Mill supports JVM 11+ for evaluating builds (configurable per-project via mill-jvm-version); native launcher needs no local JDK, JVM launcher needs JDK 17+ · Native executables: Windows/Mac/Linux on Intel, Mac/Linux on ARM. Windows-ARM has no native executable and falls back to the JVM launcher.

**Vs siblings:** No sibling overlap: ccache, Buck2, tup, and xmake all target C/C++ or polyglot native builds, not the JVM. Pick Mill specifically when the baseline pain is Maven/Gradle overhead on a Java/Scala/Kotlin project; none of the catalogued siblings apply there.

**Gotchas:**
- PowerShell 5.1 writes UTF-16LE .mill-version files that Mill can't read; PowerShell 7+ is required on Windows
- Benchmark page itself is internally inconsistent on the Mill version used: the summary text says 'Mill 1.1.0' while the detailed benchmark tables specify 'Java 17 + Mill 0.12.9-native'
- The Netty and Mockito ports used for the benchmark are not 100% complete - some subprojects, linters, and Android/Kotlin/OSGI tests were disabled to make the comparison apples-to-apples
- Open bug (#7381) shows severe negative performance scaling (thread pool grows to thousands of blocked threads) at very high --jobs counts on a 1.2.0-RC1 build; unclear if it reached a stable release

**Status:** Actively maintained: latest commit is today (2026-09-24), 2.8k GitHub stars, MIT licensed. Distributed as a self-updating bootstrap script (Maven Central-hosted releases), so it's directly usable without vendoring.

[repo](https://github.com/com-lihaoyi/mill) · [benchmark](https://mill-build.org/mill/comparisons/performance.html)

#### compilers-frontends

##### zapcc  `C++`  `NCSA`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

zapcc: a Clang fork with a persistent caching server that rebuilds template-heavy C++ 1.2-3.3x faster than GCC/Clang.

**Beats:** GCC, Clang — On Baptiste Wicht's 2016 ETL (header-only, template-heavy) benchmark on a 4-core/16GB desktop, zapcc++ (beta) built ETL's debug config at -j1 in 214s vs 469s for GCC 5.4.0 (~2.2x) and 710s for Clang 3.9 (~3.3x); the release config at -j1 took 640s vs 782s for GCC (~1.2x) and 960s for Clang (~1.5x). Colfax Research's independent 2017 compiler comparison found Zapcc 1.0.1 compiling the TMV library in 510s vs 848s for GCC 7.2.0 and 902s for Clang 5.0.0 (~1.7x) on a 2-socket Xeon Platinum 8168, corroborating the direction and rough magnitude of the gain.

**How:** The zapccs server keeps parsed ASTs, template instantiations, and generated IR/code resident in memory between compiles instead of redoing that work per translation unit, and can reuse results across source files in a way the README compares to link-time inlining decisions being made proactively. This turns repeated compilation of shared, heavily-templated headers (the dominant cost in libraries like ETL) into cache hits instead of full reparses/re-instantiations. The README claims single-file incremental recompiles are typically 10-50x faster than a cold build because only the changed dependency subgraph is reprocessed; full from-scratch builds see smaller (2-5x) gains that scale with how template/header-heavy the project is.

**Use it when:**
- Large, template/header-heavy C++ codebase (clang- or gcc-compatible source) built repeatedly on Linux x86-64, where CI or local dev-loop compile time dominates
- Iterative development where a single file changes and you rebuild often (the caching server gives its biggest wins here)
- Full debug builds of header-only template libraries similar in shape to ETL (measured 2-3.3x faster than Clang/GCC)
- You already know the project compiles cleanly with vanilla Clang and can dedicate a long-lived background process and extra RAM to the caching server
- You don't need sanitizers and can tolerate an unmaintained, LLVM-r325000-vintage (Feb 2018) fork

**Skip it when:**
- Plain C or lightly-templated C++, where the README itself says caching gives little to no acceleration
- Any build needing ASan/UBSan/TSan/MSan - explicitly unsupported
- Modern C++17/C++20 code: development stopped in 2020, last synced to LLVM trunk 2018-02-13, and -std=gnu++17 was still rejected as an invalid value as of the last activity on that issue (Dec 2018)
- Correctness-sensitive or release builds: a user reported (issue #42) non-deterministic object files and binaries that segfault at reproducible-but-build-order-dependent locations under parallel (-j>1) builds, not reproduced with plain clang, and it was never resolved
- Windows/macOS targets: only minimally/lightly tested, MSVC ABI and zapcc-cl are explicitly unsupported, and there is no one left maintaining platform fixes

**Integration:** source-drop · none beyond a standard LLVM/Clang build toolchain (CMake + Ninja, per README) · Effectively frozen at Clang/LLVM ~6.0-era conformance (last merged with LLVM r325000, 2018-02-13); build via CMake + Ninja exactly as for LLVM. -std=gnu++17 was not recognized as of the last relevant activity (issue #32, Dec 2018); treat full C++17/C++20 support as unverified/likely absent. · x86-64 Linux (thoroughly tested, primary target); Windows via MSVC or mingw-w64 targeting mingw-w64 32/64-bit (minimally tested; zapcc-cl/MSVC-ABI target explicitly unsupported); macOS via Clang (experimental, lightly tested). No aarch64 or RISC-V support (a RISC-V feature request was closed unresolved).

**Vs siblings:** Pick zapcc over MIR/c2m or TinyCC when the actual cost is template-instantiation and header re-parsing in a large, clang/gcc-compatible C++ codebase (its gains scale with template/header weight); MIR/c2m and TinyCC instead target small/simple C or C-subset inputs for fast one-shot JIT-style compiles and are both still maintained, whereas zapcc has been abandoned since 2020 with an open, unresolved correctness bug (issue #42).

**Gotchas:**
- The in-memory server can share/inline state across translation units, making -j>1 builds non-deterministic and, per issue #42, occasionally producing binaries that segfault at reproducible-but-order-dependent locations not seen with plain clang
- -std=gnu++17 was rejected as an invalid value as of the project's last active development (issue #32); it was never fixed before the maintainer confirmed (issue #47, 2021) the project is dead
- zapccs must be killed manually (pkill zapcc) to release memory or to pick up a freshly rebuilt zapcc binary; it also has a configurable memory cap (bin/zapccs.config MaxMemory) that silently resets the entire cache when hit
- README recommends -j should not exceed physical core count + 2, especially on hyperthreaded Intel CPUs that report double the physical core count — oversubscribing the server can make builds slower, not faster

**Status:** Abandoned since 2020 (last commit 2020-07-21, last synced to LLVM trunk 2018-02-13); the maintainer confirmed in a 2021 issue that the project is dead. NCSA/LLVM-Release-licensed and copyable, but it's a full compiler toolchain you'd have to build and maintain yourself, not a small vendorable file, and the known non-determinism/segfault correctness bug (issue #42) was never fixed.

[repo](https://github.com/yrnkrn/zapcc) · [benchmark](https://baptiste-wicht.com/posts/2016/12/zapcc-cpp-compilation-speed-against-gcc-54-and-clang-39.html)

#### formatters-linters-lsps

##### Oxlint (oxc-project/oxc)  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Rust-based JavaScript/TypeScript linter and toolchain that replaces ESLint with 50-100x faster linting.

**Beats:** ESLint — Oxc's own bench-linter repo (hyperfine, 1 warmup, non-zero exits ignored, ESLint v9, no ESLint cache) measured Oxlint linting the VS Code source tree at 62.10x/118.25x/60.09x ESLint's speed on an M2 Max 12-core / M4 Max / M3 Air 8-core respectively, and ~17x single-threaded (31.025s vs 1.824s on M2 Max); vs Biome on the same tree with only the no-debugger rule enabled, 2.72x/2.49x/3.31x across the same three machines; vs typescript-eslint with type-aware rules on Vue core and Sentry (M2 Max), 8.22x and 12.38x respectively.

**How:** Oxlint reuses oxc's own parser and semantic analyzer, built on an arena allocator (oxc_allocator), so most rules run in a single AST traversal instead of ESLint's per-rule/per-plugin dispatch. Files are linted in parallel across CPU cores via Rayon, with the `ignore` crate (SIMD-accelerated) walking the file tree, so throughput scales with core count. That parallelism is why the gap widens on more cores: ~17x single-threaded vs ESLint, up to ~62-118x multi-threaded on 8-12 core machines in the project's own benchmark.

**Use it when:**
- Large JS/TS monorepos where ESLint's per-file startup and plugin dispatch overhead dominates CI time
- Standard-rule linting (no exotic plugin needs) where raw throughput matters more than full rule-set parity
- Multi-core CI runners or dev machines, since the speedup scales with thread count
- Teams migrating incrementally, running Oxlint alongside ESLint to cover the remaining rule gap
- Projects wanting near-instant `npx oxlint` feedback with zero required config

**Skip it when:**
- Codebases that depend on ESLint plugins with no Oxlint equivalent or JS-plugin bridge
- Projects needing full type-aware linting parity with typescript-eslint - gain drops to 8-12x and rule coverage is narrower, and it needs the separate oxlint-tsgolint/TypeScript 7 component
- Repos still on legacy ESLint v8 config - must convert to flat config via @eslint/migrate-config before the official migration tool works
- Setups with local/custom ESLint plugins - these do not migrate automatically
- Single-core or low-core environments, where the advantage shrinks toward the ~17x single-threaded figure

**Integration:** crate · Rust workspace of internal oxc_* crates (oxc_allocator, oxc_parser, oxc_linter, oxc_semantic, ...) plus rayon, bpaf, napi, tower-lsp-server; npm CLI package ships a prebuilt native binary with no user-facing JS deps · Rust 1.96.0 (workspace MSRV, N-2 policy), edition 2024; no Rust toolchain needed to use the prebuilt npm binary · Linux (glibc/musl; x86-64, arm/aarch64, riscv64, powerpc64le), macOS (x86-64, arm64), Windows (x86-64, i686, arm64), plus wasm and OpenHarmony targets per the npm package's optionalDependencies

**Vs siblings:** Over Biome specifically: the same VS Code benchmark run by the Oxc project shows Oxlint 2.5-3.3x faster (though that test used only the no-debugger rule, so treat it as a floor, not a full-ruleset comparison). The other catalogued siblings (Ruff, Pyrefly, ty, clangd-tidy) target Python or C++, so within JS/TS linting Oxlint is the only ESLint-throughput entry here besides Biome.

**Gotchas:**
- Legacy ESLint v8 configs must be converted to flat config first (via @eslint/migrate-config) before the @oxlint/migrate tool works
- Local/custom ESLint plugins don't migrate automatically and need manual setup
- Type-aware rules require the separate oxlint-tsgolint binary, which depends on TypeScript 7
- The published Oxlint-vs-Biome benchmark enables only a single rule (no-debugger) on both linters, so the ~2x figure isn't representative of full rule-set performance

**Status:** Actively maintained (commits as recent as today, 22.9k stars across the oxc monorepo) with VoidZero backing; MIT licensed and directly usable via `npx oxlint`, though ESLint rule/plugin parity is still incomplete.

[repo](https://github.com/oxc-project/oxc) · [benchmark](https://github.com/oxc-project/bench-linter)

##### Pyrefly  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Rust type checker and LSP for Python; faster than mypy and Pyright on cold, whole-project checks.

**Beats:** mypy; Pyright — Astral's ty_benchmark harness (public, pinned revisions) ran a cold CLI type-check of home-assistant/core with no cache on an Apple M4: Pyrefly 5.32s vs Pyright 19.62s (~3.7x faster) vs mypy 45.66s (~8.6x faster). The same post's LSP incremental-recheck test on PyTorch showed Pyrefly was the slowest of the three, ~2.4-2.6s vs Pyright's ~370-386ms and ty's ~4.5-4.7ms; no compiler flags are relevant since these are prebuilt/uv-installed binaries, hardware is stated only as 'M4'.

**How:** The whole tool is a single Rust binary; type-checking is parallelized across modules with rayon, backed by concurrent data structures (dashmap, parking_lot) and jemalloc/mimalloc allocators. Per its own ARCHITECTURE.md, it deliberately favors module-level incrementality over fine-grained, binding-level incrementality (the Salsa/rust-analyzer or Roslyn/TypeScript approach): each module's bindings are solved sequentially and completely, betting that whole-module solving is fast enough that finer-grained caching isn't needed. That design gives fast cold/batch checks but is the likely reason its LSP incremental recheck lagged both Pyright and ty in Astral's benchmark.

**Use it when:**
- Cold or CI type-checks of large, multi-module Python codebases (millions of LOC) where batch throughput matters more than incremental recheck latency
- Migrating an existing mypy or Pyright project and wanting built-in tooling (`pyrefly init`, `pyrefly suppress`) to stage the rollout
- Codebases heavy on Pydantic, Django, or pytest patterns, where Pyrefly's built-in framework modeling reduces false positives
- Wanting one tool that is both the CLI checker and the editor LSP with consistent results (VS Code, Neovim, Zed)
- Multi-core CI machines, since checking parallelizes across modules with rayon

**Skip it when:**
- Editor-driven inner loop where every-keystroke/save recheck latency matters most: Astral's benchmark measured Pyrefly's incremental LSP recheck on PyTorch at ~2.4-2.6s, versus ~370ms for Pyright and ~4.5ms for ty
- Memory-constrained dev machines: multiple open issues report very high RSS, including one reporting the VS Code extension reaching up to 100GB on a large repo
- Older Linux hosts on glibc 2.17, where a memory-allocation crash has been reported
- Teams that need strict semver stability: Pyrefly's own version policy states monthly minor releases can introduce new type errors or other breaking changes
- Relying on the README's PyTorch '15x faster than mypy/Pyright' headline for capacity planning — no hardware or methodology is published for it

**Integration:** crate · none to run (pip install pyrefly ships a prebuilt Rust binary); building from source pulls a Rust workspace (rayon, dashmap, parking_lot, lsp-server, ruff_python_parser/ruff_notebook, tokio, etc.) · Rust stable, edition 2024 (Rust 1.85+) to build from source; rust-toolchain.toml pins channel=stable with no exact version · Linux x86_64/i686/aarch64 (glibc and musl), macOS x86_64/arm64, Windows x86_64/i686/aarch64 — all built as prebuilt release binaries

**Vs siblings:** Pick Pyrefly over ty (astral-sh/ty) when you value production-scale proof (Instagram's 20M-LOC codebase, PyTorch, JAX adoption) and built-in Pydantic/Django/pytest modeling over raw speed — in the same benchmark ty beat Pyrefly on both cold checks (2.19s vs 5.32s) and, by a wide margin, incremental LSP rechecks (4.5ms vs 2.6s).

**Gotchas:**
- README claims IDE rechecks 'typically complete in under 10 milliseconds,' but Astral's independent benchmark measured 2.4-2.6s for Pyrefly's LSP recheck on PyTorch — a large, credible gap
- Multiple open GitHub issues report excessive memory use, including one titled 'Pyrefly consumes A LOT of memory' and another reporting the VS Code extension using up to 100GB
- Reported crash allocating memory on glibc 2.17 (older Linux distros)
- Does not follow strict semver: any minor version bump (monthly) may add new type errors or change behavior; `pyrefly suppress` exists specifically to manage that churn

**Status:** Actively maintained — commits as of today (2026-09-24), monthly minor releases, 1.0 tagged as stable; MIT-licensed and installable as a prebuilt binary via pip, so adoption cost is low despite the non-semver upgrade churn.

[repo](https://github.com/facebook/pyrefly) · [benchmark](https://astral.sh/blog/ty)

##### ty  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Rust-based Python type checker and language server from Astral; 10-100x faster cold checks than mypy and Pyright.

**Beats:** mypy; Pyright — Astral's own blog (astral.sh/blog/ty, dated 2025-12-16) reports, on an Apple M4: cold no-cache CLI type-check of home-assistant/core at ty 2.19s vs Pyrefly 5.32s vs Pyright 19.62s vs mypy 45.66s (~9x over Pyright, ~21x over mypy), and LSP incremental re-check after editing a file in pytorch/pytorch at ty 4.5ms vs Pyright 370.5ms vs Pyrefly 2.60s (~82x over Pyright, ~578x over Pyrefly; prose cites slightly different 4.7ms/386ms/2.38s). No tool versions or exact M4 variant/RAM are stated on the page; the harness (astral-sh/ruff scripts/ty_benchmark) is public with pinned lockfiles. The repo's own BENCHMARKS.md, run separately on an Apple M3 Max (128GB) with pinned versions (ty 0.0.55, Pyright 1.1.410, mypy 2.1.0, Pyrefly 1.1.1), corroborates the same ranking on other projects (e.g. Black: ty 69.5ms vs Pyrefly 128.3ms vs mypy 1.316s vs Pyright 1.420s) though with different magnitudes than the blog.

**How:** Written in Rust and built on the `salsa` incremental-computation framework (the same query/memoization engine used by rust-analyzer), giving fine-grained incremental re-analysis so editing one file only recomputes affected queries instead of re-checking the project. It parallelizes work with `rayon`, and on Linux/other non-macOS/Windows targets swaps in `tikv-jemallocator` for allocation-heavy workloads. Cold/no-cache runs are fast because the whole pipeline (parsing, semantic indexing, inference) is Rust-native rather than Python, unlike mypy.

**Use it when:**
- Large monorepos where cold, no-cache CLI type-check latency matters (CI, pre-commit)
- IDE/language-server usage where sub-second incremental re-check after each keystroke/save matters
- Projects already on the Astral toolchain (uv, Ruff) wanting one vendor for lint/format/type-check
- Teams willing to tolerate a beta, fast-moving type checker in exchange for speed
- Python 3.10+ targeted codebases (earlier versions type-check with more false positives/negatives)

**Skip it when:**
- Projects needing a stable, versioned API/behavior contract — ty is 0.0.x with no stable-API guarantee and diagnostics can change between any two releases
- Codebases relying on mypy/pyright-specific strict-mode flags or plugins with no ty equivalent yet (see docs/coming-from-mypy-or-pyright.md rule-mapping gaps)
- Code with very complex/deeply nested expressions where bidirectional type inference has known 'dismal performance' and regression reports (astral-sh/ty#3180, #3505)
- Warm/cached CLI re-check comparisons — the headline benchmark is a no-cache scenario; only mypy supports warm cached re-checks in that comparison, so it doesn't show ty's cache-hit CLI behavior
- Teams that need mature third-party plugin ecosystems (e.g. mypy plugins) that ty doesn't support

**Integration:** source-drop (prebuilt standalone binary / PyPI wheel built via maturin from a Rust binary crate in the astral-sh/ruff monorepo) · none (Python package pyproject.toml declares zero deps; the Rust binary statically bundles its own dependencies) · none required to use it (install via uvx/pipx/pip/standalone installer/Docker); building from source requires Rust 1.96+ per astral-sh/ruff's workspace Cargo.toml · macOS, Linux, Windows (prebuilt binaries via GitHub Releases, PyPI wheels, standalone installer script, Docker image ghcr.io/astral-sh/ty)

**Vs siblings:** Versus Pyrefly (the only true sibling here — same baseline of mypy/Pyright): pick ty when incremental LSP re-check latency matters most (Astral's benchmark shows ty beating Pyrefly by ~500x on that metric) and you want a public, pinned, reproducible benchmark harness rather than Pyrefly's README claim with no stated methodology; pick Pyrefly if you need functionality ty doesn't yet have. Biome/Oxlint/clangd-tidy/Ruff aren't real alternatives here — different languages or different tool category (linting/formatting, not type checking).

**Gotchas:**
- 0.0.x versioning: no stable API yet, diagnostics/behavior can change between any two releases (README 'Version policy')
- Default checking mode is stricter than mypy/pyright defaults in several ways (e.g. always checks unannotated function bodies) with no flag to relax it, which can surface new errors when migrating
- Complex/deeply nested expressions can trigger severe slowdowns from bidirectional type inference cost (open issues: 'Dismal performance when some complex expressions exist', a sympy performance regression)
- The astral-sh/ty GitHub repo is mostly packaging/docs; the actual Rust type-checker source lives in the astral-sh/ruff repo's crates/ty* via a git submodule

**Status:** Actively developed beta from Astral (same team as Ruff/uv), with commits as recent as today; MIT licensed and usable now via uvx/pipx/pip, but the 0.0.x version policy means no stable API and diagnostics can change release to release.

[repo](https://github.com/astral-sh/ty) · [benchmark](https://astral.sh/blog/ty)

#### linkers

##### mold  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Drop-in ELF linker beating LLVM lld and GNU ld via pervasive data-parallelism across the whole link pipeline.

**Beats:** lld — On 9 real-world programs (Blender, Chromium, Clang, ClickHouse, Firefox, Godot, LibreOffice, PyTorch, TensorFlow, some ARM64 variants) linked in both debug and release configurations, mold beat LLVM lld by 4.9x at the median (per-program range ~1.5x-16.1x) and wild by 1.9x at the median. All three linkers were built from source in release mode as of 2026-08-28 with default options; measurements are wall-clock, median of 3 runs after a warm-up, on an AMD Ryzen Threadripper 7980X/Ubuntu 24.04 and an Apple M1 Ultra/Fedora Asahi Remix 42.

**How:** Per the ASPLOS 2027 paper ('mold: A Massively Parallel Linker'), mold decouples the traditionally entangled passes of Unix linking — symbol resolution, archive-member pulling, relocation, output layout — so each stage is split across a rayon-based work-stealing thread pool (capped at 32 threads by default) instead of running mostly single-threaded like lld/gold. Section-merging deduplication uses a custom lock-free, open-addressing concurrent hash map (CAS-claimed buckets, per-shard probing) whose table size is pre-estimated with HyperLogLog cardinality counting rather than grown/resized on the fly. The paper's ablation study found no single optimization dominates — the speedup is cumulative across nearly every pass being parallelized.

**Use it when:**
- Large C/C++/Rust ELF builds on Linux/Unix where the link step dominates the debug-edit-rebuild loop — mold shows 4x-16x over lld on multi-GB debug binaries (per-program table in README).
- Many-core workstations or CI runners (Threadripper-class) where lld/gold leave most cores idle during linking.
- Toolchains that already select a linker via `-fuse-ld=`/`-B` (Clang, GCC 12.1+, Rust via `.cargo/config.toml`) — swapping in mold is a one-line config change.
- Any of the 16 listed non-Windows/non-macOS ELF targets, including cross-linking ARM64 output from an x86 host.
- Teams that want bit-for-bit deterministic link output with no host-specific default paths baked in.

**Skip it when:**
- Native Windows/MSVC or macOS/Mach-O link jobs: the mold.exe binary builds and runs on Windows, but per the maintainer (issue #1658) it 'can only be used to link ELF binaries' — no PE/COFF or Mach-O support, and macOS support was explicitly ruled out (issue #1052 thread).
- Projects relying on non-trivial linker-script features (custom SECTIONS/memory layouts, embedded/microcontroller link maps) — mold supports only the minimal subset needed to parse glibc's loader script and has stated no plan to add more (open issue #243, 'SECTIONS doesn't seem to be implemented').
- Workloads needing incremental or partial linking (gold-style `--incremental`, or `-r` combined with LTO) — not supported; every invocation is a full relink.
- Small link jobs on few-core machines: on the M1 Ultra debug table mold actually regressed vs. lld for Clang (0.9x) — the parallel design needs enough cores/input size to pay for itself.
- If you need long field-history on the exact codebase in production: the linker rewrote from C++ to Rust just before this snapshot (Sept 2026, issue #1655), so 'production since 2021' applies to the predecessor C++ implementation, not the current Rust one.

**Integration:** crate (Cargo workspace building a CLI binary `mold` + companion shared object `mold-wrapper.so`; not a library you link against) · Rust crates: rayon, hashbrown, memmap2, blake3, xxhash-rust, crc32fast, zstd, flate2, libz-sys, cpp_demangle, rustc-demangle, bstr, memchr, getrandom, libc. Build also needs a C compiler (GCC/Clang) and Git. · Rust stable toolchain (Cargo.toml workspace edition 2024, i.e. rustc 1.85+); rust-toolchain.toml pins channel "stable". · Linux/Unix ELF targets: x86-64, i386, ARM32/64 (+BE), RISC-V32/64 (+BE), PowerPC32/64 (v1/v2), s390x, LoongArch32/64, SPARC64, m68k, SH-4. Also builds on Windows (CI job build-windows.ps1 produces mold.exe) but, per the maintainer, can then only link ELF output, not PE/COFF.

**Vs siblings:** Pick mold over wild when you need broader architecture coverage (16 ISAs vs. wild's more limited set) or maximum throughput on many-core Linux boxes: mold is ~1.9x faster than wild at the median, and wild is marked N/A (can't link at all) on several rows in mold's own table, including Chromium release builds because it lacks --icf=all. mold and zld don't really compete — zld targets Apple's ld64/Mach-O toolchain exclusively, so on macOS zld is the only option of the two; mold has explicitly ruled out macOS support.

**Gotchas:**
- --start-group/--end-group are accepted for compatibility but silently ignored — mold (like lld) tracks archive symbols globally so link order doesn't matter, which can surprise anyone relying on that flag's traditional semantics.
- No incremental or partial (-r + LTO) linking; every run is a full relink.
- Only a minimal linker-script subset is supported (just enough to read glibc's ASCII libc.so loader script); no plans to extend it.
- Windows builds of the CLI exist but only link ELF, not PE/COFF — don't expect an MSVC linker replacement.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-23; 140+ contributors; CI test-builds ~19,000 Gentoo packages against GNU ld as a control before each release); MIT-licensed with prebuilt binaries via most distro package managers and GitHub releases, though the linker core is a very recent (Sept 2026) full rewrite from C++ to Rust.

[repo](https://github.com/rui314/mold) · [benchmark](https://github.com/rui314/mold#benchmark)

##### Wild (wild-linker)  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`  `active`  `Tier A`

Rust linker for Linux that beats LLVM lld on debug-build link time via mmap'd input and rayon-parallelized phases.

**Beats:** lld — Verified against mold's own August 2026 README benchmark table (all three linkers built from source in release mode as of 2026-08-28, wall-clock median of 3 runs after warm-up, on a Threadripper 7980X/Ubuntu 24.04 and an M1 Ultra/Fedora Asahi 42): wild beat lld on all 28 rows where it could link (per-row ratios 1.38x-4.18x, median ~2.1x, e.g. Chromium debug 16.64s to 3.98s), while mold beat wild on those same rows by ~1.9x at the median.

**How:** Wild mmaps input files instead of read()-ing them, deduplicates merge-string sections up front, and resolves symbols through a hashmap before touching relocations — the same input-handling strategy mold uses. Its phases (symbol_db, resolution, layout, elf_writer) run on a rayon-owned thread pool, using par_iter/par_bridge to parallelize the relocation-graph traversal and the copy/relocate step in the ELF writer, with only a few phases left single-threaded. It isn't algorithmically different from mold — both are mmap-plus-parallel-ELF-writer designs — it is simply slower in practice today (mold's README puts wild ~1.9x behind mold at the median on the same benchmark).

**Use it when:**
- Iterative Linux debug builds (Rust/Cargo, or C/C++ via Clang or GCC 16.1+/CMake 4.4+) where lld's link time is the edit-compile-link bottleneck, for a program wild can link (Blender, Clang, ClickHouse, Godot, LibreOffice, PyTorch, Chromium debug all measured 1.4x-4.2x faster than lld).
- Projects already invoking lld via -fuse-ld=lld/--ld-path=lld — swapping to wild is a flag-value change, no build-system rework.
- x86-64, ARM64, riscv64gc, PPC64LE, or LoongArch64 Linux targets, especially with Clang or GCC 16.1+ / CMake 4.4+ for first-class integration.
- Teams that want an actively developed, Rust-native alternative to mold specifically because mold's author has ruled out incremental linking.
- Experimental wasm32-wasip1/wasm32-unknown-unknown linking, if you're comfortable with a feature flagged as experimental (--features wasm).

**Skip it when:**
- Release builds needing --icf=all (identical code folding) — wild doesn't implement it, so it is N/A on the mold benchmark's Chromium-release rows rather than just losing some size savings.
- Programs wild can't link at all yet: TensorFlow 2.21, Firefox debug builds, and ARM64 Chromium/Firefox are N/A for wild in the mold benchmark suite.
- Any Mach-O (Apple) or Windows target, or non-Linux host — unsupported.
- Builds depending on fuller linker-script features (SEARCH_DIR, STARTUP, TARGET, INSERT, NOCROSSREFS, REGION_ALIAS, MEMORY '>region' placement, PHDRS AT attribute) — only partially implemented per LINKER_SCRIPT_SUPPORT.md.
