**Integration:** source-drop · google/re2 (git submodule, built to obj/libre2.a) · C++11, g++-compatible CXX; Python 3 to regenerate unicodedata.h · x86-64 (Linux/macOS and similar 64-bit UNIX); other architectures only via a slower VM interpreter (ENABLE_VM=1)

**Vs siblings:** Among the catalogued RE2-beating siblings (rejit, BLARE), pick re2jit specifically when the bottleneck is \p{X} Unicode-class matching or capture-group boundary reporting on x86-64 Linux/macOS — that's its one distinctly measured edge. rejit and BLARE report broader RE2 speedups and don't share re2jit's missing \b/\B support, so prefer them for general-purpose replacement.

**Gotchas:**
- Reserves Unicode plane-15 private-use code points (roughly U+F0000-U+F0FFF) for internal use; matching against them is unsupported.
- \b/\B word boundaries are silently absent rather than erroring.
- Unanchored search with backreferences can't use RE2's DFA fallback, so it's slow by a large constant, independent of algorithmic complexity.
- Perf figures come only from two repo-bundled programs (test/30-long, test/32-markdownish, built with ENABLE_PERF_TESTS=1); no independent benchmark exists.

**Status:** Abandoned since its last commit on 2016-11-25, and the README itself says 'don't use this thing either way' — but it's MIT-licensed, depends only on RE2, and small enough to vendor if you just want the Unicode-charclass lookup-table trick.

[repo](https://github.com/pyos/re2jit) · [benchmark](https://github.com/pyos/re2jit/blob/master/README.md)

#### text-search-and-indexing

##### frg (fastripgrep)  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust CLI that indexes a codebase with sparse n-grams to search faster than ripgrep on every tested pattern.

**Beats:** ripgrep — First-party README table on the openclaw codebase (9,000 files, case-sensitive, warm cache, output to /dev/null), built with `cargo build --release` (no rustc version or CPU model stated): frg beat ripgrep on all 8 tested patterns (1.06x-5.3x, e.g. 10ms vs ripgrep's 53ms on a selective literal) and beat grep by roughly 155x on that same literal (1,553ms), excluding the one-time ~20-23s index build. benches/bench.rs only times frg against itself on synthetic 1K/5K-file repos and never runs ripgrep, so the comparison table has no independent, reproducible harness.

**How:** It extracts 'sparse n-grams' (variable-length byte substrings selected by a 256x256 byte-pair weight table so a substring's edge pair-weights exceed all interior pair-weights) into an inverted index of xxh3-hashed n-gram to file-ID posting lists, stored as delta-varint-encoded, mmap-friendly binary. A query's mandatory literals are covered by a minimum set of these n-grams, whose posting lists are intersected/unioned to shrink 9,000 files to about 5 candidates before full regex verification. Patterns with no extractable literals (`.*`, single-byte) skip the index and instead use parallel rayon file scanning with SIMD memchr byte search and zero-copy output.

**Use it when:**
- Large, mostly-static codebase (thousands of files) searched repeatedly, where the one-time ~20-23s index build amortizes
- Interactive or AI-agent-driven code search (frg ships Claude Code/Cursor/Codex integration) where sub-100ms per-query latency matters more than a one-off build cost
- Selective literal or alternation queries (function/variable names, `useState|useEffect`) — this is where the README shows the biggest indexed wins (1.7x-5.3x vs ripgrep)
- Environments where the index can be kept current via `frg watch`/`frg update` (~70ms incremental) rather than rebuilt from scratch each time

**Skip it when:**
- One-off search of a directory with no existing index — the ~20-23s build cost dominates a single query
- High-churn repos or CI checkouts that are scanned once and discarded, where index upkeep or build time outweighs any per-search gain
- Wildcard/single-byte patterns with no extractable literals — the index can't help there and speedup drops to 1.06x-2.7x, close to ripgrep
- Anywhere an independently reproducible benchmark is required — the ripgrep comparison is a first-party README table only; benches/bench.rs never invokes ripgrep
- Teams unwilling to add a `.frg/` state directory to the repo tree or manage index sync

**Integration:** crate (binary via cargo install / Homebrew tap / source build) · regex, regex-syntax, rayon, memmap2, memchr, ignore, xxhash-rust, clap, clap_complete, clap_mangen, notify, serde, serde_json, anyhow, fs4, indicatif, is-terminal, glob · Rust stable, edition 2021; no minimum rustc version pinned in Cargo.toml or CI · CI (GitHub Actions) tests ubuntu-latest and macos-latest only; no Windows CI; no CPU-specific build flags in Cargo.toml

**Vs siblings:** Same category as ngi and trigrep (both also pair an index with regex search to beat ripgrep); frg's own benchmark covers more pattern types (8, including alternation and wildcard) and ships a maintained replace subcommand plus AI-agent skill integration, but ngi reports larger peak speedups on the Linux kernel (up to 5.9x) and ugrep is the more mature, feature-complete indexed-grep option if proven adoption matters more than novelty.

**Gotchas:**
- Index must exist and be current before indexed search helps; `frg update`/`frg watch` keep it in sync after file changes (README claims ~70ms incremental via overlay/tombstone)
- Adds a `.frg/` directory (generations/<id>/meta.json, postings.bin, lookup.bin, files.bin) to the project tree
- Patterns with no extractable literals bypass the index entirely and fall back to parallel brute-force scanning
- `frg replace` writes only with an explicit `--write` flag (dry-run/diff-preview by default)

**Status:** Active as of last commit 2026-03-24 (single maintainer, 16 stars), MIT-licensed, v0.3.0, distributed via crates.io/Homebrew/source — small and copyable to vendor, but young with no third-party benchmark verification yet.

[repo](https://github.com/qhkm/fastripgrep) · [benchmark](https://github.com/qhkm/fastripgrep#benchmarks)

##### ngi (N-gram Indexed Regex Search)  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

CLI that builds a trigram index of a codebase to pre-filter files before ripgrep does the actual regex match.

**Beats:** ripgrep — First-party README benchmark on the Linux kernel source tree (92,916 files): ngi beat ripgrep by 1.7x-5.9x and grep -r by 13x-69x across 5 regex patterns (e.g. 27ms vs rg's 161ms vs grep's 1866ms for `__attribute__.*section`), with 100% result parity vs ripgrep (13/13 queries). No CPU/hardware, rustc or ripgrep version, or run count is given, and the 16s/146MB one-time index build for the kernel tree is excluded from the reported timings.

**How:** Every file is decomposed into 3-byte substrings (trigrams) and stored as an inverted index (trigram -> posting list of files), mmap'd and binary-searched at query time -- the classic trigram-index scheme (Russ Cox / Google Code Search). regex-syntax parses the pattern to extract required literal substrings, whose trigrams are intersected to shrink the candidate set before rg runs at all. If the surviving candidates exceed ~10% of files, ngi skips the index and lets rg's own file walker do a full scan instead. Note: DESIGN.md describes a fancier 'sparse n-gram' weighted/monotonic-stack extraction scheme (inspired by Cursor's blog post), but src/ngram.rs shows the shipped v0.1.0 index is plain fixed-length trigrams hashed with FNV-1a -- the sparse-gram design in the doc isn't what's actually implemented.

**Use it when:**
- Large trees (tens of thousands of files, Linux-kernel scale) searched repeatedly with the same working copy
- Queries with extractable literal substrings (identifiers, macro/symbol names) rather than pure wildcards or anchors
- ripgrep is already installed and on PATH -- ngi is a pre-filter in front of it, not a replacement matcher
- Selective queries expected to touch well under 10% of files, where the index actually narrows the candidate set
- Agentic/tooling workflows that want JSONL (`--json`) output alongside the speedup

**Skip it when:**
- Broad/unselective patterns (>10% of files match) -- ngi's own fallback logic hands the whole scan to rg, so no speedup applies
- One-off searches on a tree you won't query again -- index build (16s / 146MB for the Linux kernel) isn't worth it for a single search
- Rapidly-changing or ephemeral checkouts (CI runners, throwaway containers) where keeping `.ngi/` current adds overhead each run
- Patterns with no extractable literals (e.g. `.*`, bare character classes) -- no trigram filtering is possible
- Anything production-critical: v0.1.0, 21 stars, single first-party benchmark, no third-party validation or issue history yet

**Integration:** crate · anyhow, clap, crc32fast, ignore, memmap2, rayon, regex, regex-syntax (Rust, build-time); ripgrep recommended on PATH at runtime, falls back to the built-in regex crate if absent · Rust edition 2024 (rustc 1.85+); CI builds against Rust stable · CI covers Linux (ubuntu-latest) and macOS (macos-latest) only; Windows is untested and undocumented

**Vs siblings:** Pick ngi specifically when you already run ripgrep and just want a pre-filtering index layer in front of it (it literally shells out to rg for the match step) with an explicit >10%-match fallback rule; trigrep and frg make similar 'faster than ripgrep' claims without that documented fallback threshold, and none of the three ripgrep-adjacent siblings has more than a first-party README benchmark backing it.

**Gotchas:**
- DESIGN.md documents a weighted 'sparse n-gram' extraction algorithm that the shipped code does not implement -- src/ngram.rs is plain fixed-length trigrams; don't take the design doc as current behavior
- `.ngi/` must be added to .gitignore manually per the README -- a stale or accidentally-committed index is a footgun
- Falls back to a full rg scan silently whenever a query matches >10% of files; `ngi search --explain` is the only way to see which mode (indexed/rg-fullscan/full-scan/no-index) actually ran
- The FNV-1a trigram hash is pinned by unit tests as part of the on-disk index format, implying a future hash change would need an index rebuild/migration

**Status:** Active as of the last commit (2026-03-24) but very early: v0.1.0, 21 stars, MIT-licensed, no third-party benchmark or issue history yet; the codebase is a small single crate (8 source files under src/) so it's easy to vendor or fork if development stalls.

[repo](https://github.com/erogol/ngi) · [benchmark](https://github.com/erogol/ngi#benchmarks)

##### ugrep (with ugrep-indexer)  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

ugrep-indexer builds Bloom-filter file indexes so ugrep's cold recursive search skips non-matching files, beating ripgrep.

**Beats:** ripgrep — On ugrep's own v3.12.6 source tree (1,317 files, 12.2MB, 8 threads), cold-filesystem search for 'std::chrono' took 1.02s unindexed vs 0.0487s best-of-4 (range 0.0487-0.0983s) with --index -- a 10x-21x self-comparison; ripgrep 13.0.0 took 1.18s on the same cold search (timed with shell `time`, vs ugrep's internal --stats timer), giving a derived roughly 12x-24x gap between indexed ugrep and ripgrep. No CPU, OS, or compiler flags are stated.

**How:** ugrep-indexer builds a windowed N-gram hash table per file (Bloom-filter-like, tunable accuracy -0 to -9, default -4) using an additive prime-61 rolling hash over up to the first 16 bytes of the eventual search pattern, compiled by ugrep into a hash finite automaton (HFA) layered on top of its regex DFA. At search time ugrep tests each file's stored hash bits against the pattern's HFA before opening the file, so on a cold (uncached) filesystem it avoids the disk read and decompression cost for files that cannot match.

**Use it when:**
- Recursive greps over directories that are cold in the OS page cache: network drives, rarely-touched archives, first search after mount/boot
- Repeated searches of the same large, slowly-changing tree where the indexing pass amortizes over many searches
- Patterns with a short, selective literal prefix (first 8-16 bytes distinctive) that keep the index false-positive rate low
- Already using ugrep for its grep-compatible CLI, Unicode support, or archive/compressed-file search and want an extra lever for cold storage
- Willing to spend ~0.5KB-14KB of index storage per file depending on chosen accuracy level

**Skip it when:**
- Files are already warm in the OS page cache -- indexing adds startup/check overhead and can be slower than a plain search
- Highly volatile trees needing frequent re-indexing; re-indexing is incremental but still recurring maintenance work
- Patterns using unlimited `*`/`+` repeats or large Unicode character classes -- these raise both index-hash construction start-up time and the false-positive rate
- Need `-v` (invert), `--filter`, `-P` (Perl regex), or `-Z` (fuzzy) -- `--index` does not support these ugrep modes
- Only one small, first-party benchmark exists (1,317 files/12.2MB on ugrep's own v3.12.6 tree); no independent or larger-scale confirmation

**Integration:** source-drop · none required for core grep functionality; optional PCRE2 or Boost.Regex for -P (Perl regex), zlib for -z, and optional bzip2/lzma/lz4/zstd/brotli/bzip3 for specific compressed-archive formats · not documented -- autotools build (AC_PROG_CXX in configure.ac / ./build.sh), no pinned C++ standard flag found in configure.ac or src/Makefile.am · Linux, macOS (Homebrew/MacPorts), Windows (winget), FreeBSD, OpenBSD, Alpine, Arch; x86-64 with SSE2/AVX2/AVX512BW auto-detected (disable via --disable-sse2/--disable-avx2), ARM/AArch64 NEON (--disable-neon to turn off)

**Vs siblings:** Sibling entries (frg, ngi, trigrep) speed up ripgrep-class search on warm/in-memory data; ugrep+ugrep-indexer targets the opposite case -- cold, uncached filesystems -- and only pays off after a separate indexing pass, so pick it when your searches hit rarely-cached storage (network or cold disks) and you can tolerate index upkeep, not for ordinary warm-cache greps.

**Gotchas:**
- Index has a false-positive (noise) rate -- some non-matching files are still opened; rate rises with permissive patterns and lower accuracy settings
- Index files are hidden per-directory `._UG#_Store` files; use ugrep-indexer -d to remove them or re-index after large structural changes
- Current --index design is safe (files are always re-scanned if newer than the index timestamp) only because indexes stay per-directory; the README explicitly warns a possible future 'single combined index file' option would drop that safety guarantee
- Higher accuracy levels (-8/-9) push index storage up to tens of KB per very noisy file, versus ~4KB/file at the default -4

**Status:** Core ugrep is actively maintained (3,302 stars, BSD-3-Clause, last commit 2026-09-15); the ugrep-indexer companion repo is smaller (84 stars) with its own last commit on 2025-06-22, so the indexing feature is iterating more slowly than core ugrep.

[repo](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep-indexer/blob/main/README.md)

#### unicode-utf8

##### Boost.Text (tzlaine/text)  `C++`  `BSL-1.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Boost-style C++ Unicode library (transcoding, normalization, text types) faster than ICU only in narrow, now-degraded cases.

**Beats:** ICU — Vendor's Google Benchmark charts (GCC on Linux, no CPU model/compiler version/flags stated) on ~0.5MB of Wikipedia text show Text's NFC-normalize-from-NFC-input path on European text beating ICU's UTF-8 normalizer by ~1.02-1.24x and roughly matching ICU's UTF-16 normalizer, while ICU's UTF-16 path wins the other 3 of 4 NFC scenarios; for UTF-8->UTF-16 transcoding, Text's SIMD path matched ICU (~473k vs ~476k ns) but the code now shipped (SIMD disabled) runs the slower ~590k ns scalar path.

**How:** The fast paths write runs of already-decoded or already-normalized output in bulk rather than branching per code unit, which is what a std::back_inserter or the transcoding iterators force. A SIMD transcode path (originally from Bob Steagall's C++Now 2018 work) decoded up to 16 UTF-8 bytes per op, but commit dd2959e7 (2024-01-18, fixing issue #212 — a correctness bug that produced silently wrong UTF-16 output) force-disabled that SIMD path repo-wide, so the code now shipping runs the plain scalar path that the vendor's own charts show as slower than ICU for UTF-8->UTF-16.

**Use it when:**
- NFC normalization of already-NFC European-script UTF-8 text, compared only against ICU's UTF-8-input normalizer (not ICU's faster UTF-16 path) -- best case ~1.24x per the vendor's charts.
- You call the pointer-to-pointer bulk transcode_to_*/normalize_append APIs directly instead of back-inserters or transcoding iterators; that is the only path where any measured gain applies.
- You want one Boost-style, STL-familiar library covering the full Unicode algorithm stack (segmentation, collation, bidi) plus text/rope types, not just fast transcoding.
- A C++14 codebase (Clang 6+/GCC 6+/VS2019+) that cannot add ICU as a dependency and values API/code familiarity over ICU feature completeness.

**Skip it when:**
- UTF-8->UTF-16 throughput: since dd2959e7 (Jan 2024) disabled SIMD, the shipped scalar path is slower than ICU's UnicodeString::fromUTF8 per the vendor's own chart.
- Non-European scripts or NFD-origin input for normalization: ICU's UTF-16 normalizer beats Text in 3 of the 4 charted NFC scenarios.
- Code that pipes output through std::back_inserter or the transcoding iterators for further per-code-unit work: documented by the author as 'quite bad'/'terrible' for performance, erasing the advantage.
- Wanting an actively maintained dependency: no commits since 2024-01-18 (stale), and the last fix was for a silent data-corruption bug in the fast path.
- Header-only vendoring: the data-heavy parts (collation_data_*.cpp, normalization_data_*.cpp, break tables) are compiled sources, not header-only, so you must build a library, not just #include headers.

**Integration:** static lib · Boost >= 1.71.0 (auto-cloned by CMake if not found); Boost.Filesystem/System only for the optional ncurses example editor · C++14 minimum (Clang 6+, GCC 6+, VS2019+); C++20 mode (concepts/coroutines) needs GCC 10+/Clang 13+/VS2019+ · any platform supported by GCC/Clang/MSVC; the transcode SIMD path targeted x86 SIMD historically but is force-disabled as of 2024-01-18, so the current build is effectively scalar

**Vs siblings:** Pick Boost.Text only when you need its broader Unicode algorithm/text-type surface (segmentation, collation, bidi, rope) in one Boost-style library; for pure UTF-8 validation/transcoding speed, ada-url/idna, encoding_rs, or SimdUnicode show larger, better-documented speedups over ICU or their respective baselines without a disabled fast path.

**Gotchas:**
- SIMD-accelerated transcoding (transcode_algorithm.hpp) was force-disabled repo-wide by commit dd2959e7 (2024-01-18), fixing issue #212 where BOOST_TEXT_USE_SIMD=1 produced corrupted, non-deterministic UTF-16 output; there is no supported way to safely re-enable it in the shipped code.
- Using std::back_inserter or the transcode/normalize iterators directly forfeits nearly all the measured speed advantage -- only the pointer-to-pointer bulk APIs are fast.
- MSVC users must build with /utf8 (or at least /source-charset:utf-8) or the ~150 CLDR locale headers under boost/text/data/ will be misinterpreted.
- The published performance charts predate the 2024-01-18 SIMD disable and no longer reflect the UTF-8->UTF-16 numbers of the code you'd actually build today.

**Status:** Stale since its last commit on 2024-01-18, which force-disabled the SIMD transcode path after it was found to silently corrupt UTF-16 output; BSL-1.0 licensed and copyable, but not header-only -- vendoring means building compiled data/algorithm sources, not just including headers.

[repo](https://github.com/tzlaine/text) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tzlaine/text/blob/master/doc/performance.qbk)

##### encoding_rs  `Rust`  `(Apache-2.0 OR MIT) AND BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust implementation of the WHATWG Encoding Standard; beats ICU at UTF-8/UTF-16/legacy transcoding on Web-shaped text.

**Beats:** ICU — Author's own 2016 benchmark measured encoding_rs against ICU 55 (as built by Ubuntu 16.04) on x86_64 Haswell, with and without explicit SSE2: English UTF-8<->UTF-16 conversion was 7.23x faster decode and 7.00x faster encode than ICU, most other tested languages' UTF-8 conversions were 1.6x-3.9x faster, but UTF-16LE/UTF-16BE conversions were 0.30x-0.32x of ICU's speed (slower).

**How:** Non-streaming UTF-8 paths borrow (Cow) instead of copying when input is already valid, and UTF-8 validation itself uses the SIMD-accelerated simdutf8 crate. ASCII-heavy fast paths are hand-written and, with the `simd-accel` feature, runtime-multiversioned per target (AVX2+BMI1 detection via `multiversion`/`core_detect` on x86_64, NEON on aarch64/thumbv7neon) so a single binary picks the best code path at runtime. The README notes the ASCII acceleration was rewritten in 2026 for Zen 3/M3 Pro/Raspberry Pi 4, i.e. the code measured in the 2016 benchmark is not the code shipping today.

**Use it when:**
- Parsing arbitrary Web content (HTML/CSS/XML) whose declared or sniffed charset may be a legacy encoding, mirroring what a browser does
- UTF-8<->UTF-16 conversion in a Gecko/Servo-like pipeline where FFI-friendly, allocation-free (Cow) conversion matters
- Targeting x86_64, aarch64, i686, or thumbv7neon where the `simd-accel` feature's runtime dispatch pays off
- no_std / no-allocator embedded contexts (crate supports no_std with `alloc` feature togglable)
- You want a small, vendorable crate (only WHATWG's ~40 encodings) rather than all of ICU's converters

**Skip it when:**
- You need ICU's full arbitrary-encoding converter surface (charsets outside the Web Encoding Standard) or ICU-specific APIs (transliteration, locale-aware behavior)
- You need UTF-16LE/UTF-16BE-labeled output specifically: those labels' "output encoding" is UTF-8 per spec, a documented API surprise, not a bug
- Encoding legacy CJK (Big5/GB/Shift_JIS/EUC-KR/Hanja/Hangul) at top speed by default: those encode paths are size-optimized, not speed-optimized, unless you opt into the `fast-*` Cargo features
- You need the full SIMD acceleration path on stable Rust without qualification: `simd-accel` depends on nightly-only features (`rustversion`, `any_all_workaround` crates), so a stable build may miss it
- Deciding based on the cited benchmark: it is a decade-old first-party 2016 post against ICU 55, and the library's own code has changed materially since (2018 and 2026 rewrites) per the README

**Integration:** crate · cfg-if, scopeguard, multiversion_no_op (always); optional: multiversion (x86/x86_64 without baseline AVX2+BMI1), simdutf8 (x86/x86_64/aarch64/wasm32+simd128), core_detect (x86/x86_64), serde, rustversion + any_all_workaround (simd-accel feature) · Rust 1.88 (MSRV, per Cargo.toml `rust-version`); `simd-accel` feature further constrains to Rust versions with the nightly features it needs · any (falls back to portable code); SIMD acceleration tuned for x86_64, aarch64, i686, thumbv7neon via the `simd-accel` feature

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued siblings are narrower single-purpose primitives (UTF-8 validation: simdutf8, xutf, SimdUnicode, utf8_range, Parabix; normalization: Boost.Text, unicode-transforms; URL/IDNA: ada-url/idna); pick encoding_rs when the job is full transcoding between UTF-8/UTF-16 and arbitrary legacy Web charsets (e.g. sniffing and decoding real-world HTML), and pick one of the UTF-8-only validators instead when all you need is to validate or count code points in already-UTF-8 data.

**Gotchas:**
- Encoding to UTF-16LE, UTF-16BE, or "replacement" always yields UTF-8 output because those are their WHATWG-defined output encodings, not the input encoding
- Speed is an explicit non-goal for legacy-encoding encode paths by default; enable `fast-hangul-encode`/`fast-kanji-encode`/etc. (or the `fast-legacy-encode` bundle) if CJK encode throughput matters
- `simd-accel` requires nightly Rust features, so a plain stable build won't get the full multiversioned SIMD dispatch described in the README
- The Cargo license string is a compound `(Apache-2.0 OR MIT) AND BSD-3-Clause`: the BSD-3-Clause part covers WHATWG-derived label/encoding data, not just the code

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-24, core dependency of Firefox/Gecko and Servo); dual Apache-2.0/MIT plus BSD-3-Clause licensed and small enough to vendor ("copyable"), though the cited benchmark predates two later rewrites of the hot paths.

[repo](https://github.com/hsivonen/encoding_rs) · [benchmark](https://hsivonen.fi/encoding-perf-2016-11/)

##### unicode-transforms  `Haskell`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Haskell Unicode NFC/NFKC/NFD/NFKD normalization for Text, beating ICU's C library binding on decomposition forms.

**Beats:** ICU (ICU4C 65.1, via the text-icu Haskell binding) — The README's per-file wall-clock ms table (package v0.3.7) compares unicode-transforms against text-icu 0.x calling ICU4C 65.1, across 7 language corpora, on unstated macOS hardware (no CPU model, GHC version, or compiler flags given). unicode-transforms wins all 14 NFD/NFKD rows (+8.8% to +376.9%, e.g. NFKD/Korean 7.78ms vs ICU's 37.10ms) but loses 9 of 14 NFC/NFKC rows, including NFC/Japanese (11.90ms vs ICU's 3.04ms) and NFC/AllChars (9.72ms vs 3.58ms).

**How:** It rides text's internal stream-fusion machinery (Data.Text.Internal.Fusion) to decompose/recompose characters while writing directly into a mutable Text array, avoiding intermediate list or Text allocations. Combining marks awaiting reorder by combining class are held in a small hand-unrolled buffer (`ReBuf = Empty | One Char | Many Char Char [Char]`) rather than a general list, so the common 0-2 mark case avoids list overhead. Hangul syllable decomposition/composition is done algorithmically instead of via UCD table lookup. The library is built with `-O2 -funbox-strict-fields -fspec-constr-count=10` (optional LLVM backend via a cabal flag).

**Use it when:**
- Pure-Haskell codebases that want to drop the native ICU4C runtime dependency and FFI overhead of text-icu
- Decomposition-heavy workloads (NFD/NFKD): wins all 14 measured README rows, from +8.8% to +377% over ICU
- Batch/offline normalization of in-memory Data.Text values, e.g. Korean or Vietnamese text (largest measured wins)
- Projects on GHC 8.0.2 through 9.14.1 wanting a small dependency footprint (base, text, bytestring, ghc-prim, unicode-data only)
- Cases where a small, auditable pure-Haskell implementation is preferred over linking libicu

**Skip it when:**
- Composition-heavy workloads (NFC/NFKC): ICU is faster in 9 of 14 measured rows, e.g. NFC/Japanese 11.90ms vs ICU's 3.04ms, NFC/AllChars 9.72ms vs 3.58ms
- NFKC on Korean input specifically: open issue #106 reports NFKC is not idempotent on some Korean inputs — a correctness bug, not just a perf gap
- Need ICU features beyond normalization (collation, FCD normalization, string iteration, regex) — this package does normalization only
- Callers outside Haskell (C/C++/other languages) — there is no exposed FFI surface, it's a Haskell library only
- Need normalization numbers you can trust on your own hardware: the published table is for package v0.3.7 (current is 0.4.0.1), unspecified 'macOS' hardware with no CPU model, GHC version, compiler flags, or run date given

**Integration:** module · base (>=4.8,<4.23), text (>=1.1.1,<=1.2.5.0 or >=2.0,<2.2), bytestring, ghc-prim, unicode-data · GHC 8.0.2+ (CI tests through GHC 9.14.1); cabal-version 2.2 · any (pure Haskell); CI covers Linux, Windows (AppVeyor), and s390x

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued siblings are C/C++/Rust/Go SIMD UTF-8 validators/decoders, not Unicode normalizers, except Boost.Text (C++, also claims to beat ICU on NFC). Pick unicode-transforms over ICU (or Boost.Text) specifically when you're in a pure-Haskell codebase doing decomposition (NFD/NFKD) and want to remove the ICU4C runtime dependency; for NFC/NFKC-heavy or non-Haskell workloads, ICU or Boost.Text is likely still faster.

**Gotchas:**
- Open bug: NFKC is not idempotent on some Korean inputs (issue #106, still open as of 2026-08-17)
- Ships a deprecated Data.ByteString.UTF8.Normalize module alongside the current Data.Text.Normalize API
- For some scripts (Japanese, AllChars) composition forms are markedly slower than ICU, up to roughly 4x, not just a modest loss
- Package is still marked 'Experimental' stability in its cabal file despite a decade of releases

**Status:** Actively maintained — last master commit 2026-01-18, adding support for newer GHC releases up through 9.14; BSD-3-Clause and small enough to vendor, but stability is marked 'Experimental' and there is an open correctness bug in NFKC on Korean text (issue #106).

[repo](https://github.com/composewell/unicode-transforms) · [benchmark](https://github.com/composewell/unicode-transforms#performance)

##### utf8_range (SIMD Range-based UTF-8 validator)  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

SIMD range-based UTF-8 validator bundled in protobuf; edges out Lemire's SSE/NEON validator, mostly on ARM.

**Beats:** Lemire's SIMD UTF-8 validator (github.com/lemire/fastvalidate-utf-8, the algorithmic ancestor incorporated into simdutf) — First-party README benchmark (gcc-7.3, no optimization flags stated) compares 'range2' (a two-block NEON/SSE variant of the range algorithm) against Lemire's 2018 fastvalidate-utf-8 prototype on an unspecified ARMv8-A chip and an Intel Xeon E5-2650 (SSE4.1). On NEON, range2 beats Lemire by about 1.17x-1.78x depending on buffer size (~1.32x on the UTF-8 demo text and at 1K-1M buffers); on SSE4 it is within noise of Lemire (near parity on demo text and 1M, and slower than Lemire at 32 bytes).

**How:** Core technique is the 'range algorithm': load 16 bytes, use a SIMD table lookup (NEON tbl / SSE pshufb) to assign each byte a predicted 'range index' based on where it should fall in a 1-4 byte UTF-8 sequence, then validate all 16 bytes against their [min,max] ranges in one pass, avoiding Lemire's more branch-heavy state tracking and the classic Hoehrmann DFA table walk. The shipped wrapper (utf8_range.c) adds an 8-bytes-at-a-time SWAR ASCII fast-skip (checking the high bit of 8 packed bytes at once) before entering the SIMD range check, and falls back to a naive byte-by-byte loop for tails under 16 bytes or on platforms without SSE4.1/ARM64 NEON.

**Use it when:**
- Already depending on protobuf or Abseil in C/C++ and want its vendored validator instead of adding a new dependency
- Buffers of roughly 1KB+ on ARMv8 NEON, where range2 shows its clearest edge over Lemire-style validation (~1.3x+)
- ASCII-heavy input, where the wrapper's 8-byte SWAR ASCII skip dominates before SIMD is ever reached
- Only need a boolean valid/invalid result or the longest-valid-prefix length, not decoding
- x86-64 SSE4.1 targets where parity with a 2018-era SIMD validator is acceptable

**Skip it when:**
- Need AVX2/AVX-512 throughput: the shipped utf8_range.c only dispatches to SSE4.1 or 64-bit ARM NEON; range-avx2.c exists in the tree but is not wired into the wrapper protobuf actually links
- Targeting 32-bit ARM, RISC-V, WASM, or other platforms without SSE4.1/NEON: falls back to a naive per-byte loop with no SIMD speedup
- Small non-ASCII buffers: SSE4 numbers show range2 losing to Lemire at 32 bytes (2173 vs 2891 MB/s)
- Need UTF-8<->UTF-16/32 transcoding, not just validation: this library only validates
- Want current, independently-run benchmarks: the README table is an unmaintained ~2019 first-party benchmark against Lemire's 2018 prototype, not today's simdutf

**Integration:** source-drop · none for the C library (utf8_range.c/.h); Abseil (absl::strings, for absl::string_view) for the C++ wrapper utf8_validity.h · C99/C11 for the core C file; C++ (protobuf's current C++17 baseline) for the wrapper; README's own build was tested with gcc-7.3, CMakeLists.txt requires CMake 3.16+ · x86-64 with SSE4.1, or aarch64 with NEON, for the SIMD path; any platform via a naive byte-by-byte fallback otherwise

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only if you're already pulling in protobuf/Abseil and want its bundled C validator without adding a new dependency; simdutf8 (up to 23x over Rust std), SimdUnicode (up to 14x over .NET), and xutf (1.5-10x over simdutf) show larger and more current speedups, and utf8_range's own edge over Lemire is ARM-specific and within noise on x86 SSE4.

**Gotchas:**
- The README benchmark tables measure the original standalone research files (range-neon.c, range2-*.c, lemire-*.c via main.c), not utf8_range.c, the 2023 Google-rewritten wrapper with the ASCII fast path that protobuf actually ships and links
- No AVX2 dispatch reaches production despite range-avx2.c sitting in the same directory — the wrapper only branches on __SSE4_1__ or __ARM_NEON+64-bit
- Only static-library linkage is provided (CMake/Bazel add_library targets utf8_range and utf8_validity); a shared-library request (issue #14958) was closed without adding one
- The component's own LICENSE file is MIT (Yibo Cai 2019 + Google 2022) even though the surrounding protobuf repo is BSD-3-Clause — relevant if vendoring just this directory

**Status:** Actively maintained as part of protobuf (this component last touched 2026-06-19; the protobuf repo overall as of 2026-09-25); MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor on its own, but only static-library builds are supported.

[repo](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf) · [benchmark](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/third_party/utf8_range/README.md)

### serialization-and-formats

#### binary-schemas

##### Apache Fory (C++)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Apache Fory's C++ serializer for plain annotated structs, cross-language binary format; 1.3-11x Protobuf's throughput in its benchmarks.

**Beats:** Protobuf — Fory's own Google Benchmark suite (xlang compatible mode, reference tracking off, reused output buffer) against Protobuf v25.5, built Release with -O3 on an unnamed compiler, ran on a 12-core, 48 GB arm64 Mac (Darwin 24.6.0, chip not named). Its 2026-06-12 report shows 1.27x-10.9x Protobuf's throughput, e.g. MediaContent serialize at 8.81M vs 2.12M ops/s (4.15x). Most of the Protobuf timings include converting to and from plain C++ structs on every iteration; on Sample, the one case that uses native protobuf objects, Fory was 1.59x on serialize and 2.25x on deserialize. The older benchmarks/cpp README table (Darwin 24.5.0) shows 1.2x-4.5x.

**How:** FORY_STRUCT generates constexpr field metadata, and fields are sorted at compile time: non-nullable fixed-width primitives come first by size, then varints, then everything else. The serializer can therefore reserve the maximum size once and write the leading primitives at compile-time offsets with a single writer-index update, skipping per-field capacity checks and error propagation. It encodes straight from the user's struct with no intermediate message object, using zigzag varints for int32/int64 and a combined length-plus-encoding header for strings (Latin-1/UTF-16/UTF-8). In compatible mode, schema metadata (a TypeDef identified by a 52-bit MurmurHash3 hash) is written once per stream and cached by the reader, and per-field reads are unrolled through compile-time switch dispatch.

**Use it when:**
- C++ code that already models data as plain structs (strings, vectors, maps, nested structs) and today pays to copy them into protobuf message objects and back; that conversion is where the benchmark's biggest serialize wins (4-11x) come from
- Throughput-bound serialization of small-to-medium messages (roughly 80 B to 2 KB in the benchmarks), using one Fory instance per thread and a reused Buffer via serialize_to
- Payloads exchanged between C++ and Java/Python/Go/Rust/JS/C# services that should share one wire format, with type IDs registered consistently or types generated from Fory/protobuf IDL
- Object graphs with shared or cyclic std::shared_ptr references (track_ref(true)), which protobuf cannot express
- Rolling deployments that need add/remove/reorder field evolution (compatible mode is the default); for C++-only, same-schema traffic, .xlang(false).compatible(false) gives smaller, faster payloads

**Skip it when:**
- You need protobuf wire compatibility, preservation of unknown fields, or protobuf/gRPC tooling (reflection, interceptors). Fory bytes are not protobuf bytes, and its own docs recommend protobuf for these cases
- Payload size matters more than CPU. In the 2026-06-12 report Fory's output was larger than Protobuf's for Sample (445 vs 375 B) and MediaContent (362 vs 301 B); it was smaller only for the numeric structs
- Large messages where you read a few fields in place. Object mode decodes the whole struct; flat formats (or Fory's separate row format) avoid that
- You need a long-stable C++ API. The C++ object-graph serializer arrived in November 2025, and v1.7.0 through v1.7.5 shipped within four weeks (2026-08-28 to 2026-09-25), alongside codec-boundary hardening commits in late August 2026
- Decoding untrusted input without extra setup. The C++ security guide requires registering only accepted types and keeping the graph-memory and depth limits; Fory's Java and Python implementations have had deserialization CVEs (CVE-2025-59328, CVE-2026-50076, CVE-2025-61622, CVE-2026-48207), and none are listed for C++

**Integration:** static lib (or shared); a compiled library pulled in with CMake FetchContent (SOURCE_SUBDIR cpp, target fory::serialization) or as a Bazel module; not header-only · none at runtime (MurmurHash3 and its hash map are vendored); googletest only for tests; gRPC C++ 1.39+ only for the generated gRPC companions; the foryc compiler is optional, for IDL codegen · C++17; CMake 3.16+ or Bazel 8+. The docs disagree on compiler minimums: the install guide lists GCC 7+/Clang 5+/MSVC 2017+, the benchmark README GCC 8+/Clang 7+/MSVC 2019+. MSVC requires /Zc:preprocessor · x86-64 (CMake compiles Fory's sources with -mavx2 or /arch:AVX2 by default), aarch64 (NEON paths), plus SSE2 and scalar fallbacks; CI runs on ubuntu-latest, macos-latest and windows-2022, with ASan/UBSan jobs

**Vs siblings:** Pick Fory over YaFF, SBE or ProtoCache when you want to decode into ordinary owning C++ structs (strings, vectors, maps, shared_ptr graphs) with schema evolution on by default and readers in other languages. Pick SBE for fixed-layout, low-latency messages, and YaFF or ProtoCache when you read a few fields in place from a buffer without a full decode.

**Gotchas:**
- Each struct needs a FORY_STRUCT(...) list placed after its fields (in a public: section inside a class), plus register_struct<T>(id) on every Fory instance. A missing registration fails at runtime with 'Type not registered', not at compile time.
- The defaults are track_ref(true) and compatible(true), and both cost speed and size. The published benchmark switched reference tracking off, so disable it for value-shaped data.
- On x86-64, CMake's FORY_USE_AVX2 option defaults to ON and adds -mavx2 to Fory's compiled sources. Set it to OFF if the binary must run on CPUs without AVX2.
- With compatible(false), mismatched schemas 'may cause errors or undefined behavior' (per the docs). Even in compatible mode, renaming a field is not supported because fields match by snake_case name or tag ID. Raw pointers and std::array are listed as unsupported.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-23, v1.7.5 released 2026-09-25) and Apache-2.0 licensed, but the C++ object serializer is under a year old and is consumed as a CMake or Bazel-built library rather than vendored headers.

[repo](https://github.com/apache/fory) · [benchmark](https://github.com/apache/fory/blob/main/docs/benchmarks/object-serialization/xlang/cpp/README.md)

##### fernBuffer  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Prototype bit-packed JSON encoder (C API over a C++17 core) that beats MessagePack on size for string- and key-heavy JSON.

**Beats:** MessagePack — Only encoded byte size was measured: the 10 JSON files in benchmark/, compared with Python msgpack's defaults (floats packed as float64). Size is deterministic, so compiler and hardware do not matter, and I reproduced every number exactly (fernBuffer v1 release WASM under Node 24, msgpack 1.2.2). fernBuffer wins 6 of 10 (log -28%, flat records -47%, hex strings -46%, sparse nulls -54%, repeated strings -53%, deep nesting 18 vs 25 B) and loses 4 (floats +8%, ints +21%, bools +87%, tiny object 11 vs 10 B). The project publishes no speed numbers.

**How:** It wins on size, not speed. The JSON tree is flattened into DFS-ordered (path, value) leaves, and each path is written as push/pop deltas against the previous path (trie-style prefix sharing), all in one unaligned bit stream. Lengths, token IDs and integer magnitudes use Fibonacci (Zeckendorf) universal codes. Strings and keys seen at least twice go into two dictionaries at the front of the stream. Hex text (whole even-length hex strings, or runs of 8 or more even hex chars inside a string) is packed 2:1 into raw bytes, and floats are stored as f32 when that round-trips exactly. Every leaf also pays schema ops plus a 2-bit type tag, which is why dense numeric and bool arrays come out larger than MessagePack's 1-byte fixint/true/false.

**Use it when:**
- Arrays of records or log lines where the same keys and string values repeat. In the repo's test files this was 28-54% smaller than Python msgpack: log entries 11,156 vs 15,465 B, flat records 2,171 vs 4,093 B, sparse nulls 903 vs 1,974 B, repeated strings 557 vs 1,178 B.
- Payloads full of all-lowercase or all-uppercase hex strings (hashes, digests, hex IDs), which are stored as raw bytes: 1,898 vs 3,493 B on the hex_strings file.
- Storing or shipping blobs where bytes cost more than CPU, and your data already exists as JSON text (the API takes and returns JSON strings).
- Browser/JS experiments via the prebuilt Emscripten WASM build (fb.encode(obj) returns a Uint8Array, fb.decode returns an object), or as a reference design for bit-level JSON packing (delta paths, Fibonacci coding, token tables).

**Skip it when:**
- Numeric or boolean arrays. In the repo's own table it is larger than MessagePack on floats (+8%), ints (+21%) and bools (+87%), and the README reports [0..49] at ~2.19x MsgPack. Bool 'runs' are documented as N bits, but the encoder only ever emits one bool per field.
- Any data that must round-trip exactly. Mixed-case hex-alphabet strings come back lowercased (tested: 'Cafe' -> 'cafe', 'Facade' -> 'facade'). Repeated uppercase hex values or GUID segments lose their case. Unsigned integers above INT64_MAX come back negative (18446744073709551615 -> -1).
- Top-level scalars, {} or []: they encode fine but crash on decode (path.back() on an empty path, which is UB; the v1 WASM build traps 'memory access out of bounds').
- Untrusted input, or latency/throughput-sensitive paths. The decoder is not hardened (UB on a pop from an empty path, LEB128 shifts past 64 bits) and there are no tests or fuzzing. Each call parses JSON text with nlohmann/json and writes one bit at a time. Wide objects scale quadratically: in the v1 WASM build, a 16k-key object took 232 ms to encode and 459 ms to decode, vs 1.9/3.1 ms for 1k keys.
- Production use or large streams: the author labels it a prototype, there is no incremental/streaming decode (per the README), and the decoder reads the format version field but ignores it.

**Integration:** source-drop (one C++17 translation unit, fernbuffer.cpp plus src/*.hpp, behind the C header fernbuffer.h); release v1 also ships a prebuilt Windows x64 DLL/CLI and an Emscripten WASM+JS build · nlohmann/json (vendored as src/json.hpp, uses ordered_json); C++ standard library, including exceptions, which are caught at the C boundary · C++17 (structured bindings; the build scripts pass /std:c++17 to MSVC from Visual Studio 2017+, and -std=c++17 -O3 to Emscripten). The Makefile needs GNU make with the Windows cmd shell. · Windows x64 (MSVC build scripts, found via vswhere) and WebAssembly (Emscripten). The header has GCC/Clang visibility macros, but no Linux/macOS build script is provided. Floats are memcpy'd in host byte order, so the format assumes little-endian.

**Vs siblings:** Choose it over JSON BinPack only when you want schemaless JSON-in/JSON-out size reduction with no schema to write and can live with a prototype, since JSON BinPack's catalogued best-size results are schema-driven. For anything production-bound, numeric-heavy or needing exact round-trips, use JSON BinPack, qdf's compression tier or plain MessagePack. MTS-1 targets delta-encoded telemetry, not general JSON.

**Gotchas:**
- Hex detection is lossy. A string that is entirely hex characters and of even length (even 2 chars) is stored as bytes with a single upper/lower flag, so mixed case decodes as lowercase. Token-table hex entries drop the flag completely, so repeated uppercase hex decodes as lowercase.
- Integers are handled as int64. uint64 values above 2^63-1 are silently reinterpreted as negative, and negating INT64_MIN in the encoder is signed overflow (UB; it happened to round-trip in the WASM build).
- Decoding the output of a top-level scalar, empty object or empty array is undefined behavior; only non-empty objects and arrays at the root decode.
- Both calls return heap buffers that must be freed with fernbuffer_free (the README warns that ctypes c_char_p leaks). The WASM wrapper round-trips through JSON.stringify/JSON.parse, so JS-side number formatting applies.

**Status:** Single-author prototype: 3 commits, all on 2026-06-07, none since, one v1 release, no issues or PRs, 6 stars. It is MIT-licensed with under 40 KB of its own source plus vendored nlohmann/json, so it is easy to vendor, but treat it as a reference design rather than a production codec.

[repo](https://github.com/Escartem/fernBuffer) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Escartem/fernBuffer#benchmark)

##### flatcc  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

FlatBuffers schema compiler and runtime for pure C. Wire-compatible with Google's flatc, and roughly as fast as its C++ code.

**Beats:** Google FlatBuffers (C++) — Setup: Google's flatbench schema (a container of 3 tables with structs and strings, about 336-344 bytes), 1M iterations, -O3 -DNDEBUG, unnamed system cc/c++, on a 2.2 GHz Haswell Core i7 under OS X. flatcc encoded in 626 ns/op against 702 ns/op for flatc C++ (about 1.12x) and traversed in 28.7 vs 28.9 ns/op (a tie). The C++ baseline is a FlatBuffers 1.0.0 header from 2014 vendored in the repo, rebuilt with a fresh builder every iteration. The repo's Ubuntu run (hardware not stated) has flatcc about 3% slower on encode (531 vs 516 ns) and about 8% faster on decode (27.5 vs 30.0 ns).

**Known shortcoming:** Marginal win from 2015-2016 numbers: encode about 1.12x, decode tied, and the C++ builder is rebuilt each iteration while the C builder is reset. The repo's own Ubuntu run shows flatcc encode about 3% slower (531 vs 516 ns/op) and decode about 8% faster. No compiler named (system cc/c++, -O3 -DNDEBUG).

**Known shortcoming:** Roughly equal to the baseline, not clearly faster: the C++ side uses a FlatBuffers 1.0.0 header from 2014, rebuilt per iteration, and the maintainer calls the benchmark 'very old' and expects current flatcc to be slightly slower (#382, 2026). Its value is FlatBuffers wire compatibility from C. Use >= 0.6.4 for the schema-parser buffer-overrun fixes; the verifier does not limit DAG blow-up as Google's does.

**How:** Reader accessors are generated as static inline functions that read fields straight out of the buffer through vtable offsets. They do no allocation, need no library, and let the compiler drop any code you don't use. The typeless builder keeps its internal stacks (vtable stack, data stack, frame stack, patch log) and a hash-table vtable-deduplication cache across builds: `flatcc_builder_reset` reuses that memory instead of freeing it. Output goes to an emitter that writes fixed-size pages (about 2.9 KB) in a ring buffer, not to one growing array. Vtables are clustered at the end of the buffer, and `create` calls and direct array copies skip the stack when no endian conversion is needed. The author attributes flatcc's encode edge to making fewer allocations. In the benchmark code, the C++ side constructs a fresh FlatBufferBuilder on every iteration, while the C side resets its builder.

**Use it when:**
- A pure-C codebase (embedded, firmware, C-only services) that needs to read or write FlatBuffers. Users report it working on ESP32/FreeRTOS with newlib and on Arduino.
- Exchanging buffers with services that use Google's flatc in other languages, since flatcc produces the same wire format and flatc-compatible JSON.
- Read-heavy paths: reads are zero-allocation inline accessors with no runtime library. Traversing the benchmark message takes about 29 ns/op.
- Building many small buffers in a loop with one reused builder (`flatcc_builder_reset`), or streaming large buffers page by page through a custom emitter without holding the whole buffer in memory.
- Schema-specific JSON-to-FlatBuffer parsing and printing in C. The generated parser and printer handle a 722-byte message in about 1.2-2.2 µs.

**Skip it when:**
- A C++ project already using flatc and looking for speed. The results are a wash: encode is about 1.12x faster on the OS X run but about 3% slower on the repo's Ubuntu run, and decode is tied to about 8% faster.
- You need a large serialization speedup over FlatBuffers. This is the same format with the same costs, and only a different wire format can change those.
- Untrusted input where DAG blow-up matters. The verifier rejects cycles and caps nesting at about 100 levels, but unlike Google's verifier it does not limit the number of tables visited. Also, never modify an untrusted buffer in place, even after verifying it.
- You want vectors sorted by key while building. The builder cannot sort; you have to cast the finished buffer to mutable and sort it afterwards (in-place heap sort, not stable), and only on trusted buffers.
- You need a stable API across upgrades. Minor breaking changes to the header API happen occasionally, and generated code must match the include/flatcc version exactly.

**Integration:** static lib (runtime libflatccrt, or compile src/runtime/*.c directly). Reading needs only generated headers plus include/flatcc. The flatcc code generator must be built first (CMake). · At runtime, none beyond the C runtime library. Building the flatcc tool needs CMake 3.16+ and Ninja or make. · C11 is the reference (C++11 or C++14 for C++ code that includes the generated headers). A portable header layer supports older compilers, and weekly CI covers GCC 4.4 and 9-15, Clang 5-22, and MSVC. `--pedantic` is not supported on GCC 8+. · Any. Little-endian and big-endian hosts are supported (big-endian since 0.4.0, tested on AIX PowerPC and on s390x via QEMU, but not in regular CI). CI covers Linux x86-64 including 32-bit, macOS on Apple and Intel runners, and Windows with MSVC.

**Vs siblings:** Pick flatcc when you need actual FlatBuffers wire compatibility from C. Lite³, Karmem and YaFF report much larger wins over FlatBuffers, but each is its own format and cannot read or write existing FlatBuffers data. ProtoCache and hpp-proto target Protobuf and C++, not FlatBuffers from C.

**Gotchas:**
- The generated headers must come from the same flatcc version as include/flatcc and libflatccrt. A system-installed flatcc package can silently mismatch.
- Builder errors are not checked by default ("no hand holding"). A missing required field asserts in debug builds but writes an incorrect table in release builds. Link libflatccrt_d while developing and run the verifier on your output.
- The verifier requires the buffer to be aligned at its absolute memory address (e.g. 16-byte force_align fields). Plain malloc on 32-bit Windows gives only 8 bytes, so use `flatcc_builder_finalize_aligned_buffer` and `flatcc_builder_aligned_free`.
- Reading and verifying expect a file_identifier by default. Buffers without one, which some other language bindings produce, fail unless you pass a null identifier to the `_with_identifier` variants. If tests segfault, check strict aliasing (`-fno-strict-aliasing`, or `-DPORTABLE_MEM_PTR_ACCESS=0`).

**Status:** Actively maintained: v0.6.4 was released 2026-09-16, fixing parser overruns on adversarial schemas that had been reported as CVEs, and there are commits up to 2026-09-25. It is Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor, and in 2026 the maintainer said the benchmark code is 'very old' and has not been updated (issue #382).

[repo](https://github.com/dvidelabs/flatcc) · [benchmark](https://github.com/dvidelabs/flatcc/blob/master/doc/benchmarks.md)

##### flatty  `Nim`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Binary serializer for plain Nim types; ~38x faster serialize, ~36x faster deserialize than JSON-based std/marshal.

**Beats:** Nim std/marshal — The README's benchy table (100 runs each) for an 11,125-node ref-object tree shows serialize 2.265 ms vs 85.178 ms for std/marshal's JSON `$$` (~37.6x on min, ~38.6x on average) and deserialize 2.643 ms vs 148.723 ms (~56x on min, ~36x on average). Nim version, compiler flags and hardware are not stated (tests/config.nims only sets --path), and the numbers were recorded before the PR #55 hardening, so current deserialize is likely nearer 24-40x (derived from PR #55's 1.4-1.5x slowdown).

**Known shortcoming:** Binary format measured against Nim's std/marshal, which writes JSON text, so the 37-56x gap is binary vs JSON. Ratios use minimum times (average-time deserialize is about 36x). No compiler, flags or hardware stated.

**Known shortcoming:** The README table predates decode hardening (PR #55, 2026-07-14) that made ref-tree deserialize about 1.4-1.5x slower, so the current deserialize gap is likely about 24-40x (estimate). The gap mostly reflects std/marshal's reflection overhead; bingo, another binary Nim serializer, is only about 16% slower than flatty. Shared refs come back as copies and cyclic graphs overflow the stack on serialize. Little-endian only, int width depends on build flags, no versioning or IDL, no other-language implementation.

**How:** Encoding and decoding are generic overloads resolved at compile time per type, while std/marshal walks runtime type info (`typeinfo.Any`), writes JSON text and records every ref address in an IntSet. For seqs and arrays whose element type is 'flat' (supportsCopyMem, no pointers, variants, ranges or int-width mismatch), flatty writes a length prefix and moves the whole block with one copyMem; strings are also one copyMem, and decode allocates with newStringUninit/setLenUninit to skip zero-fill. Output is appended to a plain string with setLen plus copyMem instead of StringStream, values keep native little-endian layout with no byte swapping, and hot procs are `{.inline.}`.

**Use it when:**
- Nim-to-Nim messages or save files where both ends are built from the same type definitions, e.g. game state over UDP with netty plus supersnappy compression (the stack the README describes).
- Payloads dominated by seqs/arrays of numbers or flat objects, which encode and decode as a single memcpy per container.
- Snapshotting acyclic ref-object trees: about 2.3 ms to serialize an 11,125-node tree in the README benchmark.
- Decoding untrusted network blobs: since the July 2026 hardening, every read is bounds-checked (also under -d:danger), length prefixes are validated before allocation, and a fuzzer runs in tests.
- Hashing arbitrary nested Nim objects by content with the bundled hashy module.

**Skip it when:**
- Data read by non-Nim programs: the format is defined only by Nim types, with no IDL and no other-language implementation (the JS target is Nim-compiled JS only).
- Long-lived storage while types evolve: the README says there is no versioning, so any change to a type breaks reading old blobs.
- Graphs with shared or cyclic refs: `toFlatty` on a ref writes a nil flag plus the value with no identity tracking, so shared refs come back as copies and cycles recurse until the stack overflows. std/marshal tracks ref addresses and keeps both.
- Big-endian targets (compile-time error) or JS builds with int64/uint64 fields, which the README says are supported badly.
- Polymorphic ref hierarchies or variants with more than one `case` discriminator: encoding follows the static type, and objvar.nim reads only the first discriminator (PR #36 for multiple/nested discriminators was closed unmerged).

**Integration:** module · none (Nim standard library only) · Nim >= 2.0.0 (flatty.nimble); install with nimble or atlas · Little-endian native targets only (compile error on big-endian); CI on Linux, macOS and Windows plus the Nim JS backend under Node; the decode stack guard is off on emscripten and unrecognized platforms

**Vs siblings:** Every catalogued sibling targets another language (Rust, Go, C#, C++, Zig); none is a Nim library, so pick flatty inside a Nim-only system. Pick a cross-language schema format such as Bebop or SBE instead when non-Nim peers must read the data or the schema must evolve, since flatty has no IDL and no versioning.

**Gotchas:**
- Blobs are build-dependent: `int`/`uint` and lengths use the target's native width unless both sides compile with the same -d:flatty32 or -d:flatty64, copyable seq/array elements are raw memory images (sizeof(T) each, padding included), and every enum is written as 8 bytes.
- Malformed input raises FlattyError (bad length, count or enum), IndexDefect (truncation) or RangeDefect (range type out of bounds); the README tells you to catch both CatchableError and Defect.
- The README benchmark predates the July 2026 hardening (PR #55), which itself reports ref-tree deserialize ~1.4-1.5x slower afterwards; serialize is unchanged.
- Much of the gap to std/marshal is marshal's reflection, not binary vs text: in the same table jsony (JSON) serializes in 9.618 ms, ~8.9x faster than marshal, while the binary peer bingo is only ~16% slower than flatty on serialize (min).

**Status:** Active: nimble version 0.4.0, last commit 2026-08-13, decode path fuzzed and hardened in July 2026; MIT, pure Nim with no dependencies, small enough to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/treeform/flatty) · [benchmark](https://github.com/treeform/flatty#speed)

##### greenpack  `Go`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Go msgpack2 code generator with versioned, typed field names; ~15% faster writes than gogo/protobuf in author's 2017 benchmark.

**Beats:** Protocol Buffers (Go implementations: gogo/protobuf gogofaster, golang/protobuf, DeDiS/protobuf); FlatBuffers Go and Cap'n Proto Go are also in the table — In the author's 2017 fork of alecthomas/go_serialization_benchmarks (6-field struct, 3.1 GHz Core i7 MacBook Pro 13", Go version unconfirmed; the header says 1.8beta2), GreenPackMarshal took 129 ns/op with 0 allocs, against 152 ns/op with 1 alloc (64 B) for gogo/protobuf's proto.Marshal. greenpack wrote into a reused 512-byte buffer while gogo allocated its output on every call. The 224 vs 240 ns/op read row is invalid because BenchmarkGreenPackUnmarshal calls ZebraPack's ZMarshalMsg/ZUnmarshalMsg.

**Known shortcoming:** The benchmark's GreenPackUnmarshal row actually calls ZebraPack's ZUnmarshalMsg, so the read-side number is ZebraPack's code, not greenpack's (224 vs 236 ns is run-to-run noise on identical code). The write comparison reuses a 512-byte buffer while gogo proto.Marshal allocates per call.

**How:** It uses reflection-free code generation inherited from tinylib/msgp. Marshal pre-sizes the output with the generated Msgsize() via msgp.Require, then writes each field key as a precomputed msgpack byte literal (`o = append(o, 0xae, 0x4e, ...)`) followed by a type-specific Append* call into a caller-supplied []byte. Repeated marshals into a reused buffer therefore allocate nothing. Unmarshal reads map keys zero-copy and dispatches through a compiled Go string switch to per-field decoders, mutates existing slices and maps in place, and zeroes missing fields by replaying a msgpack nil through the same switch (a fixed-size NilBitsStack) instead of allocating.

**Use it when:**
- Go services whose structs must be readable from Python, R or JS with a stock msgpack library and no generated code or schema file.
- You want the Go struct definition to be the schema: no .proto/IDL, no protoc or C++ toolchain, just `//go:generate greenpack`.
- Write-heavy paths that can reuse an output buffer: MarshalMsg(buf) appends into the caller's slice. The 2017 run measured 129 ns/op and 0 allocs/op for a 6-field struct.
- Schemas that evolve over time: numbered zid fields, `deprecated` tombstones and conflict detection at generate time, plus signed/unsigned integer types that stock msgpack encoders lose.
- Pipelines that need serialization hooks (PreSave/PostLoad, e.g. to flatten trees) or generated MariaDB read/write methods (`-sql mariadb`).

**Skip it when:**
- Wire size matters. Every key carries the field name, zid and type clue, so the benchmark struct encoded to ~142 bytes, against ~59 for ZebraPack (derived from the MB/s and ns/op columns). Use ZebraPack, `-omit-clue`/`-alltuple`, or protobuf instead.
- You need C++ or other non-Go code generation. None exists; the author points C++ users to generic msgpack libraries (issue #16).
- You are choosing it for faster reads than gogo/protobuf. The only published greenpack read number actually measured ZebraPack, and the author's 2024 CBOR comparison shows greenpack Unmarshal at 322 ns/op with 2 allocs/op.
- Code that relies on generics or shared pointers. Type-parameterized fields are skipped unless you pass `-generics=true`, which the author says is much slower. Automatic pointer dedup has been off by default since v0.529.0 because of unresolved errors, and Marshal/Unmarshal never supported it.
- You need a large-team maintenance guarantee. It is a single-author project; a report that map[int64]map[int8]T writes no data (#12) was closed without a fix.

**Integration:** module · runtime package github.com/glycerine/greenpack/msgp (depends on glycerine/fwd, 4d63.com/tz); the generator also uses golang.org/x/tools and shurcooL/go-goon; goconvey for tests · Go 1.24.2 (go.mod directive) · any Go target; pure Go, uses unsafe string/slice casts (an appengine build tag provides a no-unsafe variant)

**Vs siblings:** Pick greenpack over ZebraPack (same author: 120 vs 129 ns/op writes, ~59 vs ~142-byte payload) when other-language consumers must decode with any msgpack library and no schema, because greenpack data is fully self-describing. Pick ZebraPack or Karmem when raw Go speed or wire size matters more, and SBE, Bebop or Apache Fory (C++) for C++-side work, since greenpack has no C++ generator.

**Gotchas:**
- `-fast-strings` makes decoded strings alias the input buffer through unsafe, so that buffer must not be reused. In current master, msgp/read_bytes.go ReadStringBytes takes the zero-copy path only when `err != nil`, so successful reads still copy with string(v). Measure allocations yourself before relying on the zero-alloc claim.
- Cross-language readers see extras. time.Time is msgpack extension type 5 (normalized to UTC), not the standard -1 timestamp, and time.Duration is extension 7. EncodeMsg streams also add an "@" struct-name key unless you pass `-no-structnames-onwire`; the MarshalMsg path does not.
- All fields are omitempty by default, so zero values never reach the wire and absent keys decode as zero. The nil-replay stack that implements this is fixed at 8 nested struct levels (MaxNestedStructPointerDepth) and panics beyond that.
- Go module versioning: tags were renamed to v0.xxx.0, and the proxy still reports the old non-module v5.1.2 as @latest. Pin an explicit v0.5xx.0 tag (tags go up to v0.541.0).

**Status:** Actively maintained by its single author (last commit 2026-01-23, tags up to v0.541.0). MIT-licensed, pure Go, and used via go generate, so it is easy to adopt in Go projects.

[repo](https://github.com/glycerine/greenpack) · [benchmark](https://github.com/glycerine/go_serialization_benchmarks#results)

##### hpp-proto  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Wire-compatible C++23 Protobuf implementation; non-owning mode decodes and builds+serializes 1.5-1.9x faster than libprotobuf arenas.

**Beats:** Protobuf (Google's C++ libprotobuf) — This is a first-party Google Benchmark run against Google protobuf 33.2 on an i9-11950H with gcc 13.3.0, plus an M1 Pro with Apple clang 17; the build flags are not stated. Decoding one ~220-byte GoogleMessage1 takes 141/160 ns (proto2/proto3) in hpp-proto's non-owning mode vs 210/252 ns for Google's arena mode, and set+serialize takes 99.6/121 vs 186/223 ns. Owning-mode decode is near parity (proto2 210 vs 215 ns), and Google wins serialize-only (64.5 vs 85.1 ns).

**Known shortcoming:** Google protobuf wins serialize-only (Linux 64.5 vs 85.1 ns; Apple M1 Pro 75.1 vs 132 ns, proto2). Owning-mode decode is about parity (210 vs 215 ns); the 1.5-1.9x headline needs non-owning view semantics, and the non-owning set_message row assigns string_views to literals while Google copies. The README's FetchContent pin (2026-01-02) predates two fuzzer-found parser fixes (heap overflow, PR #199; crash, PR #200). Pre-1.0.

**Independent measurement:** Code size: the Linux encode/decode test binary is 111,816 bytes vs 3,829,824 with static libprotobuf and 1,748,216 with libprotobuf-lite.

**How:** Messages are plain structs. Field-number-to-member dispatch uses a consteval two-level 'masked lookup table', and varints go through the branch-predicted shift-mix decoder adapted from protobuf's varint_shuffle.h. Most of the headline gain comes from non_owning_traits: string, bytes and repeated fields become string_view/span views backed by the input buffer or a caller std::pmr arena, which removes per-field heap allocations and copies. Packed varint arrays are pre-sized by popcounting terminator bytes 8 at a time. The parser walks 16-byte overlapping 'slope' regions, or a caller-promised padded_input, so inner loops skip bounds checks; proto3 UTF-8 checks call simdutf's is_utf8, and serialization is two-pass with an external size cache in a 1 KiB stack-backed monotonic buffer.

**Use it when:**
- You exchange protobuf messages with existing libprotobuf or gRPC peers and want lower per-message C++ latency on small messages (the benchmark uses a ~220-byte GoogleMessage1) without changing the wire format.
- Hot decode paths where the input buffer outlives the parsed message: non_owning_traits with a std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource decode in 141 ns vs 210 ns for Google arena (proto2, i9-11950H).
- Build-then-send pipelines that fill a message and serialize it once: set+serialize takes 139 vs 185 ns (proto2, regular) and 99.6 vs 186 ns in non-owning vs arena mode.
- Large packed numeric arrays or proto3 messages with long strings: a 1000-element packed uint64 decodes in 2511 vs 3852 ns CPU, and the raw Linux output shows proto3 decode with 512/2048-byte strings at 518 ns vs 1007 ns.
- Binary-size-constrained or embedded targets: the Linux encode/decode test program is 111,816 bytes, against 3,829,824 for static libprotobuf and 1,748,216 for libprotobuf-lite.

**Skip it when:**
- Codebases that cannot move to C++23: it needs GCC 13+ or Clang 19+ (MSVC is also in CI) and CMake 3.25+.
- Workloads dominated by re-serializing messages that are already built. Google wins serialize-only: proto2 64.5 vs 85.1 ns on the i9, and 75.1 vs 132 ns on the M1 Pro.
- When you cannot guarantee buffer and arena lifetimes. Owning-mode decode is roughly even with Google on the small message (proto2 210 vs 215 ns), and the headline gains need view semantics that Google's arena mode does not use.
- Large libprotobuf codebases that rely on the accessor API, Google-style reflection or Arena semantics: the generated types are different, so migrating means rewriting call sites. Text format is not documented.
- Risk-averse production: the project is pre-1.0 (latest tag is the v1.0.0-beta.1 pre-release) with 43 stars, and fuzzing found a heap-buffer-overflow and a crash in the parser as recently as July and August 2026.

**Integration:** header-only core (hpp_proto::hpp_proto) plus the protoc-gen-hpp plugin built from source; optional compiled hpp_proto::dynamic_message library · is_utf8 (simdutf) for UTF-8 validation; glaze for JSON; protoc for code generation. CPM fetches missing dependencies unless CPM_LOCAL_PACKAGES_ONLY=ON. gRPC is needed only for the adapter. · C++23 (README: Clang 19+ or GCC 13+), CMake 3.25+, protoc. CI also builds with MSVC and MinGW, and tests C++26 with Clang 22. · Portable C++. CI covers Linux x86-64 (GCC 13/14, Clang 20/22), macOS (macos-latest) and Windows (MSVC, MinGW); benchmarks were run on x86-64 and an Apple M1 Pro. No ISA is required: on x86-64, popcnt is detected at runtime.

**Vs siblings:** Pick hpp-proto when you must keep the protobuf wire format and .proto schemas (existing peers, gRPC) and want a faster, smaller C++ codec. ProtoCache (a flat format for protobuf schemas, 132 vs 2620 ns decode+traverse), SBE and Apache Fory report bigger wins, but they use their own encodings, so every peer has to change.

**Gotchas:**
- non_owning_traits messages hold string_view/span into the input buffer or the alloc_from memory resource, and both must outlive the message. Map fields become key/value spans that are not deduplicated (the last duplicate wins). Mixing owning string_t with view-typed repeated_t leaks, because destructors never run.
- padded_input requires at least 16 readable bytes past the payload, and the first padding byte must be 0. Passing it without those guarantees defeats the parser's bounds-check-free loops.
- read_binpb/read_json report errors through a status and do not catch std::bad_alloc from containers. A failed parse may leave the target message partly modified.
- The README's FetchContent snippet pins the v1.0.0-beta.1 commit (2026-01-02). That commit predates two ClusterFuzzLite-found fixes: a heap-buffer-overflow in segmented packed-varint decoding (PR #199, merged 2026-07-21) and a non-owning unknown-field crash (PR #200, 2026-08-03). Pin a newer commit.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last main-branch commit 2026-08-03, fuzzed with ClusterFuzzLite, CI on Linux, macOS and Windows) but still pre-1.0 with 43 stars. It is MIT-licensed and consumable via FetchContent or the in-repo vcpkg port and conanfile.

[repo](https://github.com/huangminghuang/hpp-proto) · [benchmark](https://github.com/huangminghuang/hpp-proto/blob/main/benchmarks/ReadMe.md)

##### HyperSerializer  `C#`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Contract-less .NET binary serializer built on runtime-compiled Span/MemoryMarshal proxies; ~16x faster than protobuf-net and MessagePack-CSharp in its author's benchmark.

**Beats:** Protocol Buffers (protobuf-net 3.1.26), MessagePack (MessagePack-CSharp 2.4.59) — The author's BenchmarkDotNet table (.NET 8.0.3 RyuJIT x64 AVX2, /p:Optimize=true, Intel Core i9-10980XE, Windows 11) shows 1M single-object serialize+deserialize round-trips of a 10-member POCO. HyperSerializer took 46.24 ms, against 98.81 ms for MemoryPack 1.9.16 (2.14x), 768.58 ms for MessagePack-CSharp 2.4.59 and 769.34 ms for protobuf-net 3.1.26 (both ~16.6x). Allocations were similar (~206 MB), except protobuf-net at 427 MB. The committed harness does not reproduce this exact table: its Test class has no string, and its loop and parameter setup differ. The '18x' and '3x vs Apex' figures come from an older chart with no environment listed.

**How:** On the first use of each `T`, a static constructor reflects over the type and fills C# source templates to build a proxy class. It compiles that source at runtime with Roslyn (Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp, Release optimization), loads the assembly, and caches the Serialize/Deserialize delegates in the static generic class `HyperSerializer<T>`. The generated code computes the exact output length (fixed member sizes plus string and array byte counts) and allocates one `byte[]`. It then writes each member as raw memory with `MemoryMarshal.Write` and reads it back with `MemoryMarshal.Read`. Strings are block-copied as UTF-16 through `MemoryMarshal.Cast<char,byte>`, and value-type arrays are block-copied too. The format has no field tags, no varints, no UTF-8 transcoding and no per-member type markers. Its only framing is a 1-byte null flag for each nullable and a 4-byte length prefix for each string or array.

**Use it when:**
- Both ends run the same .NET 6-9 build (a shared DTO assembly) and exchange small, flat objects over a trusted link. The README names messaging between services behind a firewall as the target.
- Short-lived caches of flat DTOs, in-process or remote, where you can flush the cache whenever a type changes.
- Hot paths that serialize and deserialize one object at a time. The published run shows ~46 ns per round trip (derived: 46.24 ms / 1M) for a 10-member POCO with Guid, DateTime, decimal, TimeSpan, an enum and a string.
- Bulk arrays of unmanaged structs, such as market ticks. Pass the whole `T[]` and it is stored as a length prefix plus one block copy (see test Test_Struct_Array_Should_Serialize and the author's advice in issue #8).
- Types you cannot or will not annotate. No [ProtoContract], [MessagePackObject] or [Key] attributes are needed.

**Skip it when:**
- Persisted data, or services deployed on different schedules. The format is positional with no field IDs, so reordering, removing or retyping a member breaks reads. The README warns that mismatched bytes can decode into wrong values with no exception.
- Any reader that is not .NET, or data exchanged across architectures. The bytes are raw CLR memory layout: Microsoft's docs say `MemoryMarshal.Write` copies private fields and implementation details. Byte order is the host's, strings are UTF-16, and no format spec exists.
- Native AOT, trimmed or single-file apps. The library compiles C# with Roslyn at runtime, loads the result dynamically, and builds compiler references from `Assembly.Location`. Native AOT forbids dynamic loading, and single-file apps return an empty `Assembly.Location`.
- Object graphs. Class-typed members and dictionaries are ignored, with no reference or cycle handling (issues #2 and #11), and a top-level `Dictionary<int,int>` throws (issue #1, open since 2022).
- Processes where cold start or footprint matters. The first use of each type runs a Roslyn compilation, and the package depends on Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp. The repo does not document the compile cost.

**Integration:** shared lib (NuGet package `HyperSerializer`, managed DLL) · Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp >= 4.9.2 (Roslyn, used at runtime to compile the per-type proxies) · .NET 6 (package targets net6.0, net7.0, net8.0, net9.0) · Any OS/architecture running .NET 6-9 with JIT and runtime assembly loading. Native AOT is not supported, and single-file publish is likely incompatible. The wire format uses host byte order.

**Vs siblings:** Bebop is the only sibling with a C# result. Pick HyperSerializer over Bebop when you want no .bop schema and no bebopc codegen step and both ends are the same .NET types. Pick Bebop when TypeScript, Rust or C++ must read the data. rkyv and Apache Fory (C++) are measured outside .NET, so they matter here only if you are not locked to .NET.

**Gotchas:**
- The async methods are synchronous wrappers, and `SerializeAsync` also copies the result with `ToArray()`. In issue #8, calling SerializeAsync per record into a MemoryStream took 1,967 ms, against 528 ms for TeaFiles, on 3.02M structs. The author's fix was the sync `Span` API, or serializing the whole array in one call.
- Setup runs in the static constructor of `HyperSerializer<T>`, so codegen failures surface as TypeInitializationException (issues #1 and #4). The generated deserializer calls `new()` and assigns every scanned member, and MemberTypeInfo.cs never checks CanWrite. So types appear to need a public parameterless constructor and settable members. Set `HyperSerializerSettings` before the first use of each type.
- Member order is public fields first, then properties, in reflection order. Microsoft documents that GetProperties order is unspecified on .NET 6 and earlier and deterministic from .NET 7. In the current source, setting `SerializeFields = false` keeps fields and drops properties, which is the opposite of what the README describes.
- The README says generic lists work, but `TypeSupport` compares against the open generic `typeof(IEnumerable<>)`, which a `List<int>` never equals. So List members appear to be skipped silently, and the V3 test that covers lists uses a comparison helper that cannot return false. Value-type arrays do round-trip (issue #5 regression test). Struct members must not contain references, because `MemoryMarshal.Write` throws ArgumentException for those.

**Status:** Maintained but slow-moving. v1.6 (2025-11-05) only added net9.0; before it, the last code change was in April 2024. The repo has 85 stars, ~44k NuGet downloads and one open issue. Usable via NuGet under Apache-2.0 (the package ships an MIT License.txt), but its runtime Roslyn dependency rules out AOT and makes it heavier than its small source suggests.

[repo](https://github.com/adam-dot-cohen/HyperSerializer) · [benchmark](https://github.com/adam-dot-cohen/HyperSerializer#benchmarks)

##### Imprint  `Rust`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Rust row format with a sorted field-offset directory, so records merge or project without decoding; ~4x faster than prost merges.

**Beats:** Protobuf (Rust prost 0.12 implementation, per the since-removed benches/Cargo.toml) — In the author's Criterion run (PR #11, May 2025, Rust prost 0.12; CPU, compiler and flags not stated; the chart unit is ns), decoding a fake Product and Order, combining them and re-encoding took 3,454 ns with prost vs 797 ns with Imprint at the largest size (~4.3x, the README's '76%') and 1,004 vs 784 ns at the smallest. A contributor's rerun in PR #27, after merges became order-deterministic, gave 2,848 vs 692 ns (~4.1x) and 748 vs 642 ns (~1.17x); the projection chart has Imprint slower at size 1 and ~2.4x faster at size 10, although the prost projection re-encodes 5 fields against Imprint's 6.

**Known shortcoming:** Baseline is Rust prost 0.12, not Google protobuf, and the protobuf merge path adds clones. Slower than prost at the smallest projection size. The comparison harness was deleted in PR #31 and survives only in history (commit f42484cf).

**Known shortcoming:** Deserialize (248 vs 769 ns) times Imprint without decoding field values (author: 'best case'). The projection comparison favours prost (5 fields re-encoded vs 6 projected). Not on crates.io (the name belongs to an unrelated crate); git dependency only. Malformed input can panic; map bytes are not deterministic despite the README; project writes a 0xdeadbeef placeholder schema hash.

**Independent measurement:** PR #11 (author): merge at size 1/5/10 prost 1003.50/2140.10/3453.90 ns vs Imprint 784.04/798.71/797.41 ns; serialize 355.53 vs 224.99 ns. PR #27 rerun (contributor, after deterministic merge): size 10 prost 2848 vs Imprint 692 ns, size 1 748 vs 642 ns.

**How:** Each row has a 15-byte header and a directory of 7-byte entries (u16 field id, u8 type code, u32 payload offset) sorted by field id. A field is found by binary search, and its byte length is the gap to the next entry's offset.
