- You want production maturity or a Rust API. It stopped at v0.0.36, nearly all commits are by one developer, and the core crate is built only as a cdylib behind C/JNI entry points, with no Rust-facing API.

**Integration:** shared lib · Core (Rust): rdkafka (librdkafka with vendored OpenSSL), tokio, aws-sdk-s3, memmap2, protobuf, jni, fxhash, flate2/tar. Runtime: a Kafka topic per store, an S3 bucket for base-index snapshots, and a gRPC gateway for config and writes. Python SDK: boto3, cffi, grpcio, protobuf. · Rust 2021 edition (MSRV not documented); Python SDK requires Python 3.8+; Go and Java minimums not documented. · The SDK loaders only know prebuilt binaries for linux-x86_64, linux-aarch64 and macOS aarch64 (no Windows, no Intel Mac). 64-bit only: the offset table uses usize and is commented as 32-bit incompatible. The prebuilt binary bucket no longer exists, so you must build from source.

**Vs siblings:** Garnet, Dragonfly, KeyDB and Pogocache are shared network servers benchmarked on server throughput against Redis, and Caffeine is an in-process JVM heap cache you fill yourself. Pick IKV only if you want every app host to hold a stream-synced, disk-spillable read replica of a feature dataset and will run and maintain its Kafka/S3 data plane yourself. Otherwise a sibling is the safer choice.

**Gotchas:**
- The 'no network calls' claim covers steady-state reads only. Opening a reader fetches config over gRPC from gateway.inlined.io, may download a base-index tarball from S3 (region hard-coded to us-west-2), and blocks until its Kafka partition is consumed to the high watermark. All vendor endpoints are now dead, so readers cannot start without code changes or a self-hosted data plane.
- Supply-chain risk: the Go and Python SDKs list a public S3 bucket named ikv-binaries, download the highest-versioned libikv from it, and dlopen it. That bucket now returns NoSuchBucket, so anyone who re-creates the name could serve the code the SDKs load. Pin and build your own binary. Also, the README's inlined.io links now redirect to an unrelated site flagged as potentially malicious.
- The Kafka consumer sets enable.ssl.certificate.verification=false while it authenticates with the account passkey over SASL/SCRAM. In a self-hosted setup, override this with the kafkaprop_ config prefix.
- Durability and robustness are thin. mmap.flush() is commented out ('TODO(critical): this fails on macos'), so value bytes are synced only when the OS writes pages back. The JNI and C entry points unwrap() or expect() on inputs and config. A comment warns that a panic in the consumer thread is not surfaced.

**Status:** The project has been stale since v0.0.36 (2024-05-14) and is effectively orphaned. As of 2026-09-26, inlined.io redirects to an unrelated flagged site, docs.inlined.io and gateway.inlined.io do not resolve, and the SDKs' binary bucket is gone. Using it now means building libikv from source and self-hosting or patching out the data plane, though the MIT-licensed Rust index is small enough to study or vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/inlinedio/ikv-store) · [benchmark](https://github.com/inlinedio/ikv-store#benchmarks--100x-faster-than-redis)

##### KeyDB  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Multithreaded C++ Redis 6.2 fork serving one keyspace from many event-loop threads; claims ~7x Redis 6 throughput under TLS.

**Beats:** Redis — KeyDB's own blog (Sept 2020) drove servers on an AWS m5.4xlarge from an m5.8xlarge with memtier_benchmark --tls --threads=32 and otherwise default settings: KeyDB with 16 server threads and TLS got close to 1M ops/s (about 800k with 8 threads) versus ~130k ops/s for single-threaded Redis 6.0 with TLS, which is 36% below non-TLS single-threaded Redis and 61% below non-TLS Redis with io-threads. CPU model, compiler, build flags and exact versions are not given, Redis was not sharded or run as several instances, and the 'up to 7x lower latency' claim has no table.

**Known shortcoming:** Dead in practice: last commit 2024-04, last release v6.3.4 (2023-10); the lead developer left Snap in early 2025 and pointed users to Valkey (#895); open deadlock/crash issues (#883, #743, #827). Stuck at Redis 6.2 (can't load Redis 7 dumps, #527). A global spinlock still serializes every command, so gains shrink for writes, hot keys and long EXEC/Lua. The benchmark used 16 server-threads (README recommends 4) against an unsharded Redis, with no CPU/compiler/flags; the '7x lower latency' claim has no data. Threading needs Linux SO_REUSEPORT; ARM startup assert (#856); FLASH is beta; multi-master consistency/crash reports (#366). An existing redis.conf 'io-threads' line silently maps to server-threads.

**How:** It runs the stock Redis ae event loop on N threads and pins each connection to one thread at accept() (spread with Linux SO_REUSEPORT plus active client balancing), so socket I/O, TLS and RESP parsing run in parallel. Command execution against the shared keyspace is still serialized by a single global lock: a fair ticket spinlock ('fastlock', with an x86-64 assembly fast path) that spins with pause/yield and falls back to a futex wait, and that uses otherwise wasted spin time to do incremental dict rehashing ('async rehash'). KEYS/SCAN, and optionally GET/MGET ('enable-async-commands') and in-process BGSAVE ('use-fork no'), read from copy-on-write MVCC snapshots of the database so they do not hold the global lock.

**Use it when:**
- A single Redis 6.x node that is CPU-bound on networking, TLS or protocol parsing (many connections, small GET/SET values) and you want more ops/s from one box without sharding into Redis Cluster or running one instance per core
- TLS-terminated Redis traffic: the benchmarked Redis 6 could not combine io-threads with TLS, while KeyDB does TLS on every server thread
- Existing Redis 6.x deployments on Linux (Redis 6 RDB files, modules, Lua) that want a binary swap and can tolerate a stale codebase
- You specifically need active-active (multi-master) replication or per-member hash/set expiry, which upstream Redis does not provide

**Skip it when:**
- New production deployments: no commits since April 2024, last release v6.3.4 (Oct 2023), the lead developer left Snap in early 2025 and told users to move to Valkey, and deadlock/crash issues (e.g. #883 replication deadlock, #743, #827) remain open
- Anything needing Redis 7+ commands or data: RDB_VERSION is 9, so Redis 7 dumps (RDB v10) fail to load (#527) and Redis 7 commands such as PEXPIRETIME are missing
- Write-heavy or hot-key workloads and long MULTI/EXEC or Lua: every command still runs under one global lock (transactions hold it for the whole EXEC), so parallelism is limited to I/O and parsing
- Non-Linux hosts, and ARM with caution: the threading model relies on Linux SO_REUSEPORT load balancing, and there are open ARM startup-assert reports (#856)
- Multi-master or FLASH setups you cannot babysit: FLASH is labelled experimental/beta, active replication has an open data-consistency report (#366), and HN users reported cluster-wide crashes and deadlocks in multi-master mode

**Integration:** standalone server binary (keydb-server, built with make; Docker image eqalpha/keydb); not a linkable library · Bundled in deps/: jemalloc, Lua, hiredis, linenoise, hdr_histogram, moodycamel concurrentqueue, cpp-statsd-client, memkind (optional), RocksDB submodule (FLASH only). System: OpenSSL (TLS on by default), libuuid, libcurl (MOTD, disable with NO_MOTD=yes), nasm (x86-64 spinlock), bz2/zstd/lz4/snappy for RocksDB builds; Makefile can link system jemalloc/RocksDB/hiredis instead · C++17 (-std=c++17 -fno-rtti) plus C11/C99 for the C files; GCC or Clang (Clang builds use libc++); GCC 13.1 build fixed in 6.3.4; minimum compiler versions not documented · Linux (tested); x86-64 gets the assembly spinlock, aarch64 builds exist but have open crash reports; FreeBSD compiles as of 6.3.4; macOS builds but README says only Linux is supported for the threading model

**Vs siblings:** No siblings catalogued yet.

**Gotchas:**
- server-threads should follow NIC queue count, not core count: the README recommends 4 (default 2) and warns more threads can be slower because the global lock is a spinlock, yet the headline TLS benchmark used 16 threads with affinity
- An existing redis.conf with 'io-threads 8' silently becomes 8 KeyDB server threads, since io-threads is an alias for server-threads
- KeyDB expects exclusive use of its cores (spinning waiters burn CPU), and keydb-benchmark/redis-benchmark are single-threaded and too slow to measure it; use memtier on separate cores
- multi-master-no-forward yes loses data unless every master is in a full mesh; enable-async-commands relaxes cross-client read-your-writes ordering and currently covers only GET/MGET

**Status:** Stale: last release v6.3.4 (Oct 2023) and last commit April 2024, and the lead developer, leaving Snap, recommended Valkey. The code is BSD-3-Clause and builds with make, but anyone adopting it maintains the fork themselves.

[repo](https://github.com/Snapchat/KeyDB) · [benchmark](https://docs.keydb.dev/blog/2020/09/29/blog-post/)

##### otter  `Go`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Caffeine-style concurrent Go cache (adaptive W-TinyLFU): 10-34x hashicorp/golang-lru throughput at 25-100% reads; slower on pure writes.

**Beats:** hashicorp/golang-lru — The numbers come from the project's own Go port of Caffeine's GetPutBenchmark: 8 goroutines (-cpu=8), with a 32,768-entry cache pre-filled from a scrambled Zipf over about 10.9K string keys, so every Get hits and every Set is an update with no eviction. Run once on an Apple M1 Pro (darwin/arm64) with an unrecorded Go toolchain, otter reached 106.4M ops/s at 100% reads vs 3.14M for hashicorp/golang-lru v2 (about 34x), about 27x at 75/25, 21x at 50/50 and 10x at 25/75, while golang-lru was about 1.4x faster at 100% writes (3.23M vs 2.32M ops/s).

**Known shortcoming:** No Go toolchain version stated (go.mod minimum only). The ~27x read-throughput lead shrinks with writes, and at 100% writes golang-lru is ~1.4x faster.

**Known shortcoming:** The benchmark flatters it: a 32,768-slot cache over ~10.9K Zipf keys means every Get hits, every Set updates and nothing is evicted; one M1 Pro run. Pure writes lose (2.32M vs golang-lru 3.23M ops/s; second-slowest of 8 caches). MaximumSize is soft with the async executor (#171 shows 1,027 entries at max 2; use the sync executor). Open bugs: drainBuffers mutex contention under Compute (#177); the loader runs more than once per key (#152, fix PR #184 open). Not a drop-in (renamed API, W-TinyLFU not LRU); Go 1.24+; no commits since 2025-12.

**How:** The hash table is a fork of puzpuzpuz/xsync's MapOf, a CLHT-style (Cache-Line Hash Table) design with 64-byte buckets of 5 entries and SWAR meta-byte probing, so Get does no memory writes and takes no locks. Policy bookkeeping follows BP-Wrapper: reads go into a lossy striped ring buffer (the stripe count grows when contention is detected) and writes into a bounded growable MPSC queue, and both are replayed in batches under one eviction mutex taken with TryLock, so readers never wait on the policy lock. By contrast, golang-lru takes an exclusive sync.RWMutex Lock on every Get to move the entry to the front. Eviction is adaptive W-TinyLFU (admission window plus segmented main space, a 4-bit count-min sketch and hill-climbing window sizing), expiry uses a hierarchical timing wheel, and node structs are code-generated per feature set so options you don't use add no per-entry memory.

**Use it when:**
- Read-heavy in-process caches shared by many goroutines on multi-core machines, where golang-lru's global lock on Get is the bottleneck (first-party: 34x at 100% reads, 27x at 75/25, 21x at 50/50).
- Bounded caches whose access pattern is unknown or shifts between recency- and frequency-biased, where the adaptive W-TinyLFU window beats plain LRU hit rates on the project's trace simulations (S3, DS1, P8, OLTP, Glimpse, mixed).
- When you want Caffeine's feature set in Go: per-entry variable TTL, loader dedupe to limit stampedes, background refresh-ahead, weight-based bounds, stats counters, and deletion callbacks.
- Generic keys of any comparable type (hashed with maphash.Comparable) and any value type, from hundreds to millions of entries (the eviction benchmark covers capacities from 100 to 1,000,000).

**Skip it when:**
- Pure-write or update-heavy workloads: at 100% writes otter measured 2.32M ops/s vs golang-lru's 3.23M, behind theine, ristretto, sturdyc, gcache and ttlcache too; the docs themselves list extreme write-heavy loads as the exception.
- When the size cap must hold at every instant (tiny caches, or entries that pin scarce resources): with the default async Executor, a tight Set loop pushed a MaximumSize=2 cache to 1,027 entries (issue #171). The maintainer's fix is a synchronous Executor, which moves the eviction work back onto the caller.
- Low-contention or single-goroutine use, or small insert-only caches. The gains come from contention; in the insert-only eviction benchmark golang-lru was faster at capacity 100 (266.6 vs 307.5 ns/op), though otter was faster at 10K and 1M.
- Hot paths built on Compute with slow callbacks: Compute holds a hash-table bucket lock while the function runs, and open issue #177 reports heavy mutex delay in drainBuffers under frequent Compute (v2.2.1, root cause not yet found).
- Toolchains older than Go 1.24, or projects that cannot track new Go releases: the README says only the two most recent Go minor versions are supported.

**Integration:** module · none at runtime beyond the Go standard library (the only direct requirement in go.mod is stretchr/testify, for tests); the slog logger plugin is a separate module (plugin/pslog) · Go 1.24 (go.mod `go 1.24.0`; uses maphash.Comparable and runtime.AddCleanup). Only the two newest Go minor versions are supported; CI runs Go 1.25.x, plus a 32-bit job on 1.24.x. · pure Go, so any GOOS/GOARCH in principle. CI runs Linux (ubuntu-latest) plus a 32-bit build; the GOARCH=wasm build was fixed in v2.3.0. Published benchmarks exist only for darwin/arm64 (Apple M1 Pro).

**Vs siblings:** go-sieve and golang-fifo also report large wins over golang-lru with SIEVE-style policies; pick otter when you also need Caffeine-style features (variable TTL, loader dedupe, refresh-ahead, weights, stats) and an adaptive policy that holds up on both recency- and frequency-biased traces. Caffeine itself is the JVM original that otter's design and benchmark are ported from.

**Gotchas:**
- Policy state is only eventually consistent with the map: eviction and expiry reordering run in batches on a goroutine started through the Executor (default `go fn()`), so EstimatedSize can exceed MaximumSize for a while. Pass a synchronous Executor if you need strict bounds, as the project's own hit-ratio simulator does.
- Get(ctx, key, loader) works like singleflight: under a burst of concurrent Gets the loader can still run more than once for the same key (issue #152). A fix PR (#184) has been open since 2026-06-25.
- Weights are computed once, on write, and never recomputed; they only decide whether the cache is over capacity, not which entry is evicted. Zero weight or an expiry of math.MaxInt64 is the documented way to pin an entry.
- When expiry is enabled, a cleanup goroutine ticks once per second. It is stopped by a runtime.AddCleanup finalizer or by an explicit StopAllGoroutines (needed under synctest, issue #158). SaveCacheTo/LoadCacheFrom use encoding/gob, so K and V must be gob-encodable.

**Status:** v2.3.0 was released 2025-12-22 and main's last commit is 2025-12-23, but the maintainer was still answering issues in 2026 and bug reports and a fix PR (#184) are open; Apache-2.0, pure Go with no runtime dependencies, and the README lists users including Grafana, Centrifugo and FrankenPHP.

[repo](https://github.com/maypok86/otter) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/maypok86/otter/main/benchmarks/throughput/results/throughput.txt)

##### Pogocache  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Multithreaded C cache server speaking RESP, memcache, HTTP and Postgres; about 2x Redis and 1.2-2.3x memcached throughput (author-run).

**Beats:** Redis, Memcached — The only benchmark is the author's cache-benchmarks suite: memtier_benchmark with 256 connections over a local UNIX socket, 1-1024 B values, persistence off, server pinned to 16 cores of an AWS c8g.8xlarge (ARM64), median of 31 runs. At 8 threads and pipeline 1, Pogocache 1.2.0 did 3.08M GET/s and 2.95M SET/s vs 1.51M/1.67M for Redis 8.2.1 and 2.60M/1.27M for memcached 1.6.38, with GET p99 of 0.119 ms vs 0.207 ms and 0.191 ms. It beats Redis, Valkey, memcached and Dragonfly in every thread/pipeline cell (smallest margin: 1.07x over memcached on GET at 1 thread, pipeline 10). No compiler flags are stated, and the older README table (about 3.5x Redis) is stale.

**Known shortcoming:** The ~3.5x-over-Redis figure is a stale July 2025 run against Redis 8.0.2; the current author-run suite shows ~2.0x Redis 8.2.1 and ~1.18x memcached GET at 8 threads. No compiler or flags. Garnet beats it at pipeline depths 25/50 (verifier downgrade).

**Known shortcoming:** Garnet wins GET in 34 of 36 pipelined cells. Strings only (no Redis data types, pub/sub, MULTI or Lua), no HA/replication, SELECT 0 only. maxmemory is enforced by polling RSS once a second (a third-party Raspberry Pi 4 test ran ~50% over the limit). memcache CAS is off by default (every cas fails without --cas yes). Embedded mode uses hash seed 0 and no memory limit. The benchmarked 1.2.0 was AGPL; MIT only from 1.3.1. Source commits sparse since 2026-01.

**How:** Keys are hashed with th64 (random seed per process) into one of 4096 shards by default. Each shard is an independent Robin Hood open-addressing table with 10-byte buckets (48-bit entry pointer, 24-bit hash fragment, 1-byte distance-to-bucket) guarded by its own compare-and-swap spinlock, so two threads rarely wait on the same lock. Each entry is one heap allocation (mimalloc by default) with keys packed at 6 bits per character ('sixpack'). Networking runs one epoll/kqueue loop per thread with connections assigned round-robin; each tick batches reads, command execution and writes, using io_uring to submit the batched reads/writes on Linux when enough sockets are ready, and low-memory eviction uses 2-random sampling instead of maintaining an LRU list.

**Use it when:**
- Plain string GET/SET caching (sessions, rendered pages, query results; the benchmark used 1 B-1 KB values) where you want more ops per core than Redis or memcached and don't need Redis data types.
- Request/response traffic with little or no pipelining (depth 1-10) from many connections. This is where the author's suite shows the largest margins: about 2x Redis at 8 threads, with GET p99 of 0.12 ms vs 0.21 ms for Redis.
- CPU- or cost-limited hosts: about 7.1K CPU cycles per operation vs about 10K for Redis and 13.4K for memcached in the author's perf runs.
- Replacing memcached for text-protocol clients when you also want TLS, a password, HTTP access and manual SAVE/LOAD snapshots in one binary on Linux or macOS.
- An in-process cache in C/C++: drop in pogocache.c for a thread-safe sharded map with TTLs, eviction/notify callbacks and CAS, with no network hop.

**Skip it when:**
- You need Redis beyond strings. There are no hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, pub/sub, MULTI/EXEC, Lua, INFO/HELLO/CLIENT, or databases other than 0 (SELECT only accepts 0). Lists and other types are an open request (issue #14).
- You need replication, failover or clustering. None exist, and high availability has been 'in the works' since Aug 2025 (issue #20). Persistence is only a manual SAVE/LOAD or a save on clean shutdown via --persist.
- Deeply pipelined clients (depth 25-50). In the same suite Garnet beats it on GETs in 34 of 36 pipelined configurations, e.g. 29.5M vs 11.4M ops/s at 8 threads, pipeline 50.
- Strict memory caps. The limit works by polling process RSS once a second. A third-party test with 1 MiB values on a Raspberry Pi 4 hit a VmHWM of 3.3 GB against --maxmemory 2 GiB (about 50% over).
- Risk-averse production. It was first released in July 2025 by a single company/maintainer, and the only published throughput benchmark is the author's own.

**Integration:** source-drop: the server binary is built with make (static release builds and a Docker image exist); pogocache.c + pogocache.h are embeddable · The server build git-clones and statically links mimalloc 3.1.5, jemalloc 5.3.0, liburing 2.12 (Linux) and OpenSSL 3.5.2, which needs cmake, autotools and perl at build time. Each can be disabled with NOMIMALLOC/NOJEMALLOC/NOURING/NOOPENSSL=1. The embedded pogocache.c needs only the C standard library. · C11 (stdatomic.h, static_assert) plus GCC/Clang extensions (__thread, __builtin_ia32_pause, -flto=auto); minimum compiler versions not documented · 64-bit Linux and macOS (documented; CI on ubuntu-latest); x86-64 and aarch64 spin hints; benchmarked on ARM64 (AWS c8g); no Windows; the Makefile also has an Emscripten/WASM target

**Vs siblings:** Pick Pogocache over Dragonfly when clients mostly GET/SET strings at low pipeline depth and CPU per request matters: it beat Dragonfly in every thread/pipeline cell of the author's suite, by 1.1x to 5x. Pick Garnet instead for heavily pipelined clients, and Dragonfly when you need broader Redis command coverage. The embedded pogocache.c plays the in-process role for C that Caffeine plays on the JVM.

**Gotchas:**
- CAS is disabled by default (--cas no). Memcache `gets` returns CAS 0 and every `cas` fails until the server is started with --cas yes.
- Hash buckets store 48-bit pointers. The build assumes heap addresses fit in 48 bits; compile with NO48BITPTRS to get 8-byte pointers on systems with larger virtual address spaces or tagged pointers.
- Embedded mode: the hash seed defaults to 0 (only the server picks a random seed), and there is no built-in memory limit; eviction happens only when the caller passes lowmem=true on store. The header comment says the default is 65536 shards, but the code uses 4096.
- It binds to loopback by default, so in Docker or Kubernetes you must pass -h 0.0.0.0 or clients get dropped connections (issue #21). The --auth password can only be given on the command line.

**Status:** Releases are still coming (1.3.2, Aug 2026), but source changes have been sparse since Jan 2026 (later commits touch only Docker and README files). It has been MIT-licensed since the Nov 2025 relicense (first MIT release 1.3.1); versions 1.0.0-1.3.0, including the benchmarked 1.2.0, were AGPL-3.0.

[repo](https://github.com/tidwall/pogocache) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tidwall/cache-benchmarks)

##### python-diskcache  `Python`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Pure-Python, SQLite-backed persistent cache that runs in-process and beats localhost Memcached/Redis on read latency, not writes.

**Beats:** Memcached (pylibmc client) and Redis (redis.StrictRedis) — The author's tests/benchmark_core.py runs 100k ops per process (90% get, 9% set, 1% delete) over only 100 keys with values of a few hundred bytes, so the whole working set stays hot in SQLite's page cache. It pits DiskCache in-process against pylibmc and redis-py talking to default-configured localhost servers. Single-process median get was 12.2 us vs 26.0 us (Memcached) and 44.1 us (Redis), and median set was 68.9 us vs 27.9 us. With 8 processes, only FanoutCache(8 shards) beat Memcached overall (59.0 s vs 68.8 s total); plain Cache took 157.9 s. The page gives no CPU, OS, Python, SQLite, Memcached or Redis versions, its tables date from 2017, and the committed tests/timings_core_p1.txt comes from a different run (19.1 us get median).

**Known shortcoming:** Sets are ~2.5x slower than Memcached, and the plain Cache loses overall at 8 workers (157.9 s vs 68.8 s); only FanoutCache with 8 shards wins. No CPU stated.

**Known shortcoming:** SECURITY: CVE-2025-69872 / GHSA-w8v5-vhqr-4h9v - the default Disk unpickles stored values, so anyone who can write the cache directory can execute code; affects <=5.6.3 with no patched release and no fix timeline from the maintainer (2026-07). Use a non-pickle Disk or trusted directories only.

**Known shortcoming:** The benchmark uses only 100 keys, so the working set stays hot in SQLite's page cache and the GET win is mostly avoiding a localhost socket. Writes are slower (set 68.9 us vs 27.9 us for Memcached; unsharded Cache at 8 processes has set P99 21 ms, max 1.85 s). FanoutCache's 10 ms timeout makes set/delete fail silently; LRU/LFU/stats turn every get into a write; no async, no NFS; macOS fork bug #325 open. Stale since 2024-03 (last release 5.6.3, 2023-08).

**How:** Gets skip the network round trip: the cache is an embedded SQLite database queried in-process, while the Memcached and Redis baselines go through a localhost socket. SQLite runs in write-ahead-log (WAL) mode so reads and writes don't block each other, with a 64 MB mmap and an 8,192-page page cache. Values under 32 KB are stored inline and larger ones in separate files, and SQLite triggers keep count and size so nothing needs a scan. Under the default least-recently-stored eviction policy a get is one indexed SELECT with no transaction and no write. FanoutCache hashes keys (adler32) across N SQLite files, so concurrent writers compete for N write locks instead of one.

**Use it when:**
- A Python app on a single host (web workers, CLI tools, data pipelines) that needs a cache shared between its processes and kept across restarts, without running Memcached or Redis.
- Read-dominated traffic (around 90% gets) with small keys and values, where in-process gets beat a localhost Memcached round trip (median 12.2 us vs 26.0 us in the author's benchmark).
- Caches larger than RAM: gigabytes on local disk, with large values written to files and readable as file handles (`read=True`).
- Memoizing expensive function results across runs (`memoize`, `memoize_stampede` for cache-stampede protection).
- Django sites that want a replacement for the built-in file-based cache, via `DjangoCache`.

**Skip it when:**
- Write-heavy traffic, or many writers on one unsharded `Cache`: writers take turns on SQLite's write lock. With 8 processes, set P99 was 21.3 ms and the max 1.85 s, against a 312 us max for Memcached. Single-process sets are also about 2.5x slower than Memcached (68.9 us vs 27.9 us median).
- Caches shared between machines: there is no network interface, and SQLite is not recommended on NFS. The docs also report poor performance on PythonAnywhere and problems in Parallels shared folders.
- Cache directories writable by less-trusted code: the default Disk unpickles values on read. CVE-2025-69872 / GHSA-w8v5-vhqr-4h9v (medium) covers all versions up to 5.6.3 with no patched release. Use JSONDisk or lock down the directory.
- LRU/LFU eviction or statistics: these turn every get into a write transaction, which gives up the fast read path the benchmark measured. The benchmark ran the default least-recently-stored policy.
- asyncio code (no native async; wrap calls in a thread executor), or many threads under a tight memory budget: each thread opens its own SQLite connection and mmap. In issue #293, 10 threads peaked at 2.15 GB RSS against 0.13 GB for one thread.

**Integration:** module · none (uses only the standard-library sqlite3 module) · Python 3 (setup.py python_requires '>=3'); CI tests CPython 3.8-3.11; current release 5.6.3 · any platform with Python's sqlite3 on a local filesystem; CI runs on Linux, macOS and Windows; not NFS

**Vs siblings:** Pick DiskCache over server caches like Pogocache, Valkey or Dragonfly when the cache lives on one machine inside a Python app and you want persistence and no server to run. Those siblings win when the cache must be shared across hosts or has to absorb heavy concurrent writes.

**Gotchas:**
- FanoutCache's default timeout is 10 ms, and set/delete swallow the Timeout and return False, so writes can fail silently (39 of 71,530 sets were dropped in the 8-process benchmark). A plain `Cache` raises Timeout instead, with a 60 s default.
- Keys are matched by their serialized bytes, not by __hash__/__eq__. Pickled container keys such as tuples can serialize differently when equal (issue #54), and 1 and 1.0 count as the same key. Use JSONDisk for consistent keys.
- In FanoutCache, size_limit (default 1 GB) is split evenly across shards, and an item larger than one shard's share is culled immediately. Culling is lazy (at most cull_limit=10 keys per write), so the cache can briefly exceed its limit.
- Open bug #325: on macOS, forking after opening two `Cache` objects on the same directory gives sqlite3 'disk I/O error'. A full disk raises sqlite3.OperationalError on any write, but reads keep working.

**Status:** Stale: last commit 2024-03-03 and last release 5.6.3 (2023-08-31), with 85 open issues. In July 2026 the maintainer declined to commit to a fix or timeline for the pickle CVE. It is Apache-2.0, pure Python and dependency-free, so it is easy to vendor or fork.

[repo](https://github.com/grantjenks/python-diskcache) · [benchmark](https://github.com/grantjenks/python-diskcache/blob/master/docs/cache-benchmarks.rst)

##### RapidKV  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Single-threaded C++20 RESP server with 13 string commands; ties Redis unpipelined, 1.45-4.2x faster when pipelined.

**Beats:** Redis — The author ran memtier_benchmark (8 threads x 25 clients) over loopback on one AMD Ryzen 7 4800H laptop running Kubuntu 24.04, CPU-pinned, with Redis persistence off; the Redis version and io-threads setting are not stated. RapidKV tied Redis at pipeline 1 (135K vs 130K ops/s; 0.99x in the 1M-key sweep) with about half the p99, then led by 1.45x at pipeline 10, 3.01x at 100 (5.18M vs 1.72M ops/s) and 4.23x at 500 (8.04M vs 1.90M) on 1:9 SET:GET with 8-byte values. The compiler is not stated beyond the CMake Release flags (-O3 -march=native -flto), and the memtier command lines are not in the repo.

**Known shortcoming:** Parity with Redis at pipeline depth 1; the 3.01x/4.23x appear only at depth 100/500. 1 star, compiler and Redis version unstated.

**Known shortcoming:** Resize bug (from reading flatMap.h, not run): during incremental doubling, keys past the migrate cursor cannot be found, so GET misses, DEL returns 0 and a stale value can overwrite a newer SET; untested. Not a Redis drop-in: EXPIRE/TTL in ms not s, SET PX only, no MGET/MSET/SELECT/HELLO, a bad request closes the connection.

**Known shortcoming:** SECURITY: no AUTH or TLS, binds 0.0.0.0, and no bulk-length cap (unbounded read buffer). README claims are wrong (the 7-bit tag equals the slot bits so it skips no compares; 'SIEVE' is CLOCK over slot order; needs GCC 13+ for std::format, not 12+). TTL clock refreshed only every 100 ms; RSS can exceed max_memory_usage. Code written over three weeks in 2026-01/02; benchmarks unscripted on one laptop.

**How:** It does less work per command rather than using more cores. The README's perf stat shows 2,144 instructions and 2,265 cycles per GET, against Redis's 5,421 and 3,813. The store is a Robin Hood open-addressing hash table in structure-of-arrays layout (2-byte PSL + tag metadata array, 16-byte keys, rapidhash with a random per-process seed) that doubles incrementally, 32 slots migrated per operation. Keys and values are 16-byte CompactStrings with a 15-byte inline SSO, and anything longer comes from a thread-local slab allocator with power-of-two classes (32 B-2 KB). The I/O path is one Asio event loop, a zero-copy RESP parser that returns string_views into a 64 KB read buffer, command names packed into a uint64 for dispatch, pipelined commands run in batches of 16 with hash-slot prefetch 4 commands ahead, and double-buffered async writes.

**Use it when:**
- A single-core, read-heavy GET/SET cache whose clients pipeline deeply. In the README's 1:9 SET:GET sweep, RapidKV was 1.45x Redis at pipeline 10, 3.0x at 100 and 4.2x at 500, with 3.8-5.1x lower p99 at depths of 100 and more.
- Bulk value transfer on one core. At pipeline 64 with 2 KB values it moved 1.52 GB/s against Redis's 780 MB/s, and a SET-only run with 128 B values (every key and value on the slab path) was 47% faster.
- Unpipelined string traffic where Redis's tail latency is the problem. At pipeline 1, throughput tied (135K vs 130K ops/s) but p99 was 1.57 ms against 3.06 ms in the README run.
- As a source of parts to study or vendor. flatMap.h is a header-only template and CompactString is small, and both are MIT-licensed. The README puts FlatMap at 1.9-2.6x std::unordered_map, but that is with 10-character random keys against std::hash and no reserve(); it was not compared with absl or boost flat maps.

**Skip it when:**
- You need anything beyond 13 string commands: lists, hashes, sets, MGET/MSET, SETNX/SETEX, Lua, pub/sub, MULTI, persistence, replication or clustering.
- Untrusted networks. It has no AUTH, ACL or TLS, binds 0.0.0.0 by default, and has no maximum request or bulk length: the per-connection read buffer keeps doubling while a declared bulk string is still incomplete.
- Multi-core throughput. A single thread does all I/O and command work, so at pipeline 1 it only matched Redis (about 125-135K ops/s in the README runs).
- A keyspace that keeps growing while you need exact answers. From reading flatMap.h: during each incremental doubling, a key whose home slot the migration cursor has passed, but which sits further along its probe run, is found in neither table. GET can miss it, DEL returns 0, and a SET issued meanwhile is later overwritten by the stale migrated value. The resize unit test finishes migrating before it reads back, so this path is untested.
- Production use in general. The project has 1 star and no releases or issues, all code commits fall between 2026-01-31 and 2026-02-22, and every Redis comparison is an unscripted first-party laptop run.

**Integration:** standalone server binary built from source with CMake (its components are internal static libs); flatMap.h can be copied out as a header-only template, while CompactString also needs compactString.cpp and slabAllocator.cpp · Asio 1.36.0 (header-only, pulled by CMake FetchContent at configure time, so the build needs git and network access) and vendored rapidhash; GoogleTest 1.15.2 and Google Benchmark 1.9.1 only with -DBUILD_EXTRAS=ON · C++20 and CMake 3.20+. The README claims GCC 12+ / Clang 15+ / MSVC 2022+, but the code includes <format> and calls std::format_to_n, and cppreference lists text formatting in libstdc++ only from GCC 13 (libc++ 17), so plan on GCC 13+. Release builds use -O3 -march=native -flto, so the binaries do not carry across CPUs. · Little-endian only (the CompactString SSO flag lives in byte 15). The README gives Linux and Windows/MSVC build steps; the only benchmarks are on x86-64 Linux. Prefetching uses __builtin_prefetch or _mm_prefetch, with a no-op fallback. macOS and aarch64 are not documented.

**Vs siblings:** For anything multi-core or feature-bearing, pick Pogocache, Dragonfly, KeyDB or Garnet. In its own suite Pogocache already doubled Redis GET throughput at pipeline 1 with 8 threads, where RapidKV only ties Redis, and Dragonfly, KeyDB and Garnet carry real Redis data types and persistence. RapidKV is the pick only for a small, readable single-threaded C++20 codebase to learn from or mine for its FlatMap and CompactString, or for a one-core cache serving deeply pipelined plain GET/SET.

**Gotchas:**
- Expiry checks read a cached steady_clock value that only the maintenance timer refreshes (every 100 ms by default, 200 ms in the sample config), so TTL resolution is that interval. The cached value starts at 0, so a key given a PX TTL before the first tick gets an absolute expiry near zero and expires at the first refresh.
- The README says the 7-bit hash tag 'avoids ~99% of false-positive key comparisons', but the tag is the hash's low 7 bits, which are also slot-index bits. Any entry that passes the PSL check therefore already has the same tag, and a full key compare always follows.
- The eviction the README calls SIEVE is really a CLOCK-style second-chance sweep in hash-slot order, with the visited bit set only by GET. It runs only after usage exceeds max_memory_usage, 10 keys per SET. If the limit is crossed mid-resize, every unvisited entry left in the old table is dropped as migration proceeds.
- Memory accounting counts the table arrays and slab slot sizes, but not unused slots in 1 MB slab pages (never returned to the OS) or the 64 KB read and write buffers of each connection, so RSS can exceed max_memory_usage. Separately, each connection has a hard 8 MB cap on unsent replies; exceeding it closes the socket without an error.

**Status:** The record calls it active because of the last push (2026-05-10), but that push only added the MIT license and deleted a CMakeSettings.json file; the code dates from a three-week burst ending 2026-02-22 (1 star, no releases, no issues), so treat it as a small, readable MIT reference whose FlatMap and CompactString can be copied out, not as a production cache without your own testing.

[repo](https://github.com/shashank2602/RapidKV) · [benchmark](https://github.com/shashank2602/RapidKV#benchmarks)

##### Ristretto  `Go`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Concurrent in-process Go cache with TinyLFU admission and cost-based eviction; ~3x a mutex-wrapped groupcache LRU's throughput in its own benchmarks.

**Beats:** The groupcache LRU (golang/groupcache/lru behind a sync.Mutex). The charts label it 'groupcache'; it is presumably the suite's 'base-mutex' entry. — Dgraph's own cachebench compared Ristretto with golang/groupcache/lru behind a sync.Mutex (plus BigCache, FreeCache, FastCache and goburrow). The 2020 README charts show ~3x the LRU's throughput at 16-64 goroutines on Mixed 25% writes/75% reads (~57M vs ~18M ops/s at 64) and ~3.3x on Zipfian read-only and write-only runs, while freecache wins Mixed at 4 goroutines and fastcache wins writes at 4-12. The only hardware named is an Intel Core i7-8700K with 16 GB, in the 2019 blog; the Go version, build flags and Ristretto version are not stated (cachebench has no go.mod), and the charts predate the September 2020 change that charges internal per-item cost by default.

**Known shortcoming:** The ~3x vs groupcache's LRU is read off blog charts (i7-8700K); a Go library whose win includes hit ratio from TinyLFU admission.

**Known shortcoming:** The 2020 charts predate PR #195 (internal cost on by default); its own cachebench still calls Set(k,v,1) without IgnoreInternalCost and the hit ratio collapses (#336: 1.05% vs ~50% on the README chart; #363 open). Lossy by design (sets dropped at the buffer or by TinyLFU; Get right after Set can miss without Wait()); weak on recency-heavy traces. A third-party otter bench shows ~32.8M vs otter's 195M reads/s, and its insert speed comes from dropping sets. One global policy mutex (#483); keys are not stored (hash + conflict hash only); go.mod needs Go 1.24 while the README says 1.21.

**How:** Values live in 256 RWMutex-sharded Go maps keyed by a 64-bit hash (runtime memhash via go:linkname for strings and []byte, the integer itself otherwise). Gets record accesses into striped, lossy sync.Pool ring buffers (BP-Wrapper-style batching), and those batches reach the policy through a non-blocking channel that drops them when full. New Sets go into a 32K-slot buffered channel drained by one goroutine and are dropped rather than block when it is full, so no caller waits on the policy lock. The policy is TinyLFU admission (a 4-row count-min sketch of 4-bit counters, a bloom-filter doorkeeper and periodic halving) paired with SampledLFU eviction (sample 5 resident keys, evict the lowest estimated frequency); the README FAQ credits the throughput to batching and eventual consistency.

**Use it when:**
- A Go service where many goroutines hit a skewed (Zipf-like) key set and a single mutex around an LRU (groupcache/lru, hashicorp/golang-lru) is the bottleneck: the project's charts show that baseline flat at about 16-20M ops/s while Ristretto reaches about 55-65M at 16-64 goroutines.
- Byte-budgeted caches with variable-size values: Set takes a per-item cost, one large valuable item can evict several small ones, and a Cost func can compute cost lazily only for sets that are not dropped.
- Frequency-biased workloads (search, database page caches, analytics), where TinyLFU admission keeps one-hit wonders out; the README Search (ARC-S3) chart shows 48% vs 23% for the LRU at 500k capacity.
- Cache-aside use where losing an occasional insert is acceptable, because hot items are Set repeatedly and eventually get admitted.
- You want per-item TTL, eviction/rejection callbacks for manual memory management, and a small per-entry footprint (keys are not stored, only hashes).

**Skip it when:**
- You need every Set to land, or read-your-writes: new items can be dropped at the set buffer or rejected by TinyLFU, and a Get straight after Set can miss unless you call Wait().
- Recency-biased or loop/LRU-friendly workloads: the 2019 blog says Ristretto 'suffers' on the CODASYL (ARC-OLTP) trace because LFU fits it badly, and otter's hit-ratio page says it may struggle on recency-biased workloads.
- You size the cache by item count (cost=1) and leave IgnoreInternalCost false: every item is also charged unsafe.Sizeof(storeItem[V]), so the cache holds far fewer items than MaxCost. A user running the project's own ARC-S3 bench at MaxCost 500000 got a 1.05% hit ratio vs ~50% on the README chart (issue #336), and issue #363 reports near-zero hit ratios in third-party benchmarks.
- You need the highest read throughput among Go caches: in otter's third-party benchmark (Apple M1, 8 goroutines, cost configuration corrected) Ristretto did about 32.8M ops/s on 100% reads vs otter's 195M, and fell behind ccache on the 75%-read and 75%-write mixes.
- You need to list keys, exact key equality or a networked/distributed cache: only a 64-bit hash plus a 64-bit xxhash conflict hash is stored, iteration gives values only, and the library is single-process.

**Integration:** module · cespare/xxhash/v2, dgryski/go-farm, dustin/go-humanize, golang.org/x/sys (testify for tests); optional jemalloc via cgo behind the 'jemalloc' build tag, used only by the z package · go.mod declares go 1.24.0 (toolchain go1.25.0); the README still says Go 1.21+ · Any Go target in principle: pure Go plus go:linkname into runtime internals (memhash, fastrand, nanotime). The z package has per-OS mmap files (linux, darwin, windows, plan9, js, wasip1) and amd64 assembly with a generic fallback, and recent releases fixed 32-bit, s390x and riscv64 builds. CI runs only on ubuntu-latest.

**Vs siblings:** Otter's own benchmarks put it well ahead of Ristretto on read throughput and on hit ratio for recency-biased traces (W-TinyLFU), so otter is the better general-purpose Go default. Pick Ristretto for a byte-cost budget with minimal per-entry memory, or for insert-heavy traffic where dropped sets are acceptable (otter measured Ristretto at 15-22M inserts/s vs its own 2.4-3.3M and attributes the gap to dropped inserts); over go-sieve or golang-fifo, which are count-bounded SIEVE/FIFO caches, it adds cost-weighted eviction, TTL and eviction callbacks.

**Gotchas:**
- MaxCost includes internal per-item overhead unless IgnoreInternalCost is true. This default arrived in PR #195 (Sep 2020), after the README charts were made; the project's own cachebench adapter still calls Set(key, v, 1) without that flag.
- Set returning true does not mean the item was admitted: TinyLFU can still reject it later. Updates to existing keys are applied immediately, but new keys only appear after the background goroutine processes them.
- Each cache starts background goroutines and a TTL ticker, so always call Close. Del does a blocking send into the set buffer, so under heavy load it can wait for the drainer. Expired entries are swept in 5 s buckets by default but are also filtered out on Get.
- Collision handling depends on key type: integer keys are their own hash with no conflict check, string/[]byte keys add an xxhash conflict hash, and a custom KeyToHash that returns 0 as the second value disables the check. The memhash seed changes per process, so hashes are not persistent.

**Status:** Actively maintained (v2.4.2 on 2026-07-07, last commit 2026-09-21) and an Apache-2.0 `go get` module, though third-party reports of low hit ratio (#363) and policy-lock contention (#483, with fix PR #489 still open) remain unresolved.

[repo](https://github.com/dgraph-io/ristretto) · [benchmark](https://github.com/dgraph-io/ristretto#benchmarks)

##### Valkey  `C`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

BSD-licensed fork of Redis OSS 7.2 whose async I/O threads give ~37% more SET throughput than Redis 8.0.

**Beats:** Redis — Momento, a vendor that sells Valkey-based services, ran the official Docker images valkey/valkey:8.1.1 and redis:8.0 (build flags not stated) on the same AWS Graviton4 c8g.2xlarge, both with io-threads 6, persistence off and 6 pinned cores, driven by valkey-benchmark with 1 KB values, a 3M-key keyspace, no pipelining and per-server tuned connection counts. Valkey reached 999.8K vs 729.4K SET RPS (~1.37x) at 0.8 vs 0.99 ms p99, and the post states +16% on GET; because Redis 8.0 has its own new I/O-threading implementation, this compares two threaded servers.

**Known shortcoming:** The 37%/16% SET/GET gains vs Redis 8.0 come from a Momento blog; Momento sells hosted Valkey, so the source is not independent.

**Known shortcoming:** No gain on small machines: parity without io-threads (239K vs 235K) and tied up to 4 threads. At 256 connections Redis 8.0 p99 (0.84 ms) beats Valkey (0.93 ms); p99 doubles at 1024 connections. Too many io-threads can be slower (#4114); CPU shows ~100% from busy polling (#4001). Cannot load Redis 7.4+/8 RDB files; Redis 8 built-in modules absent; several high-severity use-after-free advisories in 2026.

**How:** Valkey 8.0's async I/O threading (an AWS contribution) keeps all command execution on the single main thread but hands socket reads and RESP parsing, reply writes, epoll_wait and object frees to worker threads as jobs, scaling the number of active I/O threads with load (current unstable passes jobs over lock-free SPMC/MPSC/SPSC ring queues). Before running each batch of parsed commands, the main thread interleaves and prefetches the hash-table lookups for every key in the batch ("memory access amortization", memory_prefetch.c), so cache misses overlap instead of stalling one after another. AWS reports this cut lookupKey time by more than 80% and added almost 50% throughput. Valkey 8.1 also replaced the chained dict with a hash table of 64-byte, cache-line buckets (7 slots plus 1-byte secondary hashes, inspired by Swiss tables), which cuts a lookup to about two memory accesses and saves about 20 bytes per key.

**Use it when:**
- You run Redis OSS 7.2 or older on a box with 6-8+ cores and one instance is saturating its main thread on simple GET/SET. Turning on io-threads can take one node from roughly 240K to about 1M RPS (1 KB values) without sharding or pipelining.
- Many concurrent connections (hundreds) with small or medium values (512 B-1 KB), where the network syscalls and parsing, not command logic, eat the CPU.
- Memory-bound caches holding many small keys: the 8.1 hash table saves about 20 B per key (about 30 B per key with a TTL) over the old dict.
- You need a permissively licensed (BSD-3-Clause) Redis-compatible server rather than Redis 8's RSALv2/SSPLv1/AGPLv3 choice.
- Workloads that do not shard well, such as hot keys, large collections or same-slot multi-key operations, where a bigger, faster single shard helps.

**Skip it when:**
- Small boxes (3-4 cores or fewer) or io-threads left at 1. Momento measured parity without I/O threads (239K vs 235K SET RPS), and the two were neck-and-neck until the 4th thread.
- You depend on Redis CE 7.4+ or Redis 8.x. Their RDB files cannot be loaded by Valkey, and Redis 8's built-in Query Engine, JSON, time series, probabilistic types and vector sets are not part of the Valkey core server.
- You need well beyond ~1M simple ops/s on one node. Command execution is still single-threaded, and designs that execute commands on multiple threads report higher per-node numbers.
- Tail latency matters and connection counts are untuned. Going from 400 to 1024 connections doubled Valkey's p99 from 0.8 ms to 1.6 ms. At 256 connections with 6 threads, Redis 8.0's p99 (0.84 ms) was actually lower than Valkey's (0.93 ms).
- Over-provisioning io-threads: open issue #4114 (2026-07) shows io-threads 8 running slower than io-threads 4 on a 32-core host, because idle I/O threads burn cycles in their polling loop.

**Integration:** server binary built with make (CMake build is marked experimental); official valkey/valkey Docker images · Vendored in deps/: jemalloc (default allocator on Linux), Lua, libvalkey, linenoise, hdr_histogram, fpconv, lz4, fast_float. Optional: OpenSSL (TLS), librdmacm/libibverbs (experimental RDMA), libsystemd, static Zstandard >= 1.4.7, libbacktrace. · C compiler with gnu11 (C11 _Atomic). The Makefile probes for it and falls back to -std=c99. Default -O3. · Linux, macOS, OpenBSD, NetBSD, FreeBSD; big- and little-endian; 32- and 64-bit; Solaris best effort. The hash table has x86 SIMD and ARM NEON paths; the TSC/CNTVCT hardware clock is used on x86-64 Linux and aarch64. RDMA is Linux-only and experimental.

**Vs siblings:** Pick Valkey over Dragonfly, Garnet or Pogocache when you want the actual Redis OSS codebase (same RDB/AOF files, config and module API), so migration is effectively an upgrade, and ~1M RPS per 8-vCPU node is enough. Garnet's paper uses Valkey 8.1 as the baseline it beats, and Pogocache reports ~2x Redis 8.2.1 GET throughput, so those win when raw per-node throughput matters more than byte-level Redis compatibility.

**Gotchas:**
- io-threads is off by default and must be set explicitly. The count includes the main thread (io-threads 9 = main thread + 8 I/O threads). valkey-benchmark also needs --threads, or it cannot show the gain.
- With I/O threads on, the main and I/O threads busy-poll, so OS CPU usage reads near 100% even when the server is lightly loaded (issue #4001; noted in the 9.1 release post). Plan capacity with the main/I/O thread usage metrics added in 9.1.
- INFO reports redis_version:7.2.4 for compatibility. Tools must read server_name/valkey_version to detect Valkey and its real version.
- It shares Redis's Lua attack surface (CVE-2025-49844, a Lua use-after-free that can lead to RCE). 2026 brought several high-severity use-after-free advisories (TLS, stream deserialization, RDMA, the Lua debugger), plus an io-threads + TLS assertion crash (#4347, fixed), so stay on current patch releases (9.1.2 / 9.0.6 / 8.1.10, 2026-09-01).

**Status:** Very active BSD-3-Clause server under LF Projects (commits on 2026-09-26, 9.2.0-rc1 on 2026-09-16, patch releases still shipping for the 8.0, 8.1, 9.0 and 9.1 lines, 27.3k stars) that you deploy, not a library you vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/valkey-io/valkey) · [benchmark](https://www.gomomento.com/blog/valkey-turns-one-how-the-community-fork-left-redis-in-the-dust/)

##### Vettel  `C`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

A ~300-line C CLI key-value store on one flat text file; its README times it slightly faster than redis-cli.

**Beats:** Redis — A Python script ran os.system 1000 times. Each call started a shell, which ran either `vt -c "set k v"` (an unoptimized clang build appending to ~/.store.vt) or `redis-cli set k "v"` (default host, so a local Redis server; the Redis version, build and persistence settings are unstated). A single run, timed with fish's `time` on a MacBook Pro 13-inch Mid 2012 (2.5 GHz dual-core Core i5, 16 GB DDR3, macOS 10.15.7), took 10.72 s vs 13.26 s: about 10.7 ms vs 13.3 ms per key, or 1.24x (derived). This measures process-spawn plus IPC overhead, not the throughput of either store.

**Known shortcoming:** Built at -O0 (no -O flag in make.sh), and the benchmark spawns a process per key (vt -c vs redis-cli), measuring process startup rather than store speed; 2012 MacBook Pro; abandoned.

**Known shortcoming:** No speed technique: set/get are an O(n) linear scan of a flat file, and the 'win' is a process spawn plus file append vs a redis-cli TCP round trip. CLI only (no server, RESP, TTL or eviction; the old TCP server was removed); not a cache. Bugs: delete prefix-matches (del user also removes user1), exit code always 0, fclose(NULL) on first run (UB), overlapping sprintf (UB); no locking or fsync and delete truncates then rewrites (a crash can wipe the store). macOS/MacPorts-only build at -O0; abandoned since 2023-02.

**How:** It has no speed technique. `set` scans the whole store file line by line to reject a duplicate key and then appends one line with fopen("a"); `get` is the same O(n) scan. It 'wins' only because each benchmarked call is a short-lived process doing a local file append, while redis-cli also pays a TCP connect and a request/response round trip to a Redis server, and process creation dominates both timings (5.10 s vs 6.27 s sys time). The one comment on the Feb 2023 Show HN post made the same O(n) point and expected Redis to win by a wide margin with more data.

**Use it when:**
- Reading ~300 lines of C to learn how a naive flat-file key-value CLI works (parsing, append-only writes, rewrite-on-delete)
- A personal shell scratchpad of at most a few hundred string keys on a single-user macOS machine, where losing data is acceptable
- A teaching example of benchmark pitfalls: timing process spawn plus a local file append against a client/server network round trip

**Skip it when:**
- As a Redis replacement or as a cache: there is no server, no network protocol, no data types, no TTL, no eviction and no memory bound
- Any store past a few hundred keys: every set and get is a full linear scan of the file, and delete rewrites the whole file
- Concurrent writers: there is no file locking, so check-then-append can create duplicate keys, and a delete's read-truncate-rewrite can drop a concurrent append
- Anything that needs durability: there is no fsync, and delete opens the store with mode "w" (truncating it) before writing it back, so a crash mid-delete can empty the store
- Production or security-sensitive use: the C has undefined behavior (see gotchas), was built at -O0, and has no tests, CI, releases or issue tracker activity

**Integration:** source-drop (one main.c that builds a CLI executable, out/vt; a prebuilt out/vt binary is committed; there is no library API) · libedit (editline/readline.h, -ledit). make.sh hard-codes MacPorts paths under /opt/local. · Not documented. make.sh uses clang with -Wall -Wextra -pedantic, no -std and no -O flag. The code needs POSIX getline, BSD/GNU vasprintf and the non-standard `uint` type. · Only macOS (MacPorts) has a build script, and the author's benchmark machine is a 2012 Intel MacBook Pro. Linux and Windows are not documented; glibc would likely need _GNU_SOURCE for vasprintf.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only when you want a tiny, readable toy. For an embedded, serverless local store that really beats Redis on local get latency, use python-diskcache. For a faster Redis-protocol server, use Valkey, Pogocache or Dragonfly.

**Gotchas:**
- delete matches by prefix: delete_key uses strncmp with strlen(key), so `del user` also removes `user1`, `username` and so on (get uses an exact comparison)
- set is insert-only and errors with 'a record with key ... already exists', so an update means delete then set. Every command exits with status 0, even on errors and misses, so scripts must parse stdout.
- Parsing is fragile: keys containing ':' break the key:value format, values are split on spaces and rejoined with single spaces, and the code relies on overlapping sprintf plus an uninitialized malloc buffer in delete (undefined behavior)
- get_store_path calls fclose() on a NULL FILE* when the store file does not exist yet. That is undefined behavior and likely crashes the first run, after which the empty file exists.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2023-02-12 after 12 commits, with no releases, no issues and one fork that has no later pushes; the code is MIT-licensed and readable in minutes but not usable as a real store.

[repo](https://github.com/japrozs/vettel) · [benchmark](https://github.com/japrozs/vettel/blob/master/README.md)

##### warp_cache  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust/PyO3 memoization decorator for Python with SIEVE eviction, TTL, async and mmap cross-process backend; ~25x cachetools, slower than lru_cache.

**Beats:** cachetools (Python LRU/TTL cache library) — These are first-party numbers from the repo's runner. The workload is 100K calls of an identity function over Zipf keys (2000 unique, ~71% hit rate at 256 entries), median of 3, on CPython 3.13.2 (Clang 20.1.0) on an unspecified Apple M-series Mac with cachetools 7.0.1. warp_cache did 20.4M calls/s against cachetools.func.lru_cache's 826K (~24.7x; 19.1-27.0x across 32-1024 entries), while stdlib functools.lru_cache did 31.0M. With 16 GIL-bound threads warp_cache did 19.5M, against 795K for cachetools with an added threading.Lock and 11.9M for lru_cache plus a Lock. cachetools.func already locks internally with a Condition, and lru_cache is documented thread-safe, so both threaded baselines pay for a lock they do not need. Plain lru_cache under threads was not measured.

**Known shortcoming:** The ~24.5x at 16 threads is vs cachetools with a Lock; single-threaded, the stdlib lru_cache is 1.5x faster.

**Known shortcoming:** The baselines are artificially slow: lru_cache is already thread-safe (the '+Lock' adds an unneeded lock) and cachetools.func.lru_cache already locks, so 'cachetools+Lock' is double-locked; single-threaded, lru_cache is 1.3-1.8x faster. SECURITY: PyPI 0.7.0 (2026-04) predates June fixes for UB (#30), out-of-bounds (#31), a race (#37) and world-readable pickled shared memory (#39).

**Known shortcoming:** No free-threaded (cp313t) wheels and throughput falls from 15.1M at 1 thread to 3-4M at 8-32 threads without the GIL. Open bugs: methods do not bind (#52), the shm spinlock wedges if its holder dies (#38), max_size=0 caches one item (#47), a bad TTL can panic (#86). The shm name persists across restarts (stale results after redeploy); shards make max_size approximate; eviction is linear. First-party only on an unnamed M-series chip with ~5 ms runs.

**How:** The whole hit path runs inside one PyO3 `tp_call`. It hashes the args tuple with `PyObject_Hash` and picks a shard with `hash & mask`. It probes a hashbrown table through a passthrough hasher that reuses Python's hash, using a borrowed-key `Equivalent` lookup so a hit allocates no key. It compares keys with `PyObject_RichCompareBool` and returns the value. On GIL builds the per-shard lock is `GilCell`, an `UnsafeCell` wrapper that does no locking because the GIL already serializes access; free-threaded builds compile in a parking_lot `RwLock` per shard instead. SIEVE eviction (NSDI'24) reduces a hit to one relaxed atomic store of a visited bit, with no LRU list relinking. The release build uses fat LTO and codegen-units=1. Most of the gap to cachetools is simply native code against a pure-Python wrapper plus a Condition lock.

**Use it when:**
- Hot memoized functions called from thread pools or web-server threads on standard GIL CPython when you also want TTL or async in the same decorator. The author measured ~20M calls/s at 256 entries, against 0.8M for cachetools.func.lru_cache.
- Replacing cachetools.func.lru_cache or ttl_cache decorators on hot paths. The author measured 19-27x more calls/s at 32-1024 entries, and 12-14x more than cachetools ttl_cache in the TTL loop (7.2-7.4M vs 0.52-0.60M).
- Async functions. A cache hit returns without awaiting the coroutine, and concurrent misses on the same key are coalesced within each event loop.
- Gunicorn or Celery workers on Linux or macOS that should share small results through mmap: keys up to 512 B and values up to 4 KB by default, primitives preferred. The author measured 5.0M ops/s in one process and 8.1M total with 4 processes.
- Skewed or scan-heavy key streams where hit ratio matters more than call overhead. The author's Zipf tests show SIEVE with 15-22% fewer misses than LRU at the same size.

**Skip it when:**
- Plain memoization where you would otherwise use functools.lru_cache. The stdlib C cache is 1.3-1.8x faster single-threaded (31.0M vs 20.4M ops/s at 256 entries), and the CPython docs say it is already thread-safe (coherent under concurrent updates), so the repo's 'lru_cache + Lock' comparison adds a lock you do not need.
- Free-threaded CPython. PyPI 0.7.0 ships no cp313t or cp314t wheels. The only published no-GIL results are from February 2026, before the current sharded store, and show total throughput falling from 15.1M ops/s at 1 thread to 3.0-4.2M at 8-32 threads. There is no newer data.
- Code that needs features warp_cache lacks. Instance methods do not bind (open issue #52). There is no unbounded mode (max_size must be an int), no `typed=` flag, no custom key function, no dict-like cache object, no per-entry TTL, no stampede protection on sync calls, and no size-in-bytes eviction (#15 open). cachetools, cachebox or moka-py cover these.
- Shared backend where a process can be SIGKILLed or OOM-killed mid-write. The cross-process TTAS spinlock has no owner-death recovery (#38 open), so every process hangs until the shm file is deleted. The shared backend is also unavailable on Windows and unsafe across trust boundaries, because complex types round-trip through pickle (#46, #50 open).
- Production code that needs a stable release. The project has 9 stars and a Beta classifier, and the June 2026 memory-safety and concurrency fixes (#30, #31, #37, #39, #40) are on master but not in any PyPI release.

**Integration:** module · No Python runtime dependencies. Rust crates: pyo3 0.29, parking_lot 0.12 and hashbrown 0.15, plus memmap2, libc and ahash on non-Windows. Source builds need a Rust toolchain and maturin. · CPython 3.10+ on master (PyPI 0.7.0 declares >=3.9); Rust edition 2021, minimum rustc not documented · PyPI 0.7.0 wheels: manylinux2014 x86_64/aarch64, macOS x86_64/arm64 and Windows x86_64 for CPython 3.9-3.14. No musllinux and no free-threaded wheels. The shared backend is POSIX-only and raises RuntimeError on Windows.

**Vs siblings:** python-diskcache is the only other Python sibling. Pick warp_cache for in-memory memoization where per-call overhead matters, or for small primitive results shared among local workers through mmap. Pick diskcache for large or persistent values, bytes-bounded eviction, or when a crashed worker must not wedge the cache. The SIEVE and quick-cache entries are the underlying algorithm and a native Rust cache; warp_cache matters only when the caller is Python.

**Gotchas:**
- The latest PyPI release, 0.7.0 (2026-04-13), predates the June 2026 fixes. Those include unsound GilCell aliasing under reentrant `__eq__` (#30, critical), an out-of-bounds slab write with shared max_size=0 (#31), a data race on the lock-free read path (#37), and world-readable shm files holding pickled data (#39). Pin to master if you need them.
- Shared-backend files are named from the function's `__module__` and `__qualname__` and persist across restarts. On reopen they are reused whenever version, capacity, key/value size limits and TTL match. A redeploy with changed function logic can therefore serve stale results, and closures that share a qualname share one cache. Keys or values over the size limits are silently not cached; watch `oversize_skips`.
- max_size is split across up to 16 shards, each running its own SIEVE with ceil(max_size/shards) slots. Capacity is therefore approximate (max_size=100 gives 16x7=112 slots) and eviction is per shard. Also, eviction removes from a VecDeque at the hand position, which from reading the code is linear in shard size, not the O(1) the docs claim. max_size=0 still caches one entry on the memory backend (#47).
- Keys follow Python equality with no `typed` option, so f(1), f(1.0) and f(True) share one entry. Keyword arguments are sorted, so f(a=1, b=2) and f(b=2, a=1) hit the same entry, unlike lru_cache. Expired TTL entries are only dropped lazily and keep their values alive until they are evicted or overwritten. Negative or NaN TTL can panic on the memory backend (#86 open).

**Status:** Actively maintained (last master commit 2026-06-18, a batch of memory-safety and concurrency fixes), MIT-licensed and pip-installable from prebuilt wheels. The newest PyPI release (0.7.0, April 2026) lacks those fixes, and the project is small (9 stars, Beta).

[repo](https://github.com/toloco/warp_cache) · [benchmark](https://github.com/toloco/warp_cache/blob/master/README.md)

##### Yac (PHP shared-memory object cache)  `C`  `PHP-3.01`  `active`  `Tier C`

PHP extension: lock-free shared-memory key/value cache for FPM workers on one host, replacing local Memcached/APCu without a network hop.

**Beats:** Memcached — On the author's WordPress site (laruence.com; an 8-core/31 GB server running PHP 8.1 FPM behind Nginx; CPU model and compiler flags not stated), swapping the Memcached object-cache drop-in (memcached on localhost:11211) for the Yac drop-in raised full-homepage throughput from about 118.5 to about 141.5 RPS (+18.6% to +20.1%). It also cut p50 latency by about 16-17% at 20, 50 and 100 concurrent ab clients, with both setups capped by PHP rendering and MySQL; a fixed 10,000-request run gave +17.6%. Yac's own microbenchmark (16 forked workers, 100:1 read:write, Apple M5 Pro, PHP 8.5) reports 170-727x more aggregate ops/s than per-worker TCP connections to a local memcached 1.6.45, which mostly measures the removed loopback round trip rather than cache mechanics.

**Known shortcoming:** Per-host only (no cross-node sharing/invalidation) and shared only with forked children of the creating process (#124); CLI off by default. Writes are lossy under contention (set() returns false on a lost CAS) and the WordPress drop-in's incr/decr is non-atomic; 48 B key cap, and the drop-in hashes long keys to crc32b without a read-back check (silent collision risk). flush() wipes the whole host segment; capacity is fixed at startup with a 4-slot probe; a 2026 storage rewrite, with 2.4.2 fixing a get() crash and a flush race. The 170-727x microbenchmark mostly reflects removing the loopback round trip.

**How:** It removes the network: a get() is a MurmurHash64A lookup into a fixed power-of-two slot table in already-mapped memory. It probes at most 4 slots (home slot plus an odd stride) and copies the value out, with no socket, loopback TCP round trip or protocol encoding. Concurrency is lock-free. Each slot has a seqlock-style version counter: readers snapshot it and retry, and writers claim it with a CAS, giving up after 30 spins. Values sit in ring segments handed out by a CAS bump pointer. On every read a full CRC-32C check (SSE4.2 or ARMv8 hardware, detected at runtime) turns recycled or torn blocks into misses instead of taking a lock. Small scalars and strings up to 7 bytes are embedded in the slot's pointer word, and values that fit beside the key in the 48-byte key area are stored inline, so neither needs a value block. Values over 4K are LZ4-compressed by default.

**Use it when:**
- A single PHP-FPM host, or a few independent ones, where Memcached or Redis on localhost serves only as a same-machine cache: the WordPress object cache, config, routing tables, rendered fragments.
- Requests that do dozens to hundreds of cache gets each, where localhost TCP round trips per get add up. This is the WordPress case: about 19% more RPS even though the ceiling is set by PHP and MySQL.
- Read-heavy access (the project's own benchmark uses 100:1 read:write) with many small values. Ints, bools, null and strings of 7 bytes or less live in the slot and skip value allocation entirely.
- You would rather not run, secure and monitor a cache daemon, and losing the cache on every php-fpm restart is acceptable.
- PHP 7.0-8.5 on Linux x86-64/ARM64 or Windows (both covered by CI), in NTS or ZTS builds.

**Skip it when:**
- Several web nodes that must see each other's writes or invalidations. Each host's segment is private, so a delete or flush on one node never reaches the others.
- Sharing between unrelated processes such as cron jobs, standalone CLI scripts or a second FPM master. Only the process that created the segment and its forked children can attach to it (issue #124), and CLI is disabled by default.
- Write-heavy or hot-key write workloads. set() returns false when it loses the slot CAS race, and the README says to avoid several processes setting the same key at once. The WordPress drop-in's incr/decr is a non-atomic get-then-set, so counters lose updates under concurrency.
- Keys over 48 bytes (PSR-16 requires 64, issue #83), values over 64 MB raw or 1 MB after compression, or incompressible values above the compression threshold, where set() fails if LZ4 would make them bigger.
- Risk-averse production that needs a long-settled engine. The storage layer was largely rewritten in Aug-Sep 2026 (2.4.0-2.4.2): 2.4.2 fixed a get() crash under concurrency and a flush() race that could leave a slot permanently unusable. In 2021 (issue #122) the author said the older partial-CRC Yac 'has a certain probability of error'.

**Integration:** shared lib (PHP extension yac.so/.dll, installed via PECL, PIE or phpize; the WordPress path adds the wp-yac-cache plugin, which deploys wp-content/object-cache.php) · none required (LZ4 is bundled, or a system LZ4 via --with-system-lz4); optional msgpack, igbinary or json serializers. The WordPress plugin needs PHP 7.2+ and WordPress 5.6+. · PHP 7.0+ (package.xml; CI builds 7.0 through 8.5). A C compiler with the GCC/Clang __atomic/__sync builtins, or MSVC; configure fails otherwise. Needs mmap(MAP_ANON) or SysV shm. · Linux x86-64 and ARM64 (CI, including a 30-second 16-worker concurrency hammer on both), Windows x64 and x86 (named file mapping), macOS (the author's benchmark machine, not in CI). Hardware CRC-32C is used when SSE4.2 or ARMv8 CRC is detected at runtime, with a slicing-by-8 software fallback otherwise.

**Vs siblings:** Pick Yac when the application is PHP-FPM. It is the only catalogued Memcached-beater whose cache lives in memory shared across forked PHP workers; CacheLib (in-process C++) and python-diskcache (in-process Python) are the equivalents for other runtimes. Stay with a networked cache such as Memcached, Pogocache or Dragonfly when more than one host has to share entries or invalidations.

**Gotchas:**
- Yac::flush() (and so wp_cache_flush()) invalidates the entire shared segment on the host, across every prefix and every app attached to the same PHP master. delete() only writes a tombstone, and memory comes back only when the value ring wraps around.
- Without a default argument, get() returns false for both a miss and a stored false; pass a sentinel default (2.4.0+) to tell them apart. Since 2.4.0, multi-get omits missing keys instead of returning false placeholders, so code that reads $result[$key] directly can raise warnings. The WordPress drop-in writes a stored false as 0.
- In the WordPress drop-in, keys over the 48-byte budget have their key part replaced by a 32-bit crc32b hash and are not re-checked on read. Two long keys in the same group can therefore collide and silently return each other's value. A birthday estimate (derived, not documented) is about a 1% chance with ~10K live long keys in one group. Do not set yac.serializer=json for WordPress either: objects come back as arrays and cause fatal errors.
- Capacity is fixed at startup. keys_memory_size sets the slot count (8M is about 64K slots), and each key can only occupy its 4 probe slots, so live entries can be kicked long before the table fills. A value bigger than one 4M+ segment fails (the 'fails' counter goes up). Size both pools from info() hit, kick and recycle counters.

**Status:** Actively maintained by the original author: 2.4.2 stable released 2026-09-10, 2.5.0-dev on master, commits through 2026-09-24. Core is PHP-3.01 licensed (GitHub shows NOASSERTION) and the WordPress plugin is GPLv2-or-later. Install from PECL or PIE rather than vendoring, and expect fast-moving internals after the 2026 storage rewrite.

[repo](https://github.com/laruence/yac) · [benchmark](https://github.com/laruence/wp-yac-cache/blob/master/README.md)

#### columnar-analytics

##### Apache Doris  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

MPP SQL analytics database (Java FE, C++ vectorized BE); vendor sf1000 runs show 5-11x faster than ClickHouse on join-heavy benchmarks.

**Beats:** ClickHouse — On the vendor's own page at sf1000, Doris's total run times were 11.6 s vs ClickHouse 82.2 s on SSB (13 queries, joined schema), 53.8 s vs 279.0 s on TPC-H and 173.8 s vs 1913.9 s on TPC-DS (about 7.1x, 5.2x and 11.0x), with no hardware, cluster size, versions, compiler or tuning disclosed. The agent-observability numbers come from VeloDB's own AgentLogsBench on an AWS m6i.8xlarge with 100M rows (Doris 2.3/4.3/2.5 s vs ClickHouse 42.1/42.3/24.3 s; the DuckDB gaps come from DuckDB's JSON handling collapsing on specific queries), while on independent single-table ClickBench, ClickHouse is about 1.7-2.3x faster by geomean.

**Known shortcoming:** Vendor benchmarks: the DuckDB multiples (3,136x/7,118x) are derived from the vendor's own AgentLogsBench, and no hardware is given for the SSB/TPC runs.

**Known shortcoming:** Wins appear only on the vendor's side (sf1000 page with no hardware/config; report 'coming soon'). On date-matched untuned ClickBench (2026-05-10) ClickHouse is faster: c6a.4xlarge hot 33.0 s vs 48.4 s, Doris wins 5 of 43 queries. Its edge likely comes from the Nereids optimizer, runtime filters and colocated joins rather than raw scan speed.

**Known shortcoming:** SECURITY: 2026 CVEs include an unauthenticated FE admin API before 3.1.0, a privilege bypass fixed in 4.0.8/4.1.4, a meta-service auth bypass and a JDBC RCE; stay on patched versions. A server, not a library (Java 17 FE + C++20 BE, ~90 third-party dependencies, AVX2 by default); open crash/leak bugs #67619 and #67898.

**How:** The backend is a vectorized columnar engine using SIMD (SSE4.2 always, AVX2 by default, NEON on ARM); its column, PODArray and aggregation hash-table code is copied from ClickHouse and modified, and join hash tables are bucket-chained first/next uint32 arrays over the build-side block. Queries run on a pipeline engine modelled on HyPer's morsel-driven paper, which splits plans into PipelineTasks on a thread pool and uses local shuffle against skew. Most of the margin over ClickHouse on multi-join benchmarks likely comes from the Cascades-based cost optimizer (Nereids, rules plus statistics-driven CBO), runtime join filters (IN, Bloom, Min-Max, IN_OR_BLOOM) pushed into scans, and colocated/bucketed joins. Storage adds sorted compound-key prefix, min/max zone-map, Bloom and inverted indexes.

**Use it when:**
- Star/snowflake schemas and TPC-DS-style ad-hoc SQL with many large joins, where ClickHouse would need denormalized flat tables or hand-ordered joins.
- Customer-facing dashboards that need many concurrent sub-second queries over data that is ingested continuously and upserted (Unique-key tables).
- Log, trace and agent-observability data that mixes full-text search, dynamic-JSON filters and aggregations in one SQL engine, as an alternative to Elasticsearch/OpenSearch plus a separate OLAP store.
- Speeding up SQL over existing Iceberg/Hudi/Delta/Paimon lakehouse tables without copying the data.
- Teams whose BI and tooling already speak the MySQL protocol.

**Skip it when:**
- Single wide-table scan/filter/aggregate workloads (ClickBench shape). In the date-matched ClickBench results (both 2026-05-10, both untuned), ClickHouse was faster: on c6a.4xlarge the hot-run sum was 33.0 s vs Doris 48.4 s, with Doris winning only 5 of 43 queries; on c6a.metal it was 8.25 s vs 11.0 s. Doris's stored data was also larger (13.8 GB vs 9.4 GB).
- Embedded or in-process analytics. Doris needs a JVM frontend (JDK 17 for 3.0+) and C++ backend servers. The documented production minimum is 16 cores and 64 GB per node, with 3+ backends recommended; for embedded use pick DuckDB or chDB.
- OLTP or row-at-a-time transactional workloads. Doris is an analytical MPP store.
- Decisions that need independently reproducible numbers. The SQL-benchmark report is marked 'Coming Soon', and the page gives no hardware, cluster size, versions or configuration.

**Integration:** Standalone server, not a library: FE (Java) plus doris_be (C++) binaries, shipped as release tarballs, Docker images or a Kubernetes operator. There is no embeddable C++ API. · FE needs a JDK: Java 17 for Doris 3.0+, Java 8 for 2.1 and earlier. A BE source build pulls about 90 bundled third-party packages (thirdparty/vars.sh lists Arrow, brpc, Thrift, Protobuf, RocksDB, jemalloc, simdjson, Hyperscan, parallel-hashmap, the AWS/Azure/GCS SDKs and more). BE Java extensions (JDBC/Hudi scanners, Java UDFs) are on by default and can be turned off with DISABLE_BE_JAVA_EXTENSIONS=ON. · BE: C++20, GCC 11.1+ or Clang 16+ (both enforced in be/CMakeLists.txt). FE: JDK 17 and Maven. · Linux x86-64 needs AVX2 by default; a no-AVX2 package or a USE_AVX2=0 build is available. Linux aarch64 builds with -march=armv8-a+crc by default. Documented file systems are ext4 and xfs. CMake also has macOS build paths, but macOS is not documented as a production platform.

**Vs siblings:** StarRocks (started as a fork of Doris) is the closest sibling and also claims to beat ClickHouse, though on SSB-flat with a smaller 1.87x margin; pick Doris for ASF governance and its built-in inverted-index, VARIANT and lakehouse-catalog feature set, and benchmark both on your own joins. Pick it over Umbra (no public repo) or Velox (an execution library for building engines) when you want a ready-made distributed open-source database rather than a component.

**Gotchas:**
- The repo's TPC-H sf1000 DDL puts lineitem and orders in a colocate group on orderkey (768 buckets) and part and partsupp in one on partkey, with replication_num=1. Join speed depends on this kind of physical design. The benchmark page does not say whether its runs used these scripts or this layout.
- Security fixes have come in quickly in 2026. FE REST admin APIs were reachable without authentication before 3.1.0 (CVE-2026-58319). Privilege-check bypasses were fixed only in 4.0.8/4.1.4 (CVE-2026-68570, CVE-2026-72524). There is also an FE meta-service authentication bypass (CVE-2026-31377) and a JDBC-driver-URL RCE (CVE-2026-96443). Keep the FE off untrusted networks and stay on the latest patch line.
- Operational stability issues are open, e.g. #67619 (BE SIGSEGV during merge-on-write bulk load on 4.0.8) and #67898 (scanner-thread leak on every external-catalog query). Queries under memory pressure are cancelled with MEM_LIMIT_EXCEEDED or workload-group overcommit errors, so size memory and workload groups deliberately.
- The README warns that some third-party licenses are not compatible with Apache-2.0, so some features have to be disabled for a strictly Apache-2.0 build. tools/tpch-tools/README still says some TPC-H queries were rewritten for an old optimizer, but the current q9/q18/q21 files carry no such markers or hints, so that note looks stale.
