- GROUP BY or anything beyond a simple aggregate. Its own benchmark is 6.7x slower than ClickHouse on a year group-by count, the TPC-H page says performance 'has not been tuned' (only a modified Q1 at SF1 is shown), and the authors describe it as 'soon slower in more complex cases'.
- Data bigger than RAM or read from cold disk. Column files are stored uncompressed, and the benchmark notes say ClickHouse wins from a cold disk because of compression.
- Workloads that need durability or crash safety. The write path I read calls fallocate, pwrite and close, ignores their return codes, and never fsyncs. There is no WAL.
- ClickHouse schemas that use Enum8 (#114), partial-column INSERT, db.table references in the engine (#106), or string literals (#230, 'select 'abc'' returns nothing). Any feature past the short list in docs/lang.md is missing.

**Integration:** Standalone server binary: Linux release zips up to v2021.07.05, or built with cargo from the workspace. There are two binaries, server (ClickHouse protocol) and mysql_server. It is not packaged as an embeddable library. · Vendored forks of arrow 6.4, datafusion 6.0 and parquet; sled 0.34 for metadata and partition bookkeeping; tokio 1.x; tikv-jemallocator; lzzzz (LZ4, wire compression); clickhouse-rs-cityhash-sys; the mysql 21 crate; and two git-branch dependencies, tensorbase/basejit (Cranelift 0.69 expression JIT, no license file in the repo) and tensorbase/baselog. · Rust nightly-2021-12-17, pinned in rust-toolchain. The docs say nightly is required. Stable Rust is not supported. · Linux (also Windows via WSL2, VMs or Docker). docs/docs.md says macOS is not supported and that CPUs other than x86-64 are 'not tested', although a blog post reports a demo run on RISC-V hardware. CI runs only on ubuntu-20.04.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only as reference code for putting a ClickHouse wire-protocol front end on DataFusion. Otherwise use upstream Apache DataFusion (maintained and far newer than TensorBase's pinned 2021 fork) for an embeddable Rust engine, StarRocks, Apache Doris or QuestDB for a maintained server that beats ClickHouse on its own benchmarks, or chDB for ClickHouse SQL inside a process.

**Gotchas:**
- The headline '5x~10000x faster than ClickHouse' numbers belong to the closed TensorBase Frontier Edition, not this repo. On HN, a commenter (zX41ZdbW) noted that the synthetic system.numbers queries compile into a loop the compiler removes entirely, so no data is processed.
- Every query mmaps every matching column-partition file, and the mappings appear never to be released: QueryState's Drop impl is commented out, and GitHub code search finds no caller of mm_unmap. Expect virtual address space to grow on a long-running server.
- Large result sets can hang the client. #86 (open): SELECT on a string column without LIMIT times out because the server does not split big Arrow RecordBatches into smaller blocks. An INSERT block that spans 1000 or more partition-key values is rejected with TooManyPartsPerBlock.
- The runtime depends on github.com/tensorbase/basejit by git branch. That repo has no LICENSE file, so check licensing before you redistribute a build, even though TensorBase itself is Apache-2.0.

**Status:** Abandoned: code changes stopped in December 2021, the last commit (2022-05-10) only disabled dependabot, the last binary release is v2021.07.05 and 48 issues are open; it is Apache-2.0 with about 1.5k stars, but the pinned 2021 nightly toolchain and a git dependency with no license file make it reading material rather than something to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/tensorbase/tensorbase) · [benchmark](https://github.com/tensorbase/tensorbase/blob/main/docs/benchmarks.md)

##### Tessera  `C#`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Small .NET 9 columnar library whose sorted merge-sweep as-of join is about 14x faster than pandas.merge_asof on 1M x 1M rows.

**Beats:** pandas — Synthetic data: 1M trades and 1M quotes over 500 symbols, pre-sorted, with int symbol codes. BenchmarkDotNet (.NET 9 Release) reports a mean of 10.8 ms for Tessera's backward join, against 82.9 ms for a hand-written C# per-symbol binary-search join (~7.7x). A separate Python script times a single pandas.merge_asof call with perf_counter after a 1,000-row warm-up and gets 152.8 ms (~14x). The two sides generate the same data shape with different RNGs (System.Random vs numpy), not identical rows. Pandas, NumPy and Python versions and the CPU are not stated beyond 'single dev laptop'.

**Known shortcoming:** pandas was timed once with perf_counter against a BenchmarkDotNet mean for the C# side; no CPU model; the repo is about a day old with 1 star.

**Known shortcoming:** The 14x is not asymptotic (pandas' merge_asof is also a single O(n+m) sweep); the win is direct array indexing and low overhead. No sortedness check, so unsorted input gives silent wrong results (pandas raises); tolerance=0 means no limit (pandas: exact only); unmatched int columns become 0, not null. The C# and Python benches use different RNGs (not identical rows); single-threaded, no out-of-core; about a day of history with an AI co-author, no NuGet release.

**How:** It uses a sort-merge as-of join. Because both inputs are globally sorted by time, one right-side cursor only moves forward while the left rows are walked. A per-group 'last seen row' array indexed directly by the dense int symbol code replaces any per-row search, so the join is a single O(n+m) pass. Output is a gather through an int32 match-index array allocated uninitialized, which is why the result costs only about 11.4 MB. Current pandas main also does a single sorted sweep (Cython asof_join_backward_on_X_by_Y) but keys it with a khash int64 hash table and adds validation and DataFrame overhead. So the win over pandas comes from direct array indexing and lower constant factors, not from better asymptotics. The O(n+m) vs O(n log m) framing applies only to the repo's own C# binary-search baseline.

**Use it when:**
- A .NET 9 backtester or tick-processing service that must attach the prevailing quote to each trade, in memory, on arrays in the ~1M-row range
- Feeds already sorted by time with int64 nanosecond timestamps and a modest, dense symbol universe (the benchmark uses 500 symbols)
- You need pandas-style backward, forward or nearest as-of semantics with tolerance and allowExactMatches, but inside a C# process without Python
- You want a short, readable implementation to vendor and adapt: the core is a handful of source files with no runtime dependencies
- Building OHLCV+VWAP bars from ticks in the same process (supported, but not benchmarked)

**Skip it when:**
- Your pipeline is in pandas or Python: there are no Python bindings, and moving DataFrames into .NET plus factorizing keys is outside the benchmarked time
- General dataframe work: there are no equality joins, group-by, filters, expression layer or file readers and writers in the source tree
- Data larger than RAM: memory-mapped, out-of-core columns are an unchecked roadmap item
- Production-critical use: all 7 commits landed within about a day (2026-06-26 to 06-27), with AI co-author trailers. It has 1 star, no releases, no NuGet package and no issues filed, so there is no outside usage signal
- Very high-cardinality or sparse keys: the group table is sized to max code + 1 on every join (twice for nearest), and CombineCodes throws if the product of cardinalities overflows int32. The sweep is single-threaded

**Integration:** source-drop · none for Tessera.Core (BenchmarkDotNet 0.14.0 for the benchmarks, xunit 2.9.2 for the tests) · .NET 9 SDK (targets net9.0 with LangVersion latest; uses C# collection expressions and static abstract interface members) · any platform .NET 9 runs on. The as-of join is scalar code; VectorOps uses the portable System.Numerics.Vector<T>, whose width depends on hardware (the comments cite 4 doubles on AVX2 and 8 on AVX-512)

**Vs siblings:** Pick Tessera when you need an as-of join on in-memory arrays inside a .NET process. Pick QuestDB when the data already lives in a time-series database (its SQL ASOF JOIN supports ON keys and TOLERANCE), and data.table when you work in R (rolling joins via roll=TRUE/'nearest'). chDB and cuDF (cudf.pandas) are better when you want to keep a pandas-shaped workflow rather than port to C#.

**Gotchas:**
- Sortedness is not validated. Unsorted or only per-group-sorted time columns give silently wrong matches, whereas pandas raises 'left keys must be sorted'. Run Table.SortByTime first; it is a comparison-delegate Array.Sort whose cost is not in the benchmark
- tolerance <= 0 means no limit, while in pandas tolerance=0 is valid (non-negative) and restricts matches to equal timestamps
- Unmatched rows get NaN only for double and float columns. Int and long 'bring' columns get 0 (a test asserts this), which cannot be told apart from real zeros. There is no null mask
- Both sides must use one shared code mapping (Categoricals.FactorizeShared). Factorizing each table separately silently mismatches symbols, and a negative code would index out of range

**Status:** The repo is technically 'active', but its whole history spans about one day (last commit 2026-06-27). It is MIT-licensed and small enough to copy the few source files, but it is not published to NuGet and several unrelated 'Tessera' packages already exist there.

[repo](https://github.com/bpmcginley/Tessera) · [benchmark](https://github.com/bpmcginley/Tessera#results)

##### Vortex  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust columnar file format and compressed-array toolkit that aims to replace Parquet for scans, writes and random access.

**Beats:** Apache Parquet — Vortex's own CI dashboard (bench.vortex.dev build 737386b; AWS c8gd.metal-24xl ARM64 per the workflows; rustc 1.98 with target-cpu=native) reports geomean write throughput of 1,756 vs 605 MB/s and scan throughput of 84.1 vs 3.2 GB/s against parquet-rs 59 with default ZSTD, plus hot take latency of 1.85 ms vs 65 s. These are not per-core comparisons: the Vortex side runs on a multi-threaded Tokio runtime with a writer that compresses on all cores, while the Parquet side uses parquet-rs's synchronous ArrowWriter and reader. End-to-end query gains are smaller and mixed: ClickBench on NVMe is 3.99 vs 6.08 s with DataFusion and 4.65 vs 5.45 s with DuckDB, TPC-H S3 SF100 is 6.7x slower with DuckDB, and independent ClickBench runs on c6a.4xlarge are mixed to negative.

**Known shortcoming:** The vendor's 1.13x/1.32x/627x are ratios to the fastest entry, not vs Parquet; derived vs Parquet: DataFusion 1.52x, DuckDB 1.17x, TPC-H SF1 3.35x, hot random access ~545x. Write 2.97x and scan 30.73x hold. Official ClickBench contradicts it: DataFusion+Vortex 91.3 s vs DataFusion+Parquet 45.6 s; DuckDB+Vortex is slower summed and only ~5% faster by geomean.

**Known shortcoming:** Write/scan ratios are not per-core: the Vortex writer compresses on all cores while the parquet-rs side is single-threaded. On S3 at SF100, DuckDB+Vortex took 488.6 s vs 73.5 s for Parquet; epic #7716 lists losing queries. Files are ~1.07x Parquet-zstd size (0.55-1.43x), not smaller.

**Known shortcoming:** Open correctness bugs: a zone-map null leak can prune valid zones (#9205), DuckDB sum overflow (#9836), panics on malformed files. DuckDB COPY OOM (#10046); C/C++/DuckDB writers are single-threaded (#8760); small-batch writes 20-30x slower (#5861). The default session writes the newest file edition, so a library upgrade can break older readers; 0.x API churn; C++ bindings are source-only on Linux/macOS-arm64.

**How:** Each chunk gets its own chain of lightweight encodings, chosen by a BtrBlocks-style sampling compressor. Integers use FastLanes SIMD bit-packing, frame-of-reference, delta and RLE; floats use ALP/ALPrd; strings use FSST. Dictionary, run-end and sparse encodings apply across types, and zstd/PCodec are kept for the size-oriented 'compact' strategy. Arrays are lazy trees of encodings, so filters, takes and comparisons run directly on compressed data when a kernel exists, and data is fully decoded only when no kernel does. The DuckDB integration can hand FSST strings to DuckDB without decompressing them. The default file layout keeps min/max/null-count zone maps every 8k rows for pruning and targets segments of about 1 MB, a size chosen for S3 request sizing. The writer compresses chunks in parallel across all available cores, and footer metadata is zero-copy and zero-parse.

**Use it when:**
- Write-once, scan-many analytics tables that you query through DuckDB or DataFusion on local NVMe. On the dashboard, TPC-H SF1 on NVMe takes 450 ms with DuckDB+Vortex vs 1.51 s with DuckDB+Parquet.
- Point lookups and sparse row fetches (take) over columnar data such as feature vectors, taxi trips or nested lists/structs, where Parquet's lack of row-level random access hurts. Hot take is 1.85 ms vs 65 s for Parquet and 3.57 ms for Lance.
- Rust data systems or custom storage engines that want Arrow-compatible arrays with compressed-domain compute, plus pluggable encodings, layouts and storage backends (local disk, object stores).
- Bulk ingest or conversion on many-core machines, where the parallel writer can use every core. The dashboard shows 1,756 MB/s vs 605 MB/s for parquet-rs, with the threading caveat below.
- GPU decode pipelines on Linux, using the optional CUDA feature that decodes Vortex files on the device.

**Skip it when:**
- As an interchange format for arbitrary consumers. Parquet is readable almost everywhere, while Vortex needs its own library or extension. Iceberg support is still 'coming soon', and DuckDB extension updates need DuckDB maintainers to redeploy, so they can lag Vortex releases by days.
- Large queries over S3 with DuckDB. On the same dashboard, TPC-H S3 SF100 takes 488.6 s with DuckDB+Vortex vs 73.5 s with DuckDB+Parquet, and at S3 SF1 DataFusion+Parquet is fastest. Independent ClickBench runs are mixed to negative (DataFusion+Vortex 91.3 s vs 45.6 s for Parquet, Aug 2026). The project's own epic #7716 lists ClickBench, TPC-H and TPC-DS queries where it still loses to Parquet.
- Memory-constrained ingest through DuckDB. In #10046, COPY ... (FORMAT vortex) of ClickBench hits was OOM-killed on a 7.6 GiB host regardless of memory_limit, because Vortex allocations are invisible to DuckDB's accounting. The C, C++ and DuckDB write paths are effectively single-threaded (#8760). An independent May 2026 test also hit OOM reading directories of Vortex files through the DuckDB extension.
- Many small writes. In #5861, writing RecordBatches under about 1,000 rows was 20-30x slower than Parquet, although that test used uncompressed Parquet.
- When smallest file size is the goal. The dashboard's geomean Vortex file size is 1.07x Parquet-zstd (range 0.55x to 1.43x); the 'compact' strategy trades read speed for size. Also, the Rust and C++ APIs still change between 0.x releases, and the Scan API is marked as under development.

**Integration:** crate (vortex on crates.io). Also a PyPI module (vortex-data), a Maven Spark package, a DuckDB extension, and C/C++ libraries built from source with CMake as static or shared libs. · The workspace pins arrow-rs 59.x, flatbuffers, fastlanes, fsst-rs, zstd, pco, object_store and tokio. Engine integrations use DataFusion 55 or DuckDB 1.5. The C/C++ bindings need CMake 3.25+ and Cargo/rustc on PATH; nanoarrow provides optional Arrow interop. The README recommends mimalloc as the global allocator. · Rust 1.95 MSRV (edition 2024), with CI building on 1.98. The C++ bindings need a C++20 compiler and CMake 3.25+. · Rust crate platforms are not documented. The C/C++ bindings build natively only on Linux x86-64/aarch64 and macOS arm64; Windows, musl, cross-compilation and universal binaries are unsupported. The CUDA path is Linux-only.

**Vs siblings:** Pick Vortex over Lance for SQL analytics through DuckDB or DataFusion when file size matters. On Vortex's own dashboard, Lance files are 2.11x Parquet size vs 1.07x for Vortex, and Lance trails on write, scan and take (first-party numbers). Velox, StarRocks, Umbra and Sirius are query engines, not formats: Vortex sits underneath an engine such as DuckDB, DataFusion or Spark rather than replacing one.

**Gotchas:**
- Backward compatibility covers only files written by 0.36.0 or later. The default session writes the newest frozen edition, so a library upgrade can produce files that older readers cannot open. Pin an edition when readers lag behind writers.
- Open correctness bugs: #9205 (null children of a nullable struct leak into zone maps, so is_null filters can prune valid zones and return wrong results) and #9836 (sum overflow handled incorrectly in the DuckDB integration). Fuzzing has found panics on malformed files (#8848, #8823), so isolate untrusted inputs.
- Memory: take on an FSST string array grew 19 MB into 2 GB (#4784), and buffer allocations bypass host-engine memory limits until the BufferAllocator work (#9674) lands.
- C++ API: the Writer must call finish() or the file is corrupt. Literals need an explicit type, as in lit<uint16_t>(180), because there is no type coercion; a plain lit(180) fails at runtime.

**Status:** Very active: commits land daily, 0.86.1 shipped on 2026-09-11, and 0.x releases come every two to three weeks. It is Apache-2.0 and an LF AI & Data incubation project; the file format has been stable since 0.36.0, but library APIs still change between releases.

[repo](https://github.com/vortex-data/vortex) · [benchmark](https://bench.vortex.dev)

#### embedded-kv

##### Badger (BadgerDB)  `Go`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Go embedded LSM key-value store using WiscKey key-value separation; 3.7x lower random-read latency than RocksDB in Dgraph's 2017 test.

**Beats:** RocksDB — Dgraph ran this benchmark itself in 2017 on a 2-core AWS i3.large (16 GB RAM, local NVMe, ~93K 4 KB random-read IOPS). Random Gets over 250M 22-byte keys with 128 B values averaged 32.4 us in Badger vs 119.0 us in RocksDB 5.1.4 called through cgo (3.67x), and loading 75M x 1 KB took 17m10s vs 78m08s (~4.6x). RocksDB was opened read-only with its default block cache and a 16-bit bloom filter while Badger held its LSM tables in RAM (LoadToRAM), and neither the Go version nor the CPU model is stated.

**Known shortcoming:** First-party benchmark with no CPU model: RocksDB ran with default options through cgo while Badger's LSM sat in RAM. Loads with 128 B values are slower than RocksDB.

**Known shortcoming:** The benchmark does not reflect current defaults (ValueThreshold is 1 MB since v3.2103.0, so values under 1 MB are stored inline in a plain LSM; LoadToRAM removed in v3.2011.0). Loses on small values (128 B load 45 vs 39 min; 16 B ~1.9x slower); scans with values ~13x slower at 128 B and ~4x at 1 KB. Peak RSS during load ~14 GB vs 0.6 GB for RocksDB; mmap cannot be disabled.

**Known shortcoming:** Value-log GC is manual and frees at most one file per call; open GC stall (#2334) and never-compacted L6 tombstones (#2329). Use >=v4.9.6: earlier versions had deleted-data-reappears bugs (#2278/#2310), dropped acknowledged writes (#2313) and a 3x bulk-import regression in v4.9.4 (#2327).

**How:** It follows the WiscKey paper (FAST '16): values above ValueThreshold go to an append-only value log that doubles as the write-ahead log, and the LSM tree holds only keys plus 12-byte value pointers (file id, length, offset). This keeps the tree small enough to stay in RAM (Dgraph measured a 1.7 GB LSM tree for 75M keys x 1 KB, against 50 GB for RocksDB), so a point read is an in-memory table search with bloom filters plus one read from the value log. Compactions rewrite only keys and pointers, so write amplification falls as values grow. Supporting pieces are an arena-allocated, atomics-based concurrent skiplist memtable adapted from RocksDB's inline skiplist, per-table bloom filters, Ristretto block and index caches, and mmap-backed value-log files.

**Use it when:**
- Go services that need an embedded, ordered, persistent KV store without cgo. You get plain `go get`, easy cross-compilation, and full visibility in the Go CPU and memory profilers. Cgo pain is why Dgraph replaced its RocksDB binding with Badger.
- Random point reads of values around 1 KB or larger, with a dataset bigger than RAM, on local NVMe. The 2017 log shows Get latency 3.7x lower than RocksDB at 128 B, 4.2x lower at 1 KB and 5.4x lower at 16 KB. On current versions this only applies if you lower ValueThreshold so values actually go to the value log.
- Bulk loading of large values. In the same log, loading 75M x 1 KB was about 4.6x faster than RocksDB (17m10s vs 78m08s), and 5M x 16 KB about 12x faster (6m55s vs 1h22m21s).
- Key-only scans and existence checks. With PrefetchValues=false, iteration never touches the value log: 250M keys took 0.71 s, against 5.8 s for RocksDB's key+value iteration.
- Embedded use that needs concurrent ACID transactions with SSI conflict detection, TTLs or multi-version reads. Dgraph, Jaeger and go-ipfs are listed users.

**Skip it when:**
- Small values under write-heavy load. In the same log Badger loaded 250M x 128 B more slowly than RocksDB (45m27s vs 39m11s) and 1B x 16 B about 1.9x more slowly (3h04m vs 1h38m). Dgraph's blog blames Badger's slower compactions.
- Range scans that return values. Iterating 250M x 128 B with values took 75.8 s vs 5.8 s for RocksDB (about 13x slower), and about 4x slower at 1 KB, because each value is a separate read from the value log.
- Memory-limited or 32-bit deployments. Peak RSS while loading was about 14 GB vs 0.6 GB for RocksDB. Value-log files are always mmapped, since the FileIO mode was removed in v3. Users report page-cache thrashing in 500 MB containers (#2255) and mmap failures on 386 (#2287).
- Heavy delete or overwrite workloads that need disk space back automatically. The application has to drive value-log GC through RunValueLogGC, which frees at most one file per call. Open issues report GC stalls when the active file has the most garbage (#2334) and tombstones that automatic compaction never removes from L6 (#2329).
- Non-Go stacks, or anything that expects RocksDB's API, on-disk format or tools. Badger's own on-disk format also changes between major versions, and moving data across one requires a backup and restore.

**Integration:** module · Pure Go, no cgo. Depends on dgraph-io/ristretto/v2 (caches and allocator), klauspost/compress (zstd), cespare/xxhash, google/flatbuffers, protobuf, golang.org/x/sys, OpenTelemetry (zpages) and cobra (CLI only). jemalloc is optional: only the CLI Makefile builds with the `jemalloc` tag. · go.mod declares go 1.24.0, though the README still says Go 1.23+. Import path is github.com/dgraph-io/badger/v4. · Linux, macOS and BSD are fully supported (POSIX locking and fsync). On Windows, directory locking works differently. AIX has no directory fsync, and Plan9 and WASM/JS have no file locking. 32-bit builds are fragile because of mmap address-space limits (#2287), and a ppc64el test failure is open (#2079). The source tree contains no assembly files.

**Vs siblings:** Pick Badger when the application is written in Go and must stay cgo-free: every catalogued sibling (Titan, PebblesDB, SplinterDB, NuDB, ToplingDB, etc.) is C/C++. If you already run RocksDB and want the same key-value-separation gain for large values, Titan provides it as a RocksDB plugin (reported ~70% faster data loading) without changing engine or API.

**Gotchas:**
- Current defaults do not match the benchmark. Since v3.2103.0 (2021), ValueThreshold defaults to 1 MB, so values under 1 MB are stored inline in the LSM tree and Badger behaves like an ordinary LSM store. The default was 32 B until it was raised to 1 KB and then 1 MB. The 2017 run also used TableLoadingMode=LoadToRAM, an option removed in v3.2011.0. Call WithValueThreshold with a small value to get the WiscKey behaviour that was measured.
- Space reclamation is manual. Call db.RunValueLogGC(ratio) on a ticker, re-running while it returns nil. It never collects inline values or the active vlog file. TTL expiry and deletes also do not shrink a database that has stopped taking writes, because compactions only run when writes arrive.
- Use v4.9.6 or later. v4.9.3 and v4.9.4 fixed deleted keys reappearing after compaction (#2278) and after vlog GC (#2310), and fixed acknowledged writes being dropped during DropPrefix/DropAll (#2313). The v4.9.4 compaction fix then slowed large bulk imports about 3x (#2327), which v4.9.6 fixed (#2330).
- Transaction and size limits: a transaction fails with ErrTxnTooBig once pending writes pass 15% of MemTableSize (use WriteBatch for bulk loads). Keys are capped at 65,000 bytes and values at ValueLogFileSize. Calling Close twice, or writing after Close, panics with a closed-channel error.

**Status:** Actively maintained (v4.9.6 released 2026-08-05, commits through 2026-09-21), Apache-2.0, and used in production by Dgraph, Jaeger and go-ipfs. The headline numbers, though, come from an archived 2017 benchmark whose options and defaults no longer exist, so re-benchmark current v4 before relying on them.

[repo](https://github.com/dgraph-io/badger) · [benchmark](https://github.com/dgraph-io/badger-bench/blob/master/BENCH-rocks.txt)

##### CacheAdvance  `Swift`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Size-capped append-only Swift log file (optional ring-buffer eviction); appends far faster than per-row-committed SQLite inserts.

**Beats:** SQLite — The '30x faster than SQLite' tagline is a first-party README claim from April 2020 with no published numbers, hardware or Xcode/Swift version. The PR that added the benchmarks (#41) said 'more than 15x' as a lower bound and mentioned runs above 50x; two days later the README was changed to 30x. The benchmarks are XCTest measure{} tests appending about 480 JSON-encoded Lorem-ipsum strings. The SQLite side runs COUNT(*), prepares a fresh INSERT and autocommits every row under default rollback-journal synchronous=FULL (per sqlite.org, a few dozen transactions per second versus 50,000+ plain INSERTs), while CacheAdvance never fsyncs. It therefore compares durable per-row transactions with page-cache writes, and a batched or WAL-mode SQLite baseline was never tested.

**Known shortcoming:** The 30x appears only in the README (earlier 15x) and the test file has no numbers. The SQLite baseline is naive (COUNT(*) and a separate commit per append at default durability) while CacheAdvance does not fsync.

**Known shortcoming:** The 30x is a README tagline with no published data or hardware (PR #41 said '>15x'). The SQLite baseline uses COUNT(*), a fresh prepare and an autocommit per row at synchronous=FULL, while CacheAdvance never fsyncs; the author concedes SQLite is much faster at reads. messages() loads the whole cache; no keys/count/delete.

**Known shortcoming:** Not a key-value store but an append-only ring-buffer log (embedded-kv is a loose fit). Not thread-safe or Sendable, no process lock; the file must pre-exist; the README's init label is wrong (file: vs fileURL:). Swift 6 / Xcode 16+.

**How:** Each append JSON-encodes the message (encoder is pluggable), prefixes it with a big-endian UInt32 length and writes it at the current FileHandle offset. It then rewrites one 8-byte offset field in a fixed 64-byte file header; an overwriting cache also updates the oldest-message pointer and advances a read cursor. That is a few write/seek syscalls per message. There is no SQL parsing, B-tree, journal, transaction or fsync (the source never calls synchronize/fsync). The SQLite path it is compared against pays a full autocommit transaction per insert.

**Use it when:**
- Swift apps on iOS 15+/macOS 11+/tvOS/watchOS/visionOS (or Linux with Swift 6) that need a crash-surviving on-disk buffer of recent log or analytics events before upload
- Write-heavy, read-rarely workloads: many small appends (tests use about 480 strings of roughly 50 bytes), then one bulk messages() read at upload or crash-report time
- When you want a hard on-disk size cap with automatic eviction of the oldest entries (shouldOverwriteOldMessages: true) and no compaction or vacuum
- When pulling in SQLite/Core Data just for a log table is overkill and a single dependency-free Swift source package is preferred

**Skip it when:**
- You need power-loss durability: appends are plain write() calls with no fsync, and the README only promises that data is 'persisted to disk' when append returns (i.e. handed to the OS)
- You need keyed lookup, filtering, deleting specific entries, a message count or partial reads: messages() decodes the whole cache into memory, and there is no count API (proposed in issue #34, absent from the current source)
- Read-heavy use: the author's own PR #41 reports that SQLite is 'significantly faster at reading messages'; reads cost two small read calls plus a JSON decode per message
- Multi-threaded or multi-process writers: instances are not thread-safe, the class is not Sendable under Swift 6, and there is no file locking
- Large messages or caches whose size or overwrite policy may change later: messages must stay under 2 GB, and changing maximumBytes or the overwrite flag after first use makes the file unwritable (fileNotWritable)

**Integration:** module · none (Foundation only); SQLite3 is imported only by the test target · Swift 6.0 tools / Swift 6 language mode (Xcode 16+); Objective-C support removed in 4.0.0 · iOS 15, tvOS 15, watchOS 7, macOS 11, Mac Catalyst 15, visionOS 1 (podspec); Linux x86-64 tested in CI with Swift 6.0.3 and 6.1; other OSes not documented

**Vs siblings:** Every sibling here is a keyed store with point lookups (for example CalicoDB, also benchmarked against SQLite, NuDB or the RocksDB-derived engines) and mostly C/C++/Go. Pick CacheAdvance only when you are in Swift and need a bounded, append-then-dump log file rather than a key-value store; for any keyed or read-heavy workload a sibling (or SQLite itself) is the right tool.

**Gotchas:**
- The file must already exist (for example via FileManager.createFile) before init; the handles open with forUpdating/forWritingTo and fail otherwise. The README's sample uses a 'file:' argument label, but the real initializer takes 'fileURL:'.
- maximumBytes and the overwrite flag are stored in the header and must never change: a mismatch leaves the file readable but append throws fileNotWritable. The encoder/decoder are not recorded, so changing them silently breaks decoding of old messages.
- Crash windows are documented in the source: a crash between the data write and the header update loses the newest message, and a crash mid-write can yield CacheAdvanceError.fileCorrupted, after which the README says to delete the file.
- The per-append cost is dominated by JSONEncoder (the author in PR #41 put encoding at about 15x the header cost); supply a cheaper MessageEncoder if throughput matters.

**Status:** Active single-maintainer project (v4.0.0 June 2025, last push June 2026, 0 open issues, CI on Apple platforms and Linux); Apache-2.0 and 14 small Swift source files, so easy to vendor, though usage is modest (51 stars).

[repo](https://github.com/dfed/CacheAdvance) · [benchmark](https://github.com/dfed/CacheAdvance/blob/main/Tests/CacheAdvanceTests/SQLitePerformanceComparisonTests.swift)

##### CalicoDB  `C++`  `MIT`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Small C++17 embedded transactional B+-tree key-value store modeled on SQLite's WAL design; beats SQLite on large-value reads and sequential fills.

**Beats:** SQLite — The author ported LevelDB's db_bench to both engines and ran it once in GitHub Actions CI (ubuntu-latest and macos-latest runners, CPU unstated, gcc Release build with no version given) at commit 30fe767. It compared CalicoDB 0.0.1 against SQLite 3.39.5 in WAL mode, with WITHOUT ROWID, 4 KiB pages, a 4 MB cache, exclusive locking and synchronous NORMAL (FULL for the *sync tests). CalicoDB won clearly on 100 KB-value reads (4.3x/6.3x random, 1.5x/2.7x sequential, Linux/macOS) and by about 2x on batched sequential fills. It was up to ~1.3x slower on random fills and overwrites and 3.8-5.2x slower on the macOS sync-write tests (all ratios derived from the page's microseconds-per-op table).

**Known shortcoming:** Loses some benchmarks (readrandom on Linux; the *sync workloads on macOS are about 4-5x slower than SQLite). Stale; the author says it is not production-ready.

**Known shortcoming:** Numbers come from commit 30fe767 (2023-07, older API) and were never re-run over 54 later commits; the raw CI log is gone and the benchmark builds from main, so they cannot be reproduced. The v0.1.1 changelog lists a WAL sync bug 'likely' causing data loss/corruption; fuzzer crashes open (#118). Loses random fills/overwrites by up to ~1.3x; the SQLite side is the system library through SQL with a different autocheckpoint (4096 vs 1000); no Windows/MSVC.

**How:** It is essentially SQLite's storage design without the SQL layer. It uses a B+-tree over slotted pages with a fixed-width indirection vector for in-node binary search, pointer-map pages that hold parent pointers so splits and merges don't rewrite child pages, overflow chains for large payloads, and a SQLite-style write-ahead log with a shared-memory WAL index. Dirty pages sit in a page cache (LevelDB-derived hash table plus LRU list; default 1024 pages) and go to the WAL only on commit or eviction; checkpoints write each unique page back once, sorted by page number. Sequential inserts take a split_nonroot_fast path that splits at the right edge instead of redistributing cells 50/50, and pivot keys are suffix-truncated (Bayer and Unterauer's simple prefix B-tree). The benchmark page credits the gap mainly to SQLite's higher per-operation RDBMS overhead; no per-benchmark profiling is published.

**Use it when:**
- Read-heavy embedded workloads with large (about 100 KB) values: readrand100K ran 58.8 vs 252.4 us/op on Linux (~4.3x, derived) and 79.2 vs 495.5 on macOS (~6.3x, derived); readseq100K was ~1.5x and ~2.7x faster (derived).
- Bulk-loading sequential keys, especially in batched transactions: fillseqbatch ran 1.04 vs 2.03 us/op on Linux (~2.0x, derived) and 1.86 vs 4.57 on macOS (~2.5x, derived); single-op fillseq was ~1.3x and ~2.0x faster (derived).
- A C++ program on Linux or macOS that uses SQLite only as an ordered, transactional key-value file and wants snapshot readers alongside one writer without a SQL layer.
- Memory-constrained or no-exceptions builds: the library compiles with -fno-exceptions and -fno-rtti, handles malloc failure, supports 32-bit targets, and lets you plug in your own allocator (calicodb::configure), Env (filesystem/I/O) and Wal. It also has an in-memory mode (temp_database).
- As a compact, well-documented modern C++ reimplementation of SQLite's B-tree and WAL architecture to study or fork.

**Skip it when:**
- Production data. The README says it is 'not ready for production'. The v0.1.1 changelog records a WAL sync bug that 'would have likely resulted in data loss/corruption', and issue #118 says the file-format fuzzer 'produces crashes quickly' on corrupted files. There have been no commits since 2023-11-01.
- Random-key inserts and overwrites: SQLite was faster on fillrandom (~1.09x Linux, ~1.05x macOS), fillrandbatch (~1.20x / ~1.31x), overwrite and overwritebatch (up to ~1.22x on macOS), and small-value readrandom on Linux (4.61 vs 4.27 us/op). All ratios are derived.
- Per-commit durable writes on macOS: kSyncFull calls fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC). fillseqsync ran 1101 vs 291 us/op (~3.8x slower) and fillrandsync 1118 vs 214 (~5.2x slower) against the system SQLite, which the page says uses F_BARRIERFSYNC.
- Windows or MSVC (CMake stops with a fatal error), network filesystems (the README at the benchmarked commit warns it will not work there), or platforms without shared-memory primitives, which only work in exclusive locking mode.
- Workloads that need SQL, multiple concurrent writers, a stable on-disk format or API, or datasets that don't fit comfortably in one file. The README says it is 'only practical for datasets that can reasonably be stored in a single file', and each connection is single-threaded with blocking I/O.

**Integration:** static lib · none for the library (POSIX system calls only); tests need googletest (fetched by CMake FetchContent) and Python 3 · C++17, CMake 3.14+, GCC 7+ or Clang 5+; MSVC not supported · POSIX only: Linux and macOS are tested in CI (ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, gcc and clang). The -shm file must support mmap unless exclusive locking mode is used. The design doc and v0.2.0 notes claim 32-bit support. No Windows.

**Vs siblings:** Every catalogued sibling (for example Titan, ToplingDB, Nova-LSM and DiaLSM) is benchmarked against RocksDB and mostly targets LSM-scale write throughput; pick CalicoDB only when you want a tiny, dependency-free, single-file B+-tree with SQLite-style WAL transactions to replace SQLite as a plain key-value store, especially for large-value reads. Its evidence is one mixed-result CI run from 2023, weaker than most siblings'.

**Gotchas:**
- The published numbers are for commit 30fe767 (2023-07-02, labelled 0.0.1). That predates v0.1.0, predates the v0.1.1 WAL sync fix, and used an older public API with no tx.h or bucket.h. The 54 later commits (nested buckets, a larger local cell size, corruption fixes) were never re-published. The linked raw CI output (actions run 5437371027) now returns 404, and the bench workflow builds CalicoDB from main, so rerunning it today will not reproduce those numbers.
- SQLite is the system libsqlite3 that the runner links, driven through SQL statements with wal_autocheckpoint=4096. CalicoDB runs with its default auto_checkpoint of 1000 frames. The author's disclaimer says SQLite carries more per-operation overhead, so part of each 'win' is simply skipping SQL.
- If a system call fails inside a read-write transaction, the Tx is poisoned: every call returns that error until you return from the update() lambda. commit() does not release file locks until the Tx is deleted, and only one Tx can be live per DB handle.
- Handles are raw pointers you must delete yourself (DB, Tx, Bucket, Cursor), and Bucket handles must be deleted before their transaction ends. Page size (512 to 32768, default 4 KiB) is fixed when the database is created. The last connection to close checkpoints and unlinks the WAL.

**Status:** Stale since 2023-11-01 (v0.2.0 plus 54 unreleased commits, 43 stars) and self-described as not production-ready. It is MIT-licensed and about 50 source files with no dependencies, so it can be vendored for experiments, but you would own maintenance and crash-safety validation.

[repo](https://github.com/andy-byers/CalicoDB) · [benchmark](https://github.com/andy-byers/leveldb/blob/db_bench_calicodb/benchmarks/results.md)

##### count-db  `Java`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Java embedded store for 64-bit-keyed counters; first-party bigram test: ~82x LevelDB write, ~12x read throughput.

**Beats:** LevelDB — These are first-party ops/sec figures. The hardware was an i7-4770 with a 7200 rpm SATA HDD and 32 GB RAM (10 GB JVM heap); the JVM version and flags are not stated. Eight threads called increaseCount/readCount on Wikipedia bigram hashes. count-db ran with its cache and Bloom layers; LevelDB (leveldbjni), RocksDB (RocksJava) and Kyoto Cabinet ran uncached with default options. The LevelDB and RocksDB adapters do a per-key-locked get-then-put per increment, no merge operator on this path, and LevelDB gets no filter policy. At 256M bigrams count-db reached 1.12E7 writes/s vs LevelDB 1.37E5 (~82x) and 1.06E7 reads/s vs 8.90E5 (~12x). The uniform test draws 128M increments from only 1M distinct keys (Random.nextInt(1000000)), so for count-db it is effectively an in-heap counter test.

**Known shortcoming:** Unfair setup: cached count-db writes vs read-modify-write LevelDB; ratios (~82x/~12x, uniform write ~95x) are derived; benchmark links are dead (code moved to count-db-run/); abandoned.

**Known shortcoming:** The speedup is in-heap write combining plus a Bloom filter vs uncached LevelDB/RocksDB doing get-then-put per increment with no merge operator (LevelDB without a filter policy); the uniform test is 128M increments over only 1M distinct keys. No fsync (writes sit ~1 s in heap); string keys are hashed to 64 bits and not stored, so collisions merge silently; the first read on a dirty bucket triggers a synchronous rewrite. Stale dependencies (Spring 4.1, jackson-databind 2.9.7); abandoned 2019.

**How:** By default a write-combining cache sits in front of the store. Writes go into 10 in-heap hash maps, sharded by key mod 10, where repeated keys are combined in memory. A background job flushes those maps to disk in batches every second, so a hot key costs one disk write per flush instead of one read-modify-write per increment. Underneath is a hash-partitioned append-then-compact log: keys are split into 64 buckets by their low 6 bits, and each bucket is a list of key-range files that take blind appends. A periodic job, or the first read of a dirty bucket, sorts each file, merges duplicates with the Combinator and rewrites it to about 10 MB with a sparse in-memory offset index. Reads binary-search that index and scan a short run. Whole files are cached on heap up to a third of available memory, and an optional per-interface Bloom filter answers misses.

**Use it when:**
- Counting n-grams, events or per-entity tallies from Java where the same keys are incremented many times (Zipf/power-law keys) and bulk throughput matters more than durability of each write.
- Batch pipelines with separate write and read phases: it detects write phases and defers compaction, and optimizeForReading() compacts everything before the read phase.
- Keys that are already 64-bit longs (IDs, precomputed hashes) and values that are primitives or small JSON-serializable objects.
- Single-machine data sets larger than the heap, where you would otherwise hand-roll a HashMap that spills to disk.
- Legacy Java 8 code that can vendor MIT-licensed source rather than depend on a maintained artifact.

**Skip it when:**
- You need durability or crash consistency. Files are written with plain FileOutputStream append and close, with no fsync. The cache layer holds writes in heap for up to about 1 s, and writes are not visible to reads until flush().
- You need exact String or byte[] keys, or ordered scans over the original keys. Strings are hashed to 64 bits with a multiply-by-65599 hash and not stored, so collisions merge silently and iterators return hashes.
- You need transactions, snapshots, several processes sharing one data directory, or a LevelDB/RocksDB-compatible API.
- Your writes are write-once or have few repeated keys. The published speedups come from in-memory combining of repeated increments, and no fair benchmark covers this case.
- You need a maintained production dependency. The last code commit was in 2019. Master depends on master-SNAPSHOT builds of the author's utility libraries via JitPack and on jackson-databind 2.9.7, with Dependabot bump PRs left open. The only Maven Central release (1.1.12) dates from October 2015 and pulls in Spring 4.1.

**Integration:** module (Maven JAR: be.bagofwords:count-db:1.1.12 on Central from 2015; current master is com.github.koendeschacht:count-db:master-SNAPSHOT via JitPack) · master: bow-utils, bow-utils-extra and mini-dep-i (all master-SNAPSHOT via JitPack), guava 19.0, commons-io 2.5, commons-lang3 3.4, jackson-databind 2.9.7, lmdbjni-linux64 0.4.6, snappy-java 1.1.2.6; the 1.1.12 release also pulls in Spring 4.1.0 (beans/context/core/test) and jackson-databind 2.3.3 · Java 8 (maven-compiler source/target 1.8); newer JDKs not documented · Any JVM in principle, since the file backend is pure Java, though the core POM still declares lmdbjni-linux64. The benchmark comparison needs Linux x86-64 JNI libraries (bundled in count-db-run/lib). Otherwise not documented.

**Vs siblings:** HyperLevelDB keeps LevelDB's API and storage semantics for a ~3.4x write gain; HaloDB is a general value store catalogued as beating RocksDB and Kyoto Cabinet on fill-random. Pick count-db over either only for increment-heavy counters on 64-bit keys inside one JVM, where in-memory write combining and merge-on-compaction do the work. For general get/put or durable storage, use those siblings.

**Gotchas:**
- Writes only become visible to reads after flush(), which the README states explicitly. Cached writers block when the heap monitor (MemoryManager) reports low memory, and that monitor can call System.gc().
- The first read on a bucket written since its last compaction synchronously rewrites the whole bucket (lockForRead -> rewriteBucket), so read latency can spike right after write bursts.
- The default config enables the cache layer (DataInterfaceConfig sets cache=true) but not the Bloom filter. The published numbers used CACHED_AND_BLOOM, which you must request.
- Stale docs: the README's ExampleUsage.java link and the benchmark-source links in doc/performance.md are dead because the code moved to count-db-run/. The README's Maven coordinates point to the 2015 release, not current master.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2019-10-31, with only Dependabot PRs after that and the last Central release in 2015. It is MIT-licensed plain Java 8, so vendoring src/ together with the author's bow-utils/bow-utils-extra/mini-dep-i sources is the realistic way to use it.

[repo](https://github.com/koendeschacht/count-db) · [benchmark](https://github.com/koendeschacht/count-db/blob/master/doc/performance.md)

##### DBX  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Beta pure-Rust HTAP embedded database whose key-value API edges out in-memory SQLite on a 10,000-row first-party benchmark.

**Beats:** SQLite — The only comparison is a first-party Criterion run (3 Apr 2026; rustc 1.92.0 release profile; Windows 11 x64, 16 GB, CPU unstated) on 10,000 short string pairs, DBX open_in_memory against rusqlite 0.32 bundled in-memory SQLite: INSERT 25.21 ms vs 29.4 ms (~1.17x), GET 2.84 ms vs 33.8 ms (~11.9x), SCAN 51 us vs 340 us. Only the INSERT row is a like-for-like (and modest) win. The SQLite harness autocommits every insert and re-prepares SQL on every insert and lookup (conn.execute/query_row), so GET mostly measures statement compilation. The 51 us SCAN figure matches the repo's PERF_TRACKER entry for a DBX SQL SELECT count(*) (where SQLite's count(*) took 5.66 us), not the bench's db.scan(), which copies all 10,000 pairs.

**Known shortcoming:** INSERT is only 1.16x vs SQLite; the GET ~11.9x / SCAN ~6.7x are derived. The SQLite harness re-prepares statements each call and the benchmark page contradicts itself; no CPU model.

**Known shortcoming:** The only fair win is INSERT (~1.17x, 10k rows, in-memory); the 11.9x GET is inflated because the SQLite side re-prepares SQL each call. The 51 us SCAN is DBX's SQL count(*), not the benchmarked scan(); the same doc shows SQLite count(*) at 5.66 us (9x faster) and DBX file inserts at 260.6 ms vs rusqlite 47 ms.

**Known shortcoming:** Data bug: values starting 0x00 0x01/0x02, or 10+ byte keys ending 0xDB 0x58, are mangled or dropped by scan() (get() and scan() disagree). Compaction rewrites the whole table every 5k WAL entries; default Lazy durability loses acknowledged writes on crash. Heavy non-optional dependencies (arrow/parquet, tokio, s2n-quic); beta, one developer, no commits since 2026-04-13 (whose CI failed); docs stale.

**How:** Writes land in a Tier-1 'Delta' store: one crossbeam SkipMap per table inside a DashMap. There is no SQL parsing, statement preparation or per-statement transaction on the KV path. When the global entry count reaches 10,000 (the default threshold, and exactly the benchmark size), insert() drains Delta into the WOS on the calling thread. For open_in_memory the WOS is a std BTreeMap per table behind one RwLock, so the benchmarked GET is essentially a BTreeMap lookup plus a Vec clone. The file-backed 'Native WOS' is a dirty buffer, an append-only WAL and a 4 KB-page SSTable with a sparse index and LRU page cache. The v0.2.0 'Fast-Path' changes the SQL executor (it skips the distributed DAG scheduler and mpsc channels), not the storage.

**Use it when:**
- Rust services that want an in-process, ordered byte-key/value store with named tables, CAS helpers and serde struct storage (DatabaseSerde), and that value a pure-Rust API over SQLite's maturity
- Small, memory-resident datasets rebuilt at startup (open_in_memory or open_fast) where per-call SQL overhead would dominate. The only published comparison uses 10,000 short string pairs.
- Prototypes that want KV, SQL, Arrow/Parquet and optional CUDA aggregation in a single crate, and can pin a 0.x beta version and read the source when behaviour is unclear
- Replacing a naive rusqlite pattern (autocommit inserts, conn.execute/query_row re-preparing SQL on every call) where you control both sides and only need point get/put

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that relies on SQLite's durability record, stable file format or SQL compatibility. DBX is a 0.x beta from one developer with 390 total crates.io downloads, and v0.2.2 (13 Apr 2026) had to fix deletes that were never written to the WAL and get/delete calls routed to the wrong partition.
- Large on-disk tables. Native WOS compaction reads the whole table's SSTable into a BTreeMap and rewrites it every 5,000 WAL entries, so write cost and peak memory grow with table size. Nothing above 10,000 rows is benchmarked.
- Many concurrent readers on file-backed tables. Every get/scan that reaches a file-backed table's WOS takes that table's single Mutex. The in-memory WOS uses one RwLock for all tables, and secondary-index updates take an RwLock (README disclaimer).
- Counts and small aggregates. The repo's own PERF_TRACKER measured SQLite SELECT count(*) at 5.66 us against 51 us for DBX. In the same run, file-backed per-row DBX inserts took 260.6 ms against 47.03 ms for rusqlite with a prepared statement.
- Lean builds. The default dependencies cannot be turned off and include arrow/parquet 54, tokio, s2n-quic, sqlparser, zstd, reed-solomon-erasure and several crypto crates, even if you only use the KV API.

**Integration:** crate · arrow 54, parquet 54, tokio, s2n-quic + rcgen, sqlparser 0.52, dashmap, crossbeam-skiplist, rayon, zstd, reed-solomon-erasure, aes-gcm-siv/chacha20poly1305/hkdf/sha2, bincode, serde, cron, chrono, tempfile, and others (all non-optional); optional cudarc 0.19 (CUDA 12.5) behind the 'gpu' feature · Rust edition 2024 (so Rust 1.85+); no rust-version declared; the benchmarks used rustc 1.92.0 · Pure Rust. CI builds and tests on ubuntu-latest (x86-64) only, and the published benchmarks ran on Windows 11 x64. A prebuilt win32-x64-msvc Node binary is committed. macOS and aarch64 support are not documented. GPU paths need NVIDIA CUDA.

**Vs siblings:** The other catalogued SQLite-beaters, CalicoDB (C++17 B+-tree, ~4.3x faster random reads), SNKV (1.6-2x at 1M records) and ForestDB (up to 8x reads), are measured at larger scale and on durable storage. Pick DBX only if you need a pure-Rust crate that bundles KV, SQL, Arrow/Parquet and optional CUDA, and you accept beta risk. For a proven on-disk KV store, prefer a sibling.

**Gotchas:**
- The MVCC tags can collide with user bytes. scan() treats values that start with [0x00,0x01] as MVCC values and strips those 2 bytes. It treats values that start with [0x00,0x02] as tombstones and drops the row. Keys of 10+ bytes that end in [0xDB,0x58] are parsed as versioned keys and lose their last 10 bytes. The get() fast path returns raw bytes, so get and scan can disagree on binary data. A source comment wrongly assumes binary data never starts with 0x00.
- Database::open defaults to DurabilityLevel::Lazy. append_to_wal only requests an fsync at Full, so acknowledged writes can be lost on a crash. Use open_safe for per-write fsync. open_in_memory has no WAL at all.
- insert() flushes Delta into the WOS synchronously on the caller's thread when the global entry count (all tables, overwrites included) reaches 10,000, which causes periodic latency spikes. Every insert also allocates a lossy UTF-8 copy of the key for partition routing.
- The docs are inconsistent. The storage-layers guide still says the WOS is built on sled (removed in 0.2.0) and that Tier 1 is a BTreeMap (the code uses DashMap + SkipMap). The benchmarks page mixes v0.0.6 and v0.2.0 numbers. open_in_memory also spawns a background worker thread per database.

**Status:** Young single-author project: created Feb 2026, 197 commits, no issues ever filed, 4 stars. The last commit and 0.2.2 release were on 13 Apr 2026, and that commit's CI run failed in the Node-binding job. It is MIT-licensed (a donation appendix makes GitHub show NOASSERTION) and usable from crates.io, but it is too large and immature to vendor as a SQLite replacement.

[repo](https://github.com/bytelogiccore-spec/DBX) · [benchmark](https://github.com/bytelogiccore-spec/DBX/blob/main/docs/english/benchmarks.md)

##### ForestDB  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Couchbase's embedded key-value engine built on an HB+-trie; first-party 2014 tests show up to 8x faster reads than SQLite.

**Beats:** SQLite — In a first-party 2014 test, Couchbase used a Nexus 5 (Snapdragon 800, 2GB RAM, Android 4.4.2) and loaded 1M documents (8-32 byte keys, 256-byte values) into ForestDB and into a two-column SQLite 3.7.11 table in WAL mode. It then timed 80K random reads, 80K random updates at batch sizes 1-20, and a two-thread mixed read/update run: ForestDB was up to 8x faster on reads, up to 2.3x faster on writes at larger batches (slower at batch 1), and up to 7x faster on the mixed run. The figures are 'up to' values read off charts, no compiler or flags are given, and the analysis is commented out of the live wiki page.

**Known shortcoming:** The 8x/2.3x/7x figures sit in a commented-out wiki page; master abandoned since 2019-05 (cb-master branch touched 2024-04, neo 2025-11).

**Known shortcoming:** Weak evidence: 2014 first-party 'up to' values read off charts with no compiler/flags; the analysis is commented out of the live wiki page. Master is frozen since 2019 and unsupported (last tag v1.2, 2016); shipping code lives on cb-master/neo; Couchbase Lite dropped it in 2.0. C API over a C++11 implementation.

**Known shortcoming:** Batch-1 synchronous writes are slower than SQLite; only read-committed/uncommitted isolation; append-only, so compaction is needed. Open bugs: malformed-file segfault (#23), master breaks aarch64 (#24) and VS2019 (#22), MSVC C callers hit a bool ABI mismatch (#17). Handles are not shareable across threads; one writer per file advised.

**How:** The primary index is an HB+-trie. Keys are split into fixed-size chunks (8 bytes by default), and each trie level is a B+-tree keyed on one chunk. That keeps node comparisons short and nodes block-aligned, so long or random keys need fewer disk reads. 'Leaf B+-trees' that store whole key suffixes limit the skew caused by repetitive key patterns. Writes are appended to a log-structured file and found through in-memory hash-table WAL indexes. The main index is updated in batches when the WAL passes a threshold (4,096 docs by default) or at commit, which spreads write amplification across batched writes. ForestDB also runs its own buffer cache, which weights index nodes above data pages and can use O_DIRECT, instead of relying on the OS page cache.

**Use it when:**
- Embedded storage where reads must never block on a writer. MVCC allows one writer plus many readers per file, e.g. UI-thread reads while a sync thread writes, which is why Couchbase Lite 1.x offered it.
- Long or hash-like keys (8+ bytes, roughly uniform), where HB+-trie chunking keeps the index small and shallow compared with a B+-tree that stores whole keys.
- Writes that can be batched into multi-document commits. In Couchbase's SQLite comparison, ForestDB only pulled ahead on writes as the batch size grew.
- Apps that need a change feed: iterate the sequence index from a saved sequence number to drive replication, backup or external secondary indexes.
- Apps that need cheap point-in-time snapshots or rollback of the whole store to an earlier commit header.

**Skip it when:**
- Single-document synchronous commits: at batch size 1 ForestDB was slower than SQLite in Couchbase's own mobile test, because append-only storage causes more write amplification.
- You need SQL, secondary indexes, or serializable or repeatable-read isolation. Only read committed and read uncommitted exist.
- You want an active, general-purpose upstream. 'master' has been frozen and unsupported since 2019, and the last tag is v1.2 (2016). Fixes land only on Couchbase release branches, and Couchbase Lite dropped ForestDB in 2.0 (issue #19).
- Disk-constrained devices: the append-only file grows until compaction copies live data into a new file. The wiki says compaction of very large stores can take tens of minutes to hours. Circular stale-block reuse (block_reusing_threshold) is the only mitigation, and it has to be tuned.
- Opening untrusted database files: a fuzzed malformed file segfaults forestdb_dump in superblock parsing (issue #23, open since 2022, no fix referenced).

**Integration:** shared lib · pthread; Snappy for optional document-body compression (built in by default on non-Windows standalone builds unless SNAPPY_OPTION=Disable); optional libaio (Linux), jemalloc, and OpenSSL, CommonCrypto or LibTomCrypt for encryption · C++11 compiler; CMake 3.1+ per INSTALL.md (the neo branch's CMakeLists requires 3.13); applications call the extern "C" API · README lists CentOS, Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, iOS and Android. The 'master' branch fails to build on aarch64 Linux (x86-only signal-handler code, issue #24) and with VS 2019 (offsetof error, issue #22). The 'neo' branch has AArch64 fixes and disables that handler.

**Vs siblings:** Against the other SQLite challengers catalogued (SNKV, CalicoDB, DBX, CacheAdvance), pick ForestDB when you need MVCC snapshots, a sequence-number change feed and readers that never block, and can live with a dormant upstream and the oldest, least reproducible numbers of the group. Against LSM siblings such as HyperLevelDB or Badger, its case is lower write amplification (Couchbase measured 7-20x per synchronous update vs LevelDB's 166-387x), not raw throughput.

**Gotchas:**
- The default GitHub branch 'master' contains changes Couchbase never shipped. Production code lives on 'cb-master' and 'neo', so check out one of those, or tag v1.2, rather than master.
- On MSVC, fdb_types.h does '#define bool int' for C callers, so fdb_config's layout differs from the C++-built library. Issue #17 reports broken fdb_get_default_config results unless the caller is also compiled as C++.
- Nothing is durable until fdb_commit, and the async durability modes can lose data on a crash. Deletes remain as tombstones until compaction purges them. Snapshot or rollback calls to sequence numbers that a concurrent compaction has already dropped return errors.
- The buffer cache is global: buffercache_size is ignored once the first fdb_open has initialized it. A file created in auto-compaction mode cannot be opened in manual mode, or the reverse, without calling fdb_switch_compaction_mode.

**Status:** 'master' has been frozen and unsupported since May 2019, but the Apache-2.0 'neo' branch still gets occasional Couchbase fixes (last commit 2025-11-21). Current Couchbase Server Community Edition docs still name ForestDB as the standard index storage engine, and a small community fork (ForestDB-KVStore/forestdb, last push April 2025) adds Conan packaging.

[repo](https://github.com/couchbaselabs/forestdb) · [benchmark](https://github.com/couchbaselabs/forestdb/wiki/Performance-Results)

##### HaloDB  `Java`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Java embedded key-value store for point lookups: append-only logs plus an off-heap hash index. Beats RocksDB on random writes and reads in IO-bound tests.

**Beats:** RocksDB — This is a first-party benchmark from about 2018: 500M records with 8-byte keys and 1 KB values (about 500 GB) on 2x Xeon E5-2680, 128 GB RAM, one Samsung PM863 SSD and RHEL 6. It compared HaloDB with rocksdbjni 5.7.2 (WAL disabled, Snappy on L2 and above, custom 10 MB L1 tuning) and KyotoCabinet; the JVM version and flags are not stated. HaloDB won fill-random 127 vs 10 MB/s, random update 19 vs 2 MB/s, 32-thread random reads 94,409 vs 59,936 ops/s (about 1.6x) and mixed read+update 45,750 vs 8,625 reads/s and 6,144 vs 2,691 writes/s. It lost sorted-order fill to RocksDB, 133 vs 165 MB/s.

**Known shortcoming:** RocksDB wins sequential fill (165 vs 133 MB/s); the gains (fill-random 12.7x, update 9.5x, read 1.6x) are vs rocksdbjni 5.7.2; abandoned.

**Known shortcoming:** Abandoned (last release v0.5.6, 2021-05); Java 8 with sun.misc.Unsafe (deprecated in JDK 23); the jar is not on Maven Central. Keys max 127 B and all keys live in RAM (~44 GB per 1B 8-byte keys); open scans all index files (minutes). One global write lock (single writer); no range scans/batches/transactions; not durable by default. The benchmark used RocksDB 5.7.2 with WAL off and an odd 10 MB L1; JVM unstated; Windows repair bug #23.

**How:** It uses a Bitcask/Haystack-style log-structured hash design. Every write is a sequential append to a data file (1 GB in the examples). An in-memory hash index maps each key to its file id, value offset, size and sequence number, so a get needs at most one positional disk read (read amplification 1). The index lives off the Java heap to avoid GC pressure. It is derived from OHC, segmented like Java 7's ConcurrentHashMap with 2x-cores segments, and has an optional slab memory pool for fixed-size keys. A rate-limited background thread rewrites any file whose stale fraction passes a threshold, so a 50% threshold gives about 2x write amplification. Yahoo measured 10-12x for RocksDB on its own workload. Deletes go to separate tombstone files, and no key ordering is maintained.

**Use it when:**
- JVM services doing only point lookups, where the data set is much larger than RAM but every key plus about 20 bytes of metadata fits in memory (e.g. 8-byte keys with 1-10 KB values)
- Write-heavy random insert/update workloads on SSD where LSM write amplification is the bottleneck: 127 vs 10 MB/s fill-random and 19 vs 2 MB/s random update against RocksDB in the project's test
- One writer thread (e.g. a consumer draining a Kafka log) with many concurrent readers that need sub-millisecond p99 reads, the setup Yahoo ran in production
- Kyoto Cabinet replacement in Java where fast crash recovery matters: only the one or two files being written need repair

**Skip it when:**
- You need range scans, ordered or prefix iteration, write batches, transactions or column families. Stay on RocksDB.
- Keys are longer than 127 bytes, or the whole key set will not fit in RAM. Yahoo quotes about 44 GB for 1 billion 8-byte keys with the memory pool and about 64 GB without.
- Bulk loads in sorted key order: RocksDB won that test (165 vs 133 MB/s). Disk use is also higher (556 GB vs RocksDB's 504 GB after 500M random updates).
- Restart time matters: opening a database scans every index and tombstone file to rebuild the index, which the README says can take minutes.
- You need a maintained dependency on a current JDK: the code targets Java 8 and relies on sun.misc.Unsafe, which is deprecated in JDK 23 (issue #63). The last release was 2021, and the Yahoo artifacts are not on Maven Central.

**Integration:** module · slf4j-api 1.7.12, Guava 18.0, JNA 4.1.0 (native malloc for the off-heap index); lz4 1.3 optional. Jar is com.oath.halodb:halodb 0.5.6, published only to GitHub Packages (needs a token) or via JitPack as com.github.yahoo:HaloDB; not on Maven Central. · Java 8 (compiled with source/target 1.8; CI runs only JDK 8). The README says newer JDKs are untested. A user in issue #63 reports it running on Java 22. · The README says it was tested on Linux x86 and macOS. It needs a 64-bit JVM (the Uns class rejects address sizes above 8 bytes). Windows has an open bug where repair after an unclean shutdown fails (issue #23). Tuning advice: disable Transparent Huge Pages and set vm.swappiness=0.

**Vs siblings:** Pick HaloDB when you must stay inside a Java process and only need point gets, puts and deletes. Badger and Pogreb (Go) and NuDB (C++) cannot be embedded directly in the JVM. If you can leave the JVM or need ordered access, one of those siblings or RocksDB fits better.

**Gotchas:**
- The key limit is really 127 bytes (Byte.MAX_VALUE, checked in HaloDBInternal.put), not the 128 the README says. With the memory pool on, any key longer than the declared fixedKeySize is rejected.
- Writes are not durable by default. They land in the OS page cache and are synced only after flushDataSizeBytes accumulates, unless enableSyncWrites(true) is set, which the author says costs significant write throughput. After a power loss, interleaved puts and deletes keep only partial ordering.
- Interrupting a thread during IO makes the JVM close the FileChannel it was using, and the README warns not to do this.
- Set setNumberOfRecords (about 2x the expected key count) up front, or the off-heap index has to rehash. Without the memory pool every write calls native malloc, so the README recommends jemalloc against fragmentation.

**Status:** The Yahoo repository is abandoned: the last release is v0.5.6 (May 2021), the last commit is from April 2023, and an open 'Project status?' issue has no maintainer reply. It is Apache-2.0 and about 50 Java files, so it can be vendored. The live continuation is the community fork outr/HaloDB (halodb-revive 0.7.0 on Maven Central, JDK 22+, FFM instead of Unsafe, longer keys, prefix scans), but that fork is new and has almost no adoption.

[repo](https://github.com/yahoo/HaloDB) · [benchmark](https://github.com/yahoo/HaloDB/blob/master/docs/benchmarks.md)

##### HSE (Heterogeneous-memory Storage Engine)  `C`  `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Micron's embedded C key-value engine for NVMe SSDs; its own YCSB run shows about 8x RocksDB's load throughput.

**Beats:** RocksDB — In Micron's own v1 docs (YCSB 0.17.0, 2 billion 1,000-byte records, 96 client threads, a 2-socket Xeon E5-2690 v4 with 256 GB DRAM, four Micron 9300 NVMe drives striped with LVM, RHEL 8.1), HSE 1.7.0 from the mpool kernel-module era loaded at 986K inserts/s against 123K for RocksDB 6.6.4 (about 8x, 34 vs 271 minutes, p99.9 of 1.6 vs 19.5 ms), and run-phase gains of 'up to nearly 6x' on workloads A-D appear only as charts. RocksDB tuning, compiler and flags are not stated, the current 3.x storage layout was never re-measured, and no independent reproduction was found.

**Known shortcoming:** Numbers come from the v1 docs; the project is abandoned.

**Known shortcoming:** Speed numbers are Micron's own, for HSE 1.7 (2020, which needed the mpool kernel module; 2.0+ runs in userspace on XFS/ext4) vs RocksDB 6.6.4 with unstated tuning; 3.x was never re-measured and no independent reproduction exists. Archived: last commit 2023-08, last release 3.0.0 (2022-11), open bugs #630/#631; the storage format broke at 1 to 2 to 3 (dump and reload each time).

**Known shortcoming:** Linux x86-64/s390x only, SSD only, one KVDB per process, values <=1 MiB, keys ~1.3 KB; own API, not a RocksDB drop-in (no merge operator/WriteBatch/MultiGet/backup). A ~200 s startup put throttle skews benchmarks (#9); commits are async with a 100 ms journal flush; the REST socket is on by default.

**How:** Writes go into c0, an in-memory layer of RCU-protected Bonsai trees split into up to 32 hash-sharded c0_kvsets, and ingest then moves them into a shallow cN tree whose root node spills into key-range leaf nodes. Each on-media kvset keeps keys (kblocks with a 'wants to be a B-tree' index and Bloom filters) apart from values (vblocks), so k-compaction rewrites only keys and node split and join change only metadata; that key-value separation is the likely source of the up-to-85% fewer bytes written than RocksDB's leveled compaction. A scheduler driven by space amplification (sp3) uses HyperLogLog garbage estimates to decide when to spill or compact, and ingest throttling keeps tail latency down. Media-class policies can also pin keys to fast storage while values tier down to cheaper SSDs.

**Use it when:**
- Insert- or update-heavy ingest of billions of roughly 1 KB records onto local NVMe when the dataset is several times DRAM (the benchmark put 2 TB on a 256 GB host) and load time or SSD write volume is the bottleneck.
- Data with natural key prefixes, such as per-tenant, per-device or time-epoch keys. A KVS created with a matching prefix.length gives you prefix-filtered cursors and single-call prefix deletes for bulk expiry.
- Tiered SSD setups: set mclass.policy=staging_max_capacity to keep keys and the journal on TLC or pmem and move values to QLC, cutting writes to the low-endurance drives.
- Embedded C or C++ services on x86-64 (or s390x) Linux that need atomic, snapshot-isolated transactions across several KVSs and can accept an asynchronous durability window.

**Skip it when:**
- You need RocksDB's API or feature set. There is no compatibility layer, the public API has no merge operator, WriteBatch, MultiGet, arbitrary range delete or backup engine, and the issue asking for backup/restore options (#4) is still open.
- You need an engine someone maintains. The last master commit was 2023-08-17 and the last release was 3.0.0 in November 2022. Reported bugs (#630, #631) sit unfixed, and each major version (1 to 2 to 3) changed the storage format, so data had to be dumped and reloaded.
- Non-Linux targets, HDDs or small machines. The docs support only Linux on x86_64 or s390x, SSD volumes only, a filesystem with O_DIRECT and fallocate punch-hole support, and recommend 32 GB of RAM or more.
- One process needs several databases, or items exceed the hard limits: only one KVDB can be open per process, values are capped at 1 MiB and keys at about 1.3 KB.
- You need each write to be durable when it returns. Commits are asynchronous, and by default the journal is flushed every 100 ms (durability.interval_ms) unless you call hse_kvdb_sync().

**Integration:** shared lib (libhse-3, built from source with Meson; Meson can also build it static) · userspace-rcu, libbsd, libevent, lz4 and cJSON (lz4 and cJSON are built in as Meson subprojects by default), xxHash; libcurl for the CLI and tools only; libpmem (optional, for pmem on x86) · C (gnu11), Meson >= 0.63.0; minimum compiler versions not documented · 64-bit Linux on x86-64 or s390x (other architectures compile through generic fallbacks but are not listed as supported); tested on RHEL 8/9, Ubuntu 18.04 to 22.04 and Fedora 35/36; storage must be SSD or pmem on XFS/ext4 (DAX for pmem)

**Vs siblings:** Over SplinterDB, which makes a similar NVMe insert claim (6-10x RocksDB), pick HSE when you want its cross-KVS snapshot-isolation transactions, prefix deletes and multi-tier media placement. If you need the RocksDB API itself, or active upkeep, Speedb or ToplingDB is the drop-in route.

**Gotchas:**
- Puts are throttled when the engine starts and self-tune over roughly 200 seconds (issue #9), which badly skews short benchmarks. Profile the storage with `hse storage profile` and set throttling.init_policy. Under load, the put path adds short sleeps unless you pass HSE_KVS_PUT_PRIO.
- A KVS opened with transactions.enabled=true rejects non-transactional updates, and a KVS opened with it false rejects transactions. Prefix deletes need a filter exactly equal to the prefix.length fixed at KVS creation.
- Deletes and updates do not free space right away. k-compaction leaves values that are no longer referenced inside vblocks, and garbage from prefix tombstones is not counted in the space-amplification estimate (docs/space-amp.md).
- By default each process starts a REST server on a UNIX socket (rest.enabled=true), and error codes are hse_err_t, not errno. Use hse_strerror() or hse_err_to_errno(), because strerror() gives meaningless results.

**Status:** Abandoned since its last commit on 2023-08-17 (last release 3.0.0, Nov 2022); the Apache-2.0 OR MIT license makes it forkable, but it is a large Linux-only C engine rather than something to vendor lightly, and the benchmarked 1.x line depended on the mpool kernel module, whose repo (mpool-kmod) is now archived.

[repo](https://github.com/hse-project/hse) · [benchmark](https://github.com/hse-project/hse-project.github.io/blob/master/v1/docs/apps/ycsb.md)

##### lsm-tree-go  `Go`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Small learning-project LSM-tree KV store in Go; beats bbolt only on batched random writes, loses reads and sequential writes.

**Beats:** BoltDB — The README table has one win: random writes at 1.19M/s vs bbolt v1.4.3's 0.23M/s (about 5.2x). It loses to bbolt on sequential writes (1.98M vs 2.77M), reads (0.44M vs 1.17M) and misses (1.08M vs 1.96M), and BadgerDB v4.9.1 leads on every column. The run was Linux with 4 CPUs of unstated model, Go given only by go.mod's 1.25.4, 1M keys and 1,000-key batches, with keys and values described as 11 bytes although bench/compare generates 12-byte ones. bench/compare runs NoWAL, SyncAsync and SyncAlways against synced and unsynced baselines, and the README does not say which row the table shows. Older hardcoded Linux figures in bench/fulltable.go, possibly from a Lima VM, give 0.76M vs 0.27M/s (about 2.8x) for SyncAlways vs bbolt with fsync per commit.

**Known shortcoming:** Beats BoltDB only on random writes (5.2x) and loses sequential writes, reads and misses; BoltDB is not a listed baseline; README says MIT but there is no LICENSE file; a toy project.

**Known shortcoming:** Not importable (all packages under internal/ and the module path differs from the repo); the win is only random writes vs bbolt (1.19M vs 0.23M/s), losing sequential writes, reads and misses (Badger wins every column); on macOS it loses even random writes. fulltable.go prints hard-coded numbers rather than measuring.

**Known shortcoming:** From code reading: Get scans L0 oldest-first (stale reads, undone deletes possible); flush runs in the caller's PutBatch and compaction holds a DB-wide write lock; errors are dropped. Crash windows: WAL truncated before MANIFEST, inputs deleted before MANIFEST, orphan .sst deleted, NoWAL Close loses the memtable, SyncIouring broken. Two commits in one day; no scans/transactions; no Windows.

**How:** Writes are buffered. Each PutBatch is serialised into one CRC32-framed record, appended to an mmap'd write-ahead log (one fdatasync per batch in the default SyncAlways mode), and inserted into a Go map memtable pre-sized for 200k entries. At 4 MB the map is sorted and written sequentially to an mmap'd SSTable, and leveled compaction (10x per level, heap-based k-way merge) runs later. This turns random-key inserts into sequential file writes, which is why it beats bbolt's copy-on-write B+tree on random writes but not on sorted ones. Reads check the map, then probe every SSTable in every level in turn, each through a 10-bits/key FNV-1a double-hashing Bloom filter and then a sparse index (every 128th key) plus a linear scan. The README says reads touch 'one file per level', but the code does not do that, and each probe re-hashes the key and allocates strings, which fits the low 0.44M/s read rate.

**Use it when:**
- Studying or teaching LSM internals: about 52 KB of non-test Go in seven small internal packages covers the WAL, memtable, SSTable format, Bloom filter, sparse index, JSON MANIFEST and leveled compaction, and the README has pprof-driven optimization notes.
- As a starting point for an experimental Go storage engine you intend to own, where you will add range scans, write concurrency and crash-consistency work yourself.
- Batched (about 1,000 keys per call) random-order ingestion of small string keys on Linux, where bbolt's random-insert rate (0.23M/s in the author's table) is the bottleneck and point Get/Put/Delete is enough. Even there, BadgerDB was about 5.9x faster in the same table.

**Skip it when:**
- Reads or mixed workloads. In the author's own table it does 0.44M/s point reads and 1.08M/s misses, against bbolt's 1.17M/1.96M and Badger's 1.29M/1.49M.
- Sorted or sequential bulk loads (bbolt 2.77M/s and Badger 7.30M/s vs 1.98M/s), or anything that needs range scans, iterators, transactions, snapshots, []byte values or concurrent writers. None of these exist.
- macOS. The hardcoded macOS table in bench/fulltable.go shows 191k sequential, 128k random-write and 164k read ops/s in SyncAsync mode, against bbolt NoSync's 2.35M/162k/1.18M. So on macOS it loses even random writes unless both sides fsync.
- Data you cannot afford to lose. There are 2 commits from one day and no issues or releases. The tests are too small to exercise compaction, and there are the stale-read and crash-window problems listed under gotchas.
- Windows: the code calls syscall.Mmap/Munmap, which Go provides only on Unix, and Windows is not documented.

**Integration:** source-drop (every package is under internal/ and go.mod declares module github.com/aasheesh/lsmtree, which does not match the repo path, so it cannot be go-get'd or imported from another module) · none for the engine (Go standard library only: syscall mmap, hash/fnv, hash/crc32, container/heap). The bbolt v1.4.3 and BadgerDB v4.9.1 entries in go.mod are used only by bench/compare. · Go 1.25.4 (go.mod 'go' directive) · Linux (fdatasync, optional io_uring WAL mode) and other Unix systems with syscall.Mmap, such as macOS (fsync fallback). Pure Go and architecture-independent. Windows is not supported.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only when you want a small, readable Go LSM to study or fork. For a real Go embedded store pick Badger, which beat it on every column of this same benchmark (7.30M vs 1.98M sequential writes/s, 1.29M vs 0.44M reads/s) and has transactions and iterators. For read-heavy Go point lookups consider Pogreb.

**Gotchas:**
- It cannot be imported as a module. All packages sit under internal/ and the module path is github.com/aasheesh/lsmtree, so you must copy the tree into your own module and rewrite the imports.
- Possible stale reads (from code reading). Get scans L0 SSTables oldest-first and returns the first hit, so a key that was overwritten or deleted across two not-yet-compacted L0 files (up to 8 are kept) can return the older value. A file's 'max key' is taken from its last sparse-index entry (every 128th key), so L0-to-L1 overlap detection can miss files. The shipped tests cannot catch this: with at most 50k keys, writing 0.3-2 MB against 0.5-4 MB flush thresholds, the correctness and 'compaction' tests flush at most once, never compact, and read overwrites back only from the memtable. The benchmark ignores the values it reads.
- Write and read stalls. The memtable flush runs synchronously inside the caller's PutBatch, and a forced L0 compaction also runs there once L0 exceeds 16 files. The 'background' compaction goroutine holds the DB-wide write lock while it merges all of level L with all of level L+1, which blocks readers and writers. Compaction errors are discarded.
- Durability varies by mode, and there are crash windows. The zero-value WALSyncMode is SyncAlways (fdatasync per batch). SyncAsync can lose about 10 ms of writes. NoWAL, the fastest mode in bench/compare, loses the unflushed memtable even on a clean Close(), because Close never flushes.
