SyncIouring is broken as written: the ring's file offset starts at 0, writes are submitted only when the 256-entry ring fills, and the WAL cursor never advances, so Close truncates the log, and reopening an existing WAL in that mode is refused. A flush truncates the WAL before the MANIFEST lists the new SSTable, and compaction deletes its inputs before rewriting the MANIFEST. Open silently skips unreadable SSTables and deletes any .sst file not in the MANIFEST, so a crash in either window loses data. The crash test uses SIGKILL only, not power loss, a point HN commenters also raised.

**Status:** This is a single code drop: two commits on 2026-05-31, nothing since, and no releases, tags, issues or PRs. It is MIT only through a one-word README section with no LICENSE file. It is small enough to vendor by copying, but treat it as study material rather than a dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/AasheeshLikePanner/lsm-tree-go) · [benchmark](https://github.com/AasheeshLikePanner/lsm-tree-go#benchmarks)

##### NuDB  `C++`  `BSL-1.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Header-only, insert-only on-disk hash table for SSDs; its own benchmark shows higher insert and large-DB fetch throughput than default-config RocksDB.

**Beats:** RocksDB — By default the project's bench.cpp inserts 64-byte random keys with random values of 250-750 bytes in single-threaded batches of 20,000, then fetches random existing keys; RocksDB is opened with default Options, with only create_if_missing set. The README 'sample output' has NuDB at about 1.45-1.75x RocksDB's insert ops/s at 100K and 1M keys, about 10-16x RocksDB's fetch ops/s at 1M and 10M keys, and about 0.47x at 100K keys. With default settings each cell is a single 20,000-op batch. No CPU, SSD, compiler, flags or RocksDB version is given, and NuDB's commit (a close/reopen between phases) falls outside the timed insert loop.

**Known shortcoming:** Bench numbers are 'sample output' with no CPU, SSD, compiler, flags or RocksDB version; each cell is one 20K-op batch; RocksDB runs with default Options and NuDB's commit isn't timed in the insert loop. Loses fetch at 100K keys (~0.47x RocksDB). Insert-only (no update, delete or range scan), fixed-size keys, not durable until the ~1 s background commit, no multi-process access (#72), very slow on HDD (#67). Stale since 2021 apart from small fixes; CI only on GCC 5-8/Clang 6-8/Boost 1.69; no 32-bit (#2). Fetch callbacks can run under an internal lock and stall commits (#53).

**How:** The key file is a bucketed linear-hashing table (Litwin/Larson): each bucket is one device block (default 4096 bytes) of entries sorted by a 48-bit prefix of a salted xxHash64, so a fetch is usually one pread of the bucket plus one pread of the value, with no LSM levels or compaction to make reads costlier as the DB grows. Full buckets spill into records appended to the data file, which form a linked list. Inserts go into an in-memory pool, and a background context thread commits them about once per second with bulk sequential appends and a rollback log; the README says locks are never held during disk reads or writes.

**Use it when:**
- Write-once, read-many data with fixed-size keys, especially content-addressable storage keyed by a 32- or 64-byte hash (rippled/XRPL node store is the reference deployment, reported at over 3 TB and later over 10 TB).
- Random point lookups over data sets much larger than RAM on SSD/NVMe, where you want roughly constant per-lookup I/O and memory use that does not grow with DB size.
- Sustained single-writer ingestion where losing up to about one second of unflushed inserts on a crash is acceptable, but on-disk consistency after the crash is required (the log file rolls back partial commits).
- Projects that want a header-only dependency and already build with Boost.

**Skip it when:**
- Any workload that needs update, overwrite, delete, TTL or compaction: records are immutable, duplicate inserts fail with key_exists, and removing data means rewriting the whole DB offline (issue #98).
- Range scans, prefix queries, ordered iteration or variable-length keys; the only iteration is a sequential walk of the data file in insertion order.
- Spinning disks: the author says it 'will be extremely slow' on HDDs (issue #67).
- Multi-process access or several store instances on the same files: the author says this is undefined behavior (issue #72).
- Small data sets that fit in cache: in the project's own sample run RocksDB fetched about 2.1x faster at 100K keys.

**Integration:** header-only · Boost 1.69+ (Boost.System and Boost.Thread must be linked; uses boost::optional, boost::shared_mutex); bench needs RocksDB, zlib and snappy; tests need Boost.Beast · README says C++11; the CMake build sets cxx_std_14. CI covered GCC 5-8 and Clang 6-8 on Ubuntu 16.04 plus VS2019; newer compilers not documented. · 64-bit Linux and other POSIX (pread/pwrite, posix_fadvise skipped on macOS) and Windows (win32_file); 32-bit correctness is an open issue (#2). SSD or other high-IOPS storage required.

**Vs siblings:** Pick NuDB over SplinterDB, TerarkDB or Titan only when data is truly append-only with fixed-size hash keys and you want a small header-only engine with O(1) point lookups. For updates, deletes, range queries or a RocksDB-compatible API, those siblings (or RocksDB itself) are the better fit.

**Gotchas:**
- Inserts are buffered in memory and committed about once per second by a background thread, so they are not durable when insert returns; call close (or context::flush in manual mode) to commit. The destructor calls close but discards its error. After one failed commit, every later insert and fetch returns that error until the DB is closed.
- Key size, block size, load factor, salt and Hasher are fixed at create time; opening with a different Hasher fails the pepper check. Values must be 1 byte to 4 GB (a zero-length value trips an assert, issue #101). Tune block size to the device and AllocSize to the average value size.
- The fetch callback can run while an internal shared lock is held (when the key is still in the uncommitted insert pool), so a slow callback can stall the commit thread (issue #53).
- insert is not write-only: its duplicate check reads the key-file bucket (plus the data file on a hash match). Writers get 25 ms sleeps when the insert rate beats the measured flush rate and more than the 4 MB burst (set_burst) is buffered; issue #83 traced rippled latency spikes to the earlier throttle logic.

**Status:** Stale: only a missing-includes fix (July 2024) and a 2.0.9 version bump (April 2025) since 2021, and the author calls it mature with 'nothing more to do' (issue #96). It is BSL-1.0 and header-only, so easy to vendor, but CI only targeted old toolchains (GCC 5-8, Clang 6-8, Boost 1.69).

[repo](https://github.com/cppalliance/NuDB) · [benchmark](https://github.com/cppalliance/NuDB/blob/master/bench/README.md)

##### Pebble (CockroachDB storage engine)  `Go`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Go LSM key-value store that replaced RocksDB inside CockroachDB; meets or beats RocksDB on YCSB in vendor benchmarks.

**Beats:** RocksDB — A 2020-09-15 Cockroach Labs post shows unlabeled YCSB bar charts: on a 3-node CockroachDB cluster (A-F) Pebble beat RocksDB by about 0-7% (E tied), and in a storage-engine-only run through the public cmd/pebble YCSB tool (A-E) by about 1.2-1.3x, with about 1.85x on read-only C, all on in-memory datasets. The post names no CPU, instance type, Go or RocksDB version, or flags (RocksDB was presumably 6.2.1, the last version CockroachDB used), and it lists avoiding the cgo boundary as an advantage, so part of the gap may be call overhead; the project's nightly benchmark page tracks Pebble alone, with no RocksDB line.

**Known shortcoming:** Evidence is charts only: engine-level ~1.2-1.3x (YCSB-C ~1.85x) and 0-7% at the CockroachDB level; the engine-only run has no workload F; a Go reimplementation tuned for CockroachDB, not a general RocksDB drop-in.

**Known shortcoming:** Go library only (no C/C++ API). Not a drop-in: no column families, transactions, backups or universal/FIFO compaction; v2+ cannot open RocksDB databases and the README warns of silent corruption with unsupported features. Part of the storage-level gain may be cgo call overhead on the RocksDB side; in-memory data only with no hardware/versions. Must Close() the closer from Get or leak off-heap memory; tiny defaults (8 MB cache, 4 MB memtable); one-way format ratchet. Open issues: SST corruption on GCP Hyperdisk (#5726), CRC mismatch (#6175), iterator-state bug (#6168).

**How:** RocksDB groups concurrent commits into leader/follower batch groups. Pebble instead copies each batch into the WAL buffer under a short mutex, applies it to the lock-free memtable skiplist concurrently, and publishes visible sequence numbers in order through a lock-free single-producer multi-consumer commit queue, which removes the group-concatenation copy and most thread handoffs. The block cache is split into 4 x NumCPU CLOCK-Pro shards whose memory comes from C malloc, outside the Go heap so the GC never scans it; the vendor post credits this cache concurrency for the ~1.85x gap on read-only YCSB C. Smaller contributors: L0 sublevels with flush splitting, a copy-on-write B-tree for file metadata, delete-only compactions under range tombstones, block-property filters that skip blocks, separate flush and compaction pacing, and on newer formats columnar sstable blocks and value separation into blob files; inside a Go program it also avoids a cgo crossing on every call.

**Use it when:**
- A Go service that needs an embedded ordered KV store with RocksDB-style semantics (snapshots, range deletes, merge operators, SST ingestion, prefix bloom filters) without calling C++ through cgo on every operation or maintaining a C++ build.
- Read-heavy, highly concurrent workloads whose working set fits in the block cache. This is where the storage-only comparison showed its largest gain (~1.85x on YCSB C).
- Write-heavy LSM workloads where read amplification in L0 hurts during write bursts: L0 sublevels and flush splitting target exactly this case.
- Large block caches (tens of GB) in a Go process. Cache and memtable memory live outside the Go heap, which avoids the ~2x RSS blowup the docs describe for GC-managed caches.
- You want an engine that has been the production default of CockroachDB since v20.2 (Nov 2020), with metamorphic and crash testing plus nightly benchmarks.

**Skip it when:**
- C, C++ or Rust applications: it is a Go library with no C/C++ API, so from those languages RocksDB (or a RocksDB derivative) remains the practical choice.
- You need RocksDB features Pebble omits: column families, transactions, backups, universal or FIFO compaction, tailing iterators, persistent cache, plain or hash table formats, sub-compactions.
- Migrating an existing RocksDB database: v2+ refuses RocksDB-generated DBs, the path runs through v1 plus format-major-version upgrades, and the README warns that unsupported RocksDB features can silently corrupt data.
- Storage-bound or out-of-cache workloads, or when judging end-to-end impact: the published comparison covers only in-memory datasets, and at the CockroachDB cluster level the gain was about 0-7% (workload E tied).
- You depend on direct I/O or io_uring. Neither is part of the design: an io_uring prototype is only an open issue (#4684), and in a 2020 HN thread a maintainer said direct I/O hurt performance in their experiments.

**Integration:** module · Go modules only, including DataDog/zstd (cgo) or a pure-Go zstd fallback without cgo, golang/snappy, minio/minlz, cockroachdb/errors, cockroachdb/swiss, prometheus client_golang, xxhash/xxh3, google/btree. cgo is optional: with it, cache and memtable buffers come from C malloc; without it, from Go sync.Pool size classes. · Go 1.23 for the v2.1.7 tag (module path github.com/cockroachdb/pebble/v2); master's go.mod requires Go 1.25.3 and uses the unsuffixed path; CI runs Go 1.26 · PR CI: Linux amd64 (including no-cgo and race builds) and macOS 14. Nightly: Linux 386, Linux arm64, Windows, and s390x under qemu (big-endian).

**Vs siblings:** Pick Pebble over the other Go stores in the catalog, Badger and the lookup-focused Pogreb, when you need full RocksDB-style LSM semantics (range tombstones, merge operators, snapshots, SST ingestion) and CockroachDB's production track record, even though Badger's catalogued speedups over RocksDB are much larger. In C++ services, a RocksDB-derived option like Speedb or the Titan plugin keeps you inside the RocksDB ecosystem.

**Gotchas:**
- Get returns (value, closer, err), and you must call closer.Close(). Cache blocks are reference-counted, manually allocated memory, so a missed Close is a real leak rather than garbage the GC will collect.
- Defaults are small and conservative: 8 MB block cache, 4 MB memtable, and FormatMajorVersion defaults to the oldest supported format (FormatFlushableIngest). Columnar blocks and value separation stay off until you ratchet the format, and ratcheting is permanent.
- Batches are capped at 4 GB, and indexed batches need extra skiplist memory beyond that. The docs point to DB.Ingest of prebuilt sstables for larger atomic writes.
- The docs lag the code: the README's format table ends at FormatColumnarBlocks, while master defines newer formats (FormatValueSeparation, FormatV2BlobFiles, and others). Open issues include SST corruption reports on GCP Hyperdisk (#5726), an unexplained CRC32C mismatch (#6175) and an iterator-state bug in DeletableValueMerger (#6168).

**Status:** Actively maintained (last master commit 2026-09-10, v2.1.7 tagged 2026-08-24, release branches through crl-release-26.2) and usable as an ordinary BSD-3-Clause Go module, though its roadmap and format changes follow CockroachDB's needs.

[repo](https://github.com/cockroachdb/pebble) · [benchmark](https://www.cockroachlabs.com/blog/pebble-rocksdb-kv-store/)

##### Pogreb  `Go`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Go embedded key-value store with an on-disk hash index; roughly 10-23x goleveldb random-lookup throughput in the author's chart.

**Beats:** goleveldb (pure-Go port of LevelDB; the C++ LevelDB was not tested) — The README's only numbers are a 2018-2019 chart (pre-0.9 design without a WAL) of single-goroutine random Get throughput after a DB reopen on a DigitalOcean droplet with 8 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM and SSD (Ubuntu 16.04): pogreb falls from about 1.23M to 0.69M reads/s between 10K and 10M keys, while goleveldb (the Go port, not C++ LevelDB, opened with compression off and no bloom filter configured) falls from about 0.13M to 0.03M, roughly 10-23x slower; bolt is about 4-6x and badger about 10-13x slower. No Go version, CPU model or run flags are given, and at the tool's default key/value sizes even 10M keys (about 3.6 GB, derived) fit in the page cache, though a 2025 third-party test with 50M records (issue #35) agrees on direction: pogreb 2.29M QPS, pebble 1.50M, badger 0.70M, SQLite 0.14M.

**Known shortcoming:** The real baseline is goleveldb (the Go port), not C++ LevelDB; the ~10-20x is read off a 2018-19 chart that predates the 2020 WAL redesign.

**Known shortcoming:** Any unclean shutdown triggers a full index rebuild from the WAL (~8 days at billions of records, #35). No fsync by default; with compaction off the disk grows (26 GB vs bbolt 300 MB, #66); hard 2^32-key cap from a 32-bit hash (#38). No range scans, transactions or batches; one writer lock blocks reads; one process per DB. Larger-than-RAM reads collapse to ~420 ops/s (#54); Windows writes ~10x slower (#25); Windows ARM64 does not build (#76); last tag v0.10.2 (2023-12).

**Independent measurement:** Third-party test in issue #35 (2025, 50M records): pogreb 2.29M QPS vs Pebble 1.50M and Badger 0.70M reads.

**How:** Keys are hashed with seeded 32-bit MurmurHash3 into an on-disk linear-hashing table (Litwin's algorithm). The table uses 512-byte buckets of 31 fixed-size slots (hash, segment ID, key size, value size, 32-bit offset), chains overflow buckets, and splits one bucket at a time at a 0.7 load factor. A Get reads one bucket, scans its slots for a matching 32-bit hash and key length, then reads the record from the WAL segment and compares the full key: about two random reads per lookup, where an LSM tree or B+tree probes several levels. Index and segment files are memory-mapped read-only with MADV_RANDOM, and writes go through pwrite, so warm lookups are memory reads with no cache on the Go heap; the author's 2018 design post says the switch to mmap nearly doubled lookup speed over plain file I/O.

**Use it when:**
- A Go service whose on-disk map is read far more than it is written and needs only point Get/Has, for example a lookup table rebuilt daily and then served read-only (the author's original use case).
- Tens to hundreds of millions of keys (well below the hard 2^32-key cap) that are too large for a Go map but whose index and hot records fit in the OS page cache.
- You want the lowest random-lookup latency and memory use among pure-Go stores. In a 2025 third-party test with 50M records (issue #35), pogreb had a p99 of 5 us against pebble's 13 us and badger's 254 us, with about 42 MB of RAM.
- You need pure Go with zero module dependencies and no cgo, cross-compiling for Linux, macOS or Windows on amd64 or 386.

**Skip it when:**
- You need range or prefix scans, sorted iteration, transactions, atomic multi-key batches or snapshots. The hash index cannot provide any of them.
- Restart time after a crash matters at scale. Any unclean shutdown makes the next Open discard the index and replay the entire WAL; a user with billions of records estimated this at about 8 days (#35), and another user moved to pebble for this reason.
- Write- or update-heavy workloads. A single RWMutex means each write blocks all readers. Compaction is off by default, so overwrites keep growing the disk footprint: one user reported 26 GB where bbolt used 300 MB (#66). Windows writes are about 10x slower than on Linux (#25, open since 2019).
- Random lookups over data much larger than RAM. On an 8 GB Debian server with 10M keys, reads through mmap dropped to about 420 ops/s and were still slow at 100M keys without mmap (#54, open).
- More than about 1-2 billion keys: collisions rise toward the 2^32 limit (#38). Also out: several processes sharing one DB (a lock file blocks this), low-memory 32-bit ARM (1 GiB initial mmap fails with ENOMEM, #72) and Windows ARM64 (build fails in v0.10.2, #76).

**Integration:** module · none (go.mod has no require lines) · Go 1.18 (go.mod; CI tests 1.18.x and latest 1.x) · Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 (CI matrix), with GOARCH=386 build-tested; Plan 9 uses a non-mmap backend on main; Windows ARM64 does not build in v0.10.2 (#76)

**Vs siblings:** Badger is the other catalogued pure-Go store (LSM-based, with transactions); pick pogreb over it when you need only point lookups and want the lowest read latency and memory, since Badger read about 10x fewer keys per second in pogreb's chart and 0.70M vs pogreb's 2.29M QPS in a 2025 third-party test with 50M records. HaloDB (Java) and NuDB (C++) serve other language stacks, and lsm-tree-go's win over BoltDB is on writes, not reads.

**Gotchas:**
- Durability is off by default. BackgroundSyncInterval=0 never fsyncs, so set it to -1 to fsync every write, or call Sync(). Recovery then truncates each segment at its last valid CRC-checked record.
- Unclean shutdown is detected through the lock file. Open then renames the index files to .bac and rebuilds the whole index from the WAL before it returns, and that time grows with total data size.
- Space is not reclaimed automatically. Set BackgroundCompactionInterval or call Compact(); only segments of at least 32 MiB with at least 50% dead bytes are compacted.
- Get copies every value (one allocation per call). GetAppend (no allocation) and Backup exist only on main after the last tag, v0.10.2 (Dec 2023), so `go get` of the latest release lacks them. Items() is not a point-in-time snapshot: it re-takes the read lock on every Next call, bucket by bucket.

**Status:** Apache-2.0, single maintainer, zero dependencies and small enough to vendor, but 'active' overstates it: the last tag is v0.10.2 (Dec 2023), main has had only small changes since (Backup, GetAppend, Plan 9 fixes, last commit 2026-04-06), and issues years old about Windows writes, crash reindexing and the 4B-key cap are still open.

[repo](https://github.com/akrylysov/pogreb) · [benchmark](https://github.com/akrylysov/pogreb#performance)

##### Speedb  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

RocksDB fork, API-compatible through RocksDB 8.6.7, adding a hash-based memtable and gradual write throttling to beat stock RocksDB.

**Beats:** RocksDB — Speedb's own docs benchmark Speedb with the sorted hash memtable against RocksDB v7.2.2 with its default skiplist, the same RocksDB base as Speedb 2.0/2.1, using db_bench (1B objects, 1KB values, 64MB write buffers, 4 threads, 16 cores, no compression). They report headline 'up to' gains of 155% on 100% overwrite, 68% on a 50% random-read mix and 15% on random seek; per-point values appear only in charts, and no CPU model, compiler or flags are given. The README's no-stall random-write chart (80M objects, 1KB values, 50 threads, 16-core Xeon Platinum 8370C) has no numbers at all.

**Known shortcoming:** The README chart has no numbers; the Speedb docs repo gives sorted-hash memtable gains (up to 155% overwrite, 68% at 50% reads, 15% seek vs RocksDB 7.2.2 skiplist), and that memtable is opt-in. docs.speedb.io is dead; last commit 2024-03, around Redis's acquisition of Speedb.

**Known shortcoming:** Stale: last release 2.8.0 is based on RocksDB 8.6.7. Speed evidence is vendor 'up to' numbers vs RocksDB 7.2.2 with no CPU/compiler/flags. The hash memtable is memory-heavy (6040 MB vs 3292 MB skiplist in #749; memory undercounted, #540 and #618 open); docs say lock-free but inserts take a per-bucket lock; iterator Refresh unsupported.

**Known shortcoming:** Defaults differ from RocksDB (dynamic level bytes off #786, compaction readahead 0, 8 compaction threads), and migrating back to RocksDB after using Speedb-only options is undocumented. The paired Bloom filter saves memory only and its own docs say it is ~2x slower.

**How:** The sorted hash memtable replaces RocksDB's skiplist with a fixed array of hash buckets (MurmurHash of the user key). Each bucket is a short sorted linked list with its own reader-writer lock, so point writes and Gets are bucket probes instead of O(log n) skiplist walks. Each insert also goes onto an atomic, unsorted write list that a background thread cuts into sorted vectors (up to 10K keys each, or whenever a seek arrives). Iterators merge those vectors with a binary heap, so writes keep flowing while a seek waits only for its own cut to be sorted, and a pre-built standby memtable hides the cost of allocating the buckets. Separately, dynamic delayed writes (use_dynamic_delay, on by default) cut the write rate in linear steps according to how far L0 file count, pending compaction bytes or memtable count are past the slowdown trigger. RocksDB instead moves the rate by fixed +25%/-20% steps, and the README's no-stall chart credits this change.

**Use it when:**
- You run RocksDB 7.x to 8.6 and overwrite- or update-heavy workloads with roughly 1KB values are limited by the skiplist memtable; setting memtable_factory to speedb.HashSpdRepFactory is the change the vendor benchmarks (up to +155% overwrite, +68% on a 50% read mix).
- Sustained bulk random writes where RocksDB's delayed-write mechanism gives sawtooth throughput and stalls; Speedb's dynamic delay (default on) and a shared WriteController smooth the write rate across column families and across several DBs in one process.
- Many DB instances or column families in one process sharing one memory budget: SharedOptions gives them one cache, one WriteBufferManager with proactive flushes, and one write controller.
- Filters with high bits-per-key (about 20 and up) where filter memory matters: the paired Bloom filter claims about 30% less memory at the same false-positive rate.
- You want to A/B a RocksDB-compatible engine with almost no code change; the docs say you can switch back to RocksDB at any time.

**Skip it when:**
- You need RocksDB features, fixes or on-disk options added after 8.6.7 (September 2023). Speedb has not rebased since then and has had no commits since March 2024, when Redis acquired the company.
- Memory-constrained deployments using the hash memtable. In one Speedb test log (issue #749), malloc stats showed 6040 MB with hash spdb vs 3292 MB with the skiplist. Issue #540 says memtable memory is underestimated, and more so with HashSpdRepFactory. A memory-reduction ticket (#618) is still open.
- Workloads dominated by seeks or scans: the claimed gain is only up to 15%, and a seek over freshly written data has to wait for the background thread to sort the pending write list.
- Code that relies on Iterator::Refresh() or memtable insert hints: the hash memtable reports IsRefreshIterSupported()=false, and InsertKeyWithHint ignores the hint.
- Latency-sensitive point reads through the paired Bloom filter: Speedb's own doc says building and probing it is about 2x slower than RocksDB's default filter, so it saves memory, not time.

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (CMake/make targets speedb and speedb-shared) · None required for the core library. Optional: snappy, lz4, zlib, zstd, bzip2 and jemalloc. The CMake option WITH_LIBURING defaults to ON. gflags is needed for db_bench and the tools. · C++17; GCC 7+ or Clang 5+ per INSTALL.md; Visual Studio 2017+ on Windows · Linux, macOS, Windows and iOS per INSTALL.md, with CMake code paths for x86-64, aarch64 (armv8 CRC), ppc64 and s390x. The default build targets the build machine's CPU; use PORTABLE=1 for a portable binary.

**Vs siblings:** Pick Speedb over ToplingDB or PsiTri's RocksDB-API layer when you want the smallest behavioral change from stock RocksDB 8.x (same LSM engine, speedups that are opt-in memtable and filter swaps) and can live with an unmaintained fork. Pick Titan for large values, where its gains come from key-value separation, and ToplingDB if you want a RocksDB fork with larger published speedups and benchmark runs as recent as September 2026.

**Gotchas:**
- Some defaults differ from RocksDB: level_compaction_dynamic_level_bytes=false (Speedb's changelog says the flag 'is not working properly with Speedb', issue #786), compaction_readahead_size=0, 8 compaction threads, and use_dynamic_delay=true. A tuned RocksDB config can therefore behave differently.
- The docs describe hash-memtable writes as needing no synchronization, but the code takes a per-bucket write lock on every insert. ApproximateMemoryUsage() returns 0, and the bucket vector is allocated outside the arena, so memtable size accounting undercounts.
- Bucket count is a fixed cost paid per memtable: the docs cite 1,000,000 buckets (about 8 MB, and creation is slow), while main lowered the default to 400,000 (#854) after the last release. Speedb pre-creates a standby memtable to hide the creation time.
- The Speedb write flow (use_spdb_writes) is still marked experimental and uses more memory. How to go back to RocksDB after enabling Speedb-only memtable or filter options is not documented.

**Status:** Stale: last commit March 2024 and last release 2.8.0 (January 2024, on RocksDB 8.6.7) after Redis acquired Speedb, docs.speedb.io is gone, and 146 issues are still open. It is Apache-2.0 and buildable, but you would have to do every future RocksDB rebase yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/speedb-io/speedb) · [benchmark](https://github.com/speedb-io/documentation/blob/main/speedb-features/sorted-hash-memtable.md)

##### SurrealKV  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

SurrealDB's pure-Rust async LSM key-value engine with OCC transactions; vendor benchmark shows ~3x RocksDB fsync'd write throughput.

**Beats:** RocksDB — On SurrealDB's own crud-bench harness (Threadripper 9970X, 128 GB DDR5, PCIe 4.0 NVMe, bare metal; 50K keys, 48 Tokio workers, 128 clients, --sync), SurrealKV reached 105,072 creates/s vs 31,777 for RocksDB (SurrealDB's surrealdb-rocksdb 0.24.0-surreal.5 fork, as an OptimisticTransactionDB), a 3.31x gap. It also reached 1.60M vs 693K point reads/s (2.31x) and 8,361 vs 2,406 scans/s (3.47x). The Rust toolchain is not stated; crud-bench's release profile uses LTO, opt-level 3 and codegen-units 1. README git history shows the SurrealKV row re-measured at least three times on 2026-09-24/25 (point reads 901K -> 1.18M -> 1.60M, creates 88K -> 105K), while RocksDB's create and scan figures never changed. The build measured is unreleased main, while crud-bench main pins surrealkv 0.21.2.

**Known shortcoming:** Evidence is crud-bench from the same organization (SurrealDB) with toolchain/flags unstated, and its RocksDB is SurrealDB's fork crate.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmark rows are mixed: the SurrealKV row was rerun 3+ times (901K to 1.18M to 1.60M reads) while RocksDB's create/scan numbers never changed; the benchmarked code is unreleased (main is 120 commits past crates.io 0.21.4). Default durability is Eventual (no fsync) while the bench forces Immediate with vlog, a 256 MB memtable and a GB-sized cache; peak memory 1.35 GB vs RocksDB 393 MB; 50K keys fit in RAM; LMDB/libmdbx win scans.

**Known shortcoming:** A compaction OOM (#397, 16-22 GiB) is fixed on main but unreleased; recent correctness bugs #376, #390, #393, #395; the README's io_uring claim is absent from the code; needs Tokio. The crud-bench RocksDB adapter calls blocking commit() inside async tasks, which likely shrinks its fsync groups (inferred from code).

**How:** Writes use a group-commit pipeline modeled on Pebble's. Each committing transaction claims a slot in a 1024-slot lock-free MPSC ring with one atomic fetch_add, checks for conflicts against recent commits (Bloom-filter-assisted), and publishes the slot. A single background flusher drains every contiguous ready slot, writes them as one WAL append with one fsync, applies them to the arena-skiplist memtable, and advances the visible sequence number. Because commit() is an awaitable future, far more transactions than worker threads can share one fsync. In contrast, crud-bench's RocksDB adapter calls RocksDB's blocking commit() directly inside async tasks, which probably limits how many commits RocksDB can group per fsync at 48 workers; that is our reading of the adapter code, not a measured cause. Reads are lock-free MVCC snapshot lookups through the memtables and then leveled SSTables (64 KB prefix-compressed blocks, 10-bit/key Bloom filters, sharded block cache), and large values can move to a WiscKey-style value log.

**Use it when:**
- Rust services on Tokio with many concurrent small transactions that each need fsync-before-ack durability. This is where group commit pays off: 105K synced creates/s at 128 clients vs RocksDB's 31.8K in the vendor run.
- You need multi-key snapshot-isolation transactions with savepoints, or built-in versioned/time-travel reads (with_versioning, get_at, history), without layering MVCC on top of a plain KV store.
- One storage engine must also run in the browser: wasm32-unknown-unknown in a Web Worker, persisting to OPFS, with a migrator for existing IndexedDB stores.
- You want a Rust-native build and don't want to compile librocksdb-sys. Remaining native code is small C codecs such as zstd.
- Point-read-heavy workloads whose working set fits in memtable plus block cache. The vendor run shows 1.60M reads/s on a 50K-key dataset.

**Skip it when:**
- Range-scan-dominated workloads: in the same table LMDB (27,446 ops/s) and libmdbx (16,005) beat SurrealKV's 8,361 scans/s. An mmap B+tree is the better fit.
- Tight RAM budgets. Peak memory was 1.35 GB vs RocksDB's 393 MB in the vendor run. Issue #397 measured compactions needing 16-22 GiB, with an OOM restart loop on a ~16 GB store; the fix merged on 2026-09-25 is not in any crates.io release yet.
- Datasets much larger than RAM or long-running write-heavy stores. The only published benchmark uses 50K keys, which fit in memory. Compaction is leveled-only, and a maintainer agreed in issue #309 that leveled is a poor fit for versioned data.
- Code that needs the RocksDB API or ecosystem: C/C++ callers, RocksDB-specific tuning, or features the README does not document, such as column families or merge operators.
- Anything that needs a settled, well-tested release. It is 0.x, and the benchmarked 'V2' engine is 120 commits past the latest crates.io release (0.21.4). 2026 fixed several correctness bugs: broken first-committer-wins (#376), no fsync after compaction (#390), UB in the memtable arena (#393) and range-iterator boundary defects (#395). One anecdotal HN report (June 2026, older version) also found SQLite 15-60x faster per op for a single client.

**Integration:** crate · tokio (runtime required), affinitypool, arenaskiplist, byteslice, quick_cache, parking_lot, bytes, snap, zstd, lz4_flex, crc32fast, xxhash-rust, aes-gcm, chacha20poly1305, chacha20, blake3, subtle, tracing, async-trait, rand. Also rustix on Unix, windows-sys on Windows, wasm-bindgen/web-sys/getrandom on wasm. Three in-workspace migration crates (RocksDB, SurrealKV v1 and IndexedDB readers) are always compiled in. · Rust 1.86 (rust-version in Cargo.toml, edition 2021), plus a Tokio runtime. · README lists Linux x86-64/aarch64, macOS x86-64/aarch64, Windows x86-64, and wasm32-unknown-unknown (browser Web Workers with OPFS). CI also builds Apple and Android targets. The README's claim of io_uring on Linux does not match main, where WAL and SSTable I/O use the affinitypool thread pool on every platform.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over Badger when you are in Rust/Tokio or need browser OPFS support; both offer WiscKey value separation and snapshot-isolated transactions, but Badger is Go. Pick Speedb, ToplingDB or PsiTri instead when you need the RocksDB API as a drop-in or a C++ consumer, since SurrealKV only offers its own Rust API and a one-way RocksDB data import.

**Gotchas:**
- Default durability is Durability::Eventual, which writes to the OS page cache without fsync. The benchmark figures use Durability::Immediate, set per transaction. Set it yourself if you need the durability the benchmark measured.
- Needs Tokio. build() spawns background tasks with tokio::spawn and commit() is async. Call tree.close().await before exit: Drop only schedules an async close when a runtime is current, and otherwise just logs a warning.
- A commit that loses a write-write conflict returns TransactionWriteConflict and closes the transaction, so retry with a new transaction. Isolation is snapshot, so write skew is possible, and get_for_update does not stop it between transactions that only read a key.
- The benchmark config differs from the defaults. crud-bench turns on the value log (off by default), sets a 256 MB memtable (default 100 MB) and sizes the block cache in GB (default 32 MB). docs/ARCHITECTURE.md is marked WIP and still describes the older mutex-based commit path (src/commit.rs and src/oracle.rs no longer exist on main).

**Status:** Very active: 120 commits since v0.21.4 (2026-08-26), most of the V2 engine landed 2026-09-24..26, and the memtable was swapped on 2026-09-26. It is Apache-2.0, has 555 stars and ~1.06M crates.io downloads (mostly via SurrealDB), but it is pre-1.0 and the benchmarked code is not on crates.io yet, so pin a git revision or wait for the next release.

[repo](https://github.com/surrealdb/surrealkv) · [benchmark](https://github.com/surrealdb/surrealkv#performance)

##### Titan (RocksDB plugin)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

RocksDB plugin that moves large values into separate blob files (WiscKey-style) to cut write amplification versus plain RocksDB.

**Beats:** RocksDB — PingCAP's April 2019 blog ran go-ycsb against TiKV on Titan versus TiKV on RocksDB (64 GB dataset, TiKV capped at 32 GB RAM, 1 KB and 16 KB values) on a 40-core Xeon E5-2630 v4 with 128 GB RAM and a SATA SSD. It reports about 70% higher load throughput and 180% higher update throughput, better point gets, worse range scans and slightly higher space use; compiler, flags, versions and go-ycsb settings are not given, and the Raft log write in front of the engine dilutes the gain.

**Known shortcoming:** Needs TiKV's RocksDB fork (kTypeTitanBlobIndex exists only in tikv/rocksdb 8.10.tikv), so it is not a drop-in for upstream RocksDB. Merge, SingleDelete and DisableFileDeletions return NotSupported; MultiGet is a loop of Gets; rollback requires kFallback mode and a compaction pass. Upstream RocksDB's integrated BlobDB (enable_blob_files) does the same key-value separation with fuller API support. Range scans 40% to several times slower and up to ~2x disk space (TiDB docs); weaker per-record blob compression; 7 mutexes per point read vs 2 (#139). Open crash in the compaction filter from a missing blob file (#328) and a critical double-deleted blob file that prevents restart (#186). No running CI (only old Travis); last master commit 2026-04-29. Evidence is one 2019 PingCAP blog measured end to end through TiKV with Raft in front, no compiler/flags/versions.

**How:** It uses key-value separation from the WiscKey paper: compaction rewrites only keys and small blob indexes, not the large values, so write amplification and compaction I/O drop for big values. TitanTableBuilder does the separation during flush and compaction, so the foreground write path (WAL plus memtable) stays RocksDB's. Blob garbage collection is driven by table-property collectors and flush/compaction listeners that track each blob file's discardable ratio (GC at 0.5 by default); optional Level Merge rewrites blobs while the last two LSM levels compact, which keeps them sorted for scans. The smaller LSM tree also leaves more block cache for index, filter and data blocks, which PingCAP credits for faster point reads.

**Use it when:**
- Write- or update-heavy workloads with values of about 1 KB and up; PingCAP reports the gap over RocksDB widens as values grow, and its 16 KB tests gained most.
- RocksDB deployments limited by compaction I/O, write stalls or SSD wear from write amplification.
- Point-lookup-heavy reads on large values, where an LSM tree of only keys and blob indexes fits better in block cache.
- Mixed value sizes: values below min_blob_size stay inline in the SST, so only large values pay the extra blob-file read.
- You already run TiKV or can build against TiKV's RocksDB fork (tikv/rocksdb branch 8.10.tikv).

**Skip it when:**
- Range-scan-heavy workloads: PingCAP says Titan underperforms RocksDB on range queries and TiDB docs put the drop at 40% to a few times slower, because each scanned value is a separate blob-file read.
- Disk-space-limited deployments: space amplification is higher than RocksDB (TiDB docs say it can reach about twice RocksDB), and per-record blob compression compresses worse than RocksDB's per-block compression.
- Small values (well under 1 KB): they stay inline, so you take on the plugin's complexity for no gain.
- Code that needs Merge operators, SingleDelete or batched MultiGet: Titan rejects the first two, and its MultiGet is a loop of single Gets.
- Projects on upstream facebook/rocksdb: master uses the TiKV-fork-only kTypeTitanBlobIndex value type, so it does not build against upstream; RocksDB's own integrated BlobDB (enable_blob_files) gives the same key-value separation and supports Merge, SingleDelete and batched MultiGet.

**Integration:** static lib · RocksDB source tree (CMake clones tikv/rocksdb branch 8.10.tikv by default; each Titan branch pins a TiKV RocksDB fork branch); optional snappy, lz4, zstd, zlib, bzip2, jemalloc; gflags for the bench/stress tools · C++17, CMake 3.10+ (legacy CI config used g++-9 and clang) · Not documented in README; build flags cover x86-64 (SSE4.2), aarch64 (armv8 CRC) and ppc64le, the legacy Travis config targeted Linux x86-64, Linux arm64 and macOS, and production use is Linux through TiKV

**Vs siblings:** Pick Titan over TerarkDB when values are large (1 KB and up) and the bottleneck is write/compaction amplification rather than read QPS or compression ratio, and when you want a plugin tracking a recent RocksDB (the TiKV 8.10 fork) rather than a full engine forked from RocksDB v5.18.3.

**Gotchas:**
- Space is reclaimed only when blob GC runs; blob_file_discardable_ratio and max_background_gc (default 1 thread) set how far disk use lags behind deletes and overwrites.
- Point reads take several more mutexes than plain RocksDB (issue #139 counts 7 against 2), and a Get without a snapshot creates a ManagedSnapshot; the issue flags this as overhead in CPU-bound, in-memory workloads.
- There is no direct rollback: switch blob_run_mode to kReadOnly or kFallback and let compaction inline values before you drop Titan.
- Open issues report crashes or failed restarts from missing or double-deleted blob files (#328, #186), and the repo has no running public CI (only a legacy Travis config), so pin a branch that matches a TiKV release.

**Status:** Maintained by the TiKV team at a slow pace (last master commit 2026-04-29) under Apache-2.0, and enabled by default for new TiKV clusters since v7.6.0, but usable outside TiKV only if you adopt TiKV's RocksDB fork.

[repo](https://github.com/tikv/titan) · [benchmark](https://pingcap.com/blog/titan-storage-engine-design-and-implementation/)

##### UnisonDB  `Go`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Go KV database that puts a WAL and memtable in front of LMDB; about 3x LMDB's SET throughput (first-party).

**Beats:** LMDB — The author's harness runs redis-benchmark against a Redis-protocol Go server (tidwall/redcon), 50 runs of 200k SET then 200k GET with 1 KB values, 10 clients, pipeline 10 and 4 threads, on an Apple M2 Pro with 16 GB RAM. The Go version is not stated. On the SET-only chart, UnisonDB (LMDB backend, 1 s WAL sync, 16 MB memtable) reaches about 100k-133k req/s at 0.21-0.40 ms p50, against about 35k-42k req/s at 0.69-0.86 ms for PowerDNS/lmdb-go. The LMDB baseline was opened NoSync, synced every 1 s, and used one write transaction per SET. Durability windows are similar, so the roughly 3x comes from write buffering and batching, not a faster B-tree.

**Known shortcoming:** The win is architecture, not a faster core: the LMDB baseline commits one NoSync transaction per SET while UnisonDB batches through its WAL and memtable (it also wraps LMDB itself); numbers are chart-derived with no Go version/flags.

**Known shortcoming:** Only SET is charted (no GET numbers); both sides have a ~1 s fsync window and acknowledged writes are not fsynced for up to ~1 s; no backpressure on sealed memtables; LMDB map 4 GB by default. Alpha with no tagged releases (the author said in 2025-12 it is not in production; Raft removed 2026-09-12); possible SIGSEGV in the replicator (#186); cgo required, releases linux/amd64 only, Go 1.25.2+; documented as a server only.

**How:** Writes do not touch the B+tree inline. Under one engine mutex, each Put appends a FlatBuffer-encoded record to WALFS, an mmap-backed segmented log (msync every 1 MB by default, full fsync on a 1 s ticker), and inserts into an arena skiplist memtable (Badger's skl package) with a Bloom filter. When the arena fills, the memtable is sealed and a background goroutine flushes it to LMDB in key order, 16 puts per write transaction. Compared with raw LMDB doing one copy-on-write transaction per SET, this is ordinary LSM-style write buffering and batching. The B-tree underneath is still LMDB (or bbolt).

**Use it when:**
- You need one writer fanning out to tens or hundreds of read replicas and want the WAL to be the replication stream, with no separate Kafka or CDC pipeline.
- Write-heavy KV workloads with values around 1 KB, where you would otherwise run LMDB with one small write transaction per update and can accept about 1 s of fsync lag.
- Replicas should keep serving local reads while offline and catch up later from a stored (segment, offset) or LSN.
- Rows where only a few columns change per update, or large objects written as chunks that must commit atomically.
- Linux deployments (the only release target is linux/amd64) with cgo and LMDB headers available.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a mature embedded KV store: the README marks it alpha, there are no tagged releases, and in December 2025 the author wrote on HN that it was still being hardened in test/staging and not yet in production.
- Every acknowledged write must be durable: SETs return after the mmap append, and the WAL is fsynced only on the 1 s ticker (msync every 1 MB), so a power loss can drop recent writes.
- Read-dominated workloads: GET results are not charted, and a GET can check the active memtable and every sealed memtable before reaching LMDB, so plain LMDB reads should be as fast or faster.
- Windows, or pure-Go builds without cgo: the docs list only Linux and macOS, and the LMDB backend needs cgo.
- Datasets larger than RAM, or sustained writes faster than the LMDB flush can drain: the benchmark keyspace (200k x 1 KB, about 200 MB) fits in page cache, and engine.go has no write stall or backpressure on the sealed-memtable queue.

**Integration:** module · LMDB via cgo (PowerDNS/lmdb-go) or bbolt; Badger v4 (skiplist arena), bits-and-blooms/bloom, FlatBuffers, gRPC, and AWS/Azure/GCS SDKs for blob replication; ZeroMQ (libzmq) only when built with -tags zeromq · go.mod declares go 1.25.2 (the docs say Go 1.24+ and the Dockerfile uses golang:1.24); cgo required · Linux and macOS per the docs; goreleaser builds linux/amd64 only; the benchmark ran on Apple M2 Pro (arm64)

**Vs siblings:** Among the Go siblings (Badger, Pebble, Pogreb, lsm-tree-go), pick UnisonDB only when built-in WAL-streaming replication to many read replicas matters more than engine maturity; on its own chart it also beats Badger v4 on SETs (about 133k vs 67k-80k req/s). For a single-node embedded store, Badger or Pebble are far more mature and have documented Go APIs.

**Gotchas:**
- The default LMDB map size is 4 GB (btree_config.mmap_size); LMDB fails writes once the map is full, so raise it before loading more data.
- Sealed memtables wait in RAM until the background flush (triggered by rotation or a 30 s ticker) writes them to LMDB. Each is 4 MB by default and 16 MB in the benchmark config. If LMDB falls behind, memory grows and GETs probe more skiplists.
- WAL readers hand out zero-copy slices of mmapped segments. Open issue #186 describes a possible SIGSEGV if the replicator closes a reader, and so unmaps a deleted segment, while the streamer still holds those slices.
- Churn is high: on 2026-09-12 alone the Raft implementation was removed and fixes landed for LMDB/Bolt queue leakage and a replicator busy-loop, so pin a commit.

**Status:** Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-12, single main author, 426 stars) and Apache-2.0, but it is an alpha with no tagged releases, recent large architectural changes and an open SIGSEGV issue, so use it only if you can vendor it at a pinned commit and test it yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/ankur-anand/unisondb) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ankur-anand/unisondb#redis-compatible-benchmark-unisondb-vs-badgerdb-vs-boltdb-vs-lmdb)

#### embedded-kv-lsm

##### RocksDB integrated BlobDB  `C++`  `Apache-2.0 OR GPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

RocksDB's built-in key-value separation: large values go to blob files, cutting compaction write amp versus stock leveled RocksDB.

**Beats:** stock RocksDB (leveled compaction, no blob files) — RocksDB's own 2021 blog post ran a customized version of its standard benchmark suite: 1 TB of raw values, 1KB-1MB values, six load/overwrite/read phases, on a build equivalent to 6.18.1 and an 18-core Skylake DE @ 1.6GHz with 64GB RAM and two M.2 SSDs in RAID0; the compiler and flags are not stated. Against stock leveled compaction it reported 2.3-4.7x faster initial load, 2.1-3.5x higher overwrite throughput with 75-78% less write amp, and up to 1.4x faster reads for large values, but it lost on range scans at 1KB and 4KB; an independent 2025 paper (BVLSM: RocksDB 9.7.3, Xeon Gold 5218, NVMe, authors of a competing design) implies about 4x over stock RocksDB for 64KB random writes with async WAL, but only about 0.4-0.6x on sequential writes.

**Known shortcoming:** A feature of RocksDB itself (enable_blob_files), listed separately from RocksDB's other features; range scans lose at 1-4 KB values; evidence is RocksDB's 2021 blog (v6.18.1) with no compiler/flags.

**Known shortcoming:** DATA-LOSS RISK: RepairDB/ldb repair drops blob files (#13884, #13090, open). Blob GC is off by default (space amplification); insert-only with GC gives write amplification of 7+ (#11570); blobs always go to the first cf_path (#8535). Open bugs: force_threshold=0 causes endless compaction (#15256); MultiGet soft-limit never ends (#15247); the last tag 11.8.1 lacks the #14897 fix.

**Independent measurement:** BVLSM paper (2025, competitor authors, RocksDB 9.7.3): ~4x vs stock RocksDB on 64 KB random writes but only ~0.4-0.6x on sequential writes, and below stock on sustained 4 KB random writes.

**How:** It uses WiscKey-style key-value separation. Compactions sort and rewrite keys plus small pointers instead of the large values, so write amplification drops and compaction keeps up with ingest, which removes the write stalls that throttle stock leveled compaction under heavy overwrites. Blob files are written by the background flush and compaction threads, one writer per file, using large I/Os and doing compression off the foreground path; they are also tracked in the MANIFEST as part of the Version, so the read path is mostly lock-free. Garbage collection piggybacks on compaction: live blobs in the oldest blob_garbage_collection_age_cutoff fraction of blob files are relocated as their keys pass through compaction, and files holding nothing but garbage are dropped whole. This avoids WiscKey's GC, which issues a Get plus a Put for every blob it checks.

**Use it when:**
- Write-heavy or overwrite-heavy workloads with large values, where leveled compaction's write amp or write stalls cap throughput. The 2021 tests saw write-side wins at every value size from 1KB to 1MB.
- Flash-endurance- or bandwidth-sensitive deployments. The blog measured 75-90% lower write amp than leveled across its overwrite and mixed read/write phases.
- Point lookups on large values. The blog found BlobDB matched or beat leveled (up to 1.4x) for larger values, because the LSM holding only keys and pointers stays small.
- Cases where you would otherwise switch to universal compaction only for lower write amp. The RocksDB team recommends BlobDB with leveled compaction instead, which read up to 5.6x faster than universal in their tests.
- Large-value TTL or size-budget workloads on FIFO compaction. Since 11.0, FIFO can trim by combined SST and blob bytes, and a KV-ratio intra-L0 picker is built specifically for BlobDB.

**Skip it when:**
- Small values (1KB-4KB) with range scans. The blog's own results show BlobDB behind leveled on scan workloads at those two sizes, since each value costs an extra indirection into a blob file.
- Tight disk budgets. Overwritten or deleted blobs stay on disk until GC relocates them. GC is off by default, space comes back only in whole-blob-file increments (blob_file_size), and lowering space amp costs extra write amp.
- Insert-only or sequential-key loads. With GC on, the default 0.25 age cutoff kept relocating blobs in a pure-insert test, giving write amp of 7+ (issue #11570; the maintainer's advice is to disable GC). An independent 2025 paper (BVLSM, RocksDB 9.7.3) also found BlobDB slower than stock RocksDB on sequential writes and on sustained 4KB random writes.
- Deployments relying on multiple cf_paths/db_paths, RepairDB/ldb repair, or secondary instances. Blob files always go to the first cf path (open issue #8535, confirmed in blob_file_builder.cc). Repair drops blob files from the MANIFEST, so the next open deletes them and loses the data (open issues #13884 and #13090). The wiki lists secondary instances and blob-file ingestion as unsupported.
- Very large values under sustained overwrite. The blog's own overwrite runs were stall-free at every size except the largest, 1MB.

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (part of librocksdb itself; turned on per column family through options, not a separate component) · None required. zlib, bzip2, lz4, snappy and zstd are optional, for blob_compression_type; gflags is needed only for the tools (db_bench, ldb). · C++20: GCC 11+ or Clang 10+, per INSTALL.md (which still lists Visual Studio 2017+ for Windows) · Per INSTALL.md: Linux, macOS, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, Windows (CMake/vcpkg), iOS, AIX and Solaris SPARC. No BlobDB-specific platform limits are documented. The published benchmark ran on x86-64 (Skylake DE).

**Vs siblings:** No siblings catalogued yet. Compared with the baseline, pick it over stock leveled RocksDB when values are large and writes or overwrites dominate, and over universal compaction when you wanted universal only for its lower write amp.

**Gotchas:**
- min_blob_size defaults to 0, so enable_blob_files=true on its own sends every non-empty value to a blob file. Set a threshold.
- enable_blob_garbage_collection defaults to false. blob_garbage_collection_force_threshold=0.0 passes validation but makes an idle DB compact forever (open issue #15256, Sept 2026). blob_cache cannot be changed through SetOptions.
- Recent open bugs: MultiGet with value_size_soft_limit keeps returning Aborted when the first key's value is in a blob file, so the documented retry loop never ends (#15247). Another open issue reports FIFO max_data_files_size dropping far more data than its budget (#15252). A blob GC compaction failure (#14897) is fixed per the HISTORY.md 11.9.0 entry, but the newest tagged GitHub release is 11.8.1.
- Blob direct write (experimental, 2026) writes large values straight to blob files on the write path. Its v1 cannot recover still-active direct-write blob files by WAL replay after a crash, and it requires the ordered single-memtable-writer path, so no allow_concurrent_memtable_write, pipelined, unordered or two_write_queues writes.

**Status:** Actively developed inside RocksDB: HISTORY.md shows 11.11.0 on 2026-09-21 with blob and wide-column work, and blob direct write and FIFO KV-ratio compaction landed in 2026. It is in production use and dual-licensed Apache-2.0/GPLv2, but you adopt it as a RocksDB configuration, not as a component you can vendor on its own.

[repo](https://github.com/facebook/rocksdb) · [benchmark](http://rocksdb.org/blog/2021/05/26/integrated-blob-db.html)

#### indexes

##### Bw-Tree (Open BwTree, wangziqi2013)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Open-source lock-free Bw-Tree (concurrent B+-tree multimap) from CMU; its own benchmarks show it slower than std::map and stx::btree.

**Beats:** BerkeleyDB (B-tree mode) — The BerkeleyDB wins are not this code: ICDE'13's 10.40M vs 0.56M ops/s (about 18.7x, Xbox LIVE trace), 3.83M vs 0.66M (5.8x, synthetic) and 8.6x (deduplication) were measured on Microsoft's unreleased implementation on a Xeon W3550 with 8 threads. This repo's own numbers put it behind the incumbents: a single-threaded benchmark-all screenshot (g++ -O3, jemalloc, sequential long keys, a ThinkPad T440s per the shell prompt, libstdc++ inferred) shows it slower than std::map, std::unordered_map and stx::btree, and the authors' SIGMOD'18 evaluation (2x Xeon E5-2680 v2, g++ 5.4, tcmalloc) finds it 1.1-2.5x faster than a reimplemented original Bw-Tree but slower than B+Tree-OLC, Masstree and ART, ahead only of a lock-free SkipList.

**Known shortcoming:** NOT FASTER: the 18.7x/5.8x vs BerkeleyDB are Microsoft's closed Bw-Tree numbers; this open implementation's own benchmarks show it slower than std::map and stx::btree, and the SIGMOD'18 evaluation found it slower than B+Tree, Masstree and ART.

**Known shortcoming:** The repo's own single-thread numbers (4.65M inserts / 9.58M reads per s) trail std::map (5.91/17.85) and stx::btree (10.60/21.50); in SIGMOD'18 ART-OLC is >4x faster on lookups and B+Tree-OLC/Masstree ~2x; it beats only a skip list. Fixed 2^20-node mapping table with no resize (#45). Open bugs: epoch-GC use-after-free (#69), std::string segfault (#62), clang build failure (#64), C++17 'register' (#70).

**Known shortcoming:** Delete is not wait-free (ABORT delta; a dead thread blocks writes, #40); >10 aborts per insert under high contention. Debug and stderr logging on by default (-DBWTREE_NODEBUG needed); ~16 MB object can crash the stack (#65); multimap with no update/size. Abandoned 2018-11; x86-64 g++-5 era (16-byte CAS, -mcx16); in-memory only; Microsoft patent question unanswered (#71).

**How:** Nodes are addressed through a mapping table of logical node IDs. Writers prepend delta records (insert, delete, split, merge) to a node's delta chain and publish them with one compare-and-swap on that node's slot, and threads 'help along' unfinished structure modifications instead of waiting on latches. A chain is consolidated into a new base node after 8 deltas, and nodes split above 128 entries and merge below 32. On top of Microsoft's design, the SIGMOD'18 paper adds delta records pre-allocated inside the base node's memory chunk, decentralized per-thread epoch GC, fast consolidation, node-search shortcuts using delta offsets, and non-unique key support; together these give 1.1-2.5x over a good-faith original Bw-Tree, but the indirection and delta-chain traversal still cost more instructions and cache misses than a latch-based B+Tree.

**Use it when:**
- Research or teaching where you need a working lock-free Bw-Tree (mapping table, delta chains, help-along SMOs, epoch GC) to study, instrument or port to another language.
- As a baseline in an index benchmark, or to reproduce or extend the SIGMOD'18 'Building a Bw-Tree Takes More Than Just Buzz Words' results (YCSB-style Insert-only, Read-only, Read/Update and Scan/Insert on integer or email keys).
- A prototype that specifically requires a latch-free, comparator-based, non-unique (multimap) ordered index over small trivially-copyable keys such as 64-bit integers, where you run a fixed thread pool registered up front and stay well under the ~1M-node mapping-table cap.

**Skip it when:**
- Whenever speed is the reason. The repo's own single-threaded benchmark-all screenshot shows 4.65M inserts/s and 9.58M reads/s, against 5.91M/17.85M for std::map and 10.60M/21.50M for stx::btree. With 20 threads in SIGMOD'18, ART with optimistic lock coupling was more than 4x faster on point lookups, and a B+Tree with optimistic lock coupling and Masstree were often about 2x faster (3.7x for B+Tree on monotonic insert-only).
- High-contention appends such as monotonic keys from many threads: in SIGMOD'18 it saw more than 10 CAS aborts per insert, and lock-based Masstree, ART and B+Tree held up better.
- Large or growing indexes: the mapping table is a fixed std::array of 2^20 node IDs with no resizing (a README 'Known Problem'; issue #45 still open). That caps the tree at roughly tens of millions of keys at 32-128 entries per leaf. The SIGMOD'18 paper describes lazily-backed virtual-memory expansion, but that is not what master ships.
- std::string or other non-POD keys and values: issue #62 (a segfault during the first GC cycle with std::string keys) was never fixed, and the author notes that the tree moves keys and values often, so non-POD types are slow.
- Production systems. Delete is not wait-free: a thread that dies between posting and removing its ABORT delta blocks all writes under that parent (#40). There is an unfixed use-after-free race in epoch cleanup (#69), and a question about Microsoft's Bw-Tree patents (#71) was never answered. It is in-memory only, with no persistence (#72), unlike the BerkeleyDB baseline.

**Integration:** source-drop · none for the index itself (C++11 STL plus pthreads; bwtree.h also includes sorted_small_set.h, bloom_filter.h and atomic_stack.h). The test/benchmark harness uses PAPI (disable with -DNO_USE_PAPI) and jemalloc via LD_PRELOAD, and the full-speed make target links boost_system and boost_thread. · C++11. Only g++-5 is used in the Makefile and Travis. clang++ fails on private nested-class access unless patched (#64). The 'register' keyword in bloom_filter.h is invalid in C++17 (#70). Needs -mcx16 for the 16-byte CAS. · x86-64 Linux is the only tested platform (Travis on Ubuntu). It relies on a 16-byte std::atomic CAS (LOCK CMPXCHG16B) and GCC builtins and attributes. Other architectures, macOS/Windows and MSVC are not documented.

**Vs siblings:** For real concurrent in-memory indexing, pick ART Synchronized: the SIGMOD'18 authors measured ART with optimistic lock coupling more than 4x faster than this tree on point lookups, and LIPP's evaluation also lists BwTree among the indexes it beats. Choose Open BwTree only when the requirement is specifically a latch-free, comparator-based B+-tree multimap, or a reference implementation of the Bw-Tree/Hekaton design.

**Gotchas:**
- Debug mode is the default. Unless you compile with -DBWTREE_NODEBUG, BWTREE_DEBUG enables assertions and per-operation atomic counters, and bwt_printf logs every call to stderr while print_flag is true, which is its initial value in bwtree.cpp. ALL_PUBLIC is also hard-defined, so internal members are public.
- A BwTree object is about 16 MB, because the mapping table and the free NodeID stack are in-object arrays. Declaring one on the stack crashes (#65), so always allocate it with new. The constructor also starts a background epoch/GC thread unless you pass start_gc_thread = false.
- Not header-only: you must compile src/bwtree.cpp (it defines print_flag, the thread_local gc_id and the thread counter). A thread with no assigned GC ID (gc_id = -1) trips an assert or causes undefined behavior. The GC slot count is captured when the tree is constructed.
- Multimap semantics: Insert only fails if that exact (key, value) pair already exists, so repeated keys accumulate values, and there is no update, so 'replace' means a non-atomic Delete + Insert. Iterators copy one leaf page at a time and give no snapshot across pages.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2018-11-14, with 14 open issues (use-after-free race, std::string segfault, clang build failure) unanswered; it is Apache-2.0 and small enough to vendor (CMU's now-archived NoisePage vendored it under third_party/bwtree), and the last known-good toolchain is g++-5 on Ubuntu.

[repo](https://github.com/wangziqi2013/BwTree) · [benchmark](https://db.cs.cmu.edu/papers/2018/mod342-wangA.pdf)

##### libmdbx  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

LMDB fork: embedded memory-mapped ACID B+tree KV store; author reports 10-30% faster in-tmpfs CRUD than LMDB.

**Beats:** LMDB — All numbers are first-party: the README says in-tmpfs CRUD runs of the ioArena harness show libmdbx 10-20% faster than LMDB, and up to 30% faster in builds that drop runtime checks. It publishes no result tables, hardware, compiler flags or LMDB version. The repo's make bench targets default to 25M operations in nosync mode with 4 reader threads for get/iterate, on upstream ioArena's defaults of 16-byte keys and 32-byte values. The '10-100K times faster' line names no cases; separately, the author claims mdbx_cache_get speeds up get by 'several tens of thousands of times'.

**Known shortcoming:** The measured claim is 'up to 30% faster than LMDB in CRUD benchmarks' (10-20% in tmpfs runs; up to 30% only with build options that relax runtime checks); the README's '10-100K x' line is an unmeasured assertion about extreme cases (verifier downgrade). Canonical origin moved to sourcecraft.dev; GitHub is a mirror.

**Known shortcoming:** The 10-30% over LMDB is first-party only, with no tables, hardware, flags or LMDB version; the claim dates to 2019 and was never re-run against LMDB 1.0 (2026-07, faster large-transaction commits). The 30% needs MDBX_DISABLE_VALIDATION, which weakens corruption detection; bench defaults are nosync, 16 B keys, 32 B values. The '10-100K x' names no cases (the author ties it to mdbx_cache_get). Slower than LMDB by default on Windows (LockFileEx) and macOS (F_FULLFSYNC); WSL1 refused. 2026 bugs fixed: nested drop+abort data loss (#361), OOB read on malformed DB in mdbx_env_chk (#375), commit flush error reported as success. Still 0.x with one lead author; the successor MithrilDB may be withheld from sanctioning countries.

**How:** The core is LMDB's design: a copy-on-write (shadow-paging) B+tree in a memory-mapped file with MVCC snapshots, so reads are zero-copy pointer walks with no buffer pool and no WAL, and readers are wait-free without atomic operations. On top of that libmdbx adds LIFO reuse of freed pages (shorter page circulation, better write-back cache hit rates), 'refund' auto-compaction that truncates freed tail pages at commit, 'Big Foot' chunking of huge retired-page lists, bulk deletion by cutting whole B-tree branches, and mdbx_cache_get, which stores a key's version and mmap offset client-side and stops the B-tree descent at the first page that has not changed. The top '30% faster' figure needs builds that relax runtime checks (the MDBX_DISABLE_VALIDATION option, described as bringing corruption detection 'closer to the LMDB').

**Use it when:**
- Read-dominated embedded workloads that need ACID transactions, sorted keys and range scans, where readers must never block the single writer and read throughput should scale across cores.
- Several processes on one host sharing a single database file without running a database server.
- You already run LMDB and hit its limits: keys longer than 511 bytes (libmdbx allows 2022 bytes at 4 KiB pages, 32742 at 64 KiB), a data file that never shrinks, bloat from slow readers, or corruption after crashes in no-sync modes (MDBX_SAFE_NOSYNC keeps the DB consistent).
- Hot point lookups on keys that rarely change, where mdbx_cache_get can skip most of the B-tree descent.
- Bulk loading pre-sorted data with the append operation on Linux, the platform the author recommends for speed; Ethereum clients (Erigon, Reth, Silkworm) use it in production.

**Skip it when:**
- Write-heavy workloads with strict durability: only one write transaction runs at a time and the README says syncing shadow pages to disk can bottleneck write-intensive loads. The write-optimized LSM engines in this category are a better fit.
- Performance-sensitive Windows or macOS deployments: by default Windows uses LockFileEx and macOS/iOS use F_FULLFSYNC, and the README says both make libmdbx slower than LMDB. WSL1 is refused outright (ENOLCK) and shrinking the file on Windows is limited.
- Long-running read transactions (analytics scans, backups by iteration) alongside steady writes: pinned pages make the file grow and throughput drop unless you use transaction parking or the Handle-Slow-Readers callback.
- You need a current head-to-head against LMDB: the 10-30% figures are old first-party claims (an 'up to 20% faster' version was posted in 2019) and have not been republished against LMDB 1.0, which shipped in July 2026 with faster large-transaction commits.
- Processes that open untrusted or corrupted database files, or strict supply-chain policies: 2026 fuzzing found an out-of-bounds read in mdbx_env_chk (issue #375) and a null dereference on corrupted DBs (#297), both since fixed. The project is still 0.x and led by one author after corporate funding ended in 2025, and the README says the successor MithrilDB may be withheld from countries that sanction Russia.

**Integration:** source-drop (amalgamated mdbx.c + mdbx.h, optional mdbx.c++ + mdbx.h++); CMake or GNU Make builds it as a static or shared lib · none beyond libc and pthreads (ntdll.lib on Windows); bash, GNU Make or CMake to build · C99/C11 (CMake picks C23, C11 or C99; GNU Make uses -std=gnu11); C++ API needs C++11 and prefers C++17 to C++23. Tested since 2026 with GCC 11.3+, Clang 14+, MSVC 19.44+ (VS 2022), Elbrus LCC 1.28+; MinGW 10.2+ on Windows · Linux, Windows (not WSL1), macOS, iOS, Android, FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, DragonFly, Solaris/illumos, HarmonyOS and other POSIX.1-2008 systems; the file format depends on endianness only, not 32/64-bit; the header prints a warning when built for RISC-V

**Vs siblings:** SplinterDB, NuDB, TerarkDB and Titan are all write-optimized engines benchmarked against RocksDB on insert and load throughput (for example SplinterDB reports 6-10x faster inserts and Titan about 70% faster loading). Pick libmdbx when the workload is read-dominated, needs ordered range scans with zero-copy reads and snapshot isolation, or has several processes sharing one file. Pick a sibling when ingest rate is the bottleneck.

**Gotchas:**
- Values returned by get/cursor calls point into the map and stay valid only until the next update or the end of the transaction. Writing through them causes SIGSEGV, or silent DB corruption under MDBX_WRITEMAP or on dirty pages.
- mdbx_dbi_close is not synchronized with transactions running on other threads. Nested-transaction DDL had data-loss and assertion bugs fixed in mid-2026: a drop inside a child transaction that was then aborted emptied the table (#361), and rename caused a commit assertion (#360). Pin to the stable branch or a release.
- Sharing a DB across containers requires one kernel page cache, a shared PID namespace (e.g. --pid=host) and matching libmdbx/libc build options (compare the 'options:' line of mdbx_chk -V).
- Since December 2025 only amalgamated source ships and most tests are not included, so you cannot rerun the full test suite from a release tarball.

**Status:** Actively maintained: stable v0.14.4 shipped 2026-09-19, master is v0.15 development, and the last commit was 2026-09-25. It is Apache-2.0 amalgamated C and easy to vendor, but still pre-1.0, driven by one lead author, and developed on SourceCraft with GitHub (Mithril-mine) only as a mirror.

[repo](https://sourcecraft.dev/dqdkfa/libmdbx) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Mithril-mine/libmdbx#improvements-beyond-lmdb)

##### PGM Extra (pgm-extra-rs)  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust PGM learned index with BTreeSet/BTreeMap-style Set and Map; beats BTreeSet on u64 lookups, loses to binary search.

**Beats:** std::collections::BTreeSet / BTreeMap (Rust) — In the author's Criterion benchmark on an Apple M1 Pro (rustc version not stated; bench profile LTO with codegen-units=1), 10K lookups (half hits) against 1M uniformly random u64 keys took 489.5 us with Static::lower_bound at epsilon 256 versus 851.6 us with std BTreeSet::contains (1.7x). Find-then-scan-100 range queries took 120.5 us versus 174.3 us with BTreeSet::range (1.4x). The same table shows slice binary search (266.8 us) and HashMap (68.2 us) beating PGM, and the 7.7 MB vs 25.0 MB memory figures count construction-time allocations, not resident size.

**Known shortcoming:** In its own table binary search and HashMap beat PGM for lookups; rustc version unstated.

**Known shortcoming:** NOT FASTER THAN BINARY SEARCH in its own README (266.8 vs 489.5 us for binary search; HashMap also wins), so the '2-4x over binary search' claim is wrong. Correctness bugs: strings sharing an 8-byte prefix give wrong answers (a port of v1.3.0 gave 9,934/10k false negatives on URLs) and dense u64 above 2^53 collapse in f64 (23,853/100k misses). The memory table counts total bytes allocated during build, not resident size.

**Known shortcoming:** Map::build/extend keeps the first value on duplicate keys (docs and BTreeMap keep the last); Dynamic::insert can duplicate keys; Set/Map have no remove and each insert is an O(n) rebuild; the 'simd' feature does nothing; greedy shrinking-cone segments rather than optimal PLA. Code frozen since v1.3.0 (2025-12); 536 downloads, 0 reverse deps.

**How:** Each bottom-level segment is a linear model (first key, slope, intercept) that predicts a key's position to within ±epsilon. Upper levels index the segment start keys recursively with epsilon_recursive (default 4), so a lookup is a few multiply-adds plus a search over about 2·epsilon+2 array slots, not a pointer walk through B-tree nodes. Segments come from a greedy shrinking-cone pass (a feasible-slope interval anchored at each segment's first key), not from the optimal convex-hull PLA (OptimalPiecewiseLinearModel) that the reference C++ PGM-index uses, so it can produce more segments for the same epsilon. The code is safe Rust with no hand-written SIMD; the `simd` feature is declared in Cargo.toml, but nothing in src/ checks it.

**Use it when:**
- Read-mostly sets or maps with up to millions of unique u64/i64 (or narrower integer) keys, built once from sorted data and then queried many times, where you would otherwise reach for BTreeSet/BTreeMap.
- Ordered queries a HashMap cannot serve (lower_bound, range, find-then-scan). There the README measured 1.3-1.7x faster point lookups and 1.4x faster 100-element range scans than BTreeSet at 1M keys.
- Memory-sensitive keyed data: the retained model is a small fraction of a byte per key on top of the sorted Vec, so storage is close to that of the raw sorted array.
- You already keep keys in a sorted Vec or memory-mapped slice and want an index that stores only segments (Static/OneLevel), persistable with serde or zero-copy rkyv, including no_std + alloc builds (CI checks --no-default-features).

**Skip it when:**
- Exact-match or even plain ordered lookups on a static sorted array. In the README's own table, HashMap (68.2 us) and binary search on the sorted Vec (266.8 us) both beat the best PGM variant (489.5 us) on 10K queries over 1M keys. That contradicts the README's 'speedup of 2-4x over binary search' line, and a sorted Vec with partition_point already gets most of the memory win.
- String or byte keys where many keys share their first 8 bytes (URLs, 'user_000...' IDs). All such keys map to the same numeric key, and the segment builder accepts equal keys without checking the error bound. A line-by-line Python port of the v1.3.0 build/search/Set::get code, run this session, returned 9,934 false negatives out of 10,000 lookups on 'https://example.com/itemNNNNN'.
- Dense integer keys above 2^53, such as consecutive nanosecond timestamps near 1.7e18. Keys are converted to f64, so neighbours collapse to the same value, and the same port broke the epsilon bound: 23,853 of 100,000 lookups missed. Random full-range u64 keys and small integers came out correct.
- Write-heavy or mixed workloads. Set::insert and Map::insert re-sort and rebuild the whole index on every call, and Dynamic::range filters the entire base Vec linearly instead of using the index.
- Where maturity matters: single author, 536 total crates.io downloads, zero reverse dependencies, and no issues or PRs ever filed. The property tests cover only deduplicated u64 keys below 1,000,000, with no strings, large keys or duplicates.

**Integration:** crate · num-traits (with libm); optional rayon (parallel feature), serde, rkyv 0.8 · Rust edition 2024, so rustc 1.85+; no rust-version field is declared and CI tests only stable · any: safe Rust with no architecture-specific code, and no_std + alloc supported (Dynamic needs std). CI runs only on ubuntu-latest, and published benchmarks exist only for an Apple M1 Pro.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over the reference C++ PGM-index or PGM++ only when you need a pure-Rust, no_std-capable crate with serde/rkyv and BTreeSet-shaped wrappers, and can accept non-optimal segmentation and much thinner testing. Over indexset, pick it for read-mostly integer keys where memory matters; pick indexset for concurrent or frequent writes.

**Gotchas:**
- Map::build, FromIterator and Extend do a stable sort and then Vec::dedup_by, which keeps the first of equal keys. A duplicate key therefore keeps its earliest value, and extend() does not overwrite an existing key, even though the doc comments say 'last value wins (like BTreeMap::from_iter)'. No test covers duplicates. Map::insert does overwrite correctly.
- Dynamic::insert does not check the base data, and force_rebuild does not dedup. Inserting a key that is already indexed gives an inflated len() and a duplicated element after the next rebuild.
- Construction errors are swallowed. FromIterator/Extend fall back to an empty collection, and Set::insert on a set created with epsilon 0 returns true without storing anything.
- The published numbers are not measurements of the Set/Map wrappers. The benchmarks call Static::lower_bound on a Vec, while Set/Map get() scans the ±epsilon window linearly and is not benchmarked. The memory table uses stats_alloc bytes_allocated, which is cumulative bytes requested during construction. The PGM figure is mostly Static::new's temporary copy of the keys, and the BTreeSet figure includes from_iter's temporary Vec and sort, so it does not measure resident size.

**Status:** The metadata says active, but the last functional release is v1.3.0 (2025-12-29, rkyv support), with only CI and README commits since (latest 2026-07-28). It is MIT-licensed, safe Rust and small (about 4.8K lines under src/, including inline unit tests), so it is easy to vendor and patch, but there is no issue history to show how responsive the single maintainer is.

[repo](https://github.com/itsfoxstudio/pgm-extra-rs) · [benchmark](https://github.com/itsfoxstudio/pgm-extra-rs/blob/main/README.md)

##### redb  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Rust embedded ACID key-value store on copy-on-write B+trees; beats RocksDB/SQLite on durable single-key commits and reads; LMDB still reads faster.

**Beats:** RocksDB and SQLite (also benchmarked against LMDB and fjall, with mixed results) — On the author's redb-bench-compare harness (Ryzen 9950X3D, Samsung 9100 PRO NVMe, 5M random entries with 24-byte keys and 150-byte values, 4 GiB cache, all engines driven from Rust), 1,000 fsync'd single-key commits took 920 ms for redb, against 2,432 ms for RocksDB (rust-rocksdb 0.24 OptimisticTransactionDB, lz4) and 7,040 ms for SQLite (rusqlite 0.38 bundled, synchronous=FULL and otherwise default journal and cache), and 1M in-cache random reads took 1,138 ms against 2,911 ms and 4,283 ms. LMDB (heed 0.22) won every read row, the rustc version and flags are not stated (the repo pins toolchain 1.90), and the current harness emits rows the README table lacks, so the table may predate it.

**Known shortcoming:** LMDB wins every read row in redb's own table; RocksDB/fjall win batch writes and removals; redb uses the most disk. No rustc version or flags. The README's benchmark link is stale (real path crates/redb-bench-compare/benches/lmdb_benchmark.rs).

**Known shortcoming:** LMDB wins every read row (1.5-3.3x); batch writes 3.5-4.5x slower than RocksDB/fjall, removals ~3.4-3.9x slower, bulk load 1.85x slower than LMDB. No compression, so the largest file (4.00 GiB vs RocksDB 893 MiB), and long-lived readers grow it further. The SQLite baseline sets only synchronous=FULL (default journal and cache). Full repair after a crash by default (slow on big databases); +26% commit time on HDD since 4.2 (#1507). No C API; C++ needs FFI.

**How:** LMDB-style copy-on-write B+trees with MVCC: readers pin a root snapshot and never block the writer, and freed pages are recycled by epoch-based reclamation once no reader can see them.
