**Gotchas:**
- There is no disconnection handler, so closed sockets stay in Room::sockets and keep getting sends. In uWS v0.12 a WebSocket is a thin wrapper around a raw uv_poll_t*, so reusing that handle after close is unsafe.
- The lockstep walk assumes every publisher is also in the sorted subscriber vector. If a sender is not subscribed, the index stops advancing, and every later sender in that batch gets the shared frame, including its own messages.
- The benchmark client never parses a batched frame. It counts deliveries as frame length / 16, which works only because every deepstream test event is exactly 16 bytes.
- addSubscriber calls push_back and then re-sorts the whole vector on every connect, and broadcast() copies each map entry by value. The author's own comments mark both as unoptimized.

**Status:** Abandoned since the last commit on 2016-11-25. This copy re-uploads Alex Hultman's repo (the original URL now returns 404; one typo-fix commit comes from a contributor). It is Zlib-licensed and small enough to copy, but it builds only against 2016-era µWebSockets. The maintained path is current µWebSockets' own Apache-2.0 pub/sub (src/TopicTree.h), which also queues per-subscriber publishes and drains them in batches.

[repo](https://github.com/skyformat99/High-performance-pub-sub) · [benchmark](https://github.com/skyformat99/High-performance-pub-sub/blob/master/README.md)

##### LavinMQ  `Crystal`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

AMQP 0-9-1/MQTT 3.1.1 broker in Crystal with a very small RAM footprint; one customer replaced managed Kafka with it.

**Beats:** Apache Kafka — The only evidence against Kafka is a customer story on the vendor's blog (DAT Systems, 25 Oct 2024, Elixir/Broadway clients). It reports memory falling from 5 GB to under 40 MB on a development instance, consume times 3x lower and publish times 300x better than its earlier integration with an unnamed serverless Kafka service that had 'broker not found' and 'leader missing' errors. No hardware, sizing, Kafka configuration or method is given, so read these numbers as a migration anecdote, not a benchmark.

**Known shortcoming:** A vendor customer case study: the baseline is an unnamed serverless Kafka and the 5 GB to 40 MB memory figure is a local dev install.

**Known shortcoming:** Not Kafka wire-compatible (AMQP 0-9-1 and MQTT 3.1.x only; no AMQP 1.0, no MQTT 5, QoS2 downgraded to QoS1). Single-leader cluster (more nodes add redundancy, not write capacity), etcd required, zombie-leader bug on disk stall open (#2151). Since 2.9.0 confirms wait on syncfs and ISR followers, so the case study's numbers predate this. mmap risks: SIGBUS after a disk alarm (#2180), use-after-munmap (#2181), 30-200x disk write amplification (#2176), redelivery state lost on restart (#1911).

**How:** Storage is disk-first. Each queue is a series of 8 MB segment files mapped with mmap (MAP_SHARED). A publish is a memcpy appended to the last segment. Consumers read the segments sequentially. An ack writes a 4-byte position to a per-segment ack file, and a segment is deleted once every message in it is acked. Messages are not cached on the heap: the OS page cache does the caching and madvise(DONTNEED) releases pages, so resident memory stays flat as queues grow (the README says 25 MB of RAM with 100M messages enqueued). Publisher confirms are group-committed: one syncfs(2) call on a dedicated thread flushes every pending confirm in a batch. The code is compiled by LLVM to a native binary and uses a fiber/CSP event loop for I/O.

**Use it when:**
- You use Kafka as a plain work or event queue at modest volume (the case study ran ~4,000 to 50,000 messages a day) and the JVM broker's memory or operational weight is the main cost.
- You run RabbitMQ-style AMQP 0-9-1 workloads and want the same client libraries with lower RAM: the README lists 35 MB for 1,000 queues and 70 MB for 1,000 connections.
- Queues sometimes build very deep backlogs and you do not want broker RAM to grow with queue depth (messages live in mmap'd segments and the page cache).
- You want one small broker for both IoT MQTT 3.1.1 devices and AMQP backend consumers, or a replayable stream at moderate scale with header, key-value or geo filtering on the server.
- You run on small instances: vendor lavinmqperf runs show ~570k msg/s at 16 B with one producer and one consumer on a t4g.micro (2 vCPU, 1 GiB).

**Skip it when:**
- You depend on the Kafka API or its ecosystem (Connect, Streams, existing Kafka clients) or on partitioned topics with consumer-group rebalancing. LavinMQ is not wire-compatible.
- You need write throughput spread across nodes. The cluster has a single leader that takes all writes and replicates everything to followers, so adding nodes adds redundancy, not capacity.
- You need AMQP 1.0, MQTT 5 or MQTT QoS 2. QoS 2 publishes are downgraded to QoS 1, and only AMQP 0-9-1 and MQTT 3.1.x are listed.
- You need long-term or tiered log retention. Blob/S3 storage for streams is still an open feature request (#1070), so the log is bounded by local disk.
- You need mature failure handling in clustered mode. Open issues include a leader that never fails over when its disk stalls (#2151) and a stream-replay memory spike that killed a production node (#2226).

**Integration:** standalone server binary (deb/rpm packages, Homebrew, AUR, Docker image cloudamqp/lavinmq) · Runtime: libssl and liblz4 (per the Dockerfile); etcd for clustering. Build: Crystal plus the shards amqp-client, amq-protocol, systemd, lz4 and mqtt-protocol. · Crystal 1.21.0 to build from source (shard.yml); prebuilt packages need no toolchain · Linux (x86-64 and arm64; vendor benchmarks run on Graviton), macOS via Homebrew, Windows only through WSL. The syncfs group commit is Linux-only; other OSes fall back to a global sync().

**Vs siblings:** Pick LavinMQ over Redpanda, AutoMQ or Fluvio when you are willing to leave the Kafka protocol for AMQP routing (exchanges, DLX, TTL, priority and delayed queues) and want the smallest footprint. Pick it over RabbitMQ when you want the same AMQP 0-9-1 clients with a single-binary, low-RAM broker and can live without AMQP 1.0, MQTT 5 or QoS 2 and with a younger clustering implementation.

**Gotchas:**
- Confirm semantics changed in 2.9.0 (2026-06). Confirms now wait for a filesystem-wide syncfs and, in a cluster, for every in-sync follower. Before that, the broker confirmed once the message was in the mmap. The October 2024 case study predates this change, and --no-sync gets the speed back at the cost of durability.
- The mmap-per-segment design has sharp edges: SIGBUS when bursts of writes hit mapped pages right after a disk-full alarm clears (#2180), an open use-after-munmap SIGSEGV when stream retention runs during delivery (#2181), and one CPU core pinned during queue churn on Linux 7.0 to 7.1.8 on arm64 (a kernel bug, #2259).
- Write amplification: page-granular mmap writes plus a syncfs per confirm batch produced 30-200x more disk writes than network bytes received in the reporter's clusters (#2176). This matters on IOPS-billed volumes.
- Requeue and redelivery state lives only in memory. After a restart the redelivered flag and x-delivery-count reset, so a poison message can dodge x-delivery-limit (#1911). Stream consumers also inherit a default prefetch of 65,535.

**Status:** Very active: v2.10.0 shipped on 2026-09-25 after 2.9.3 on 2026-09-09, with frequent patch releases. It is Apache-2.0 and deployed as a packaged server, and CloudAMQP sells a hosted version.

[repo](https://github.com/cloudamqp/lavinmq) · [benchmark](https://lavinmq.com/blog/dat-systems-user-story)

##### Liftbridge  `Go`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Go server adding Kafka-style partitioned, replicated logs on top of NATS; self-reports ~1.1x NATS JetStream publish throughput on one node.

**Beats:** NATS JetStream — Using its own bench/producer tool, the repo reports ~241K msgs/sec (P99 2.0 ms) for 4 concurrent publishers, each pipelining 100 async publishes, on a single node with RF=1 and 256-byte messages. The message size comes from the CHANGELOG, and the ack policy is not stated, but the tool's default and the README example are both leader. The ~220K msgs/sec NATS JetStream figure is quoted as 'similar settings (pubbatch=100, file storage, RF=1)' with no source, version, hardware or harness, and no hardware, OS, Go version or run length is given for either side, so the ~1.1x is a cross-run comparison, not a side-by-side measurement.

**Known shortcoming:** Only ~1.1x vs JetStream (241K vs ~220K msgs/s); the 241K is the RF=1 leader-ack fast path, the JetStream figure has no source and no message size is given.

**Known shortcoming:** SECURITY/PRIVACY: telemetry is on by default (telemetry.basekick.net); open issues include authorization after group replace (#470, fix PR #471 open) and NATS credentials written to logs (#468). No fsync on segment writes, a 5 s high-watermark checkpoint and default LEADER ack with RF=1, so acknowledged messages can be lost on crash; data dir defaults to /tmp/liftbridge. The headline config (4 publishers x batch 100) is one the client's own bench tool warns 'may hang'; 256 B messages, no hardware/Go version. No compression/metrics/exactly-once/tiered storage; no release since v26.01.1.

**How:** Streams replicate with a Kafka-style in-sync-replica (ISR) protocol and use Raft (hashicorp/raft) only for cluster metadata, so each message goes into one log rather than a Raft log plus a message log. The partition leader drains its NATS subscription into batches of up to 1,024 messages (batch.max.messages). It appends each batch to a segmented commit log with a memory-mapped offset index, and segment writes go to the OS page cache with no fsync. The January 2026 release that added the benchmark also added an RF=1 fast path. For LEADER/NONE acks it skips the commit queue and advances the high watermark once per batch, and clients can pipeline publishes over the streaming gRPC PublishAsync call.

**Use it when:**
- You already run NATS and want durable, replayable, partitioned streams on existing subjects without changing the publishers.
- A Go shop that wants Kafka-like semantics (consumer groups, compaction, retention, offset/timestamp replay) from a single self-contained binary with embedded NATS instead of a JVM cluster.
- Small-message ingest (the benchmark uses 256-byte messages) in the roughly 100-250K msgs/sec per-partition range, where the client can batch or pipeline publishes.
- A single-region cluster run with RF=3, AckPolicy_ALL and min.insync.replicas=2 to get quorum-acknowledged, at-least-once delivery.
- Edge or IoT nodes running RF=1, where losing leader-acked but unflushed messages on a crash is acceptable.

**Skip it when:**
- You need fsync-level durability. Segment writes are never fsynced and the high watermark is checkpointed only every 5 s by default. A configurable sync policy exists only as a proposal in the repo's own bottleneck analysis.
- Multi-region clusters: an engineer who deployed it reported on HN that cross-region latency throttles the Raft metadata protocol, which slows stream creation and ISR changes. Federated clustering is only on the roadmap.
- You need transactions, exactly-once or idempotent producers, message compression, tiered storage, Prometheus metrics or SASL auth. The roadmap lists all of these as not done, and no release has shipped since v26.01.1.
- Read-heavy fan-out: the repo's own analysis flags one-message-at-a-time reads, one gRPC Send per message and per-message allocations on the subscribe path.
- Choosing it over JetStream mainly for speed: the ~1.1x margin is against an unsourced JetStream figure, and no replicated or AckPolicy_ALL throughput is published.

**Integration:** module (standalone Go server; prebuilt linux/darwin/windows tarballs, .deb/.rpm packages and a ghcr.io Docker image; clients speak gRPC) · NATS Server v2.10.0+ (external, or embedded in-process via nats.embedded); hashicorp/raft + raft-boltdb (metadata), gRPC, tysonmote/gommap (mmap index), google/tink (encryption at rest), casbin (authorization); clients: go-liftbridge v2 (official), plus Java and Rust official clients and community Node.js/Python clients · Go 1.25.6+ to build from source (raised from Go 1.21 in v26.01.1) · Release binaries for linux, darwin and windows on amd64 and arm64; CI tests run only on ubuntu-latest

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over NATS JetStream when you want Kafka-style partitioned logs with ISR replication, consumer groups and compaction layered onto an existing NATS deployment; if you want the default, better-supported choice inside nats-server, pick JetStream, since the throughput edge is marginal and unverified. Redpanda and Fluvio are catalogued as Kafka replacements with multi-level published numbers (Redpanda up to 1 GB/s). Choose those when throughput or tail latency at scale is the main requirement, and Liftbridge when you want a lighter, Go-native service tied to NATS.

**Gotchas:**
- The headline configuration (4 concurrent publishers with pub-batch=100) is the same combination the repo's bench/producer tool prints a warning about possibly hanging because of go-liftbridge client limitations.
- The default ack policy is LEADER, which acks after the leader's page-cache write. With RF=1 (the default replication factor) and no fsync, acked messages can be lost in a crash; uncommitted messages can also be lost during a leader change.
- Two defaults to change: anonymous telemetry is on and sends instance ID, OS, CPU and memory info to telemetry.basekick.net every 24 h (turn it off with telemetry.enabled: false or LIFTBRIDGE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false), and partition data lives under /tmp/liftbridge/<namespace> unless you set data.dir.
- Open security reports: #470, where Subscribe applies the consumer-group replacement (closing the legitimate subscriber) before checking authorization, with fix PR #471 still open; and #468, where NATS credentials embedded in server URLs are written verbatim to the startup log.

**Status:** Active in name: Basekick Labs revived it with v26.01.1 in January 2026 after no releases since v1.9.0 in September 2022. Commits since then are mostly dependabot bumps plus one Docker fix (last 2026-07-15), and the roadmap's v26.02 items have not shipped. It is Apache-2.0 with prebuilt binaries and packages, so it is usable as-is.

[repo](https://github.com/liftbridge-io/liftbridge) · [benchmark](https://github.com/liftbridge-io/liftbridge/blob/master/README.md)

##### msgq (comma.ai)  `C++`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

comma.ai's shared-memory ring-buffer pub/sub for one machine, callable from Python and C++; about 3.2x pyzmq IPC on Python-driven ping-pong.

**Beats:** ZeroMQ — The README's chart comes from msgq/examples/benchmark.py: two Python processes play 1 KiB ping-pong on an unspecified x86 Linux machine, taking the median of 5 randomized repeats. msgq reached 362.13k msgs/s against 113.97k for pyzmq XPUB/SUB over ipc:// (about 3.2x), with multiprocessing.Pipe at 231.66k, LCM UDP at 173.68k and Zenoh over a Unix socket at 86.03k. Counting both directions, that is about 181k round trips/s, or roughly 5.5 us per round trip including Python overhead. This is not native libzmq, no CPU, kernel or compiler is given (the SCons build uses -O2), and the 64 B and 64 KiB runs are not published.

**Known shortcoming:** The ~3.2x vs pyzmq is a Python ping-pong test (latency-bound, not streaming), shared-memory IPC on one host.

**Known shortcoming:** Same host only (no network); lossy: a slow subscriber is silently reset and there is no backpressure; one publisher per topic and the 26th subscriber evicts all readers (#702). Live assert()s abort the process on messages over segment/3 (~349 KB default) or empty messages. SIGUSR2 is sent per message to the subscriber's creator thread, so a recv on another thread waits out the poll timeout; lost-wakeup race (#208). macOS polls every 10 ms; /dev/shm files are never unlinked; copies on send and recv (not zero-copy). CPU not given; 64 B/64 KiB runs unpublished.

**How:** Each endpoint is a file in /dev/shm that every process mmaps. It holds a header of 64-bit atomics, each packing a 32-bit wrap-cycle counter with a 32-bit offset, one for the writer and one per reader, followed by a single-producer, multi-consumer byte ring of 8-byte-size-prefixed records. A send is a memcpy into the ring plus an atomic write-pointer update, then a tkill(SIGUSR2) to each reader thread to interrupt its nanosleep-based poll. A receive is a memcpy out, bracketed by checks of a per-reader validity flag in the style of a seqlock optimistic read, so there are no locks and no kernel socket copies. The writer never waits for readers: readers it laps are invalidated and reset, so there is no backpressure work on the hot path.

**Use it when:**
- Same-host sensor or telemetry pipelines where Python and C/C++ processes publish and subscribe to the same topics (openpilot's use case).
- Latest-value streams where dropping stale messages is acceptable or wanted; conflate=True returns only the newest message.
- Small to medium messages (64 B to 64 KiB are exercised by the benchmark) at high rates, where per-message syscalls and kernel copies (Unix sockets, pipes) cost too much CPU.
- Linux on x86-64 or aarch64 with /dev/shm, using CPython 3.11 to 3.14 (prebuilt manylinux, musllinux and macOS wheels on PyPI as msgq-ipc).
- Tests that need to step a pub/sub system deterministically, via the bundled fake backend (CEREAL_FAKE).

**Skip it when:**
- Any cross-host messaging: there is no network transport, and the subscriber address must be 127.0.0.1 (enforced by assert).
- Workloads that need reliable delivery, backpressure, acknowledgements or persistence: a slow subscriber is silently reset to the write head and loses messages.
- Topics with several producers, or request/reply and fan-in patterns: a new publisher takes over the endpoint and the old one's send fails with MultiplePublishersError.
- More than 25 subscribers on one topic, or messages larger than a third of the segment (about 349 KB with the default 1 MiB segment) unless segment_size is raised.
- Latency-sensitive work on macOS, which has no tkill and polls every 10 ms instead; processes that already use SIGUSR2; containers without a shared /dev/shm.

**Integration:** module (pip wheel msgq-ipc with Cython bindings); static libs libmsgq.a / libvisionipc.a via SCons for C++ · none at runtime (librt on Linux); build needs SCons, Cython>=3.1 and setuptools>=77 · C++17 (-std=c++1z), C gnu11; Python >= 3.11 · Linux x86-64 and aarch64 (CI and wheels); macOS x86-64/arm64 wheels, where wake-ups fall back to 10 ms polling

**Vs siblings:** Pick msgq over Monocoque (ZeroMQ-style REQ/REP over IPC and TCP) or TCPSHM (point-to-point TCP/SHM round trips) when you need one-to-many same-host pub/sub that Python and C++ can both use, and lossy latest-value delivery is fine. Choose those siblings or Zenoh when you need request/reply, reliable delivery or a network hop.

**Gotchas:**
- Despite folklore calling it zero-copy, the README says it copies on both send and receive. Large frames go through VisionIPC instead.
- Hard limits are enforced with assert(), and the SCons build does not define NDEBUG. A message over segment/3 aborts the publisher, and an empty message trips the receiver's size>0 assert. A 26th subscriber evicts every reader on the endpoint, which then re-registers (open issue #702 calls the fixed cap a footgun).
- Creating a queue installs a SIGUSR2 handler, and every send signals each subscriber's thread. The signal targets the thread that created the subscriber, so receiving on another thread waits out the poll timeout (100 ms slices when blocking). A rare lost wake-up in poll is acknowledged in closed issue #208.
- Creating a publisher resets the endpoint's reader table, so create publishers before subscribers (the benchmark barriers on this). Queue files in /dev/shm are never unlinked. OPENPILOT_PREFIX namespaces them.

**Status:** Actively maintained: v1.0 went to PyPI as msgq-ipc in September 2026, the last commit was 2026-09-09, and it runs in production in openpilot as a git submodule. It is MIT-licensed, and its roughly 500-line C++ core is easy to vendor, but the packaging depends on SCons and Cython.

[repo](https://github.com/commaai/msgq) · [benchmark](https://github.com/commaai/msgq/blob/master/README.md)

##### SMF write-ahead-log (Seastar Message Fabric)  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Seastar thread-per-core O_DIRECT write-ahead log from the smf project; ~48x lower worst-case produce latency than Kafka 1.0.

**Beats:** Kafka — On one localhost Linux 4.14 host (NVMe + XFS; CPU and compiler version not stated; release builds of that era used -O2 -ggdb per CMake/base_flags.cmake), using Seastar epoll + AIO without DPDK, smfb's slowest write took 34 ms versus 1618 ms for Kafka 1.0.0's ProducerPerformance (100M 100-byte records, acks=1, lz4, 32 partitions). That is about 48x on maximum latency only, with no percentile table or throughput. An earlier, since-deleted docs page (2 bare-metal dual Xeon E5-2640 v3 servers, SATA SSD, DPDK server, Kafka 0.11.0.1) reported 34-43x lower latency percentiles and 1.71M vs 0.42M msgs/s with 1 producer, or 2.27M vs 0.96M with 3 producers.

**Known shortcoming:** The 48x is max latency (1618 ms vs 34 ms against Kafka 1.0.0, acks=1); SMF starts about 1.3x slower. Last real commit 2021-10-17 (the 2023 activity is a dependabot branch).

**Known shortcoming:** The WAL was removed from master on 2018-02-24 (issue #203); the repo is now RPC-only and the WAL survives only in history (772474eb02). Weak durability: no fdatasync in the write path, a 1-minute default timer flush, and dma_write not awaited, so acks precede disk writes. Broker get() always returns 500; no Kafka protocol, replication or consumer groups.

**Known shortcoming:** Tied to the 2018 Seastar API (needs porting); Linux x86 SSE4.2 only, expects XFS and >=1 GiB per shard; built -O2 -ggdb. The author's numbers disagree across sources (blog 48x max latency, deleted docs 34-43x, a commit message 91x, issue #195 10x); a deleted docs page shows 1.71M vs 0.42M msg/s throughput.

**How:** It uses Seastar shard-per-core ownership. Each topic/partition is routed to one core by jump consistent hash and has a single reader/writer, with no locks or atomics. Writes are copied into page-aligned 4 KB chunks and sent as O_DIRECT dma_write calls (up to 4 concurrent per segment) once 1 MB is pending or a flush timer fires, with segments rolled at 64 MB and tagged with Seastar IO priority classes. The 48x result came from a perf/toplev pass: removing a per-put std::sort (74% of CPU), replacing a map.find with std::lower_bound over a std::deque (offsets are monotonic), and caching each entry's on-disk size to cut LLC misses.

**Use it when:**
- You are building a Seastar service and want a reference O_DIRECT segment writer with page-aligned chunking, bounded concurrent DMA writes, and a size-or-time flush policy to port.
- Write-heavy ingest of small records (about 100 B) in large client batches, where acknowledging after in-memory buffering (log-writer semantics, as the author concedes) is acceptable.
- Single-node, per-core-partitioned append logs on Linux + XFS + NVMe, where you can pin cores and route each partition to its owning shard.
- Studying a documented profiling case (perf record/stat, toplev, LLC-miss hunting) on a real log-write path.

**Skip it when:**
- As a Kafka replacement. It has no Kafka protocol, no replication (chain_replication_service::put only appends locally), no consumer groups, and broker-side reads return 500. The reader code has an in-progress 'XXX working on this' path.
- When you need per-write durability. The write path has no fdatasync, the timer flush defaults to 1 minute (smfb used the default), and acks return before DMA writes finish.
- When you want a maintained dependency. It was deleted from master in Feb 2018, is written against the 2018 Seastar API (old <core/...> include paths), and was built with an Ansible-provisioned Seastar, so expect a port before it compiles.
- Non-Linux, non-x86 or small hosts. smfb refuses to start without SSE4.2, throws below 1 GiB of memory per shard unless --developer is set, and logs an error when the log directory is not on XFS.

**Integration:** static lib · Seastar (early-2018, with libaio; DPDK optional), Flatbuffers, Boost, zstd, lz4, xxHash, RE2, Roaring bitmaps, HdrHistogram; smf RPC for the smfb broker · GCC with Seastar-era flags (CMake enables -fconcepts for GCC > 6.1); CMake 3.3+; C++ standard inherited from Seastar pkg-config flags, not stated · Linux x86-64 with SSE4.2 (broker check); XFS expected; O_DIRECT/AIO required

**Vs siblings:** Pick Redpanda (a maintained, Kafka-API-compatible C++ broker also built on Seastar) for any production Kafka replacement, and Walrus (maintained Rust log engine) when you need an embeddable log. Pick the SMF WAL only as a small, Apache-2.0 reference design for a Seastar-native O_DIRECT log writer that you will port and harden yourself.

**Gotchas:**
- In wal_segment, append() and do_flush() launch dma_write in the background without awaiting it (commented 'send in background - safely!!'). As written, flush() and close() do not wait for in-flight writes, and write errors are not propagated to the ack.
- wal_segment::open() throws if the segment file already exists, and files are opened with create|truncate. Recovery and reopen depend on epoch-named new files, not on appending to old ones.
- Partition routing is the caller's job (jump_consistent_hash(partition, smp::count)). Misrouting shows up as directory or system_error failures, per the header comment.
- The headline numbers disagree across the author's own sources: the blog says 48x (max latency only), the deleted docs page says 34-43x across percentiles, commit 5585e52f45 says '4x faster than kafka to 91X', and issue #195 says '10x lower latency'.

**Status:** Abandoned: the WAL was deleted from master in Feb 2018, and the repo (last master commit 2021-10-17) is now RPC-only. The Apache-2.0 code can be recovered from commit 772474eb02, but it is tied to a 2018 Seastar API and has unfinished reads and weak durability, so treat it as reference code, not a dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/smfrpc/smf) · [benchmark](https://www.alexgallego.org/perf/toplev/2018/02/08/performance-debugging.html)

##### StrangeQ  `Go`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Single-node Go AMQP 0.9.1 broker speaking RabbitMQ's wire protocol; author measures 1.1-4.5x RabbitMQ 4.3's durable, confirmed throughput.

**Beats:** RabbitMQ — On one 16-core Apple Silicon Mac (chip model and Go version not stated), the author ran RabbitMQ 4.3 (default classic queue, in an OrbStack ARM64 Linux container; the README does not say whether the container's fsyncs reach the host disk) and host-native StrangeQ under the same amqp091-go perftest: one durable queue, persistent 1 KB messages, confirms with up to 1000 in flight per producer, fsync on, prefetch 100, 20 s runs, median per-second consumed rate. StrangeQ was 1.67x RabbitMQ at 1 producer/1 consumer and about 4.4x at 10/10 and 30/30, mostly because RabbitMQ fell from 64.5K to about 25K msg/s while StrangeQ stayed at 107-114K; with 64 KB bodies it was 1.10x.

**Known shortcoming:** The 1.10-4.48x vs RabbitMQ 4.3 is the author's own README benchmark comparing classic queues with different fsync settings, container vs native; RabbitMQ is not a listed baseline; 5 stars, AI-assisted.

**Known shortcoming:** Lopsided benchmark: RabbitMQ ran in an OrbStack Linux container while StrangeQ ran native; the ~4.4x comes mostly from RabbitMQ falling to ~25K msg/s at 10-30 producers on one queue (only 1.10x with 64 KB bodies). No clustering/HA, priority/lazy queues, global QoS or management UI. LLM-written, one maintainer; a WAL deadlock and acked-message redelivery were fixed in 2026-08, after the July bench and after the latest release v0.10.0; WAL v4 cannot read older WAL files (--unsafe-recovery discards them); the README's go install is broken (module path not resolvable).

**How:** All queues share one write-ahead log whose writer goroutine does drain-then-flush group commit: every record that queued up while the previous fsync ran (up to 1000) goes out in one write and one fdatasync (Linux) or os.File.Sync (other OSes), and a publish is confirmed only after its batch is synced. Confirms are batched too: each channel tracks a contiguous durable watermark with atomics, and a per-connection flusher sends a single basic.ack with multiple=true for the whole range. Each queue keeps an in-memory ring of message pointers where the slot is the delivery tag masked to the ring size, claimed with a per-slot CAS (64K slots by default); messages spill to the WAL at 80% full and are later checkpointed to segment files. On the connection side, separate reader/processor goroutines and a dedicated ack goroutine feed batched deliveries that go out as one write per batch (writev for bodies of 32 KB or more), with frames pooled via sync.Pool.

**Use it when:**
- Go services or CI suites that need a real AMQP 0.9.1 broker without an Erlang runtime or Docker: embed it in the process or ship one static binary (release builds exist for linux-386/amd64/arm64 and darwin-amd64/arm64).
- Single-node, durable, publisher-confirm workloads where many producers feed one queue with small (~1 KB) messages. In the author's table StrangeQ holds about 107-114K msg/s at 10-30 producers, while RabbitMQ's default classic queue drops to about 24-25K.
- Integration tests for code written against RabbitMQ clients, where a quick-starting in-process broker matters more than full RabbitMQ feature parity. The repo has a conformance target (make conformance-rabbitmq) that checks behavior against RabbitMQ 4.3.
- Teams that want to profile and debug the broker with standard Go tools (net/http/pprof, go tool pprof) and scrape Prometheus metrics, instead of using Erlang tooling.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that needs clustering, replication or HA; the README lists these as not implemented. It does not mention quorum queues, streams, or plugins such as shovel or federation.
- Apps that depend on priority queues (x-max-priority), consumer priorities, lazy queues, global QoS, prefetch_size > 0 (rejected with 540), SASL EXTERNAL, connection.secure, or the management UI/CLI.
- Large-message workloads: with 64 KB bodies the author's lead shrinks to 1.10x.
- Production systems where the durability track record matters. The Show HN says an LLM wrote the code; it has one maintainer, 5 stars and no third-party bug reports. Fixes for a WAL read-path deadlock and for acknowledged records being served again from the segment tier landed in August 2026, after the benchmark was run.
- Code that relies on RabbitMQ edge semantics the README lists as divergent. Zero-TTL messages are dropped when no consumer is ready. A malformed per-message expiration is treated as no TTL. reject-publish is not enforced inside a transaction. A mandatory publish to a full reject-publish queue is returned with code 312.

**Integration:** module (Go module github.com/maxpert/amqp-go in src/amqp-go of the strangeq repo; also prebuilt server binaries) · go.uber.org/zap, knadh/koanf (yaml/env/file), prometheus/client_golang, RoaringBitmap/roaring, fxamacker/cbor, HdrHistogram/hdrhistogram-go, golang.org/x/crypto, x/sys, x/sync, gopkg.in/yaml.v3 (plus rabbitmq/amqp091-go for perftest/tests and stretchr/testify for tests) · Go 1.25.1 (go.mod directive) · Linux (uses fdatasync) and macOS (uses os.File.Sync). Release binaries cover linux-386/amd64/arm64 and darwin-amd64/arm64. There are Windows-specific source files but no Windows release binary.

**Vs siblings:** Pick StrangeQ when you want an AMQP 0.9.1 broker you can embed in a Go program; it is the only catalogued sibling benchmarked directly against RabbitMQ 4.3 on durable, confirmed traffic. Prefer LavinMQ (AMQP 0-9-1 plus MQTT, about 1K stars, actively developed) when maturity matters, and skip SocketPro if you must keep AMQP clients, since its RabbitMQ win comes from its own C++ framework (repo last pushed 2023).

**Gotchas:**
- The module path in go.mod (github.com/maxpert/amqp-go) does not match the repo, and proxy.golang.org returns 'not found' for it. So the README's `go install github.com/maxpert/amqp-go/cmd/amqp-server@latest` and plain library imports do not resolve: clone and build in src/amqp-go, or use a replace directive.
- The latest release, v0.10.0 (2026-07-02), predates both the benchmarked build (measured 2026-07-14) and the August 2026 data-loss and deadlock fixes. Build from main if you want the benchmarked and fixed code.
- The WAL format v4 is a deliberate clean break: files from older versions are rejected with ErrUnsupportedWALVersion. The --unsafe-recovery flag lets the broker start but discards the unparseable file, so drain queues before upgrading across formats.
- The README says a bare `amqp-server` runs 'in-memory', but DefaultConfig writes to ./data with fsync and per-record CRC32 turned on (the sample config puts the CRC cost at about 8% CPU; fsync:false is an opt-in that transactions ignore). Each queue keeps unacked messages in its RAM ring (64K slots by default, 262144 in the README's production example) and spills to the WAL at 80% full.

**Status:** Actively developed by one maintainer (last commit 2026-08-29, many July-August commits fixing races, deadlocks and a data-loss path) and MIT-licensed, but it has 5 stars, no outside issues, and a latest release older than the fixes: fine for tests and experiments, unproven in production.

[repo](https://github.com/maxpert/strangeq) · [benchmark](https://github.com/maxpert/strangeq#performance)

##### TCPSHM  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++11 framework for crash-recoverable point-to-point messaging over TCP or shared memory; claims ~4.8x lower RTT than ZeroMQ.

**Beats:** ZeroMQ — The author ran an echo ping-pong on one Ubuntu 14.04 host (Xeon E5-2687W, 3.1 GHz, threads pinned), measuring average RTT only (total elapsed time divided by message count, no percentiles): 8.82 us over TCP loopback against 42.27 us for ZeroMQ REQ/REP over TCP (about 4.8x), and 0.338 us in SHM mode against 30.65 us for ZeroMQ IPC over a Unix domain socket (about 90x, but that compares busy-polled shared memory with a kernel socket). TCPSHM was built with g++ -std=c++11 -O3 (version not stated) while the ZeroMQ version, build and benchmark code are not published, and the README's 16/36/68/200-byte message mix matches the 2018 test code, but a 2020-05-04 commit changed HEAD's test to 4-16-byte payloads and a different clock, so HEAD does not reproduce the published numbers.

**Known shortcoming:** The ZeroMQ bench code and version are not public; the shared-memory vs ZeroMQ IPC comparison is not apples-to-apples. Abandoned since 2020. Flags are g++ -std=c++11 -O3 (test/build.sh).

**Known shortcoming:** README bench predates HEAD (a 2020 commit changed message sizes and the clock), so HEAD doesn't reproduce it; average RTT only, no percentiles. The ~90x SHM figure is busy-polled shared memory vs Unix sockets; the echo example busy-spins 2 client and 3 server threads. The SHM queue uses compiler-only barriers (no atomics/fences), so it is only correct on x86-TSO, not ARM. Linux + IPv4 only; no fsync or power-loss durability; no TLS; shm files mode 0666 and the code assumes logged-in clients won't attack. Documented constructor argument order is wrong (#6); slots stay bound to a client name until Stop(); tiny compile-time default queues.

**How:** SHM mode uses a bounded single-producer/single-consumer variable-length ring buffer (SPSCVarQueue, from the author's SPSC_Queue project) in a shm_open segment: 64-byte cache-line blocks, read and write indices on separate 128-byte-aligned lines, a producer-side cached read index, and messages built in place, synchronized only by compiler barriers with no atomics, locks or syscalls on the data path. Both sides busy-poll, so there is no kernel wakeup cost. TCP mode is a non-blocking, TCP_NODELAY socket polled from the user's thread, with the ack sequence piggybacked in each 8-byte message header, optional batching via PushMore(), and a send queue that is an mmap-ed file with no fsync/msync. The library creates no threads and does no logging, exceptions or clock reads.

**Use it when:**
- Same-host IPC between two C++ processes where latency dominates, for example a trading gateway and a strategy, and you can give a core to each busy-polling thread. SHM mode measured 0.34 us average RTT on the author's machine.
- Point-to-point streams or request/response of small binary structs (under 64 KB including the 8-byte header) that must resume automatically after either side crashes or reconnects, without running a broker.
- Sessions that should reset on a schedule: renaming the server (for example 'Server20180714') discards the previous session's unhandled messages, as the README's daily trading example describes.
- A small, known set of clients where you want to map connection groups to threads yourself, and a dependency-free header-only codebase (nine headers, about 56 KB) that you can vendor and audit.

**Skip it when:**
- You need durability through power loss or host reboot. The README says it does not persist data to disk: queues live in the page cache (mmap-ed files with no fsync) or in /dev/shm.
- You need pub/sub, fan-out, topics, brokered storage or clients in other languages. It is C++-only and point-to-point.
- The host is CPU-constrained or shared, or you need many connections. Every polling thread spins (the bundled echo example spins 2 threads in the SHM client and 3 in the server), and the README says performance degrades past about 1000 live connections.
- Non-x86 or weakly ordered CPUs such as ARM. The shared-memory queue orders memory with compiler-only asm barriers and no hardware fences or atomics, which relies on x86 total store order. Issue #4 about ARM was only fixed in the test timer code. It is also Linux-only and IPv4-only.
- Untrusted networks or multi-user hosts. There is no TLS, and authentication is only a user-defined login blob. The code assumes a logged-in client 'will not attack us' when it processes acks, and shared-memory files are created with mode 0666 (before umask).

**Integration:** header-only · none beyond Linux POSIX APIs (sockets, shm_open, mmap). The test build links -lrt -lpthread. · C++11 (test/build.sh uses g++ -std=c++11 -O3). It uses GCC builtins (__builtin_bswap*, __BYTE_ORDER__) and GNU inline asm, so it needs GCC or Clang. Tested compiler versions are not documented. · Linux only; x86-64 is the only tested architecture (the benchmark host is a Xeon E5-2687W); IPv4 only

**Vs siblings:** Every sibling is a broker or pub/sub system (Wisp/NATS, Zenoh, FluxMQ, Redpanda and Woodpecker as Kafka-class systems, SocketPro), so pick TCPSHM only for one C++ point-to-point link that needs sub-microsecond same-host latency and automatic resend after a crash, with no topics, fan-out or disk durability. Zenoh is the closer, maintained alternative if you need pub/sub with optional shared memory (a feature flag you must enable).

**Gotchas:**
- The interface doc and examples show the constructor as (ptcp_dir, name), but TcpShmClient and TcpShmServer actually take (name, ptcp_dir) (open issue #6). The examples pass the same string for both, which hides the mismatch.
- All capacities are compile-time Conf constants with small defaults: ShmQueueSize is 2048 B (32 64-byte blocks) and TcpQueueSize is 2000 B, and Alloc() returns nullptr when the queue is full, so the caller has to retry. In SHM mode every message takes whole 64-byte blocks, so a 12-byte message uses 64 B.
- A server connection slot is bound to a client name at first login and stays bound until Stop(). Once MaxShmConnsPerGrp or MaxTcpConnsPerGrp distinct names have logged into a group, new names are rejected with 'Max client cnt exceeded'. If persisted sequence numbers disagree at login, the connection fails through OnSeqNumberMismatch and must be fixed by hand.
- There are no transactions. A crash between Pop() and Push() can drop a response, and doing Push() before Pop() can duplicate one on recovery. The TCP side closes the connection if a message is larger than TcpRecvBufMaxSize, or if a send splits an 8-byte block and then gets EAGAIN; the connection recovers when it reconnects.

**Status:** Abandoned: the last commit (2020-05-04) was a cache-padding tweak, and the open issues #5 (2020) and #6 (2025) have no replies. It is MIT-licensed, about 56 KB of dependency-free headers, and easy to vendor and patch.

[repo](https://github.com/MengRao/tcpshm) · [benchmark](https://github.com/MengRao/tcpshm#performance)

##### Walrus (embedded log/WAL storage engine)  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Embeddable Rust per-topic write-ahead log engine; ~8% more unsynced writes/s than a local single-broker Kafka, tied when fsync'd.

**Beats:** Kafka — On unstated Linux hardware, 10 threads each wrote bursts of 500-1024-byte records to their own topic for a default 120 s: Walrus through its per-record pwrite() path averaged 1,205,762 unsynced writes/s, against 1,112,120 (~1.08x) for a Java producer (acks=all, idempotence, linger.ms=0) feeding one unreplicated Kafka broker on localhost:9092, and with fsync per write the result was 4,980 to 4,921 with RocksDB's WAL at 5,222. No CPU, disk, kernel, filesystem, Kafka version or broker flush setting is given, and the Kafka harness counts a record when send() enqueues it, not when the broker acknowledges it.

**Known shortcoming:** Only about 8% faster unsynced; with fsync it ties. Benchmark code is public but no CPU/compiler/OS is stated.

**Known shortcoming:** The Kafka harness counts messages at send() enqueue, not ack, against a broker on localhost (a loopback hop exists). No latency numbers; hardware given only as 'Linux'. Not a Kafka drop-in: one cursor per topic, no offsets or consumer groups; distributed mode replicates only metadata; crates.io stuck at 0.2.0 (2025-10).

**Known shortcoming:** Durability bugs: the pwrite result is discarded and fsync errors are only printed, so appends return Ok on a full disk. Where io_uring is blocked (Fargate/gVisor/seccomp) the background flush thread panics and fsync and file deletion stop silently (#25 open). No Windows (#26 wontfix). Prints to stdout per append unless WALRUS_QUIET; fsync/backend settings are process-global; 256 B header per entry (docs say 64).

**How:** Each topic has one writer that puts a 256-byte rkyv-serialized header (length, owning topic, FNV-1a checksum) plus the payload into 10 MB blocks cut from sparse, preallocated 1 GB files with a single pwrite(). So the append path has no network hop, no wire protocol and, in NoFsync or Milliseconds mode, no fsync; a background thread deduplicates dirty files and fsyncs them as one io_uring batch every N ms. The newer batch_append_for_topic path submits up to 2,000 planned writes in one io_uring submission, but that path was not used in the Kafka comparison.

**Use it when:**
- One Rust process needs a durable append-only log or queue per topic (event log, job queue, local WAL), and you would otherwise run a local Kafka broker just for that.
- Many independent topics written from separate threads: writers are per topic and do not contend with each other (the benchmark used one topic per thread).
- Throughput-first ingestion that can accept a bounded loss window (FsyncSchedule::Milliseconds, default 200 ms) or no durability at all; the measured edge over Kafka exists only in that unsynced mode.
- Linux hosts that permit io_uring, if you plan to rely on the batch append/read APIs; the author says their non-io_uring fallback is roughly 5-10x slower.
- Records of roughly 0.5 KB and up; every entry carries a fixed 256-byte header, so tiny records mostly write overhead.

**Skip it when:**
- You need Kafka semantics or ecosystem: wire/client compatibility, consumer groups, offset-based seek or replay, time-based retention. Walrus has one consumable cursor per topic and deletes a file once every block in it has been read. On HN the author said a Kafka translation layer was dropped because Walrus is message-based, not offset-based.
- You need per-record durable throughput: with fsync on every write it measured 4,980 writes/s, a tie with Kafka (4,921) and behind RocksDB's WAL (5,222).
- You have latency SLOs: no p50/p99 latency figures are published (a gap called out in the Show HN thread); only throughput was measured.
- Linux sandboxes where io_uring_setup is blocked (AWS Fargate, Lambda, gVisor, restrictive seccomp). The background flush/cleanup thread panics at startup while Walrus::new() still returns Ok, so periodic fsync and file deletion silently stop (open issue #25).
- Windows (does not compile; the maintainer said support is not planned, issue #26), or setups that need replicated data: the distributed mode's README describes Raft for metadata only, with each segment's data held by its leader node.

**Integration:** crate (walrus-rust on crates.io; latest published release is 0.2.0 from 2025-10-19) · rand 0.8, memmap2 0.9, libc, rkyv 0.7 (validation), rkyv_derive, bytecheck 0.6, tracing; io-uring 0.7 on Linux only · Rust edition 2024, so Rust 1.85+; no rust-version declared in Cargo.toml · Linux primary (io_uring for batch I/O and background fsync; mmap backend as alternative); non-Linux Unix code paths exist without io_uring (not benchmarked); Windows does not compile

**Vs siblings:** Pick Walrus when you want a library inside a Rust process rather than a broker to operate; SMF's Seastar-based write-ahead log is the only sibling of similar shape. To replace Kafka as a networked, replicated service, Redpanda (Kafka-compatible, 12-70x lower p99.99 latency), Fluvio (~1.5x throughput) or Woodpecker (3.5x MB/s in local-FS mode) all claim larger margins than Walrus's ~8% unsynced edge.

**Gotchas:**
- The fd backend throws away pwrite's result (`let _ = self.file.write_at(...)` in src/wal/storage.rs), and background fsync errors are only printed. So append_for_topic can return Ok after a failed or short write, for example on a full disk.
- Debug output goes to stdout via println! on every append unless the WALRUS_QUIET env var is set. The benchmark sets WALRUS_QUIET=1, so production callers should too; even in quiet mode each check is an env-var lookup on the hot path.
- Process-wide state leaks across instances. The fsync schedule that decides O_SYNC is a OnceLock set by the first Walrus created, and the fd/mmap backend choice is a global atomic. So the v0.2.0 post's pattern of several instances with different FsyncSchedules in one process does not give each instance its own file-open behavior. Also, SyncEach on the fd backend opens files O_SYNC and still calls fsync after every append.
- Each entry costs a 256-byte header (docs/architecture.md still says 64 bytes). The header embeds the topic name and must serialize into 254 bytes, so very long topic names are rejected. The published MB/s figures count payload bytes only.

**Status:** Active but effectively single-author (last commit 2026-05-13, MIT, ~1.9k stars) and small enough to vendor (~4.8k lines under src/), but crates.io still serves 0.2.0 from October 2025, so the WALRUS_DATA_DIR race fix (PR #22) and the ~13% write-throughput struct-packing change (PR #24) are git-only.

[repo](https://github.com/nubskr/walrus) · [benchmark](https://nubskr.com/2025/10/20/walrus_v0.2.0)

##### Woodpecker  `Go`  `Apache-2.0 (server/ directory dual-licensed AGPL-3.0-only OR SSPL-1.0)`  `active`  `Tier C`

Go WAL library storing append-only logs on S3/object storage or local disk; vendor test shows 3.5-5.8x Kafka single-stream write throughput

**Beats:** Apache Kafka — One first-party single-node, single-client, single-log-stream write test, published identically in the README, the Milvus docs and a May 2025 Milvus blog post. Woodpecker to local FS: 450 MB/s at 1.8 ms; to S3: 750 MB/s at 166 ms; to MinIO: 71 MB/s at 184 ms. Kafka: 129.96 MB/s at 58 ms; Pulsar: 107 MB/s at 35 ms. No CPU or instance type (only 'single EC2 instance' for the S3 ceiling), message size, batching, Go version, or Kafka/Pulsar settings (acks, fsync, replication) are given, the repo has no Kafka/Pulsar harness, and the numbers come from early-2025 development builds.

**Known shortcoming:** Vendor-only single-stream benchmark from early-2025 builds; no hardware, message size or Kafka/Pulsar acks/fsync/replication settings; no Kafka harness in the repo. Not uniformly faster: MinIO mode 71 vs Kafka 130 MB/s; S3/MinIO latency 166/184 ms vs Kafka 58 ms; embedded mode 200-500 ms. Licence trap: the embedded client imports server/ (AGPL-3.0/SSPL), so embedded use links copyleft code. Not a Kafka replacement (own Go API, no Kafka protocol, partitions or consumer groups; one exclusive writer per log; needs etcd; Go 1.25+, Linux only). v0.1.x: quorum-mode bug losing acknowledged data after compaction (#320) fixed only 2026-09; open reader bugs (#277, #352); README drifts from code.

**How:** Group commit: appends land in an in-memory sequential buffer (entries ordered by id, gaps held back) that is flushed when it hits an entry/byte cap or a timer (defaults 200 ms for object storage, 10 ms for local FS, 1 ms in service mode), turning many small writes into large sequential ones. On object storage each flush is cut into ~2 MB blocks uploaded as separate objects in parallel from a goroutine pool (maxFlushThreads, default 32) while acks are still released strictly in entry order; blocks of a sealed segment are later compacted into merged objects (up to segmentCompactionPolicy.maxBytes, default 2 MB). Local-FS mode appends CRC32-framed records to one segment file and fsyncs once per flushed block. Writer fencing uses object-store conditional PUT (If-None-Match) instead of lock round-trips where the backend supports it; the vendor frames the result as reaching 60-80% of each backend's raw bandwidth.

**Use it when:**
- A Go system (vector DB, database, event-sourced service) that needs an ordered, durable WAL and already runs etcd plus S3/MinIO, and you want to stop operating a Kafka or Pulsar cluster for it.
- Bulk single-stream appends to S3 where ~100-200 ms commit latency is fine: the vendor measured 750 MB/s from one client/stream vs 130 MB/s for Kafka.
- Single-node deployments on local disk that want fsync-acknowledged appends at millisecond latency (vendor: 450 MB/s at 1.8 ms).
- Log retention priced at object-storage rates with stateless compute, where catch-up/replay reads can come straight from object storage.
- Multi-AZ durability via the 3-replica quorum service mode (ack after 2 of 3 replicas, async flush to object storage), if you can run the extra LogStore service.

**Skip it when:**
- You need the Kafka API or ecosystem (wire protocol, partitions, consumer groups, Connect/Streams, transactions): none of it exists here.
- Latency-sensitive writes over object storage: the vendor's own table shows S3/MinIO modes at 166/184 ms vs Kafka 58 ms and Pulsar 35 ms, and the Milvus docs put embedded MemoryBuffer mode at 200-500 ms.
- Self-hosted MinIO backends: the same table has Woodpecker at 71 MB/s, about half of Kafka's 130 MB/s.
- Many concurrent producers into one log: each log has one exclusive writer (etcd session lock or conditional-write fence); in lock mode failover can wait up to the 10 s session TTL.
- Risk-averse production outside Milvus: still v0.1.x, and a quorum-mode bug that lost acknowledged data after compaction (#320) was only fixed in September 2026.

**Integration:** module · etcd (required; only metadata backend supported) plus an S3-compatible object store or local filesystem; Go deps include minio-go, Azure SDK, etcd client/server v3.5, gRPC, Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, zap and hashicorp/memberlist (service-mode gossip). Service mode also ships a LogStore server, Docker images, a Kubernetes operator and the wpcli admin tool. · Go 1.25 (go.mod declares go 1.25.0) · Pure Go; Docker build images target Linux only (Ubuntu 20.04/22.04, Rocky Linux 8, Amazon Linux 2023); other OSes not documented

**Vs siblings:** No siblings catalogued yet. Against the Kafka baseline, pick it only when you want an embeddable Go WAL on object storage rather than a general-purpose broker.

**Gotchas:**
- License trap: the embedded client (woodpecker/client/logstore_client_local.go) imports the server/ package, which is AGPL-3.0-only or SSPL-1.0, so embedded mode compiles copyleft code into your binary; only the non-server packages are Apache-2.0.
- Writers can be invalidated under you: when the etcd session expires writes fail with ErrLogWriterLockLost and the app must reopen a writer. With fencePolicy 'auto' on a new cluster, startup fails outright if the object store's conditional-write check fails; there is no silent fallback to locks.
- Docs lag code: the README reader example calls OpenLogReader(ctx, start), but the interface is now OpenLogReader(ctx, from, readerBaseName), and the README config shows 4 MB flushes / 64 threads while current defaults are 2 MB / 32.
- Open reader issues: ReadNext keeps serving data after the reader is closed (#277), and an idle tail reader polls etcd plus a quorum-wide RPC every 200 ms (#352).

**Status:** Actively developed (v0.1.45 released 2026-09-21, releases roughly weekly) and shipped as the default WAL in Milvus 2.6+, but still pre-1.0. Client packages are Apache-2.0 and server/ is AGPL-3.0/SSPL, so embedding it in proprietary software needs legal review.

[repo](https://github.com/zilliztech/woodpecker) · [benchmark](https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus-docs/blob/v3.0.x/site/en/reference/architecture/woodpecker_architecture.md)

##### Zenoh  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0 OR EPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust pub/sub and query protocol that can run with or without a broker; in one 2023 study it moved 10-65x Kafka's bitrate.

**Beats:** Kafka — A National Taiwan University team ran Zenoh 0.7.0-rc against a Kafka 3.2.1 broker driven by the Rust rdkafka 0.28.0 client (linger.ms=0, batch.size=400KB, acks=0, no compression) on a Ryzen 7 5800X fixed at 4.0 GHz with Ubuntu 20.04, reporting medians. Single-machine, Zenoh peer mode got 65x Kafka's bitrate at 8 B, 24x at 8 KB and 10x at 32 KB. Over 100 GbE, Zenoh reached ~50 Gbps P2P and ~34 Gbps brokered against Kafka's 5 Gbps. No compiler or flags are given, Kafka could not be run above 512 KB, the benchmark repo now returns 404, and the page's multi-machine iperf ceiling (44 Gbps) is below Zenoh's own 50 Gbps figure.

**Known shortcoming:** The benchmark URL 404s (branch master, not main; now the zenoh.io blog) and the ZettaScaleLabs/zenoh-perf bench repo is gone; no compiler stated; the arXiv comparison is a non-peer-reviewed preprint (verifier downgrade from A).

**Known shortcoming:** Not a Kafka drop-in: no durable log, offsets or consumer groups; storages keep only the latest value per key. The benchmark is a 2023 vendor blog on 0.7.0-rc (before the Tokio port and 1.0 batching rework); the page's multi-machine iperf 'ideal' (44 Gbps) is below Zenoh's own P2P figure (50 Gbps); Kafka ran with linger.ms=0, acks=0 via rdkafka; nothing measured above 512 KB. Default publisher congestion control is Drop (silent drops; the bench used Block); multi-MB drops (#2258) and Block stalling the router (#1876) are open. 'Reliable' only selects the link; Zenoh itself doesn't retransmit.

**How:** The wire protocol is compact: variable-length integer encoding, and key expressions are declared once and then sent as small numeric resource IDs. That gives a minimum of 5 bytes of overhead per message. A multi-stage transmission pipeline serializes many small messages into each frame (automatic batching), reuses pre-allocated batch buffers, and fragments large ones. The team says it keeps heap allocations off the critical path and limits async to the network-facing code, to keep future stack frames small. Payloads are zero-copy ZBytes. There is an opt-in shared-memory transport for same-host traffic and an opt-in io_uring receive path on Linux. In peer mode the broker hop disappears, and nothing is appended to a durable log on the data path.

**Use it when:**
- High-rate small messages (8 B to 8 KB) between services, sensors or robots. In the NTU test Zenoh passed 4M msg/s, while Kafka stayed at 56K-63K msg/s for payloads under 2 KB.
- Latency-sensitive fan-out where losing the broker hop matters: 10 us (Zenoh P2P) vs 73 us (Kafka) single-machine median one-way latency with 64 B pings.
- Topologies that span edge to cloud (robotics, V2X, IoT) and need to switch between peer-to-peer, client and routed modes without changing application code.
- Large payloads between processes on the same host, using the opt-in shared-memory feature (reference-counted SHM buffers, automatic conversion to non-SHM when data leaves the host).
- Mixed-language systems, including microcontrollers through zenoh-pico, that need one protocol from C/C++ through Python to Rust.

**Skip it when:**
- You need Kafka's durable, replayable, partitioned log: retention, consumer groups, offsets, rewinds. Zenoh storages keep only the latest value per key. AdvancedPublisher history is an in-memory per-publisher cache (default depth 1) behind the unstable feature.
- You depend on the Kafka ecosystem (existing clients, Connect, Streams, schema tooling). Zenoh is not wire- or API-compatible.
- You need exactly-once or transactional delivery. The docs read for this entry do not cover either.
- Large messages over slow or lossy links with default settings: the default Drop congestion control can discard multi-MB messages even without real congestion (open issue #2258).
- You plan to size a deployment from the headline ratios. They come from 2023's 0.7.0-rc, which predates the 0.11 Tokio port and the 1.0 batching rework, and the benchmark code is gone.

**Integration:** crate (Rust); zenoh-c builds a C library from the same Rust core; zenoh-cpp is header-only C++ over zenoh-c or zenoh-pico; zenohd router binary · tokio, rustls/tokio-rustls, quinn (QUIC), serde, lz4_flex, flume/crossbeam and others; the Cargo features transport_tcp/udp/tls/quic/ws/unixsock are on by default; shared-memory, uring, transport_serial/vsock/unixpipe and unstable are opt-in · Rust 1.75 (some dependencies may need newer; zenoh-pinned-deps-1-75 pins compatible versions); zenoh-cpp needs C++17 · Linux, macOS, Windows (all in CI); io_uring receive path is Linux-only; zenoh-pico covers microcontrollers

**Vs siblings:** Pick Zenoh over Redpanda or Woodpecker when the job is moving live data with low latency, not keeping a durable log. Those two stay Kafka-style storage systems. Over TCPSHM, pick it when you need many-to-many routing, discovery and multiple languages rather than a single point-to-point C++ link with sub-microsecond latency.

**Gotchas:**
- Publications default to CongestionControl::Drop, so a full queue silently drops data. The benchmark used Block. BlockFirst was added to mitigate large-message drops.
- Block can stall a router: open issue #1876 (still reported on 1.9.0) shows a router looping on 'Unable to push non droppable network message' when a link is cut or congested, without closing the transport.
- Reliability::Reliable does not retransmit at the Zenoh layer; it only selects a reliable link such as TCP. Loss detection and recovery need AdvancedPublisher and AdvancedSubscriber, which are in the unstable API.
- The express flag turns batching off: better latency, lower throughput. Batching behaviour changed with the 0.11 Tokio port and was reworked in 1.0, and 1.0 was not backward compatible with 0.11.

**Status:** Actively maintained Eclipse project (release 1.10.1 on 2026-09-07, last main commit 2026-09-15), dual Apache-2.0/EPL-2.0 licensed; use it as a Cargo dependency or through zenoh-c/zenoh-cpp, not as a small vendorable source drop.

[repo](https://github.com/eclipse-zenoh/zenoh) · [benchmark](https://zenoh.io/blog/2023-03-21-zenoh-vs-mqtt-kafka-dds/)

#### probabilistic-filters

##### BinaryFuseFilter (.NET)  `C#`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Managed C# binary fuse filter: about 9 bits/key at 0.39% FPP, queried ~21x faster than BloomFilter.NetCore.

**Beats:** Bloom filter (BloomFilter.NetCore package) — In one BenchmarkDotNet run on .NET 10 x64 (CPU not stated), with 4,096 half-hit/half-miss lookups against filters built from 1M random 64-bit keys, BinaryFuse8Filter was 20.76x faster than BloomFilter.NetCore 3.0.0 at the same 0.39% FPP and 8.68x faster than XORFilterDotNet 1.2.0, and it built from 1M keys 2.32x faster than creating the Bloom filter and adding every key (86x less allocation). Only ratios are published, and both baselines hash 8-byte arrays internally (the Bloom filter also locks on every call), so the ratios compare these libraries, not Bloom vs binary fuse as algorithms.

**Known shortcoming:** The Bloom/XOR baselines hash key bytes while the fuse filter takes pre-hashed keys, so part of the 20.76x is hashing; NuGet ~131 downloads.

**Known shortcoming:** The Bloom baseline (BloomFilter.NetCore) takes an AsyncLock on every Contains and hashes byte[], so the 20.76x is a library gap, not an algorithm gap; FrozenSet<ulong> is only 1.13x slower at 1M keys, so the real win is ~7x less memory. One noisy run with a cache-resident 1.1 MB filter. Immutable, FPP fixed at 8/16/32 bits, deterministic seeds stored in the header (false-positive keys are computable); v1.0.0 written in one afternoon; deserializing Generic<T> with the wrong hasher gives silent wrong answers.

**How:** It implements binary fuse filters (Graf & Lemire, JEA 2022, arXiv:2201.01174): each key maps to three fingerprint slots in adjacent power-of-two segments, and construction peels the 3-uniform hypergraph (a queue of degree-one slots, then back-substitution from a stack) so that fingerprint(key) = F[h0] ^ F[h1] ^ F[h2]. A query does one Murmur64 finalizer on key+seed, a 64x32 multiply-high and two masked offsets, then three loads through `Unsafe.Add` refs with no branches or bounds checks, where a Bloom filter needs k probes (optimal k is about 8 at 0.39% FPP). Construction is a port of FastFilter/xorfilter's Go code with bounds-check-free refs, ArrayPool scratch buffers and a Vector256/Vector128 scan for degree-one slots on net8.0+. Much of the measured gap is the baseline's cost, though: BloomFilter.NetCore's `FilterMemory.Contains` computes all k Murmur3 positions from the byte span, takes an AsyncLock on every call, then reads BitArray buckets.

**Use it when:**
- In-process .NET sets that are static or rebuilt now and then (blocklists, known-ID sets, 'definitely not in cache/DB/disk' pre-checks), queried far more often than built, where memory is the limit: about 9 bits/key, against 64+ bits/key for a FrozenSet<ulong>.
- You already have 64-bit IDs or hashes. The ulong API mixes each key with a Murmur64 finalizer, so raw sequential IDs work. For string, byte[] or Guid keys, the generic wrapper hashes with XxHash64.
- Replacing BloomFilter.NetCore's in-memory filter for a fixed set on a hot path. Its per-call lock and byte[] hashing are what the 20.76x query and 2.32x build ratios expose.
- Filters built once and shipped to other processes or to disk. The 32-byte little-endian header is checked field by field before load, and the same keys on the same library version serialize to identical bytes.
- Codebases targeting anything from netstandard2.0 to net10.0 that want no native dependencies. Hashing and serialization have explicit big-endian paths.

**Skip it when:**
- The set changes over time, or you need a shared or distributed filter. There is no Add or Remove, so every change is a full rebuild. BloomFilter.NetCore supports inserts and has Redis backends.
- Memory is not tight. In the same run, an exact FrozenSet<ulong> queried only 1.13x slower than BinaryFuse8 at 1M keys and has no false positives. What you gain here is mainly about 7x less memory, not speed.
- Filters far larger than CPU cache. The published query ratios use a 1M-key filter of about 1.1 MB, which the author calls cache-resident. Every lookup makes three random reads, and there is no Bloom comparison at the 32M-key (~36 MB) scale that the BatchScale benchmark runs.
- You need an FPP between the fixed steps, or the smallest static filter possible. Only 8/16/32-bit widths exist, with no 4-wise fuse or ribbon option. Ribbon filters (BuRR, RocksDB Ribbon) get closer to the space lower bound.
- You need a proven dependency. It is at v1.0.0 only: all 22 commits landed in about 2.5 hours on 2026-08-03, and there are 1 star, about 131 NuGet downloads and no issues or PRs. The netstandard2.0 build compiles, but CI runs tests only on net8.0 and net10.0 on ubuntu-latest.

**Integration:** module (NuGet package BinaryFuseFilter; a pure managed assembly of about 15 small .cs files, easy to vendor under MIT) · System.IO.Hashing (XxHash64 for the generic hashers), plus System.Memory on netstandard2.0. MinVer and SourceLink are build-only. · Consumers need netstandard2.0 or net8.0/net9.0/net10.0. Building the repo needs .NET SDK 10.0.100 (global.json) and LangVersion latest. The SIMD construction scan and Math.BigMul path are compiled only for net8.0+. · Any .NET runtime and architecture (pure managed code). On net8.0+, construction uses Vector256 or Vector128 when hardware-accelerated and falls back to scalar code otherwise. Queries are scalar everywhere. Serialization and built-in hashing are endianness-independent.

**Vs siblings:** It is the only .NET entry in this category, so pick it for a static key set in C#; in C, Go, Rust or Java, use the older and far more widely used xor_singleheader, FastFilter/xorfilter, xorf or komiya-atsushi/xor-filter. If the set needs inserts or deletes, a cuckoo or quotient filter (efficient/cuckoofilter, CQF) fits instead.

**Gotchas:**
- BinaryFuseFilter<T> serializes only the core filter. Deserializing with a different hasher than the one used to build it gives silently wrong answers, as the README warns. The built-in string hasher hashes UTF-16 code units, so hashes of the same text as UTF-8 bytes elsewhere will not match.
- Seeds are deterministic: the first is SplitMix64 from a fixed state of 1, and the seed is stored in the serialized header. The built-in integer hashers are identity functions. Anyone who knows the filter can therefore compute false-positive keys, so do not use it as a security boundary against attacker-chosen queries.
- From the code, construction rents about 24 bytes/key of scratch (13 B per slot at about 1.125 slots/key, plus 9 B per key) from ArrayPool<T>.Shared, and those arrays can stay pooled after the build. Create(IEnumerable) and the generic Create also copy the input to arrays. The fingerprint array is capped below 2^31 elements, and Create throws InvalidOperationException if 1,024 seeds fail, which the code says should not happen.
- The benchmark source warns that 'the benchmark machine is busy: judge by the Ratio column within one run only'. BinaryFuse32 queried faster than BinaryFuse16 (ratios 1.32 vs 1.41), which points to noise. The batch Contains(span) API is no faster than a plain loop (README; a 4-wide interleaved version lost by 13-17%).

**Status:** A brand-new single-author MIT project whose v1.0.0 shipped on 2026-08-03 after one day of work, with no commits since; it is small and well-tested enough to vendor, but has almost no users yet.

[repo](https://github.com/Dissimilis/BinaryFuseFilter) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Dissimilis/BinaryFuseFilter#performance)

##### Bloomsday (blocked/split-block Bloom filter, Rust)  `Rust`  `MIT (declared in Cargo.toml; no separate LICENSE file detected by GitHub)`  `active`  `Tier C`

Safe-Rust Parquet-style split-block Bloom filter whose inlined, auto-vectorized lookups ran ~2.3x faster than sbbf-rs in its own benchmark.

**Beats:** Bloom filter (sbbf-rs Split Block Bloom Filter crate) — The README's Criterion table (CPU and rustc not stated; repo flags at the time were +avx2,+fma with target-cpu=haswell) times 1,000 pre-hashed xxh64 lookups into a 1M-key filter at 10 bits/key (~1.25 MB). Negative lookups took ~1.17 µs and positive ~1.26 µs, vs ~2.81 and ~2.93 µs for sbbf-rs 0.2.8 called through its dyn-dispatched FilterFn, or about 1.2 vs 2.8 ns per lookup. Each iteration repeats the same 1,000 hashes, so only about 32 KB of blocks is touched and stays cache-hot; the table also predates the bench's shrink to 10k keys and the switch to bounds-checked code, so `cargo bench` at HEAD does not reproduce it.

**Known shortcoming:** The ~2.3-2.4x is derived from README numbers on a 10k-entry bench (not 1M); sbbf-rs is called through dynamic dispatch per lookup; the fastbloom comparison was dropped and never published; not on crates.io; no CPU model.

**Known shortcoming:** Uses the same SBBF math as sbbf-rs (same salts and fastrange mapping), so the 2.3x comes from sbbf-rs's dynamic dispatch vs bloomsday's inlining, not a better layout. The bench repeats the same 1k hashes (~32 KB stays cache-hot) and predates a bounds-check commit and a shrink to 10k keys, so HEAD does not reproduce it. Its sizing undersizes an SBBF (per the Parquet spec a 0.01% request gets ~0.04%, 10% gets ~18%).

**Known shortcoming:** The repo's AVX2 flags in .cargo/config.toml do not reach downstream crates (no runtime dispatch); the key API uses std Hash, which is not portable, so persisted filters can mismatch across builds/platforms. Not on crates.io, no LICENSE file, no CI; 9 commits over 3 days in 2026-02.

**How:** The filter math is the same as sbbf-rs. A multiply-shift fastrange of the top 32 hash bits picks a 32-byte block, and eight salted multiplies of the low 32 bits each pick one bit per word, so a probe touches a single block within one cache line. The difference is code generation. bloomsday's probe is an `#[inline(always)]` safe iterator fold that LLVM can inline into the caller's loop and auto-vectorize (the README cites vpand/vpor/vpsllv under AVX2). sbbf-rs selects an AVX2, SSE4.1 or fallback kernel at runtime and calls it through a `&'static dyn` trait object, which the compiler cannot inline. The measured gap therefore reflects dispatch and inlining overhead rather than a better filter layout.

**Use it when:**
- Hot-loop membership probes on pre-computed 64-bit hashes, such as join or scan pre-filters and dedup checks, where the probe loop can be inlined and each probe should touch one 32-byte block.
- x86-64 binaries you build yourself with AVX2 enabled (`-C target-cpu=native` or `-C target-feature=+avx2`) for known server hardware.
- You want sbbf-rs's split-block bit layout (a given hash sets the same bits in the same block) behind a safe, owning Rust API instead of unsafe calls on a raw buffer.
- FPR targets around 1%: the 10 bits/key it picks there gives about 1.26% FPR according to the Parquet spec's table.
- You are willing to vendor about 110 lines of safe code or pin a git dependency, because nothing is published on crates.io.

**Skip it when:**
- Portable binaries built for baseline x86-64 or for ARM. The README warns that without AVX2-class target features the code may fall back to scalar. sbbf-rs detects AVX2/SSE4.1 at runtime and also ships NEON and WASM kernels.
- Tight FPR targets. Sizing uses the classic ceil(-ln p / ln^2 2) bits/key, which undersizes a split-block filter. Per the Parquet spec, a 0.01% request gets 20 bits/key, which is about 0.04% (4x over), and a 10% request gets 5 bits/key, which is about 18%.
- Concurrent writers (insert takes &mut self and there is no atomic variant), or any need for deletion, counting, union, or Parquet-compatible serialized bitsets.
- no_std or embedded targets: it requires std, while sbbf-rs supports no_std.
- Production dependencies that need a track record. It has one author and 9 commits over three days in February 2026, with no CI, no LICENSE file and no crates.io release.

**Integration:** crate (git-only, not on crates.io; the README's `bloomsday = "0.1.0"` line does not resolve); small enough to source-drop · xxhash-rust 0.8 (xxh32/xxh64/xxh3 features enabled, only xxh64 used); optional serde 1.0 behind the `serde` feature; requires std · Rust 1.85+ (edition 2024); no rust-version/MSRV declared · Pure safe Rust, so any std target compiles. Performance depends on auto-vectorization with AVX2-class target features. The repo's .cargo/config.toml (`+avx2,+fma`, `target-cpu=native`) applies only to cargo runs inside the repo, not to crates that depend on it, so downstream users must set their own flags. Only x86 AVX2 speed is claimed; ARM/NEON behavior is not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over fastbloom (on crates.io, works with any hasher, and has AtomicBloomFilter for concurrent inserts) only when you specifically want the Parquet/sbbf-rs split-block layout for pre-hashed u64 keys and can build with AVX2; bloomsday once wrote a fastbloom comparison but removed it without publishing results. For a static key set where memory matters, xorf or pleat need fewer bits per key.

**Gotchas:**
- The key API hashes through Rust's std `Hash` trait. Its docs say the data fed to a Hasher is not portable across platforms and, for most std types, not stable across compiler versions. A filter serialized after `insert_key` may not match after a rebuild or on another platform. Use `insert_hash` with a stable hash of your own for anything you persist.
- The README table predates the 2026-02-06 'safety first' commit. That commit replaced `get_unchecked` with checked indexing in both hot paths, adding a bounds check per probe, and the numbers were not re-measured afterwards.
- An invalid fpr (<= 0 or >= 1) silently falls back to 10 bits/key instead of returning an error. `new(0, _)` still allocates one block.
- Despite the 'cache-line' naming, blocks are 32 bytes (half a 64-byte line), with 32-byte alignment. serde output is the struct's own shape (word arrays plus num_blocks and seed), not the Parquet bitset format.

**Status:** Listed as active, but all 9 commits landed 2026-02-04 to 2026-02-06 with nothing since; it has 14 stars, no issues and no CI, and MIT is declared only in Cargo.toml, so treat it as a small, safe, copyable reference to vendor rather than a maintained dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/sidd-27/Bloomsday) · [benchmark](https://github.com/sidd-27/Bloomsday#performance)

##### Boost.Bloom (block / multiblock filter configurations)  `C++`  `BSL-1.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only C++11 Boost filter template whose cache-local block and SIMD multiblock subfilters run 2.6-5x faster than a classical Bloom filter.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — In the project's own boost_bloom_benchmarks (GCC 14 x64, -O3 -march=native, unique random ints from splitmix64, single-threaded element-at-a-time loops, self-hosted runner with an unnamed CPU), at N=1M and equal bits/element (c=8-16) block<uint64_t,K> inserts in 3.99-5.55 ns vs 11.04-20.28 ns and looks up in 4.6-6.0 ns vs 12.1-22.0 ns for the classical filter<int,K> (about 2.6-4x), rising to about 5x for insert and successful lookup at N=10M, c=16 but only about 1.8x for unsuccessful lookup (18.7 vs 34.2 ns). The baseline is the library's own classical configuration, not another library, and block pays about 10x the FPR at c=16.

**Known shortcoming:** The numbers are for block<uint64_t,K> configurations, not multiblock; block filters have ~10x worse FPR at c=16; self-hosted CI runner with no CPU stated.

**Known shortcoming:** First-party numbers vs its own classical configuration on an unnamed self-hosted CPU. At N=10M, c=16 unsuccessful lookups are only ~1.8x faster (18.7 vs 34.2 ns; inserts/successful lookups ~5x), and boost::unordered_flat_set<int> lookups are in the same ballpark in its own bench, so the win is memory rather than speed. SIMD is chosen at compile time and AVX2 vs SSE2 fast_multiblock32 use different hash bits, so saved arrays are not portable across builds.

**Known shortcoming:** Insert-only with fixed capacity (no size/delete/try_insert/runtime K); thread safety undocumented (no atomics); the capacity argument is in bits.

**How:** It uses blocked Bloom filtering: block<Block,K'> sets all K' bits inside one hash-chosen Block (a uint64_t, or a 64-byte uint64_t[8]), so an operation touches one cache line instead of K scattered ones, while multiblock sets one bit in each of K' consecutive words (split-block layout; fast_multiblock32<8> matches the Impala uint32_t[8] bucket). Each element is hashed once: Lemire's fastrange picks the subarray, a multiplicative congruential generator (Steele-Vigna constant) re-mixes the hash, bit positions are sliced from it, and a 128-bit multiply-xor mix is applied first for hashes that do not avalanche, such as boost::hash<int>. The fast_multiblock variants build the bit masks with SIMD (AVX2 _mm256_sllv_epi32, an SSE2 float-exponent trick, or little-endian Neon). The core issues software prefetches for the target cache lines, and since Boost 1.90 bulk insert and bulk may_contain pipeline hashing and prefetching over batches of up to 64 elements, with branchless lookups for block and fast_multiblock.

**Use it when:**
- Filtering negative lookups in front of disk, network or database accesses, when you need tens to hundreds of millions of inserts or probes per second per core and can accept a higher FPR at the same bits/key (or spend a few extra bits/key to get it back).
- Filters much larger than the CPU cache (N of 1M and up, tens of MB): the gap grows with size. At N=10M, c=16, GCC 14 x64, the classical filter takes 86.0 ns to insert and 95.7 ns per successful lookup vs 16.9/18.7 ns for block<uint64_t,6>.
- Builds with AVX2 enabled (-mavx2, -march=native or /arch:AVX2), or AArch64 with Neon: fast_multiblock32<K'> gives the best speed/FPR mix. At N=1M on GCC 14 x64 it runs at 2.7-3.2 ns per operation at c=8-12 with 0.54% FPR at c=12, vs 1.05% for block<uint64_t,5>.
- Batch workloads that can use insert(first,last) or bulk may_contain: the docs' GCC 14 x64 table at N=10M shows a further 1.2-3.5x for most configurations.
- Projects already on Boost 1.89+ (or vcpkg boost-bloom or Conan) that want a maintained, allocator-aware, header-only C++11 filter with built-in capacity_for/fpr_for sizing helpers.

**Skip it when:**
- When FPR per bit is the priority: at c=16, block<uint64_t,6> has 0.42% FPR vs 0.045% for the classical filter<int,11>. Use the classical config, a wider multiblock, or more bits/key.
- When you need deletion, counting, growth, an element count, try_insert or a runtime K. The filter is insert-only with a fixed capacity and no size(); try_insert, size estimation and runtime K are listed only as future work.
- Static key sets built once: the library's own future-work page says cuckoo and xor filters are 'more space efficient and potentially faster', and it offers neither.
- Many threads writing to one filter: there are no atomic or concurrent insert operations, and thread safety is not documented.
- When memory is not the constraint and keys are small: in the same benchmark, an exact boost::unordered_flat_set<int> looks up in 5.63/4.24 ns (successful/unsuccessful) at N=1M and 23.11/14.68 ns at N=10M. That is comparable to block filters (4.6 ns at c=8, N=1M; 18.7 ns at c=16, N=10M), though its inserts are much slower (38.9 and 58.1 ns).

**Integration:** header-only · Boost.Assert, Boost.Config, Boost.ContainerHash, Boost.Core, Boost.ThrowException, Boost.TypeTraits (all header-only, per CMakeLists.txt) · C++11.
