Header-only, x86 AVX2 only; std::random_device mask table (not reproducible); the 8-hash batch reads past the end; int overflow above 2^28 keys; hashing not timed. The same design ships in Apache Arrow Acero's BlockedBloomFilter.

**How:** Register blocking (Lang et al., VLDB 2019; Putze et al., 2010) maps each key to one 64-bit word, so an insert or query is one memory access plus one AND/compare. Instead of computing k bit positions, the Patterned variant uses 10 hash bits to pick one of 1024 overlapping 57-bit masks (4-5 bits set) from a 136-byte table and 6 more bits to rotate it ('mask rotation'), with the remaining bits picking the block, so one 64-bit hash is enough. The AVX2 path handles 8 hashes per call, using _mm256_i64gather_epi64 to read the mask table and, on query, the filter words.

**Use it when:**
- You are writing your own filter for a hash join or columnar scan and want a short, readable reference for the register-blocked bit-pattern design. It uses the same layout as Apache Arrow Acero's BlockedBloomFilter: 57-bit masks, 4-5 bits set, 1024 masks, 6-bit rotation.
- Negative-heavy probe workloads on x86-64 with AVX2, where 5-7% false positives are acceptable because an exact check runs afterwards.
- Filters that stay in cache. The checked-in results show the largest gain over Basic (19-20x) at 1K-16K keys, which is 2-32 KB of filter, and only 8-10x at 4M-67M keys.
- Batch probing where the 64-bit hashes already sit in arrays whose length is a multiple of 8.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a target false-positive rate. PatternedSimdBloomFilter ignores eps: it always allocates max(512, 8n) bits, rounded up to the next power of two strictly above that. It measured 6.0-6.9% FPR when asked for 1%.
- Production use. This is benchmark code with no tests, no key hashing, no releases and no handling of batches that are not a multiple of 8. Its int sizing (8*n) overflows above about 2^28 (268M) keys.
- Targets without x86-64 AVX2, or MSVC. The header includes <immintrin.h> unconditionally, uses __builtin_clz, and has no NEON path and no runtime CPU dispatch.
- You need reproducible or shareable filters. Each instance seeds its mask table from std::random_device, so bit vectors differ between instances and processes. Arrow's version uses a fixed seed.
- Using SimdBloomFilter (the plain AVX2 register-blocked variant) as is. Its block index (h1 & (num_blocks-1)) and its bit positions ((h1 + i*h2) & 63) both use the low 6 bits of h1, so keys in the same block share a bit offset. That plausibly explains the 7.4-9.8% FPR the author says he could not explain.

**Integration:** header-only · None for bloom_filters.h beyond the standard library and <immintrin.h>. The bench/fpr harness bundles nanobench.h. · Not stated. Built with g++ 12.2.0 at -O3 -mavx2 with no -std flag, so GCC 12's default C++17. Needs GCC/Clang builtins (__builtin_clz). · x86-64 only. The SIMD variants require AVX2 (gathers, variable shifts). No ARM/NEON and no runtime dispatch.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only to study or copy the bit-pattern and mask-rotation trick in about 540 lines. For real use, Boost.Bloom's block<uint64_t,K> filters give the same one-word-per-key layout with FPR control and active maintenance, and the Impala-derived AVX2 blocked filter in efficient/cuckoofilter has been tested and benchmarked by independent researchers.

**Gotchas:**
- The published numbers predate bug fixes. Every CSV comes from the initial commit of 2023-05-30. PR #1 (July 2024) fixed two bugs. First, PatternedSimdBloomFilter ANDed the hash with its own uninitialized variable instead of the 10-bit mask-index mask. Second, BlockedBloomFilter::Query read the filter's first 32 bytes instead of the key's block. No results have been published for the fixed code. The Blocked probe cost stays flat at ~27 cycles at every size, which is an artifact of the Query bug. The Patterned filter's ~6% FPR is consistent with a near-constant mask index: 64 rotations with about 4 keys per word.
- Memory per key is not matched across variants. The Patterned sizing, 32 - __builtin_clz(m), doubles exact powers of two. At every benchmarked size (powers of 4) the Patterned filter therefore used 16 bits/key against Basic's 9.57, about 1.7x the memory for about 6x the FPR. A Hacker News commenter raised the equal-FPR question in 2023, and it got no reply.
- The SIMD Insert and Query always read 8 hashes with unaligned 256-bit loads. Pad the input to a multiple of 8, or they read past the end.
- Timings exclude hashing. The harness feeds pre-generated random 64-bit values as hashes, and the probe keys are fresh random values, so nearly all probes are negative lookups. Hashing real keys adds cost to every variant and narrows the speedup ratio.

**Status:** Stale (five commits, last on 2024-07-15, 21 stars, no tests or releases) but MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor as a reference to re-benchmark, while Apache Arrow Acero's BlockedBloomFilter is a production implementation of the same design with AVX2 dispatch, prefetching and folding.

[repo](https://github.com/save-buffer/bloomfilter_benchmarks) · [benchmark](http://blog.krassovsky.com/bloom_filter.html)

##### Ribbon Filter (ribbonGo)  `Go`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Pure-Go static Ribbon filter (Dillinger-Walzer 2021) storing 7.3-7.5 bits/key at 0.78% FPR, below textbook Bloom and Xor sizes.

**Beats:** Bloom filter, xor filter — Only self-measurements from the repo's go test BenchmarkPaper_* suite with r=7 and sequential 8-byte integer keys, Go version and flags unstated. At w=128, build was 106.3 ns/key at 7.33 bits/key for n=1e6, and 384.7 ns/key at 7.51 bits/key for n=1e8, on an Apple M3 Pro. Queries at n=1e6 were 43.2/31.7 ns positive/negative, a warm-cache loop over 8192 cycled probes on an unnamed Xeon Platinum; no n=1e8 query numbers are published, and the README says only the query table was re-measured after the July 2026 storage-layout change. The Bloom (9.6 bits/key at 1%) and Xor figures are textbook constants, not benchmark runs, and FPRs are not matched: against a Bloom filter at the same 2^-7 FPR (about 10.1 bits/key by the README's 44% figure) the saving would be about 27%, not the quoted 23.6%.

**Known shortcoming:** The Bloom 9.6 bits/key comparison is a textbook constant, not a benchmark; FPRs are not matched (r=7 is about 0.78%).

**Known shortcoming:** Static only: no add/delete and no serialization (issue #23), so it cannot be persisted. At matched 2^-7 FPR a Bloom filter needs ~10.1 bits/key, so the saving is ~27%; the Bloom baseline is never benchmarked (#26). Duplicate keys or a 64-bit XXH3 collision (~3% at 1e9 keys) make all 256 seeds fail.

**Known shortcoming:** Real slot overhead is 4.7-45% (doc comments say 1.8-7.2%); w=32 at 1e8 keys is no better than Bloom; r<=8 gives an FPR floor of 0.39%; build needs ~25 B/key. The README benchmark command runs no benchmark; query numbers are warm-cache at n=1e6 only; the w<=64 build lacks prefetch (#42).

**How:** Each key is hashed once with XXH3 to 64 bits. That hash is cheaply remixed per seed into a start slot, a w-bit coefficient row and an r-bit fingerprint. The rows form a banded linear system over GF(2), solved by on-the-fly Gaussian elimination (the paper's 'Rapid Incremental Boolean Banding ON the fly') plus back-substitution, retrying with a new seed if banding hits a linear dependence. At w=128, RocksDB's empirical slot tables put the slot count only about 5-7% above n, so storage stays near the r-bits/key minimum. The README puts Bloom at about 44% overhead. The solution is stored in RocksDB's Interleaved Column-Major Layout. A query is one hash plus up to r shift/AND/POPCNT parity checks over two adjacent w-bit words, and it exits on the first mismatched column, so negatives are cheaper than positives.

**Use it when:**
- Go programs (no cgo) that build a filter once over a known, de-duplicated key set of about 1e6-1e8 keys and query it many times in the same process, for example per-snapshot or per-shard membership sets.
- Memory-bound cases at about 0.4-1% FPR. At w=128 the author measured 7.33 bits/key (n=1e6) and 7.51 (n=1e8). The textbook figures, from the README's own overhead percentages applied to 7 bits, are about 8.6 for Xor with 7-bit fingerprints and about 10.1 for Bloom at 2^-7. That is roughly 13-27% smaller.
- Relatively high FPR targets (r=1-8, so 50% down to 0.39%): the Ribbon paper says the design is most competitive for f >= 2^-7.
- Read-heavy services where build time of about 0.1-0.4 microseconds per key is acceptable and queries of about 30-45 ns (warm cache, n=1e6) are fast enough.

**Skip it when:**
- Sets that grow or change: there is no Add or Delete. Every change is a full rebuild costing 57-385 ns/key in the author's M3 Pro runs, with per-key cost rising at larger n.
- Filters that must be persisted or shipped, such as LSM table blocks or on-disk indexes. No serialization API exists (issue #23 is open). The hash is final XXH3, which the code notes is not byte-compatible with RocksDB's on-disk Ribbon blocks.
- FPR below about 0.39%: ResultBits is capped at 8. The Config comment lists r=10, but validateConfig panics above 8.
- Memory-tight build hosts. Construction holds 8 B/key of stored hashes plus 17 B/slot of banding arrays at w=128 (9 B/slot at w<=64), on top of the caller's key slice. The benchmark file warns of about 8 GB peak at n=1e8, including the test keys.
- Narrow widths at large n. w=32 at n=1e8 used 10.17 bits/key (45% slot overhead, from extrapolated non-RocksDB sizing constants), no better than a textbook Bloom at the same FPR. w=64 at n=1e8 (8.23 bits/key) is only about 4% under textbook Xor.

**Integration:** module · github.com/zeebo/xxh3 v1.1.0 (indirect: klauspost/cpuid/v2, golang.org/x/sys) · Go 1.24.2 per go.mod; CI runs tests on Go 1.25 · Any Go target: the library is pure Go, and the xxh3 dependency ships amd64 SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512 and arm64 NEON assembly with a generic fallback. Published numbers cover arm64 (Apple M3 Pro) and x86-64 (Xeon Platinum); CI runs on ubuntu-latest.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it when you need the smallest static filter at about 0.4-1% FPR in pure Go without cgo. If C/C++ is acceptable, BuRR (bumped Ribbon; the Ribbon paper reports load-balanced Ribbon below 1% overhead, against 4.7-7.3% here) or xor_singleheader (simpler, with published head-to-head benchmarks) are stronger picks. The cuckoo-family siblings (Vacuum, Windowed cuckoo) fit better if you need inserts after build.

**Gotchas:**
- Keys must be unique, and uniqueness really applies to the 64-bit XXH3 hash. Every seed retry remixes only the stored hash, and the bander rejects even consistent redundant equations. So a duplicate key, or two distinct keys whose 64-bit hashes collide (birthday odds of about n^2/2^65: about 3e-4 at 1e8 keys, about 3% at 1e9), fails every seed. Build then runs all MaxSeeds (default 256) banding attempts before returning ErrConstructionFailed.
- The Config doc comments quote the paper's asymptotic overheads (w=32 about 7.2%, w=64 about 3.6%, w=128 about 1.8%). Measured slot overhead is much higher: 31.8/12.0/4.7% at n=1e6 and 45.3/17.6/7.3% at n=1e8. That is because slot counts follow RocksDB's tables for a 5% per-seed failure rate and grow with log n.
- NewWithConfig and NewFromKeysWithConfig panic, rather than return an error, on an invalid CoeffBits or ResultBits. Keys are []string only; the pre-hashed build path (buildFromHashes) is unexported.
- The README's benchmark commands (-bench='BenchmarkRibbon...') match no benchmark function; the real ones are BenchmarkPaper_Build/Query_Positive/Query_Negative/Space, and -short skips n=1e8. The w<=64 build loop also lacks the prefetch load that the README credits with a 20-36% gain at scale (open issue #42); only the w=128 path has it.

**Status:** Active but young: created March 2026, v1.0.10 released 2026-07-18 after the ICML storage rewrite, 15 stars, 10 open issues including serialization (#23) and Bloom/Cuckoo/Xor benchmarks (#26). It is MIT-licensed, seven source files and one dependency, so easy to vendor, but not production-proven.

[repo](https://github.com/RibbonFilter/ribbonGo) · [benchmark](https://github.com/RibbonFilter/ribbonGo#benchmarks)

##### Windowed Cuckoo Filter (WindowFilter, implements 'Smaller and More Flexible Cuckoo Filters')  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Safe-Rust (2,2) windowed cuckoo filter: 12.8 bits/key at 2^-10 FPR, 12% under Bloom, 7-25% under cuckoo; slower inserts.

**Beats:** cuckoo filter, Bloom filter — In one run of the author's benchmark binary (100k string keys, 200k queries half present, target rate 2^-10, release build with thin LTO on unpinned stable Rust, CPU not stated), the windowed (2,2) filter used 1.596 bytes/key vs 1.803 for the author's own classic Bloom and 2.130 for the author's own (2,4) cuckoo; lookups tied with cuckoo (60.3 vs 61.2 ns) and beat Bloom (81.6 ns), while inserts were 2.8x slower than cuckoo (163 vs 59 ns). Most of the 25% memory gap to cuckoo is power-of-two rounding at n=100k, which leaves the cuckoo table at 76% load: against a well-sized cuckoo the code's parameters give about 7% (12/0.94 vs 13/0.95 bits per key), matching the paper's overhead factors of 1.272 vs 1.365.

**Known shortcoming:** Baselines are the author's own Bloom/cuckoo implementations; no CPU model; inserts 2.8x slower than cuckoo (162.97 vs 58.74 ns); 0 stars.

**Known shortcoming:** The '25% smaller than cuckoo' is mostly an artifact: its own cuckoo baseline rounds to a power of two (76% load at n=100k); against a well-sized cuckoo filter the gain is about 7% (matching the paper's 1.272 vs 1.365). Baselines are self-made (unblocked Bloom), cache-resident 100k keys, one run, no CPU stated; FNV string hashing dominates lookup time.

**Known shortcoming:** Inserts are 2.8x slower than cuckoo; no resize (~2% headroom); no dedup (a fifth copy fails after 10k kicks); a 160 KB rollback Vec per kicking insert. &str keys only, fixed hash seeds (unsafe for adversarial keys), no serialization. A one-day repo (18 commits on 2026-09-03), not on crates.io, 0 stars; the paper authors' own implementation is gitlab rahmannlab/cuckoo-filters (Python/numba).

**How:** The gain is in memory, not speed. It implements (2,2) windowed cuckoo hashing from Schmitz, Zentgraf and Rahmann (arXiv:2505.05847): each key has two candidate windows of two adjacent slots, neighbouring windows overlap by one slot, and the theoretical load threshold is 0.965 with only four candidate slots (vs 0.980 with eight slots for (2,4) buckets), so a 2^-k rate needs k+2 bits per slot instead of k+3 and the table is sized for 94% load. The second window is the first plus a fingerprint-derived offset modulo the window count (a signed offset instead of the classic XOR), so the table size need not be a power of two; each slot also stores a choice bit and a window-offset bit, which let an evicted fingerprint find its other window and count as extra match bits. Slots are bit-packed into a Vec<u64>, and lookups check the four slots one at a time: no SIMD, no bit-parallel matching, no prefetching.

**Use it when:**
- A Rust service needs a deletable 'definitely absent' pre-check in front of a disk, database or network lookup, the maximum key count is known, and bytes per key matter more than insert speed: about 12.8 bits/key at a 2^-10 rate vs 14.4 for a classic Bloom filter.
- Key counts that fall just above a power-of-two boundary, where a standard XOR-addressed cuckoo filter must round its bucket count up and can waste up to about 2x (the author's own cuckoo sits at 76% load for 100k keys).
- Read-mostly workloads: fill once or slowly, then query often. The author's run measured lookups on par with (2,4) cuckoo and faster than an unblocked Bloom filter, on a cache-resident 100k-key filter.
- Keys are already strings, or converting them to &str is cheap.
- You want a short, readable reference for the windowed layout (about 740 lines of library code including tests, #![forbid(unsafe_code)], no dependencies) that you can vendor and adapt.

**Skip it when:**
- Insert-heavy or streaming fills. Inserts were 2.8x slower than the author's (2,4) cuckoo (163 vs 59 ns) and 1.7x slower than Bloom. The paper's own implementation also shows windowed (2,2) inserting about 2x slower than bucketed (2,4), and about 10x slower than the Prefix filter (3.1 vs 33 M keys/s at 2^-8).
- Untrusted keys. The hash is FNV-1a plus a splitmix finalizer with fixed seeds, and the relocation RNG is a fixed-seed xorshift, so crafted keys can collide and force failed inserts; the README says it is for experiments and trusted input only.
- Unknown or growing key counts. There is no resizing: the table is sized for 94% load at the declared capacity, and the author's max-load run failed at 95.75%, which leaves only about 2% headroom before insert returns false.
- Static key sets known up front. At a 2^-10 rate, Xor filters (1.23x overhead, per the paper) and BuRR are smaller than this filter's ~1.28x and need no relocation.
- Production dependencies that need persistence, integer or byte keys, batch or SIMD lookups, concurrent inserts, or a maintained crate. None of these are provided; the crate is not on crates.io, has 0 stars, and all 18 commits landed within one day. Performance on DRAM-sized filters was never measured (the benchmark stops at 100k keys, about 160 KB).

**Integration:** crate (git dependency only; not published on crates.io) · none (std only; Cargo.lock lists no external packages) · Rust 1.85+, implied by edition 2024. No rust-version field; rust-toolchain.toml pins only the floating 'stable' channel. · any Rust std target: pure safe Rust (#![forbid(unsafe_code)]) with no SIMD or architecture-specific code; CI runs only on ubuntu-latest, and the benchmark hardware is not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only when you need a deletable filter in dependency-free safe Rust and can live with slow inserts; Vacuum Filter (a similar ~25%-smaller-than-cuckoo claim) and Morton Filter (1.3-2.5x faster lookups) are more heavily engineered C++, and Prefix Filter inserts about 10x faster but needs AVX-512. For key sets known up front, Xor Filter or BuRR is smaller.

**Gotchas:**
- Any insert whose four candidate slots are all full allocates a rollback log with Vec::with_capacity(max_kicks) before the first kick: 16-byte entries x 10,000 is about 160 KB per such insert at the default setting.
- Inserts are not deduplicated. Repeated inserts of one key each take a slot, and once the key's four candidate slots (three when its two windows are adjacent) all hold its copies, the next insert runs all 10,000 kicks and fails.
- delete on a key that was never inserted can remove another key's matching entry and create false negatives. The README warns about this, as with cuckoo filters in general.
- Bad parameters panic instead of returning errors: new asserts capacity > 0 and fpr_bits in 1..=30 (1..=29 for CuckooFilter). A fingerprint of 0 is remapped to 1 so that 0 can mean an empty slot, which slightly raises the false-positive rate (the paper makes the same trade).

**Status:** Listed as active, but it is a one-day project (18 commits on 2026-09-03, CI green, no issues, releases or crates.io publication) that is MIT-licensed, dependency-free and small enough to vendor, so treat it as a readable reference rather than a maintained library; for the full design (bit-parallel probes, prefetching, parallel subfilters), see the paper authors' MIT-licensed Python/numba code at gitlab.com/rahmannlab/cuckoo-filters.

[repo](https://github.com/EvanGruhlkey/WindowFilter) · [benchmark](https://github.com/EvanGruhlkey/WindowFilter#benchmark)

##### xor-filter (Java, komiya-atsushi)  `Java`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Small Java xor filter (8/16-bit) built on Guava Funnels; about 2x faster Long-key queries than Guava BloomFilter at equal FPR.

**Beats:** Bloom filter (Guava com.google.common.hash.BloomFilter) — This is first-party JMH (Gradle jmh plugin 0.5.0 defaults, time unit ms) on an undisclosed JVM and CPU. Each filter was built from 8,192 keys (every other of 16,384 pregenerated keys) and queried round-robin over all 16,384, so half the queries hit, everything stayed cache-resident, and hashing went through Guava 28.2 murmur3_128 for both filters. XOR8 did 17,458 vs 8,879 queries/ms against Guava BloomFilter at fpp 0.389% for boxed Long keys (1.97x) and 7,122 vs 5,318 for 20-character strings (1.34x). A separate 100,000-key run gave 9.84 vs 11.55 bits/key serialized (1.17x smaller). All ratios are derived from the README tables.

**Known shortcoming:** Ratios derived from JMH numbers vs Guava 28.2's BloomFilter at 16,384 elements only.

**Known shortcoming:** Not on Maven Central (vendor source only). Build-once with all keys in memory plus ~35 B/key temp; an empty collection throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; writeTo/readFrom close the caller's stream and readFrom trusts the header. The benchmark filter held 8,192 keys (cache-resident, 50% hits, no JVM/CPU); the gain shrinks to 1.34x for strings. Abandoned 2020; FastFilter/fastfilter_java is the maintained alternative.

**How:** It implements Graf & Lemire's xor filter (arXiv 1912.08258), a Dietzfelbinger-Pagh / Bloomier-style construction. Each key maps to three slots, one in each third of an array of about 1.23n+32 fingerprints, and a query is just fingerprint == B[h0] ^ B[h1] ^ B[h2]: exactly three array reads, with multiply-shift range reduction instead of division. Both this library and Guava's BloomFilter (MURMUR128_MITZ_64 strategy) compute one Guava murmur3_128 per query. Guava then tests numHashFunctions bits by double hashing, with a 64-bit modulo per probe; the xor filter adds one MurmurHash3 fmix64 and the three reads. Because the expensive hash is shared, the gap shrinks when hashing dominates (1.97x for Long keys vs 1.34x for 20-character strings). Construction is hypergraph peeling: a queue of singleton slots, a stack, then back-assignment, retried with a new seed if peeling fails.

**Use it when:**
- JVM service with a static key set built once, queried many times and shipped as bytes, e.g. a nightly blocklist, known-ID set or per-segment key set.
- You already use Guava Funnels/BloomFilter and want about 2x faster Long-key queries at the same ~0.39% FPR with about 15% less memory (XOR8: 9.84 vs 11.55 bits/key).
- You need a very low FPR. XOR16 vs Guava Bloom at fpp 0.002% ran 2.6x faster on Long keys (16,976 vs 6,535 q/ms) at 19.69 vs 22.52 bits/key.
- Workloads with many positive lookups, where a Bloom filter must test all k bits while the xor filter always does exactly three reads.
- You want a tiny, auditable piece of code to vendor: two source files (about 516 lines), Java 8, Guava as the only dependency.

**Skip it when:**
- Keys arrive incrementally, or the set changes: there is no put/remove/merge, so every change means rebuilding from a complete in-memory Collection. Guava BloomFilter supports put/putAll.
- You need it as a Gradle/Maven dependency. me.k11i:xor-filter was published only to Bintray, which is gone, and Maven Central has no me.k11i artifacts. FastFilter/fastfilter_java is maintained (Apache-2.0, pushed 2026-07) and adds binary fuse and xor+ filters, but it takes pre-hashed long keys.
- Space is the priority. There is no binary fuse or xor+ variant, so XOR8 costs 9.84 bits/key at 100k keys, and the fixed +32-slot overhead inflates tiny filters.
- Very large sets under tight heap. Construction holds all keys plus temporary arrays of roughly 35 bytes/key: sorted hashes, per-slot xor and count, queue, and stack (derived from the source). Bloom filters build by streaming.
- Long or expensive-to-hash keys (e.g. strings), where the query gain falls to about 1.34x and may not justify adopting unmaintained code with no issue history and tests only at 5,000-10,000 keys.

**Integration:** source-drop · Guava (built against 28.2-jre; uses Funnel, HashFunction, Hashing.murmur3_128) · Java 8 (0.1.1 was built with sourceCompatibility 8; 0.1.0 targeted Java 11) · any JVM

**Vs siblings:** Every catalogued xor/binary-fuse sibling targets another runtime: xor_singleheader (C), xorfilter (Go), xorf (Rust), exor_filter (Erlang) and BinaryFuseFilter (.NET). Pick this one only when you need a pure-JVM xor filter keyed through Guava Funnels. If native code or another language is an option, those siblings are maintained and offer binary fuse filters, which sit within 13% of the space lower bound vs 23% for xor, per the Go sibling.

**Gotchas:**
- writeTo/readFrom wrap the caller's stream in try-with-resources and close it. writeTo also emits one byte/short per call through DataOutputStream, so wrap file or socket streams in a BufferedOutputStream.
- build() on an empty collection throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, because HashedElements reports size 1 for zero keys. The peeling queue is a fixed n+1 ring buffer with no overflow check; in a Python port of the construction loop, sets under ~32 keys peeled on only ~20-50% of seeds vs ~95% for larger sets. Such sets need extra retries but still come out correct.
- The serialized bytes store strategy, seed and capacity but not the Funnel. readFrom must get the identical Funnel (including charset) or it silently returns false negatives. readFrom also trusts the header (strategy index, capacity), so untrusted bytes can throw or allocate up to 2^31 slots.
- The default build() seeds from ThreadLocalRandom, so identical inputs give different bytes; pass rngSeed for reproducible artifacts. The code relies on Guava APIs flagged unstable (the source suppresses UnstableApiUsage).

**Status:** Abandoned since January 2020 (v0.1.1, zero issues ever filed); the Bintray-hosted artifact no longer resolves, but the MIT-licensed code is two small files that are easy to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/komiya-atsushi/xor-filter) · [benchmark](https://github.com/komiya-atsushi/xor-filter#benchmark)

##### xorf (Rust xor / binary fuse filter crate)  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust static xor/binary-fuse filters: about 9 bits/key at 0.4% FPP versus about 11.5 for an optimal Bloom.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — Nothing in this crate measures a Bloom filter: its doc tests only assert BinaryFuse8 stays under 9.1 bits/key with under 0.406% false positives on 1M random u64 keys, and its Criterion benches time only xorf's own filters (the lookup bench repeats one hot key). The Bloom comparison (binary fuse within 13% of the storage lower bound vs 44% for Bloom, i.e. about 9 vs about 11.5 bits/key at 2^-8) comes from the binary fuse paper (JEA 2022), which benchmarks the authors' C++ code (GCC 10 -O3 -march=native, Intel i7-6700 Skylake), not this Rust port; the 9-bit figure carries over by construction, but speed does not.

**Known shortcoming:** The paper's numbers come from the C++ reference code and never mention xorf; the crate never benchmarks a Bloom filter (its docs say ~9 bits/entry and a test asserts <9.1).

**Known shortcoming:** Static only, with fixed 8/16/32-bit fingerprints (#61/#69). Duplicate keys make Xor loop forever in release builds (#25) and BinaryFuse errors after 1000 seeds; boundary-size build failures fixed only in 0.13.0. HashProxy cannot wrap BinaryFuse (#72). Build scratch ~24 B/key; lookups are cache-miss bound (280 to 51 M/s from 1M to 99M keys, #84); its own lookup bench uses one hot key.

**Known shortcoming:** The README says 0.14 but crates.io's latest is 0.13.0, whose optional bincode dependency is flagged unmaintained (RUSTSEC-2025-0141). Serialized bytes are native-endian and non-reproducible; unsafe from_raw_parts; u32 index caps it at ~3.8B keys.

**How:** Each key maps to three fingerprint slots: construction peels a random 3-uniform hypergraph so that fingerprint(key) = F[h0] ^ F[h1] ^ F[h2], and a query is one MurmurHash3 finalizer mix plus three array reads, with no SIMD. Binary fuse filters (Graf & Lemire, arXiv:2201.01174) put the three slots in adjacent power-of-two segments (a binary-partitioned fuse graph), so the array needs about 1.125n slots instead of the xor filter's 1.23n + 32. Fingerprint width alone sets the FPP (about 2^-8, 2^-16 or 2^-32) at about 9, 18 or 36 bits/key, where a Bloom filter needs about 1.44·log2(1/ε) bits/key. The code is a port of Go FastFilter/xorfilter and uses only the 3-wise variant.

**Use it when:**
- Static or rebuild-occasionally sets that are queried far more often than built, such as SST/segment filters, blocklists, dedup pre-checks and 'is this key on disk' guards, where filter RAM is what you are trying to cut.
- You already have 64-bit hashes, or can hash keys yourself, and a fixed FPP of about 0.39% (8-bit), about 0.0015% (16-bit) or effectively zero (32-bit) suits you.
- Rust services or embedded/no_std targets with an allocator. CI checks thumbv7em-none-eabi with default features off.
- Filters persisted to disk and loaded without copying: `BinaryFuse*Ref::from_dma` borrows the fingerprint bytes from an mmap'd buffer and copies only a 20-byte descriptor.
- Sets of about a million keys or more. The paper measures the 3-wise layout reaching 9 bits/key there, while below about 20k keys the xor filter can be as small or smaller.

**Skip it when:**
- You need inserts, deletes or counting. Every filter is rebuilt from the full key set; use a cuckoo or quotient filter instead.
- You want to tune FPP against space continuously, the way Bloom parameters allow. Only 8, 16 and 32-bit fingerprints exist, and the maintainer says in issues #61 and #69 that space per item cannot be reduced.
- Query latency on huge filters is the goal. Each lookup touches three random cache lines. A user in issue #84 measured about 280 M lookups/s at 1M keys falling to about 51 M/s at 99M keys, and in the binary fuse paper an AVX2 blocked Bloom filter queried faster than any xor-family filter.
- Building very large sets under a memory cap. From reading the code, BinaryFuse construction allocates about 13 bytes per slot plus 9 bytes per key of scratch (about 24 B/key) on top of your u64 key array, for a result of about 1.1 B/key.
- You need the smallest possible static filter. xorf has no 4-wise binary fuse (8.6 bits/key in the paper), and Ribbon filters (BuRR, RocksDB) get closer to the lower bound.

**Integration:** crate · libm (via the default `binary-fuse` feature) and rand (via the default `uniform-random` feature, which needs std). Optional: serde plus serde_bytes. The published 0.13.0 also has an optional `bincode` 2.0.0-rc.3 dependency, which is flagged unmaintained (RUSTSEC-2025-0141, issue #98). Unreleased master (0.14.0) removes it and keeps `bincode` only as an alias for `serde`. · Rust 1.85 on master (edition 2024, MSRV job in CI). The published 0.13.0 is edition 2021 and declares no rust-version, so its MSRV is not documented. · Any Rust target with `alloc`. The code is portable and has no arch-specific intrinsics. no_std builds are CI-checked on thumbv7em-none-eabi without default features.

**Vs siblings:** Pick xorf when you are in Rust and want the xor_singleheader/xorfilter algorithms natively, with no_std support and zero-copy mmap loading; use those C/Go originals in their own languages. Choose BuRR or RocksDB Ribbon instead when the last few percent of space matter more than query speed (the binary fuse paper measured ribbon queries slower), and a cuckoo filter or CQF when the set must accept inserts or deletes.

**Gotchas:**
- Keys must be distinct. Debug builds check this with a BTreeSet and panic; in release, BinaryFuse drops exact duplicate hashes, but the Xor family's unbounded retry loop never terminates on duplicates (issue #25). BinaryFuse gives up after 1,000 deterministic seeds with Err("Failed to construct binary fuse filter."), and before 0.13.0 about 1 in 60k distinct key sets just past a segment-length step (n ≈ 11.5k) could never build (PR #100).
- `HashProxy` requires `From<Vec<u64>>`, which BinaryFuse types do not implement (they only have TryFrom), so the recommended filters cannot be wrapped. Issue #72 is closed, but the code still lacks the impl. Hash keys yourself or wrap Xor8 instead.
- Filter bytes are not reproducible by default. The `uniform-random` feature fills unused slots from the thread RNG (issue #77); disable default features for byte-identical output. DMA fingerprints for the 16/32-bit types are raw native-endian memory, although the descriptor is little-endian, and `from_dma` panics on misaligned buffers (it uses unsafe `from_raw_parts` after assert checks).
- The README on master says `xorf = "0.14"`, but crates.io's newest version is 0.13.0, so that line does not resolve yet. BinaryFuse index arithmetic is u32, so one filter addresses at most 2^32 slots (about 3.8B keys); this limit is not documented.

**Status:** Actively maintained and MIT-licensed, with about 6.7M crates.io downloads: 0.13.0 shipped on 2026-08-21 with the segment-boundary construction fix, and master already carries an unreleased 0.14.0 (edition 2024, MSRV 1.85, native bincode support removed).

[repo](https://github.com/ayazhafiz/xorf) · [benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.01174)

##### cfilter (Cuckoo Filter implementation in Go)  `Go`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier D`

Unmaintained pure-Go cuckoo filter (Fan et al. 2014) offering deletion as a Bloom-filter alternative; speed claims unmeasured, known item-loss bugs.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — Nothing was measured. The 'higher performance than Bloom filters' line restates the Fan et al. paper, whose figures come from the authors' C++ efficient/cuckoofilter. The repo's only benchmark inserts and deletes one constant key, with no Bloom baseline, no published results and no stated hardware. The only third-party numbers for cfilter (issue #11: 100M random 16-char hex keys, Go on an unspecified Mac, no Bloom comparison) show roughly 0.5M inserts/s and 1M lookups/s, with 5,162 inserted keys missing afterwards.

**Known shortcoming:** No benchmark numbers of its own: the 'faster than Bloom' claim comes from the paper's C++ implementation (efficient/cuckoofilter, listed separately). A popular Go port (751 stars) with directional evidence only.

**Known shortcoming:** Known lost items: 5,162 of 100M missing (#11) and misses past ~300k (#13), both closed unfixed; 'no longer maintaining' since 2019-11. `go get` resolves v0.1.1 (2016), which panics in the eviction loop (#8). On master the XOR alt-bucket works only for power-of-two sizes (otherwise false negatives) and a failed kick drops an old key without fixing Count. A slice per slot (24 B header plus a heap allocation per fingerprint, ~7.5 MiB preallocated) contradicts the README's space claim; not goroutine-safe; no serialization.

**How:** It uses partial-key cuckoo hashing from Fan, Andersen and Kaminsky (CoNEXT 2014). Each key stores a short fingerprint (the leading bytes of its FNV-1 64 hash) in one of two 4-slot buckets, i1 = djb2(key) mod m and i2 = (i1 XOR djb2(fingerprint)) mod m. A lookup therefore reads at most two buckets instead of k scattered Bloom bits, and a delete just clears a slot. When both buckets are full, Insert evicts random fingerprints to their alternate bucket, up to 500 times. This Go implementation gives up most of the paper's cache-locality advantage: every slot is a 24-byte []byte slice header pointing at its own heap allocation, and every Insert/Lookup/Delete allocates twice (hash.Sum plus the fingerprint slice). Nothing in the repo measures the resulting speed.

**Use it when:**
- Reading a short, clear Go walk-through of partial-key cuckoo hashing (insert, evict, XOR alternate bucket, delete) while learning the Fan et al. design.
- Small, single-goroutine, throwaway sets of []byte keys that stay well below the 262,144-slot default capacity (the issue #13 reporter saw no losses at 200k keys but did at 300k), with Size left as a power of two, where an occasional false negative is acceptable.
- Maintaining legacy code that already imports it (pkg.go.dev lists older OWASP Amass utils, finogeeks/ligase and osamingo/shamoji), where you need to understand its failure modes before replacing it.

**Skip it when:**
- Anything that relies on the usual no-false-negatives property. Users reported inserted items that later cannot be found: 5,162 of 100M keys in issue #11, and lookups failing past about 300k keys in issue #13. Both issues were closed without a fix, with the note 'No longer maintaining this' (2019-11-20).
- Memory-sensitive use, which is the README's own headline claim. Each slot costs a 24-byte slice header whether it is used or not (about 7.5 MiB preallocated for the default 262k-slot filter), and each stored fingerprint is a separate heap allocation. At the default ~5e-7 FPR an optimal Bloom filter needs about 3.8 bytes per item (my arithmetic from the code and the paper's formula, not a measurement). A commenter in issue #13 estimated the footprint at 7x larger than necessary.
- High load factors. The issue #11 reporter could not get past roughly 36-50% load before Insert failed, against the ~95% the paper reports for 4-slot buckets.
- Concurrent access (no locking of any kind), persistence across restarts (the serialization request in issue #5 was closed unimplemented), or fingerprint sizes that are not a whole number of bytes.
- Any setting where you want a maintained, tagged release. The last commit was 2017-07-05, and the only tags (v0.1.0 and v0.1.1, both 2016) predate every bug fix.

**Integration:** module · none (Go stdlib only: hash, hash/fnv, math/rand, bytes) · Not formally stated. There is no go.mod, and .travis.yml tested Go 1.3-1.6 plus tip in 2016-2017. Module mode resolves @latest to v0.1.1. · any Go platform (pure Go, no unsafe or assembly)

**Vs siblings:** In practice, never for production. In Go, go-qfext (a quotient filter with measured 20-31 ns lookups against 74 ns for bits-and-blooms Bloom) or FastFilter/xorfilter (for static sets) are measured, working alternatives. efficient/cuckoofilter is the C++ reference whose paper numbers this README borrows. In 2017 the author himself pointed users to seiflotfy/cuckoofilter instead.

**Gotchas:**
- `go get github.com/irfansharif/cfilter` resolves to v0.1.1 (proxy.golang.org @latest), tagged 2016-09-11. That version still has the `i ^= hashfp(f) % cf.size` precedence bug, which panics with 'index out of range' once eviction starts (issue #8, fixed on master 2016-12-28), and a `rand.Intn(len(b)-1)` bug that never evicts the last slot (issue #10). panmari/compare_probabilistic_filters, which pins v0.1.1, commented cfilter out for exactly this panic. To get the fixes you must pin a master pseudo-version.
- Even on master, the alternate-bucket XOR trick only round-trips when Size (the bucket count) is a power of two, which the default is. With any other Size, a fingerprint that gets evicted can land in a bucket Lookup never checks, so the filter returns false negatives. The losses reported in issue #11 used Size(20,000,000) and Size(35,000,000).
- When Insert gives up after MaximumKicks, the fingerprint it is still holding is usually an earlier key's, and that key is silently dropped: Insert returns false, but Count() is not decremented and the lost key now fails Lookup. Insert also never checks for duplicates, so a key inserted twice is stored twice. Delete of a key that was never inserted can remove another key's matching fingerprint, as the README warns.
- FingerprintSize is in bytes, not bits. Its doc comment says the default is 2, but master's configure() uses 3 bytes (v0.1.1 used 2), so the effective FPR, about 2*BucketSize/2^(8*bytes), depends on which version you got.

**Status:** Abandoned. The last commit was 2017-07-05, and on 2019-11-20 the author closed all remaining issues with 'No longer maintaining this'. It is MIT-licensed, stdlib-only and about 240 lines, so it is easy to vendor, but the false-negative bugs above (power-of-two sizing, dropped eviction victim, stale v0.1.1 tag) would need fixing first.

[repo](https://github.com/irfansharif/cfilter)

### toolchain-and-build

#### build-systems

##### Buck2  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Meta's Rust rewrite of the Buck build system; up to 2x faster than Buck1 in Meta's internal monorepo usage.

**Beats:** Buck1 (Meta's original Buck build system) — The only first-party number is the README's 'up to 2x faster than Buck1 in practice,' sourced from Meta's internal production usage comparing Buck2 to Buck1 across Meta's monorepo. No specific workload, project, methodology, compiler/stdlib, or hardware is given, and the README itself says comparisons against Bazel-class systems 'have yet to be performed.'

**How:** Core build graph runs on `dice`, Meta's own incremental computation engine, so only invalidated nodes recompute on a change. Remote Execution support (Bazel's REAPI, works with BuildBarn/BuildBuddy/EngFlow/NativeLink) enables distributed/cached builds and, when used, hermeticity: all rule inputs must be declared or the build fails. A persistent background daemon (buckd) plus filesystem watching avoids repeated startup/scan cost on ultra-large repos. Build files and rules are parsed/evaluated with `starlark-rust`, Meta's own fast Starlark interpreter.

**Use it when:**
- Large, multi-language monorepos already paying the cost of Make/Bazel-style top-down builds and needing better incremental-rebuild accuracy
- Teams that can invest in Remote Execution infrastructure to get real hermetic, cacheable builds
- Projects wanting a single build/test/query tool across languages with cross-language dependencies (e.g. Rust crate <- OCaml <- Python)
- Teams willing to write/port BUCK/Starlark rule definitions instead of reusing existing CMake/Make/Cargo build files
- Users comfortable tracking a fast-moving HEAD with no stable release tag

**Skip it when:**
- Small or single-language projects where Make/CMake/Cargo already work fine — migration cost isn't justified
- Teams wanting hermetic guarantees without standing up Remote Execution: local-only build steps are not sandboxed/hermetic (README footnote)
- Projects needing precompiled-header support: open issue #368 says PCH 'don't seem to be working'
- Workloads sensitive to daemon startup latency: open issue #507 notes 'daemon startup is a bit slow'
- Anyone needing a stable, versioned release: no stable release tag exists, Meta itself tracks HEAD

**Integration:** source-drop · none (self-contained Rust workspace; Remote Execution backend optional and external, e.g. BuildBarn/BuildBuddy/EngFlow/NativeLink) · prebuilt binaries via GitHub releases or dotslash; building from source uses a pinned Rust nightly (rust-toolchain.toml: nightly-2026-07-05) · Linux, macOS, Windows (CI has setup_linux_env/setup_macos_env/setup_windows_env and a Cross.toml)

**Vs siblings:** Pick Buck2 over Mill/tup/xmake when you need true multi-language monorepo builds with Remote-Execution-backed hermeticity and are willing to adopt Starlark BUCK files; its 2x number is Meta-internal Buck1-vs-Buck2 only (evidence tier C, no workload/hardware given), so it is not a verified head-to-head against Make/CMake/Ninja/Bazel/Cargo the way tup's or Mill's numbers are.

**Gotchas:**
- Local-only build steps are NOT sandboxed/hermetic; only Remote-Execution-backed builds get full hermeticity (README footnote)
- Open issue #340: buck2 recompiles *all* source files when a link-only dependency changes
- No stable release tag; Meta itself runs latest HEAD, so 'rough edges' are expected for outside users (README warning)
- Precompiled headers reportedly not working (issue #368)

**Status:** Actively maintained (commits as of 2026-09-24, 4.4k stars, used in production at Meta), but usability is 'copyable' rather than a stable package: no stable release tag, dual MIT/Apache-2.0 licensed.

[repo](https://github.com/facebook/buck2) · [benchmark](https://github.com/facebook/buck2/blob/main/README.md)

##### xmake  `C`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Lua-scripted cross-platform build tool with built-in package manager; beats CMake+Make, roughly matches plain Ninja.

**Beats:** Make (via CMake-generated Makefiles) — First-party README benchmark building xmake's own in-repo xmake-core (C) target: on Termux (8-core, -j12) xmake finished in 24.890s vs cmake(gen+make)'s 5.416s+28.473s=33.889s total (~1.36x), but plain ninja ran in 25.682s, barely behind xmake; on macOS (8-core, -j12) xmake was 12.264s vs cmake(gen+make)'s 1.203s+14.030s=15.233s total (~1.24x), while plain ninja was faster than xmake at 11.327s. Single-threaded (-j1) gaps vs cmake+make were smaller (~1.08-1.15x). Exact CPU model and compiler/flags are not stated.

**How:** xmake's core engine (xmake-core, written in C, bundled with a modified Lua/tbox runtime) parses xmake.lua and runs the resulting dependency DAG directly in one process and one invocation, the same way Ninja does, instead of the two-stage 'generate Makefiles, then run recursive make' path CMake+Make requires. The measured speedup is specifically against that generate+make baseline (~1.24-1.36x at -j12, ~1.08-1.15x at -j1); xmake does not claim to beat Ninja's own scheduler and is measurably not doing so here. It also ships an optional content-based local/remote build cache (not exercised in this particular benchmark).

**Use it when:**
- Migrating off raw CMake+Make (not CMake+Ninja) where a single tool that configures and builds without a separate generate step is the goal
- Want a built-in cross-platform package manager instead of wiring vcpkg/conan into CMake by hand
- Targeting niche platforms/toolchains in one config file (WDK drivers, CUDA, Zig, Rust, embedded compilers like Keil/IAR/TI, arbitrary cross toolchains) that CMake supports poorly
- New small-to-medium C/C++ project where xmake.lua's terser syntax is a feature rather than a migration cost
- Want distributed/remote build or a build cache without separately standing up distcc/ccache/sccache

**Skip it when:**
- Project already builds via CMake+Ninja or Meson: per this same README, xmake is on par with or slightly slower than plain Ninja, so there is no measured win there
- Team depends on CMake's mature IDE/CI/third-party tooling ecosystem; xmake's own IDE plugins (VSCode/Sublime/IDEA/Zed) are official but far smaller in adoption
- Large existing CMake codebase: there is no automatic CMakeLists.txt -> xmake.lua converter in this repo, so migration means hand-porting build logic
- Treating the claimed multiplier as portable: this is a first-party, tier-C benchmark with no CPU model, OS version, or compiler/flags disclosed
- Need airtight incremental-build correctness across all language backends: open issues report gaps for at least one backend (see gotchas)

**Integration:** CLI binary (not a library) — precompiled install via curl/wget/PowerShell script or OS package managers · none to install (self-contained binary); requires whatever C/C++/other-language toolchain the project itself needs (GCC/Clang/MSVC/etc.), which xmake detects rather than provides · not documented as a minimum — no dependencies outside the standard library per README; current release v3.1.1 (2026-08-27); source-build requirements (compiler for xmake-core, Lua) not stated in README · Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD/NetBSD/OpenBSD/DragonflyBSD, Solaris, Android, iOS, watchOS, tvOS, visionOS, MSYS/MinGW/Cygwin, Wasm, Haiku, HarmonyOS, and arbitrary cross-toolchains, each with multiple listed architectures

**Vs siblings:** None of the catalogued siblings are direct substitutes: ccache caches compiler invocations and composes with any build system including xmake; Mill/Buck2 target JVM/Meta monorepo ecosystems, not general C/C++; tup targets the specific pathology of huge (100k-file) trees with slow no-op/rebuild checks under Make. Pick xmake over CMake+Make when you also want a bundled package manager and one-file multi-language config, but pick tup instead if your real bottleneck is Make's no-op/rebuild-check cost at large scale, since xmake's own numbers show it merely tying Ninja rather than tup's claimed order-of-magnitude jump.

**Gotchas:**
- The repo's default branch is 'dev', not 'master'; benchmark_url points at master but the same numbers appear on dev's README
- README's headline claim is 'on par with Ninja' — in this exact benchmark table xmake (12.264s parallel / 39.937s single, macOS) is slower than plain ninja (11.327s / 38.995s), so 'faster' here means faster than CMake+Make, not faster than Ninja
- Benchmark hardware is described only as '8core' with no CPU model, OS version, or compiler/flags disclosed
- Open issues report incremental-build gaps for at least one language backend ('rust project not being rebuilt when modified', #4790) and occasional flaky build failures fixed only by restarting (#4796); verify incremental correctness for your specific toolchain before relying on it

**Status:** Actively maintained: last commit 2026-09-22, latest release v3.1.1 (2026-08-27), 259 open issues, 12.2k stars, no open security advisories found; Apache-2.0 licensed and distributed as a self-contained precompiled binary, so it's cheap to adopt or vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/xmake-io/xmake) · [benchmark](https://github.com/xmake-io/xmake/blob/master/README.md)

#### compile-caching-and-distribution

##### FASTBuild  `C++`  `Zlib`  `active`  `Tier C`

Full build system combining object caching, unity builds and distributed compilation; replaces make/MSBuild, not a wrapper.

**Beats:** the same build without FASTBuild's object cache, Unity/Blob builds or distributed compilation (implicit; no baseline tool is named) — fastbuild.org's features page gives first-party, unqualified figures — object caching 'up to 10x', Unity/Blob builds 'improvements of 10x or more', distributed compilation 'speedups of 5x are common' — each measured against the same build without that FASTBuild feature enabled. No workload, hardware, compiler, or flags are given, so these are vendor round numbers, not a reproducible benchmark.

**How:** Unity/Blob builds merge many .cpp files into fewer translation units, cutting per-file compiler startup/parse overhead. The object cache stores compiled objects keyed by build inputs and reuses them across machines instead of recompiling identical code. Distributed compilation preprocesses source locally then ships it to idle worker machines running FBuildWorker, so object compilation runs in parallel across a farm rather than being limited to one machine's core count.

**Use it when:**
- Large multi-platform (PC/console/mobile) C/C++ game or engine codebase, where you're willing to author the build in FASTBuild's own BFF language
- Team has spare workstation or render-farm capacity to run FBuildWorker for network distribution
- CI or local dev with deterministic compiler output, where object-cache hits repeat across builds and machines
- Cross-compiler shop needing one build tool across MSVC, GCC, Clang, SNC, GreenHills, CodeWarrior, NVCC
- Want unity-build automation without hand-writing jumbo .cpp generation scripts

**Skip it when:**
- Want to keep an existing CMake/Make/MSBuild/Ninja build and just add caching or distribution without rewriting build files
- No dedicated worker machines or spare network compute — distributed mode adds nothing without hardware to distribute to
- Non-deterministic compiler output or unusual toolchains: issue #1021 (cache errors when system locale differs) and #992 (clang-cl PCH + cache 'fatal error in some situations') show real cache-correctness edge cases
- Linux build farm with >32 cores per worker: issue #1197 reports the CPU-affinity mask is 32-bit, giving a wrong mask on wider machines
- Small or single-machine project where compile time is already short — BFF authoring and cache/worker setup cost may not pay off

**Integration:** source-drop · none documented for the core build; the OSUI component links native OS UI frameworks (WinAPI on Windows, Cocoa .mm files on macOS) · not documented as a stated minimum; Linux CI (Linux.yml) builds and tests with GCC 10 and Clang 15 on Ubuntu 22.04 — Windows/macOS minimum compiler versions not checked this session · Windows, Linux and macOS as build hosts (README); used to target PC, Mac, Linux, consoles, smartphones and retro systems as build outputs — specific host CPU architectures not documented

**Vs siblings:** Pick FASTBuild when you're building (or willing to rebuild) a multi-platform C/C++ project around its own BFF language and want unity builds, object cache and worker-farm distribution bundled in one tool. Pick NativeLink or HOMCC instead when you need to keep an existing Bazel/REAPI or distcc-compatible build and only add remote caching or distributed compilation without rewriting build files, or octobuild when the target is specifically Unreal Engine's UBT/UAT pipeline.

**Gotchas:**
- Cache correctness assumes deterministic compiler output; issue #1021 shows cache errors when the system locale differs and #992 shows clang-cl PCH + cache producing a fatal error in some situations
- Distributed compilation is reported to intermittently fail (issue #1058, open, 'Need More Info')
- Linux CPU-affinity helper uses a 32-bit mask (issue #1197), so it can compute the wrong core mask on machines with more than 32 cores
- GitHub's UI reports 'no license' for this repo because the license file lives at Code/LICENSE.TXT rather than repo root, even though it is zlib-licensed

**Status:** Actively maintained — the dev branch (where patches land) was last committed 2026-09-20, days before this entry — and zlib-licensed (Code/LICENSE.TXT), so it's free to vendor; its 1.4k GitHub stars understate real usage since it's mainly distributed via fastbuild.org binaries and used by many closed-source game studios.

[repo](https://github.com/fastbuild/fastbuild) · [benchmark](https://www.fastbuild.org/docs/features.html)

##### HOMCC  `Python`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Distributed C/C++ compiler wrapper replacing distcc with server-side dependency caching and compression for thin uplinks.

**Beats:** distcc — On an internal, non-public Celonis C++ codebase built with clang++-14 (server job limit 112, 60 compilation threads), the README's bar chart shows homcc beating distcc by about 6.3x at 5/25 Mbps (~9.2 vs ~57.5 min), narrowing to ~1.4x at 40/200 Mbps, and homcc being slightly slower than distcc at gigabit (~5.8 vs ~4.9 min). No CPU/hardware spec, raw data, or runnable benchmark script is published; the numbers are estimated from bar heights in an image, and the README's prose claim of gains 'by some orders of magnitude' overstates what its own chart shows.

**How:** On a cache miss homcc still sends preprocessed sources like distcc, but homccd keeps a persistent, size-bounded (LRU, `HOMCC_MAX_DEPENDENCY_CACHE_SIZE`) cache of dependency files keyed by content hash, so once warm only genuinely new headers/sources cross the network instead of the full preprocessed unit every time. Transferred sources and resulting object files are additionally compressed with lzo or lzma. Both mechanisms specifically target bandwidth, not CPU parallelism, which is why the reported gains shrink to nothing as link speed rises.

**Use it when:**
- Remote/distributed C or C++ builds (gcc or clang) over thin or variable-bandwidth links (roughly 5-40 Mbps in the README's own numbers), e.g. work-from-home developers hitting an office build farm
- Teams already using a distcc-style CCACHE_PREFIX or conan-profile hook and willing to swap in a different client/server pair
- Need sandboxed remote compilation per client via schroot profiles or docker containers rather than running arbitrary code directly on the build host
- Debian/Ubuntu-based build infrastructure (packaged and tested as .deb on Ubuntu 22.04)
- Want to tunnel remote compiles over SSH (multiplexed ControlMaster) instead of exposing a plaintext TCP service

**Skip it when:**
- Gigabit or otherwise unconstrained links to the build farm — the project's own chart shows distcc is not slower (slightly faster) once bandwidth stops being the bottleneck
- Untrusted/public networks without a VPN or SSH tunnel — there is no built-in TLS; homcc transmits source over plain TCP by default and the README explicitly warns not to expose homccd publicly
- Environments needing per-client connection limits on the server — homccd does not cap simultaneous connections from one client, so a single client can exhaust the job pool
- Non-Debian/Ubuntu targets or languages other than C/C++ — schroot sandboxing and the packaging are Debian-specific, and gcc/clang are the only supported compilers
- Projects wary of small-team tooling — 24 stars, single corporate maintainer (Celonis), no independent adopters visible; internal benchmark numbers cannot be reproduced by outsiders

**Integration:** source-drop · python-lzo (>=1.12, needs liblzo2-dev/apt python3-lzo) for compression; sysv_ipc for the client's semaphore-based concurrency control; optional schroot or docker for sandboxed remote execution; ssh for tunneled hosts · Python 3.9+ (debian/control declares X-Python3-Version >= 3.9; CI runs on 3.9); gcc or clang on both client and server · Linux, packaged and CI-tested for Debian/Ubuntu (ubuntu-22.04); schroot sandboxing is Debian/Ubuntu-specific, docker sandboxing is more portable but the server itself targets Linux

**Vs siblings:** Pick homcc over NativeLink, FASTBuild, or octobuild specifically when your bottleneck is a thin/variable uplink to an existing distcc-style distributed build farm and you want server-side dependency caching plus compression to shrink that — NativeLink targets single-machine local build acceleration (no distribution), FASTBuild is a from-scratch build system with its own distribution/unity-build model, and octobuild is scoped to Unreal Engine's UBT/UAT toolchain; none of them are distcc drop-in replacements for bandwidth-constrained remote C/C++ compilation.

**Gotchas:**
- No built-in transport encryption: plain TCP hosts send source unencrypted; use an SSH-tunneled `@HOST`/`user@HOST` entry or a VPN, and never expose homccd on an untrusted network
- homccd does not limit simultaneous connections per client, so one misbehaving client can consume the entire server job pool
- docker sandboxing requires the container to bind-mount the host's /tmp to /tmp so the server-side dependency cache is reachable inside the container; schroot sandboxing has the same /tmp-mount requirement
- Client relies on SysV semaphores for concurrency bookkeeping — historically a source of race-condition bugs (see issues 'Fix SysV semaphore race', 'AttributeError on HostSemaphore __exit__'), now fixed but worth knowing if debugging odd hangs

**Status:** Actively maintained by Celonis (last commit 2026-08-18, v1.0.4 tagged the same day, zero open issues) under the MIT license; small adoption (24 stars) but the codebase is compact and copyable/vendorable if you accept the Debian/Ubuntu-oriented packaging.

[repo](https://github.com/celonis/homcc) · [benchmark](https://github.com/celonis/homcc#readme)

##### octobuild  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust compiler cache for Unreal Engine that impersonates IncrediBuild's xgConsole to speed up re-compiles vs. no cache.

**Beats:** stock Unreal Build Tool / Unreal Automation Tool build without octobuild (README 'Without octobuild' column) — The README's first-party benchmark table (unnamed UE 5.0.3 game project, DebugGame configuration, no stated compiler flags) shows a fully warm (100%) cache beating a build without octobuild by about 2.4x-6.5x across platforms — e.g. Linux 3m54s to 36s, Win64 8m4s to 2m15s (MSVC 2019) — on an AMD Ryzen 7 3700X/32GB (Linux) or Intel Core i7-9700F/32GB (Windows/console) with SSD storage; a cold (0%) cache showed no speedup and was up to ~25% slower on Win64 (8m4s to 10m6s).

**How:** It is a content-addressed disk cache of individual compile actions, similar in spirit to ccache/sccache, avoiding re-invocation of cl.exe/clang for translation units it has already built. The repo also ships octo_agent/octo_builder/octo_coordinator and a src/cluster module, suggesting optional distributed-build support beyond local caching, but this is undocumented in the README and not covered by the benchmark. Per the README's own numbers the entire measured speedup is cache-hit driven: at 0% cache hit rate it is roughly neutral to slower than no octobuild at all, presumably from added hashing/IPC overhead.

**Use it when:**
- Unreal Engine or UE-based game project doing iterative DebugGame rebuilds after small source edits, with a cache that can stay warm between builds
- Team already using, or willing to enable, IncrediBuild-style XGE executor integration in UBT/UAT
- Windows target with MSVC 2019/2022 (the benchmarked and best-documented path)
- Linux or macOS target where you can apply the listed UE engine patches (some already merged in UE >= 5.2 / >= 5.3)
- Dev or CI machines with spare local SSD space for a large (default 64GB) persistent cache

**Skip it when:**
- Cold-cache or from-scratch CI builds: the README's own table shows octobuild is equal to or up to ~25% slower than no octobuild at 0% cache hit rate (Win64 8m4s -> 10m6s)
- You need a validated comparison against ccache, sccache, distcc, or IncrediBuild itself — none appears in the README; the only baseline is 'without octobuild'
- Non-Unreal C/C++ projects: it's UE-specific (vs/clang compiler pre/postprocessing, XGE action-graph parser), not a general-purpose compiler cache
- You can't spare disk for a multi-GB persistent cache, or your build environment is ephemeral so the cache never warms up
- You need compiler flags and an exact reproducible harness for the benchmark numbers — the README doesn't state flags and uses an unnamed game project

**Integration:** source-drop · Rust crates (bincode, crossbeam-channel, petgraph, reqwest, serde, sha2, xml-rs, figment, thiserror, uuid, etc.) plus the octobuild/daemon-rs and octobuild/ipc-rs git dependencies; winapi/winreg on Windows. Also distributed as prebuilt packages via Chocolatey, WinGet, Homebrew, and apt/deb. · Rust stable (edition 2021 crate, CI builds against dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable with no pinned MSRV); Windows build additionally needs Visual Studio 2019 or 2022 with the C++ desktop workload · Win64 (MSVC 2019/2022), Linux, macOS, plus PS4/PS5/Xbox One/Xbox Series X and Android/iOS listed as supported; console/mobile targets build through UE's own toolchains

**Vs siblings:** Pick octobuild specifically because the project is Unreal Engine or UE-based — its xgConsole/ib_console impersonation and MSVC/clang postprocessing are UE-specific integration points that NativeLink, FASTBuild, and HOMCC don't provide. Those siblings target generic CMake/Ninja or distcc-based C/C++ builds and would need a custom UE integration to be used at all, whereas octobuild works with UBT/UAT's existing XGE executor path out of the box.

**Gotchas:**
- Cold cache makes the build slower than not using octobuild at all (README: Win64 8m4s without octobuild vs. 10m6s at 0% cache hit)
- Default disk cache is 64GB; tune via OCTOBUILD_CACHE_LIMIT_MB, and OCTOBUILD_CACHE_MODE can set it to read-only or fully disabled
- On Windows, long command lines can hit 'ERROR: The filename or extension is too long (os error 206)' — fix is OCTOBUILD_USE_RESPONSE_FILES=true, which is already the Windows default
- Source tree contains cluster/agent/coordinator/builder binaries implying distributed (multi-machine) build support, but this is undocumented in the README and unmeasured in the benchmark

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-15, 285 stars, packaged for Chocolatey/WinGet/Homebrew/apt) and MIT-licensed, but it's a set of UE-specific CLI binaries rather than a general library, so 'copyable' means vendoring the tool, not embedding source into another project.

[repo](https://github.com/octobuild/octobuild) · [benchmark](https://github.com/octobuild/octobuild#benchmark)

#### compilers-frontends

##### MIR / c2m (C2MIR)  `C`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Lightweight JIT toolkit whose C11 front-end (c2m) compiles a header-free C function ~80x faster than gcc -O2.

**Beats:** GCC — On an Intel i5-13600K (Fedora 37, GCC 12.3.1), c2m -eg compiled a single header-free C function (Eratosthenes sieve) in 336us vs gcc -O2's 27.1ms (~80x) and gcc -O0's 26.1ms (~77x, with gcc reading source from an in-memory filesystem to remove disk I/O); the resulting c2m-generated machine code then ran at ~92% of gcc -O2 speed on that same sieve and ~91% geomean (0.96 average) across 15 small C benchmarks from the repo's own suite.

**How:** c2m uses a hand-written 4-pass pipeline (PEG-based recursive-descent parser, no yacc/flex, then context checking, then MIR generation) instead of a heavyweight preprocessor/parser/optimizer stack. MIR-generator itself runs only a short, deliberately minimal optimization pipeline (SSA built via Braun's algorithm, global value numbering, copy/dead-store/dead-code elimination, and a priority-based linear-scan register allocator with aggressive coalescing) instead of GCC's full middle end, keeping per-function compile overhead in the hundreds-of-microseconds range.

**Use it when:**
- Embedding a C-based JIT inside an interpreter or dynamic-language runtime (the README's own target: CRuby/MRuby-style hot-path specialization)
- Latency-sensitive compile paths where a single small function needs microsecond-scale turnaround rather than a whole translation unit
- Lazy or basic-block-level code generation (-el/-eb) to defer codegen cost until a function or block is actually executed
- Targeting x86-64, aarch64 (including Apple Silicon), ppc64le, s390x, or riscv64 on Linux/macOS and willing to vendor a small (~55K LOC), MIT-licensed compiler
- Compiling small, self-contained C programs (no large #include trees) from the command line without installing GCC

**Skip it when:**
- Code needs VLAs, `_Complex`, `_Atomic`, or `_Thread_local` -- c2m's C11 subset omits them (c2mir/README.md lists them as unimplemented; issue #394 is an open request for `_Thread_local`)
- Large, multi-file, header-heavy production builds -- the quoted ~80x is a single function with no #include files on an in-memory gcc run; a real build sees a much smaller gap per the record's own tradeoffs note
- You need GDB-quality source-level debug info for compiled/JITted code -- still an open feature request (#442, opened Jul 2026)
- Untrusted or adversarial C input -- several open heap-buffer-overflow/segfault issues in the parser and preprocessor (#353, #360, #362, #364, #365, #366) mean the front-end isn't hardened
- You need generated code to match or beat gcc -O2 at runtime -- c2m -eg trades that away, running at ~91% geomean / ~92% on sieve of gcc -O2 speed

**Integration:** static lib + shared lib + source-drop (also builds a standalone `c2m` compiler binary) · none to build (self-contained, builds with system gcc/clang); programs it compiles link libc/libm at runtime · C11/gnu11 to build MIR itself (GCC or Clang); c2m implements a C11 subset (no VLA/_Complex/_Atomic/_Thread_local) plus some GNU extensions · x86-64, aarch64 (incl. Apple Silicon), ppc64le, s390x, riscv64 on Linux; x86-64/aarch64 macOS; Windows (MinGW/MSVC) is built by GNUmakefile though the README disclaimer only warranties the Linux/OSX/ppc64le/s390x/riscv64 CI-tested platforms

**Vs siblings:** Pick MIR/c2m over TinyCC when you need an embeddable JIT library (interpret-or-generate, lazy per-function/per-block codegen, MIR IR you can also build directly via API) rather than just a fast standalone `cc`; TinyCC's ~9x-over-gcc number is for a traditional whole-program compile-and-link and doesn't offer c2m's lazy JIT interfaces. Neither zapcc (a caching Clang wrapper for incremental full C++ builds) nor cg_clif (a Rust/Cranelift backend) is a real alternative here -- both target different languages and build workflows entirely.

**Gotchas:**
- No `_Thread_local`, `_Atomic`, VLA, or `_Complex` support in c2m (c2mir/README.md; issue #394 open)
- Thread safety is per-MIR_context: separate contexts per thread need no synchronization, but sharing one context across threads isn't documented as safe
- Using C as the JIT input (instead of building MIR IR directly via the API) can slow compilation up to 2x, per README
- Multiple segfault/heap-buffer-overflow issues remain open in the parser/preprocessor path (e.g. #360, #362, #364, #365, #366), so malformed C input isn't guaranteed to fail safely

**Status:** Actively maintained -- commits and issue activity continue through Sep 2026 (last commit 2026-06-19, new issues as recent as #475 on 2026-09-03); MIT-licensed and small (~55K LOC per README) enough to vendor, with 'copyable' usability meaning a source/library integration rather than a packaged install.

[repo](https://github.com/vnmakarov/mir) · [benchmark](https://github.com/vnmakarov/mir/blob/master/README.md)

##### rustc_codegen_cranelift (cg_clif)  `Rust`  `MIT OR Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Drop-in Cranelift codegen backend for rustc that replaces LLVM to cut debug-build compile times.

**Beats:** rustc — First-party numbers only. bjorn3's Nov 2024 progress report says that on the rustc-perf suite, after enabling lld for non-LLVM backends, cg_clif was '10-50% faster' than cg_llvm on most benchmarks, with a couple of pathological benchmarks still regressed; no hardware, exact rustc version, or raw data are given. Separately, issue #878 (2020) reported debug-profile clean and baseline-incremental builds about 10-60% faster (often ~40%) versus cg_llvm, but clean-incremental builds up to ~200% slower due to uncached object files.

**How:** Cranelift is a simpler, JIT-oriented code generator with far less optimization machinery than LLVM, so it spends much less time per function translating MIR to machine code, trading away optimized codegen quality that doesn't matter for debug builds. The Nov 2024 progress report attributes the bulk of the observed win to switching the link step to lld for non-LLVM backends (rust-lang/rust PR #132774) and to adding a BufWriter around object-file writes, which fixed a specific regression on the 'coercions' rustc-perf benchmark.

**Use it when:**
- Local dev-loop cargo build/cargo check cycles where debug binaries are compiled and rerun repeatedly and compile latency matters more than runtime speed
- Projects already on Rust nightly, running on Linux, macOS, or x86_64 Windows
- Codebases that avoid heavy std::arch SIMD intrinsics and unwinding-based panic handling (or already build with -Cpanic=abort)
- Willing to opt in per-profile via Cargo.toml/.cargo/config.toml so only the debug profile uses cg_clif
- Crates that hit an unsupported feature can fall back to the default LLVM backend without any code change

**Skip it when:**
- Release/optimized builds -- cg_clif is not a target here and produces slower-running code than LLVM -O
- Code leaning on std::arch SIMD intrinsics beyond the partially-supported subset (std::simd portable SIMD does work fully)
- Programs that unwind on panic when targeting Windows or macOS -- unwinding support there is experimental and unsupported
- Crates with 'pathological' codegen shapes -- the Nov 2024 report notes a few secondary benchmarks still regress vs cg_llvm
- Anyone who needs stable (non-nightly) Rust, since it's only distributed for nightly via rustup

**Integration:** compiler backend, distributed as a rustup component and loaded via -Zcodegen-backend · none for the user; Cranelift is pulled in by the backend itself · Rust nightly (requires the unstable -Zcodegen-backend / codegen-backend cargo feature) · Linux x86-64/AArch64/RISC-V/s390x, macOS x86-64/AArch64, Windows x86-64 (fully tested per README matrix); FreeBSD and some Linux targets are unverified

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued siblings (zapcc, MIR/c2m, TinyCC) all target C/C++ toolchains; cg_clif is the only Rust-ecosystem entry here, so it's the pick whenever the baseline being replaced is rustc/cargo rather than gcc/clang.

**Gotchas:**
- -Cpanic=abort is enabled by default because stack unwinding is experimental and unsupported on Windows/macOS
- std::arch SIMD intrinsics are only partially supported; std::simd portable SIMD is fully supported
- 2020 measurements (issue #878) showed clean-incremental builds up to ~200% slower because compiled object files were not cached in the incremental cache (#760); the Nov 2024 report does not say whether this was fixed
- JIT mode requires all dependencies to be available as dynamic libraries and lacks incremental compilation, so it can be slower than normal AOT builds

**Status:** Actively maintained (commit as of 2026-09-23) and distributed as an official nightly-only rustup component, but still labeled experimental overall; MIT/Apache-2.0 dual-licensed and adopted by adding a build flag rather than vendoring a library.

[repo](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustc_codegen_cranelift) · [benchmark](https://bjorn3.github.io/2024/11/14/progress-report-nov-2024.html)

#### formatters-linters-lsps

##### Biome  `Rust`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust toolchain combining a formatter (97% Prettier-compatible) and linter (500+ rules) that replace ESLint and Prettier/dprint.

**Beats:** ESLint (linting); Prettier and dprint (formatting) — The only public numbers are Nov 2022 hyperfine runs on a MacBook Pro 13-inch M1 (2020) comparing Biome's Rome-era predecessor against Prettier, parallel-prettier/xargs -P prettier, and dprint for formatting (~25x, ~20x, ~20x, and 1.5-2x faster respectively, single-threaded ~7x), and against ESLint for linting (~15x faster, rules both tools support, no type-aware rules, single-threaded ~4x), plus a separate M1 Max 10-core run cited for a '100x faster than Prettier' figure. No compiler flags, tool versions, or raw output are given, and the benchmark/ directory that produced these numbers was deleted from main in commit 8e4ada5 (2026-05-13).

**How:** It's compiled Rust, avoiding Node.js/V8 startup and interpreter overhead. Formatting and linting run against one shared lossless CST (biome_rowan, a rowan-style Green/Red tree that preserves full trivia) instead of each tool doing its own parse. Biome's own benchmark notes say the linter batches rule matching against one semantic model and control-flow graph rather than running each rule as an independent AST visitor, and the CLI parallelizes file processing across threads (tunable via the BIOME_THREADS env var). The scanner also skips filesystem traversal into folders irrelevant to the current run when project-wide type rules are disabled.

**Use it when:**
- You already run Prettier (or dprint) + ESLint on JS/TS/JSON/CSS/GraphQL and want one faster CLI/LSP, bootstrapped from existing configs via `biome migrate`.
- Editor-in-the-loop formatting/linting on medium-large monorepos where ESLint's per-keystroke latency is the pain point — Biome's LSP targets interactive use.
- CI wants a fast cold full-repo check across JS/TS/CSS/GraphQL without needing type-aware rules.
- You want a self-contained native binary with no Node.js dependency for the CLI itself (the npm package just wraps a platform binary).
- You want broad out-of-the-box rule coverage (500+ rules pulled from ESLint/typescript-eslint/jsx-a11y/unicorn) without assembling an ESLint plugin stack.

**Skip it when:**
- You depend on ESLint plugins or custom rules with no Biome equivalent — `biome migrate eslint` only maps recognized rules (eslint, typescript, jsx-a11y, unicorn, jest), not arbitrary plugins.
- You need full type-aware lint parity with typescript-eslint: Biome's type-aware 'project domain' rules (noFloatingPromises, noUnresolvedImports, noImportCycles) are new in v2, opt-in, and docs cite performance dropping from ~800ms to ~2s per 2,000 files when enabled.
- You rely on incremental/cached formatting for large repos with few changed files — Biome has no incremental formatting like Prettier/dprint; every run is a cold run.
- You want to cite the headline speedup numbers as current: the published ~25x/~15x figures are Nov 2022 Rome-era hyperfine runs, never re-measured, and the benchmark/ code that produced them was deleted from main in May 2026.
- Your codebase has deeply parenthesized object expressions in arrow functions (`() => ({...})`) — a real regression made formatting 'dramatically slower' on that shape between 2.5.10 and 2.5.11 (GH #11747), a sign perf isn't uniformly stable release-to-release.

**Integration:** crate (Rust workspace of 100+ biome_* crates), distributed as a prebuilt native CLI binary via the @biomejs/biome npm package · none to run (self-contained native binary; npm install only adds one platform-specific optionalDependency binary, no JS deps). Building from source needs the Rust toolchain. · Rust edition 2024 (~1.85+) to build from source; via npm, Node.js >=14.21.3 is only the install mechanism, not required to run the binary · linux-x64/arm64 (glibc + musl), darwin-x64/arm64, win32-x64/arm64 (per npm optionalDependencies); also compiles to WASM for the online playground

**Vs siblings:** Pick Biome over Oxlint when you need one tool for both formatting and linting plus LSP/editor support and a Prettier-config migrator; Oxlint's README claims ~2x faster linting than Biome and 50-100x vs ESLint but is lint-only with no formatter. Ruff is the closest analog outside JS (Rust linter+formatter replacing Flake8+Black) if you're evaluating the pattern rather than a JS-specific tool.

**Gotchas:**
- Type-aware lint rules (project domain: noFloatingPromises, noUnresolvedImports, noImportCycles) are opt-in and materially slower — docs cite ~800ms to ~2s per 2,000 files when enabled, plus higher memory use.
- No incremental/cached formatting: every `biome format`/`check` run reformats cold, unlike Prettier/dprint — confirmed in Biome's own benchmark notes.
- Formatter hit a real perf cliff on large parenthesized object expressions in arrow functions, reported as 'dramatically slower' between 2.5.10 and 2.5.13 (GH #11747).
- Dual-licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0 per Cargo.toml/package.json, though GitHub's repo-level license detection reports just Apache-2.0.

**Status:** Actively maintained (pushed 2026-09-24, 25.9k stars, not archived); dual MIT/Apache-2.0, published as compiled binaries for every major OS/arch, so it's safe to adopt for day-to-day formatting/linting today — just don't cite the 2022 speedup numbers as current without re-benchmarking.

[repo](https://github.com/biomejs/biome) · [benchmark](https://github.com/biomejs/biome/blob/fdf8555f57dbb763f5dfcbe27be89814b2d0df0c/benchmark/README.md)

##### clangd-tidy  `Python`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

CLI wrapper around clangd that reports clang-tidy diagnostics much faster than standalone clang-tidy.

**Beats:** clang-tidy — The README's 'Comparison with clang-tidy' section states clangd-tidy is 'significantly faster than clang-tidy (over 10x in my experience)' when running the same checks over a codebase, because clangd only builds an AST from included headers where clang-tidy checks all headers. No benchmark script, target codebase, compiler flags, or hardware are given — it's the author's stated personal experience, not a reproducible measurement.

**How:** Standalone clang-tidy parses and checks the full AST of every included header for every translation unit, even though it suppresses warnings from headers by default. clangd instead builds and caches an AST scoped to what a file actually needs, the same incremental analysis it uses for live editor diagnostics, so clangd-tidy inherits that lighter-weight AST construction instead of clang-tidy's from-scratch per-file header checking.
