No other technique (caching, parallel dispatch beyond clangd's own worker pool, etc.) is described in the README or source.

**Use it when:**
- Running clang-tidy-style checks in CI on a C/C++ codebase where wall-clock time matters
- You already have clangd installed/configured and a working compile_commands.json
- You want per-file grouped diagnostics instead of clang-tidy's duplicated per-header warnings
- You want incremental linting of only changed lines via clangd-tidy-diff (e.g. gradual rollout of checks on a legacy codebase)
- You also want code-formatting checks (clang-format) folded into the same CI step (-f/--format)

**Skip it when:**
- You need --fix / automatic fixups; clangd-tidy has no fix-application support, only editor code actions
- You rely on clang-tidy checks that clangd's TidyProvider doesn't support; those are silently dropped, not reported as skipped
- Exact diagnostic parity with clang-tidy matters (there are open, acknowledged behavioral discrepancies, e.g. issues #7, #15, #16)
- You can't install/configure clangd in your CI image, or don't have a compile_commands.json
- You want a large, heavily-used, battle-tested tool; this is a small single-maintainer project (161 stars)

**Integration:** source-drop · clangd (external binary); Python 3.8+; attrs, cattrs, typing-extensions (auto-installed via pip); tqdm optional for progress bar · Python 3.8+; a clangd binary (version affects available .clangd diagnostics config, e.g. UnusedIncludes needs clangd-14+, MissingIncludes needs clangd-17+) · POSIX (per PyPI classifiers: Operating System :: POSIX); no Windows classifier listed

**Vs siblings:** Not directly comparable to the other sibling entries (Biome, Oxlint, Pyrefly, ty, Ruff), which target JS/TS or Python; clangd-tidy is the only C/C++ formatter-linter-LSP entry in this category so far, so 'no siblings catalogued yet' for its actual competitor set (clang-tidy variants).

**Gotchas:**
- Silently disables clang-tidy checks unsupported by clangd's TidyProvider (listed in LLVM's TidyProvider.cpp) rather than erroring or warning
- No --fix option; the README suggests using editor code actions instead since the tool targets CI, not local fix workflows
- Known behavioral discrepancies vs clang-tidy are tracked as open issues (#7, #15, #16), not resolved
- Default -j (clangd async workers) is 1, so out-of-the-box throughput depends on tuning -j for parallelism

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-02-09) and MIT-licensed, but a small, single-maintainer project (161 stars) — usability tagged 'copyable' rather than a heavyweight dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/lljbash/clangd-tidy) · [benchmark](https://github.com/lljbash/clangd-tidy#comparison-with-clang-tidy)

##### Ruff  `Rust`  `MIT`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust linter and formatter replacing Flake8, Black, isort, pyupgrade, and more with one fast CLI.

**Beats:** Flake8 (linting); Black (formatting); also compared to pycodestyle, pyflakes, pylint — CONTRIBUTING.md's reproducible hyperfine benchmark (Ruff release build vs. the CPython 3.10 tree, pinned tool versions, Python 3.11) shows Ruff at 294ms cold vs Flake8 12.26s (41.66x), pyflakes 15.79s (53.64x), pycodestyle 46.92s (159.43x), and autoflake 6.18s (20.98x) — but states no CPU model. The larger headline figures (~150x vs Flake8, ~60ms incremental re-lint) come from the founder's 2022 blog post on unspecified macOS hardware, not this repo benchmark; the Black formatting-speed claim appears only in the README, with no benchmark numbers given anywhere.

**How:** Written in Rust and shipped as a single native binary, it avoids the per-file Python interpreter and plugin-subprocess overhead that Flake8's plugin architecture incurs; rules are natively re-implemented in Rust rather than shelled out to separate Python checkers. It also has built-in result caching so unchanged files are skipped on incremental runs. CONTRIBUTING.md's own benchmark shows most of the incremental win comes from that cache: a cold lint of CPython takes ~294ms, a cached rerun ~48ms.

**Use it when:**
- Python 3 codebase already on Flake8 with few/no exotic plugins, run alongside a formatter
- Want one tool for both linting and Black-style formatting instead of two separate ones
- Large codebases or monorepos where whole-repo lint/format time matters in CI or pre-commit
- Need editor/LSP integration (VS Code and others via ruff_server) with fast on-save checks
- Want built-in autofix for import sorting, unused imports, and pyupgrade-style modernization in one pass

**Skip it when:**
- Team depends on specific Flake8 plugins Ruff hasn't re-implemented natively
- Need output byte-identical to Black on code that wasn't already Black-formatted (FAQ notes more deviation there)
- Need full Pylint parity; coverage is partial and some Pylint-style rule requests are still open
- Using `--extend-per-file-ignores` together with leading recursive glob patterns — open issue reports an extreme performance penalty (#8626)
- Autofixes for PERF401/PERF403 rules have open bug reports of making code slower in some cases (#21890, #21891) — review fixes before accepting

**Integration:** CLI binary (installed via pip/pipx/uv/cargo); source is a Rust crate workspace (crates/*) · none for the prebuilt binary (self-contained, no Python runtime required to run it) · Rust 1.96 (edition 2024) to build from source; prebuilt wheels declare Python >=3.7 as the package requirement · PyPI classifier lists 'OS Independent'; wheels are published for common platforms but no explicit CPU-architecture list was found this session

**Vs siblings:** No catalogued sibling targets Python lint/format specifically: Biome and Oxlint are the JS/TS equivalents (ESLint/Prettier), Pyrefly and ty are Python type-checkers (a different job than linting/formatting), and clangd-tidy is the C/C++ equivalent. Pick Ruff whenever the baseline being replaced is Flake8, Black, isort, or pylint on a Python codebase.

**Gotchas:**
- Formatting non-Black-formatted code produces more diffs than the near-100% match figure implies (FAQ)
- `--extend-per-file-ignores` combined with leading recursive glob patterns triggers an 'extreme performance penalty' (issue #8626, open)
- PERF401/PERF403 autofix suggestions have open bug reports of producing slower code in some cases (#21890, #21891)
- Ruff's linter and Black/ruff-format treat line-length enforcement differently, so E501 can still fire even with the formatter enabled

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-24, 49,764 stars, MIT license); copyable either as a pip-installed prebuilt binary or as a vendorable Rust crate workspace, so there's little build/toolchain risk for adopters.

[repo](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff) · [benchmark](https://notes.crmarsh.com/python-tooling-could-be-much-much-faster)

#### linkers

##### zld  `C++`  `MIT`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Drop-in fork of Apple's ld64 that speeds up incremental Xcode debug linking; archived, maintainer now recommends lld instead.

**Beats:** Apple ld (ld64) — First-party misc/benchmarks.md (with the full captured ld command lines) shows zld beating stock Apple ld64 on three real Xcode/Mach-O debug links on a 'high-end Mac desktop': Signal's iOS app binary 390ms->250ms (~1.6x), Firefox macOS's XUL framework 5.2s->2.20s (~2.4x), and Firefox iOS's Storage.framework 495ms->340ms (~1.5x), with similar percentage gains reported on a 2014 MacBook Pro. No specific CPU model, run count, or variance is given, and the exact Xcode/clang version used for the benchmark itself isn't stated (the captured ld invocations reference clang 11.0.0 and 9.0.1 runtime libs).

**How:** Replaces ld64's STL hash maps/sets with Abseil's Swiss Tables (open-addressing, SIMD-probed hash containers) for the linker's internal symbol/string tables. Parallelizes stages that ld64 runs serially, including library parsing, output-file writing, and sorting. Also caches and speeds up string hashing (hash caching plus a faster hash function) and persists some object/library-name metadata under /tmp/zld-... between runs to warm later links.

**Use it when:**
- Xcode, Bazel, or Cargo debug builds on macOS/iOS where a single ld64 link already takes >=500ms and faster edit-build-run loops matter
- Projects that must stay on Apple's own ld64 codebase for behavioral/stability reasons rather than switching linker families entirely
- Debug-only linking (not release, not App Store archive builds) where a small correctness/regression risk is acceptable
- Teams that can pin to a matching Xcode/ld64 vintage (repo's last activity is 2023, roughly Xcode 13-14 era) and won't chase newer toolchains
- x86_64 or arm64 Xcode debug targets where the arm64_32/Mac Catalyst fallback gap (see gotchas) doesn't apply

**Skip it when:**
- Any release, App Store, or otherwise correctness-critical build -- the README states it is untested/unintended for that
- Newer Xcode/ld64 versions past 2023: repo is archived (last commit 2023-02-15), so toolchain drift bugs like the Xcode 14 undefined `_objc_msgSend$...` selector-stub issue (#113, #125) won't be fixed
- Apple Silicon (M1) hosts, where users reported SIGKILL crashes and codesigning issues with certain Rust/Cargo link setups (#110, referencing #85)
- arm64_32 or Mac Catalyst link targets: zld knows it has issues there and silently falls back to the real ld unless you also pass `-zld_original_ld_path`
- New projects generally: the maintainer's own 2022 RFC (#112) says lld is faster and more reproducible and is what they'd pick today; the README's top line now tells readers to use lld instead

**Integration:** source-drop · cmake (build-time); vendors Abseil (for Swiss Tables) and Apple's ld64/corecrypto sources in-tree; requires the full Xcode.app (not just Command Line Tools) to build and run · macOS with a full Xcode install; built via `make`/cmake; benchmark and issue history point to an Xcode 13-14 / clang 11.0.0 / ld64 vintage, unmaintained since 2023-02-15 · macOS hosts only (Intel and Apple Silicon), producing Mach-O output for macOS/iOS/watchOS/tvOS targets; not applicable to Linux/Windows/GNU/MSVC toolchains

**Vs siblings:** mold and Wild are ELF/Linux linkers competing with lld; neither links Mach-O/Xcode debug builds, so they aren't substitutes for zld's use case. Pick zld over them only when the job is specifically Xcode/Bazel/Cargo debug-linking on macOS/iOS -- and even then, the maintainer's own RFC and the archived README both point to lld as the better current choice for that same job.

**Gotchas:**
- Without also passing -Wl,-zld_original_ld_path,<real ld>, zld silently falls back to Apple's stock linker for cases it knows are broken (arm64_32, Mac Catalyst) with no warning
- Needs the full Xcode.app installed, not just Xcode Command Line Tools, or builds/runs fail (#106, #109)
- Caches metadata under /tmp/zld-...; README says to run a link twice before judging speedup because the first run pays cold-cache cost
- Reported SIGKILL/codesigning crashes on Apple Silicon with some Rust+Cargo configurations (#110, #85), and an Xcode 14 undefined-symbol bug with ObjC selector stubs (#113, #125)

**Status:** Archived since 2023-02-15 (MIT license, 1,191 stars); the README's own top line now says to use lld instead, echoing the maintainer's 2022 'Future of zld' RFC (#112) that lld is faster, more reproducible, and what they'd choose for a new project today.

[repo](https://github.com/michaeleisel/zld) · [benchmark](https://github.com/michaeleisel/zld/blob/master/misc/benchmarks.md)

#### preprocessors-and-codegen

##### FlatBuffers  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Zero-copy binary serialization with schema-generated accessors; reads fields in place without unpacking, unlike protoc.

**Beats:** protoc — FlatBuffers's own C++ benchmark page (docs/source/benchmarks.md) reports, per 1M iterations on a ~10-object struct (array, 4 strings, mixed int/float scalars): Decode+Traverse+Dealloc 0.08s (FlatBuffers binary) vs 302s (Protocol Buffers LITE C++ runtime from protoc), ~3775x, and Encode 3.2s vs 185s, ~58x. Run on 'Windows 7 64bit' with no compiler, flags, or CPU model stated.

**How:** Tables are encoded as offset-linked vtables and structs as fixed, aligned inline scalar layouts, so field access is pointer arithmetic through the received buffer rather than a parse pass — no intermediate object graph is allocated on decode (0 bytes/blocks reported vs Protobuf LITE's 760B/20 blocks in the project's own benchmark). `FlatBufferBuilder` constructs buffers back-to-front to avoid backpatching offsets during encode. There's an optional slower object API (`--gen-object-api`) that unpacks into STL containers, but the default zero-copy path is what produces the measured speedup.

**Use it when:**
- Game engines or real-time systems reading many small/medium structured messages per frame (scene data, network packets) where allocation-free decode matters
- Read-many, build-once workloads: mmap'd assets, IPC payloads, or config blobs accessed repeatedly after being written once
- Cross-language data exchange needing schema-driven forward/backward field compatibility without adopting full gRPC/protobuf tooling
- Memory-constrained platforms (mobile, embedded) where avoiding a fully parsed object graph saves RAM
- You control both producer and consumer and can regenerate code from `.fbs` schemas as part of your build

**Skip it when:**
- Data arrives from an untrusted source and you don't run flatbuffers::Verifier first — direct field access does no bounds checking on malformed offsets
- You need protobuf's broader ecosystem (gRPC-first tooling, dynamic/reflective message manipulation, established schema registries) with minimal migration cost
- Wire size is the priority over decode speed: FlatBuffers's own benchmark shows its binary format larger than Protobuf's for the same object (344B vs 228B)
- You need a fully mutable object graph by default — that requires the object API, which unpacks the tree and gives up most of the zero-copy advantage
- Team is unfamiliar with offset/vtable-based wire formats and wants protobuf's simpler 'parse into a plain object' mental model

**Integration:** header-only · none for the core C++ runtime (all headers under include/flatbuffers); optional grpc.h integration needs gRPC if used · C++11 (README: works on 'any [platform] with a recent C++ compiler (C++ 11 and newer)'); CMake exposes an optional C++17 test target, not a runtime requirement · Windows, macOS, Linux, Android per README, plus 'any others with a recent C++ compiler'; no architecture-specific (SIMD/AVX) requirement found in headers

**Vs siblings:** Pick FlatBuffers over RapidProto, Zserio, or vtprotobuf when you want true zero-copy field access with no unpack step at all — those alternatives still build or touch a parsed object on decode, just cheaper than stock protoc. Pick one of them instead if you must stay on the actual Protobuf wire format/schema/gRPC ecosystem while cutting decode cost.

**Gotchas:**
- Direct field access skips validation; run flatbuffers::Verifier (include/flatbuffers/verifier.h) before trusting a buffer from an untrusted source, or bad offsets can read out of bounds
- Accessors return pointers into the original buffer, not owned copies — the backing buffer must outlive every object/string pointer you keep
- The convenient, fully mutable object API (--gen-object-api) unpacks the whole tree into STL containers, forfeiting most of the zero-copy speed this entry is cataloged for
- The wire format carries no self-describing type tag/version — a reader must already know the schema (or use the separate reflection API) to interpret a buffer

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-14, 26.5k stars, used at Google, Unity, Facebook, and many game engines), Apache-2.0 and copyable; but the specific protobuf-comparison benchmark code lived in a now-deleted `benchmarks` git branch and isn't reproducible today, so the >3000x decode figure should be read skeptically (likely an unoptimized/debug protobuf build) even though the library's own speed reputation is well established elsewhere.

[repo](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers) · [benchmark](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/blob/master/docs/source/benchmarks.md)

##### RapidProto  `C++`  `Apache-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Header-only codegen protobuf decoder for C++: arena and streaming models beating protoc's Arena decode and protozero.

**Beats:** protoc — On the project's own in-repo harness (tests/bench.py), decoding a 2000-record mixed Dataset (strings, nested/repeated messages, packed scalars) serialized by protoc, the arena decoder ran ~7x protoc+google::protobuf::Arena's throughput at 0.49x its peak payload memory on g++-13 (~6x on clang++-20), and the streaming decoder ran ~12x protoc+Arena and ~1.8x protozero; on protobuf's own google_message1/2 corpora and a 20MB OSM PBF extract the arena/streaming decoders beat protoc's protobuf-layer throughput by roughly 28-155% depending on payload shape. All figures use protobuf 4.25.3, -O3 -DNDEBUG; no CPU model is documented, only 'a quiesced box' with SMT/turbo off and core pinning.

**How:** Per docs/optimizations.md, the gains stack from compile-time specialization: borrowed string_view fields instead of copies, packed-array pre-sizing (a bulk memcpy for fixed-width packed fields, a length-bounded allocation for varint arrays), forced full inlining of the wire-read call tree (RP_FLATTEN), a fused single-bounds-check tag read, SWAR (SIMD-within-a-register) 64-bit varint kernels that decode multiple bytes' continuation bits per branch instead of one byte at a time, a one-byte dispatch hub for low field numbers, and field-order threading that jumps straight to the next expected field's label when fields arrive in ascending wire order (protoc's own emission order). Together these moved the arena decoder from 2.4x protoc to 6-7x protoc on the project's mixed Dataset benchmark.

**Use it when:**
- Hot decode path for schemas you can regenerate ahead of time via codegen (not reflection-based), where protoc+Arena decode throughput or peak memory is the bottleneck
- Read-mostly consumption of a message tree needing random/repeated accessor access (arena model), e.g. a mixed record with strings, nested/repeated messages, packed scalars
- Extracting a handful of fields or forwarding data without materializing objects (streaming model) — zero allocation, faster than protozero on most shapes
- Input strings/bytes can be safely borrowed as views into a buffer you keep alive (or you accept the cost of decode_owned for a self-contained handle)
- Linux/macOS/Windows C++17 projects on GCC/Clang/AppleClang/MSVC that can add a header-only generated decoder without a new link dependency

**Skip it when:**
- You need to serialize, mutate, or produce protobuf messages — RapidProto is decode-only; keep protoc for the write path
- You need real closed-enum semantics or strict proto3 string UTF-8 validation — RapidProto decodes all enums open and does not validate UTF-8 (part of where its speed margin over protoc comes from)
- You rely on protobuf's normal merge behavior for a repeated singular sub-message on the wire — the arena decoder rejects the buffer (RepeatedSingularMessage) instead of merging it
- You decode large packed scalar arrays mainly through the streaming model — it is slower than protozero there since a callback can't batch a bulk store; use the arena model for that shape
- The project is 3 stars, about three months old (created 2026-06-28), with first-party-only benchmarks that don't state a CPU model — weigh that immaturity against protoc for anything load-bearing today

**Integration:** header-only · none (generated headers are self-contained; rapidprotoc itself needs only a C++17 toolchain to build, or use a prebuilt release binary) · C++17; GCC, Clang (incl. AppleClang), or MSVC — CI/benchmarks use g++-13 and clang++-20 · Linux, macOS, Windows (all three CI-covered); no documented CPU-architecture requirement (SWAR only, no SIMD intrinsics)

**Vs siblings:** Pick RapidProto over Zserio or vtprotobuf when you're staying on the .proto/protoc ecosystem but want a much larger raw C++ decode throughput and memory win than Zserio's ~1.17-1.2x over protoc, and can accept a narrower, decode-only, C++-only tool (vtprotobuf targets Go). Pick FlatBuffers instead when you can drop the protobuf wire format entirely for true zero-copy access with no decode step at all.

**Gotchas:**
- Arena tree strings/bytes/raw payloads are borrowed views into the input buffer: the tree is valid only while both the Arena and the input outlive it, unless you use decode_owned
- A duplicate singular sub-message field on the wire is rejected outright (ArenaDecodeError::RepeatedSingularMessage), not merged the way protoc merges two concatenated messages
- Enums always decode open, even proto2/editions-CLOSED enums — an unrecognized value arrives as a raw integer instead of routing to unknown fields
- Recursion-depth guards against pathological nesting are sized for an 8MB stack; Windows defaults to a 1MB stack, so untrusted deeply-nested input needs a larger linked stack (/STACK:8388608) to stay safely rejecting

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-09-14) and Apache-2.0-licensed, but a brand-new, 3-star project (created 2026-06-28) with no independent benchmark or adoption track record yet; it is copyable/vendorable since the consumer-facing output is generated header-only code, but treat the maturity as early.

[repo](https://github.com/VeaaC/rapidproto) · [benchmark](https://github.com/VeaaC/rapidproto/blob/main/docs/benchmarks.md)

##### vtprotobuf (protoc-gen-go-vtproto)  `Go`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

protoc plugin generating reflection-free Marshal/Unmarshal/Size/Equal/Clone helpers for Go protobuf APIv2; ~1.7x faster unmarshal than stock protoc-gen-go.

**Beats:** protoc — Per the author's 2021 Vitess blog post (Vicent Marti), a synthetic VReplication stress test replicating a large MySQL table between keyspaces measured 7.17 CPU-seconds of unmarshal overhead with stock protoc-gen-go (APIv2) vs 4.15 CPU-seconds with vtprotobuf's UnmarshalVT (~1.7x), falling to 0.63 CPU-seconds (~11x) when vtprotobuf's generated memory pooling is also used; the post gives no hardware, Go version, or compiler flags, and the repo ships no benchmark code to reproduce the numbers.

**How:** All (de)serialization logic is fully unrolled per-field at codegen time (ported from gogo/protobuf's approach to the APIv2 API), so there is no reflection walk over the message descriptor at runtime. SizeVT precomputes the exact encoded size so MarshalVT allocates its output buffer once. UnmarshalVTUnsafe casts wire bytes directly into string/[]byte fields instead of copying them. The optional generated sync.Pool-backed object pools (ResetVT/ReturnToVTPool/FromVTPool) let callers reuse whole message structs across unmarshal calls, avoiding allocation entirely, which is where most of the reported speedup comes from.

**Use it when:**
- Go services already on google.golang.org/protobuf (APIv2) with (de)serialization visible as CPU cost in profiles (RPC hot paths, replication/streaming row processing).
- gRPC, DRPC, or Twirp services that can install vtprotobuf's provided codec so all messages benefit without touching call sites.
- Teams that can explicitly opt into memory pooling per message type and manage single-owner reuse lifetime carefully, where most of the >10x gain reported by the author lives.
- Want reflection-free CloneVT/EqualVT/SizeVT even without wiring the whole RPC path.
- Comfortable checking in generated *_vtproto.pb.go files as part of the normal protoc build step.

**Skip it when:**
- Still generating APIv1/gogo code: vtprotobuf targets APIv2 only and is explicitly not compatible with APIv1-generated code per the README.
- Can't tolerate unsafe byte aliasing: UnmarshalVTUnsafe pins the entire input buffer alive via GC for the life of any string/bytes field taken from the message (open issue #167), which can silently balloon retained memory if a field is cached long-term.
- Messages are small or short-lived: the author's own post notes many protobuf messages are too small for pooling to help, and the ~1.7x codegen-only gain (no pooling) is the realistic floor.
- Need pooling correctness for repeated fields, maps, or nested messages: multiple open issues report pooled ResetVT/ReturnToVTPool bugs with repeated fields (#92) and note pooling only reaches the outer message, not nested children (#162, 'Recursive Pool Usage').
- Want a single drop-in replacement for proto.Marshal/Unmarshal with zero call-site changes and no RPC codec registration step.

**Integration:** source-drop · google.golang.org/protobuf (APIv2) required; optional integration deps on google.golang.org/grpc, storj.io/drpc, or github.com/twitchtv/twirp for the provided codecs · go.mod pins `go 1.26.4` to build the plugin/runtime as of the last commit; the `unique` string-interning field option additionally needs Go 1.23+ in consumer code · any (pure Go, no architecture-specific code in the repo tree)

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued siblings (RapidProto, Zserio, FlatBuffers) are all C++ alternatives to protoc's C++ output; pick vtprotobuf instead whenever the stack is Go on google.golang.org/protobuf APIv2, since it optimizes protoc's existing Go codegen and wire format rather than replacing either.

**Gotchas:**
- UnmarshalVTUnsafe keeps the whole input wire buffer alive via GC for as long as any string/bytes field from the message is reachable (unsafe.String aliasing); documented as an open gap in issue #167, not yet in the README.
- UnmarshalVT on a non-zeroed message behaves like proto.Merge rather than a fresh Unmarshal; call Reset() first or use a freshly allocated message.
- Memory pooling is opt-in per message (`option (vtproto.mempool)` or `--go-vtproto_opt=pool=...`) and, as of issue #162, only pools the outer message — nested/child messages are still freshly allocated on each unmarshal.
- Returning a pooled repeated-field message has open correctness bugs (issue #92, generated ResetVT); verify pool behavior with your own message shapes before relying on it in production.

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-07-02, 1118 stars, used in production by Vitess/PlanetScale and widely adopted in the Go gRPC ecosystem); BSD-3-Clause and small enough to vendor, but 'copyable' here means installing the plugin and wiring it into your protoc invocation, not literally copying a header.

[repo](https://github.com/planetscale/vtprotobuf) · [benchmark](https://vitess.io/blog/2021-06-03-a-new-protobuf-generator-for-go/)

##### Zserio  `C++`  `BSD-3-Clause`  `active`  `Tier C`

Own-IDL C++/Java/Python serialization framework; bit-packed decode 1.2x-2.6x faster than protoc.

**Beats:** protoc — Per-decode time (protobuf ParseFromString vs zserio read, pre-serialized blob, JSON load/serialize untimed) on 4 schemas, gcc 11.3.0 CMake-Release build, Intel i7-9850H/Linux Mint 21.1: Zserio beat protoc-generated C++ by 1.17x-2.63x (addressbook 1.478 vs 1.731ms, apollo 0.244 vs 0.641ms, carsales 1.374 vs 2.053ms, simpletrace 0.221 vs 0.386ms); byte-aligned variants reached 2.05x and 2.22x. Benchmark is first-party (same org as Zserio, 6-star companion repo), evidence tier C.

**How:** Zserio packs fields at the bit level rather than byte level, and its default schemas carry no per-field tag IDs or explicit length prefixes the way protobuf's wire format does, so there is less to scan per field during decode. Byte-aligning fields (the '_align' schema variants) trades blob size for speed by removing bit-shift work, cutting decode time roughly another 40-45% versus the default schema on addressbook and carsales in this benchmark. No SIMD or algorithmic trick is documented; the win is wire-format layout, not a decode algorithm.

**Use it when:**
- Designing a new wire format from scratch where blob size matters as much as decode speed
- Multi-language C++/Java/Python project willing to author .zs schemas instead of .proto
- Need built-in SQLite table serialization, JSON debug export, or generic reflection/services without hand-rolling them
- Functional-safety-conscious C++ codebase: C++11 runtime, >600 unit tests, ASan/UBSan clean, 99% line coverage
- Deserialize-heavy workloads (parse once, read many) where a 1.2x-2.6x per-decode win compounds

**Skip it when:**
- Already invested in protobuf schemas, tooling, or cross-org interop; migration cost likely exceeds the modest measured speedup
- Need protobuf-style forward/backward field compatibility; Zserio's compactness comes partly from dropping field IDs and lengths
- Team can't add a Java-based external compiler step (zserio.jar) to the build
- Need platforms beyond 64/32-bit Linux and 64-bit Windows; macOS/ARM are not in the stated Supported Platforms list
- Want a larger, independently verified speedup: siblings RapidProto (~7x) and vtprotobuf (~1.7x) show bigger measured wins over protoc

**Integration:** source-drop · none for the C++ runtime itself; bundled SQLite3 only if using the SQL-database extension; Java (JRE) needed at build time to run the zserio.jar code generator, not at runtime · C++11; gcc 7.5.0+ (11.4.0/7.5.0 tested), clang 11.0.0+ (14.0.6/21.1.8 tested), MinGW 7.5.0+, MSVC 2017+; CMake 3.15+ if using the bundled CMake helper · 64-bit Linux, 32-bit Linux, 64-bit Windows per README's Supported Platforms list; macOS/ARM not stated

**Vs siblings:** Pick Zserio when you want a full schema framework (SQLite mapping, JSON debug strings, services/pub-sub, one schema for C++/Java/Python) and can move off .proto. Pick RapidProto or vtprotobuf instead if you must keep .proto files and want a bigger measured decode speedup with less schema-language lock-in.

**Gotchas:**
- Byte-aligned (_align) and delta-packed (_packed) schema variants trade blob size against decode speed in opposite directions; pick per workload
- Compact wire format omits field tags/lengths, so schema-evolution/compatibility rules differ sharply from protobuf's
- Code generated by the zserio compiler inherits the license of the input .zs schema, separate from the BSD-3-Clause runtime license
- Open issue #577 'Consider to optimize C++ serialization performance' (still open) indicates maintainers see further headroom

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-09-17, frequent releases); BSD-3-Clause runtime, with generated code separately licensed under the input schema's license.

[repo](https://github.com/ndsev/zserio) · [benchmark](https://github.com/ndsev/zserio-protobuf-benchmarks)

## Copyleft

### networking-and-servers

#### event-loops-io

##### uring_exec  `C++`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only liburing adapter for stdexec (std::execution) senders; beats Asio's io_uring backend on loopback TCP ping-pong.

**Beats:** Boost.Asio (io_uring backend) — Loopback TCP ping-pong on one AMD 5800H box (Linux 6.4.8, GCC 13.2 -O3, 16 KiB blocks, 5 s): a uring_exec echo server beat an Asio coroutine echo server built with ASIO_HAS_IO_URING and ASIO_DISABLE_EPOLL by 1.27x-3.46x across 2/4/8 threads and 10/100/1000 sessions (e.g. 4 threads/1000 sessions: 4.411 vs 1.275 GiB/s). The client was uring_exec's own ping in both cases, and there was one run per cell with no variance reported. A newer 10 s table in benchmarks/README adds Asio on epoll, which beats uring_exec at 10-100 sessions with 2+ threads.

**Known shortcoming:** Beats Asio's io_uring backend (1.27-3.46x) but Asio on its default epoll backend beats uring_exec at low session counts (4 threads/100 sessions: 8.744 vs 3.226 GiB/s); the author says io_uring cannot beat epoll on the current kernel and calls the project effectively archived since 2025.

**Known shortcoming:** Loopback benchmark with uring_exec's own client; its run() loop busy-polls (keeps a core busy when idle) while Asio threads block; single runs, no variance. Against Asio on epoll it loses in 5 of 6 rows at 10-100 sessions with 2-8 threads (epoll 1.4-3.2x faster). No TLS or multishot/zero-copy; noexcept constructor terminates if io_uring is unavailable.

**How:** Each thread that calls run() lazily gets its own thread-local io_uring ring, created with IORING_SETUP_SINGLE_ISSUER and IORING_SETUP_COOP_TASKRUN, and all rings share one kernel worker pool through IORING_SETUP_ATTACH_WQ. Operation states are immovable and intrusive, with a per-object vtable for type erasure, and the CQE user_data points straight at them, so the library itself does no per-I/O heap allocation. Work scheduled from other threads goes through lock-free CAS intrusive queues split into 16 buckets that run threads drain by round-robin plus random pick. The default run loop submits without blocking, harvests completions in batches with io_uring_peek_batch_cqe (64 per batch, up to 512 per step) and calls yield() when idle instead of sleeping in the kernel. The author gives no explanation of why this beats Asio.

**Use it when:**
- Your code base already uses stdexec/P2300 senders and you want Linux socket or file I/O as composable senders with stop-token cancellation and when_any timeouts.
- Many concurrent TCP connections (1,000-100,000) served by several threads on one box. The author's newer table has it beating Asio epoll there, e.g. 8 threads/10,000 sessions 6.662 vs 2.118 GiB/s.
- A single-threaded event loop: at 1 thread it beat both Asio backends at every session count in the author's table (e.g. 100 sessions: 4.026 vs 3.600 io_uring, 3.052 epoll GiB/s).
- You can give the event loop dedicated cores, because the default run loop polls and yields rather than blocking.
- As a small, readable reference (about 1,600 lines of headers) for mapping io_uring onto sender/receiver before writing your own.

**Skip it when:**
- Few connections spread over several threads. In 5 of the 6 rows with 10-100 sessions and 2-8 threads, Asio's default epoll backend was 1.4-3.2x faster in the author's own table (4 threads/100 sessions: 8.744 vs 3.226 GiB/s), and the author says io_uring cannot beat epoll on the current kernel.
- Production services that need a maintained dependency: the README calls it effectively archived since 2025, there is one author, the repo has only two test files and no CI config, and the build follows stdexec main, whose upstream changes have broken compilation (issue #2, the 2026-05 fix commit, a ~10x compile-time regression noted for ping_when_any).
- You need TLS, DNS or higher-level socket types. The API is raw file descriptors, and the author says in issue #3 that async OpenSSL is out of scope (workarounds: poll-based SSL or kTLS).
- You want advanced io_uring features: the sender list has no multishot accept/recv, provided buffer rings, registered files/buffers or zero-copy send.
- Non-Linux targets, kernels older than about 6.1 (the recommended minimum), or environments where io_uring is disabled. Also workloads that cancel every I/O, since per-operation cancellation adds overhead according to the benchmarks README.

**Integration:** header-only · stdexec (NVIDIA, tracked at main), liburing (link -luring, recent enough for io_uring_prep_futex_wait/bind), pthread; Asio only for the comparison benchmark · C++20; benchmarked with GCC 13.2; the benchmarks README says Clang also works (there is a clang-19 workaround commit) · Linux only (io_uring), kernel 6.1+ recommended; architecture support not documented (benchmarked on x86-64 AMD 5800H)

**Vs siblings:** Pick uring_exec when you specifically want io_uring exposed as std::execution senders. For a maintained C++20-coroutine io_uring runtime that aims to cover most io_uring features and also posts wins over epoll and Asio, Condy is the safer choice. At low connection counts, stock Asio on epoll (or PhotonLibOS, which edges out boost::asio in its own ping-pong) is faster than uring_exec according to the author's own data.

**Gotchas:**
- The default run() never blocks in the kernel. It calls io_uring_submit without waiting, peeks the CQ and calls std::this_thread::yield() when nothing moved, so each run thread keeps a core busy even when idle. run_policy{.waitable=true} switches to io_uring_submit_and_wait.
- An I/O sender submits its SQE to the thread-local ring of whichever thread calls start(). Hop onto the scheduler first (stdexec::schedule or starts_on, as every example does), or the operation sits in a ring that no run() loop drains.
- Thread-local rings are keyed by the io_uring_exec constructor's call site through a template lambda parameter. The header warns that constructing it repeatedly at one site (e.g. in a loop) reuses the same per-thread ring, so treat it as a long-lived singleton. The constructor is noexcept, but ring setup throws std::system_error on failure, which means std::terminate if io_uring is unavailable.
- async_read/async_write default to offset 0, so on a seekable file every call hits byte 0 unless you pass an offset. Errors arrive as set_error(exception_ptr to std::system_error), and -ECANCELED arrives as set_stopped.

**Status:** The author declares it effectively archived since 2025 (the last commit, 2026-05-01, only follows stdexec API renames); it is header-only and MPL-2.0, so it is easy to vendor, but you inherit stdexec churn yourself.

[repo](https://github.com/Caturra000/uring_exec) · [benchmark](https://github.com/Caturra000/uring_exec/blob/master/README.md)

#### http-servers-frameworks

##### Lwan  `C`  `GPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

C HTTP/1.1 server and embeddable library; topped TechEmpower Round 10 JSON at ~5.8x Go net/http's throughput.

**Beats:** Go net/http — TechEmpower Round 10 (April 2015), Peak Hosting dual-Xeon E5 v2 servers (40 hyperthreads) over 10 GbE, JSON-serialization test: Lwan rev 49607add (CMake Release, compiler not stated) peaked at 2,200,066 req/s at 256 connections, #1 of 145, versus 379,662 req/s for TFB's Go 1.4.2 net/http + encoding/json entry (5.8x); the ratio was 1.7x at 8 connections. In the same round's plaintext test the gap was ~2.6x (2,075,046 vs 799,052 req/s, Lwan #7, far behind ULib's 6.9M), and Lwan's JSON handler then built a ccan/json DOM per request, so the win comes from the server core, not from JSON encoding.

**Known shortcoming:** The evidence is TechEmpower Round 10 (2015, Go 1.4.2 baseline), about 5.8x on JSON; no recent independent rounds are cited. No compiler or exact CPU model stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Evidence is TechEmpower Round 10 (April 2015, Go 1.4.2); the maintainer reported a big regression in later preview rounds (#291). The 5.8x is the 256-connection best case (1.7x at 8, 2.6x at 32); plaintext in the same round is ~2.6x. September 2026 fixed an out-of-bounds read in the URL decoder (#380), request desynchronization via stale pipelining state (#381, #382) and a WebSocket worker spin (#383); lost/stuck socket reports still open. HTTP/1.x only, TLS experimental (Linux, TLS 1.2), no chunked uploads, 40 KB default body cap, >4 KB pipelined requests fail (#218). Default CMake build is Debug; Release uses -march=native; no coroutine stack guard page. GPL-2.0-or-later.

**How:** One worker thread per online CPU, pinned using the sysfs thread_siblings topology, each with its own SO_REUSEPORT listening socket (with a CBPF steering filter where available) and its own edge-triggered epoll set; connection state lives in one preallocated array indexed by file descriptor. Every connection runs in a stackful coroutine switched by a hand-written x86-64/aarch64 swapcontext that skips floating-point registers and the signal mask, so handlers read like blocking code with no per-request thread or callback chain. The request parser dispatches on methods and headers by loading 2/4/8 bytes as integers (`STRING_SWITCH`), finds line ends with memchr/memmem, and decodes URLs with SSE/SWAR; idle keep-alive connections expire through a timeout queue driven by a timer wheel. Release builds add LTO and `-march=native`.

**Use it when:**
- Small, CPU-cheap HTTP/1.1 responses (JSON, plaintext, cached small files) at high connection counts, where per-request server overhead dominates; in Round 10 its lead over Go net/http grew from 1.7x at 8 connections to 5.8x at 256.
- Linux x86-64 or aarch64 hosts where you build from source for the target CPU and want one pinned worker per core.
- Embedding an HTTP endpoint in a C program via liblwan without a C++ runtime or an external event library.
- Config-only static file or Lua serving: files under 16 KiB are mmap-cached with precompressed deflate/gzip/Brotli/zstd variants, and larger files go out via sendfile.
- A fast backend stub or load target for benchmarking proxies and gateways (the README lists Kong, KrakenD and Istio using it this way).

**Skip it when:**
- You need HTTP/2 or HTTP/3: Lwan is HTTP/1.x only (issue #17, open since 2014).
- You need production TLS: TLS is marked experimental, works only on Linux through kTLS (tls.ko plus mbedTLS), and supports TLSv1.2 only; the README suggests a separate terminator such as Hitch.
- Uploads without Content-Length or of large size: a request body with no Content-Length gets 400 (no chunked request bodies), POST/PUT bodies are capped at 40,960 bytes by default, and issue #218 (open) reports pipelined requests over 4 KB failing.
- An internet-facing edge that needs a hardened parser: September 2026 reports fixed request desynchronization via stale pipelined state (#381, #382), a WebSocket-FIN busy-spin that pinned a worker (#383), and an 8-byte out-of-bounds read in the SWAR URL decoder (#380); lost/stuck socket reports #348 and #353 remain open.
- Proprietary software that ships the binary: Lwan is GPL-2.0-or-later, so distributing a program linked with liblwan carries GPL obligations (the README notes that only serving over HTTP does not).

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (liblwan-static / liblwan.so with installed headers), or the standalone `lwan` server binary · Required: CMake 3.20+ (CMakeLists.txt; the README still says 2.8) and one of zlib, zlib-ng or libdeflate. Optional: Lua 5.4, Brotli, zstd, mbedTLS (kTLS), mimalloc/jemalloc/tcmalloc, SQLite and MariaDB client (samples only); libucontext on architectures other than x86-64/aarch64. · C compiler that accepts -std=gnu11 (GCC or Clang; uses GNU extensions, inline assembly and linker sections) · Linux x86-64 is primary (CI build, tests, static analysis, OSS-Fuzz); FreeBSD and OpenBSD x86-64 build (epoll emulated on kqueue); aarch64 has a native context switch; other CPUs fall back to libucontext, which fails on Apple Silicon macOS (issue #366). Windows not documented.

**Vs siblings:** Pick Lwan over Drogon, Crow, Oat++, CWIST or Agoo-C when you want a pure-C HTTP/1.1 server with the widest measured margin over Go net/http (5.8x in TFB JSON versus ~1.5x for Crow in the catalog), and GPL plus no HTTP/2 is acceptable. If you need HTTP/2 or production TLS, Lwan is the wrong choice; look at H2O or a C++ framework instead.

**Gotchas:**
- The default CMake build type is Debug, which logs every request while holding a lock; benchmark only with -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release.
- Release builds default to -march=native/-mtune=native (MTUNE_NATIVE=ON), so a binary can fail on other CPUs; pass -DMTUNE_NATIVE=OFF when packaging.
- Coroutine stacks are fixed-size (4x SIGSTKSZ, 8x with Brotli, page-rounded) and in release builds come from the heap with no guard page, so deep recursion or large stack buffers in handlers can silently overflow (see issue #130).
- At startup Lwan raises RLIMIT_NOFILE and preallocates max_file_descriptors (default 524288) x sizeof(struct lwan_connection); max_file_descriptors must be at least 10x threads. A crash when threads < online CPUs was fixed only on 2026-09-18.

**Status:** Active (last commit 2026-09-22; latest tag v0.7, June 2025; September 2026 security reports were fixed within days), GPL-2.0-or-later, built from source with CMake or pulled as GHCR container images and Alpine/Arch/NixOS packages.

[repo](https://github.com/lpereira/lwan) · [benchmark](https://www.techempower.com/benchmarks/results/round10/peak.json)

#### tls

##### wolfSSL  `C`  `GPL-3.0 (the LICENSING file lets certain listed projects, e.g. MariaDB and OpenVPN, use it under GPL-2.0 instead)`  `active`  `Tier B`

Embedded-first C TLS 1.3 library, not an OpenSSL fork, that beat every OpenSSL version in HAProxy's 64-core Graviton4 tests.

**Beats:** OpenSSL — HAProxy Technologies ran HAProxy 3.1-dev1 on a 64-core Graviton4 (AWS r8g.16xlarge, gcc 11.4, mid-2024) with wolfSSL 5.7.0 and with OpenSSL 1.1.1w, 3.0.x and 3.1-3.4-dev. At 64 threads wolfSSL handled 59.7k full RSA handshakes/s vs 48.3k for 1.1.1w, ~43k for 3.1+ and ~21k for 3.0.x, and ~150k end-to-end ticket resumptions/s vs 17.8k (1.1.1w with pthread locks), 23-28k (3.1+) and 1.6-3.7k (3.0.x). It was second to AWS-LC in both tests, and neither wolfSSL's build flags nor the test harness were published.

**Known shortcoming:** GPL-3.0 (commercial licence otherwise), so not freely copyable into proprietary code. Test scripts and flags for the HAProxy benchmark unpublished.

**Known shortcoming:** Benchmarked on 5.7.0 (mid-2024) with unpublished configure flags; a plain ./configure leaves the SP and CPU assembly off, and --enable-haproxy is not implied by distro builds. Use >= 5.9.4 for three High-severity certificate-verification CVEs (one widened in OpenSSL-compatible builds); open ASan use-after-free with HAProxy's test suite (#10123). Only ticket resumption was measured; session-ID resumption uses a global cache under one rwlock. AWS-LC beat it in both tests.

**How:** Public-key math runs on wolfCrypt's 'SP' (single-precision) backend. This is generated code with a fixed size per key length (2048-bit RSA is 32 x 64-bit words) that does Karatsuba multiplication and Montgomery reduction in inline AArch64/x86-64 assembly (sp_arm64.c alone is ~7 MB). It is paired with ARMv8 Crypto Extension/NEON and AES-NI/AVX2/AVX-512 code for AES-GCM, SHA-2, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and X25519. For multi-core scaling, the manual says the library is 'thread safe by design' because it 'avoids global data', and reference counts use C11 <stdatomic.h> or GCC __atomic builtins (wc_port.h). In HAProxy's profiles, wolfSSL's resumption curve did not change between pthread locks and HAProxy's lightweight locks ('it clearly doesn't need locks'), while OpenSSL 1.1.1w and 3.x spent most of their CPU in pthread_rwlock calls and atomics.

**Use it when:**
- HAProxy, or another OpenSSL-API server that already has a wolfSSL port, taking many short-lived TLS connections on many cores, where OpenSSL 3.x lock and atomic contention caps throughput. At 64 threads HAProxy measured 59.7k vs ~43k RSA full handshakes/s (OpenSSL 3.1-3.4-dev) and ~150k vs 23-28k ticket resumptions/s.
- Workloads heavy on ticket resumption, such as a proxy re-encrypting to backends or clients that reconnect often, where you want linear scaling to 64 cores without special lock builds.
- Embedded, RTOS or kernel-module targets that need TLS 1.3/DTLS 1.3 in tens of kB. The repo ships ports for Zephyr, ESP-IDF, STM32, Renesas, NXP and others, custom allocators (wolfSSL_SetAllocators) and a static memory pool (WOLFSSL_STATIC_MEMORY).
- You need a FIPS 140-3 validated module and a vendor that sells commercial licenses and support contracts (HAProxy notes an LTS period is 'probably negotiable').
- Post-quantum TLS work: ML-KEM/ML-DSA with AVX-512/AArch64 assembly plus native Falcon and FrodoKEM, with no liboqs dependency as of 5.9.4.

**Skip it when:**
- You need a binary drop-in for libssl/libcrypto or exact OpenSSL behavior. The compatibility layer is a macro mapping, and HAProxy reports 'minor differences' and says deploying it 'requires a lot of testing and feature validation'.
- Proprietary distribution without buying a commercial license: the code is GPL-3.0, and GPL-2.0 is allowed only for a named list of projects (MariaDB, OpenVPN, U-Boot from Cisco, ...).
- You want the absolute top numbers on Graviton. AWS-LC (v1.32.0+30) beat it on full RSA handshakes (63.1k vs 59.7k/s), and AWS-LC built with C11 beat it by ~20% on resumption (183k/s).
- You depend on distro packages and automatic OS security updates. HAProxy found that the Debian/Ubuntu wolfSSL packages lacked the HAProxy options and CPU optimizations it needed, so it had to build and maintain wolfSSL by hand.
- You can't upgrade quickly. 5.9.4 (2026-09-25) fixed three High-severity certificate-verification CVEs, and one of them (CVE-2026-93302, trusted-peer CA check) widens to all CA loading in OPENSSL_COMPATIBLE_DEFAULTS builds, which --enable-haproxy, --enable-nginx, --enable-all and --enable-distro all turn on.

**Integration:** static lib | shared lib (autotools ./configure or CMake; also source-drop with user_settings.h for IDE/RTOS builds) · none beyond libc (optional hardware or crypto-callback ports; the liboqs dependency was removed in 5.9.4) · ANSI C (a C89 build is supported via --enable-c89); autoconf/automake/libtool for git checkouts or CMake 3.16+ (CMake support described as 'still under development'); asm is auto-enabled only for GNU-C-compatible compilers; the benchmark used gcc 11.4 · any C target; assembly for x86-64 (AES-NI/AVX2/AVX-512), AArch64 (ARMv8 crypto extensions/NEON), ARM32/Thumb-2/Cortex-M, RISC-V 64 and PPC32/64; Linux, Windows, macOS/iOS, Android, many RTOSes and a Linux kernel module

**Vs siblings:** Pick wolfSSL over AWS-LC when you need a small, embeddable or FIPS 140-3 stack across many CPUs and RTOSes, a vendor support contract, or good multi-core scaling from a default build (the AWS-LC versions tested needed CMAKE_C_STANDARD=11 to avoid lock collapse, since fixed upstream); pick AWS-LC for the highest Graviton numbers and an API descended from BoringSSL/OpenSSL. Tempesta FW is a complete web accelerator and DDoS-protection proxy rather than a library, so wolfSSL is the choice when you link TLS into your own server.

**Gotchas:**
- Speed depends on configure flags. The fixed-size SP assembly and the ARMv8/Intel assembly are off by default in a plain ./configure (--enable-sp, --enable-armasm and --enable-intelasm all default to disabled). You enable them with --enable-sp --enable-sp-asm, --enable-armasm/--enable-intelasm, or --enable-all-asm; configure.ac turns all-asm on automatically only under --enable-all/all-crypto on 64-bit GNU C. HAProxy did not publish the flags it used.
- The ABI depends on the build configuration. configure generates wolfssl/options.h, which you must include before any other wolfSSL header (or define WOLFSSL_USE_OPTIONS_H). Struct layouts vary with options and between releases (5.9.4 changed OcspRequest, so code that embeds it must be rebuilt).
- Unlike OpenSSL, a client verifies the server by default: without loaded CAs, connect fails with -188 (README Note 2). Static-key RSA/DH/PSK cipher suites are disabled unless you enable them with WOLFSSL_STATIC_* defines.
- The benchmark only measured ticket resumption. Session-ID resumption goes through the process-global SessionCache under one rwlock unless ENABLE_SESSION_CACHE_ROW_LOCK is defined (ssl_sess.c). Issue #10123, still open, reports an ASAN use-after-free when HAProxy's vtest suite runs against wolfSSL master.

**Status:** Actively maintained by wolfSSL Inc. (5.9.4 released and last commit 2026-09-25) under GPL-3.0 or a commercial license. It is production-usable, but you build it yourself with the right configure flags and must keep up with frequent security releases.

[repo](https://github.com/wolfSSL/wolfssl) · [benchmark](https://www.haproxy.com/blog/state-of-ssl-stacks)

#### websocket-grpc-rpc

##### wtx (gRPC server)  `Rust`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Rust crate with its own HTTP/2 and gRPC stack. Its unary gRPC server served 3.7-5.5x grpc-go's req/s on HttpArena.

**Beats:** gRPC (grpc-go, official google.golang.org/grpc implementation) — HttpArena ran a unary GetSum gRPC call over plaintext h2c, driven by h2load with 256 and 1024 connections, 100 streams each, 5 s runs, best of 3. The machine was a Threadripper PRO 3995WX, with the server pinned to 32 cores plus their SMT threads. wtx 0.49 (nightly Rust, target-cpu=native) served 3,990,708 req/s against grpc-go v1.72.0 (Go 1.24, default grpc.NewServer) at 720,798 req/s with 256 connections (5.5x). With 1024 connections it served 3,620,970 against 969,718 (3.7x). Two limits apply: wtx used about 64 logical CPUs against grpc-go's 44, and the two results come from different run dates (grpc-go on 2026-04-12, wtx re-validated on 2026-08-24).

**Known shortcoming:** Rust. The wtx and grpc-go HttpArena runs were weeks apart, the author contributed the entry, and earlier wtx numbers were invalid (empty reply body, fixed in PR #1300). Several other entries (zix, cardigan, swerver) reach ~6.8-7.0M rps on the same board.

**Known shortcoming:** Unary gRPC calls only, with hand-written service definitions (#231) and third-party message codegen. The author calls it a free-time project that probably shouldn't be used in production (#452); no security audit, including its own TLS 1.3. An independent grpc_bench run (discussion #559, 2026-04, Xeon Gold 6548N, wtx 0.40) had it behind go_grpc (93,004 vs 117,082 req/s at 4 CPUs) and tonic, while an earlier run (#547, Ryzen 5900X) had it ahead, so the result depends on environment. HttpArena p99 is 69.9 ms at 256 connections vs a 6.55 ms average, and grpc-go's p99 field repeats its average, so tail latency cannot be compared. Returning () or a string type from a handler silently sends an empty body with grpc-status 0 (behind the invalid HttpArena results fixed in PR #1300). Needs nightly Rust; 7 breaking releases in 3 months (benchmarked 0.49, current 0.52.1). Plain HTTP/2 is slower than hyper (4.08M vs 6.97M req/s). Missing crypto feature fails at runtime, not build time.

**How:** Http2ServerFramework::run_in_threads uses a runtime-per-thread, shared-nothing design. It starts one single-threaded tokio LocalRuntime per available thread. Each runtime binds its own listener (SO_REUSEPORT is on by default) and runs its connection and stream tasks locally, so the hot path has no work-stealing and no cross-thread handoff. The HTTP/2 framing, HPACK and Huffman code are written in-house, and the response is built in the same buffer as the request, so a reply no larger than the request needs no new allocation. The benchmark binary also used target-cpu=native, thin LTO, codegen-units=1, panic=abort and wtx's optimizations-std feature (memchr, simdutf8, socket2).

**Use it when:**
- A Rust service whose hot path is small unary gRPC calls at very high request rates on a many-core Linux box. On HttpArena, wtx served 3.99M req/s against grpc-go's 0.72M with 256 h2c connections.
- Workloads with hundreds to thousands of connections, each carrying many concurrent streams. These spread well across the per-thread listeners; the benchmark used 256-1024 connections with 100 streams each.
- gRPC over TLS without a separate TLS stack: in HttpArena's unary-grpc-tls test, with wtx's own TLS 1.3, it reached 3.69M vs 0.70M req/s (256 connections) and 3.63M vs 0.93M (1024).
- Internal services, prototypes or benchmark rigs where you control the .proto files and both ends, and you can type the service routes by hand.
- Projects that want gRPC, HTTP/2, WebSocket and Postgres from one crate with a small dependency tree and fast builds. The README reports 2 required dependencies and a 6.53 s clean optimized build for the gRPC client.

**Skip it when:**
- You need server, client or bidirectional streaming RPCs. The gRPC module supports unary calls only.
- You need generated service stubs or the usual gRPC ecosystem. Services must be typed by hand; the macro for this is still open issue #231. Reflection, health checking and interceptor libraries are not documented.
- Production or security-sensitive systems. The README says wtx has had no security audit. In issue #452 (Nov 2025) the author calls it 'a fun project developed in my free-time that probably shouldn't be used in production' and advised a user to stay on tokio-tungstenite.
- Small CPU budgets or strict tail-latency targets. In grpc_bench's 2026-04-23 run (wtx 0.40, 1-4 server CPUs, 1000 clients), wtx trailed go_grpc (93,004 vs 117,082 req/s at 4 CPUs) and tonic, and its p90 stayed at about 42 ms. On HttpArena its p99 was 69.93 ms at 256 connections (average 6.55 ms), and it used 727 MiB of memory against grpc-go's 310.5 MiB.
- Teams that require stable Rust or a stable API. lib.rs enables nightly features, and crates.io lists 7 breaking minor releases (0.46 to 0.52) between 2026-05-16 and 2026-08-10.

**Integration:** crate · For the benchmarked gRPC server: tokio, quick-protobuf, hashbrown, foldhash, plus memchr, simdutf8 and socket2 through optimizations-std. pb-rs (or another generator) is needed at build time to generate message types. TLS or other crypto needs one backend feature: crypto-ring (ring), crypto-alr (aws-lc-rs), crypto-graviola or crypto-ruco (RustCrypto). · Rust nightly only. lib.rs uses #![feature(random, return_type_notation)] even though crates.io lists rust-version 1.96. The repo pins nightly-2026-09-03, the crate uses edition 2024, and HttpArena built wtx 0.49 with nightly-2026-06-27. · The core is no_std + alloc, and the README says it works on embedded devices with a heap allocator. Targets with 16-bit pointers are not supported. The multi-threaded server needs std; the executors are tokio, wtx's own std executor, and embassy-net. Benchmarks exist only for x86-64 Linux.

**Vs siblings:** Pick wtx when the service is written in Rust and must keep standard gRPC-over-HTTP/2 clients: its measured gain over grpc-go (3.7-5.5x) is larger than that of Kitex (1.5-1.7x) or rpcx (2.3-2.6x), both Go, though each was measured on a different harness. grpcxx is the closest C++ analogue that also speaks gRPC; brpc is the more mature C++ multi-protocol choice.

**Gotchas:**
- The response is built in the request buffer, and the handler's return type decides what happens to that buffer. ResFinalizer for () (and for &str, String and Vector) calls req.clear(). A handler that writes its reply into req.msg_data.body and returns () therefore sends an empty body with grpc-status 0. This bug invalidated wtx's own HttpArena entry until PR #1300; return StatusCode or VerbatimParams instead.
- If no crypto backend feature is selected, crypto calls panic or halt at runtime instead of failing the build. TLS and secure cookies need one of crypto-ring, crypto-alr, crypto-graviola or crypto-ruco.
- HTTP/2 has no HTTP/1.1 Upgrade path. Clients must use prior-knowledge h2c or ALPN over TLS. Stream prioritization and server push are not supported.
- The README warns that wtx assumes the summed length of any number of slices cannot overflow. On 32-bit targets, oversized input can overflow and cause unexpected behavior. The docs also flag PlaintextCtx (the TLS config used for plain h2c) as dangerous if misconfigured.

**Status:** Actively developed, almost entirely by one author (764 of about 790 non-bot commits; last commit 2026-09-08; 0.52.1 released 2026-08-14; about 70k crates.io downloads). The crate is MPL-2.0 and easy to depend on, but it is pre-1.0 with breaking releases every few weeks, nightly-only, unaudited, and its author does not recommend it for production.

[repo](https://github.com/c410-f3r/wtx) · [benchmark](https://www.http-arena.com/data.json)

### numerics-and-science

#### blas-lapack

##### Eigen  `C++`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier A`

Header-only C++ template library for dense/sparse linear algebra; beats OpenBLAS at small-to-mid sizes without linking BLAS.

**Beats:** OpenBLAS — On an Intel Xeon Gold 6444Y (GCC 13.3.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG -mavx512dq -mfma, single-threaded), Eigen's own kernels beat OpenBLAS 0.3.26's geometric-mean GFLOP/s on GEMV, DOT, TRSM, POTRF and SYEV across most size bands (roughly 1.1-4.9x), are near parity on large GEMM, and lose on GEEV and GESDD; against Intel oneMKL 2025.3, Eigen is generally slower at large sizes. The harness (Google Benchmark 1.8.3, median of 10 reps) is public but still an unmerged GitLab merge request (!2903), and frequency was not locked during the run.

**Independent measurement:** Eigen 5.0.1 reached 193.1 GFLOP/s on f32 matmul N=1024 (91% of the host's measured single-core FMA peak of 212.2, 1.42x a hand-written xsimd kernel, 1.85x Blaze), but lost fixed 4x4 multiplies to a naive triple loop (5.87 vs 3.20 ns, naive 1.83x) and 3x3 to hand-rolled xsimd (5.59 vs 2.26 ns, 2.5x). At N=64 hand-rolled xsimd also beat it 1.41x (187.4 vs 133.2 GFLOP/s), and the naive 4x4 win is gcc-specific (clang 18 leaves that loop scalar and Eigen wins there). (developer source, private repo; selection harness in docs/linear-algebra.md, gcc 13 -O3 -march=native, Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz, run 2026-09-03-third-party)

**Independent measurement:** Built without -march=native, Eigen fell from 193.1 to 34.6 GFLOP/s on f32 matmul N=1024 (5.6x loss), while OpenBLAS with runtime CPU dispatch went from 575.9 to 569.2. sizeof(struct{Eigen::Matrix4f; char;}) is 80/96/128 bytes under SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512, so translation units built with different arch flags silently disagree on layout. (developer source, private repo; selection harness in docs/linear-algebra.md, gcc 13, Intel Xeon @ 2.10GHz, run 2026-09-03-third-party)

**How:** Expression templates fuse chained operations into a single loop at compile time, avoiding temporaries. Eigen's own GEMM kernel does three-level cache blocking -- mc x kc panels packed for L2/L3, mr x kc micro-panels kept in L1, and a register-blocked micro-kernel -- the same family of technique GotoBLAS/BLIS use, confirmed in the header comment of GeneralBlockPanelKernel.h. Kernels are explicitly SIMD-vectorized (SSE/AVX/AVX-512/NEON/etc.), and small fixed-size matrices get compile-time loop unrolling that skips packing overhead entirely, which is why Eigen's edge over OpenBLAS is largest at small sizes (DOT 4.9x, GEMV 2.2x at n<=16) and shrinks or reverses as size grows.

**Use it when:**
- Small and medium dense ops (roughly n<=1024) where OpenBLAS's dispatch/call overhead dominates -- GEMV and DOT measured 1.1-4.9x faster than OpenBLAS here
- You want a header-only dependency with no external BLAS/LAPACK to build, package, or version-pin
- Fixed-size or compile-time-sized linear algebra (small transforms, small solvers) where Eigen's unrolled kernels apply
- TRSM, POTRF, SYEV workloads at small/mid size, where Eigen beat OpenBLAS by 1.25-3.6x per this benchmark
- C++ codebases that want expression-template ergonomics instead of raw BLAS call signatures

**Skip it when:**
- Very large dense GEMM/SYRK (n in the 1500+ range) where Eigen is roughly at parity with OpenBLAS and often slower than oneMKL
- GEEV (nonsymmetric eigenvalues) -- measured at 0.45x OpenBLAS at 192-1024, and well behind oneMKL at large sizes
- GESDD (SVD) at mid-to-large sizes -- measured 0.6-0.9x OpenBLAS
- Large-scale multi-threaded numerics -- this benchmark and Eigen's own kernels are single-threaded; OpenMP only parallelizes some ops (dense GEMM, PartialPivLU, a few iterative sparse solvers), not the full LAPACK surface
- Storing fixed-size Eigen objects in STL containers or passing them by value without alignment care -- triggers runtime alignment assertions on SIMD builds

**Integration:** header-only · none (STL only); optional external BLAS/LAPACK backend for large-matrix offload · C++14 (target_compile_features cxx_std_14 in CMakeLists.txt); CMake 3.18+ only needed for the optional install/test build, not for using the headers · x86-64 (SSE2 baseline, AVX/AVX2/AVX-512 optional), aarch64/ARM NEON, PowerPC Altivec/VSX, MIPS MSA; this benchmark ran on AVX-512

**Vs siblings:** no siblings catalogued yet

**Gotchas:**
- Fixed-size vectorizable types (Vector4d, Matrix4d, Quaternionf, etc.) assert at runtime if misaligned -- avoid storing them by value in STL containers or passing by value without EIGEN_MAKE_ALIGNED_OPERATOR_NEW
- OpenMP thread count should match physical cores, not logical/hyperthreads -- oversubscription slows things down since Eigen's kernels already saturate a core
- Heavy expression-template usage increases compile times
- For very large dense problems, Eigen's own docs and this benchmark both point toward linking an external BLAS/LAPACK backend instead of relying solely on Eigen's kernels

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-23) with a large downstream user base (ROS, TensorFlow, Ceres Solver, OpenCV, Blender); MPL-2.0, header-only, trivial to vendor.

[repo](https://gitlab.com/libeigen/eigen) · [benchmark](https://libeigen.gitlab.io/benchmarks/2026-09-xeon-gold-6444y-blas-lapack-avx512/)

### parsing-and-text

#### parser-generators-and-combinators

##### PAPAGENO (PArallel PArser GENeratOr)  `C`  `GPL-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier A`

Bison-style generator that emits pthreads-parallel operator-precedence parsers, up to 5.5x faster than Flex+Bison on ARM.

**Beats:** GNU Bison + GNU Flex (sequential LALR(1) parser/lexer) — The paper (Barenghi et al., preprint for Science of Computer Programming) benchmarks the PAPAGENO-generated parallel lexer/parser against the authors' own sequential Flex+Bison LALR(1) reference parser, both built with gcc 4.9.1 -O3 -march=native, on a 16-core quad-Opteron 8378 server and a 4x-Cortex-A15 Odroid-XU ARM board, over real-world JSON (2.7KiB-75MiB) and Lua (7KiB-35MiB) inputs. It reports up to 5.5x speedup on the ARM board and a separate maximum 7x speedup for parallel lexing alone vs. sequential Flex (not vs. the full Flex+Bison pipeline); the 16-core server JSON comparison (Fig. 13b) is a 3D plot with no stated exact peak number against Flex+Bison.

**How:** Exploits the OPG property that the shift/reduce decision between two adjacent terminals depends only on a fixed precedence relation, not on global parse state, so the input can be split into chunks and reduced independently on separate POSIX threads with no wasted re-computation when recombining partial trees. Lexing can likewise be split into an independent parallel pass (test/JSON_parallel_lexer). The README states throughput scales close to linearly with thread count on JSON workloads.

**Use it when:**
- Files large enough for parallelism to amortize thread overhead (paper shows real gains mainly on multi-MB inputs, up to 75MiB JSON / 35MiB Lua)
- A grammar that is already an Operator Precedence Grammar, or small enough to convert without exploding the rule set (e.g. arithmetic expressions, JSON)
- Batch/offline C parsing on multi-core x86_64 servers or ARM big.LITTLE boards where lexing/parsing is a proven bottleneck
- You can vendor and maintain generated C source yourself (Python 2.x generator, no upstream releases since 2015)

**Skip it when:**
- General LALR(1) or ambiguous/context-free grammars: converting real-world Lua to OPG+Fischer-normal-form blew productions up from 144 to 8547 plus required manual lexer transforms
- Small or streaming inputs (KB-scale) — paper reports negligible or negative speedup there from thread migration/NUMA overhead
- Anywhere you need Bison's GLR mode or ANTLR-style handling of ambiguous grammars — OPG is a strict LALR(1) subset
- Projects needing an actively maintained tool or Python 3 support: last commit 2015-04-20, generator is Python 2.x only, one unresolved GitHub issue
- Anywhere a true drop-in Bison/Flex replacement is required — grammar syntax is Bison-like but the generated parser's call signature and build process differ

**Integration:** source-drop · Python 2.x to run the generator; GNU Flex, gcc/clang, Make, and POSIX threads (pthreads) to build the generated parser · Python 2.x (generator); C with pthreads and GNU Flex for the generated code (paper's own build used gcc 4.9.1, -O3 -march=native) · x86_64 and ARM (tested on Cortex-A15/A7); requires a POSIX threads implementation (tested on Linux NPTL)

**Vs siblings:** Pick PAPAGENO only when the win you need is multi-core parallelism on a Bison-compatible C grammar that is (or can be forced into) Operator Precedence form; the catalogued siblings (flap, re2c, Pika Parser, winnow, chumsky, MPL/FastParse) are all single-threaded OCaml/Rust tools that get their speedups from fused lexing, code generation, or SIMD/table specialization, not from splitting work across cores, so they don't compete on this axis.

**Gotchas:**
- Generator statically rejects non-OPG grammars (consecutive nonterminals, precedence conflicts) and only prints diagnostics — you must manually restructure the grammar
- Real-world grammars can blow up drastically under OPG conversion: Lua went from 144 to 8547 productions in the paper's benchmark
- README states terminal/nonterminal names may not start with '_'
- Generator itself is Python 2.x only; no indication of a Python 3 port

**Status:** Abandoned: no commits since 2015-04-20, GPL-2.0 licensed, one open GitHub issue and no CI/releases; small enough (a handful of C files plus a Python 2.x code generator) to vendor and maintain yourself if you accept the OPG grammar restriction.

[repo](https://github.com/PAPAGENO-devels/papageno) · [benchmark](https://re.public.polimi.it/retrieve/handle/11311/971391/67830/papaj-final.pdf)

### serialization-and-formats

#### binary-schemas

##### gencode  `Go`  `GPL-2.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier B`

Go code generator for a compact schema-driven binary format; marshals ~2.3x and unmarshals ~2.7x faster than protobuf-go.

**Beats:** Protobuf — alecthomas/go_serialization_benchmarks measures a struct of two strings, a time.Time, an int, a bool and a float64 in a user-generated report that gives no Go version or CPU. There, gencode marshals in 122 ns/op and unmarshals in 132 ns/op, against 287/356 ns/op for protobuf-go (~2.3x/~2.7x), with 3 allocations each; gogo/protobuf on the same page is 115/166 ns/op. The gencode/unsafe_reuse row (reused buffer, -unsafe numeric stores, time as int64) reaches 48/104 ns/op, but protobuf-go has no matching buffer-reuse row.

**Known shortcoming:** Not safe for untrusted input: Unmarshal has no bounds checks (truncated input panics, #20) and wire lengths go straight into make(). The generator does not build today without pinning andyleap/parser to db5a13a7cd46 (#29). The unsafe_reuse row mixes buffer reuse, unsafe numeric stores and a cheaper time encoding, and strings are still copied. Time values with LMT zone offsets fail to round-trip silently. No schema evolution; colfer, mus-go, benc and 200sc/bebop beat its safe path. Unclear whether GPL-2.0 covers generated code.

**How:** The generator emits straight-line, type-specialized code with no reflection. The wire format is positional: fields are written in declared order with no field numbers or wire-type tags, so there are no tag bytes to write, read or switch on. Marshal runs Size() first and allocates the output once, or reuses the caller's buffer if it is big enough. Offsets of fixed-width fields are folded into constants at generation time (`buf[i+9]`), so a run of fixed fields becomes plain byte stores without advancing the index (the author explains this in issue #24). Ints are written little-endian by byte shifts, or with `-unsafe` as one unaligned native-endian pointer store; strings, slices and `v`-prefixed ints use LEB128 varints, with zigzag encoding for signed varints.

**Use it when:**
- Go-to-Go payloads (RPC messages, cache values, on-disk records) where you own both ends and regenerate both from one schema file; there is only a Go backend.
- Small flat structs of ints, floats and short strings where per-message CPU cost matters: about 120-130 ns per marshal/unmarshal on the shootout's 6-field struct, against 287/356 ns for protobuf-go.
- Structs made mostly of fixed-width numbers, where offsets fold to constants: in the author's README run (hardware not stated), an all-fixed 4-field struct deserializes in 20.7 ns/op.
- Length-prefixed message streams over sockets or files: mark the struct `framed` to get Serialize(io.Writer)/Deserialize(io.Reader).
- Messages that can be one of several struct types: a `union` field becomes a Go interface you can type-switch on, with a varint type tag on the wire.

**Skip it when:**
- Decoding untrusted or possibly truncated bytes. Unmarshal has no bounds checks and panics with 'index out of range' on truncated input (issue #20, open since 2018). Lengths read from the wire go straight into make(), so a hostile length can force a huge allocation.
- Any schema evolution. The format is positional with no field numbers, defaults or unknown-field skipping, so adding, removing or reordering a field breaks existing data and older readers.
- Cross-language use or map-heavy data. There is only a Go backend and no map type; PR #12, which added maps and C++, was never merged.
- Anything that needs a maintained, easy-to-build tool. The last commit was 2017-11-24 and the repo has no go.mod. The generator no longer builds against the current andyleap/parser unless you pin the 2016 version (issue #29). The parser silently accepts a garbage schema (#19), and `[][N]byte` fields produce code that does not compile (#23).
- Wire size against protobuf. On the shootout struct the safe variant encodes to 53 bytes, against 51 for protobuf-go.

**Integration:** source-drop · The generated code imports only the Go standard library (io, time, unsafe) and needs no runtime package. The generator CLI depends on github.com/andyleap/parser, which must be pinned to db5a13a7cd46 from 2016 because the 2021 generics rewrite breaks the build (issue #29), and on github.com/kr/pretty. · Not documented. The repo predates Go modules and has no go.mod, and issue #23 reports use with go1.11. Building the generator with current Go needs a manual go.mod that pins andyleap/parser. · Default mode runs on any Go target because it uses explicit little-endian byte shifts. With -unsafe, fixed-width ints and floats use unaligned native-endian pointer loads and stores, so the wire format matches the safe mode only on little-endian hosts. PR #11 for big-endian support was never merged.

**Vs siblings:** In the same shootout, colfer (115/123 ns), mus-go (92/122), benc (81/103) and 200sc/bebop (94/112) all beat gencode's 122/132 ns safe path, so pick gencode only for what they lack: tagged unions decoded to Go interfaces, a framed io.Reader/io.Writer API, or time kept with its zone offset (gencode's row is labelled fulltzoffset; mus and benc are labelled no time support). It is also a small, readable reference for how offset folding in a code generator works.

**Gotchas:**
- Unmarshal almost never returns an error. Only nested and framed paths return one (the framed length check returns io.EOF), and other malformed input panics. Wrap decoding of external bytes in recover().
- `-unsafe` changes only fixed-width ints and floats; strings are still copied on unmarshal. The shootout labels its gencode/unsafe_reuse row as unsafe-string with full-tz-offset time. In fact that row's schema stores BirthDay as an int64 UnixNano, and it reuses a 1 KB marshal buffer, so its 48 ns marshal mixes three changes.
- time fields reserve exactly 15 bytes for time.MarshalBinary, and the error from UnmarshalBinary is ignored. Current Go writes 16 bytes when a zone offset has leftover seconds (LMT zones), so those times fail to round-trip without any error.
- Marshal(buf) writes into buf when its capacity is big enough and returns a slice of it, so the next Marshal into the same buffer overwrites earlier output. Size() also runs on every Marshal, which is an extra pass over strings and varints.

**Status:** Abandoned since 2017-11-24, and the generator is GPL-2.0 (the project does not say whether that covers generated output). The generated code needs only the standard library, so you can vendor it once the generator is built with a pinned parser dependency, but treat it as a technique reference rather than a live dependency.

[repo](https://github.com/andyleap/gencode) · [benchmark](https://github.com/alecthomas/go_serialization_benchmarks/blob/master/report/data.js)

#### yaml-toml-xml

##### Parshred  `C++`  `AGPL-3.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier A`

C++20 SIMD XML parser with a flat 32-byte-node DOM; 1.6-3.3x pugixml's read-only parse throughput on synthetic XML.

**Beats:** pugixml — Setup: generated <item id name status>text</item> records at 64 KB-128 MB, single thread, Ryzen 5 7640U, GCC 16.1 -O3 -mavx2. fast_dom_parse<FDOM_FASTEST>, which builds no text nodes, ran at 1317-2722 MB/s against pugixml 1.14 load_buffer(parse_minimal) at 641-1585 MB/s, a 1.6x-3.3x gap. It matched RapidXML 1.13 parse_fastest within ~5% up to 16 MB and was 1.5-1.8x faster at 64-128 MB. These are first-party numbers, and pugixml copies the buffer and still builds PCDATA nodes, so the pugixml ratio overstates a same-work comparison.

**Known shortcoming:** Its fast DOM parsers do not validate: end-tag mismatches are not reported (the project's own W3C run accepts 928 of 1,383 not-well-formed cases), fast_dom_parse drops CDATA and leaves entities undecoded unless FDOM_NORMALIZE is passed, values over 65,535 bytes are truncated, and deep nesting silently produces a wrong tree. The SIMD path needs the caller built with -mavx2.

**How:** It makes a single pass over the input. AVX2 32-byte compare+movemask+ctz scans (_mm256_cmpeq_epi8/_mm256_movemask_epi8) jump to the next '<', closing quote or comment/CDATA end, and names are read with a scalar lookup table. Nodes are 32-byte structs written in order into one malloc'd array, which starts at len/35 nodes and doubles with realloc. They are linked by uint32 indices, not pointers, and names and attribute values stay as pointers or offsets into the input (zero-copy). The benchmarked FDOM_FASTEST mode also skips building text nodes. The parser never matches end-tag names or reports errors, so it does less work than pugixml. The author puts the 64 MB+ gap over RapidXML down to RapidXML's per-node allocation versus this one flat array.

**Use it when:**
- Read-only extraction of element structure and attributes (not text) from trusted, well-formed UTF-8 XML, which is exactly the FDOM_FASTEST shape that was benchmarked
- Large documents (64-128 MB) on x86-64 with AVX2, where the README shows 1.5-1.8x over RapidXML and 1.85-2.6x over pugixml
- Replacing a pugixml load_buffer + walk used only for reading, when you can adopt an index-based API with string_view results and keep the input buffer alive
- Python batch jobs over trusted XML that need more than lxml's roughly 90-106 MB/s (README reports 527-575 MB/s), provided raw, entity-undecoded text is acceptable
- Open-source projects already under AGPL-3.0-or-later, or teams willing to buy the commercial license

**Skip it when:**
- Untrusted or possibly malformed input: neither fast_dom_parse nor dom_parse checks that end tags match or reports parse errors. The project's own W3C run shows 928 of 1383 not-wf cases wrongly accepted (SAX path)
- Closed-source products or SaaS without a paid license: AGPL-3.0 §13 network-use copyleft, whereas pugixml (MIT) and RapidXML are permissive
- Files of 64 KB-16 MB where you already use RapidXML: Parshred's own table shows parity within ~5% there, and RapidXML is header-only
- Needs beyond read-only DOM: editing the tree in place, pugixml's full XPath 1.0 (ancestor/preceding axes and variables are missing), namespace-aware DOM/XPath, or UTF-16/Latin-1 input (UTF-8 only)
- Workloads that need production maturity: single author, 0 stars, and all code landed 2026-07-11 to 07-29 with no commits since. The weekly fuzz job has failed twice in fuzz_xpath (out-of-memory in xpath::eval_step and UBSan float-to-integer overflow in xpath.hpp)
