- Products that cannot take a GPL-3.0 dependency, or that need an actively maintained one. There have been no commits since April 2022 and there is no CI. A January 2026 request to relicense (issue #12) has had no reply.

**Integration:** shared lib (make builds libwh.so) or source-drop (lib.c, kv.c, wh.c plus lib.h/kv.h/wh.h/ctypes.h) · pthread and libm; librt on Linux/FreeBSD and libexecinfo on FreeBSD. The Makefile links libbacktrace and liburing only if their headers are found. No other libraries. · C (the Makefile uses -std=gnu18) with Clang (default, and faster per the README) or GCC. Minimum versions are not documented. The author reported a 2-4% regression with Clang 9. The headers are wrapped in extern "C", and the author's issue #11 benchmark includes them from C++17. · Linux, FreeBSD, macOS. x86-64 with SSE4.2 required (AVX2 used if enabled), or AArch64 with NEON and the crc extension. Builds with -march=native by default. No Windows support.

**Vs siblings:** Pick Wormhole over HOT or ART Synchronized when keys are long, binary or variable-length and you need a complete thread-safe ordered map with deletes, range deletes and merge. The author's single-thread numbers in issue #5 put it ahead of HOT on string keysets (1.80 vs 1.27 MOPS on Amazon keys). Cuckoo Trie beat Wormhole by up to 50% on YCSB-C in its SOSP'21 paper, but its own README says it is not robust enough for use in real programs.

**Gotchas:**
- Linking lib.c installs process-wide constructors. Unless it is built with -DNOSIGNAL (make O=ns), a SIGSEGV, SIGFPE, SIGILL or SIGBUS anywhere in the host process prints a backtrace and then sleeps forever 'waiting for GDB' instead of crashing. Internal fatal errors (debug_die) do the same. It also tries to mlock() every mmap'd region and prints 'mlock disabled' to stderr when that fails.
- With the struct-kv APIs, the caller must keep each key's CRC32C hash current (kv_update_hash / kref_refill_hash32). Only debug builds assert this.
- Keys are compared as byte strings, so integer keys must be byte-swapped to big-endian (e.g. __builtin_bswap64) to sort numerically.
- The main tuning knobs are compile-time macros in wh.c and lib.c: keys per leaf (WH_KPN, default 128; 256 is 5-10% faster for point operations, 64 is better for scans), slab and hugepage size, and QSBR capacity. A split fails if 129 keys share a common prefix of 65,535+ bytes. In-place update callbacks must change only value bytes, or the index is corrupted.

**Status:** Abandoned since an April 2022 'minor sync' commit; a copy of wh.c also ships in the author's RemixDB, last pushed March 2023. It is GPL-3.0, which rules out permissive-license products, but at about 10k lines of plain C in three modules it is small enough to vendor.

[repo](https://github.com/wuxb45/wormhole) · [benchmark](http://web.archive.org/web/20211016045757/https://www.cs.uic.edu/~wuxb/papers/wormhole.pdf)

#### probabilistic-filters

##### Clubcard  `Rust`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier B`

Rust exact-membership filter (partitioned two-level Ribbon cascade) that replaced Firefox CRLite's Bloom filter cascade at under half the size.

**Beats:** Bloom filter — This is a size-only comparison on Mozilla's production CRLite data. The 2024-08-29 snapshot (816M certificates, 795 issuers, 11.7M revoked) encodes to an 8.5 MB clubcard, versus 19.3 MB for Mozilla's own multi-level Bloom filter cascade, 56% smaller. The IEEE S&P 2025 paper reports issuer-partitioned clubcards averaging 54% smaller than the cascades for 2024-10-29 to 2024-11-11. There is no compiler or query-speed comparison. The crate docs also cite a preliminary build of 8.5 MB in 200 s versus 19.8 MB in 293 s for the cascade (Ryzen 3975WX, 64 GB).

**Known shortcoming:** The win is size (clubcards ~54-56% smaller than Bloom cascades for revocation sets), not lookup speed; designed for static certificate-revocation sets.

**Known shortcoming:** Batch build only and it must enumerate the whole universe U (exact only inside U); unstable API and format, serde required, non-deterministic builds (thread_rng). Weak on uniform unpartitioned sets (+10% over optimum vs ncrlite's +1.4%); part of the win comes from issuer partitioning (a sharded Bloom is ~13 MB vs 8.5 MB); size blows up near 50% block density. No query-speed benchmark (~10 us per clubcard query in the paper); epsilon hard-coded at 0.02.

**How:** It uses Mike Hamburg's two-level cascade (RWC 2022). A Ribbon approximate filter, a homogeneous GF(2) system with k = floor(log2(|U\R|/|R|)) columns, cuts U down to R plus about |R| false positives. A one-bit Ribbon retrieval function over those survivors then corrects them, for roughly (k+2)|R| bits in total, where a Bloom cascade needs many levels. Both systems are solved by Dillinger-Walzer Ribbon banded elimination with back-substitution (band 64*W bits, 256 in CRLite; epsilon 0.02). Each partition block (the issuer, in CRLite) gets its own ribbons, stitched into one matrix sorted by descending rank. Total size therefore tracks sum n_i*H(r_i/n_i), which falls below the unpartitioned bound when member density varies across blocks. Blocks denser than one half are encoded by their complement using an inverted flag.

**Use it when:**
- Static set membership over a universe you can list in full at build time, such as revoked certificates among all CT-logged certificates, when in-universe keys must never be false positives.
- Filters shipped to many clients where bytes matter more than build time or per-query nanoseconds. CRLite ships a roughly 4 MB snapshot every 45 days plus 12-hour deltas.
- Data with a natural partition whose member density varies a lot across blocks, such as issuer or expiry hour. In the README's example, partitioning by issuer lowers the information-theoretic bound from 11 MB to 7.6 MB.
- Replacing a CRLite-style multi-level Bloom filter cascade that you already rebuild in batches.
- Snapshot-plus-delta distribution. A clubcard for R2\R1 inside U2 zstd-compresses to about 26 kB per 6-hour WebPKI delta when the previous snapshot is used as the dictionary.

**Skip it when:**
- Online inserts or deletes. Construction is batch-only, and the exact stage must see every element of U, not just the members. For streaming use, pick a Bloom, cuckoo or quotient filter.
- An open or unknown key universe, such as arbitrary strings. Answers are only defined for items in U: unchecked_contains is undefined outside it, and contains is only as good as the in_universe predicate you write.
- Hot paths that need nanosecond lookups. The paper puts a CRLite query at about 10 microseconds per clubcard (one SHA-256 plus some memory accesses), and query cost grows linearly with the number of delta clubcards. The crate has no published query microbenchmarks.
- Unpartitioned sets of uniform density. In the paper's simulation (n=1M, r=10k), clubcards were 10% above the optimum while Westerbaan's ncrlite was 1.4% above. Without partitioning, the win over Bloom shrinks to the Ribbon part alone: the README estimates an issuer-sharded Bloom cascade at about 13 MB versus 8.5 MB.
- Projects that need a stable API or wire format, or need to avoid serde. The README says neither the API nor the serialization format is stable. The crate is 0.x, has one main author, and requires serde (issue #6 asking to make it optional was closed). Blocks near 50% density also blow up in size: the paper's hypothetical 180M-certificate issuer grows from 0.29 MB to 25.4 MB if half its certificates are revoked.

**Integration:** crate · serde with derive (required); rand 0.8 only with the `builder` feature; sha2 is a dev-dependency only, since you supply the hash yourself · Rust edition 2021 with no rust-version declared; the code uses let-else (Rust 1.65+) and const generics. The CRLite wrapper clubcard-crlite declares rust-version 1.85. · any: pure safe Rust with no SIMD and no unsafe outside tests. It is vendored in Firefox (third_party/rust/clubcard) and runs on Windows, Linux and macOS desktop.

**Vs siblings:** BuRR, RocksDB Ribbon, ribbonGo, xorf and xor_singleheader are approximate filters: they have a false-positive rate but need only the member keys. Pick Clubcard when you can enumerate the whole universe and need exact answers for every in-universe key, especially if a partition with uneven densities exists. For a general-purpose static approximate filter in Rust, xorf or a Ribbon implementation is simpler and has published speed numbers, which Clubcard does not.

**Gotchas:**
- Builds are not deterministic. Back-substitution fills free variables and the solution tail from thread_rng, so the same input gives different bytes each time. This matters for reproducible builds and binary diffing.
- You write the hash. AsQuery::as_query must return an Equation with s uniform in [0,m) and a[0]&1 == 1 (asserted). A weak hash causes insertion failures, which go into a per-block exceptions list that every query scans linearly.
- Answers are only exact for items inside U. When you combine a snapshot with deltas, merge the results in precedence order: member > non-member > no data > not in universe.
- Epsilon is hard-coded at 0.02. Bumped ribbon retrieval (#2), false-positive herding (#3) and a compact index encoding (#5, about 50 kB saved) are open TODOs. The README says 8.5 MB is 12% above the bound and that about 8% is reachable.

**Status:** Active but slow-moving: a single-author Mozilla crate at v0.3.4 (2026-07-31), MPL-2.0, about 1,300 lines including tests, vendored in Firefox and the default desktop CRLite backend since Firefox 137. Fine to depend on, but pin the exact version because the API and format are declared unstable.

[repo](https://github.com/mozilla/clubcard) · [benchmark](https://github.com/mozilla/clubcard#application-to-crlite-and-performance)

## Copyleft — Unverified claims (tier C/D)

### networking-and-servers

#### tls

##### Tempesta FW (Tempesta TLS)  `C`  `GPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Linux-kernel TLS 1.2 server stack in the Tempesta FW proxy; 6-83% more handshakes/s than Nginx+OpenSSL in vendor tests.

**Beats:** OpenSSL — The authors' NetDev 0x14 (2020) paper ran TLS 1.2 ECDHE-ECDSA P-256 handshakes against Tempesta FW on Linux 5.7 and Nginx 1.19.1 + OpenSSL 1.1.1d, using tls-perf and wrk; on a 1-vCPU KVM guest (i7-6500U host, no vAPIC), Tempesta reached 2,180 vs 1,545 handshakes/s with 307 vs 1,340 ms average latency. On bare-metal Xeon E3-1240v5 limited to one physical core (2 hyperthreads) with 10GbE, it gained 83% on resumption but only 6% on new sessions (7,921 vs 7,426), with worse average, p95 and max latency; compiler and build flags are not given.

**Known shortcoming:** First-party NetDev paper; on bare metal Nginx/OpenSSL had lower average and 95th-percentile latency, and Tempesta showed tail-latency spikes up to +3000%. In-kernel TLS tied to Tempesta FW, not a drop-in library. No compiler or flags stated.

**Known shortcoming:** Not a drop-in for OpenSSL: an out-of-tree kernel module inside the Tempesta FW reverse proxy with no OpenSSL-compatible API. TLS 1.2 server-side only (TLS 1.3 open, #1031), secp256r1 and AES-GCM/CCM only (no ChaCha20). Needs a patched kernel, x86-64 with SSE4.2/BMI2/ADX, 8 GB RAM and huge pages. Mixes constant-time and non-constant-time code with RDRAND randomization. Self-described Beta.

**How:** The handshake runs in SoftIRQ right after the TCP handshake, with a zero-copy state machine on skbs, so there are no user/kernel context switches, socket syscalls or extra copies. Hot paths make no heap allocations: each cipher suite has a precomputed 'MPI profile' that is copied in one shot, and temporary big integers come from per-CPU page pools. P-256 uses hand-written x86-64 BMI2/ADX Montgomery arithmetic (after Gueron-Krasnov) in Jacobian coordinates, with fixed-base comb tables (window 7) for m*G, RDRAND randomization in place of full constant-time table scans, and the Linux crypto API for AES-GCM/CCM. The paper reports 40x the original mbed TLS port's rate (2,180 vs 51 handshakes/s), but raw ECDSA/ECDHE op/s stay below OpenSSL's, so the gain over Nginx comes from where the code runs, not from faster math.

**Use it when:**
- Dedicated x86-64 Linux edge servers where full or resumed TLS handshakes/s is the bottleneck, for example short-lived HTTPS connections or TLS handshake floods (DDoS), and you can replace Nginx/HAProxy with Tempesta FW
- Traffic dominated by session resumption through RFC 5077 session tickets: the paper measured 35,263 vs 19,203 conn/s (+83%) against Nginx/OpenSSL on bare metal
- Small VMs without virtual APIC, where fewer VM exits matter: on a 1-vCPU KVM guest, the paper measured +41% handshakes/s and 77% lower average latency
- ECDSA P-256 certificates with ECDHE P-256 and AES-GCM suites, serving HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 (the only ALPN protocols supported)
- Deployments that want private and session keys held in non-swappable kernel memory, away from the application's address space

**Skip it when:**
- You need TLS 1.3, X25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305, P-384 or client-side TLS: only TLS 1.2 server-side with AES-GCM/CCM on secp256r1 is supported, and TLS 1.3 (issue #1031) is still open
- You need a library to link into your own application or into Nginx/HAProxy: there is no OpenSSL-compatible API, and the kernel TLS socket API (issue #1433) is only a proposal
- Bare-metal services that care about tail latency: in the paper, Nginx/OpenSSL had 50-170% lower average and p95 latency for new sessions, and Tempesta's max latency was up to 30x worse (28,262 vs 925 ms) under load
- Non-x86-64 hardware (ARM/Graviton), CPUs without BMI2/ADX, or managed kernels: the product needs a patched kernel (linux-6.12.12-tfw for 0.9/master, 5.10.35-tfw for 0.8), at least 8 GB RAM, 2 MB huge pages and an RSS-capable NIC
- RSA-certificate workloads (the docs say RSA isn't performance-optimized), or teams that cannot accept a Beta, GPLv2 in-kernel TLS stack that enlarges the kernel TCB

**Integration:** module · Patched Linux kernel (tempesta-tech/linux-6.12.12-tfw for 0.9/master, linux-5.10.35-tfw for release-0.8); Linux crypto API for symmetric ciphers and hashes; build packages listed in the install docs include gcc, g++, libboost-all-dev, libssl-dev, libelf-dev, flex, bison and dwarves · not documented (no GCC version given); Ubuntu 24.04 is the preferred build and run environment; needs kernel headers and 35-40 GB of disk for the kernel build · x86-64 Linux only; SSE4.2, BMI2 and ADX are required by the Makefile. AVX2 is listed as required in the docs, and the Makefile warns not to use builds without it in production. Needs RDRAND and huge-page support.

**Vs siblings:** AWS-LC and wolfSSL are user-space libraries that link into HAProxy or Nginx, support TLS 1.3 and ARM, and scale across many cores (their benchmarks use a 64-core Graviton4). Pick Tempesta only when you can replace the whole HTTPS proxy on dedicated x86-64 Linux and TLS 1.2 ECDSA-P-256 handshake cost per core is your limit, since its gain comes from kernel placement and its own crypto is slower than OpenSSL's.

**Gotchas:**
- Side-channel protection mixes constant-time code with non-constant-time code plus RDRAND randomization (as in mbed TLS) rather than OpenSSL's constant-time-everywhere approach. A CRYPTO_CONST_TIME build flag exists. On SRBDS-affected Intel CPUs, the microcode mitigation cuts RDRAND to about 3% of its original speed, and the requirements page says the mitigation is needed in public clouds.
- Curve25519 source (tls/ec_25519.c) is present but marked 'slow and incomplete' and is not in the supported-curve list; secp256r1 is the only ECDHE curve offered.
- Heavy public-key math runs in SoftIRQ with kernel_fpu_begin/end. The paper links this to tail-latency spikes and packet drops under heavy load on bare metal.
- The master branch is a development (unstable) branch. The README says to use release-0.8 for a stable version, and the project calls itself Beta.

**Status:** Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-25; Ubuntu 24 package release 0.8.2 in October 2025) but still self-described Beta; GPL-2.0 kernel module deployed as a complete reverse proxy, not a TLS library you can vendor into another program.

[repo](https://github.com/tempesta-tech/tempesta) · [benchmark](https://netdevconf.info/0x14/pub/papers/35/0x14-paper35-talk-paper.pdf)

#### websocket-grpc-rpc

##### Lightstream  `Rust`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust/Python Arrow-table transport over raw TCP, QUIC, HTTP/2 and WebSocket; 1.06-1.71x Arrow Flight throughput between AWS hosts.

**Beats:** Apache Arrow Flight (gRPC/HTTP2) — The project's own ECS rig ran 2x AWS i3en.12xlarge in one cluster placement group (50 Gbit/s): RAM-resident 1M-row tables in 4 shapes, warm median of 5 runs, Lightstream's parallel protocol over plaintext TCP vs arrow-flight 59.2 DoGet over tonic/HTTP/2 (8 MiB windows, default 2 MiB slicing, dictionary Resend), built with unpinned Rust nightly --release. Lightstream led in all 16 cells by 1.06x-1.71x, but its 1-stream cells (1.108-1.109 GiB/s, about 9.5 Gbit/s) sit at AWS's ~10 Gbps per-flow cap and its 16-stream cells (5.75-5.79 GiB/s, about 49.4-49.7 Gbit/s) sit at the link limit, so the ratios mostly show how far Flight falls short of the network ceiling; Lightstream's timing also includes a global reorder that Flight does not do.

**Known shortcoming:** Lightstream's results sit at the network ceilings (1 stream ~9.5 Gbit/s = AWS per-flow cap; 16 streams ~49.5 Gbit/s = the 50 Gbit/s link), so the ratios mostly show how far Flight falls short of the link; no CPU-per-byte data. Framing differs: run.sh defaults to 8 MiB batches (its header comment says 0) while Flight slices at 2 MiB; the table doesn't say which was used. The benchmark image patches minarrow to a sibling checkout and uses an unpinned nightly. Lightstream pays for a global reorder Flight doesn't; latency chart is single-stream only. Nightly-only (allocator_api, portable_simd). Not a Flight drop-in: minarrow Table API, no Flight wire compatibility, parallel writer is plaintext TCP only (max 256 connections, u32 frames, 2 GiB virtual reservation per decoder). One maintainer, 41 stars, 938 downloads, 0.1-0.4 yanked; 0.7.0 can't read back Parquet-with-nulls from earlier releases. Doc errors (missing benchmarks/ path, 'cargo install' for a library).

**How:** Each table goes on the wire as Arrow IPC inside a 5-byte TLV frame ([u8 tag][u32 LE length]) directly over TCP, skipping gRPC/HTTP/2 framing, protobuf FlightData wrapping and arrow-flight's default 2 MiB batch slicing. Buffers are minarrow 64-byte-aligned Vec64, and the receive path reads socket bytes straight into decoder-managed buffers from a reused per-stream arena, so steady-state decode does no per-batch allocation (per source comments). Parallel mode opens one TCP connection per stream, feeds them round-robin through bounded tokio channels (depth 8), decodes each connection on its own task, and restores global order by pulling connections in the same rotation, with no sort. The project publishes no profile that attributes the gain to any one of these parts.

**Use it when:**
- Bulk transfer of multi-MiB Arrow batches between Rust or Python services on a LAN/cluster, especially over one connection, where the published gain is largest (1.18x-1.71x at 1 stream).
- You need one globally ordered table stream spread across several parallel TCP connections and do not want to write the merge yourself.
- You want Arrow tables and typed Protobuf/MessagePack side messages on the same connection instead of hand-rolled adjacent-bytes framing.
- You want one API to swap between TCP, UDS, QUIC, WebSocket, HTTP/2, stdio, Arrow IPC/Parquet files and mmap, and can build on nightly Rust or use the Python wheels.

**Skip it when:**
- You need Flight ecosystem interop (Flight SQL, DoPut/DoExchange, existing Flight clients/servers, GetFlightInfo endpoint discovery); Lightstream is not wire-compatible with Flight.
- Your build must use stable Rust: the crate needs nightly (allocator_api, portable_simd via minarrow/vec64), and rust-toolchain.toml pins only channel = "nightly", no date.
- The link is already the bottleneck: at 8-16 streams the published lead shrinks to 1.06x-1.26x, because both systems approach the 50 Gbit/s limit.
- Small request/response RPC or general service APIs; this is a bulk columnar transport, not an RPC framework.
- Production-critical paths that need a mature project: one maintainer, 41 stars, 0 issues ever filed, versions 0.1-0.4.x yanked on crates.io, and 0.7.0 cannot read Parquet files with nulls written by earlier releases.

**Integration:** crate (also Python package lightstream-io) · tokio, futures-*, flatbuffers, minarrow 0.18, vec64, tracing, log; optional per feature: quinn, h2/http/bytes, tokio-tungstenite, wtransport, tokio-rustls (ring), prost, rmp-serde, zstd, snap, simd-json, tokio-uring · Rust nightly (edition 2024; unpinned nightly channel); no stable MSRV. Python >=3.9 for the wheels. · CI runs Linux x86-64, macOS x86-64/arm64 and Windows x86-64 (Windows without uds/mmap); io_uring and vmap64 are Linux-only; PyPI also ships manylinux aarch64 wheels. Published benchmarks are Linux x86-64 only.

**Vs siblings:** The catalogued siblings (DRPC, fRPC, brpc, rpcx, cmd-stream) are general RPC frameworks benchmarked on small-message QPS against gRPC, and none carries Arrow tables natively. Pick Lightstream when the payload is bulk Arrow columnar data or you need ordered multi-connection streaming; pick DRPC, fRPC or brpc for many small request/response calls.

**Gotchas:**
- Ordered mode stalls on the slowest connection: a lagging stream holds back every table behind it (documented on SortBehaviour::Ordered), with 8 buffered frames per connection.
- LightstreamParallelWriter caps at 256 connections (each connection announces its index as one byte), and each frame's payload length is a u32, so a single frame must stay under 4 GiB; split big tables into views.
- Each streaming decoder reserves 2 GiB of virtual address space (tunable via LIGHTSTREAM_ARENA_CAPACITY); many parallel streams add up under strict overcommit or ulimit -v.
- LightstreamParallelWriter::connect opens plain TcpStreams from a SocketAddr, and that file has no TLS variant; TLS exists on the single-connection TCP/WebSocket/HTTP/2 writers (tls feature) and in QUIC. The Rust README's 'cargo install lightstream' is wrong for a library crate; use cargo add.

**Status:** Active (v0.7.0 released 2026-09-19; one maintainer, 7 self-merged PRs, 0 issues) and MPL-2.0 with file-level copyleft, so it is fine to link as a dependency, but it is pre-1.0, nightly-only and still making format-breaking changes.

[repo](https://github.com/SpaceCell/lightstream) · [benchmark](https://github.com/SpaceCell/lightstream/blob/main/rust/README.md)

### parsing-and-text

#### lexers-tokenizers

##### CrossDB (hand-written SQL lexer/parser)  `C`  `MPL-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Hand-written SQL scanner/parser inside CrossDB's embedded RDBMS, claimed 10x faster than Flex/Bison-generated code.

**Beats:** Flex/Bison — CrossDB's docs FAQ claims its hand-written scanner+parser is 'over 10 times faster than Flex/Bison parser tools' and about one-third the code size, stated as a single unsourced bullet in docs/faq.md with no linked benchmark script, hardware, or compiler/flags, and it bundles scanning and parsing together rather than isolating lexer-only throughput.

**Known shortcoming:** Compared against Flex/Bison, which is not in this category's baseline list, and the ~10x figure is an unsourced FAQ number with no benchmark behind it.

**How:** A hand-written recursive-descent parser calls a hand-written scanner directly, skipping the generated DFA table-walk that Flex output uses; the scanner classifies characters with a 256-entry static lookup table (s_tok_type) and switches on token type inline. Because xdb_token.c is textually #included into xdb_parser.c, the compiler can inline across the scanner/parser boundary in a way two separately compiled Flex/Bison translation units cannot. The ~10x and ~1/3-code-size figures come from a single unsourced FAQ bullet with no published benchmark script, hardware, or compiler flags.

**Use it when:**
- Embedding a small in-memory/on-disk OLTP relational engine in C/C++/Go/Python/Rust and wanting its internal SQL parsing fast without adding Flex/Bison to the build
- High-frequency, short OLTP-style SQL statements parsed repeatedly rather than parsed once and cached
- Needing portability across Linux/macOS/Windows/FreeBSD and x86/ARM/PowerPC/MIPS without a Flex/Bison toolchain dependency
- Wanting a reentrant, thread-safe SQL front end with no shared global parser state across connections
- Accepting CrossDB's own MySQL-flavored SQL dialect rather than needing a general-purpose or standard SQL grammar

**Skip it when:**
- You need a standalone, reusable SQL lexer/parser library: CrossDB's scanner and parser are internal to the engine and not exposed as an independent API
- You need the 10x claim substantiated: no benchmark script, workload, hardware, or scanner-only vs parser-only breakdown is published
- You need a mature, standard SQL dialect: the project itself says it is 'still in its early stages and currently lacks stability'
- You need active upstream development: last commit 2025-06-20, 268 stars, 21 forks, and only 3 open issues suggest limited real-world usage exercising parser edge cases
- Your dataset won't fit in available memory or lives on network-mounted disks, which the project's own FAQ lists as limitations of the engine the parser serves

**Integration:** source-drop · none (single C source tree; optional Go/Python bindings and JNI wrapper ship separately in the repo) · not documented precisely; uses _GNU_SOURCE, stdint.h/stdbool.h; built with GCC via Makefile/CMake, MinGW64 for Windows · Linux/macOS/FreeBSD/Windows; x86 32/64-bit, ARM, PowerPC, MIPS per README

**Vs siblings:** All the catalogued siblings (logos, LRSTAR, simd-lexing, lexer-exp, Gigatoken, Accelerated-Zig-Parser, StreamTok, Ragel) are extractable, general-purpose lexers/tokenizers you drop into your own project; CrossDB's parser is only worth it if you're embedding the CrossDB RDBMS itself and want its SQL front end's speed as a side effect, not as a standalone lexer replacement.

**Gotchas:**
- Scanner and parser aren't separable: xdb_token.c is #included directly into xdb_parser.c, so the tokenizer can't be linked or used on its own
- Parsing is tied to CrossDB's own metadata structs (xdb_stmt_t, xdb_tblm_t, xdb_tblm lookups) — output is not a generic, reusable AST
- Functions use XDB_STATIC internal linkage and file-scope static tables, confirming this is compiled as one amalgamated unit rather than a modular library
- One closed GitHub issue documents a parser bug on inequality expressions (Aug 2024), fixed before the 2025-06-20 last commit but indicative of a young grammar

**Status:** Stale by this catalog's threshold (last commit 2025-06-20) with only 268 stars/21 forks, and the project's own README/CONTRIBUTING call it early-stage and not yet stable; MPL-2.0 and copyable as source, but not a drop-in component outside the full CrossDB engine.

[repo](https://github.com/crossdb-org/crossdb) · [benchmark](https://github.com/crossdb-org/docs/blob/main/docs/faq.md)

##### lexer-exp (SIMD NEON lexer experiments, dist1ll)  `Rust`  `MPL-2.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Hand-rolled NEON SIMD lexer for a toy language; beats the Rust logos crate 20-35% on Apple M1.

**Beats:** logos (Rust lexer-generator crate, v0.13) — First-party `cargo bench` results (unpinned Rust nightly, single Apple M1 machine) show lnpl's NEON lexer at 118,476 ns/iter vs logos 0.13 at 174,476 ns/iter tokenizing a 100KB synthetic pseudocode file (~35% faster), and 89,151 ns/iter vs logos's 108,257 ns/iter (~1.21x) on real Hubris-kernel source snippets (5KB-1MB); the author separately reports 20-30% gains across that Hubris file-size range.

**How:** The aarch64 path loads input in 512-byte chunks into an aligned SIMD buffer and uses NEON 128-bit vector loads to classify 16 ASCII bytes at once (ident/whitespace/number/etc. character classes), with hand-written NEON assembly (aarch64.s) pulled in via global_asm!. Keyword matching uses a perfect hash that packs each keyword into a 64-bit word for single-instruction comparison instead of a DFA/trie walk. The author also reports a 5-10% gain from replacing a computed classification mask with a precomputed lookup table.

**Use it when:**
- You're targeting aarch64 (Apple Silicon or ARM servers) specifically -- there is no x86_64 SIMD path
- You want a worked example of NEON-based ASCII token classification plus perfect-hash keyword matching to adapt into your own lexer
- Your token stream is dominated by short, repetitive keyword/identifier patterns, where the gain over logos is largest (~35% on the synthetic benchmark)
- You can build with an unpinned Rust nightly and are comfortable vendoring unsafe/asm source rather than depending on a published crate
- Throughput on medium files (5KB-1MB) matters more than lexer generality or ergonomics

**Skip it when:**
- x86_64 targets: the author's own numbers show the naive scalar lexer beating logos there, and no NEON-equivalent path exists
- You need a drop-in replacement for logos's `#[derive(Logos)]` API -- lnpl's token types are hardcoded to the author's toy language
- You need stable Rust: the crate uses `#![feature(core_intrinsics)]` and `#![feature(stdsimd)]`, unstable nightly-only features
- You need a maintained dependency: no crates.io release found, last commit April 2024, no README, and it's explicitly experimental research code
- Your workload looks like realistic, non-repetitive source rather than synthetic pseudocode -- the measured gain shrinks from ~35% to ~20% on the real Hubris kernel snippets

**Integration:** source-drop · logos 0.13 (used only for parity testing / bench comparison, not by the aarch64 lexer itself) · Rust nightly (unpinned; requires core_intrinsics + stdsimd unstable features; .cargo/config.toml sets rustflags = -Zpolonius) · aarch64 (NEON) for the benchmarked/optimized path; a generic fallback exists for other architectures but is not benchmarked or discussed

**Vs siblings:** None of the catalogued siblings target Rust + logos on aarch64, so this is the only entry showing that specific pairing; pick it only as a technique reference for NEON ASCII classification + perfect-hash keywords, not as an installable lexer -- for an actual drop-in tokenizer, Accelerated-Zig-Parser or simd-lexing are more complete SIMD lexers, and logos itself (already catalogued) remains the safer general-purpose choice off aarch64.

**Gotchas:**
- Contains raw NEON assembly (aarch64.s) loaded via global_asm! plus unsafe SIMD intrinsics -- review before vendoring
- Uses a fixed 512-byte, 128-byte-aligned SIMD input buffer (SimdBuffer); behavior at buffer boundaries wasn't verified in this review
- Depends on nightly-only, unstable compiler features (core_intrinsics, stdsimd) with no pinned rustc version
- The published benchmark numbers on the blog labeled the lnpl result 'logos:' (apparent typo) -- read the repo's bench source (benches/lexer.rs), not just the blog table, to confirm which number is which

**Status:** Stale since April 2024 with zero open issues and no crates.io listing found; MPL-2.0 licensed research code from a personal toy-compiler project, small enough to vendor the lexer module but not maintained or packaged as a library.

[repo](https://github.com/dist1ll/lexer-exp) · [benchmark](https://alic.dev/blog/fast-lexing)

#### markup-html-markdown

##### MarkupEver  `Rust (Python bindings)`  `MPL-2.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

Rust HTML/XML parser with CSS selection for Python; faster than BeautifulSoup4 and html5lib, slower than lxml-based Parsel.

**Beats:** BeautifulSoup4 (html.parser and lxml backends) and html5lib — On the maintainer's own micro-benchmark (Manjaro Linux x86_64, 8GB RAM, Intel i3-1115G4; Python version and compiler flags unstated), MarkupEver parsed a test HTML page in 4,927us avg vs BeautifulSoup4(lxml)'s 22,809us (~4.6x) and html5lib's 63,489us; CSS-selected in 310us vs BeautifulSoup4's 2,995us (~9.7x); and serialized in 1,952us vs BeautifulSoup4's 14,900us (~7.6x). On the same table, Parsel (using lxml/libxml2 directly) beat MarkupEver on all three operations (4,072us parse, 161us select, 1,276us serialize).

**How:** Tokenizing and tree-building run through html5ever (Rust's spec-compliant HTML5 parser) and CSS matching uses servo's `selectors` crate, both compiled natively instead of going through Python's html.parser or the tree BeautifulSoup builds on top. The DOM is a single Vec-backed Rust tree (treedom crate), avoiding per-node Python object churn until a node is touched, and the release build uses fat LTO, one codegen unit, and panic=abort.

**Use it when:**
- Parsing/selecting/serializing many small-to-medium HTML or XML documents from Python where BeautifulSoup4 or html5lib is the measured bottleneck
- Need CSS-selector querying (soupsieve-style syntax) without switching to XPath
- Building a DOM from scratch and serializing it (e.g. generating HTML), not just parsing existing markup
- Large or streamed input where incremental parsing via Parser.process() avoids buffering the whole document
- Deploying to Linux, Windows, or macOS with a prebuilt PyPI wheel - no local Rust toolchain needed

**Skip it when:**
- You already call lxml/Parsel directly - on the project's own benchmark table, Parsel beats MarkupEver on every measured operation (parse, select, serialize)
- You need the CSS :has() pseudo-class - an open issue says it does not work
- You need a BeautifulSoup-compatible API (Tag, NavigableString, .find()) - MarkupEver's dom/select API is different, so adopting it is a rewrite, not a swap
- You need airtight cross-thread sharing of parser objects - an unsound `impl Sync` on Tendril-based parser/matching types was reported (issue #10) and fixed later, but the exact fixed version is not documented
- You want independently reproduced numbers - only the maintainer's own benchmark exists, with no published benchmark code, no stated Python version, and no stated build flags

**Integration:** module · Rust build deps only (pyo3 0.29, parking_lot 0.12, hashbrown 0.17, plus html5ever/selectors pulled in via the treedom and matching workspace crates); Python runtime has no extra dependencies · Rust edition 2021 (build-time only, via maturin); Python >=3.8, with wheels published for CPython 3.9-3.14 and PyPy - no Rust toolchain needed to install from PyPI · Linux, Windows, macOS per PyPI classifiers; benchmarked on x86-64 (Manjaro), no documented architecture restriction

**Vs siblings:** Pick MarkupEver over html5-parser when you also want CSS selection and DOM construction/serialization in the same library, not just fast HTML5-to-lxml-tree parsing; pick selectolax or Parsel/lxml directly instead when you don't need MarkupEver's DOM-building API, since both outperform MarkupEver on this same class of parse/select/serialize benchmark.

**Gotchas:**
- CSS :has() pseudo-class does not work (open issue, unresolved as of this session)
- Historical unsound Sync impl on parser/matching types tied to html5ever's Tendril type (issue #10) - fixed later, but pin a recent version if you share parser objects across threads
- A separate 'attaching a node to itself causes crash' bug was reported and closed - confirm you're past that fix
- pyproject.toml's PyPI classifier lists the license as MIT while the actual LICENSE file and Cargo.toml both say MPL-2.0 - a metadata inconsistency, not an alternate license grant

**Status:** Actively maintained (last commit 2026-07-21, CI running on push) and MPL-2.0 licensed, but it's a compiled PyO3/maturin extension rather than a source-drop, and it's a small, largely single-author project (37 stars) with an unresolved CSS-selector gap and a past thread-safety soundness bug, so treat it as promising but young.

[repo](https://github.com/awolverp/markupever) · [benchmark](https://awolverp.github.io/markupever/#performance)

##### MyHTML  `C`  `LGPL-2.1`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Pure C99 HTML5 parser using a thread-pool tokenizer/tree-builder; beats Gumbo and html5ever on parse throughput.

**Beats:** gumbo and html5ever (Rust, via html2html_lib C binding) — On the author's own 2016-era benchmark (466 Alexa Top-500 homepages parsed sequentially in one process, 'ex vivo'), threaded MyHTML totaled 0.509s vs Gumbo 6.130s (~12x) and html5ever 4.505s (~8.9x) on an Intel Core i7-3615QM / 8GB DDR3 Mac built with Apple LLVM 7.0.2 (clang-700.1.81); the harness Makefile default is only -O2 and library-specific build flags for myhtml, gumbo, and html5ever are unstated. MyHTML's Single Mode (single-threaded, the fairer comparison against the single-threaded baselines) totaled 0.722s, about 8.5x over Gumbo and 6.2x over html5ever.

**How:** myhtml_init takes a thread_count and internally fans tokenization and tree construction out across a worker thread pool (thread_queue) backed by custom pool allocators (mcobject/mcsimple/mchar_async) instead of per-node malloc/free, so parsing one page overlaps tokenizing and tree-building work across cores. A single-threaded path (MyHTML_OPTIONS_PARSE_MODE_SINGLE, or building with MyCORE_BUILD_WITHOUT_THREADS=YES) exists for when thread overhead isn't worth it or POSIX threads aren't available.

**Use it when:**
- Bulk/offline HTML5 parsing where you can dedicate a thread pool per parser instance (e.g. batch crawling, corpus processing) and want the threaded mode's throughput
- C or C99 codebases that want a dependency-free, spec-conformant HTML5 tokenizer/tree builder without pulling in Rust or a GC runtime
- Existing consumers via the Perl, Crystal, Elixir/Erlang, or Swift bindings who need a fast HTML5 parse step without CSS selectors
- POSIX or Windows targets (source ports exist for both) where you don't need a selector engine and can build the library or vendor the source

**Skip it when:**
- New projects: the project's own README tells users to use the lexbor project instead, which is the maintained successor
- Anything needing CSS selectors or a renderer — MyHTML only builds the tree; you'd need Modest/lexbor on top
- Latency-sensitive single-page parsing on a resource-constrained host — thread-pool setup/teardown per page adds overhead unless you use Single Mode
- Code that touches token/attribute text from a different thread than the parser's workers without calling myhtml_token_node_wait_for_done first, since after-token-done callbacks fire on worker threads in the default threaded mode
- Projects wanting active upstream support: last commit 2025-01-15 and status is stale

**Integration:** source-drop · none (pure C99; POSIX threads optional and can be disabled at build time) · C99; GNU Make (or CMake) build; POSIX threads unless built with MyCORE_BUILD_WITHOUT_THREADS=YES · POSIX (Linux/macOS/BSD) and Windows source ports (source/myport/posix, source/myport/windows_nt); benchmarked on macOS/x86-64

**Vs siblings:** Prefer lexbor (its own successor, already catalogued) for any new work — same author says so. MyHTML is only worth reaching for if you're maintaining an existing MyHTML integration or need one of its non-Rust/non-C bindings (Perl, Crystal, Elixir/Erlang, Swift) and don't need CSS selectors.

**Gotchas:**
- In default threaded mode, token/tree callbacks run on worker threads; reading node text/attributes from the caller thread without waiting (myhtml_token_node_wait_for_done) races with the parser
- No CSS selector engine — pair with Modest or lexbor if you need selectors or rendering
- The upstream README itself redirects new users to lexbor, the maintained successor already in this catalog
- Build flags used for the Gumbo/html5ever comparison binaries in the benchmark are not documented, so the exact magnitude of the speedup depends on how optimized those baselines were

**Status:** Stale: last commit 2025-01-15, and the project's own README now directs users to the lexbor project instead; still LGPL-2.1 and small/dependency-free enough to vendor if you're stuck maintaining an existing integration.

[repo](https://github.com/lexborisov/myhtml) · [benchmark](https://lexborisov.github.io/benchmark-html-parsers/)

#### regex-engines

##### rejit  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Prototype non-backtracking JIT regex compiler for x86-64 that beats RE2 and grep on throughput, unmaintained since 2015.

**Beats:** RE2 — First-party README benchmarks on an Intel Core i5-2400 (quad-core, SSE4.2, Fedora 17, RE2 commit aa957b5e3374 from ~2013): multi-threaded Rejit vs. the Benchmarks Game RE2 regex-dna program is 1.68x-2.1x faster in real time across 500KB-500MB inputs, and Rejit-powered jrep is 1.68x faster than GNU grep 2.14 on `grep -R` over the Linux 3.10.6 source tree (0.370s vs 0.622s real); the compiler and optimization flags actually used for these runs are not stated.

**How:** Each regex is JIT-compiled at runtime into native x86-64 machine code using a V8-derived assembler/codegen (src/x64/assembler-x64.*), avoiding backtracking entirely. Matching uses SIMD to test up to 4 characters per instruction (kMaxParallelChars=4 in src/cpu.h, requires SSE4.2, disable with simd:off) and a 'fast forward' skip-ahead mechanism that jumps past non-matching regions instead of scanning byte by byte. The multi-threaded benchmark samples (jrep -R, regexdna-multithread.cc) add throughput by splitting input across threads manually.

**Use it when:**
- Bulk, offline x86_64 Linux/macOS text-scanning jobs where you can vendor a small unmaintained C++11 GPLv3 static lib for extra single-machine regex throughput on large inputs (tens of MB+)
- Simple find/match/replace patterns that don't need capture groups, back-references, word boundaries, Unicode/UTF-8, or POSIX BRE syntax
- You already split work across threads yourself (as jrep and the DNA benchmark samples do) and want a non-backtracking engine per thread
- Studying or extending a small, readable non-backtracking SIMD regex JIT implementation
- GPL-3.0 licensing is acceptable in your project

**Skip it when:**
- You need capture/submatch extraction: issue #6 'Support submatches extraction' has been open since 2014 and unresolved; Match only exposes begin/end of the whole match
- You need word boundaries (\b), back-references, Unicode/UTF-8 encoding, or POSIX BRE syntax: all are open, unimplemented feature requests (issues #1, #3, #5, #7)
- Non-x86_64 targets: issue #10 'Support other architectures' is open and unaddressed; SConstruct only builds arch:x64
- Production or long-lived use: no commits since April 2015, and the SConstruct build script itself prints a warning that 'top-of-tree is not maintained any more, and contains some bugs. In particular, some regular expressions are incorrectly evaluated,' pointing to an apparently-unfinished successor (arames/regit)
- You need permissive licensing or static linking into a non-GPL product: license is GPL-3.0

**Integration:** static lib · none for the core library at build time (SCons is the build tool, not a runtime dependency); the benchmark harness separately depends on RE2, V8, and PCRE for comparison only · C++11 (SConstruct sets CXXFLAGS -std=c++11); specific compiler/version not stated; built with SCons · x86_64 only, SIMD path assumes SSE4.2 (kMaxParallelChars=4 in src/cpu.h); SConstruct has Linux and macOS build configs; other architectures are an open, unimplemented issue (#10)

**Vs siblings:** Pick rejit over BLARE or re2jit only if you want a from-scratch, dependency-free non-backtracking JIT engine to study or extend and don't need RE2-compatible behavior; BLARE reports broader RE2/PCRE2/Boost comparisons and re2jit stays API-compatible with RE2 (it falls back to RE2 for cases it doesn't optimize), while rejit offers neither RE2 API compatibility nor capture groups.

**Gotchas:**
- The project's own SConstruct prints a build-time warning: 'top-of-tree is not maintained any more, and contains some bugs. In particular, some regular expressions are incorrectly evaluated.'
- No capture-group/submatch API — Match exposes only begin/end of the whole match (issue #6 open since 2014)
- x86_64-only; the SIMD fast path assumes SSE4.2 and can be turned off at build time with simd:off
- The public header include/rejit.h has `using namespace std;` at file scope, which can leak std:: names into including translation units

**Status:** Abandoned since its last commit in April 2015; GPL-3.0, C++11, and small enough (~20 source files) to vendor as a source-drop, but the build script itself warns of known incorrect-match bugs and never reached a maintained successor.

[repo](https://github.com/coreperf/rejit) · [benchmark](https://github.com/coreperf/rejit)

#### text-search-and-indexing

##### Manticore Search  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `active`  `Tier C`

SQL/HTTP full-text and analytics search database, C++ core, positioned as a faster Elasticsearch alternative.

**Beats:** Elasticsearch — Vendor blog (Manticore, Jul 2022) benchmarked Manticore 5.0.0-5.0.2 against Elasticsearch 7.15.2/8.3.2 on a 32-core SSD server (CPU model and compiler flags unstated): 4x faster on a 1.7B-row taxi dataset, 15x on 1.1M Hacker News comments, 22x on 10M nginx log lines, 25x faster bulk-load of the 1.7B-doc set (1h08m vs 28h33m via Logstash), and roughly 2x higher direct-load throughput for 50M docs (894,856 vs 416,788 docs/s, sharded configs) — though unsharded default Elasticsearch was actually 21% faster in that same test. The db-benchmarks.com suite behind these numbers is maintained by the Manticore team itself.

**How:** Query execution is multi-threaded across all CPU cores with a cost-based optimizer choosing execution plans from indexed-data statistics. It offers both row-wise storage (faster, more RAM) and a separate columnar storage engine (Manticore Columnar Library) for datasets too large for RAM. Automatic secondary indexes use a PGM-index (Piecewise Geometric Model) for key-to-location mapping instead of classic B-trees. The core inverted-index/search engine descends from the Sphinx search engine, rewritten and extended in C++17.

**Use it when:**
- Log/analytics workloads (e.g. nginx logs, time-series) where columnar storage plus the cost-based optimizer avoid JVM/Lucene overhead
- Teams that want SQL over full-text/analytics search rather than learning Elasticsearch's Query DSL, especially existing MySQL-protocol tooling
- Ingest-heavy pipelines where bulk-load throughput matters more than incremental refresh latency
- Resource-constrained deployments: README states ~40MB RSS for an empty instance
- Single query needing both full-text and vector/KNN retrieval (hybrid search) without a separate vector DB

**Skip it when:**
- Need Elasticsearch's mature aggregation framework, Query DSL, or its large ecosystem of plugins/native Kibana support
- Can't accept GPL-3.0 copyleft for embedding into proprietary systems (vs Elasticsearch's SSPL/Elastic license)
- Require strict ACID guarantees: README states Manticore is 'not fully ACID-compliant', offering only isolated transactions and binary logging
- Basing a purchase decision on the cited speedup numbers: the db-benchmarks.com suite behind them is maintained by the same Manticore team, so treat 4x/15x/22x/25x/2x figures as vendor-reported, not independent
- Need multi-master replication stronger than Galera-based 'virtually synchronous' replication provides

**Integration:** source-drop · Bundled Manticore Columnar Library (git submodule) for columnar storage; optional ICU for CJK/Chinese segmentation; various vendored libs under .gitmodules. Not a linkable library — ships as searchd/indexer binaries. · C++17, CMake 3.17+ · Linux (Debian/Ubuntu, RHEL/CentOS/Amazon/Oracle/Fedora families) and macOS via Homebrew per install script; Windows has its own CI test template (win_test_template.yml). x86-64 assumed; ARM support not documented in README.

**Vs siblings:** The sibling entries are either embeddable Lucene-replacement indexing libraries (IResearch, Tantivy, SeekStorm) or single-machine grep-replacement CLIs (frg, ngi, trigrep, ugrep); Manticore is the only full standalone SQL/HTTP search server in the set. Pick it when you need a deployable, replicated, multi-user database with backup/restore and SQL access rather than a library to embed in your own indexing pipeline, and specifically over Elasticsearch when your workload matches log/analytics/full-text patterns and you can accept GPL-3.0 and a smaller ecosystem.

**Gotchas:**
- README explicitly states Manticore is 'not fully ACID-compliant' despite having isolated transactions and binlog
- Columnar storage saves RAM but README says it gives 'lower performance than row-wise storage for some kinds of queries' — pick per-table
- GPL-3.0 licensed and historically forked from the Sphinx search engine — copyleft terms differ materially from Elasticsearch's license
- The benchmark suite (db-benchmarks.com / github.com/db-benchmarks/db-benchmarks) used for the headline multipliers is run by the same Manticore team (top contributor sanikolaev), not an independent third party

**Status:** Actively maintained (record's last_commit is current, large nightly/CI test matrix in .github/workflows) and free to install via package manager, Docker, or source build; GPL-3.0 licensing is the main friction point for proprietary embedding rather than any maturity concern.

[repo](https://github.com/manticoresoftware/manticoresearch) · [benchmark](https://manticoresearch.com/blog/manticore-alternative-to-elasticsearch/)

### serialization-and-formats

#### binary-schemas

##### JSON BinPack  `C++`  `AGPL-3.0-or-later`  `active`  `Tier C`

JSON Schema-driven binary JSON format; its prototype matched or beat Protobuf, Avro, MessagePack on encoded size across 27 documents.

**Beats:** Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, Cap'n Proto, MessagePack (and Apache Avro, Thrift, CBOR, BSON, UBJSON, Smile, FlexBuffers) — This is a size result only: on the author's json-size-benchmark (27 SchemaStore documents, one per JSON Taxonomy class), the archived TypeScript prototype (npm jsonbinpack 1.1.x) in schema-driven mode produced the smallest or tied-smallest uncompressed encoding against Protobuf 3.12.4, FlatBuffers 1.12.0, Cap'n Proto 0.7.0, MessagePack 1.0.0, Avro, Thrift, CBOR, BSON, UBJSON, Smile and FlexBuffers (e.g. ESLint config 64 B vs Avro 100 B, Protobuf 161 B, JSON 1,141 B), and it beat GZIP/LZ4/LZMA-compressed JSON on all 27 documents. Compiler and hardware are irrelevant for byte counts, no speed was measured, and the C++ code in this repo is not what was benchmarked.

**Known shortcoming:** Not a speed win: its advantage is encoded size only (smallest or tied-smallest on all 27 documents in the benchmark), and its own README recommends FlatBuffers or Cap'n Proto when runtime speed matters. The size numbers come from the archived TypeScript proof of concept, not this C++ implementation, and the papers are arXiv preprints.

**Known shortcoming:** The C++ implementation cannot yet produce the benchmarked schema-driven sizes: its compiler maps only integer, number and enum/const schemas, and object, array and string schemas fall back to schema-less encoding (maintainer, issue #896, Dec 2025). The benchmarked sizes come from the archived TypeScript prototype. Encoder and decoder bounds checks are assert() only, so release builds skip them, and there are no fuzz tests.

**How:** It does not make serialization faster; it makes output smaller by turning schema constraints into bit-level choices. Bounded integers (minimum/maximum/multipleOf) become an offset from the minimum in one byte or a Base-128 varint (ZigZag when unbounded), enums become a one-byte or varint index (zero bytes for the first choice of a top-level enum), const costs zero bytes, and decimals become a ZigZag varint of their digits plus the decimal-point position instead of an 8-byte IEEE double. Strings of 3 or more bytes already seen in the stream become a backward offset (dedup cache capped at 20 MiB), and schema-less values pack a 3-bit type tag with a 5-bit small length or integer into one byte. The largest benchmark gaps, such as ESLint at 64 B schema-driven vs 969 B schema-less, come from schema-typed object and array encodings, which the C++ compiler does not generate yet.

**Use it when:**
- Payloads crossing metered, slow or lossy links (mobile, IoT, constrained radio), where bytes on the wire cost more than CPU cycles. This is the use case the README names.
- Small to medium JSON messages, from tens of bytes to a few KB, where general-purpose compression does not pay off. On all 27 benchmark documents, the schema-driven output was smaller than JSON compressed with GZIP -9, LZ4 -12 or LZMA -9.
- You already keep JSON Schema 2020-12 definitions (for example in OpenAPI or AsyncAPI) with tight constraints (bounded integers, enums, const, string length bounds) and want to reuse them instead of writing Protobuf or Avro schemas. That is the enum-heavy, Zod-generated-schema storage use case raised in issue #896.
- Storing or sending many schema-conforming records where repeated string values dominate. Even schema-less, string deduplication gave TravisCI config 185 B vs MessagePack 627 B, and .NET project 748 B vs 919 B (benchmark page).
- Integer, number and enum payloads you can encode with the C++ code today. For fully schema-driven objects, the benchmarked Apache-2.0 TypeScript prototype (npm jsonbinpack, archived) is the implementation that has those encoders.

**Skip it when:**
- Latency- or throughput-bound paths (IPC, intra-datacenter RPC, zero-copy reads). The README itself points these to FlatBuffers or Cap'n Proto. The repo has no speed benchmark, and decoding always builds a sourcemeta::core::JSON DOM.
- You need the benchmark's schema-driven sizes from C++ today. The compiler maps only integer, number and enum/const schemas; object, array and string schemas fall back to schema-less encoding. The status page lists those mappers and nine object/array/string encodings as missing, and the e2e tests cover schema-less only ('TODO: Test schema-driven too'). The maintainer wrote in issue #896 that this repo is not at feature parity with the JS prototype.
- Schemas that rely on $ref, allOf/anyOf/oneOf, if/then/else, dependentSchemas, unevaluated* or recursion. The project's status page lists all of these as not covered yet.
- Decoding untrusted bytes. The README calls decoding non-conforming data undefined behavior. Index and range checks in the decoder are assert()s, which disappear in release builds (for example BYTE_CHOICE_INDEX indexes the choices vector unchecked). The repo has no fuzz tests.
- Schema-less-only use as a MessagePack replacement for tiny documents: the gain is often zero. From the benchmark page data, schema-less mode ties MessagePack byte-for-byte on 10 of 27 documents (e.g. TSLint 51 B vs 51 B) and ESLint is 969 B vs 971 B. Also skip it for closed-source network services that cannot accept AGPL-3.0 and will not buy the commercial license.

**Integration:** static lib or shared lib (CMake, BUILD_SHARED_LIBS), in two components: runtime (encoder/decoder) and compiler (schema to encoding) · Sourcemeta Core (json, uri, jsonpointer, jsonschema, numeric, regex, io) and Sourcemeta Blaze (alterschema, canonicalizer), both vendored and pinned by commit in DEPENDENCIES. Core in turn vendors PCRE2 and mimalloc, which is linked into executables on Linux/macOS unless SOURCEMETA_CORE_USE_SYSTEM_ALLOCATOR is set. · C++23 (CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 23 from vendored Core defaults). The top level declares CMake 3.16, but vendored Core requires 3.24. CI builds on current GitHub runners with GCC and Clang on Ubuntu, Clang on macOS and MSVC on Windows. No minimum compiler versions are documented. · Linux, macOS, Windows per CI (static and shared builds, plus ASan/UBSan jobs). No architecture-specific code was seen in src/.

**Vs siblings:** Pick it over fernBuffer or qdf when your data is already described by JSON Schema and you want the fewest bytes per small document from schema-level savings (enums, bounded integers, constants, string dedup), not a MessagePack-style or compression-tier layout. Pick Bebop, SBE, rkyv or YaFF instead when encode/decode latency is what you are buying, because JSON BinPack publishes no speed numbers at all.

**Gotchas:**
- The Encoder's string cache survives across write() calls. A string repeated in a later document on the same Encoder is written as a backward offset into an earlier document's bytes. Create a fresh Encoder per message if each message must decode on its own (inferred from runtime_encoder.h and cache.cc).
- Resolving shared strings makes the Decoder seek backwards (InputStream::rewind calls seek), so it needs a seekable std::istream. Buffer forward-only socket data first.
- Validate against the schema before encoding. The encoder checks bounds, multipleOf and string lengths with assert() only, so in NDEBUG builds an out-of-range value in an 8-bit encoding is silently cast to uint8_t instead of rejected. compile() also mutates the schema you pass in.
- Sizes from this C++ repo won't match the published benchmark. The e2e fixtures show schema-less sizes equal to the prototype's on some documents (ESLint 969 B, package.json 1,957 B), slightly larger on others (GeoJSON 127 vs 117 B; JSON Resume 2,619 vs 2,612 B, where a TODO notes Smile's 2,613 B now wins) and smaller on Road Risk (254 vs 261 B). Wire compatibility with npm jsonbinpack 1.1.x is not documented.

**Status:** Flagged active, but since late 2024 nearly all commits are Core/Blaze dependency bumps (last encoding work October 2024, README revised August 2026), with no tagged releases and a single contributor; the code is copyable under AGPL-3.0-or-later or a paid commercial license, and the benchmarked TypeScript prototype is archived but Apache-2.0.

[repo](https://github.com/sourcemeta/jsonbinpack) · [benchmark](https://benchmark.sourcemeta.com/)

#### json

##### jist  `Rust`  `GPL-3.0`  `stale`  `Tier C`

Rust CLI that pulls one value by exact key/index path from multi-GB JSON files, far faster than jq.

**Beats:** jq — The author's single-run test on an Intel i7-12700H with 64 GB DDR5 used a generated, pretty-printed 3.3 GB array of 10M objects and extracted [9999999].bar.baz. jist's simdjson path took 2.05 s and 4.5 GB, against jq's 34.17 s and 18 GB (about 16.7x, 1600 vs 96 MB/s). On a 28.9 GB file the streaming lexer took 1:30 with 9.7 MB of memory while jq ran out of RAM. The jq and compiler versions are not stated. The repo's jist_vs_jq.png shows the jq run timed with /usr/bin/time -v (0:34.17, 18.2 GB max RSS) next to an earlier jist run of 10.21 s at 7.8 MB RSS on the same query, which matches the streaming lexer, so there is no screenshot of the 2.05 s simdjson run.

**Known shortcoming:** Rust CLI whose speed comes from a bundled copy of simdjson (C++); for C++ use, take simdjson directly. Works on JSON array files, not NDJSON. GPL-3.0; stale since 2025-02; 23 stars.

**Known shortcoming:** The ~16.7x ratio compares two different sessions (no screenshot of the 2.05 s run; the screenshot's own streaming run is about 3.3x faster than jq), and jq and compiler versions are unstated. The simdjson path loads the whole file (4.5 GB RSS on 3.3 GB). One path lookup per run, no filters; not a jq replacement. 'cargo install jist' installs an unrelated crate. Missing keys print an error with exit status 0; the streaming fallback fails on single-line files over 1 MB (source reading).

**How:** For files under 4 GiB (u32::MAX bytes), a small C++ wrapper, called from Rust through autocxx/cxx, loads the whole file into a simdjson padded_string. It then runs simdjson 3.11.3 On Demand `document::at_path()`, which the header says supports only key and index paths that convert directly to JSON Pointer. The file gets SIMD structural indexing and lazy navigation that skips unrequested values without building a DOM, while jq builds a full tree (18 GB RSS for the 3.3 GB file). Larger files, or runs with -s, use a Rust fallback: the json-tools token lexer runs over 1 MB newline-aligned chunks, tracks depth and array-index counters, and reads the matched byte range back from the file by seeking to it. This keeps memory at about 10 MB but runs at about 300 MB/s.

**Use it when:**
- Scripts or ad-hoc shell work that need one known value (a token, a config field, the Nth record) from a JSON file of hundreds of MB to about 4 GB, and jq is slow or runs out of RAM
- Files larger than RAM or larger than 4 GiB, where the streaming fallback holds memory near 10 MB and still ran the author's 28.9 GB file at 321 MB/s
- Linux x86-64 machines where you can drop in the prebuilt v0.3 release binary rather than build the C++/Rust bridge
- Pretty-printed or NDJSON-style input with regular line breaks, which matches the benchmark data and suits the streaming fallback's newline-aligned chunking
- A quick schema summary of a JSON or NDJSON file (the schema feature is newer than the v0.3 binary, so this needs a source build)

**Skip it when:**
- Any real jq work: filters, select/map, wildcards, several outputs per run, reshaping or recursive descent. jist does exactly one key/index lookup
- Memory-tight machines with files under 4 GiB: the simdjson path loads the whole file (4.5 GB RSS on the 3.3 GB benchmark). Use -s to force the ~300 MB/s streaming path
- Minified single-line files (or single lines longer than 1 MB) in streaming mode. From reading buf_parser.rs, a 1 MB chunk with no newline returns 'result not found' instead of being processed (not tested)
- Pipelines that rely on exit codes or on stdin streaming. On the simdjson path a missing key or parse error is printed to stdout as 'JSON error: ...' with exit status 0, and stdin is always read fully into memory even with -s
- Projects that want a maintained, packaged tool: one author, 23 stars, no commits since 2025-02-15, GPL-3.0, and not on crates.io under this name

**Integration:** static lib · Vendored amalgamated simdjson 3.11.3 (C++, compiled by build.rs). Crates: cxx, autocxx, json-tools, serde_json (preserve_order), clap, regex, futures, json_value_merge, lazy_static, log. Build-time: autocxx-build and miette. autocxx needs LLVM/libclang installed · Rust 2021 edition. Probably Rust 1.79+, because src/schema_parser.rs uses std::path::absolute; no MSRV is stated. A C++17 compiler (build.rs passes -std=c++17 or /std:c++17) and LLVM/libclang for autocxx are also needed. Compiler versions are not documented · Prebuilt binary is Linux x86-64 only (the jist.linux.x86_64 asset on v0.2 and v0.3). A source build should work wherever Rust, a C++17 compiler and libclang are available, but that is not documented or tested; build.rs has clang and MSVC flags. simdjson picks its SIMD kernel at runtime (no -march is set)

**Vs siblings:** Pick jist over the catalogued simdjson library when you want a ready-made shell command instead of writing C++; its speed is simdjson On Demand's at_path, so inside a C++ or Rust program call simdjson (or simd-json/sonic-rs) directly. Pick it over fastgron when you know the exact path and want one value rather than a greppable flattening of the whole file; JSONSki and Pison are research libraries for large-record path queries, not end-user CLIs.

**Gotchas:**
- `cargo install jist` installs an unrelated crate: the crates.io name 'jist' belongs to a programming-language project (v0.1.9). Build from the repo or use the GitHub release binary
- The v0.3 release binary (2025-01-11) predates the schema/NDJSON summarizer commits (from 2025-01-12), so it only does path search. The Cargo.toml version still says 0.1.0
- Output is not jq -r output. String values come back with JSON escapes still in them, and leading/trailing quote characters are trimmed greedily: the repo's own unit test expects the value "\"q\"" to print as \"q\ . Objects and arrays are re-serialized compactly through serde_json
- The simdjson path does not validate the whole document (simdjson's iterate docs say invalid JSON may not trigger an error), and the README says malformed input is tolerated in streaming mode as long as the target value is complete. From reading the code, the streaming path may also panic when a 1 MB chunk boundary splits a multi-byte UTF-8 character (not tested)

**Status:** Stale: one author, last commit 2025-02-15, 0 open issues and only two self-merged PRs. It is usable today as a GPL-3.0 Linux x86-64 binary or a small (~63 KB of Rust) source build, but for anything beyond one-off lookups treat it as a personal tool.

[repo](https://github.com/adelamodwala/jist) · [benchmark](https://github.com/adelamodwala/jist#benchmarks)

#### yaml-toml-xml

##### VTD-XML  `Java`  `GPL-2.0-or-later`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Java XML parser building a compact offset/length token index, not a tree; beats libxml2 DOM parse, loses XPath.

**Beats:** libxml2 — On bemayer/xml-benchmark's 2026-09-01 run (GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest, Docker, CPU not published), VTD-XML 2.13.4 on Temurin 21 (no JVM flags, parse(false), input array cloned inside the timed loop) built its token index 1.6x-4.9x faster than Debian libxml2 2.9.14's xmlParseMemory + xmlFreeDoc (C++ harness, -O3) at 100KB-100MB. VTD-XML's rows cover only the wide file because it rejects the deep files, while libxml2's rows also average in a deep file it halts at depth 256; VTD-XML also loses at 1KB (2.8x) and on XPath //*[@id] at every size (6.8x-17x).

**Known shortcoming:** Rows do not compare the same files: VTD-XML refuses documents deeper than 254 levels, so its 100KB-100MB rows cover only the wide file, while libxml2's rows average in a deep file it truncates at depth 256. 6.8-17x slower than libxml2 on XPath at every size, and the suite's overall score ranks libxml2 above it. GPL-2.0-or-later with patent notices and a litigation-termination clause. Abandoned: last release 2.13.4 (2017), last commit 2018-06.

**Known shortcoming:** JVM only; on the same page quick-xml's DOM parse is faster at every size and RapidXml wins at 1 KB and 100 MB, so pick VTD-XML only if you must stay on the JVM. The 256 GB memory-mapped edition (VTDGenHuge) caps depth at 30. parseFile() swallows exceptions and returns false. Open bugs in the GitHub copy (#6, #8, #13, #15) with no release after 2.13.4.

**How:** It uses non-extractive tokenization, which the project calls Virtual Token Descriptor (VTD). The raw bytes stay in memory undecoded, and each token becomes one 64-bit long: 4-bit type, 8-bit depth, 20-bit length and a 30/32-bit offset. These longs are appended to pooled long[] buffers, so parsing creates no node objects, no strings and almost no GC work. Random access comes from 'location caches': per-depth arrays whose entries pair an element's record index with the index of its first child. The FAQ puts these at about 10% of parse cost and total memory at 1.3-1.5x the document size. End tags are not stored, and setDoc_BR() reuses the buffers across parses.

**Use it when:**
- JVM services that parse many shallow (<255 levels) 100 KB-100 MB documents and read a few fields by navigation, where building DOM objects and the GC they cause is the cost. On bemayer/xml-benchmark its index build posted 0.54-239 ms vs libxml2's 0.87-647 ms, with the caveat that the file sets differ.
- Replacing Xerces or JDK DOM in Java code that only reads. On the same page, VTD-XML's DOM Parse time is lower than Xerces's at every size (0.036 vs 0.232 ms at 1KB; 238.9 vs 489.0 ms at 100MB). Again the file sets differ.
- Parse once, use many times: save the index with writeIndex() and reload it with loadIndex() so you do not re-tokenize the same large file.
- Small edits or fragment cut/paste on large documents (XMLModifier, getElementFragment), which avoids a full DOM round trip and re-serialization.
- Files larger than RAM, up to 256 GB, using the extended edition (VTDGenHuge in MEM_MAPPED mode), provided nesting stays at 30 levels or fewer.

**Skip it when:**
- XPath-heavy workloads. On //*[@id] it was 6.8x-17x slower than libxml2 at every size (3837.5 vs 565.6 ms at 100MB), and slower than Xerces from 1MB up.
- Deeply nested XML. The standard edition throws 'Depth exceeds MAX_DEPTH' past 254 levels, and the 256 GB extended edition allows only 30. The standard edition also caps documents at 2 GB, or 1 GB with namespaces on.
- Tiny documents or short-lived processes. At 1KB it is 2.8x slower than libxml2, and its peak RSS on the page is 57 MB vs 5.4 MB (JVM baseline).
- Anything that needs DTD-declared or external entities, schema validation or a W3C DOM API. The FAQ calls DTD and external entities effectively deprecated, VTDGen parses a DTD but does not resolve declared entities, and a DOM interface is ruled out.
- Projects that cannot take GPLv2 plus patent notices and an unmaintained codebase. The last release was 2017, and bugs such as namespace shadowing in getElementFragmentNs (#13) are still open.

**Integration:** module (Java jar, Maven Central com.ximpleware:vtd-xml 2.13.4); C, C++ and C# ports are source-drop from the repo · none (the 2.13.4 POM declares no dependencies) · Java; the FAQ lists Java 1.2 through 8 as tested, and the benchmark ran 2.13.4 on Temurin 21 JRE. The C port builds with a makefile, or with Visual Studio set to 'Compile as C'. · any JVM; the C, C++ and C# ports cover Linux, Windows and .NET/Mono per the FAQ

**Vs siblings:** Pick it only when you must stay on the JVM and want random access, a saved index or in-place byte edits. Every catalogued sibling is native: on the same bemayer page quick-xml's DOM Parse is faster than VTD-XML at every size, and RapidXml beats it at 1KB and 100MB. For XPath, prefer simdxml or libxml2 itself.

**Gotchas:**
- parseFile(), parseGZIPFile() and similar catch IOException and ParseException, print them to System.out and return false. Use setDoc() + parse() if you need the exception.
- Hard limits in VTDGen throw ParseException: depth 254, prefix 511 bytes, qualified name 2047 bytes, and 2 GB file size (1 GB with namespaces). Text tokens longer than 1M-1 bytes are split across several records.
- The byte[] passed to setDoc() is the document. Records only point into it, so it must stay alive and unmodified for as long as the VTDNav is used.
- toNormalizedString() collapses whitespace by design (issue #9); use toString(), or toRawString() to keep entities. Issue #6 reports toString() mishandling multibyte characters, with a fix promised for '2.13_2'.

**Status:** Abandoned: the last release is 2.13.4 (Maven Central, 2017) and the last commit on the maintainer's GitHub copy is 2018-06-28. The jar has no dependencies and is easy to adopt, but GPLv2 (commercial license on request), the listed US patents and a license-termination clause for parties in litigation with XimpleWare make it a legal-review item.

[repo](https://sourceforge.net/projects/vtd-xml/) · [benchmark](https://bemayer.github.io/xml-benchmark/)

### stdlib-replacements

#### io-and-filesystem

##### FastReader  `C++`  `GPL-3.0`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

Windows memory-mapped line reader using memchr; ~4x faster line iteration than std::ifstream::getline on a 9 KB file.

**Beats:** std::ifstream — On the repo's own Google Test 'Timing' suite (mean of 10 samples x 3 full passes over the repo's 9,194-byte TestFile.txt), CFileHandler averaged 56,700 ns versus 241,000 ns for std::ifstream + std::getline against the MSVC STL — about 4.25x faster — with no CPU disclosed and the Debug-vs-Release build configuration used for the published numbers unstated.

**How:** Maps the file into the process address space once instead of streaming through libc/CRT buffered I/O, avoiding per-getline syscalls and intermediate buffer copies. Line boundaries are found with memchr, which uses a vectorized/optimized scan, rather than std::getline's char-by-char sentry loop with locale-aware traits comparisons. Each line is copied exactly once, directly from the mapped pages into the returned std::string.

**Use it when:**
- Windows-only tool that repeatedly parses a small-to-medium text file line-by-line and can absorb the one-time CreateFileMapping cost
- Read-only, whole-file-fits-in-memory workloads (log parsing, config files) where std::ifstream + getline overhead is a measured bottleneck
- Codebases already linking ATL (atlbase.h/CHandle), so the extra dependency is free
- Prototyping or benchmarking where GPL-3.0 licensing of the file itself is acceptable

**Skip it when:**
- Any non-Windows target - code compiles only against WinAPI + ATL
- Files without a trailing newline: memchr returning nullptr on the last unterminated line yields (BYTE*)0 + 1, an invalid non-null pointer bug present in both the constructor and operator++
- Proprietary/closed-source projects that cannot take on GPL-3.0
- Anything needing formatted input, seeking, writing, or multi-threaded access - no documented thread safety, and CFileHandler holds raw pointers with no locking
- Production use generally: single-maintainer, 5 stars, no commits since 2019-11-13, no issues or PRs on record

**Integration:** source-drop · WinAPI (CreateFile/CreateFileMapping/MapViewOfFile) and ATL (atlbase.h, for CHandle) · Visual Studio 2019, PlatformToolset v142 per FastReader.vcxproj; uses std::iterator<> as an iterator base, which is deprecated in C++17 and removed in C++20, so it will not compile unmodified under /std:c++20 · Windows x86 and x64 (Win32 and x64 configs in the vcxproj); WinAPI-dependent, no POSIX path

**Vs siblings:** Neither catalogued sibling (CPath, reckless) targets line-by-line file reading, so this is the only io-and-filesystem entry solving that specific std::ifstream problem; pick it only if the workload is Windows-only line iteration and the GPL-3.0 license, ATL dependency, and unterminated-newline bug are all acceptable.

**Gotchas:**
- Unterminated final line (no trailing '\n') triggers memchr returning nullptr, which the code adds 1 to unchecked, producing an invalid pointer instead of a clean end-of-file marker
- Copy constructor and assignment are deleted with no move alternative provided, so CFileHandler cannot be stored in most STL containers directly
- CFileHandlerIterator::operator* allocates a new std::string per line, so iteration is not zero-copy despite the memory-mapped backing
- Requires ATL (atlbase.h) solely for CHandle's RAII wrapper around HANDLE, pulling in more than a plain WinAPI call would need

**Status:** Abandoned since 2019-11-13 (single maintainer, no open issues or PRs, 5 stars); GPL-3.0 plus the ATL dependency make it copyable only into GPL-compatible, Windows-with-ATL projects.

[repo](https://github.com/GeorgiiFirsov/FastReader) · [benchmark](https://github.com/GeorgiiFirsov/FastReader#test-results)

#### perfect-hash-static-tables

##### cmph / cxxmph (mph_map)  `C`  `LGPL-2.1-only OR MPL-1.1`  `abandoned`  `Tier C`

C minimal-perfect-hash library (BDZ/CHD/BRZ) plus cxxmph::mph_map, claimed 10-50% faster than std::unordered_map on >100k URLs.

**Beats:** std::unordered_map (cxxmph's dense_hash_map / sparse_hash_map are its own flavors named after the sparsehash classes; cxxmph/bm_map.cc benchmarks only against std::unordered_map) — The only figure is the author's prose in mph_map.h: on large (>100k) URL sets the cxxmph maps were 'about 10%-50% faster than unordered_map'. The repo harness (bm_map.cc) runs 10M lookups over a 100k-URL file with StringPiece keys at 0% and 90% miss rates, plus 100k uint64 keys, against std::unordered_map with a Murmur3 hasher. The URL file is not shipped, no results are published, and neither compiler nor hardware is given; the header only advises -O3 -DNDEBUG.

**How:** The core is BDZ (Botelho, Pagh, Ziviani): each key hashes to one edge of a random 3-partite 3-uniform hypergraph; construction peels degree-1 vertices to prove the graph acyclic, then assigns 2-bit g values so that (g[v0]+g[v1]+g[v2]) mod 3 selects a slot unique to that key. In cxxmph a lookup is one MurmurHash3 x64_128 call, three 2-bit reads from a table of about 2.93 bits per bucket, a presence bit and at most one key comparison, with no chain walk or probe sequence; that is why the header says gains grow with key size, set size and miss rate. mph_map uses the non-minimal PHF (~81% slot occupancy, modulo), dense_hash_map rounds partitions to a power of two so a mask replaces the modulo (~50% occupancy), and sparse_hash_map adds a rank table for a minimal, 100%-occupied layout at extra lookup cost. The C library also offers CHD (~2.07 bits/key, fastest build) and BRZ (external-memory build for billions of keys).

**Use it when:**
- Read-mostly string-keyed maps with 100k+ long keys (URLs, paths) that are expensive to compare, especially with many lookup misses: the header's only stated win case. Bulk-load, call rehash(), then serve lookups.
- Assigning dense ids to a fixed set of 10^6 to 10^9 keys (URLs, words, n-grams) through the C API, with values stored in your own array indexed by the id.
- Key sets that do not fit in RAM: the BRZ algorithm builds in external memory with a memory budget (-M) and temp dir, producing functions under 8 bits/key.
- You need a compact, serializable static index: CHD ~2.07 bits/key or BDZ ~2.6 bits/key, dumped to a file or packed with cmph_pack into a blob that can be mmapped and queried with cmph_search_packed.

**Skip it when:**
- Insert-heavy or interleaved insert/lookup workloads: new keys go to a side std::unordered_map that every lookup checks first, and when the value vector fills the whole BDZ index is rebuilt in O(n).
- Small maps, integer keys or cheap comparisons: the author warns the classes 'are not necessarily faster than their existing counterparts' and gives a figure only for >100k URLs; no numbers exist for other shapes.
- Code that relies on std::unordered_map guarantees: any insert can relocate every element (invalidating all iterators and references), value_type is pair<Key, Data> so keys are mutable through iterators, the Alloc parameter is unused, and count/at/emplace/equal_range/reserve are missing.
- Looking up keys that were not in the build set through the C API: cmph_search returns an arbitrary id for them (zvelo issue #4), so you must store and compare the keys yourself.
- Projects that need a maintained or MSVC-ready codebase from this URL: the zvelo copy is frozen at 2012, cxxmph uses __builtin_expect and POSIX random(), and in this copy every mph_map unit test except erase_iterator is commented out.

**Integration:** shared lib (autotools/libtool builds libcmph, and libcxxmph with --enable-cxxmph); cxxmph is 'header-mostly' and can be source-dropped as mph_map.h plus mph_index.cc, trigraph.cc, mph_bits.cc and MurmurHash3.cpp · none at runtime beyond libm; autotools to build; the check library only for the optional unit tests · C library: portable C with autotools. cxxmph: C++11 (configure adds -std=c++0x or gnu++0x) on GCC or Clang · C library: GNU/Linux and WIN32, reported to work on OpenBSD and Solaris (README). cxxmph: GCC/Clang on POSIX systems, because of __builtin_expect and random(). No SIMD or architecture requirements.

**Vs siblings:** Pick cmph when the key set is built at run time and is far too large for compile-time tables such as frozen, constexpr-phf or ConstexprCore/perfect_hash: 10^6 to 10^9 keys, a serialized or mmapped function, or an external-memory build with BRZ. For a runtime std::unordered_map replacement, fph-table's dynamic perfect-hash map has published figures; cxxmph::mph_map has only an unquantified header claim.

**Gotchas:**
